you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

So where does this game succeed? Though the game is not very fun to replay, whenever continuing into NG+1 there are new enemy encounters which create a new experience for the player's second playthrough. Additionally, the game greatly succeeded in increasing PvP and Multiplayer connectivity and opportunities. I would say that PvP is the most intriguing part of Dark Souls II. However, with the emergence of Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin, there is going to be a different servers for players and may pull the online players from Dark Souls II to its newer version. The DLC for the game is said to be wondrous, and if you were to buy the game I would highly recommend getting them.

I've been playing the free version since 2009 when my PC could barely run it. Now I've got a much beefier PC and decided to take the plunge and buy a membership. $54(CAD) for the Trailrunner starter pack (Best deal IMO) gives you a very nice selection of weapons/equipment, and all licenses for a year.
All I can say is wow. I'm not dissappointed at all with my purchase. I love the fact that this game is 6 years old and still amazing. At first I wasn't a fan of the whole "pay-to-play" sales model, but I completely understand why the dev's did it that way.
If this game was a "buy once and keep playing" type of game it would have been released in 2009, and stayed in basically the same shape it was is at the time of release.
Instead, we've got a game that is constantly being updated, even 6 years after it's initial release, and that's due to the fact that the devs are still seeing an income from the game, which allows them to spend time/resourses updating it, and adding fresh new content, as well as fix bugs and add new features over time.
In my opinion, that makes it worth the $34(CAD) I need to keep paying in order to hunt all the animals after my licenses expire.
Don't get me wrong, if I decide to not pay next year, I can still keep all of the weapons/equipment that came with my initial purchase and use them to hunt Mule Deer and Cottontails (I believe those are the only free animals), but I will definitely be buying my licenses again next year.
I would even consider buying a higher priced "lifetime license" if the devs ever thought to release something like that, but I understand why they decided to go with the current business model.
Now, if only they would do something similar with theHunter:Primal so it could be anywhere close to as amazing of a game as this is.

I've known this game was out for a while, but recently got it. Why? A lot of Alien games are just not good. And I thought this would be a bad game. Man was I wrong.
First, Alien Isolation's story is outright AWESOME, and never gets repetitive. Every mission is different from that last, and stays scary and enjoyable without seeming dull. Next, the graphics....OH MY, they're just outstanding. My FPS on this game is through the roof, and my temperatures on my GPU and CPU barely go past idle. Aside from performance, the game looks looks beautiful, and the effects and lighting are killer. Meanwhile, the alien itself is just outright terrifying. It's complex and unpredictable AI makes this game even more fun and scary, while having fluid animations and sounds.
Only thing I don't like about Alien: Isolation are some of the characters you meet, who are rather dull. Honestly, other than that, this game is perfect for you if you want some nice scares and want a horror game that isn't 10 hours long (the length of playtime on Alien: Isolation averages around 25 hours I've heard, but for me I'm at almost 30 and I am barely halfway!)
Anyways, this game is a solid 10/10, best alien game and one of the best horror games ever!

I honestly did not expect anything less from SuperGiant Games and they did not fail to please. Transistor is beautifully constructed, utterly gorgeous to look at, and the soundtrack lives up to the action too. The only sad thing about this game was that it didn't get the hype that it deserved :(

If you loved Bastion, and especially it's soundtrack, you will love Transistor. It's got another silent protaganist who's a bit easier on the eyes, and so is the landscape. Bastion was beautiful, but there wasn't much left in that world. Transistor takes place in a city and the landscape is accordingly more populated. And the music, oh the music. Master Korb has done another wonderful job, and you can even have Red hum along to the background music for a bit if you want.
The combat is considerably differernt from Bastion. You have many more moves available and you can play along the same lines, whale on the enemy  and take a few hits; you do heal after every battle more or less. The true difference though, is the ability to "program" an attack sequence via Run(). It has some cooldown, but you can do anything from string together a sequence of attacks to just get out of harms way; allowing for a considerable number of tactics.
If you missed out on the Summer Sale, it's still entirely worth getting, but if you are tight on funds it might go on sale again this holiday season if we are lucky. Hopefully I'll have someone needing a cool gift like this that I can surprise.

Absolutely amazing. Bastion was great, but Transistor brings the game style to a whole new level. Particularly with the Turn() mechanic, the gameplay stays challenging and interesting throughout, the customization options are extraordinary, and the story... oh god, that story.
Amazing graphics, beautiful music, charming characters. What are you waiting for. Buy this game already!

If you are a fan of Bastion, I'd definitely pick up this game. First thing, I'd like to say that I was skeptical, to say the least, about the "turn" system implemented in this game. Upon playing Transistor I was pleasantly surprised. Don't let the idea of the turn fool you, this is a fast paced game and you will find yourself implementing "turn" with joy time and time again, I know I did. I think SuperGiant games is starting to become a studio I'll follow. While feeling INCREDIBLY similar to Bastion (you can definitely tell this was done by the same studio: the narrator is the same voice actor, the music is scored by the same person, the challenges share similar ideas to those implemented, and the main character stay [mostly] silent), the game establishes it's own differences, even if rather minor, in the art of the game. SuperGiant has a way of using overall theme in their games so far, and it shines here:
The narrator is as charismatic as ever, the visuals are abosutley stunning and keep the painterly feeling that was present in bastion, and the soundtrack is absolutely breathtaking.
If the theme of bastion was the Wild West, the theme of this is definitely Jazz Noir with a twist of dystopian future. The game doesn't exactly hold your hand either. The story isn't exactly minimalist, yet while you are being fed information on the city, enemies, or events, it never feels spoon fed.
I could go on and on about this game, but really I don't want to spoil to much. I say if you are reading these reviews, take the dive. You'll have tons of fun tinkering over your abilities and testing them out on the Process.

This game is amazing! As expected from Supergiant Games, the soundtrack and art direction are both stellar. There are two different choices for combat: real-time combat and turn based combat. In the turn based combat you can plan out your moves and execute them at the end of the planning turn. Your moves are called functions and can be implemented as an active, upgrade, or passive. The number of combinations surpasses even Bastion which leads to lots of flexibility to match all kinds of play styles. The story and cutscenes are also great.
The game is a little short, it took me about 6 hours to beat. The whole experience was worth it though. You can also recurse through the story after you beat the game and keep all of your old functions. To recurse through the story and get all of the acheivements it took me an additional 12 hours (I liked wasting time testing out function combinations).
If you liked Bastion, you will love Transistor. I can't recommend this game enough. Amazing.

The Elder Scrolls Online:
- Tamriel Unlimited -
The Elder Scrolls Online is an absolutely stunning game and I would recommend this to any fan of The Elder Scrolls, any MMO, RPG or Open-World lover. If your debating on buying it, I highly suggest you do, you most likely will not regret it. If you think this game is like The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, you are wrong. ESO replaces Skyrm's hack-and-slash combat system with an ability focused combat system. Although the freedom of the Elder Scrolls games carries over to ESO.
There is something about the world of the elder scrolls online that give me the chills. It gives us the oppertunity to go where ever we want and do what ever we want. We have the oppertunity like any other elder scrolls game, to skip the main quest line and wander off to do whatever you want. You can spend your time just slaying monsters if that is what you want. The oppertunities are limitless. The content we get in this game is out of this world. If you think the world of Skyrim or Morrowind was huge, you will be blown away by the size and the content of this game. The in-game world of Tamriel are made up of individual zones. The size of the zones varies, but they can be as large as size of Skyrim.
ESO started out as a "meh" kinda game. I've played it since the closed beta early in 2014. Although I enjoyed the game, it was not a very good game. With all the patches and updates like One-Tamriel, it has changed the game completely. If you compare the game in 2014 with how the game is today in 2017, it will be like two different games. I've invested over 1500 hours into this game. Its an absolutely breath-taking and social-life-destroying game. It has now broken some off the barriers which the post-One Tamriel game did have, like not being able to go where ever you wanted to go and not being able to play with your friends that arent in the same alliance as you.
I've loosely touched some of the positive topics about the game, but now its about time to visit the dark side of ESO. I feel like the developers of ESO has focused more on their cash shop, the crown store more than the core game. They've added gambling aspects to the game by introducing Crown Crates, which are crates that contains four random items from a specific loot table. While they have been fleshing out their cash shop, we have yet to see the dungeon group-finder being fixed or the immense server issues we have. If we look at what they are selling in the crown store, we can see that they sell costumes and other cosmetic items like mounts and pets for half or the same price as the major DLCs in the game. Sometimes.... or rather most of the time, when the developers makes an update to the game to balance out the four classes (Dragonknight, Sorcerer, Templar and Nightblade) in the game, it seems they are just screwing things up even more. By the updates they are released previously, it seems like they dont even play the game. I just cant understand their logic sometimes. Instead of balancing out the classes, they just nerf everything to the ground. I feel like they should hire the top tier players from every aspect of the game like PVE, PVP... and even questing and exploration. It isnt very often we are very happy with the updates they release.
But after all, nobody is perfect....

A VERY GOOD RPG that can totally be played as a single player game, and gets even more interesting in groups. The quests are what makes TESO very different from its competitors: very well written, very rarely repetitive, very few Fedex-style ones. Sometimes the dialogues are really funny, too. Crafting is fun and efficient: no need to spend a whole year focusing solely on it to make useful items. As soon as on levels 1-20, a few good crafted potions, meals and gear can make a difference. While in other games you can rarely make gear that matches your level, at least not before months of practice, in TESO you can craft good stuff right away, and awesome stuff at high levels, while not having to sacrifice precious, scarce skill points: they are awarded in numbers. Exploration is rewarded by a number of great features: numerous chests, secret places, crafting ressources, etc., can be found while sticking to the edge of rivers and moutains. No need to fight everything if you don't want too, either: you can cross a whole map and fulfill most quests without even fighting one mob if you don't want to, thanks to stealth, invisibility potions and to the fact that monsters don't come in unavoidable packs. Last but not least, the game's quite beautiful and natural-looking enough to make you forget you're playing an MMO.

Inspired by resource manager games like Dwarf Fortress and Minecraft, Factorio is an industry-building RTS that takes the means of production to the extreme. The player is stranded on a hostile alien planet after a botched space colonization attempt. Using furnaces, assembly machines, an army of machines, and more, he strikes out against the endless alien swarm in every direction. Yet, the biters and spitters are enraged by his factories' pollution, and attack from every direction.
In a nutshell:
Excellent RTS resource management game, developed by an independent studio based in the EU
Great community, though not very large
Multiplayer support still in the works, but this should be an excellent game with other people
Well optimized game, runs very well
Big updates in the works
Some downsides:
Tedious game play - essentially, this game puts into into an infinite management loop, forcing you to continually jump through hoops that force you to expand your production.
Poor mod, multiplayer support - at the time of writing, steam workshop and servers have not been integrated into the game's system. It's currently easiest as a single player game.
Rating: 94/100

Alright I'll be very brief and frank here (and fair as much as possible)
The game is great, amazingly well made maps and art is one of the pillars of this game for me. The environment totally immerses you into the game. The music, the design, the gameplay all flow very well to draw you into the MMORPG world and never look back. If you appreciate a well designed world for exploration and role playing, this is the game for you.
However, the issues people have with this game are almost all on SERVER/DEVELOPER SIDE. It feels like a half-baked cake. This is probably not for you if you're into the competitive scene or the hardcore pvp/skill and reflex thrill seeker.
Overall, the game can be experienced at a leisurely pace while rewards those who dedicate time and effort as well. But unfortunately, it falls short on the technical performance side. The gameplay is great but we can't fully appreciate it with FPS and server issues. I'd like to compare it to a good book which can be taken slowly and properly savored with each chapter but a bad movie with messy and confusing action scenes.
It's free, give it a go. If you like what you see then continue playing at your own pace, but if you're the type of person who wants to invest a ton of resources to the game, then there are probably better options for you.

Where to start NOT to buy / play the game..? The game is said to be the 'spiritual successor' of Ragnarok online, but it's not. Though I haven't played Ragnarok a lot, the 2 games differ a lot (too much to be honest), so don't be fooled by that silly 'spiritual successor' crap...
I bought this game during early access and even then the game was loaded with goldsellers - yes this pest really buys into early access games to get a market. Sadly though, the developer (and publisher) is not doing much to battle the goldsellers and you can't even report them from chat (all you can do is block them). That being said, there is said to be a tool available that can recognize, report and block this pest for you. And while it's a helpfull tool, this kind of tools SHOULD NOT be able to be used with an online game, because if this can be used, cheaters can also use hacking tools easily as well!
Then the gameplay... Where to start... If you want to 'kill 10 rats' over and over again, then this game is for you. As a MMO (which is hyped to death!) it's not bringing anything new. It's the same old over and over again and a huge grind for levels to hit cap.
And talking about grind... Changing jobs is yet an other grind. Yes, you can easily select what new job you want, but to get it done be prepared to do numerous 'kill 10 rats' quests before you're even able to talk to that one NPC that can help you progress to your next job.
It's not all too bad though... Graphics are isometric and a very appealing anime style, sound on the other hand feels pretty much out of place for this game and story telling is pretty decent (and corny, but what to expect when almost every tale has been told already :p).
In general I can say it's 'yet an other MMORPG' to fill the ranks. Nothing real special here for my taste and certainly not living up the hype (yes I did read into the game before buying that early access).

Supergiant Games have done it again. This game is as beautiful, if not even more beautiful than Bastion. However, before I go on with the rest of my review, I should say that even if you loved Bastion, you may not love this game. A lot of people fell in love with Bastion, not just because of the gameplay and music, but because of the storyline and the narrator that made you feel like you were part of the story.
Now, that's not to say that Transistor doesn't have an interesting storyline, it's just that the storyline isn't as clear as it was in Bastion. That's not necessarily a bad thing either, some people like these sort of stories, I'm one of them. Transistor's story is a little more open to interpretation, whereas Bastion's was straightforward, so in this regard, some Bastion lovers may be disappointed. It's also a little hard to understand the story, even after two playthroughs, I mean, I get what's going on, but I'm left with a why at the end of the game. It's explained why in the game, but the reason just seems a bit flawed, I can't talk much more about it without spoiling things, so I'll leave it at that.
As for the narrator, Logan Cunningham, I'm really glad to see that he's back in this game. The only issue I had, was that his impact on the game felt like it fell short in comparison to Bastion. The reasoning behind that, is because in Bastion, he actually played a bit more of an important role, in Transistor, however, he just seems like a big question mark the entire time. Now, while he is considered a main character, I mean, he's with you the entire time after all, it's just that they never really give much information on him. His lines in the games were mostly reactionary as well, instead of in Bastion where it felt like he was telling the story, in this game, it just feels like he's living through the story along with us.
With all of that said, I still love Transistor more than Bastion.
While Transistor might not be as good as Bastion on the storytelling side, the story of Transistor is still rather interesting in it's own way. Bastion was really clear cut with it's story, and that's fine, but I love the way Transistor is a lot more open with it's own story. It takes awhile to figure all of out, but I find it to be more interesting that way.
The soundtrack of this game is just amazing. I don't know how Supergiant Games did it again, I usually don't keep in-game music/sounds on, unless if they're really good, and I kept mine on the entire time while playing Transistor. I'm even listening to it now while writing this review, I'll probably end up buying the soundtrack on Steam later on. The music just matches so perfectly with the game itself, it doesn't feel like a distraction, it only enhances the experience.
The gameplay of Transistor is a bit more interesting than Bastion as well. Though I should warn you to look up some videos on youtube of the gameplay before buying Transistor. Personally though, I love the mix of using the turn-based system, along with just attacking without the turn system. It's a pretty interesting way to play, a good mix of both is the best way to go, in my opinion. The ability to use your functions (skills) as actives, passives or upgrades is a pretty cool concept as well. A bit limiting in some cases, but that just adds a bit more to the challenge.
In terms of achievements, this is rather easy to perfect in comparison to Bastion and perhaps most games in general. There isn't much difficulty involved in many of the achievements, they're more time consuming than anything. However, since the game is rather short, it only takes like 6-7 hours for your first playthrough and then perhaps 4-5 more for your second playthrough. I finished both of my playthroughs in a little over 11 hours and got all of the achievements, so it's definitely a bit shorter than Bastion.
To conclude, Transistor is a beautiful and wonderful game on it's own. If you think it'll be exactly the same as Bastion however, you may be a bit disappointed. However, Transistor is my favorite game so far this year, it did not disappoint me one bit and it only surpassed the expectations I had. I am merely warning those who think this is almost an exact copy of Bastion, it is not.
Pros:
+ Interesting gameplay
+ Beautiful art style
+ Wonderful music
+ Decent replay value
+ Lots of different combinations for functions (skills)
Cons:
- A bit on the short side (6 Hours for first playthrough)
- Some parts of the story could use a bit more explaining

If ever there was a game that was deserving of the title "flawed masterpiece", this is it. The biggest flaw is that the game does start to overstay it's welcome and could quite easily get away with being half as long. This wouldn't be so egregious if not for the fact that the fatigue starts to impinge on the sense of dread and terror. There are only so many times you can get sent on a fetch quest before the sense that you're playing a video game eats away at the immersion.
The game has it's fair share of glitches, too. More than once I've had to stand like an idiot moving the cursor around while I try and interact with something and once it bugged out completely leaving me unable to exit out of interacting with something and inevitably dying because of it. Lip syncing can also be pretty bad at times.
However, what this game does right it does really,
well. And what it does right is scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you. If you're a fan of the original Alien film and a fan of survival horror games you're in for an absolute treat. I have no doubt that in the future this game will be considered a classic of the genre. Few games have come close to the sense of abject dread I felt when I first encountered the
. I'm not sure any game has managed to make me feel as if I'm really there like AI does.
The sound and visuals in this game are absolutely stellar and do a fantastic job of conjuring up the atmosphere of the original movie. As much as I love Aliens, the original is my favourite and this game is the sequel it deserved.

This is a cinematic sci-fi horror game, and as such it works brilliantly. The graphics, lighting, sound effects and music all work towards the end of terrifying you, and in this they succeed. It is probably the least fun or relaxing game I've ever played, but it's also one of the most exciting.
This is stealth in its purest form; you cannot bail and start blasting your way out of trouble as in many FPS games with stealth elements. In this game, if you're discovered, you're generally dead within seconds. This is not an FPS. Bear that in mind. What this amounts to is spending 90% of your time fearfully cowering and creeping around (other than in those few missions where the alien is not present) whilst trying to accomplish basic tasks toward the goal of escaping a dying space station.
The DLCs don't add a whole lot to the experience; only Safe Haven is really worth paying for. But so long as you know what you're getting into, the main game itself is worthwhile. Just don't expect a shooting game (most of the time, shooting someone is immediately followed by the sound of a galloping xenomorph followed by its arm bursting out of your chest).

As someone who loves the Alien franchise, I'm insanely happy with what Alien: Isolation brought to the table and I think everyone should enjoy it.
Pros:
+atmosphere is amazing
+it can be truly terrifying
+gameplay is fantastic
+crafting is fun
+story and lore are very rich
+graphics are solid
+audio is far too good
+animations and voice acting are top notch
+alien nostalgia is great but not used as a crutch
Cons:
-ending is okay but not as coherent as I'd like
-in order to get some of the collectables you have to do some serious backtracking at the end
I picked this game up when it was on sale, I knew it was good but didn't think it was this good so I put off playing it (which I regret deeply).
I was skeptical about Amanda Ripley (our main character) going in but the writing for her is great and she's very likeable. The story and gameplay are superb. Although I will say the game becomes a little less fun once you're geared up. The last 1/4 of the game was actually the least fun for me (it's still fantastic though). But there's something to be said for having no way to combat the alien and all you can do is avoid it. I think that's where the most intense moments come from. Also I love exploring every corner of a game and at times it was pretty hard to do with the alien stalking me but that made it even more challenging/fun.
The story is really solid. I think this whole game is even more enjoyable if you've seen at least the first Alien movie. And if you haven't seen it by now you should anyway (it's a great ♥♥♥♥ing movie). But the lore is built upon and it's so cool to see more of the universe. The attention to detail is damn amazing. The fact they used the font from the original Alien movie poster for the menus brings me absolute happiness. The fidelity of the ships, equipment, and audio is stunning. I felt like I was on set for the 1979 classic.
One gripe I have with Isolation is that in order to get some of the collectables, you have to wait until near the end of the game and then backtrack through the whole ship trying to remember where this stuff was. Couple this with the fact that once you can backtrack the story is getting pretty intense so you really don't wanna wander around. It just seems like they could've made the collectables harder to get but in a more creative way. Instead you're flat out incapable of exploring certain rooms because you don't have the tool upgrades and you don't get those until literally the last few missions.
I just have one little issue with the ending. It's ambiguous. But not in a way that helps the overall lore/story. A little disclaimer though, this in no way is game breaking, it doesn't effect how I feel about the rest of the game, and I actually really like one of the theories about the ending. But what it basically boils down to is that in order for the movie Aliens (which takes place after this game) to make sense we have to assume certain things happen in an ending that's meant to be ambiguous and not tell us exactly what happened. So the ending I'd like to believe is made invalid by the state of the story in Aliens. This is only an issue though if you want to believe one particular theory about how it ends.
If you're interested in a discussion about the ending, this thread proved to be pretty enlightening and in it there's an explanation as to what has to happen in order for the second movie to make sense.

A VERY GOOD RPG that can totally be played as a single player game, and gets even more interesting in groups. The quests are what makes TESO very different from its competitors: very well written, very rarely repetitive, very few Fedex-style ones. Sometimes the dialogues are really funny, too. Crafting is fun and efficient: no need to spend a whole year focusing solely on it to make useful items. As soon as on levels 1-20, a few good crafted potions, meals and gear can make a difference. While in other games you can rarely make gear that matches your level, at least not before months of practice, in TESO you can craft good stuff right away, and awesome stuff at high levels, while not having to sacrifice precious, scarce skill points: they are awarded in numbers. Exploration is rewarded by a number of great features: numerous chests, secret places, crafting ressources, etc., can be found while sticking to the edge of rivers and moutains. No need to fight everything if you don't want too, either: you can cross a whole map and fulfill most quests without even fighting one mob if you don't want to, thanks to stealth, invisibility potions and to the fact that monsters don't come in unavoidable packs. Last but not least, the game's quite beautiful and natural-looking enough to make you forget you're playing an MMO.

This game was a tremendous disappointment. As a fan of the first Dark Souls (over 300 hours logged), I had very high hopes for this one. However I felt unbelievably cheated by what I purchased.
I will admit that I've only played through the first level of the game, but that was all that I could really stomach to do. This game fell apart for me at the tutorial level. The control scheme is nowhere near polished, and the game immediately takes this chance to punish you for it. The timing from button press (I used controllers as I expected poor port conversion from the beginning) to action felt so long that I thought something was wrong with my computer. After finding this not to be the case, I drudged on hoping I would adjust to this as I continued to try and re-learn some of the techniques that you almost had to learn in order to do well in the first one (parrying & backstabbing).
After gaining enough confidence in my skill (or perhaps I just got bored looking at the same tired scenery of the tutorial), I prepared myself to face some sort of boss like the first one. Nope. I was immediately granted passage to a plain looking beach cliff with no adversity in between, and I think that represents where this game majorly misses the point of the difficulty of the first one: satisfaction and reward.
Difficulty is important for a game to have, otherwise what's the point, right? But what this game fails at is making a reward out of triumphing over that difficulty. By the time I had finished the boss of the first level, I didn't feel the need to continue. I didn't feel proud of my accomplishment in any way, I felt underwhelmed and bored. I didn't feel like I was a better player of the game for what I had done, I felt like I made a bunch of cheap hits and got out of the way without learning anything.
I didn't even want to bother with PvP and co-op with this game, as I felt the newly implemented system of Soul Memory to determine matching would've made it so my grinding in an attempt to learn the game would've skewed the level of players I could interact with. I may be wrong in my assessment, but I've not tried it myself.
In conclusion, if you like bland, uninspired difficulty in a tired world of disconnected legs (not the open world promised so long ago) then you will find your money well spent here. Otherwise, steer clear of this game, and spend it on more worthy titles.

Wayward, at it's current state, is very enjoyable and quite different than anything I've played before (from Minecraft, Terraria, Final Fantasy, etc). I recommend it to anyone that enjoys old-school pixel graphic sandbox games with rpg, crafting, and building elements.
It is in alpha/beta phase, so just keep in mind that many things ought to change over time. Devs appear to be very professional and friendly, also active in the community (on reddit, Steam Discussions, their own webpage, etc) which is a huge plus. This little gem has great potential.
Things to consider:
- Turn-based (when ya move, craft, consume something, build, etc; other creatures move, time/game ticks forward)
- Very old-school pixel graphics (which I personally love)
- Lots of craftables, though building options are a bit limited right now.
- RPG elements: tons of different skills to level up as you use them/craft stuff, which increase your 'Talent' points (purple points to right of health points)
- Combat is very simple, so far. Ranged weapons and traps add a bit of tact to it.
- You will most likely die and it will most likely frustrate you
- Perma-death (you die, you have to start a new randomly generated world. I'd recommend the Reincarnate Mod, by dev in Workshop, to randomly respawn in same world so all your progress isn't down the drain. Though, your skills do carry over, no matter if you use mod or not)
- Micromanagement is tedious and clunky right now, takes a bit to get use to. As well as using some tools.
- Tutorial is very brief, the basic of the basics. No hand holding and you're left to figure most things out on your own. I don't mind it, but you may.
- Difficulty is sporadic, especially if you haven't read up on the mechanics. (Some folks find it very difficult while some find it very easy, though I wager that a lot of it depends where you randomly spawn at and what creatures randomly spawn in your vicinity).
- Difficulty does scale with your progression/Talent points (purple numbers by health), so keep that in mind. It means that stronger/different monsters can spawn and I believe their hp and damage does increase, but not too significantly.
- It's a lot like Minecraft, where I'd advise to mess around to figure out some things until ya die a few times, then take a few to read up on some tips/advice/game mechanics, etc before restarting again to ensure your survival.
- Music is great
Some folks have beat it pretty quick, indicating that it's not necessarily that long of a game (at the moment of development), but if you take your time, build a place or town or whatever, collect stuff, explore the large world, hunt down different monsters, etc; you should easily get 20 to maybe 30 hours or more before ya run out of stuff to do. Not considering the additional content that will most likely be added within the near future. ^.^

This is a great survival game.  It features hunger, thirst and day/night cycles and has many many skills to learn such as Blacksmithing, Fletching, Anatomy, Cooking, Clay Throwing, Glas♥♥♥♥ing and about 12 more skills.  You discover crafting recipes as you collect items from the world which persist with you through each play-through.  The crafting system is very robust but sometimes tedious.  This game also features perma-death but there is a mod that allows for resurrection so you don't lose all your progress if you like to play that way. Transistor is made by Supergiant Games, the creators of Bastion. Where Bastion was a hack n slash, Transistor is a very strategic, very challenging game. Fights play out in either real time or in a turn-based strategy form. You will be using the turn-based style more often as it adds a needed level of planning to fights. Planning is imoortant because the enemy is NOT a pushover. The enemies are not brutal but pose enoguh of a challenging to make survivng each encounter feel like an accomplishment.
The game drops you immediately in to the game and gives you the bare minimum in terms of background story about the city of Cloudbank. If you're looking for more depth to the story, you will find it within each abilites information tab. What the ability information!? Yes, each ability you obtain in the game comes at the cost of a persons life, and their death grants you an ability that can be used as main ability, an upgrade, or a passive ability. The people associated with the various abilities are key figures in the city of Cloudbank and help flesh out the city and its story.
The story, while somewhat vague in the beginning and very thick in the middle, concludes brilliantly in both the final boss fight and the story's ending. This game was an amazing experience and I will definetly be returning to Cloudbank to learn more of its story and enjoy the deep, rewarding, and fun gameplay.

When I bought Call of Juarez Gunslinger during the Steam summer sale I was looking for a game to satisfy my shooter cravings.  What I got, and admittedly didn't expect was one of the coolest storytelling and educational history experience in any FPS game.
The game unfolds as we listen to the story of this salty old gunslinger being told to 3 captivated listeners in a saloon.  As he tells his tall tales of confrontation against some of histories infamous bandits we play out the battles wonderfully narrated in gorgeous wild west landscapes.
What I loved most about playing out the narration was how it could abruptly change the environment.   When anybody tells an old story there's always mistakes or embellishment, and when you get called out for bull ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ you got to tell it again with truth.  This is depicted in game by rewinding the scene you just played and replaying it with the "true" way things went down.
The gunplay is super tight and fun.  Racking up kills gradually fills a concentration meter which allows you to slow time and see enemies better.  Concentration is best used in situations when you're severely outnumbered or surrounded.  With unlocked abilities concentration can be further improved to auto target and execute enemies very quickly.
There are 3 skill trees to support 3 different weapon / play styles.  You can unlock abilities in any tree, so you're never pigeonholed into one style.  The styles are for pistols, rifles, and shotguns.  Choosing one doesn't mean you can't use the others, it just improves the one you choose with various enhancements like faster reloading or larger ammo capacity.
The history buff and collectables fan will enjoy searching for Nuggets of Truth hidden throughout story mode.  Each collectable reveals a little slice of history with an old photograph and write up of an actual person, place, or historic event. If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

I  jumped over a fence leading into a dark alleyway, lit only by a dim yellow lamp. Four others stood waiting for me. Out of the pitch blank on the opposite side of the path, an infected girl walked into the light. One survivor starts to strike at her with his wrench, saving bullets for later. Strike after strike, the infected girl finally latched onto him, and started to chew on him. With an effort to survive, the man pulled out his handgun, and fired 4 shots into her abdomen. Having little effect, she continued to eat him, and the man fell. Another survivor who wore a black cap, Deven, shot an arrow into the infected's head, dropping her onto the cement. As we search our fallen brother's corpse, one of the other screams "no!" With one brother less, We move on.
A few minutes after the incident, I found a chainsaw, which still worked. We also caught up with more survivors whilst trying to get across the city. All of us had to escort Devin whilst he pushed a cart down to grab some fuel for our escape. I was in the front, mowing down a lot of infected, while the others shot down the rest. Gun shots covered the city. After a while of sawing down infected, I ran out of fuel, decided to get back for a few, looting houses and such. I managed to grab a shotgun, and some shells. Then, all of a sudden, the gunshots died down. I ran out to the streets to see no friends in sight, not even Devin, but only the walking dead.
"Dammit..."
I walked down the streets, shooting the heads of my now dead friends and others. "This is it," I thought. "I'm the last one alive." No one was anywhere. No one was talking. No one was in sight. I was thinking about putting the gun to my head, but then I heard what was a handgun nearby a truck. I grabbed a pistol off the ground, and made my way to the gunfire.
As I made my way to him, an infected ran up to me, and grabbed me. I pulled out my pistol, and emptied my mag into her brains. There was only one bullet left. I ran up, and saw a survivor, Felix. He was pinned in the truck, shooting off hordes of infected. I pulled out both my handgun and my shotgun, and helped him out. As he got out, I covered the area. There were still many more infected in the area. We couldn't turn back. Not yet. So we set forth. I knew there were still others out there, right?
We went forth, and killed a bunch of infected. I soon ran out of ammo for both guns, so I dropped them. The only thing I could use was a wrench. After bashing some infected brains, we went to the corner of a street. Felix had 2 guns; a sniper rifle, and a pump action shotgun. I looked at him, with our guns pointed at the infected. So I finally spoke.
"Give me one of your guns."
"Alright." He handed me his sniper rifle. I took the gun, and looked at the horde of infected, inching slowly towards us.
"You thinking what I'm thinking?" He looked at me. He and I both knew this was going to happen eventually.
"Yeah."

Pretty game. Nice graphics, very realistic when it comes to tracking, stalking and waiting for your prey.
That being said, this game has by far the worst, most greedy f2p business model I've ever seen. All of the gear and weapons you absolutely MUST pay real money for. There is no option for buying any of it with in game currency. In fact, the only thing the in game currency is good for is ammo, taxidermy and hunting licenses, but the costs vs the earnings is such a grind that it's not even worth it. I have never seen a business model for a f2p so forceful in making you cough up actual money, that it can easily be argued that it's not even a free to play. We're not talking pay to win, we're talking pay to do just about anything.
They've recently added game rotations, enabling certain animal to be open for hunting by non members without a license. However, the weapons required to hunt those animals are weapons you must pay premium currency for: the starting revolver and rifle can't be used on most of them. Which essentially makes the free game rotation nearly useless. And that uselessness can barely even be realized when you're sitting in an area, waiting for your game, and you see all these other animals in the area that you can't shoot because you don't have a license. And God have mercy on your soul if you come across a bear you can't shoot, because you don't have the license. Stock up on first aid kits, which also cost premium currency...
They've recently added new content, such as taxidermy, trophy lodges, and even hunting dog companions. Those, of course, cost more premium currency. So you have to shell out even more money for content in a "free" to play game.
I'd rather they simply put a $60 price tag on the game and that's that. But that would be the right thing to do.

Y'know all those bad games out there that are impossible to play, get bad reviews, and no one liked them?
Somewhere out there is someone with an old console and a stack of used games who plays those games religiously. And no review site ever told him those games he plays are "bad". So when he's presented with obtuse and frustrating problems, he doesn't have other games to play so he just powers through them; dying again and again and sometimes needing to start from the beginning. Eventually, he's played enough that he understands the illogical and unfair systems; a bizarre network of exploits and unexplained rules, combined with more patience dodging attacks than the game is really owed. Someday I think he'll discover the internet, find that the games he now loves are "bad", and be kind of shocked.
By some illogical measure, this is Dark Souls (and the sequel, Dark Souls 2); a bad game that has received just enough attention that the population of people understanding these systems enough to play with them and have fun with them grants it some meritous presence.
Dark Souls 2 is in no way special in its "innovative decisions to barely tutorialize". What you need to understand is that you could get this anywhere; find any poorly-reviewed game on Steam with "Blood" or "Drak-", or "Dragon-", or "Warrior" in the title, and play it until you die. Then keep playing, and forcing yourself into it, convincing yourself you have some need to write the next GameFAQ on it. Eventually, you'll find that way to get that one boss stuck in a corner so you can kill him with a pickaxe; that one place you can semi-clip through the environment to get that one upgrade early. Who knows, maybe someday you'll be playing it as a joke during Summer Games Done Quick, like their play of Shadow the Hedgehog.
I've played and beaten plenty of games considered pretty damn hard. There tends to be a difference, though, between a game that treats its players gently with its harsh difficulty, always making success seem just a hair out of grasp, and a lazily-balanced game like Dark Souls 2 that just decides to work it into its marketing, going "I BET YOU THINK YOU CAN BEAT THIS."
No, no I don't think I can beat this. I also can't beat Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde for the NES, because I didn't devote endless pointless hours to understanding why I just died in it.

First Impression Video:
Wayward is an enjoyable turn based survival game. It has everything you could want: procedural generation, crafting, and smashing rats in the face.
Wayward is definitely not an easy game, but it's also not a game that will beat you down for one wrong move. You have to work to get some meager living and a single rat can push you into a rush to find a suture. Bleeding out ain't no fun people.
At this point, Wayward is a fully fledged game. It needs some serious overhauls to the tutorial, but if you're willing to try and fail, this game is a fun time. I haven't found any bugs in the game so far.
One negative point that i would give this game is that it can put you in situations that you can't survive in. Being placed on an island with no rock (which is needed for every tool except wood spears, and harvesting without a tool can hurt you) means that you're doomed to a slow death.
Overall, Wayward is a seriously fun game. If you're into survival and crafting games, it's definitely worth picking up.

So, Call of Juarez is, straight up, an arcade based western first person shooter, with a comical twist and pure action and shooting. Literally everything is done in first person, and it almost feels like a On the Rail shooter that you freely can move through, with a minimal hud and a unreliable narrator telling people the story as you go through it, almost like riding through a book. It just feels like pure action, when your running through whizzing bullets and seeing blood gush everywhere with a bonus +100 points coming out of their head, along with a nice sound effect and a "HEADSHOT". (If you've ever played "Bulletstorm", when you get a skilled kill it's almost like that)
There is also an RPG element in the game, and thankfully, it's not a dominant thing, more of a side thing. when you kill bad guys you get experience, and from there you can unlock some skills (and eventually better guns) that you can choose. Maybe your a gunslinger, utilizing your revolvers, or perhaps, you prefer to snipe people from a distance? Maybe you get close and dirty as a shotgunner, it's your choice. The great thing about each class is that the bonuses aren't exclusive to just one weapon. In fact, in the sharpshooter tree, you can unlock ammo smashing which allows you to rapidly hit the reload button to reload all of your weapons faster, not just the rifle.
All in all, and I have played many, many games, I haven't had this much fun in a long time. It feels more like a interactive movie than just a game. Along with gameplay and graphics that I feel haven't aged, or if anything, barely aged, i would give this shooter a 9/10, and I recommend this arcadey FPS above anything else I've played.

As a fan of the (now) old Outlaws game from Lucasarts, I was surprised by this offering.  At first, I shunned this title, as my previous brush with the CoJ series was a bit lack-lustre.  After watching a a youtube stream of VideoGameCarnage, it piqued my interest and I can say now, I have no regrets.
+Gameplay is fast, but satisfyingly lethal.  The guns "feel" right, bringing back that Good, Bad, and Ugly sense of difficulty from Outlaws.
+Storyline is told as a series of narratives from the protaganist's view, with a bit of Prince of Persia-style "That's not the way it occurred" revisions mid-level to adjust for player error and humorous effect.  Also allows player to reasonably complete missions in shorter sessions.
+Surprisingly in-depth, with level progression, unlockables (in-game), and a good number and variety of levels that smacks directly of Outlaws (the comparison is deserved).
+Pricing makes it well within any gamer's budget, and you will get your money's worth...
+Shootouts at the end of the levels remind me favourably of the C64 game High Noon and are a welcome and varied take on a boss fight, giving you a sense of satisfaction that is only equaled in 'Souls games when you know it was pure skill that yielded a victory.
-No multiplayer, but can be re-played with a New Game Plus style mode and variety of difficulties.
-Is somewhat linear, but does give branching paths in some missions with hidden items and factoids to unlock.
-Pricing makes people believe it is a Budget Bin title, when it has a 1st class engine, voice acting, and is clearly a labor of love.
The fact that I've taken the time to write a review is a rare-enough occurance to suggest this game for your serious consideration.

While it certainly looks as good as Bastion, the gameplay and story just are below the high bar set by that game. The combat is stuck in the middle of real time action and semi-turnbased, and it does not mesh well. It is too slow for the real time action to feel fun, and yet too fast for the turn based stuff to be any more enjoyable. Every fight felt like a slog. If the story was good, then getting through the combat would be worth it, but sadly, it's not. The silent protaganist in Bastion worked since the narrator told us what he was thinking and doing; here Red is just silent and a non-entity. We get some artsy shots of her humming and taking breaks, and thats about it.

Negatives: Game is pretty short (although NG+ changes up the encounters), combat feels clunky and slow at first, final boss takes frustratingly long amounts of time to do anything
Postives: Literally everything not mentioned above. The way skills work takes a little while to sink in, but when it does and you've got access to enough abilities to make use of it, it's incredibly powerful. The mechanic where further lore is revealed by using a skill in each slot possible encourages you try out different skills in different roles and play the game differently, and as a result I found myself actually using every skill in the game in some way or another. The atmosphere is incredible. Once you actually get used to how combat works and have a bit more experience with the flow of things, it's excellent. A mechanic returning from Bastion is that you can activate a variety of 'limiters' that hurt you or help enemies, but give you bonus experience, which is great.
Buy this game.

The successor to Bastion from Supergiant Games had some big shoes to fill. I think it filled them well if not perfectly. From the beginning, the art direction and music direction is easily identifiable as coming from the same studio. The story begins in the middle of things, dropping the player into a brilliant world with a dark undertone.
The gameplay itself is solid. Combat can be played real time or turn based or a combination of the two, but it leans heavily toward turn based. There is no difficulty setting, only limiters, artificial difficulty modifiers you can select ingame to give youself a challenge. (Very similar to Bastion again). Without any limiters, the game would likely be very easy. With most of the limiters, some of the fights become quite nearly unbeatable. The middle ground is probably best for someone looking to enjoy the game. There are many different combat abilities that can be combined in crazy amounts of way to tailor to your style. For someone looking for a lot of customization this should satisfy.
Visuals and Audio is fantastic. There is not much here that needs to be said, as anything you would have likely seen in the trailers is what you are going to get. A good looking, good sounding indie game.
The story is where the game falls a bit short. The narrative is delivered through voiceover and digital entries, but this somewhat breaks up the flow of the game.  Unlike Bastion where there were nice long areas of narration, this game opts for small tidbits interspersed throughout gameplay. While this isn't bad, it doesn't entirely flesh out the world as much as I would have liked. The slightly "film noir" style of the game keeps up suspense up through the ending, but fails to deliver on the climax. Again, comparing the game to Bastion, the final moments of Transistor simply don't stand up to a climactic finish.
Overall however, the game is definitely worth playing for a beautiful world and engaging gameplay.
Your total play-time for a once through run will be somewhere in the 6-10 hour range.

A thoroughly and completely disappointing game and an insult to fans of the series, this is a disaster in every category.  If you liked the story or clean combat mechanics of the first game you will despise this entry.
The world is absurdly designed with "time is convoluted" explanation tying everything together about as strongly as a rubber band.  Drangleic Castle is somehow across an entire continent but is somehow easily accessible with a short jog.  The same is true of most locations in the game and is easily observed as early as Heide's tower of Flame.  Another famous example of folly is how a small tower with an elevator at its peak, travels UPward into mystery and ends up in a molten lava lake in a caldera of a previously non existent mountain many times wider than the tower now somehow below it.  Again this insanity is visible as early as Heide's tower, after defeating the dragon rider an elevator is taken down deep below the water level where there is somehow an above water cave with a protected cove and entrance open to the sea.  World design was essentially the crowning jewel of Dark Souls.  You could see everything from Anor Londo to Blighttown from the first area in the game and one step will take you one step closer to your destination; the entire world has a nearly 1:1 scale with a design that is simply awe inspiring.
The one thing they improved in this game is multiplayer connectivity, but the even scuttled that game mechanic by introducing the ridiculous soul level mechanic making it impossible to reasonably match opponents or ever play with friends, and also somehow managed to ruin the network coding of the first game taking lag from an unfortunate reality and turning it into a core game mechanic.  This somehow carries over into the single player experience, parrying and rolling were once essential mechanics as well but in this entry their results are what is "convoluted."  Even in controlled tests the same actions in the same circumstances yield wildly unreliable results.  To this end, YouTube PVPers that cut their teeth and gained their fame in previous Souls games have generally returned to Dark Souls (especially since the conversion from Games for Windows Live to Steam); this speaks volumes more than I even could.
Next we have the story; what a mess.  Look it up on youtube and see how many of the different authorities on Souls interpretation have wildly different interpretations of the stories in DS2.  This is mostly because the story was seemingly never written.  Rather than getting rich vignettes presenting tiny views into a detailed world, DS2 presents shattered fragments of unrelated events that have been forcibly linked by wild leaps of faith based around shoddy translation.   While the community generally agrees on the central (and painfully obvious) parts of the story, the rest is "convoluted."
The audio of the Souls series hasn't been perfect, but this is the worst entry in this regard as well.  The players have been given annoying screams on their death, and weapon hits now make a sad wet thump noise no matter what weapon is used.  To imagine the noise, think of what you would hear if a kitschy 1970s kung fu movie showed a person hitting a wet bag full of hamburger... you hear this noise constantly.
Finally the art direction.  In Dark Souls and even Demon's Souls, the hollowed undead are withered malkempt corpses, slowly being eroded by time and circumstance that are powered only by their hunger for souls.  In Dark Souls 2, they are a green skin zombie caricature whose lumbering motions do not reflect the damage they're capable of by swinging their limp arms toward you be jerking about at the shoulder.
All in all, this game was a hastily assembled disaster.  It betrayed players by overpromising and underdelivering on wild promises and poor effort.  The promise of a "complete game" for players purchasing at release was a lie from the get-go with three planned DLCs, and From continues this with their planned re-release of the game repackaged with the DLC claiming in to be a completely new game.
This type of insanity usually only present in the worst game developers has crushed the community's faith in From.

Wayward is a turn-based survival and crafting game with procedural world generation which would be well worth playing at 2-3xs the price. At $8 it's a bargain, especially for an Early Access Game this well developed.
The world is interesting and worth exploring, although the backstory is sparse. Crafting is well thought-out and strikes an excellent balance between reality and gameplay. Crafting recipe discovery is a very strong draw, and you can build atop your early failures with a system that brings what you learned the previous playthrough into each new start (unless you’d rather start from scratch, which you can do!). There's a wide array of skills and possible gameplay strategies, although they are not all fully balanced just yet.
There are some bumpy spots, as expected of a game in development, but the dev team is incredibly responsive. I've yet to encounter any instability with the game engine. As I write this the in-game tutorial already does a good job of easing you into the survival gameplay. The difficulty spikes up fairly harshly right now, but balance is a moving target for any game in development. Modding is enthusiastically supported by the devs, who have provided tutorials and open-source examples to get the modding scene started.
This game has apparently been in-dev for years. You can play the previous version of this game for free on their website, and it should be a great demo. If you like the free version, quickly buy it on Steam to support their great team. They’re quick to reply to feedback and take suggestions seriously. They even provide a link to the team’s dev tracker tool, where you can watch each new update come together as it progresses.
I’ll say it again: if you happen to enjoy TBS, survival, crafting, exploration or just supporting an indie team doing good work, you could hardly do better than giving this game a try.

While I ultimately settled on a "No" rating for this game, that's not entirely reflective of how I feel about it. It's not a bad game by any means, just not the game I wanted it to be. I was hoping for something right in that sweet spot between Don't Starve and Minecraft, with some fun turn-based elements to keep it interesting. Wayward was almost able to scratch that itch, but it didn't quite land there. The gameplay and interface are just awkward enough to keep me from really enjoying it. The learning curve wasn't exactly steep, but the more I learned about how to play the less I actually felt like playing.
That said, I don't want to dismiss the quality of the game. If you're looking for a top-down Minecraft-like game at a fraction of the Mojang price, you could do a lot worse. But in its current state, there was nothing new or exciting in the experience for me to latch onto.
As the game goes through revisions and updates, I'll check back in. Maybe there will be a new feature that will change my mind. I hope so. But at the moment, I can't recommend it.

I absolutely hated this game for the first 2 hours, and absolutely loved it for (almost all of) the last 18 hours.
This game is a rarity in that it takes a beloved film and manages to transfer the reasons why people love the film into the game. It captures the coherent and consistent visual style of the film to create a grimy, utilitarian environment, and backs it up with a remarkable attention to detail and sound design that is not only reminiscent of the film but also utterly fantastic on its own merits. Then they took that audio-visual design and wrapped it around a stealth horror game with terrific set pieces, a badass protagonist, and an interconnected level design that really makes you feel like you're on a spaceship without resorting to making you go through the exact same locations multiple times without there being any differences or any reason to do so.
The design of this game is really quite impressive, and it puts me in mind of one of my favourite last-gen titles - the original Dead Space, one of only a handful of games to capture the same sense of space being a lonely and utterly terrifying place. But whereas Dead Space was an action game, as you had more of an ability to fight back against the threats you face, Alien: Isolation goes in the opposite direction. While so many games have succeeded in drawing inspiration from the Alien franchise to create great games, almost all of them end up being reminiscent not of Ridley Scott's Alien, but of James Cameron's AlienS, with its big guns and . Isolation set out to be an homage and side-story to the original film, the 1979 horror sci-fi classic, and they absolutely nailed it.
But the most important question regarding any game based on a film like Alien is this: is it scary? Does it capture the same intensity and atmosphere of dread that makes the film such a classic?
The short answer is: yes.
The long answer is: yes, absoHOLYGODTHEXENOMORPHISCOMINGHIDEINACUPBOARDHIDEHIDEHIDEHIDEOHCRAPOHCRAP.
Now let me elaborate on my opening line. When I started playing the game, I was immediately blown away by the audio-visual design, and intrigued by the premise of playing as Amanda Ripley. But before long, the game started to frustrate me with its level design and set pieces. Several of the early missions force you into a position where you are almost completely powerless, and are at the mercy of the pathing and environmental awareness of the enemies. This results in a lot of trial and error, which brings me to the biggest reason why I began to hate the game: the lack of a quick save.
In hindsight, forcing the player to save at certain demarcated areas on the map is a fantastic way to increase the tension of your encounters with the Xenomorph later in the game, and ends up being a positive, not a negative. But in the beginning, when you haven't even met the alien yet and you're just trying to trial-and-error your way through these rigid environments, having to restart because you got unlucky or made one mistake is incredibly frustrating. Quick save is included in games that require stealth and navigating the environment (Dishonored, for example), because it encourages trial and error by minimising the consequences of failure. In a horror game, quick saving makes the player a bit too powerful and in control of the situation, which is exactly the opposite of what you're trying to achieve. But in that case, the game shouldn't force you to play a stealth section with the same restrictions and disempowerment of a horror game when you haven't even encountered the thing you're supposed to be horrified of yet.
Just how fed up and frustrated was I with the obnoxious and infuriating early missions? Enough to actually uninstall the game and write it off as a total failure. Fortunately, I was encouraged by a friend to give it another try, and I'm glad I did, because once the game starts to hit its stride, it grabbed hold of me and didn't let go. In truth, my enthusiasm did begin to waver towards the end of the game, and I think the pacing becomes a bit onerous. They tried to maintain the same level of game-ending tension and excitement for a bit too long, and they pull the same trick of "thinking everything's finally okay, oh wait no its not it's still terrible aaahhh" a couple of times. This conditioned me to expect the unexpected, to predict another sting in the tail, to the point where I was actually a little surprised when I finally got to the credits.
So the short version of this review is this: in terms of capturing the essense of one of the truly iconic films, a seminal, archetypal masterpiece of sci-fi and horror cinema, and turning that magic into a videogame, Alien: Isolation is a massive success. As a videogame, divorced from that baggage and expectation, it might have been an all-time great if the game's introduction wasn't a big pile of wank and if they stuck a landing a bit better. But even with those faults it's a very good game, carried by incredible audio-visual design, well-designed levels and environments, and one of the most genuinely terrifying enemies in recent memory.
And it still weird me out that this game was made by Creative Assembly. I guess this is what all their talented staff was doing when they should have been testing and refining Rome II.

While Bastion did a lot with a little, Transistor does a lot with a lot, and this is like 80/20 good thing/bad thing. The worldbuilding is great and you get a good feel for the setting with the great combination of music and locale. Even Logan Cunningham's reprisal of An Iconic Voice helped, although it was maybe beating a dead horse a little bit. However, you can tell that these lovingly handcrafted areas took a toll on the designers: Transistor is really, really short. I beat it in 3 hours, and that was a pretty casual playthrough. Of course, there's NG+ and the limiters (similar to the Gods from Bastion), but it's still a great - albeit short - game. Is it worth $20? If you /really/ liked Bastion, sure. $15? Maybe, still a bit pricey for the length though. Definitely worth $10, though!

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

There is a lot of hate about the monetary policy of this game. It is a little underhanded, and there are things I definitely disagree with, but if you approach the game from a neutral standpoint, and appreciate how much, how in depth the content of this game is, it's easy to justify purchasing the $50 starter bundle, and, eventually dropping a few dollars here and there on the game.
I play this game frequently, and I find myself continuously coming back to it for more when I lose interest in other games. It helps if you have friends to play with, this game is especially fun to play in a group, and you can help distribute the cost a bit between friends, purchasing callers, or bird hunting equipment for instance. I have probably spent about 75-90 dollars total on this game, which in purspective, is the cost of purchasing World of Warcraft and 2-3 months of game time. I'm not broke, and I don't mind spending money on entertainment, and this game is really high quality for what you are getting with that money.
The animal AI is incredibly good. The sounds and environments are so detailed and immersive that I can definitely lose track of time playing it. This game is hard, often unforgivable, and you really have to put some work into hunting. Sometimes you won't find anything. Other times you will hit something but fail to track it down. This game isn't for the faint of heart, and is definitely the most authentic hunting simulator on the market.
I find myself playing this game early in the morning before starting my work. It's a really good game to play with a cup of coffee or tea, or to play with online friends with some beer. It's hard to give this game a try because you really have to spend money on it, but if you have some extra money laying around, and you have a passion or fascination with hunting, I can't recommend this game enough.
