The equivalent of a summer blockbuster movie, this game is a fun, short, six-hour jaunt through the old west., spaghetti western-style.  The storytelling mechanisms are fun and interesting, with the protagonist telling the tale to bar patrons and sometimes forgetting pieces of the story or going off on tangents.
Shooting controls are relatively tight, my only issues were with the duel controls.  They seemed somewhat floaty, most likely to intimidate the lack of precision of revolvers of the era and to account for draw speed, versus the pinpoint accuracy you have using your mouse and keyboard.
Story is fun, but not super memorable, some fun spots and I enjoyed the ending.  Overall interesting choices by the developer in terms of pacing and choices.
Purchased on a Steam Sale, but would absolutely recommend at full price.

I absolutely hated this game for the first 2 hours, and absolutely loved it for (almost all of) the last 18 hours.
This game is a rarity in that it takes a beloved film and manages to transfer the reasons why people love the film into the game. It captures the coherent and consistent visual style of the film to create a grimy, utilitarian environment, and backs it up with a remarkable attention to detail and sound design that is not only reminiscent of the film but also utterly fantastic on its own merits. Then they took that audio-visual design and wrapped it around a stealth horror game with terrific set pieces, a badass protagonist, and an interconnected level design that really makes you feel like you're on a spaceship without resorting to making you go through the exact same locations multiple times without there being any differences or any reason to do so.
The design of this game is really quite impressive, and it puts me in mind of one of my favourite last-gen titles - the original Dead Space, one of only a handful of games to capture the same sense of space being a lonely and utterly terrifying place. But whereas Dead Space was an action game, as you had more of an ability to fight back against the threats you face, Alien: Isolation goes in the opposite direction. While so many games have succeeded in drawing inspiration from the Alien franchise to create great games, almost all of them end up being reminiscent not of Ridley Scott's Alien, but of James Cameron's AlienS, with its big guns and . Isolation set out to be an homage and side-story to the original film, the 1979 horror sci-fi classic, and they absolutely nailed it.
But the most important question regarding any game based on a film like Alien is this: is it scary? Does it capture the same intensity and atmosphere of dread that makes the film such a classic?
The short answer is: yes.
The long answer is: yes, absoHOLYGODTHEXENOMORPHISCOMINGHIDEINACUPBOARDHIDEHIDEHIDEHIDEOHCRAPOHCRAP.
Now let me elaborate on my opening line. When I started playing the game, I was immediately blown away by the audio-visual design, and intrigued by the premise of playing as Amanda Ripley. But before long, the game started to frustrate me with its level design and set pieces. Several of the early missions force you into a position where you are almost completely powerless, and are at the mercy of the pathing and environmental awareness of the enemies. This results in a lot of trial and error, which brings me to the biggest reason why I began to hate the game: the lack of a quick save.
In hindsight, forcing the player to save at certain demarcated areas on the map is a fantastic way to increase the tension of your encounters with the Xenomorph later in the game, and ends up being a positive, not a negative. But in the beginning, when you haven't even met the alien yet and you're just trying to trial-and-error your way through these rigid environments, having to restart because you got unlucky or made one mistake is incredibly frustrating. Quick save is included in games that require stealth and navigating the environment (Dishonored, for example), because it encourages trial and error by minimising the consequences of failure. In a horror game, quick saving makes the player a bit too powerful and in control of the situation, which is exactly the opposite of what you're trying to achieve. But in that case, the game shouldn't force you to play a stealth section with the same restrictions and disempowerment of a horror game when you haven't even encountered the thing you're supposed to be horrified of yet.
Just how fed up and frustrated was I with the obnoxious and infuriating early missions? Enough to actually uninstall the game and write it off as a total failure. Fortunately, I was encouraged by a friend to give it another try, and I'm glad I did, because once the game starts to hit its stride, it grabbed hold of me and didn't let go. In truth, my enthusiasm did begin to waver towards the end of the game, and I think the pacing becomes a bit onerous. They tried to maintain the same level of game-ending tension and excitement for a bit too long, and they pull the same trick of "thinking everything's finally okay, oh wait no its not it's still terrible aaahhh" a couple of times. This conditioned me to expect the unexpected, to predict another sting in the tail, to the point where I was actually a little surprised when I finally got to the credits.
So the short version of this review is this: in terms of capturing the essense of one of the truly iconic films, a seminal, archetypal masterpiece of sci-fi and horror cinema, and turning that magic into a videogame, Alien: Isolation is a massive success. As a videogame, divorced from that baggage and expectation, it might have been an all-time great if the game's introduction wasn't a big pile of wank and if they stuck a landing a bit better. But even with those faults it's a very good game, carried by incredible audio-visual design, well-designed levels and environments, and one of the most genuinely terrifying enemies in recent memory.
And it still weird me out that this game was made by Creative Assembly. I guess this is what all their talented staff was doing when they should have been testing and refining Rome II.

While Bastion did a lot with a little, Transistor does a lot with a lot, and this is like 80/20 good thing/bad thing. The worldbuilding is great and you get a good feel for the setting with the great combination of music and locale. Even Logan Cunningham's reprisal of An Iconic Voice helped, although it was maybe beating a dead horse a little bit. However, you can tell that these lovingly handcrafted areas took a toll on the designers: Transistor is really, really short. I beat it in 3 hours, and that was a pretty casual playthrough. Of course, there's NG+ and the limiters (similar to the Gods from Bastion), but it's still a great - albeit short - game. Is it worth $20? If you /really/ liked Bastion, sure. $15? Maybe, still a bit pricey for the length though. Definitely worth $10, though!

TL;DR: Tree of Savior isn't for everyone to play with as where it stands, Gameplay wise.
Overall its a game with potential to grow but with its current state and management, I wouldn't recommend it.
Hello, Just writing down a review for Tree of Savior.
Let's start off with Graphics and Music/Sound:
Graphics: 7
The game being 2.5D is quite uncommon from most MMO's. Characters models shows decent and distinct design from each class and to each gender. Though at most times you'll be finding yourself to be looking similar to other players for Tree of Savior doesn't go indepth into character customization.
Due to the character style and maps, this does give off the "RO" Nostalgia for most veteran MMO players.
Art for NPC's are good, it gives of a different feeling from just being another "Anime-esque art".
The environment and Map backgrounds are decent, they give off the right feel for each map for their theme.
Music: 9
BGM, Here is one of the good things from Tree of savior. The BGM for each map are different and gives out off the right vibes depending on the map and its theme. Boss Battle BGM makes you feel that you're fighting something extra ordinary, THOUGH this wil get repititive until later on for each boss fights.
Here but not the least: Gameplay, Community and Management, and oh also Replayability.
Gameplay: 7
The game starts of quite good to decent until you hit poor, rock bottom.
Tree of savior revolves MOSTLY around on auto-attacking. From each class, to swordsman, to cleric, to wizard, and archer based classes will be relying on auto attacking whenever their skill rotations are in cooldown or as such until they reach the cherry on getting their supposedly rank 6-7 classes.
Skills and Combat gets really stale for a while since Characters to Enemies, from mobs to Bosses will all likely be using/re-using the same skill animation and combat animation.
Progression in the game is very, linear the only spice that adds to it is that some quests are hidden from the quest log, in which A) You either consult a guide online or B) You spend the time exploring and talking to every NPC you'll be seeing in one map. Questing in the game can get REALLY STALE until the higher levels, in which some are riddled with RNG-based item fetching and etc..
Dungeons. The Dungeons in Tree of Savior are either your to go to for EXP at lower until high level grinding but as how it is the the entrance limit for such instances are limited to only 2 runs globally for all dungeons, and 3 runs for token users. Though I do not find any necessity to even limit such runs to a minimum to 2-3 runs daily globally tied to exactly just 2 tickets to use for once a day to a dungeon, which you wont be able to run others after.
Tree of savior possesses a number of different classes branching from their main class from Either, Swordsman, Cleric, Wizard or Archer, with a total of more than 80 classes.
Diversity for each class in a game is a plus to me as it divides classes into roles in a party.
This is a plus in my book, BUT at most times thanks to the META only a number of class builds and combos are gonna be significant for end game or PVP, in which making a number of class combinations irrelevant. Another thing, Diversity, like I've said just now; Diversity in roles but the issue is that each class branch either feels the same feel in regards to combat or skills, only difference are in terms of bonuses, weaponry used or gimmick.
The game's cash shop is quite empty as many would wonder but most of the part it doesnt have any pay-to-win niche items aside from the enhancement scroll that boosts RNG-based stats on a headgear accessory. Though one more thing, at early levels you might be bothered that some features are locked from the usual free to player, such as trading, storage being shared between your characters, limited amount of items listed on Market(Auction) and having an outstanding 30% tax from selling anything in the market. Not to mention taking money from the auction takes up to  48 hours.
Premium, aka Token is the answer to most of these locked features and limited slots but it doesnt reduce amount of days to take out the money from the auction/market but reduces the tax to 10% though!
I can't really complain much but this is quite a wall for someone starting from the ground up which maybe inconvenient for the new player in the early levels.
The good thing about Token(s) are they aren't exclusive to paying players only. They can be sold in the market by other players, but they cannot be traded amongst token users thru normal trading means. Even though Tokens can be sold in the market/auction, The Price for it stands near the point where you should already even invested where their price stands. Which would take you either to be around getting near Fedimian or already around level100+ to even afford one through silver means.
Although Tokens and auction/market are riddled with such walls, they did help combat RMT at some point of level but RMT/Bot users are getting smarter each day and are still eager even with the ban waves from IMC (Good Job IMC for being active in doing so!).
Community: ?
In terms of the game community, The game itself has a friendly bunch but at the same time there are hardcore white knights in terms of either light or heavy criticism; Ranging from the Developer's stand point of deciding things and from the game's core gameplay. But overall the game's players are friendly enought or either too quiet enough.
Oh for the love of all bad things, the game also has bots around.
Management: 6
IMC has been "transparent" and been working hard to serve the game to the international audience.
But with decisions made in the past in announcing Open Beta to be free from sometime ago into a sudden change of plans into deciding hosting an early access with a price tag of 50$.
With such action this suddenly took a great turn into dividing the playerbase, though in light of the majority of the community disliking the early access model. IMC had rather made tiers of purchase for it, In which the community has approved.
One more thing, the fight against RMT and Bots. IMC has stated the reason for having the early access was to combat such illegal activity but the community are divided into either thinking they're just doing this for PR or are actually honest about it. Though no deterrent really last that long if it wasn't really supervised or well made, as bots and RMT were rampant during the early access and with some exploits on the background but IMC has been doing quite well combating them.
Though at the current state of management IMC has really been sloppy with assisting the game's needs and stability. Which I hope be improved upon in the future.
Replayability:
Game gets really stale even for a grinding game. It doesn't offer much any feel of accomplishment or triumph. PVP is unbalanced for most of the part and it needs to be polished. PVE aspects as like I said it gets stale as it doesn't offer other gimmicks or necessities besides  stated above even with Guilds.
Conclusion, The game may not be for everyone to play on but it does have its own gimmick and perks. It also gives off the same Nostalgia from playing RO from long ago but it just doesn't feel the same way.
The state of the game and how it's being handled is quite so-so.
The game right now feels unfinished and still needs tending to.
Gameplay and  Management-wise, "Premium" aspect of the game feels like a necessity more than a "want". Overall its a game with potential to grow but with its current state and management, I wouldn't recommend it.
Well, That's pretty much it.. Thank you for your patience reading until down here.

Whenever I talk to people about rome 2 the immediate reaction is that rome 1 is more fun and more accurate than rome 2. It may not seem like a make or break thing in a game but the free for all defined rome, sure the javelinmen sucked♥♥♥♥♥and if your spearmen couldn't form a phalanx they sucked♥♥♥♥♥as well and all the barbarian infantry on an equal leg (without upgrades) would get beaten up by romans everyday of the week, furthermore the carthagianian mecernaries were underrepresented, the spanish suck many things as a faction and Spain at the time compromised of multiple tribes, armenian spearman are to pufta, macedon do not have the right symbol to represent them, the historical accuracy of what artillery pieces each faction had available are sketchy at best, unit details in general are misleading from being culturally inaccurate like seleucid archers are less likely to have resembled greek archers to german spearmen having a pike phalanx formation WTF???
On these many point I am therefore a greater fan of Rome 2 because Rome 2 allows you to fight battles with much more accurate unit compositions meaning the battles are more realistic, javelin units suddenly have a purpose and the tactics you can employ with them much more sophisticated this is no longer a swords vs archers vs cav vs large, tactical game it is way more expansive.
Campaiging has also been a touchy subject when I have discussed it but given that not many people buy all the expansions it can be hard to explain nonetheles wasting that amount of money just to make it a full game is criminally insane and certain people should experience ancient warfare without any safeguards or be sent back in time to appreciate why dividing the cost between the main game and so called expansions damages what the game is trying to achieve for the player, an immersive experience with a context of historical warfare that is far superior to Rome 1.
it is easy to point fingers that greece was not divided betwen sparta and athens and that in reality there were many city states but why would the total war team have added the greek states campaign. In reality it is impossible to include every singe faction in history into a grand campaign as the map and interface would become incredibly distorted not to mention the change in where settlements are, routes, roads etc. For instance for a armenian history buff where is tigrano? Nowhere is a good answer. That is why Rome 2 with everything packed in is a great game provided all the extras are stuffed in sure it still falls short of real history but hey everything does as we find ourselves increasingly finding holes in the past the further forward we go, its time people just learnt to improvise again (just not to a Rome 1 standard more sort of stop picking small holes and making them larger).
My only concerns are the lack of a free for all mode in multiplayer, the cost of the so called expansion packs which you need to make the game run and as always with Rome 2 the accuracy of siege engines available to all factions, but don't let that ruin the game it still feels more realistic than Rome 1 ever will.

Another masterfully implemented mod of the source engine, No More Room in Hell will give you a lot of fun.
The game uses a more realistical approach on the zombie survival genre while offering two game modes: survival and objective missions.
While the survival missions are quite simple, they are very enjoyable and fun, holding the zombies while you wait for extraction at wave 10.
The objective ones are more broad and offer variation within big maps, and while some are easier than others they are still a good adventure. Another fact is that such maps possess variation between rounds, so you will have another route of objectives to execute.
Most of the maps also contain secrets and special features.
You are not a superhero: you will bleed, you will be infected and you can also suicide yourself for the greater good of the group.
Overall review:
Pros:
- Free game.
- Extremely fun with friends (the more people you play, the better).
- Realistic gun mechanics and decent melee combat while keeping a good gameplay.
- Nice graphics (taking in account the fact that the game was made in 2011).
- Extremely well made animations of itens and weapons in first person.
- Very good optimization (very few bugs, and no performance issues at all).
- Good gun and attack sounds.
- Characters possess a varied soundbank of quick chat commands, giving you quick communication with your fellow survivors.
- The VOIP inside the game simulates real conversation, the far you are from another player, the lower is your voice (you can use an in game walkie talkie to communicate from afar without issues).
- Lots of maps with good level design.
- Two map types with lot of variation.
- Very good amount of guns and melee weapons (arround 20 firearms and a bow, and 20 melee weapons, there are also 3 throwable explosives).
- People still play this game to this day (so you will find people to play with you without a problem).
Cons:
- Few zombie models (you will kill the same zombies all over again).
- Some animations of ammo checking are wrong.
- Playing alone is difficult in most cases (not recommended to play alone, this is a cooperative game after all).
- Sometimes the zombie attack animation can be quite poor (depending on you position).
- The music is quite boring (my personal opinion, maybe you will like it).
While the game has minor flaws, it is a very enjoyable experience and will bring you and your friends lots of desperating moments and agony (the good kind of it).
A good adventure.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a linear gallery shooter, and in this case, that's all but a bad thing. Shooting galleries always evoke a bit of a Western vibe: Gunslinger takes that, rolls with it, revels in it, rubs it all over its skin, and lives on a diet of nothing but that for six months, and the result is wonderful in all manners of ways.
The aesthetics and storytelling are top-notch; every scene and setpiece looks straight out of a Wild West postcard, and the stories are right out of a dime novel (a term I also learned about through this game - there's actual history lessons in here, too!).
And the gameplay, as said, is the ultimate, perfected shooting gallery. Gunplay is quick and satisfying; shootouts are frantic but never run out of hand; and you have classic high noon duels to boot. There's an upgrade system, too, but it doesn't impact the game too much; I'd moreso say it acts as a motivator to make you wanna get those skillshots for larger point bonuses. Did I mention point bonuses yet? 'Cause if you like big numbers popping out of enemies after you shoot them the right way, this game is DEFINITELY for you.

Western themed first person shooter with a fun narrative. You are Silas Greaves recounting his life as a bounty hunter to patrons in a bar. As Silas drinks more, the story becomes malleable. He incorrectly remembers who he is fighting or gets sidetracked or embelishes the story which in turn affect gameplay mechanics. There are essentially two modes throughout the game, FPS and duel. The FPS is combo focused, racking up kills makes the multiplier go up, and from this you can gain more "concentration" which slows down time and can speed up your own movements. There is a light RPG element to the FPS/arcade mode. The duels rely upon you focusing on an enemy, getting your hand placement right, and reacting to your opponents pistol draw. The only downside is that is a pretty quick game and duels can be frustrating.  Good FPS with some humor that spans the mythos of the Old West makes this a pretty fun game.

If I had to review this game in one sentence, I'd review it as follows: "What you see is what you get."
Gameplay is just like in the video in the store, it's definitely a single dev indie game, so temper your expectation accordingly, but there's still plenty of playability to it.
Just a warning right off the bat; There is alot of item and user interface micromanagement such as equiping tools every time you want to gather resources and switching back for the occasional bit of combat, so that still needs some tweaking. On the plus side, resources aren't particularily generic like "wood" and instead there are five different groups of harvested tree material- leaves, bark, twigs, branches, and logs, all of which have multiple and different uses.
If you're still on the fence, go try the alpha. There's an old version available online that you can play in your browser. There are numerous differences between the web version and the Steam version, most notably smoother animations and slightly better graphics & interface. If you enjoy that version, you'll definitely enjoy the up to date version.
There's mod support and there's been two updates with significant tweaks and a couple new items since I got the game last Friday, so that's cool. I have high hopes for continued development and look forward to seeing the workshop become populated with mods.

A fantastic indie puzzle game that has you playing as a border control worker.  You're tasked with checking people's passports and documents against various rules and regulations that become more and more strict as the game progresses.  It's very atmospheric too, which doesn't really come across in the trailers.
My only problem with the game is that it can give you a headache, as you will have to look through and check a lot of forms - which has the same effect on you as doing so in real life would.  This means you'll probably struggle to play it for longer than one hour at a time.
The game is also kind of strict when it comes to saving your progress.  You progress through the game one day at a time, and it saves your progress after each day.  The problem is that when you fail the game, the mistake that caused the failure could have occurred at any point in the game, so you can't just start from the previous day and carry on.  This essentially means you'll have to restart from the beginning each time you mess up, which can become annoying when you're checking through forms you already checked on your first playthrough.
It's an excellent game though, and I'd reccomend picking it up if there is any money off.

I'm not going to lie to you... I have no idea why this game is so dang satisfying to me. I'm not the casual gameplayer type (not that there's anything wrong with that) but my consoles and PC are filled with AAA titles. I rarely play mobile games unless they connect to larger titles (See: Injustice 2, Assassin's Creed, etc.) but this one stuck out because it has the encouragement of a clicker without the clicking. I dig simulators and team-building games, mind you and that is what Soda Dungeon feels like. You go through and build up a team, you watch that team go through a Dungeon (You can set these fights on Auto, which just becomes entertaining to watch) and gather up the rewards to disperse further in your Tavern.
Honestly, it's simple and free and has given me some mindless entertainment in-between working, meetings or just winding down before bed. There ARE Microtransactions but they're also not a necessary evil. They make your fight easier if you don't want to spend thirty something hours on it -- but if you're okay with some grinding and tactics, it can work without needing them.
The art style is endearing because I grew up in a time where these kinds of graphics are what we had AND WE LIKED IT. (Garshdurnit) Extra dungeons like one for gear and one for farming gold and tokens make it so you actually have to put thought into team composition. Yes, there is a LOT for team composition in this game. While it does have a 'set-it-and-forget-it' feel -- that definitely isn't this game. There are times the game makes sure you're not just asleep at the wheel by giving you dungeon bosses that you MUST interact with and learn their fighting styles. To me, that's clever as hell.
So, is it worth a couple bucks? And more. It's free though and if you appreciate a title like this, chuck a couple bucks at these devs and get yourself some good pets or even some special fighters. They deserve it for the love they put into this game and I can't wait to see how they outdo themselves with Soda Dungeon 2.

Whenever I talk to people about rome 2 the immediate reaction is that rome 1 is more fun and more accurate than rome 2. Well agreed there is no free for all mode in Rome 2 which sucks majorly,  I mean what is the point of a 2v2 if you can't beat up your ally for being incompetent or backstabbing everyone around you. It may not seem like a make or break thing in a game but the free for all defined rome, sure the javelinmen sucked♥♥♥♥♥and if your spearmen couldn't form a phalanx they sucked♥♥♥♥♥as well and all the barbarian infantry on an equal leg (without upgrades) would get beaten up by romans everyday of the week, furthermore the carthagianian mecernaries were underrepresented, the spanish suck many things as a faction and Spain at the time compromised of multiple tribes, armenian spearman are to pufta, macedon do not have the right symbol to represent them, the historical accuracy of what artillery pieces each faction had available are sketchy at best, unit details in general are misleading from being culturally inaccurate like seleucid archers are less likely to have resembled greek archers to german spearmen having a pike phalanx formation WTF???
On these many point I am therefore a greater fan of Rome 2 because Rome 2 allows you to fight battles with much more accurate unit compositions meaning the battles are more realistic, javelin units suddenly have a purpose and the tactics you can employ with them much more sophisticated this is no longer a swords vs archers vs cav vs large, tactical game it is way more expansive.
Campaiging has also been a touchy subject when I have discussed it but given that not many people buy all the expansions it can be hard to explain nonetheles wasting that amount of money just to make it a full game is criminally insane and certain people should experience ancient warfare without any safeguards or be sent back in time to appreciate why dividing the cost between the main game and so called expansions damages what the game is trying to achieve for the player, an immersive experience with a context of historical warfare that is far superior to Rome 1.
it is easy to point fingers that greece was not divided betwen sparta and athens and that in reality there were many city states but why would the total war team have added the greek states campaign. In reality it is impossible to include every singe faction in history into a grand campaign as the map and interface would become incredibly distorted not to mention the change in where settlements are, routes, roads etc. For instance for a armenian history buff where is tigrano? Nowhere is a good answer. That is why Rome 2 with everything packed in is a great game provided all the extras are stuffed in sure it still falls short of real history but hey everything does as we find ourselves increasingly finding holes in the past the further forward we go, its time people just learnt to improvise again (just not to a Rome 1 standard more sort of stop picking small holes and making them larger).
My only concerns are the lack of a free for all mode in multiplayer, the cost of the so called expansion packs which you need to make the game run and as always with Rome 2 the accuracy of siege engines available to all factions, but don't let that ruin the game it still feels more realistic than Rome 1 ever will.

It has great and stylized visuals. This game really shows how, graphics-wise, less is more. The soundtrack is really good and the storytelling perspective is well done. Your character runs around and uses skills to kill stuff like any other adventure/rpg game. But that's the generic stuff. On to the interesting:
You have timestopping where you plan out moves, and then execute them [nearly] instantly before any enemies have time to react. The system is really well done and I absolutely adore it.
That being said, the precise implementation of this type of combat mechanic needs some work. Your skills are completely disabled while timestop is on cooldown. Your skills become usable again, both for timestop and regular time, after your timestop bar is full. Watch a trailer to see how timestop works.
When you use your timestop, you perform upwards of 8 moves on the scale of milliseconds (compared to normal time). Casting a single spell in normal time takes around half a second. When you run out of timestop, you are basically neutered for about 4 or 5 seconds where all you can do is run. There are some (very few) tactical decisions you can make in normal time, but I would almost argue that the real time aspect of combat is an illusion, and that it heavily heavily leans on turn based combat.
It's a splice between real time combat and turn based. But you HAVE to use a combat system where you plan and use your skills in a turn based fashion (Which is totally awesome). But then in regular time you just run around with your hands in your pants until timestop is available again.
This game gets so many congeniality points in my book that I would heartily recommend it. The mechanic introduced is so refreshing and engaging, but it definitely needs some work before it becomes the second coming of Jesus.

Presentation:
So I start the game up and are greated to some screen ajustments. I type it in and proced to the main screen. Here I can chose to do a fast game, or simply costemize a match.
I start a match as a NATO country, and NOTHING on the screen makes any sense. I tryed to press some buttons, but nothing happens, and the game has no toturial to tell me how to acually play the game. I find the next turn button and 5 minutes of the other contries turns go by. At this moment I was so bored from looking at the computer make it's moves, that I then did nearly nothing and said next turn and the 5 minut hell continued.
I was avare you could play as more than one country, but really if you let the computer do it`s thing, it will either win or lose you the match, so I chose small countries and did nearly nothing, yet won!
The game really needs a toturiel. I palyed like 10 hours of this game, and I still don`t know, what half of the buttons do. And trust me I tried to find out, but in many cases, the interfase is so bland and have no explenation to what anything dose. Bottom line, look up a toturiel if you want to enjoy this game to it`s fully.
Gameplay:
So the gameplay sounds simple, but again there is no explenation to tell me what i'm doing, why I win or lose a battles with my units and so on. Simply put You buy units and attack the oponents. If you win you take over some land. The one to have the most land after 100 turns, wins.
You can gang up on land units by surounding the tiles around the unit, yet sometimes the other unit still win. I figured it had something to do with the number under it, or the stars, but I attacked with the same amount of numbers and stars, yet still lost. It seems there is some RNG number rolling, but the game dose not show that.
You can also buy planes and boats, in order to cross rivers and seas, and make bombing of other enemy units. The plane stragey seems to be good, but There was a time where my planes got shot down, without any explanation.
Charecters:
So there are 2 factions to join. The Russians or the allied forces. From there you can pretty much chose any county as long as it is European, Russia or USA.
There are a few expetions whitch are the neural countries, but I never found out what they were doing in the game, other than just waste turns. I never palyed one of them, simply becouse they seemed to just be there, imprisoned by there own borders.
Whatever you do, chosse the russian team. It starts with a massive army, and wins pretty much every time, duo to the fact that USA have to sail over all there units. I played a couple of matches and Russia won every time, no matter what I did. This makes the game so boring, since you just have to wait, in order to win or lose.
Visuels:
The game looks like an old reboot of an older game, whitch I normally don`t complain about, but the graphics are really lazy on the map and units. You never really feel like you are in a great world or anyhing, it`s just a plain and boring map, with a lot of symbols of other players on it.
Music/Sound:
The main theme is acually ok, but the music in-game is downright terrible. It is full of anoying repitisians and loud noises. To top it all off you are never going to hear the music that well, since the sound effects to this game, are so loud and get`s repetetive fast!
The mash of bad music and soudeffects, made me turn off the sounds and find my own music. Luckely I listen to metal so it seemed more exiting, but the 5 minuts waiting every turn, really put me off. I must have listend to every single Iron Maiden song by the time I finished a match!
Story:
I don`t really know if this game is based on historical events, since I don`t know too much about history. I could imagen it is a aftermatch to the 2. World War, but I don`t really know.
The game has no story really, other than the fact that Russia Wins this war.
Conclution:
I did not enjoy this game. After the dreadfull start by not knowing what to do at all, I slowly learned how to buy, and deploy units and attack the enemy. But the russian army simply dose all the work for you, I was just running aorund the map, while the computer won for me.
The gamplay is really slow, if you don`t chose more than one county since the waiting and loading can take such a long time. I think I would have liked it better, if the gameplay was speed up in some way.
Overall I can`t really recorment this game, it is one of the most boring games I ever had to sit through and there are a ton of better strategy games out there, as a better alternative.
Now I am aware this is a early access game, so amybe a review like this will make the developer take out some of my cretices

Ok, so here's the rundown on this game. I absolutely hate overview mobas so smite has become my main moba that I play. I have over 1000 hours recorded since launch and about 400 hours of beta play time.
For those who dont believe
Pros:
* 3rd person action
* The lore is interesting and every gods ability is unique to their lore
* Multiple gamemodes, for those who do not only want to play the classic moba style gamemode
* The VGS commands is probably one of the best things ive ever seen in any game that does not use direct chat without another program.
* Overall its a really good game, yeah its hard to get used to but in time it gets easier
* For 30$ US (or 15$ on sale most of the time) you get every single god released and future god, thats incredible because if you think about it most other mobas require you to pay per each champion but have about 80+ champs.
* It is completely free to play with no pay to win. Yeah you may not have every god but you can unlock them pretty easily by just playing.
* You get free gems (in-game currecy) by signing in 7 days in a row and they do promotions that let you get around 150 gems, which is almost half a skin for doing a simple task. I dont know about you but free skins for simply playing a certain gamemode three times is nice.
Cons:
* So since release (I was a beta tester) the community has gotten pretty toxic. This is in both recreational players and pro players.
* Not many players still play because they cannot catch on to the gameplay, this could be avoided if players just dedicate themselves to learning,
* Ranked queues take forever, and some casual queues also. Mainly because not many play but even in release days queues were slow.
* HiRez uses the chest system, making it so that certain skins can only be obtained through chests. This is okay for special promotion skins and such but almost every skin gets thrown in the chest with 6-50 other random skins/voice packs/ward skins and so your chance to get a certain skin you want is lower than 50%.

If you're an Elder Scrolls fan and you don't have too much interest in MMOs, and you want to try this out purely because it is an Elder Scrolls game, this review is for you (if you're more of an MMO person, look elsewhere). I bought this for that same reason, and I don't want you making the same mistake, as I believe this game is not worth its asking price, for what it offers.
Review is PvE only, as I have no interest in PvP.
There's PLENTY of things that ESO does right. There's a massive world to explore. A ton of quests to do, with plenty of variety. The combat is okay. The game looks very pretty, especially the effects (fire, magic and so on). The writing is okay, not quite Skyrim level (and definitely not Oblivion or Morrowind level, but still okay). The community is good, lots of people willing to help. Unfortunately, there's also a few major issues that shatter what should be a great game into something that ends up being completely forgettable and dull.
The most important element in every Elder Scrolls game so far has undoubtedly been unparalleled world immersion. It is the primary reason why the previous games were so succesful. Understandably, this is easier to achieve in singleplayer games, because the world they present is explorable only by one player. When the player receives a quest, when he strolls through the streets of an ancient city, or is simply trying to get to the end of an exhilarating story, there is no one around to bother him. The world is free for him to explore at his own pace, without any intrusions from unwanted sources.
Multiplayer games however, have a much more difficult task of achieving good world immersion. And I'm sorry for saying this, but ESO is the best example of how everything in the game suffers because there is no world immersion. Every time you are on a quest (which like I said, should be exciting, judging by the writing and the variety), you are unable to take it seriously because there's always someone next to you, doing the exact same thing as you are, killing the same enemies, looking for the same piece of paper or trying to find the same NPC. I can only really remember one great quest where I truly felt immersed in the game world, and that was because there was no one around to break me out of it. But pretty much every quest I was on, there were people everywhere, either doing the same thing I was, or simply farming a boss for its loot.
This makes everything in ESO feel more like a chore than it should be. You do quests to level up or to complete areas, but not for the quests themselves. You might say that all MMOs are like this, but I disagree. Not every online game has quests that are so specifically designed for one player. A good example of this is Guild Wars 2. In that game, your personal story is completely detached from the rest of the experience, you do all of the important story content in your own personal instance. But when you do events and tasks in the open world, they're directed towards not just you, the player, but to every other player that happens to be in the vicinty. So when you do events with other people, it still fells immersive.
When I think about it, ESO is probably the least social MMO I've ever seen (except for the dungeons). I kept wishing there was a button to hide all players in the world so I could play this game completely by myself, without any intrusions. In terms of design, this is really more of a singleplayer game than a multiplayer game (since all of the quests are designed exclusively for your character). But for some reason, they decided to put it online and now it feels like everyone is playing their own singleplayer game in the same online world. There's honestly not many reasons why this game should be online, since I didn't see many exciting world events happening that would require multiple people to show up and do something together.
ESO tries to be both a good game for people who enjoy playing alone, and those who rather play with friends/guilds. But in doing so, it fails to be a good game for either side: the people who want to immerse themselves in the world/story can't do so because there's other people around, and because the quests represent such a large chunk of the game, I can't see too many reasons why an MMO enthusiast would want to play it with his guild (other than PvP, which might be great for all I know, but like I said, it doesn't interest me in the slightest).
This is not the only issue that this game has, but it's by far the biggest. The game also wants you to pay more money for it every step of the way, very "in your face" stuff. You can't select the imperial race in the character creator if you don't have the special edition of the game. You have to purchase guilds (What?!). Want a mount? Get ready to grind or pay some money. Even when you open the map, there's already four or five DLC locations on it that when you hover over them, they scream "Click to purchase this and unlock this and that and whatever". There's also crates (the same ones you see in every Online game ever), there's even a special section of the character menu devoted just to open these things. I don't know if you can get the keys for these crates to drop without paying for them, and frankly I don't even care. I would be able to look past all of this if the game was fun and exciting, but it's not so I have to point these things out. There's other things that bothered me too, but there's too many to write them all down.
Since this game is currently 30€, I can't recommend it. If you're an MMO fan and you're still reading this, go and play Guild Wars 2. It does pretty much everything this game does except it's better and more unique in every single department (and it's even free for you to try as long as you like). If you're an Elder Scrolls fan however, you have two options. You can buy this game when the price drops a little bit (or maybe one day it'll go free to play and play it then), but know that the only unique experience you're going to get is from the locations in the world you haven't seen before (you get to go to many different places - Auridon, High Rock, parts of Black Marsh and many many more). You'll probably enjoy visiting the locations you've only heard about so far, and learn a little bit about the era you're in. But that's really the only reason to play this. Option two, you can forget about this game completely (since it's really like a spinoff) and just wait for the next proper singleplayer entry in the series from Bethesda Game Studios and visit the unique locations then, when there will be a lot more detail and meaningful quests that extend the lore of the Elder Scrolls. It's up to you. It's quite possible you'll even enjoy the quests this game will present to you, but if you're used to Oblivion and Morrowind levels of quality, you will most likely be disappointed in the way this game handles its quests and worldbuilding (when you walk around and see that people are riding sparkling polar bears in outrageous attires while advertising their guild in the chat box, you'll probably begin to hate the world that is presented here, since none of it makes sense anymore and it's so far away from the compelling, interesting world that BGS created in the past 15 years).
I don't think this is a bad game, and I can see why people are having fun with it. But I also think that this is a few steps back for the franchise, and it's not what the Elder Scrolls should be. It should continue what it set out to do: revolutionise singleplayer fantasy games, with one of the most immersive and detailed worlds we have seen in videogames. It has done that successfully all the way until this game came out. But now, I'm starting to dislike the direction Bethesda (the publisher) has taken this franchise. Games like these have a right to exist, but not in this franchise and not when they are setting a lower quality standard for the future of said franchise.

I'll preface my reveiw this by saying that I am a seasoned Dark Souls player having completed the first on on NG+++. I give Dark Souls 2 a solid 7/10. Furthermore, I would recomend it to someone that has not even touched the previous Souls games.
I intently relished playing Dark Souls 1 and I enjoyed every minute of it. This marks the eighth time I have tried to get into Dark Souls 2. I just can not seem to be able to break through the "wall" like I could with Dark Souls 1. In my reasoning I will be comparing this game to its forebearer, Dark Souls 1, because first, Dark Souls 2 is a sequal and second, sequals should be judged by how much they improve upon the franchise.
My first concern about this game, in light of its predecesors, is the controls. Dark Souls 1 had tight and responsive feeling controls. While hard to get used to, I never actually fought the controlls. I would say that over 90% of my deaths in Dark Souls 2 were not due to actual combat, but simply fighting the regretably uncontrolable camera. The last time I played a game where the camera was this bad, it had a "64" somewhere in the title. I am not joking here....its unfortunate......highly unfortunate. Whereas the first game was responive, this one feels like your character is walking on ball bearings. I see what they were trying to do. They wanted to give the player a sense of momentum and force, which is admirable but ultimatly a flawed idea. It just clutters up combat and the feel of the gameplay.
My second concern is the design. Dark Souls 1 felt like it had more in common with an older RPG; in that there was no fast travel and if you could see it, you could go there. In Dark Souls 2 the developers sacrificed the first formula for a limited version of a fast-travel mechanic. It causes the world to have a less cohesive feeling and it stutters the gameplay. Next, the story and bosses are just a lazy redo of Dark Souls 1. Yes, the developers wanted to focus on another aspect of the Dark Souls universe, but there is no new material addressed. In Dark Souls 1, it felt like you already missed the party a long time ago, but are just expected to act like an insignificant janitor cleaning up the mess. I Dark Souls 2 it makes it clear that you are the party and all the boss monsters are invited to be shredded by yours truly. Finally, the pace of battle has been changed. This is primarily why I wouldn't recomend it to another Dark Souls player. If you have mastered the timing and rythm of combat in of Dark Souls 1; you will be lost in Dark Souls 2. Dark Souls 1 had fast-paced, well-timed combat that a begining player could begin to pick up on rather quickly. Dark Souls 2's change of pace to a slower tempo is crippling. Everything just feels sluggish and slower which leads me to my last concern.
The game runs like a beached whale. I am serious. Dark Souls 1 had its moments where my pc would begin to experince poor frame-rate such as the notorious Blighttown area. To be fair, I was playing on a laptop and I expected that. Now I have a top-of-the-line desktop tower built to take anything that I can throw at it. Dark Souls 2 consistently has cripplingly poor framerate issues. It honerstly feels like its processing an advanced lighting engine that is not there. Dark Souls 1 actually had better graphics and lighting that this game. It feels like perfomance was traded for some beautiful skyboxes and an excluded lighting mechanic. This game feels as though there are huge pieces that, for whatever reason, were just not included.
In short, If this was just more of Dark Souls 1, I would be aboard for the whole ride. This simply is neither an improvmet on nor just more Dark Souls 1. This actually feels like a step back from the perspective of a souls player.  Dark Souls 1 was a well-rouned, well stitched together, and tight felling game. Dark Souls 2 on the other hand, simply feels like it is blatently unfinished and I regret its controlls, design choices, and performance. This game had such potential and every once and awhile you can feel something better trying to happen within it. If this had been its own stand-alone game, not of the Dark Souls franchise, I would probably think better of it. On its own, its not a bad game by any means, but it has much to live up to and it does not come close to delivering.

The most stressful game I've ever played. This survival horror title is a faithful tribute to Ridley Scott's 1979 film; homages are plenty, and the art design is definitely reminiscent of the Nostromo. If you're a fan of Alien and the horror genre, this is a must buy - you MUST play in a dark room with headphones. The atmosphere is incredible.
Pros:
+ Excellent art design - the space station Sevastopol is incredibly detailed, right down to the way the walls are designed in each room - it's claustrophobic, gritty, dark and has that retro feel of the film.
+ The sound design - adding to the feeling of a living, breathing space station are the ambient sound effects. They are spot on, making you feel tense even when nothing is really happening. The individual sound effects for the various gadgets on the staton are direct homages to the film, right down to the terminals. The save station sound is particularly great, especially after several minutes of searching for one. But the show stealer is the alien - when it appears, its footsteps are terrifying - the constant "THOOM THOOM THOOM" as it searches for you is something I'll never forget.
+ Level design - the rooms that you'll explore all make sense, and are filled with nooks and crannies that help you avoid your enemies, but at the same time also makes you feel vulnerable - vents are all over the place, and the alien can and will drop down at random. Navigating through a single room is both super intense and satisfying.
Cons:
- Pacing - by far the biggest negative of the game is its pacing. The first half of the game feels great - it really builds and builds, with you starting off with no weapons at all and having to hide against all enemies, to getting a motion tracker so that you can more easily navigate around them, to getting weapons so that you can actually combat androids, to finally getting a flamethrower to scare the alien away. But after that, the game gets SUPER repetitive. It becomes a series of menial tasks that don't give the player any reward. For example, there are multiple points in the game where you'd be tasked with fixing something, only for it to ultimately not work and you are literally back at square one. This goes on for a tad bit too long - the game could easily have shaved off a good few missions that are nothing more than fetch quests. HOWEVER, the final few missions are phenomenal, and incredibly intense.
- Difficulty - I played on hard difficulty, which added to that feeling of intensity - save stations are harder and harder to get to. But I do think the game punishes you far too often, and the alien is RELENTLESS on that difficulty. A lot of the times, it's frustrating to play because you're trying to explore as much as you can, but the alien is present and does not allow you to. A great deal of patience is required to complete this game, and it's not always balanced.
All in all, Alien: Isolation is a great game. It's a stressful but ultimately rewarding experience that pulls the best from its source material.

I've got a decent amount of time put into the game so I think I can say thoroughly how I feel about it.
First off about the earlier version of the game I must have played it equally if not more hours than the steam 2.0 version; Wayward 2.0 is a huge leap in improvement over the earlier version, many bugs were fixed, art was improved, movement controls feel a lot more natural, and it has modding available which just opens the game to endless possibilities. I may even try making a simple mod or two.
For the price of $7.99 for what the game offers currently is a definite steal and it supports the team to work on it further down the road. They've already intended to continually add to it whether or not they make millions. They interact with the community through Twitch streams, and show what they intend on adding through their Wayward Trello.
Okay so with all that said maybe you are completely new to the game and haven't played the earlier version; this is a roguelike, you die and lose your world then you need to start a whole new one. It's a bit of a challenge for a new player, you will probably die the first night and perhaps again the second night, but that's okay! You'll learn from your deaths and continue to improve in survival until you get to the end game which is full of riches!
Pros:
-Can spend hours playing.
-Can save and resume whenever. (thank you turn base!)
-Each world is a new experience since it auto generates.
-Crafting, there are a ton of things to craft.
-I love that I can hotkey all my windows to one button to open and close my inventory, equipment,  crafting, milestones and skills all at once.
-The caves are extremely fun exploring, more so than the world above in my opinion. Having true darkness in a game that can only be illuminated by a torch is the best.
-Hand Drill is probably by far the best item in the game. This has to be the biggest pro of them all as this item has nearly no weight to it and provides so many fire starting.
Cons:
-Combat is simple yet not simple. You walk into creatures to attack the complexity of combat comes down to which weapons you have equiped. Although since the devs are continually adding to the game and modders will have a shot the combat could get really interesting.
-It's still early access so there's very few choice of mods and whatever small kinks are in the game are still being iron out, although any kinks there are get patched quickly or aren't noticed through normal gameplay.
-Early game at times can feel unfair only leaving you the option of running and hiding from creatures. This is mostly a personal peeve, the game needs danger of course.

This is a nice game, seems to offer a lot of depth on gameplay, the crafting system uses item "categories" for the recipes (eg: the "string" recipe requires 2 "cordage" items, so you might use two "spider silk" or one "spider silk" with one "seaweed" etc). it reminds me of the abandonware "Schiffbruch", another castaway game.
Pros:
- Good crafting system
- Proceduraly generated maps
- Replayability
- Novelty (ie: mixing rogue-like with turn-based tactics and survival. With a plus of not being another zombie survival game)
- Modable
Cons:
- Awful UI - Hotkeys (You can put itens on hotkeys, this is nice but the hotkey use will only apply the first "option" of the "actions" menu of that item. Ie: an axe has the options "Carve" and "Gather"; if you assign the axe to the hotkey 1, when you press 1 it will try to "Carve" with the axe, even if the target is not carveable)
- Micromanagement (All the time you will need to have your inventory open. Do you want to mine rocks ? Change your equiped itens on hand for a pickaxe; Do you want to cut down a tree ? Change your equiped items to an axe, is an enemy incoming? Change your equiped itens. )
- Awful UI - Itens action menu (The way the action menu is set on the itens, you are prone to missclick and do bad things. Ie: The "Glass Bottle with Seawater" actions are "1 - Drink", "2 - Pour"; you would not want to drink the saltwater for various reasons but pour it's water on a still to clean it. But unfortunately the option 1 apears right in front of the item as soon as you click, so chances are you will drink it)
- Almost no help (The only help you have is a simple tutorial quest to get you to make a campfire and water still, and a set of hint messages. Itens also have a standard description related to their main use, but many times it is not clear their function at all, nor does the game tells you that the purple number at the top of your interface increases as you skill up and get milestones and it affects the spawn rate)
Overall, it is a good game if you don't care that much to graphics nor to it's dificulty curve. If you don't like micromanagement and prefer action focused games, run away from it.

QuantZ isn't bad, and has some surprising plus points. Visually the game has aged remarkably well, slowdown on some transitions aside, and the audio is pleasant, if repetitive. In fact, 'pleasant but repetitve' sum this puzzle game up quite neatly. It has a decent amount of content for a puzzler, is easy to pick up and play, and has a fairly interesting premise. It just gets dull too swiftly.
The idea is to fling coloured balls down towards a cube that you can rotate at will - a match game with the twist that you can reposition the balls already in play by spinning the cube. This sounds good, and you can do some bizarre and wacky things with the physics, but in practice you're cracking a nut with a sledgehammer. The game was designed for a touchscreen, and it's difficult to finesse individual spheres about the place; mostly you'll resort to flailing the cube wildly and hoping that everything resettles in a more favourable configuration. There are other gimmicks to spice up gameplay, but the tried-and-tested formula is always present.
I spent a decent amount of time with the game, and found that although Action and Strategy modes both have twelve distinct worlds, they may as well be the same game mode. You'll very rarely run out of time or balls in the latter, so you can treat it in the same manner as you would the former. I blitzed through the Action section and had a decent time of it, but things got stale pretty sharpish. The Puzzle mode consists of preset playing fields with a very low number of balls to play with...you'll have to caress them with a delicate touch, and complete the eruptions in as few strokes as possible. Ahem. It was a welcome distraction, but ultimately when things got difficult (and some of the achievements are absolutely dastardly), I found myself wondering why I was still playing.

This is a good game, but it has too many problems for me to recomend it. First of all, there are online leader boards for this game that pops up when you're trying to play. The pop ups and having to log in are a mild annoyance, but the real problem with the online leaderboards is that they make it so you can't download any mods, because then you could cheat on the leader boards. This causes lots of probelms, besides the fact that you can't turn Rico into a charactor from My Little Pony. THe real probelm is the progression system, instead of getting xp for blowing stuff up or killing people, you need to get gears to get the upgrades. The problem with these gears are that to get them you need to play boring minigames. At the end of the minigame you are given a score that determnes how many gears you get. Unfortunately, the gears don't stack, so if you do a minigame and get 2 gears, then you play again and get 3 gears, you'll only have 3 gears to get upgrades with. Also, each minigame corresponds to a certian upgrade tree, so if you're bad at one of the minigames, you can't get any upgrades in that tree. Even worse, upgrades have to be earned in order, so you might have to unlock an upgrade you don't want before you can upgrade one that you do, even if the two upgrades are on differnet trees inside of the bigger tree. In conclusion, this game would be one of the best sandboxes ever if
1. You could go offline and download mods without the fear of being banned
2. The progression system was remade
OR
A sandbox mode where all weapons, vehicles, and upgrades were unlocked for you to play with.

I just wanted to preface this review by saying that. I devour all information I can find of this universe and I even follow two podcasts on the topic (if you haven't already, go check out Twin Humanities and Bonfireside Chat, they are both awesome)
Dark Souls is my favourite game of all time. It's the game I keep coming back to just to experience the combat, the world, the story and the characters. It is what made me buy a PS3 just so that I could experience more Souls in the shape of Demon's Souls. It also made Dark Souls 2 my first in terms of buying pre-order as well as buying a collectors edition (that statue is gorgeous) after what is nearly 30 years of gaming experience.
Dark Souls 2 is an amazing game, it really is. The art design is beautiful, the combat is super-tight as expected from the Souls series and it is a world that is both scary and interesting to explore. On the technical side it is also very polished for the PC (something Dark Souls can't brag about until you apply the mandatory DSFix mod).
I think it does a slightly better job at explaining some of the important core mechanics than Dark Souls did, but if you've never played a Souls game before you will probably still need some time to adjust to how these games play.
Hints and directions are subtle and you either pay attention or you learn the hard way, death is a natural part of the game so don't get discouraged by it. Also be careful with your weapons around NPCs, if you hit them you will make them agressive until you pay for your sins
or kill them, and that will make your playthrough a whole lot tougher.
If I can give but one tip to a new Souls player it would be to pay attention when you talk to NPCs, and you should keep talking to everyone until their dialog starts to repeat, and revisit them after you've made more progress to see if they have new information or sometimes even gear to spare.
My biggest gripe with the second part of the series is mostly a result of my expectations from countless hours in the first game. The vertical and connected world of Dark Souls is the best level design I've ever experienced in any game. Instead of running a "flat" linear path from start to finish, almost every area loops back with unlocked shortcuts or elevators (that move in a sensible way) to where you've been before. Dark Souls 2 is much more spread out in a sort of hub-and-spokes kind of way, almost like the discreete levels of Demon's Souls.
The bosses also feel a bit less imaginative than the previous game, but you will still experience the Souls'y jaw-dropping boss battles we've come to expect.
I love Dark Souls 2, but for me Dark Souls and Lordran is what I would call "home" and Drangleic is left as the occational vacation destination.

Game: Dark Souls II
Score: 8/10
Recommended? Yes, but not THIS version
Worth a buy at full price? No, buy Scholar of the First Sin, instead
WARNING: BUY SCHOLAR OF THE FIRST SIN, NOT THIS VERSION
The new version of this game came out that uses DX11 graphics is bundled with all of the DLC. Saves from this version of the game do NOT carry over. Do NOT buy this version unless you want to spend more money and waste time.
Now that that's out of the way, here's for the real review.
Dark Souls II, more challenging than the first, still is very enjoyable. The game still retains difficult enough combat to be considered a souls game, and if you've played the first game, you will for sure enjoy this one.
For those of you new to the series, I would recommend you pick up a copy of the first game while you wait for Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin to be released. It will be a good gauge of whether or not you will like this game, and it is only $20 instead of $40.
Gameplay wise, the game is much smoother. 60fps and 1080p is a HUGE improvement. Movement feels much more fluid and controls more responsive.
Creativity wise, the game is OKAY. It is not as bad as many claim it to be; that said I still think the first game holds much more value in creative boss/enemy design and lore, as far as the story goes. The majority of bosses in this game are some variant of "humanoid in armor," and with a friend, can be easily conquered.
There are many more weapons and armor in this game than in the first, which I also consider a nice touch. It's fun being able to swap looks whenever you decide to change things up.
In PVP/Coop, the game is somewhat unbalanced. Rather than basing matchmaking on soul level (the level of your character based on the attributes you choose to upgrade), the game bases matchmaking on soul MEMORY, the total number of souls collected. This makes for fights where your opponent may have much, much higher/lower stats than you, depending on how they spent their souls collected overtime.
That said, I haven't seen nearly as many hackers/cheaters/glitchers as in the first game. Many players have a finite amount of health and can be beaten if fought correctly.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game to others as a good entry in the souls series. However, for the love of all that is good in this world, DO NOT BUY THIS VERSION OF THE GAME. Go grab the remastered edition, Scholar of the First Sin, instead.

Game without crashes: Recommend
Game with progress preventing crashes (AI.exe stopped working) that never received a fix from the developers: Do not recommend.
You might get lucky and get to enjoy what looks like (and played like for 3 missions) a very polished and enjoyable horror experience- if not, you just threw your money in the bin, sorry to say.

Before we start: Beware of Spoilers (seriously, you've been warned)
Alien Isolation sets out to redeem the franchise after the trainwrecks which were "Aliens: Colonial Marines", "Prometheus" and "Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem" and does a very competent job at that.
The graphics are nice, the environments are very detailled and the art design is on point (every set reminds you of the movie). The most outstanding part is the sound design, in particular the music (with one or two exceptions near the end of the game where the intention was terror but the execution was irritation).
Central part of the game is the "Alien" or xenomorph and its hunt after the player. The part works nice (especially in the medical facility), switching between moving and hiding/avoiding your hunter keeps the adrenaline level high. However, as soon as you grasp the basic concent of avoiding the creature it goes from "Oh god, its hunting me again" to "Seriously, you came out of the vents again?". Once you obtain the flamethrower, the "Alien" is simply annoying because it interrupts your progress constantly with its erratic behaviour and its constant teleporting through the level. And it brings facehuggers later in the game. These pop up in the weirdest places and most times they kill you simply because you can't see where the buggers approach you.
The other enemies are humans with guns and very basic synthetics. The humans can't aim and the robots can be outrun by simple walking. The synths get a little upgrade later in the game (raincoats) which protects them from electrical damage but even that doesn't help much.
Storywise: Everybody who saw the "Aliens" movie will not take this game very seriously, simply because Amanda Ripley dies at a later date on earth.
That being said, the first part of the game is very nicely done, some minor plot twists (except, "Hurray, we killed the "Alien" in mission 5 out of 18 --> spoilers: no, you didn't) and the environments are very diverse.
Sadly, the second part of the game feels very stretched with some degree of backtracking (not as bad as Halo but bad enough to notice). Worst segment in this regard is the detour to the docking bay with 4 trips trough the same 3 rooms while the music gets more and more annoying each time a console is activated.
Once the game is finished there is practically no replay-value and the additional "Survivor"-mode is pretty lackluster.
It's a recommendation if you like the movies or get scared easily, if not you might still want to give it a look but you should probably wait for a sale. Don't buy the DLC, even if you are a completionist or fanatic for the franchise, its overpriced and offers only challenges for "Survivor".

If you're looking for a good stealth game, look no further. A few gimmicks, especially near the end, but for the most part there's no hand holding. Just you and your wits against everything trying to kill you.

Factorio is addictive. As I have stated, I have really only scratched the surface of the game. I have really tried hard to avoid looking up any tutorials or YouTube clips and so far have stuck to that fairly well. I want to figure this stuff out myself. So, that said, I am still on the second or third level of the campaign - something but probably should only take about half an hour (? no idea - never compared to anything) but I am easily up to 10+hours just on that alone (and I now think I need to start again!)
The game will do your head in but in a good way. There is something very rewarding about nutting out a manufacturing chain that works. Watching all your bits humm along and progress is made.
The tutorial is ok, it gives you enough but it's not a lot. Kinda like saying, "Did you know nuclear power is very complicated. Now, here's some uranium and some bricks, off you go then!" That said, it worked.
The campaign ramps things up significantly and seems to act as a more advanced tutorial. BUt this ain't baby steps, more like giant leaps. BUt it has worked and I am loving the challnege.
When I couldn't figure out one thing, I looked at some YouTube clips and saw technologies and features WAAAAAAAY beyond what I am up to - and I already feel barely in control.
The crafting system is pretty easy and unlike other crafting based games, you don't need to use time wasting trial and error to discover recipes. They are all there which makes things so much easier. Want to build an "x"? Hover over the icon and it will tell you it needs some "a's" and "b's" to make it. It gets tricky when the "a's" need "c's" and "d's" to be built and thus, the complexity and mind breaking begins.
You will love this game if you like exploratory, survival, crafting games that really make you think. As I said in my intro, I won't ever be an expert a tthe game but I am loving the almost perfect learning curve - it's hard but not alienating. I'm NEVER bored. It's not treating me like a baby with breadcrumbs through every possible action. Let's be honest, there is a lot this game does not tell you, but it's not impossible for a regular Joe like me to nut it out...eventually.
Can't wait to see where this game goes....scared to see where this game goes given what it has already!

I highly recommend this game, and I think it's one of the few single player ego shooters that have really managed to stand out of it's category in the last few years.
The story is set in the year 1910 in the late years of the wild west, where the sixty years old bounty hunter Suarez meets a few of his fans in a bar and tells them about his greatest adventures. You play through these adventures while Suarez narrates in the background, often while having arguements with the people around him. The funny thing is that that the memory of Suarez isn't as good as it used to be, so the mistakes he makes while telling the story affect the gameplay while you are in it.
For instance, one time he was fighting a gang of criminals called "the cowboys", but when he says "Suddenly the apaches were all around me, and they started attacking me from their higher ground", one of his fans will say "Apaches? Weren't you fighting the Cowboys?", to what Suarez responds: "Did I say Apaches? Oh, I meant to say the Cowboys were attacking me like apaches!" and all of sudden the apaches around you turn into even more aggressive cowboys.
The story itself ends with a satisfying finale, and all cutscenes are handdrawn single frames to thicken out the western atmosphere.
Pros:
-Awesome gameplay, you use western-typical weaponary to defeat hundreds of evil foes that are in your path
-Concentration mode brings Max Payne-elements into an ego shooter
-Cool story with funny humour
-Skill System, you earn XP by killing enemies and chaining combos.
-Rare connection with story and gameplay
-You can collect "nuggets", which are bits of information about the real wild west
-You meet tons of important characters of that time, Billy the Kid, Pat Garret, etc
-Graphics create a good wild west atmosphere
-Voice acting is very good, only english though
-Arcade mode can entertain for a long time, has one duel-mode and a shoot em up-mode
-Very good boss-battles, some of them can actually be surprisingly hard
Cons:
-Could have used more weapons, there are only 8 different weapons in the game, and that's only if you count dynamite and the sawn off rifle that you'll rarely ever use.
-Shotguns are pretty much useless, since they can only fire 2 shots before reloading, and most of your enemies will be at middle to far distances
-Main story is finished after a max of 5 hours, (note that the game is only 15 bugs which makes up for that)
-The dueling minigame sometimes is just not working like it should
-You'll quickly have seen all types of enemies (Revolver-bad guy, Rife-bad guy, bigger Shotgun-Bad guy and Door-bad Guy)
-The shoot em up of the arcade mode should have let you use all of your skills, or atleast given you the oppurtinity to learn all of your skills.
-An endless mode should have been added since all shot em up-missions are done in under a few minutes

This title has been in active developement for some time now, and it definately shows. First-and-foremost, what is most notable about
that sets it apart from other similiar titles is that it is turn-based.
Sound familiar? Sure. While
seems to share similiar characteristics with other clones - it is truly exceptional. What really makes this title stand out is an excellent user-interface, a truly deep crafting system, and steep-yet-fair difficulty which combine to create a really addicting experience.
With that being said, this isn't
- it has a personality all of its own. I would highly recommend trying the free version - get past the moderate learning curve and then the addiction begins :)
+Everything is fairly logical. With each death you will have an 'aha' moment, where you will almost immediately know how to correct your actions on your next run. This really makes an addicting experience.
+The user interface is really easy to use and makes a complex system fairly intuitive.
+Tons of items and crafting recipes that make sense.
+Tutorial is a warm welcome from the web version.
+Graphics are well done and fitting.
+The moderate-to-steep difficulty is great, and keeps you coming back for more.
+Super cheap asking price for the quality hours you can get out.
-Sometimes I get stuck with trying to figure out a simple crafting recipe. Perhaps a recipe list has been added in-game since the Steam launch, but I haven't found it yet. I usually just alt+tab to the Wiki, but this can be tedious at times. Once you learn the recipes, this is not a big deal.
-Just be aware this is a much slower paced game than others in this genre. Not necessarily a 'con' per se, but be aware.
-Sometimes movement can feel janky - ie. accidentally walking into a fire pit or bumping into trees and gathering stuff you don't want to.
This stands far ahead of the others. I totally recommend this game.

TL;DR: Glorious art. Game is far from perfect, but dev team is on it. Play now if you played RO and aren't fussy.
10/10 for Art, Style and Concept
4/10 for Implementation and Gameplay**
(However - dev team and community managers have stepped up their game a little, and have become more proactive in keeping the player base updated. It will get better. How much better? I have no idea.)
I play this because:
1) I played RO, and *love* the visuals.
2) I'm not affected by most of the bugs/problems that others face. Some inconveniences yes, but that's about it.
But for others...? Take your chances if you wish.
Other thoughts:
- There's no "end game" content - game is planned to have 600 levels, and we have content up to 280 or so. There's no indication of when the next major release will be, and how far it will go. Some players and guilds have experienced burn out, so try and pace yourself. :)
- Manage your expectations if you're gonna play - the forums have people talking about quitting and what not, boohooing about the game not having this/that. Too melodramatic, IMO. But there's some fair points in what they say.
- I will recommend this game once they improve the game balance, start regularly implementing the fixes that have been done for Korean TOS, and do something about quality of life. (Like increasing movement speed, adding warp points and allowing characters to do more stuff while queuing for dungeons. The list goes on.)
