Transistor lives up to the expectations set by Bastion. Super Giant Games are proving themselves to be a top notch indie studio even though they've only released two games.
The set up stands that you are Red, a popular controversial singer in the Utopian Cloudbank city where literally everyone has a voice. Heck, they vote on what color their sky is. You awake to find the Transistor a sudo cybernetic buster sword that provides company to Red on her journey across the vast city as they try to unveil mysterious disappearances and the invasion of hive mind bots called The Process.
The game is gorgeous that it's sensual art style will leave you entranced accompanied by the games masterful soundtrack. Gameplay wise, things can be turn-based by pausing at intervals to plan your strategy of attack or you can go out in real time combat, why not do both? The leveling system depends on RPG elements to combine and upgrade your attacks by stacking abilities to preform on certain play styles or enemy types. Let me say that the amount of customization for your abilities is staggering that you'll be experimenting through out your playthrough.
The story I don't want to spoil since there are true moments of good story telling elements, that also combine with gameplay. It's a bit like Bastion, in fact if you look close how the game was designed you wouldn't be mistaken for thinking Transistor was Bastion's spiritual successor. That's just a big plus cause your in for about 12 hours of gameplay depending if you do challenges and turn on difficulties enhancements.
In all honesty the game is phenomenal for its presentation and story that you'll be sure to visit again and have the soundtrack playing your head for a experience that triple A games can seem to always muster. Yes.

Transistor is Beautiful. As soon as you start up the game you play it. There are no Difficulty selections to pick, you simply start the game. The graphics are stunning showing that a game doesn't need to be 3D with crazy graphic engines. The music for Transistor also makes this game feel more emotional, drawing you in with it's great selection. The combat is wonderful. You can both normally use attacks that you have equiped, or plan out your move in a paused turn selection. The selection of moves will benifit you in combat overall. I would recommend this game as it is absolutely Beautiful.

Overall, Transistor is a great game worth recommending, with only one draw back.
The combat system is both fantastic and refreshing, as the wonderful offspring of action and turn based strategy. It allows for a great amount of customization, strategy, and challenge as you unlock more and more skills, and the ability to combine them. The graphics and music are absolutely gorgeous, much like Bastion. And don't get me started on the great voice acting. These things alone make the game worth a play through.
However, where the story is concerned, it falls flat. At first, I just thought that Transistor was slow to develop, similar to Bastion. Bastion took an hour or so to really begin. Unfortunately, this is not the case with Transistor. You randomly wake up, find out that you have a talking sword and you are chasing after some mysterious organization, who may or may not be evil, called "The Camerata". Oh, and you have to kill an enemy, that vaguely reminds you of The Matrix, called "The Process" along the way.
Now, this would be a great point to start developing a storyline about propaganda, conspiracy theories, maybe a love story... and they touch on all of these, but they never really develop anything. They give you a couple one liners, maybe a monologue that's meant to be deep and profound, yet they really don't explain that much. You're left with a general sense of what happened, a couple of unanswered questions and nothing more.
I feel if they had spent less time being vague in an attempt to be mysterious and deep, and more time developing both the characters and story, not only would the story have been longer than five hours of gameplay, but it would have been much more satisfying and worth replaying.
The combat and aesthetics of Transistor really make it worth playing, but realize that the story is only about five hours long and pretty vague.

The pop ups and having to log in are a mild annoyance, but the real problem with the online leaderboards is that they make it so you can't download any mods, because then you could cheat on the leader boards. This causes lots of probelms, besides the fact that you can't turn Rico into a charactor from My Little Pony. THe real probelm is the progression system, instead of getting xp for blowing stuff up or killing people, you need to get gears to get the upgrades. The problem with these gears are that to get them you need to play boring minigames. At the end of the minigame you are given a score that determnes how many gears you get. Unfortunately, the gears don't stack, so if you do a minigame and get 2 gears, then you play again and get 3 gears, you'll only have 3 gears to get upgrades with. Also, each minigame corresponds to a certian upgrade tree, so if you're bad at one of the minigames, you can't get any upgrades in that tree. Even worse, upgrades have to be earned in order, so you might have to unlock an upgrade you don't want before you can upgrade one that you do, even if the two upgrades are on differnet trees inside of the bigger tree. In conclusion, this game would be one of the best sandboxes ever if
1. You could go offline and download mods without the fear of being banned
2. The progression system was remade
OR
A sandbox mode where all weapons, vehicles, and upgrades were unlocked for you to play with.

I wanted to like Alien Isolation, but the game is just riddled with bad choices that shouldn’t have made it past the first Beta test let alone still be in the game more than two years after release.  Consequently the game is just tedious and frustrating.
-There are way too many items to use and the selection system is clunky, even worse accessing it doesn’t even slow down combat, so you end up awkwardly scrabbling around trying to select items while getting beaten to death by androids.
-The making items out of junk is cute, but in reality it just adds a tedious level of micromanaging.  We should just find these items readymade.
-The map doesn’t make it clear where there are entrances and exits.  The map objective icon also shows up on multiple levels, which does nothing but create confusion!
-The Alien isn’t fun to play against.  It’s always around, a lot faster, finds you easily and kills you instantly.  Hiding in cupboards all of the time and sneaking throughout the entire game isn’t fun!  And there was nowhere the alien couldn’t get you, so when I saw the alien I didn’t panic knowing I’d have to run for my life, I just  resigned myself for another insta death and the tedium of replaying the level.
-The saving system is annoying.  Being forced to save at specific places is just irritating.  The game should just auto save periodically or once you reach objectives.  For me getting to the next save felt good simply because (on this level) I will never again have to repeat the tedious task of hiding in a box for ten minutes so I can gather all the bits of junk from the rooms (for the nth time!) before inexplicably receiving a insta-death.

Game without crashes: Recommend
Game with progress preventing crashes (AI.exe stopped working) that never received a fix from the developers: Do not recommend.
You might get lucky and get to enjoy what looks like (and played like for 3 missions) a very polished and enjoyable horror experience- if not, you just threw your money in the bin, sorry to say.

Before we start: Beware of Spoilers (seriously, you've been warned)
Alien Isolation sets out to redeem the franchise after the trainwrecks which were "Aliens: Colonial Marines", "Prometheus" and "Aliens vs. Predator: Requiem" and does a very competent job at that.
The graphics are nice, the environments are very detailled and the art design is on point (every set reminds you of the movie). The most outstanding part is the sound design, in particular the music (with one or two exceptions near the end of the game where the intention was terror but the execution was irritation).
Central part of the game is the "Alien" or xenomorph and its hunt after the player. The part works nice (especially in the medical facility), switching between moving and hiding/avoiding your hunter keeps the adrenaline level high. However, as soon as you grasp the basic concent of avoiding the creature it goes from "Oh god, its hunting me again" to "Seriously, you came out of the vents again?". Once you obtain the flamethrower, the "Alien" is simply annoying because it interrupts your progress constantly with its erratic behaviour and its constant teleporting through the level. And it brings facehuggers later in the game. These pop up in the weirdest places and most times they kill you simply because you can't see where the buggers approach you.
The other enemies are humans with guns and very basic synthetics. The humans can't aim and the robots can be outrun by simple walking. The synths get a little upgrade later in the game (raincoats) which protects them from electrical damage but even that doesn't help much.
Storywise: Everybody who saw the "Aliens" movie will not take this game very seriously, simply because Amanda Ripley dies at a later date on earth.
That being said, the first part of the game is very nicely done, some minor plot twists (except, "Hurray, we killed the "Alien" in mission 5 out of 18 --> spoilers: no, you didn't) and the environments are very diverse.
Sadly, the second part of the game feels very stretched with some degree of backtracking (not as bad as Halo but bad enough to notice). Worst segment in this regard is the detour to the docking bay with 4 trips trough the same 3 rooms while the music gets more and more annoying each time a console is activated.
Once the game is finished there is practically no replay-value and the additional "Survivor"-mode is pretty lackluster.
It's a recommendation if you like the movies or get scared easily, if not you might still want to give it a look but you should probably wait for a sale. Don't buy the DLC, even if you are a completionist or fanatic for the franchise, its overpriced and offers only challenges for "Survivor".

I've been watching this game for awhile. I played the free betas before the Steam release quite a lot. So what can I tell you about Wayward? Well, it's a turn-based island survival game. There's a lot of crafting, there's a lot to discover, and there's a hell of a lot of danger. This game does not hold your hand.
The crafting system is surprisingly pretty easy to use. You make discoveries through crafting basic things that guide you towards what resources you will need and what you will want to consider crafting yet. The hints that pop up give you a bit of insight, but it leaves most of the hard work up to you.
Survival is hard. It's easy to starve, it's easy to become dehydrated, it's easy to become overtired or overencumbered, and it's sure as hell easy to run into an enemy that you weren't ready to face. The first little while you play the game will consist of you figuring out the basics. If you're turned on by games that force you to die a ton before you can actually get anywhere, this game won't be for you.
All that being said, the game is crazy charming. The graphics are very simple and cute. The sound effects are very basic, but certainly not bad at all. There isn't a whole lot of animation, but somehow the game doesn't need it. The music is actually fantastic. It coats the game in an atmosphere the seems to flesh out the game world in a way that it wouldn't be otherwise. It almost reminds me of the Donkey Kong Country 2 OST or something.
It's a great little survival game that's always growing. It's hard as hell, but it's harder not to love it. Not only that, it's pretty darn cheap. A very easy recommendation for me.

(Pay no attention to the playtime above, I've played the non-Steam betas of this game for at least 40+ hours in total.)
Wayward is an island survival roguelike, with heavy emphasis on the survival part. (For those of you who like ancient obscure freeware, it's basically the game Schiffbruch but with many more features and a lot more to discover.) It's the kind of game where you can die within the first five minutes, or do awesomely for an hour and then die to some silly mistake. Easily frustrated people be warned-- this game will kick your butt!
If you can get past that, however, Wayward is a game that can be strangely peaceful, punctuated with moments of intense drama. You've finally finished building a little shelter of wooden walls and you got a campfire started...but oh no! There's a zombie at your doorstep. Do you hurriedly craft a snare, or run out the back of your shelter and hope to lose it in the nearby woods?
You got a ton of awesome loot in the cave, but a pirate ghost is suddenly chasing after you!
Oh no, you forgot to get a second glass bottle or flask before constructing your water desalinator-- how are you going to carry water from the ocean to distill??
You forgot to repair your axe, and now you have to dig stone with your bare hands! It's okay though, you have 50% in mining...
What's great is that even when you inevitably screw up and die, there's always something to be learned. Fight spiders and snakes before taking on a shark. Supplement your health with berries and sutures while you're hurriedly running around trying to find freshwater to save yourself from dehydration. Don't walk into the campfire because it REALLY hurts. It's a game that appears simple on the surface, but is actually complex and has quite a bit to discover.
The best part is, there are many paths to success. You can become a burly tough guy and beat up all the monsters. You can build a small farm and create your own pixely homestead. You can be an explorer and hunt after that sweet, sweet ectoplasm to enchant your armor. You can build a raft and explore the seas, collecting treasure and fighting krakens.
Or you can just die a bunch. That will probably happen too. As with many roguelikes, this game needs to be approached with a good sense of humor and a bit of an inner masochist. I recommend watching streams, or playing with friends if it gets frustrating-- it's hard not to laugh when you build an awesome cabin in the woods, only to have a fire elemental burn it all down. Sometimes you accidentally drink the unpurified water, and you get poisoned. And sometimes you just can't hit that rat, no matter how many times you try....
I've been following Wayward's development since at least 1.5, and it's wonderful to see how far it's come! The graphics are even more beautiful, in all their pixely glory, the 80bit music is still adventurous and lends an aura of wonder and imagination, and the gameplay is better streamlined.
My main complaints are mostly cosmetic-- for example, the font size is a bit small still, and the various game windows you have to navigate can, at times, be overwhelming or feel cluttered, especially if you're new to the game. And I do unfortunately still have some lag, even though i'm using a newer computer than i had the last time i played the 1.9.2 pre-Steam release (it appears to have something to do with how much weight i'm carrying? I'm confused). But all of these issues are to be expected in a beta and can be ironed out easily.
IMO, the biggest and most promising new feature in this release is the Steam Workshop support! The possibilities for this game are now endless. Even before this release, there were quite a few nice mods on the Unlok forums. It will only get better!
Please, grab this game while it's on sale! 7 bucks is a steal, and if you don't like it at first, you can come back to it tomorrow, or in a week, because every game is a little different.

Super Giant took what made Bastion such an amazing title and refined it even further to create Transistor, and understandably you can only go up from there.
To me, Transistor feels like a spiritual successor of Bastion. The tropes, themes, and presentation of the game play as well as the narrative are all very familiar. It's as if this is a retelling of Bastion in some sort of permutation in a cyberpunk parallel universe.  At times, it feels very intentional. This being said, the dramatic art style and soundtrack are very unique and moving.
The mechanics of how you outfit yourself, as well as the tactics that will play into it, afford an incredible amount of flexibility to how you'll approach what you're up against. I can see a lot of replayability coming out of this title because of that, although there will likely be a way to do it all again in an even more engaging manner if Super Giant is following the template that I believe they are.
All in all, Transistor is well worth it's full price. Fans of Bastion will likely feel right at home, like finding a broken in tshirt that still fits really well despite having been misplaced in the closet for 6 months.  I'm looking forward to what will be coming out of Super Giant next, and to see if they will continue to morph the themes from their two recent games.

Coming from the dudes who made Bastion it looks and sounds very good but beneath that is a pretty indepth combat system aswell.
Bastion was abit simple, you found different weapons and could dual wield them. This time around you get 4 active slots for skills and each of these skills can have up to two other skills attached to it to alter or boost its effects and you also have passive slots. Theres no designated passive or support skills, each skill can fit in any slot.
For example the basic attack can just be the basic attack - or you could take it out of the active slot and attach it to another skill which then gains a stun attribute or the like. In the passive slot it provides damage resistance. Theres about 12 different skills and its really quite fun to experiment around with what combinations do what, you can make your own "builds" so to speak.
Another thing is two combat modes, Real Time and "Turn" (Matrix i guess). In Real time you run around in real time. Turn mode stops time and you can plan your movement and skill use within a fixed budget (altho that can be altered with certain skills in a passive slot) which then gets executed lighting fast. The catch is Turn mode has a cooldown during which you cant use any skills in realtime either (generally).
Its somewhat linear, theres a new game plus but i guess the replay value depends on how much you would be willing to shake up a tried and true combination :P

Transistor has beautiful visuals, wonderful voice acting, two very worthwhile characters and a story to tell with them that, in my opinion, is well worth experiencing. On its own, I feel it holds water, but mileage may vary as personal taste dictates.
The gameplay itself is initially simple and straight forward, but the manner in which you can augment abilities, with other abilities, and then use multiple augmented abilities together to devastating effect, is a 'easy to learn, fun to master' affair that should be taken note of.
There is a timestop mechanic of sorts, more akin to super speed or bullet time, than a turn based pause function, that further enhances your combat options. Intelligent use of this function can turn a drawn out encounter into a graceful and elegant cascade of quick decisive moves that end the battle in a matter of seconds.
It is short, but it does have a mixed up newgame+ function, with enemies scaled up. You'll likely have to replay the game in this harder mode to see all the tests and play with the late level ability combinations. This is not a bad thing, the encounters in newgame plus aren't simple scaled up, you'll encounter new mixtures of enemies, not just harder enemies.
In short, it's good. Buy it. Play it. Do it.

Updated for Alpha 16: (I changed it from not recommended to recommended)
This review is for version Alpha 14. The devs do seem to be working on it regularly so take what I am about to say with a grain of salt. I will update the review as items improve.
Lots of ups and downs with this game. I have a fair amount of time into it so I think I can pen a decent review. First this really is a fun and immersive game. It is not for the faint of heart. It is not for anyone with less than 'good' to 'better' computer specs. My computer would be considered in the 'epic' (4.5Ghz, 32GB RAM, 290X, 6 Drive cached RAID, Liquid cooled) and STILL freezes briefly for draw distance related loading.
I purchased 4 copies of this game. 3 for friends - only 1 can actually play. The other 2 unfortunately stand in the game frozen more than 80% of the time. They have laptops and the game even on the minimum settings is hopeless for them.
For those who can play it such as myself this game is good. It is a survival game similar to Rust with Minecraft'ish building mechanics and 100% looting of anything you see or kill with few limits. They have a 'crest' system that allows you to have at least some minor protection of your buildings. The problem is people can 'glitch' through ceilings and doors. This has caused almost all buildings built to be built floating in the air to avoid entry. The game does support creation of traps that can make intruders think twice if you plan your structure well. Another issue is if you don't quickly build a good structure with a bed and a crest so you can logout there is a 90% chance someone will come along while you are gone - kill you and destroy your entire structure. This is an alpha and there is an unfortunate bug where if your client crashes during a logout there is about a 20% chance you will lose all the items you are carrying. Make sure you DON"T ALT-F4 to close the client, let it close on it's own even if it takes 30 seconds and seems frozen. I lost everything twice due to this issue.
All that said the game is certainly rewarding. Battles are fun, building is fun and planning your structures to avoid intrusions or punish them for that matter is also fun. The current issues though cause me to lean towards not recommending this game until more of these large problems are fixed. They ARE working on it and evidenced by the number of patches since the initial release and the large number of changes each one includes. My suggestion would be if you play this plan to begin by playing your initial session long enough to build your base along the lines I described above all the way. Perhaps 3-4 hours play time. I read a lot about the hackers but really haven't seen much in that area, it's mostly people who glitch into your base and destroy it oriented things rather than hackers outright making themselves invincible though I have heard of that happening on occasion too.
PROS
Fun fighting and battles
Fight and possibly become the king - even tax the populace
Lots of items you can create
Anything you see you can kill/lloot 100%
CONS
Large performance issues for those with slow PC's even on minimum settings (A16 improves this somewhat)
Very difficult to find your friends - No Compass, No in-game MAP, No Coordinate System what-so-ever... Terrible.  (Issue Persists)
Game start is hard because if you log out without a base 90% chance you will be dead when you log back in (this is better somewhat in A16)
If the client crashes  there is a chance when you log back in you will lose all items. (This seems to be fixed, hasn't happened to me again)

Game: Dark Souls II
Score: 8/10
Recommended? Yes, but not THIS version
Worth a buy at full price? No, buy Scholar of the First Sin, instead
WARNING: BUY SCHOLAR OF THE FIRST SIN, NOT THIS VERSION
The new version of this game came out that uses DX11 graphics is bundled with all of the DLC. Saves from this version of the game do NOT carry over. Do NOT buy this version unless you want to spend more money and waste time.
Now that that's out of the way, here's for the real review.
Dark Souls II, more challenging than the first, still is very enjoyable. The game still retains difficult enough combat to be considered a souls game, and if you've played the first game, you will for sure enjoy this one.
For those of you new to the series, I would recommend you pick up a copy of the first game while you wait for Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin to be released. It will be a good gauge of whether or not you will like this game, and it is only $20 instead of $40.
Gameplay wise, the game is much smoother. 60fps and 1080p is a HUGE improvement. Movement feels much more fluid and controls more responsive.
Creativity wise, the game is OKAY. It is not as bad as many claim it to be; that said I still think the first game holds much more value in creative boss/enemy design and lore, as far as the story goes. The majority of bosses in this game are some variant of "humanoid in armor," and with a friend, can be easily conquered.
There are many more weapons and armor in this game than in the first, which I also consider a nice touch. It's fun being able to swap looks whenever you decide to change things up.
In PVP/Coop, the game is somewhat unbalanced. Rather than basing matchmaking on soul level (the level of your character based on the attributes you choose to upgrade), the game bases matchmaking on soul MEMORY, the total number of souls collected. This makes for fights where your opponent may have much, much higher/lower stats than you, depending on how they spent their souls collected overtime.
That said, I haven't seen nearly as many hackers/cheaters/glitchers as in the first game. Many players have a finite amount of health and can be beaten if fought correctly.
Conclusion:
I recommend this game to others as a good entry in the souls series. However, for the love of all that is good in this world, DO NOT BUY THIS VERSION OF THE GAME. Go grab the remastered edition, Scholar of the First Sin, instead.

The game is about as big as the first one despite having much more areas. This comes as the areas themselves are mostly smaller. There were weird transitions which didn't make much sense - totally unlike Dark Souls 1 - but I could forgive them as during playing the game it didn't take me out (I didn't even notice them very far in).
From made some very good changes here. I have to laud them for that. Being able to go human at any point, health items, magic items, the revamped UI. All of them brilliant. I understood that even more after I started up Dark Souls 1 immediately after Dark Souls 2. Wow, the UI seems so unintuitive compared. The Co-Op part also feels much better as you can be summoned even when going very far from your sign (which totally hurts DS1 imo). Technically I find it astounding how much FromSoftware improved from their first game. Really, the technical department of From gets to little praise for that. The game runs so well, it's crazy. Bodes very well for inevitable sequels.
Visually the game obviously has more to offer but I feel the torch mechanic wasn't as fully realized as it could have been. Having areas which absolutely force you to forgo shields in favor of torch would have made some pretty unique and tense moments but alas it was just a little gimmick I totally forgot after the first couple hours.
About the areas again. It feels a bit disjointed at some points but it was still fun to go from a pirate-themed area to a castle-themed one. It was fun, so I can overlook that.
There is a big part which disappointed me though which I can't forgive that easily. The bosses. There were generally speaking more bosses than ever but the majority felt like stronger regular enemies. Humans with lots of damage and health. That's not bad on its own but it was like this in just too many cases. I missed memorable bosses like the Gaping Dragon, Manus, Priscilla, Gwyndolin. Instead there were tons of sword-wielding human(oid) enemies like Throne Watcher/Defender, Dragonriders, Ruin Sentinels and even much worse, total rehashes like Bell Gargoyles, Sif and others (!). Very lame indeed. The ones that stood out were not that great either; Old Iron King, Nashandra, Ancient Dragon (most satisfying imo). I also feel they went a bit to overboard with taking influences from O&S - arguably the fan favorites from DS1. Too many dual bosses. I found O&S so memorable because they were the only boss fight with multiple bosses at once. In DS2 there were so many it just lost its uniqueness. Generally lazy boss design.
That would be my biggest complaint with the game. All other things I could forgive as the game itself was still fun but the bosses just have to be special for me.
That said, I still can totally recommend Dark Souls 2 to anyone - especially Souls veterans. It plays great and is a lot of fun which really counts.
Even after 130 hours I have the urge to go back at it. I still don't have the DLC, so there will be at least 20 hours to come on top of that :)

Alien: Isolation is one of the best and most terrifying and most exhilarating game experiences that I've had for years. Stranded on the crumbling deep-space outpost Sevastopol, you must sneak or fight your way through civilians, androids and the, erm, Alien, and find a way to get back to your own ship. The civilians are armed and nervous, the androids are merciless, and the Alien is a ruthless pain in the neck.
Everything about this game is beautifully made. The controls are complicated, but well though out, and you're introduced to the mechanics fluently and naturally. The design is lovely, from the flickering video messages to the engineering of the station itself, and lighting is used incredibly. In fact, the lighting may be one the very best features of the game; whether you're hiding in it or getting lost in it, it creates an atmosphere of constant tension and mystery. The characters and weaponry are also really good to look at.
Now, the main thing you'll be doing in this game is hiding from the Alien. And you need to hide, because it is brutal and fast and clever. This means that whole chunks of the game are spent in terror-filled suspense, ducking and diving between inadequate hiding spots and plotting routes through the areas. Certain tasks require you to be exposed for a while, and the panic as you hear the Alien getting closer to your position is something I've felt in very few games.
My minor problems with the game are that the missions are somewhat repetitive, and the later equipment just takes the edge off slightly, but neither stopped me from eagerly completing the game.
Basically a classic, and highly recommended.

This game is based on fun... not story or character or anything like that, just plain old fun and it IS fun... when it isn't crashing.
There are many things you can do in this game to make you feel like a real marvel super hero, and once you get the jetpack the game is insanely fun! This is a real sandbox, where you want to play after a long day of work, and you can play for just a little bit or for hours.
The wingsuit mechanic is great, and with the brilliant graphics, I found myself having fun just gliding around between trees and through caves, around mountains etc. The jetpack makes it a bit OP, but nothing says you have to use it, and it is fun in its own right. Flying around launching missiles from your shoulder makes you feel like Iron Man or something.
Lots of pretty explosions and the destructability is right up there with the battlefield franchise, great physics usually (although sometimes things can go a little crazy).
The grapple mechanic is intuitive and fun once you start experimenting with how to attach things together. Nothing more satisfying than attaching a helicopter to a tower so it suddenly gets yanked around and eventually nosedives into the dirt.
I've only played a few missions as I have mostly just been playing around in the open world, but the biggest BIGGEST annoyance so far with the gameplay is that the camera is always auto-adjusting and there is no option to change it. Yes you can change it for vehicles, but for parachute and wingsuit (which is what you will probobly be doing most the time because it's so damn fun) it keeps turning forward causing you to miss some of the mayhem you may have caused behind you.
The other big thing is that the game crashes. I have a high-end rig and don't remember the last time I had a game crash on me, but with 12 hours of game time I have had 2 crashes so far. It's not a huuuuge deal since you aren't too concerned with progress being lost as it is saving constantly, but it's definitely annoying and this long after release I would expect this to have been ironed out.
I think the guns are lacking some punch to them, the machine guns and pistols just don't seem to have enough oomf, and for all the death and explosions it just doesn't feel 'violent' ... crazy assessment but you will see what I mean when you play.
Usually the crashing would kill a game for me, but I gotta say, this game is just so much fun I will keep playing it for a while. The game sets itself apart from the rest of the open world games, and makes sure to NOT be a GTA V clone, making it a big breath of fresh air in a world full of GTA wannabes. This over WatchDogs II all day.
I would probably give this game an 8.5/10 but with the crashes and some of the other minor issues I'd say it's a 7.5.
Definitely worth the buy when it's on sale.

Super Giant took what made Bastion such an amazing title and refined it even further to create Transistor, and understandably you can only go up from there.
To me, Transistor feels like a spiritual successor of Bastion. The tropes, themes, and presentation of the game play as well as the narrative are all very familiar. It's as if this is a retelling of Bastion in some sort of permutation in a cyberpunk parallel universe.  At times, it feels very intentional. This being said, the dramatic art style and soundtrack are very unique and moving.
The mechanics of how you outfit yourself, as well as the tactics that will play into it, afford an incredible amount of flexibility to how you'll approach what you're up against. I can see a lot of replayability coming out of this title because of that, although there will likely be a way to do it all again in an even more engaging manner if Super Giant is following the template that I believe they are.
All in all, Transistor is well worth it's full price. Fans of Bastion will likely feel right at home, like finding a broken in tshirt that still fits really well despite having been misplaced in the closet for 6 months.  I'm looking forward to what will be coming out of Super Giant next, and to see if they will continue to morph the themes from their two recent games.

Coming from the dudes who made Bastion it looks and sounds very good but beneath that is a pretty indepth combat system aswell.
Bastion was abit simple, you found different weapons and could dual wield them. This time around you get 4 active slots for skills and each of these skills can have up to two other skills attached to it to alter or boost its effects and you also have passive slots. Theres no designated passive or support skills, each skill can fit in any slot.
For example the basic attack can just be the basic attack - or you could take it out of the active slot and attach it to another skill which then gains a stun attribute or the like. In the passive slot it provides damage resistance. Theres about 12 different skills and its really quite fun to experiment around with what combinations do what, you can make your own "builds" so to speak.
Another thing is two combat modes, Real Time and "Turn" (Matrix i guess). In Real time you run around in real time. Turn mode stops time and you can plan your movement and skill use within a fixed budget (altho that can be altered with certain skills in a passive slot) which then gets executed lighting fast. The catch is Turn mode has a cooldown during which you cant use any skills in realtime either (generally).
Its somewhat linear, theres a new game plus but i guess the replay value depends on how much you would be willing to shake up a tried and true combination :P

Transistor has beautiful visuals, wonderful voice acting, two very worthwhile characters and a story to tell with them that, in my opinion, is well worth experiencing. On its own, I feel it holds water, but mileage may vary as personal taste dictates.
The gameplay itself is initially simple and straight forward, but the manner in which you can augment abilities, with other abilities, and then use multiple augmented abilities together to devastating effect, is a 'easy to learn, fun to master' affair that should be taken note of.
There is a timestop mechanic of sorts, more akin to super speed or bullet time, than a turn based pause function, that further enhances your combat options. Intelligent use of this function can turn a drawn out encounter into a graceful and elegant cascade of quick decisive moves that end the battle in a matter of seconds.
It is short, but it does have a mixed up newgame+ function, with enemies scaled up. You'll likely have to replay the game in this harder mode to see all the tests and play with the late level ability combinations. This is not a bad thing, the encounters in newgame plus aren't simple scaled up, you'll encounter new mixtures of enemies, not just harder enemies.
In short, it's good. Buy it. Play it. Do it.

I just copied all the commanders from Time of Fury, made the necessary text changes, and have 100 commanders. Of course, I have no interest in building a game with the actual historical military commanders from 1953 :)
In fact, I am considering downgrading the superpowers' unit levels to maybe "3" to give them more to research, while Hungary would be Level 1. Also interesting to bring Turkey into the mix on the NATO front to give USSR something more to worry about. Not really interested in the nuke part of the game, but that may well be very important for the design.
Only bug I found so far is when you open the Diplomacy box, it blocks the other hex box options and I can't close it. I could be missing something, of course. So for modders, a very nice engine and template has been provided here. For regular users, it plays okay, but backup those csv files and give modding a try.
A big part of the war (I guess) would be getting U.S. men and materiel to Europe. I don't think this is handled by the convoy system (I leave it on automatic), only supply (PP). Otherwise, the game will have to come up with some kind of cargoship mechanic to get U.S. units over there - while possibly avoiding WP anti-shipping efforts.
Anyway, I was pleasantly surprised. Not to be rude, but Fall Weiss (IMO) was the worst. This effort is the exact opposite.

Not quite a masterpiece as some have said but a pretty good effort nonetheless. The suspense comes from the save system. You do this manually at set points throughout a level but the problem is the alien which is stalking you. Reaching these save points is essential to preserve your progress and hence the suspense.
As far as the story goes it is pretty solid and well acted.  Scatered about are terminals and audio journals  which provide additional story background and in some cases are essential for you to proceed.
The game also includes a crafting element which seems obligatory these days. It works well enough. When you find a blueprint you then gain the ability to craft that item using the junk you have collected.
In addition to the alien you will have to contend with the synthetics which become increasingly hostile as the game progresses.  They can be killed but this is generally a last resort because of the limited weaponry at your disposal. You can only carry 3 of each of the device based weapons and ammunition for the rest is limited.
A few other bits and pieces complete the picture. Some terminals and doors require hacking which consists of various simple mini games. When doing these the game does not pause so you can still be killed. Finally there are the rewire junctions which give you the option to divert power from one system to another. A good idea but unfortunately it is used less and less as the game goes on.
I'd give it 4/5 but not for its current price of £29.99. I think £15 is more realistic. It's a good game but comes up short as far as variety is concerned. A lot of going backwards and forwards to complete various tasks. A minor bug as well. You can slow to a crawl sometimes and the only cure I found was to quit and restart.  Thankfully this is not very often but it's a shame they never fixed this.

It took me quite a while to work through Alien Isolation, mainly because the gameplay was very different than I'm used to. For one, I had to adjust to the whole stealth/sneaking aspect. Rarely do you have the firepower to deal with threats, and after playing Doom or KF2, this was a dramatic shift.
That said, after completing the story, I loved this game. The slow, plodding, and suspenseful gameplay was extremely well done. The ever-present, sinking horror of the alien and encounters with other enemies keeps the game very tense until literally the last few seconds of the game, and I breathed a very huge sigh of relief upon completing it (similar to Dead Space).
This is a horror/survival game well done. The crafting is simple and not over-complicated (I hate complicated crafting). The combat is very satisfying if you ever have the right tools to do so. I highly recommend Alien: Isolation if you enjoy horror, space, first person games.

The Western genre is well-known as one of the most oddly under-represented themes in videogames. Despite the fact that the genre is particularly ideal for FPS games - having a focus on gunplay, simplistic stories, spectacular settings, and a reputation for stylised cool - the Call of Juarez series are among the only shooters to plough this particular furrow.
After the car crash that was Call of Juarez: The Cartel, it was widely felt that the series was doomed. In a bold, calculated response Techland went very much back to basics with Gunslinger. Here you will find no multiplayer, extreme linearity, an arcade focus, and attractive but evidently low-budget cutscenes. However, eschewing all these elements allowed the developers to create an extremely focused, polished, and thrilling experience.
It's no overstatement to say that Gunslinger captures spaghetti Western gunplay more perfectly than any game ever has. While the weapon selection is realistically small, each one is a completely distinct experience which demands specific skills to master. The emphasis on rapid targeting and extreme accuracy coupled with the extremely polished shooting design makes the gunplay in Gunslinger among the best - if not the best - that can be found in an FPS. It's that good.
Alongside the great environments, voice acting and models the other standout feature of Gunslinger is its genuine love and understanding of the Old West and spaghetti Western cinema. This isn't just a game set
the complex web of myth and history that is the Wild West; it is also a game
that web. Gunslinger genuinely has something to say about the way we perceive a period of history and very few games can make that claim.
It is fascinating to go along on this ride with Silas Greaves, the main character. Each stage of the game is a fascinating mix of truth, fiction, flawed memory, exaggeration and outright lies. That the gameplay every step of the way is so slick and exciting makes the player feel like a cross between Doc Holliday and The Man with No Name - and that's the way it should be.
Highly recommended.

I really enjoyed Gunslinger.  It's a very well crafted, fun, and charming little shooter.  It's short and that's exactly as long as it should be.  Tells a tale that captures the feeling of the dime novels and old western films surprisingly well, and you get a strong sense that the developer had a reverence for the source material despite being in Poland.
The game has narrator a driven delivery, somewhat similar to Bastion, but it's more guiding than reactive.  There are several moments where the game reacts to changes in the story as it's being told and they're just little visual tricks or gimmicks in level design, but I found these bits to be quite clever and a lot of fun.

If you've been eye-balling this game I'd recommend that you pick it up. It's not in your standard faire of ARPGs. This game does not hold your hand. It's a challenge for the sake of the challenge and I love it.
Combat is almost puzzle-like. You need to learn and understand what each of your moves do and how to best use them. Then you need to learn what your opponets move set is and how to counter, parry, backstab, block, and generally move through their attacks.
This game is difficult in the sense that their is so many skills to master and so much to take in. Nothing is automated so you could potentially play through most of the game before you realize that different types of shields have differing movesets. You could also go multiple playthroughs without fully understanding how your equipment load effects your stamina, rolls, run speed, etc etc. This game encourages trial and error. Whether that means falling off cliffs to see if you can get to a secret area, walking along stretches of wall and tapping your action key looking for secret passages, to figuring out whether poison works on what bosses. There will never be a popup saying go to this area next. It's all on you. Each time you die you also lose all your souls, which is a combination of currency and XP, with a single chance to go back and reclaim it or it'll be lost for good. You'll probasbly backtrack a lot trying to figure out what's next. The story isn't spoonfed to you. It's found through talking through each NPC's dialog, reading equipment descriptions, and observing the environment. If you kill the enemies enough, they respawn everytime you rest to regain health etc, they will eventually stop respwning potentially making an area easier, but also opening up the option of farming for souls and equipment.
There is also a metagame referred to as "fashion souls" among DS players. There is so much gear and equipment to collect, and potentially upgrade, that you can darn well look like whatever you like, using whatever weapons you like. Cosplaying is common.
Then you get PvP/CoOp. CoOp is done through leaving summoning signs or joining covenants that summon you to other players worlds (to aid them against PvP'ers). CoOp is helpful for getting through an area or challenging a boss. PvP is done with summoning signs, joining covenants that summon other people to your world or you to theirs (territory defense style), it's also done with items that allow you invade someone else's world. PvP/CoOp is useful for advancing levels in covenants which provide gear/spells, but it's also bring new dimensions to this game after you put in dozens of hours messing around PvE.
The Souls game all have a New Game+ mechanic. After you beat the game you can restart it with your gear, but everything is more powerful and difficult. DS2 has a mechanic that allows you to NG+ and area after beat a boss. There's a cap on how high it can go (I've never reached it but I've never tried to either), but I've seen people on their Original NG and having one or two areas NG+8. A quick warning, if you NG an area and then beat the game and NG the whole game, that area that has already been NG+ will roll over to the next difficulty (e.g. NG+ overall, but that one NG+3 will roll over to NG+4). Each NG+ will introduce new equipment and enemies (and more enemies).
DS2 is rereleasing with a type of "game of the year" style for the new consoles (DS2 Scholar of the First Sin). It's going to come with all the previous DLC plus a new one. The game will also have better frame rates, upgraded graphics, better and new enemy AI/move sets, enemy placement, and some new NPCs. It's still not completely clear if the new stuff will be available as DLC or if the prior owners will have to buy the new game, which has caused all sorts of anst in the Souls community. A patch has already hit that includes some of the content for SotFS.
There are still bugs in this game, and each time Fromsoft releases content they just add more bugs, much to the hackers delight. You can be invaded by people that hack anything from invincibility to superpowers to even having different skins. This causes some major frustration, especially for me. I've been avoiding reviewing this game, being my number one favourite I couldn't think of a way to make it unbiased. But after the resurgence of Open world games, the downfall of AAA and the battle between TF2 and Overwatch, I think I can finally pinpoint what makes it so beautiful.
. Everything is cartoony and exaggerated, it's filled with colour and despite being cartoony it feels more realistic than the grim grisley greyness of Skyrim, Morrowind, Witcher etc. It's not perfect of course, with clipping and terrible lip sync but with the cartoony atmosphere it adds to the exaggerated charm that it provides.
. If you compare how they were designed to Mass Effect: Andromeda, the way it has been presented is genius. There are a lot of gay characters, black characters, female characters- but these characteristics do not define who they are. The characters still have peronalities, they just happen to be these things- they are not just addons, it just adds to the depth of the world.
I suppose the most important thing in a game is
, and this Borderlands nails too. A lot of games can't tell whether they want to be simple or complicated, they can't tell what gimmicks they want to use, so they use everything and it turns into an incoherent mess
. Borderlands knows exactly what it wants to do. It's a Single Player or Co-Op FPS with RPG mechanics with levelling and loot systems. The RPG mechanics make it feel more open worldy than most open world games. It defines what towns exist, and gives you fast ways to get to them, and while games like Skyrim use the open world idea to make you travel for hours, Borderlands 2 just adds a lot of depth with; secret loot boxes, experience, Cult of the Vault logos or mini easter eggs.
Something that I noticed in my most recent playthrough is how much freedom you have throughout and
. One example is the first area, the entirety of Southern Shelf. You fight Knuckle dragger, to a new player they find out how brilliantly designed the bosses will be: They aren't walls of health, they aren't stupidly damaging, they are balanced with weaknesses and phases. An expert player on the other hand could then debate whether they would want to farm Knuckle Dragger for the legendary pistol Hornet, or just move on. This can also be seen in Southern Shelf Bay when you have to kill Midgemong. A new player could rush right towards Midgemong or maybe explore the boats, while an expert player would take the long route around for some extra loot and instead of calling the bridge over to get across the lake, they can just run across the chain, significantly increasing the pacing and replayability of the game.
Of course Borderlands 2 isn't perfect, the majority of the fun is in the UVHM playthrough which is a DLC. The bugs might throw people off while I enjoy discovering two or three new ones every new playthrough. Even despite this, just the first playthrough with a friend is highly worth your time. Let's hope Borderlands 3 will be another great one. Iron out the issues of Borderlands 2, while still being able to provide replayability where Borderlands: The Pre-sequel couldn't.

is a blast, and an absolute must-play for anyone who likes shooters, dungeon crawlers, humour, and/or epic stories!
Graphically, the game holds up better than most of its contemporaries. Why? Cel-shaded art style, that's why! Just like the first game, this game uses cel-shading to give everything an almost cartoony look, which really helps the game in having its own distinct look and feel. I have little to no criticism on the graphical prowess of this game, although I have to note I particularly dislikle it when games give you 'new' enemies which are really old enemies with a new paintjob. Sound-wise, the game is actually kind of the same: beautiful, with a cartoony edge. The voice acting is wonderfully close to that of an animated series, and all important characters have great lines and great actors. A lot of other NPCs share voices and lines, which is a shame, but you'll be spending most of your gameplay far away from them anyway. The guns sound brilliant, and each type of gun or barrel has its own distinct sound, which contributes to the distinct feeling they all have. The music is epic and apt for the levels, although I have had some instances where battle music would not end after a battle, or start too soon, when there were no enemies yet in sight.
Gameplay-wise,
is amazing. It plays just like the first game, which means guns blazing, run-and-gun action, extremely responsive controls, great aiming, and special skills and powers that are fun to play with. There is really nothing wrong with the controls (although the car controls are a little clunky), the combat mechanics, or the game mechanics. The randomization of loot will have you opening all the chests in the hope of finding an even better gun than the one you already have, and the feeling you get when striking gold every once in a while is oh so satisfying. The sheer amount of customization will also keep you at the game, going through your inventory, switching up your weapon type, grenade type, and even your looks once in a while. In all, you just feel immensely
when wielding guns in
, even when if an end-level baddy is stomping you into the ground time and again with infinite ease. What makes all of the gameplay
better is co-op. I have had no problems whatsoever with saving/loading/drop-in/drop-out, and this is one of the very few games that plays out amazingly both in single-player and in co-op. It's just a load of fun to share this adventure, exploration, and combat with a friend! If you have never played co-op, this is the place to start! If you're looking for a new co-op game, look no further!
When it comes to the story and world, the game is splendid. The world is much larger and more diverse than that of the first
, and this, I believe, is the main novelty this second game brings with it. The story is in principle very basic: bad guy wants to destroy stuff using bad weapon, and you need to stop him. The motivations and backstory of big baddy Jack, however, will have you wondering all game long, which is a good thing in this case. The four main characters you get to choose from in this game (two more if you've got the DLC) are new ones, not the main good guys from the previous game
For players who love a good story, though, there are many side quests that flesh out the world and provide you with more intricacies regarding the main plot, and the writing in most of these is superb, while in some of them it is simply okay.
The story actually varies a little depending on which character you play, which, combined with the diversity of their skills, the difference in weapon types, and the sheer amount of quests in the game, give
and extremely high replay value. I am already looking forward to my second playthrough, and hope I can do several more afterwards. This replay value is further enhanced by the extra content that the DLC adds, and oh man, is there a lot! I have played two of the DLC packs so far, and they were both a load of fun, although the writing is a bit less great than in the main game.
In all,
is just great fun, whether you are used to this type of game or not. I think every gamer will find pleasure in the streamlined gameplay that it provides, and laugh at the funny yet amazing story. The game captured my dreams for a while, and will be a favourite of mine forever!

Transistor has beautiful visuals, wonderful voice acting, two very worthwhile characters and a story to tell with them that, in my opinion, is well worth experiencing. On its own, I feel it holds water, but mileage may vary as personal taste dictates.
The gameplay itself is initially simple and straight forward, but the manner in which you can augment abilities, with other abilities, and then use multiple augmented abilities together to devastating effect, is a 'easy to learn, fun to master' affair that should be taken note of.
There is a timestop mechanic of sorts, more akin to super speed or bullet time, than a turn based pause function, that further enhances your combat options. Intelligent use of this function can turn a drawn out encounter into a graceful and elegant cascade of quick decisive moves that end the battle in a matter of seconds.
It is short, but it does have a mixed up newgame+ function, with enemies scaled up. You'll likely have to replay the game in this harder mode to see all the tests and play with the late level ability combinations. This is not a bad thing, the encounters in newgame plus aren't simple scaled up, you'll encounter new mixtures of enemies, not just harder enemies.
In short, it's good. Buy it. Play it. Do it.

Okay. First things first, I have over 600 hours off of steam with this game. I do not write reviews for games that often, but since that I have been playing this for sometime now, I decided to give it shot, so bear with me.
First things first... if you REALLY want to play this game... it's not free, unless you want to spend hours and hours beyond imaginable grinding favor (an in game currency) to buy every god you want to play. However, you can unlock the ultimate god pack which unlocks every past, present or future god in the game, and trust me, they release new gods like hot cakes, while there is currently 83 gods in the game. It's a great deal in my opinion.
Secondly, the gameplay. This is an MOBA, which if you are not familiar with, you're living under a rock. League of Legends is a MOBA as well, so think of three lanes, with a jungle, and minions (or creeps) with jungle monsters, buying items to increase your damage or defense and getting xp, with the main gamemode being 5v5. However, what makes SMITE different from many differnet MOBAs is the third person perspective. Trust me. If you honeslty hate normal MOBAs, give this game a try. The third person perspective allows the user to make skill shots (95% of the time) with every ability and basic attack, and it also makes the game more fast paced in my opinion. Overall, great gameplay. Shows a real test of skill and aim with each god.
Third, the gods. Now do not get me wrong, there will be broken things. What's new? Every game has broken items or characters. If they are op, play them.  Simple as that. Since there are 83 gods in the game, there is a huge variety of what you can play as, from a robot who can portal through walls, to a bowmaster horse man with a canadian skin, to a dragon with a sword who can one shot you late game. Even though there is technically a meta of what gods are better than others, you can almost get away with anything in this game. If you are really comfortable with a god, you can beat some of the best gods in the game, no sweat.
Lastly, the community. Now I'm gonna be honest here, the community could be a little better, ESPECIALLY towards junglers. You are always gonna find people who are annoying and mean in game, but some of these people are brutal. If you are a new player, I reccomend just muting everyone at the start of the gane, cause if you feed, you're gonna get bashed for it. Overall though, most people are nice, so it should not be TOO much of a problem.
In conclusion, SMITE is a third person MOBA with a brilliant esports scene, good devs that keep the game updated every two weeks with balance changes and meta shifts, and great faced paced gameplay. If you want a semi-free game that you want to play with friends, definilty give this a try. If you hate MOBAs, definitly give this a try. Great game with a lot of potential. Also, did I mention the amount of memes this game has?

Not quite a masterpiece as some have said but a pretty good effort nonetheless. The suspense comes from the save system. You do this manually at set points throughout a level but the problem is the alien which is stalking you. Reaching these save points is essential to preserve your progress and hence the suspense.
As far as the story goes it is pretty solid and well acted.  Scatered about are terminals and audio journals  which provide additional story background and in some cases are essential for you to proceed.
The game also includes a crafting element which seems obligatory these days. It works well enough. When you find a blueprint you then gain the ability to craft that item using the junk you have collected.
In addition to the alien you will have to contend with the synthetics which become increasingly hostile as the game progresses.  They can be killed but this is generally a last resort because of the limited weaponry at your disposal. You can only carry 3 of each of the device based weapons and ammunition for the rest is limited.
A few other bits and pieces complete the picture. Some terminals and doors require hacking which consists of various simple mini games. When doing these the game does not pause so you can still be killed. Finally there are the rewire junctions which give you the option to divert power from one system to another. A good idea but unfortunately it is used less and less as the game goes on.
I'd give it 4/5 but not for its current price of £29.99. I think £15 is more realistic. It's a good game but comes up short as far as variety is concerned. A lot of going backwards and forwards to complete various tasks. A minor bug as well. You can slow to a crawl sometimes and the only cure I found was to quit and restart.  Thankfully this is not very often but it's a shame they never fixed this.

A fantastic looking game, with shaded art reminiscent of games like Borderlands. The visuals, especially the characters and their introductions, are done very well, and this is complemented by the audio and the cut scenes. The depictions of dead enemies are also done masterfully, with both the ragdoll physics and the theatrical sprays of blood complementing the rest of the game, especially the beautiful background setting - whether it be an Wild West town, a train, a gold mine, swamps, or the mountains - the scenery can be breathtaking.
The gameplay mechanics themselves are also quite solid; and this game is very unique in how the Old West quick-draw stand-offs are depicted - tricky to master, but great fun. With several things you need to take note of; including focus and speed, and maybe even the ability to dodge, duels are a fun, if potentially frustrating addition to the game. This is complemented by the ability to slow down time and dodge bullets, in the style of Neo - it always brought a smile to my face when I dodged a bullet and heard an enemy say "Did he just dodge a bullet?!" The skills also work quite well, with 3 short skill trees, each leading to the ability to unlock two unique weapons, superior to the default weapons, while giving other bonuses such as to reload speed, etc.
But by far my favourite part of the game is the story. While it is not incredibly long, the way the story is told is unique and I found it utterly compelling. This is because the story is not happening as the game is played, the story is narrated by your own character, Silas Greaves, telling some young 'uns many years after the events occurred in a saloon while downing shots of whiskey. As such, hearing the conversation going on as you play, as well as situations in which the game rewinds as... "this isn't how the story goes, what actually happened was THIS..." Not too long, but long enough to be enjoyable.
'Twas a great game folks.

Pre-Review: This game took the very small amount of emotion that I had, made me feel something with it, and then stomped it into the ground. For that, I commend it. That was fascinating.
As a narrative, I recommend this game wholly. Play it through, three or four times, and grasp the hopelessness of the relationship. However, do so in this mindset. Get the emotional experience and get out.
As a game, it falls woefully short. The choices you make do not affect the core story. You can control very minor details, such as who Emily dated in her Freshman year of college, yet other details will happen due to the very forced arc. The message of the game could be recieved much better if there were some actual differences leading to different paths to the same ending, or, preferably, different paths leading to similar endings. I understand that a main point of the narrative was to show how the relationship wouldn't work, but to be truly effective, it needs to not be so forced.
In the end, it's a feeling that could arise from a short video or a short story, and that's not a very good thing if this game wants to stand out.
TL;DR: Play it once or twice, get the message, get out. Do not analyze as a game, analyze as an art work in game form. Recommended for the feeling that the first three playthroughs get you.

Holy crap, Supergiant Games really outdid themselves with this one. I was a huge Bastion fanboy from the get-go due to its unique atmosphere and its fusion of gameplay mechanics and story flavor. Combined with the fact that Supergiant is a tiny studio holding its weight against the massive giants in the industry, I was eagerly rooting for Transistor. It completely exceeded my expectations and is hands down my favorite game of all time. The gameplay itself is nuanced and is built off of one of the most interesting upgrade systems I've seen to date; instead of upgrading stats, you unlock functions that can be used as an active ability, a modifier to another active, or as a constant passive boost. This leads to an absurd number of combinations, each of which have value in different situations. The story itself is jam-packed with feels and left hooks. I won't give too much away, but suffice to say it definitely turns the standard "see antagonist group, fight antagonists one by one" formula way on its head. Darren Korb (the audio director at Supergiant) definitely upped his game on this one, so I highly recommend picking up the OST along with it. Can't recommend this game enough.

Playing this game was an absolutely beautiful experience, and here's why:
-The concept is original and so well excecuted that it leaves me begging for more, yet I feel completely satisfied.
-The battle system is revolutionary. Turn() adds a lot of strategy to something that could very well have been just another normal hack and slash game.
-The customization of The Transistor that allowed for every program you get in the game to either be used as an active skill, an upgrade to a skill, or simply a passive skill for your character, leaves infinite possibilites for customization. It is hard to find something like that in a linear game such as this.
-The art. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ man. I was enthralled when I played Bastion because of the craftsmanship that went into every little detail, but this game was on a whole other level.
-THE MUSIC. Bastions music, which was conducted by Darren Korb, was flawless. When I saw the preview for this game at E3 last year and heard "We All Become" I knew that Supergiant Games and Darren Korb would not dissapoint me with this title. And guess what: They ♥♥♥♥ing didn't
-All the little things. The narration of the Transistor throughout the game, the fact that you can have the protagonist hum along to the soundtrack, etc.
-Last but definitely not least: the characters. For a silent protagonist, Red found a way into my heart very fast. The relationship between Red and The Transistor was beautiful. Simple, yet complicated.
I am honestly so happy that I played this game. Absolute 10/10.

It took me quite a while to work through Alien Isolation, mainly because the gameplay was very different than I'm used to. For one, I had to adjust to the whole stealth/sneaking aspect. Rarely do you have the firepower to deal with threats, and after playing Doom or KF2, this was a dramatic shift.
That said, after completing the story, I loved this game. The slow, plodding, and suspenseful gameplay was extremely well done. The ever-present, sinking horror of the alien and encounters with other enemies keeps the game very tense until literally the last few seconds of the game, and I breathed a very huge sigh of relief upon completing it (similar to Dead Space).
This is a horror/survival game well done. The crafting is simple and not over-complicated (I hate complicated crafting). The combat is very satisfying if you ever have the right tools to do so. I highly recommend Alien: Isolation if you enjoy horror, space, first person games.

Fantastic horror (kinda) survival game that gives the Alien universe a very refreshing look into the story of Ellen Ripley's daughter, Amanda, and her story aboard the Sevastopol Station. If you're a fan of the Alien universe you will absolutely love this game, the resemblance it bears to the aesthetics of the ship in the first movie Alien (1979) is striking. The gameplay is as immersive and suspenseful as it can possibly be, with the Xenomorph, among other creatures, posing constant threats throughout your exploration of this space station, and as you discover the story of what happened to the station. This isn't strictly a horror game in a way, as it relies pretty much only on the tense atmosphere than on any sort of jump scares, as opposed to games that are about split (Outlast, Amnesia). You'll never feel as unsafe with a gun as you will in Alien: Isolation.
I can't recommend this game enough, if you're reading this I'd pick it up immediately. Well worth the money, I wish the developers would've developed a sequel.

I purchsed Alien: Isolation and the first hours were purely terrifying! The Alien is massive creature and the purest of threats you encounter in the game. It kills you on sight within one punch.
Another threat are the Synthetics, which I don't like at all, because fighting them is really difficult without a stun baton.
And as everything good comes in three parts, humans are partially a threat, too.
Alright, Amanda, lets make the Sevastopol great again!
The visuals of the game are beyond fantastic. Even though the game is now almost 3 years old, it is gorgeous! The 80s themed style of the interior feels so natural, that they translate the look&feel of the movies perfectly into a game. Something else I like alot is the smoke effects here. Everything looks volumetric and beyond a wall of smoke you fear to encounter the Xenomorph. The lighting also has an effect on the smoke here and both are giving you the most intense visuals you will see in any horror game!
In terms of visuals the level of detail is astonishing! So many small items you will see on tables, floors and so on.
The audio contacts the footsteps of the visuals. It's intense. You always here the Xenomorph running behind the walls or the ceilings. At the very beginning you are mostly afraid of these sounds, as you fear the encounter with the "Boogey-Man". In certain parts the music will erupt to a fearful nightmarish and intense music, where you only like to run away. But this would be a death sentence. Running will make noise. Noise will attract your enemies. Attracting your enemies will mostly lead to death. So the game plays with your fears but you have to stay calm and clear in your head. Otherwise you die. The music is essencial in such a game and the developers did everything right here.
The gameplay consists mostly of a sneaky walk and hide. You get objectives to fulfill and you are mostly lead by a map to those points. You also have combat situations but those are only against humans and synths. Both of them can be killed. In terms of the Xenomorph, you will only get tools to distract it or making it flee. This makes the game great and feels intense!
In terms of gameplay, the game has some minor weaknesses:
But that's it for gameplay. There are other minor things I did not like, for example the flight to the Anesidora. The game always gives you a vivid story of showing awesome stuff. A good example is
. But later you will have to enter the Anesidora, a ship orbiting around KG-348 - a gas giant where the Sevastopol Station is also orbiting. You will have to use a small rescue ship for that but you won't see the Anesidora exterior, nor will you experience the flight to the ship. This is very pity, as you could experience everything else before. This was the most massive "downer" in this game for me, unfortunately.
Nonetheless: This game is great. It has a great story, that fills you up for up to 16hrs.

I think this game is very well put together. I am a big fan of the original Alien movie, and this game does a great job of getting the look and feel of the series. All with the help of a lot of the original sound, music, “props” and “areas” from the movie.
So, if you’re a fan of the original movie as well, then, I would recommend trying this game.
The “levels” are very well designed, and It doesn’t feel like a quick “reuse” for the sake of making the game longer, when you have to go to the same areas, multiple times throughout the game.
The old-school 70’s and 80’s like computer systems and old text fonts used in the varies menus and terminals, also make it feel like the Alien movie.
The only small negative thing I experienced was that the alien would sometimes glitch, and some of it would be visible in for example a locker you’d be hiding in.
I played the game on the hard difficulty, as that was the recommended setting, and it took me about 18 hours of playtime to complete the game.

Most people remember this game as the last good Call Of Duty Game. The multiplayer is good, but you should probably buy this on console. The multiplayer is entirely plagued with hackers. The neglect from Infinity Ward and hacking has gotten so bad to the point where hackers can ruin your game, and since Steam cloud saves your data, it's impossible to fix in some cases. There's no word from Steam when the community asks for soloutions.
There are groups of legit players who play private matches, if you can find one, it's fun, but that's more of a tactic to avoid hackers for people who already have the game.
Some of the things hackers can do is change your resoloution, your minimap size (to the point where it takes up the whole screen.) These problems can be fixed by deleting you config files and verifying your cache.
They can also corrupt your rank, and this can't be fixed, unless you get into another hacked lobby and they rank you up to 70.
This is a GOOD multiplayer game, but I'm going to thumb it down because of how prevelent hackers are, and people should know about. Unless you already have people to play with, I wouldn't buy it for PC.

I bought this game on a whim because I enjoyed Bastion, and I gotta say what a friggen gem this is.
The artwork is simply breathtaking. The colorful painting style images create an immersive atmosphere and is simply gorgeous to look at, I've been screenshotting various images throughout the game left and right for wall papers and background simply because of how well drawn they are.
The music is hauntingly beautiful as well, it blends well with the sci-fi feel and gives me goosebumps, especially the humming feature they added in game. I mean wow, that voice is so beautiful, sometimes I just let my game run with the alt tab key down while doing other tasks just so I can be enriched by the ear candy.
I should probably also mention this game's combat system and central gameplay is incredibly innovative and unique. The fighting plays with a combination of free style combat and turn based VATS style targetting. It's very well fleshed out, and your attack commands can be customized in countless ways. The game's not too hard, but there are in-game options to amp up the difficulty just like in Bastion so you can adjust to your liking. Even though the game probably plays for about 7 hours, there's a new game+ mode with new features to extend replayability. In short, there's something for everyone.
TL;DR: This game better win indie GOTY, or there's no justice in this world.

...This game is a work of art. From the gorgeous style, to the genre choice, to the fantastic music, to the characters who initially just seem like ghosts of what they could be, yet slowly grow on you. The lines are well done, and everyone winds up having a personality of some kind that you begin to relate to them.
The combat is fresh, not something I've seen before (and I've been gaming a long time mind you), and they didn't slack there either. I played with a lot of limiters, but even without them, I can tell you that this one will take you a little while to get used to and will definitely test you. It's a strange blend of action, strategy, RPG, turn based combat, and even shooter all mixed together into a masterful blend that I initially dreaded, and by the end of the game (fantastic ending) was in love with.
This is the sort of game that was made with passion and dreams. This is the quality of game and the determination to make a fantasy that stands out amongst other dreams real for us gamers. I highly recommend this game, and I'm not entirely sure what audience I could think of that wouldn't find something appealing here. Talking swords, sci-fi, angry hardware trying to take over the world, over-eager scientists, lasers, giant explosions, godzilla-esque monsters, and VERY frustrating hairstyles... yeah, this game has a lot of nice quirks worked in all throughout. You'll love it.
