Billed as a hybrid of pinball and old-school shoot em' ups, this game isn't good as either. The pinball tables are incredibly simplistic and there really is nothing of a shmup in this. There are geometric shapes that fly around the board that you have to hit with your ball but there really isn't resembling a shmup as fans of that genre would think of it. Old-school games like Pinball on the NES have more complicated tables than the ones found here. The physics also don't feel like a traditional pinball table and the enemies move randomly and cause your ball to bounce off them on impact, depending what powerup you have equipped. This takes most of the elements of skill out of the game. Pinball and shmups often feel random but are ultimately skill-based games that reward persistence and learning the mechanics. This involved a lot of true randomness that will ultimately make it more frustrating, especially since the 20+ level campaign has no checkpoints or saves, meaning it will take hours and hours to get to the end and only if you're lucky. There is also a boss rush and endless mode which are nice but nothing unique. The presentation is bland and flat. It's colourful but there is a ton of wasted screen space and the music and effects sound like they came from royalty-free sites.
There are so many better video pinball games like Zen Pinball, Pinball Arcade, Balls of Steel and more that do a better job than this does and many are far cheaper as well. This would have been a fun $1 mobile game maybe but $8.50US is way too much to ask for this sparse and mechanically weak package. Enhanced Steam says this is currently $2 on Desura. If you want to buy there or wait for a big Steam sale, that might be worth it but I think the regular price is way too high for what you get. There's better pinball and better shmups out there. I love the idea of combining these two genres but this isn't a good attempt at that.

I don't have much time in on "Hyperspace Pinball" yet, but as there is only one review, I suspect something is in order. Updates as appropriate, hopefully very soon.
First off, this shouldn't be compared to what you currently play as pinball: TPA, FX2, or even Balls of Steel. The physics of “Hyperspace Pinball” will most likely leave players of the aforementioned trio of pinball tables cold. It just doesn't feel much like a ball rolling, or struck, or arcing, or pretty much anything you're accustomed to. But as this is "Hyperspace Pinball", quite likely this is a deliberate choice to do things differently. If you're accustomed to playing 15-minute games in FX2, be prepared to be thrilled if one of these one-ball games lasts over 30 seconds. (Some are 4-ball.)
Though you hit balls with flippers, it just doesn’t have the feel of pinball, but rather of something else, something that deserves thoughtful consideration.
While pinball is traditionally a game of developing the skills to hit primarily stationary targets, the goal of “Hyperspace Pinball” is to hit both stationary and moving targets. The table field is almost empty in all modes, with the edges containing the stationary targets, and the otherwise empty center consisting of moving targets.
The only way to lose the ball is down the center between the lower flippers. There are in-lanes, but no out-lanes.
The balls are frequently blocked from going down the center, often explosively, by barriers created through player actions.
All tables are essentially symmetrical, with a second set of flippers just above the halfway point.
“Hyperspace Pinball” has three modes: Campaign, Boss Run and Endurance.
Campaign Mode has more the look a traditional pinball, but not the physics. It’s very easy to get extra balls, and involves leveling-up within each game. A 4-ball game, averaging perhaps 2 - 3 minutes.
Boss Run Mode is basically an attempt to get to a larger block that is protected by other blocks or barriers, and has eight choices in the menu. Each of the eight unlocked selections offers a different objective and/or targets, but on similar fields. The menu previews each table, some of which are quite complex and interesting. Possibly the strongest feature of "Hyperspace Pinball". A one-ball, win or loose game unlikely to last a minute.
Endurance Mode has the physics that seems most similar to the pinball we all know. Apparently the goal is to hit the highest number of moving targets on an otherwise almost empty field, and that total number of targets hit is your score. A one-ball game averaging only seconds.
But even though this doesn't FEEL like pinball, that's no reason to write it off, especially since this is clearly meant to be pinball in name only. This is no sloggy, "wait 5 minutes for the ball to land" game. It's very fast paced, the leveling within a single table in Campaign mode is interesting, and the methods of obtaining points are creative. I won't go so far as to say the price is reasonable (even on sale), but I still have much of the table yet to play. And with bosses and 20 levels, there is certainly plenty of potential to explore.
I’m having trouble getting used to the erratic ball movement in places, though it seems possibly to be deliberate. And the table is sometimes dark, and not always easy to see just what’s going on. While I can appreciate the bright flashes that express some accomplishment, they can be very distracting in the midst of a game, so much that balls must frequently be artificially saved in the aftermath. It's not always possible to understand cause and effect in a completely "flashed-out" screen. I suspect with player input we will see a better game soon.
“Hyperspace Pinball” does have a leaderboard, but I didn’t recognize any of the names. Perhaps at this early stage they’re mostly in-house, but in this short time I did get as high as #31, and I didn’t look much beyond that. There are very few controls, and “portrait mode” is not among them. Unfortunately, this game makes very poor use of portrait mode should you change your PC's setting. The achievements affered are primarily for beating bosses, or cummulative actions that can only be accomplished over time, but basically by any patient (or obsessive) player.
"Hyperspace Pinball" is a very challenging game, more in the arcade mode than strictly as pinball. Each pinballer will have to take a chance with this game, as it may not satisfy a traditionalist. IF you don’t mind spending the money, this seems likely to be worthwhile, but ONLY if the price is acceptable to you. Otherwise, I’d suggest waiting until players more skilled and literate than I put in their two cents worth (plus $8.47US, on sale.)
EDIT #1: Having played for an hour, I must say I'm quite enjoying "Hyperspace Pinball", and am up to #20/96. (yipee) BUG - There's no way to see the names associated with the second screen of the leaderboard. It doesn't shift from the page 1 names until you reach page 3, which is correct for page 3.
EDIT #2: Played a bit longer last night offline. EVen though I'm a fairly average FX2 player, I managed to get 4/8 bosses, and a Campaign Mode score of 521K, good for 3rd place. A very nice feature is that offline scores ARE included in the LB (but takes a minute.) THANKS! 5 achievements total.
While a pretty cool game, it still needs to be twice as big or half the price to be successful. Especially since most (or all) of the Boss Run features are repeated in Campaign Mode. And I've only gotten to Level 8. (IMHO)
Thank you.

Factorio, What is it?
Factorio, is in short a logistics simulator. Two "end goals", Either make the player completely obsolete and expendable or play through the research tree, build a rocket and leave the planet you crash landed on. So, what do i think of it?
Graphics:  Top down almost RTS style-2D combined with sprites made from 3D models.....etc. Works perfectly.
Sound: -Music: Works considering you have to think you're crash landed on another planet.
-SFX:  Production quality isn't too impressive but again, they have made it work perfectly. The buzzer for when you are getting attacked even comes toe in toe with a flashing red icon, not disimilar to if you were to be looking at a screen or dashboard in a airplane cockpit. With the stylization of the basic UI it works.
Gameplay: Extremely enjoyable, addicting (maybe too much so) and very tough to beat, but rewarding every step of the way. Research tree could use a small amount of tweaking in regard to what science packs are required. this also goes for what is required for some science packs, however that would turn Factorio on to easy mode which is actually one of the reasons i consider it to be so rewarding. Its hard but play around a bit and you can work it out in no time. When i got this game, i binged it to death.
Final rating: Insanely Addictive! 8.5/10

The Call of Juarez series isn't one most say as particularly good, more so considering how it's last title The Cartel was rated pretty poorly. So it comes to great surprise just how enjoyable Gunslinger actually is. It embraces its Wild Western theme and delivers the story via a narrator and his audience. In a very clever mechanic, the maps and the gameplay changes on the fly as the story is revised or corrected, adding an extra layer of challenge to the game.
It also helps the gunplay is very solid, with skills in 3 areas that can improve your guns in a variety of ways. Along with a slo-mo ability and a last life dodge mechanic rounds out your abilities.
The particular highlight is the duels. A fairly simple system where you have to watch your oppenant as you prepare your aim and draw. You can kill them before they draw of course, but that just makes you a dishonourable coward. And we can't have that.
It's not a particularly long game however. My current running time is around 3 hours or so, however it does come with new game plus, an arcade mode and a duelling challenge mode. Not to mention collectables that tell you the real story of the various outlaws, villians, hero's and events that the game is set in if you're into that kind of thing.
I came into Gunslinger with low expectations, but the narrative, it's gameplay and even it's stylistic visual comic tones makes Gunslinger a very well rounded title that should be checked out, even if you don't have any interest in the Wild West.

The single greatest example of buyer's satisfaction and the definition of a hidden gem.
On the hardest difficulty it was challenging without being frustrating, daunting like hard mode should be without feeling cheap. The extra modes are great fun but pale in comparison to the story mode.
John Cygan pulled off an amazing performance narrating the game as Silas Greaves and moments where I normally mute a game or roll my eyes at the unfitting voice work, this time I took it all in; "O, Death" was the definition of a well-performed bit of voice acting at just the right moment.
The settings are either lush and dense or proper dusty and drab, but more importantly, always immersive - Cell-shading was a great stylistic choice for this particular game, I feel it brought out the west in a way no other style could.
Details like blowing on your gun barrels after pulling off a particularly wicked bit of shooting are satisfying rather than cheesy, especially when coupled with the great gunplay Gunslinger offers.
All this and much more stuffed into a single game made for an amazing experience, it caught me unawares and is now part of my all-time top 10 list of games.
It's the game I was looking for without knowing it.

This game is fantastic. Beautiful art style, fun combat and gameplay, and boasts strong replay value (a rarity for me).  Instead of the weapon choices of Bastion, you have four separate slots in which you can make different and unique combinations of three different programs each, in addition to four passive slots.  The variety will keep you playing without a doubt. "Dying" removes one of your slots and the program within it until you reach a checkpoint, which forces you to experiment with new combinations if you aren't careful. Soundtrack is breathtaking and truly draws you into the game with the "hummed" overlay when you go into VATS / planning mode. Finally, it's all wrapped up with a cute love story featuring a Narrator™.
Cons:
- Mildly short, but the side content and the replay value does make up for it quite a bit.
- UI is unintuitive and unfriendly (actually a rather large downside considering how much time you spent mixing and matching different programs), but can be navigated once you get used to it.

Shootmania Storm is a really awesome Arena FPS with loads of possibilitys.
It is a very fast paced game, in wich everything is purely about skill. It is easy to learn, but very hard to master.
There is an editor for near to everything, and the community has already made very good use of them and created loads of new gamemodes, maps and other features. That is one of pros.
Also, there is no 'leveling', no skillpoints, no items, every player is playing under exactly the same conditions (except for hardware of course), what also makes this game perfect for competition, wich is one of the main goals of the game: To be an innovative, competitive, popular new e-sports game.
And there lies the problem, among these words: 'popular'.
One of the only cons that come to my mind, no, actually, THE only is the lacking of popularity the game deserves. The community is awesome, but small. Too small. But instead of giving a negative review because of that, I think this is the best reason to give a positive review: Because then more people might notice how good this game is, and play it, instead of being put off by negative reviews. It may be true, there aren't a lot of servers with people on them, but there are servers, at least enough to still properly play the game.
And finally:  The game is free. Well, not officially, but the demo is free. And the demo lets you play the whole game, with the only tiny exceptions being name customization (with colours and stuff) and custom player skins. So you can technically play the whole game, and at the moment (and for quite a while already) the demo can be played infinetly. No 30-day limit or only certain gamemodes.
But if you should play the demo and enjoy it, I would recommend buying the game to support NADEO and even be able to have awesome names like " ツ 〢 ξ〤ה०ा・". In colour!

Dark souls 2 is NOT a sequel to Dark Souls. Though, it retains many of the mechanics of Dark Souls. Dark Souls 2 does fix specific problems in the first game, but for every fix their's a new issue.
The smithing system is greatly improved. Magic is greatly improved, featuring greater balance. This game is also more forgiving of long term mistakes that felt downright unfair in the last game, allowing for respec and providing the player with more upgrade materials.
I'm a PvE player primarily, so all I can say about PvP is that it's fun, but lag continues to trouble From Software's titles. I feel like there were a lot of design oversights in this game. A lot of reviews on youtube and such talk about how this game is nothing compared to what fans were shown in the demo. The graphics are worse, there's no significant need for the lighting system, etc. I feel this focus on graphics and lighting downgrades are valid, but there are more significant issues. The agility stat and item placement being the major ones. Though I personally enjoy this game a lot more than most Souls fans. I can't say it's better, but I pick this game up more often than the last title.
In spite of all the negative points, this remains one of my favorite games and I'd recommend it to anyone interested in a mechanic driven RPG.

This game is fun, but it's extremely casual.

Every time you advance past the boss for that dimension you will essentially be reset to your beginning point, no items, no heros, no gold.  You will keep any tavern upgrades, except, of course the sodas.
Each dimension is essentially the exact dungeon you just went through, only they add 100 levels.  Gameplay gets extremely repetative.
In my experience, you can employ strategy to aid you against certain bosses by changing your party or equipped items, but you'll likely find yourself auto-equipping out of pure boredom and laziness by dimension 3.  There are 10 dimensions.  This means going through 5500 rooms, repeatedly, on auto (most likely).
Somehow, this game is still highly addictive.  The cash shop is reasonably priced, especially considering that with the resets and the amount of grinding you'll have to do, I can't see any reason to spend any money in game.
I leave this review with a recommend.  It's a fun game, I sunk days into it, it's just that after awhile, it became difficult to want to play.  There didn't seem to be much incentive for finishing it.  Still, for the laughs I had, the nerdy references, and the hours saved from complete monotony, I appreciate this game.

If I were to sum up Just Cause 3 in one sentence. I would say that Just Cause 2 is to a Big Mac as Just Cause 3 is to a hastily prepared Double Big Mac. Which may sound like a good thing at first, but because Just Cause 3 came out after Just Cause 2, it just couldn't quite delivers the same impact. So if you haven't played Just Cause 2, go play that instead as it is much better composed overall.
Pors:
1. More weapons, especially the explosive kind. Which isn't a bad thing per say. But personally, the only addition that I find interesting is the Eden Spark, which isn't even included in the base game.
2. Nice graphics/environment. I really wish you could jump into the world of Just Cause 3 with Oculus Rift because it looks like a really nice vacation spot. However, perhaps it's because the dev put so much more attention to finer details, there weren't as many big cityscape like in Just Cause 2, or interesting location like the mile high club, or that really fancy casino at the start of Just Cause 2.
3. Nice soundtrack. Especially the open world music. Again, with Oculus Rift, it feels like I could spend an entire after noon just chilling on a beach and maybe reading a book (if someone figure out how to add an overlay that lets me read books in a virtual environment)
Cons:
1. Story. After I play Just Cause 2 I comment during a stream somewhere that Just Cause 2's story really lack luster. but when I started playing Just Cause 3, my low expectation was completely shattered. Because not only was Just Cause 3's story bad, it's near incoherent; most character and faction wasn't properly introduced and merely got thrown at your face. I think partly it's because it's an open world game, and then there's additional DLC added to the mix that made the progression that much more unpredictable (i.e: new player could play DLC 3 before playing DLC 1). In short, story in Just Cause series are the things that you really shouldn't think too much about or else you get a headache.
2. Bad facial animation. I don't generally hold a high standard with in game cutscene. Imagine how bad it has to be for me to notice it's inadequacy. There is this scene where the antagonist ordered one of his soldier to kill himself where as the soldier swallowed a bullet with a poker face. Come on Dev, I'm not expecting Oscar performance, but please at least put in some half decent effort to emote, pull an eyebrow for christ sake.
3. Everything blows up, sometimes on it's own. Some people might wonder how this is a bad thing. I got two word for you : "escort mission". I like explosion as much as the next guy but when they make your escort target equally flamable it gets really annoying when you have to babysit your target to safety.
4. Multiplayer. Honestly I'm not sure how this went over their head. Maybe the suits is squeezing the dev hard to release the game early or they figured multiplayer could come out as a DLC. But for some reason, after the success of Just Cause 2 fan modded multiplayer mode, the Dev decided to release Just Cause 3 without multiplayer. Amazing.
In short. It's hard to recommend Just Cause 3 at this price. It's certainly prettier compare to Just Cause 2. But it plays out more or less the same compare to its predecessor. It even hides some additional fun content in DLCs as well. So even though the game isn't inherently bad per say, but it definitely lackluster and expensive at it's full price. Don't get this game unless it's on sale.

This game topped my charts as my all-time favorite. The combat is complex yet wonderful, allowing for dozens of different weapon combinations, from extra range to making enemies fall in love with you and help you out for a little while. The combat has two functions: One that lets you pause and plan your moves strategically, and another that lets you go all out and spam your abilities till you kill all those ♥♥♥♥ing dogs that- ahem, moving on. The story is really well done, ensnaring the player and making you want to push forward to find out what happens next. But be forewarned- If you're looking for a story telling experience similar to SuperGiant's last game, Bastion, you've come to the wrong place. The main character Red is incredibly well developed, a singer in the city of Cloudbank who mysteriously loses her voice when injured lightly by yet another mystery: The Transistor. The game's music leaves nothing to be desired, sung by non other than Ashley Lynn Barrell, who voiced Zia and sang the female parts in Bastion. The music fits the game perfectly, and hits the heart like truly good music should.

God this is such a good game. Worth every cent. Beautiful art, soundtrack, gameplay. I'm not saying I am experienced at critiquing video games, but I really can't find a flaw with this game. The combat system is somewhat alike to that of VATS in the Fallout series (3 and Vegas). Except it's much better. This isn't as much hack and slash as Bastion. Transistor takes quite a bit more thinking involved if you want to get out of a battle unscathed. Hell, I have trouble keeping my abilities from crashing in boss battles. I would have definitely have paid full price for this had I known how good it was beforehand. Worth keeping Supergiant in business so that they can produce more amazing games.

Transistor is pretty much everything you'd expect from the creators of Bastion: beautiful soundtrack, beautiful art, beautiful story, and beautifully unique gameplay. If I have any complaint about it, it's that the main story doesn't offer a long enough stay in a world as captivating as Cloudbank, but there's plenty of reason to play through again to uncover as much as you can about it. An absolutely superb game.

This game is fantastic. Beautiful art style, fun combat and gameplay, and boasts strong replay value (a rarity for me).  Instead of the weapon choices of Bastion, you have four separate slots in which you can make different and unique combinations of three different programs each, in addition to four passive slots.  The variety will keep you playing without a doubt. "Dying" removes one of your slots and the program within it until you reach a checkpoint, which forces you to experiment with new combinations if you aren't careful. Soundtrack is breathtaking and truly draws you into the game with the "hummed" overlay when you go into VATS / planning mode. Finally, it's all wrapped up with a cute love story featuring a Narrator™.
Cons:
- Mildly short, but the side content and the replay value does make up for it quite a bit.
- UI is unintuitive and unfriendly (actually a rather large downside considering how much time you spent mixing and matching different programs), but can be navigated once you get used to it.

I picked this up for $13.50 when it was on sale. I figured if I got a few hours of enjoyment out of it, it'd be worth it. Just playing as a single player, I've been able to go quite far and have enjoyed my time in Tamriel thus far. I've even had the itch to spend real money on micro transactions. Only problem is.... they're not so micro... and the pay plan is convoluted and not very user friendly. I decided to dig in for the long haul and grinded until I could afford a horse. That was the first milestone! What I'm finding though is that no amount of grinding can get you all the items you may want, you're just gonna have to pay up. Nope, not this boy.... and not at the prices it would cost. I'm just gonna keep playing until it looses its lustre. That being said, Elder Scrolls Online is a fun online game, and the single player experience is pretty good too. Definitely worth the purchase, and definitely recommended!
Edit - Although I do recommend it, EOS can feel like a cash grab if you buy into the Crown Store. It's bloody expensive. I actually regret not getting the Gold verion for $39.99 with all DLC, because now to add it, I have to buy $50 worth of crowns just to add it to the Tamriel edition. Everything in the Crown Store is stupid expensive... and really, I would have spent money if I felt the pricing was fair, but no, the pricing is over inflated for EVERYTHING and just feels like a greedy cash grab.
- at this point in any other game I would have had the ability to add to my storage. You'll be surprised how fast 60 slots fills up. So you're constantly running to merchants to sell stuff. Every time you enter a big battle, you get the "no room left" warning when you go to pick up loot, so looting almost becomes pointless... and you ccan't buy extra bags.
- mounts in most other games are achievable if you've grinded enough. EOS gives you access to basic mounts only, through in game gold. Anything special, you have to open your wallet.
- the addition of housing.... forget it, unless you have lots of cash to sink into it.
- merchants offer nothing better than what you've found in-game. The only value to merchants is to sell stuff quickly, repair damaged armor, and to grab potions and lockpicks if you need them.
- You have to make sure you carry extra weapons as they cannot be repaired. The repair all function at merchants only applies to armor.

I'm loving the game, but refuse to support the bottomless money pit this experience threatens to be. It's unfortunate too, because I think there's probably a lot of players out there like me who wouldn't mind spending the money if prices were more consumer friendly. As it is, if you love these type of games and treat them like second lives, you've probably already sunk a month's rent into it by now... and really, you're the type of players this game is catering to.
Even after all that, I still recommend it, and feel you'll get your money's worth in hours alone.

Amazing game! I purchased this during the 2014 Steam Summer sale and I can say that I don't regret the purchase at all..... This is a true wild west tale with a deep story, beautiful environments, fast gameplay, focus on REAL historical Wild West figures, and more! I thoroughly enjoyed the title, so much so that I sat down and played it through in one sitting. It took me about 5 hours to complete the story on Normal difficulty. Now i've unlocked New Game+ and True West difficulty. Now i just have to start my achievement hunting and play the Arcade and Duel modes all the way through!
There were a few things that I can say that were annoyances rather than flat out bad..... The paths are EXTREMELY linear in this game, so don't worry about getting lost. Along the same lines, there is a fairly repetitive setup for the gun fights with the standard bandit NPCs....
1) Run down path
2) Get ambushed by 10-20 NPCs
3) Kill all NPCs
4) Repeat
Now this doesn't REALLY take away from the enjoyability of the gun fights as you're constantly gaining levels to add to your 'skill tree' which changes the mechanics. Also, the variability in the environment keeps it fresh enough through the game, but I know this is going to be an issue for some people.
The last slightly negative aspect of the game for me was visibility in some of the areas. Most of the issues were with the areas with dense foliage, as the enemies tend to blend in really badly and as we all know, they have perfect vision through brush... I would say that this was intentional to up the difficulty a little bit, but it was actually to the point of hurting my eyes.... There was also one point in the game where it's dusk and you're defusing dynamite on the wooden supports for train tracks. The light, wood, and rock were practically the same color, so I spent a lot of time squinting trying to see the bandits as well as my path.
Overall I'm actually going to give this game an 8/10. It's highly enjoyable and is a must buy for any fan of Westerns and FPS.
I plan to update this review once I replay the story mode through the different difficulties and added modes.

Massive lag, cumbersome multiplayer features, riddled with glitches; none of it stops the unstoppable
from being an absolute blast to play with my bros.
A delightful and hilarious alternative to
, this 2D bullet hell side scroller from
goes deep with the "bro" humor on everything. Just look at that character roster: Rambro, Bro Dredd, the Brominator, Bro in Black, Indiana Brones, Bronan the Brobarian?! The list goes on. Truly ridiculous, over the top boss fights (that eventually become doable) are part of the laughs. The enemies, camera shake, story cutscenes, achievements, the "Area Liberated" screen with one liner captions, a kill counter and electric guitar riffs at the end of every mission; every little detail feeds into the theme. I've never been so impressed with a homage to the greatest action flicks of all time and their heroes.
I'm no expert on this genre but from what I can tell the gameplay is very tight and well executed. I like how each Bro gets a distinct weapon, special ability and unique trait. Those are fun to figure out. I especially enjoyed how you can find Bros in the field and switch to them on the fly. Adds some fluidity that very much feels like it belongs in a game like this. It's great in cooperative play to be the last man standing and pull off a comeback by finding some Bros along the way (dead teammates can respawn as Bros you rescue).
There's a ton of environmental hazard and incoming fire. Destructible terrain has hysterical, deadly result when you drop a pile of boulders on a friend or blast the ground out from under his jump. I find myself losing lives left and right. You definitely have to stay on your toes the entire time or wind up dead and letting your friends carry (bro, that is shameful). For the pros, difficulty can be upped from Normal to Hard; and there's Ironbro mode. Versus gameplay includes deathmatch and races. Arcade mode skips all story stuff to focus on action.
Audio fits the theme admirably. On visuals I have equally little to say except that I think they did a great job with the characters. I love that pixilated chopper you cruise around in for mission selection on the world map, too.
For a game that offers fast paced fun, it's not as accessible as it could be. Bear in mind for Steam users, you'll need to have the setting for playing online with Steam users set to "NO" under the options. Baffling. The ping was pretty bad at times, though I'm not sure what the server situation is. I would sometimes get stuck, or camera positioning would go crazy, or respawning would stop working. Inability to invite or join others, disconnections and so on. Actually being able to join and remain in a game together with friends for any length of time proved taxing. We did manage to get through parts of the game and see the end together.
I played with the Steam Controller which worked just fine once I had it properly configured. Decidedly more natural than mouse & keyboard for this game. The same level editor the developers use is included in game. There's a pile of custom campaigns, but I haven't tried those yet.
There's my serious review for a silly game.

The story goes : a squad of Earth’s greatest heroes (and heroines)  –  against the worst that international terrorism, the galaxy, and the underworld itself can throw at humanity. Frankly, it’s bloody fantastic (and spectacularly bloody).
Unforgiving but (mostly) fair, frantic yet tactical, and oozing with 16-bit 2D charm, if Broforce had been released two decades ago I expect it probably would’ve been the greatest thing to happen to gaming back then. To me Broforce remains an incredibly confident, refined, unique, and content-rich run ’n gun shooter for up to four co-op players to this very day.
The objective of most levels is simple; you just need to blast and/or dart your way through several different locations and very literally get to the chopper. Some of the later levels change this up somewhat as the enemies segue from enemy soldiers to aliens, and later again to supernatural nasties.
Mechanics are fairly simple : normal enemies die in 1 shot ; you die in 1 shot. Broforce’s nearly completely destructible environments makes for really interesting engagements. Blast through walls to access buildings and get the drop on the enemies inside, or fire through the ground itself to tunnel beneath potential engagements.
The large team of varied bros themselves are the big stars, and there are plenty of them. Rambro, Brommando, B.A. Broracus, Double Bro Seven, The Brofessional; by now you’re probably picking up on the theme. Every single bro has its unique ability and weapons. Some are melee-focused, some have powerful, short-range weapons, some can fire longer distances, and some are unfortunately completely useless.
Controls are fully customizable. Your bro can shoot, climb walls, crouch, sprint...
You run around and kill people or aliens. When you die if you have lives (you can see how many you have in bottom left of the screen) you are forcibly swapped to a random new bro. You can get more lives by saving people in cages (by deastroying the cage)
You can make you own levels, play with people online or play community made maps.
If you like silly and
run 'n gun platformer this is a game for you! If you have some friends this game will be forth your money. Singleplayer is about 16 hours long (depending on how good you are). There are some really hard achivements if you want a challenge. I personaly recommend it!

It's Friday night. When you don't have anywhere to go, you're a fan of spending Friday nights sitting on your computer playing games until past midnight. One week, you're looking to get yourself invested into something new. Not just a quick hour or two of gameplay. With beautiful visuals, a goosebump-inducing soundtrack, and puzzle-like combat inspired by turn-based games, Transistor is just this kind of game. Centered around the adventures of Red and and the titular techno-sword "the Transistor," you journey through a city with a mysterious digital and steampunk hybrid aesthetic fighting off an unknown enemy trying to seek justice for the past.
I highly recommend this game for those looking for replayability, a short, invested storyline, puzzle mechanics, power combining mechanics, music, and visuals.

What can I say about this game that already hasn't been said. If you liked Bastion, you'll enjoy this. It's not quite as action RPG oriented as Bastion, but the Turn() system is actually really intuitive and easy to pick up. If you enjoyed the narrator from Bastion, he's back as well - though in a role that's a little different, though I think is much better than his previous one. There's also a little less story and immediate exposition given to you this time, you'll have to play around with the different skills (called Functions()) in different slots in order to get some more background and story. With that being said however, I can understand why people wouldn't like this as much as Bastion - it's definitely a different game, not just Bastion with a reskin. However, I highly recommend it if you want beautiful artwork, a wonderful soundtrack, an interesting (if somewhat sparse) story, and a unique take on action RPGs.

I just completed my first playthrough of the main campaign on normal difficulty and I have to say that this is one of the most atmospheric games I have ever played!  As a true Alien fan (movies, books, etc.), I really feel that CA captured the feeling of being aboard a spaceship in the Alien universe out in deep space.  I won't ruin any storyline elements, but the pacing is on par, in my opinion.  The alien itself is scary and you'll find yourself feeling like you want to hold your breath in real life when you see/hear it nearby.  The humans/synthetics aboard the station are also very well done, though my one complaint is the way the characters' mouths move when speaking.  I spent about 20-25 hours on my playthrough, as I took a bit of time to explore the station as carefully as I could with the alien around.  I plan to play it again at some point in the future on hard difficulty, as I did find that I had maxed out items towards the end of the game.  I would suggest normal for your first playthrough, as it is still difficult and allows you to really enjoy the environment that is dripping with the Alien movies' major and minor details.  On a scale of 1-10, I would give Alien: Isolation a 9!
As a side note, I have barely scratched the surface of the DLC content, but I would highly suggest the main game and the DLC be purchased together, especially if you are able to get them on sale.  Please don't miss out on this masterpiece, especially if you consider yourself a true Alien fan.

1. Yes, hackers can be a problem but I haven't had too much of an issue with them. I found a server with good admin and hackers don't make it far. It took some time but they're out there. Now with anti-cheat, it's even better.
2. Many negative reviews are from people who get creamed because they obviously don't know how to be tactical and patient. You can't run around in the open and expect to be left alone. There are a lot of nice players out there but there are plenty that only want your head for the thrill. Use your head to keep your head!
I typically stay under radar. Keep your head down until you're strong enough to fight off people. Learn to fight! You can't pull out a sniper rifle and one shot here. Combat takes patience and understanding of weapons, armor and moves. There's a lot to learn so don't expect to be a pro anytime soon. For practice, go play Chivalry.
Harvest at night and stay indoors in the day! Don't be stupid, people.
If you don't like being KoS'ed then stay away from other players. That means you may have to hide until their gone and run from the resources until you can come back. That's called surviving people. It's not the game's fault.
3. Toughest thing is if you play by yourself. It's tough to keep your base strong and unraided but its totally possible if you stay low-key or go play a role play server.
4. Tons of content in this game. I haven't laughed so hard in a game before. I was LMAO as soon as I started creating a character.
5. Sure - this game has♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off a lot but with time and practice I've become a lot better. Just like with DayZ, WarZ, Chivalry, Rust, 7DTD and any other game.
There's a lot more to be said about this game but I really like it. I've met some cool players in this game and I'm looking forward to seeing what else it will become. It's what Rust could've and should've been.

I downloaded this game a few years back. I saw Cry and Pewds play it back int he day and I decided I'd get it when I could. I finally did. I mostly played with my brother but after that, after having put nine hours into the game , I dropped it because it became boring to me.
The game felt very unfinished, as if it hadn't actually left greenlight. Setting up servers proved to be a hassle, and I found you could only really play with friends who weren't local, was to play on a pre-existing server. Either I was doing something wrong, or this game's Gui wasn't properly implimented. Again, very unfinished and rushed. I'm hoping the sequel will be done better, that is assuming they're hoping to improve upon what they did last time.
That being said, the game was fun at the time. I fondly recall shooting myself without any rhyme or reason, leaving my brother to fend for himself, and, in cases I found most humorous, fight off a hord that has surrounded him with no hope of escape.
It's a game of survival, and survivability is pretty low with a two man squad so bring mate's for a good time. You'll need to work together, it's very unforgiving. Limited weapons, limited ammo, mostly melee weapons, aim for the head, classic Romero zombies.
To clarify, I haven't played enough of it to make a big enough review, this is just my initial impressions from the nine hours I gathered, I haven't even touched the game in over two years so if they've made improvements to the Gui, which I doubt, I wouldn't know.
My hopes for the sequel, is that they focus more on developing the server setup, map selection, gameplay. The realistic approach they've taken is perfect, what I mean is, character customization, that seems to be very lacking in this game, if not implimented badly from my experience. Better maps would be nice too. And a Steam workshop if at all possible. I wouldn't mind downloading a Raccoon City based map and playing with some buds with that.
I fully trust the Dev team and understand if they can't focus real big like that. We'll have to see but that's half my hopes for the sequel, which I pray will improve over this game.

Factorio is a great game with loads of content, and I love that they are still adding more stuff. This review will not focus on why I think the game is awesome, because there are thousands that will make that point for me. So instead, I will try to help you understand how you co-op.
I've had loads of trouble trying to play multiplayer, and I've spent hours trying to fix it. I've tried Hamachi, Dedicated servers, starting my own headless server, and Evolve. Playing co-op wasn't an easy task, but finally I've managed it. For me what works was Evolve.
Now I'm going to explain a little bit on how you do it.
If you are doing it simple, install Evolve and form a party with your friends, and then connect to the Evolve host IP. No port needed, no portforwarding needed, just simple. There are also a lot of help found on forums and simple google searches for troubleshooting. The only problem I encountered with Evolve was that my network would not connect to the party. That was fixed through some weird stuff I really didn't understand, but it included setting a value number (0) on the Evolve Network.
Hamachi, I never got you to work...
Headless server: Now this, this was the problem I wrapped my head around for a long time. In short: if you do NOT have access to your router, you should probably skip this one, as it requires port forwarding. If you do, however, you would need two computers to host and play on a server. This is because one of the computers will function as a server, and the other as player. If you do NOT have two computers, but still want to create a headless server, you may want to google "Virtual Ocean" (have fun with that, not for beginners). However, if you DO have two computers, then it's fairly "easy". You just need to create a batch file that says: start /wait Factorio.exe --start-server "YOURSAVEFILE.zip". You do this in a txt document and save it as server.bat as "all files", not "text files". Then, start the server and you should be able to join it by using your IP address and the port: 34197 (unless you altered it in a config file). There are detailed guides all over the forums, so it shouldn't be too hard. However, you may encounter the problem that I had: "Request for connection denied", and something like another peers is allready in use or something. I didn't figure this one out, but I suspect it's due to my lack of port forwarding, which I can't do, due to school network.
If you just want to play on a dedicated server, you shouldn't worry. Then just copy their listed IP and port. If there isn't any port, the Factorio port is as mentioned 34197. Example of full IP+port: 10.245.25.31:34197 (not real btw).
So, to sum up: get evolve.
Also, protip: beware of trains. They are more dangerous than any enemy.

It's Friday night. When you don't have anywhere to go, you're a fan of spending Friday nights sitting on your computer playing games until past midnight. Centered around the adventures of Red and and the titular techno-sword "the Transistor," you journey through a city with a mysterious digital and steampunk hybrid aesthetic fighting off an unknown enemy trying to seek justice for the past.
I highly recommend this game for those looking for replayability, a short, invested storyline, puzzle mechanics, power combining mechanics, music, and visuals.

Emily is Away is an... interesting game indeed.
This is one of those games I can't decide if I should or should not reccomend it, but the fact that it is a free experience, and that for the first run, at least, I think that makes it worthwhile for an hour or two time waster.
Tl;DR: The game has an amazing premise but the thing that spoils the experience is the ending, while pretending to have multiple endings there is really only 1 with variations and it spoils the idea of choice. A good and bad ending should have been implimented, maybe not full hate or full love, but at least one that lets you keep in touch or one where she is very hurt and decideds to end the friendship herself, something to make it seem worthwhile and give each choice some heft.
Full Review:
The Premise of EiA is that you live the life of a boy who is friends with Emily, and the two of you interact with an interesting story crossing a 5 year span from 2002-2006 where you both grow up trying to stay in contact, but ultimately failing by the end. The idea is the whole "its not the destination, but the journey" type of concept, and while it seems good on paper, the end result feels... unfufilling. Its one of those instances where one might stand there and wonder to one's self "What was the honest point? Sure its fun but after the first run or 2... eh."
The meat of the game comes in the journey as you, the player, talk to emily on good ole' AOL in Windows XP. As you go through your lives you talk about what is happening between each other, console each other, and try to continue your friendship as you grow ever more distant, all hitting a climax in '04 where, to prevent spoiling, things happen and Emily becomes distant from you in some way, depending on the thing, and eventually you can trade small talk in '06 before YOU are away (Deep I know *sliiiight sarcasm*)
What the game loses me on is the buildup to one big *PFFT* of nothing. After that one sad moment, another runthrough shows... drumroll... NOTHING NEW. Sure there are varients but its always the same goodbye emily, you are no longer friends because reasons.
It really kills the potential for replayability; but more importantly this lack of branch endings leaves a sour taste to the pallets of those looking for at least some semblance of choice, or even deeper meanings in the lack there of. Sure the game doesn't need the whole get the girl thing, but its such a dull note that makes one sit there and question the validity of even trying again. It kills the whole buildup all these choices the player makes, and just makes the whole game feel hollow at its core. I know this seems like rambiling on a small part of the game, but it is the fundemental part that the game leads up to the entire time.
2 Things are needed, in my opinion, and potentially yours, to make this game feel complete.
1: A slightly happier ending, sure it doesn't need to be a "you get the girl and live happily ever after" thing, but at least one where the player stays in touch. And yes, try some variation on that note to help give meaning to choices.
2: A more Somber ending, again, no need for extremes, but maybe the bad ending(s) have Emily feel more... distant than the neutral, maybe a bit uncomfortable to talk to the player and she decides to end the friendship.
Its not that the game is bad, but it needs something to give the game more weight. Not just 2 tacked on good and bad endings but a scale of at least ok to not the best feeling. The game has an ending premise that is meant to build that feeling of lack of choice, but there is giving the FEELING of lack of choice, which can be deep and meaningful, and then just giving us the ILLUSION of choice and ripping it out from under us, making the game feel like every choice will just lead to the same goodbye. I feel as though the game could have been much better if the lack of choice came from you not being able to go out with emily, but still at least being friends, as it would give the heft to each choice needed to make the game feel more filling and give a much bigger impact the 2nd 3rd, 4th, and so-on time around.
Overall I'd say this game just needs some meat at the end to give it more weight and fill out some extra replayability. As a FREE 1-2 hour time waster, I can see it. But don't be surprised if you get bored of it after 1 or 2 playthroughs.
*Kind of a personal opinion but I think the story is so cheezy in the whole "long distance kills relationships of all forms" department, that even though its really enticing, you could still slap some tomato sauce in there and pull a lasagna out.

I just completed my first playthrough of the main campaign on normal difficulty and I have to say that this is one of the most atmospheric games I have ever played!  As a true Alien fan (movies, books, etc.), I really feel that CA captured the feeling of being aboard a spaceship in the Alien universe out in deep space.  I won't ruin any storyline elements, but the pacing is on par, in my opinion.  The alien itself is scary and you'll find yourself feeling like you want to hold your breath in real life when you see/hear it nearby.  The humans/synthetics aboard the station are also very well done, though my one complaint is the way the characters' mouths move when speaking.  I spent about 20-25 hours on my playthrough, as I took a bit of time to explore the station as carefully as I could with the alien around.  I plan to play it again at some point in the future on hard difficulty, as I did find that I had maxed out items towards the end of the game.  I would suggest normal for your first playthrough, as it is still difficult and allows you to really enjoy the environment that is dripping with the Alien movies' major and minor details.  On a scale of 1-10, I would give Alien: Isolation a 9!
As a side note, I have barely scratched the surface of the DLC content, but I would highly suggest the main game and the DLC be purchased together, especially if you are able to get them on sale.  Please don't miss out on this masterpiece, especially if you consider yourself a true Alien fan.

Fun, compelling game, arguably one of the best of the franchise. The plot seems to have a few holes, but the locations are varied and interesting enough and the action is intense enough to make you not notice for the most part.

NOTE: This game does NOT require Ubisoft's UPlay!
Despite Call of Juarez's sometimes claustrophibic sheep-herding, as it urges you through falsely narrow towns and forests, the game's mode of story telling makes it stand out as an enjoyable 6-hour adventure and good old-fashioned, Western shoot-em-up.
Silas, the protagonist and unreliable story teller, manages to make the re-telling of his (and your) adventures interesting and engaging. The voice acting throughout is well done and believable. The game is often little more than a carnival shooting gallery, but the theme carries it past its flaws and leaves a good taste, after the dust settles.
Aside from its story mode, it also offers the chance to challenge and improve against onself and friends alike, by way of the secondary "Arcade" and "Duel" modes. These are quick and hectic fun, especially great if you only have a few minutes on hand and want a game to gobble those minutes up.
In all, I'd recommend this game if you catch it on sale at the $10 or less range, or are otherwise gnawing your hands off looking for a straight and fun shooter that offers a great, thematic experience outside the typical fare.

So after I took my first Early Access shot with Offworld Trading, I decided that I should try some of these smaller independent projects instead of bigger AAA titles and the Russian roulette of pre-order. I wasn't disappointed.
Factorio is deceptively simple and amazingly complex, and I found myself easily getting sucked in as I continually gathered, built, and repaired. The mechanics are simple, the crafting system relatively easy to understand, and even though I've barely made it to the stage of the game where I can build radar systems, I'm not easily able to stop and turn to something else on my computer. Only Fallout has immersed me more, and this game managed to do it for the low price of $20. Definitely a game for when you get home after a long day and just want to relax.
As far as downsides go, I can't see where the eventual endgame is, though this will probably arrive with the final product. Also, perhaps the factories can produce materials more quickly? I keep hitting walls when it comes to production. But then, that's a nitpick, and nitpicks are the specks of dust on what is in this case a full three-course meal.
I can't wait to see the full version, and hope that the developers continue to expand an already amazing game world.
EDIT: Having said all this, I do notice that certain objects in the game aren't readily obvious as to their function. Maybe some short tooltips or an encyclopedia that the player can view to get a better picture of what certain machines do?

8/10
50 hours of mind-twisting fun, 5 hours of boredom. The progression of difficulty is almost perfect. Most of the time, your production can always be done the slow and manual, or the complicated automatic way, so that you will never feel overwhelmed by new items and their production lines, since you could also just produce the items by hand without much thought. Tus, it almost always feels like it was your choice to develop new factory systems and you will not quit playing the game because the next step is to hard to achieve.
Some say, the enemies are just annoying and should be turned off, but I think they add a lot to the game, since you always need to consider, if a new production is really necessary to build, or if the resulting pollution could lure in too many enemies.
The only thing I didn't like is the late game shortly before you finish it. Your goal is to build a giant rocket with a satellite aboard and to send it to space. As soon as you managed to develop every production line for this, the last 5-10 hours of the game are just an annoying repetition of firstly fending of the same enemies over and over again with no chance of destroying their spawn ultimately and secondly of finding new sources of ore as soon as the old mines are depleted. The rest of the time is waiting for the damn production to finish, as speding up your production would only lure in more enemies.
Some features of the game seemed relatively useless though: The train system looks nice, but you will not really need many trains to finish the game and thus a complex rail signal network seems pointless. The same is true for the signal network, which I did not use at all (also because the game does not explain anything about how it works). And as cool as the logistic robots seem to be, most of the time they just seem to be useful, when you are too lazy to set up organized transport belts, as the robots are just too expensive, slow and lacking inventory space. In general, most of the technology you can research in the game is a bit disappointing when you finally come to use it. Why build a sophisticated armor with energy fields, when your trusty old tank is still the best bet in the end? Why should you surround yourself with extremely expensive short-lived combat drones that require huge amounts of research, if you never face an enemy without walls or a tank between you?
But apart from the rather boring last hours and many pointless, though interesting features, it is still a great game that pushes your strategic thinking to the limit so that you can stare at your own factory in awe.

**I have played this game in iCBT 2 (I think it was 2) and I have watched enough streamers to know what I am talking about**
Edit: Spruced up review a little, fixed a couple of grammatical mistakes that I missed. Improved clarity of some parts. Prefaced my F2P experience with my iCBT experience.
I wanted to like this game, I really, really really did. I've been waiting for months for it to come out for F2P, I watched Etup grind for hours on his stream, basking in the huge variety of classes (like one class that can plant grass, friggin grassplanter support dude...) and hyping me and some friends up for it for the longest time.
And it only took two days before we got completely fed up with the bullsh*t.
Now, I didn't get all too frustrated when I was playing iCBT, I was gunning for the Alchemist class (which is probably a mistake, fair warning) but was stuck on Tenet Chapel at around Level 35~40 because I didn't have any leveling guides at the time. I fell into the same "trap" that I will explain later on in this review. There was nothing to tell me that I could have gone to the Orsha side of the map after starting on Klaipeda.
Further, I was experiencing a HUGE problem with MP consumption. I was nearly bankrupted all the time because of how much I had to spend on MP potions and how I have to chug them constantly. Again, without some sort of leveling guide to tell me that spellcasters who love to spam spells should heavily prioritize SPR over INT (and maybe get some CON for solo survivability but I was doing that anyway).
First of all, lets look back at the catastrophe that was the Closed Beta. It was a bit of a lagfest then and apparently IMC didn't get the memo that it was time to beef up their servers in anticipation of the huge influx of players that would come on F2P release. They didn't do a damn thing except release a 2nd SEA server. There are STILL too few channels in critical maps and STILL too many channels in spots people will breeze by or not even smirk at.
Second we have how awful it is to party sometimes. All of you are on the same quest, but when one of you turns in that quest and it just so happens to lead into a boss fight immediately with no warning, your friends are pulled into your instance, and upon beating the boss, there's a very good chance that you will have to fight that same boss again (and again depending on how many are in your party) so your friends can complete their quests, because I'm sure it's because you didn't coordinate turning in the same quest at the same time and waiting before moving onto the next part. It's still bullsh*t that this is even a thing. Don't force people into boss fights upon accepting a quest.
Next we have spawn rates, amount of mobs, and drop rates and how, when these factors are tied with how many people need a certain mob for something. The spawn rates are absolutely abysmal in most areas. The quest mob needed for the Hoplite advancement in Tenet B1? Takes roughly 2 minutes to spawn.
Everyone knows this. Everyone has complained about this on the forums as far back as Closed Beta. And yet IMC doesn't do anything about it.
The amount of mobs needed for quests (even critical advancement quests) are too few and sometimes the spawn rates are abysmal to compensate for this issue. The quest mob for the Hoplite advancement? There are only two of them, period.
Everyone knows this. Everyone has complained about this on the forums about it. IMC doesn't do anything...
Then when you add in a *chance* for a quest item to drop on these mobs that are too few and take too long to spawn, you're adding salt to the wound and giving a big middle finger to the players (especially some Swordsmen advacement quests). The Hoplite advancement? Yep, you guessed it. That mob that takes a long, long time to spawn and are too few and far between... has a *chance* to drop his quest loot.
Everyone knows this. Everyone has complained about this on the forums about it. And IMC hasn't done a d*mn thing about this.
Now lets talk about the one thing that is probably on everyone's mind:
How bad is the grind?
It can get bad. Really bad. Back to what I said during my iCBT experiences, about how I didn't have any leveling guide on-hand and thought it was a good idea to pop your Level 3 (and up) EXP Cards instead of saving them to skip past the grind spots, well, if you did that... you're in for the ride of your life, because good luck kid, you're gonna be stuck grinding in a known "horrible grinding spot" that the people who wrote those leveling guides compel you to skip past.
And even still, when you hit the higher levels (200+), most of your time will be spent grinding quite a bit per day just to hit one or two levels (and I'm talking 10-15-ish hour sessions).
Now most people won't mind this, it's not like Dungeon Fighter where there's a Stamina system in place, and there's nothing to pressure you into leveling in a certain amount of time, but I would want the leveling and grinding experience to be a little more smoother and a lot less tedious and monotonous. I'm sure if I had played as long as it would take to reach the level 200s~, I would've already made 50 alt characters/accounts to experience all of the different classes and give up on it, because the endgame... well...
All of the experienced and battle-beaten players who have managed to reached endgame knows...
there is no f*cking endgame except one dungeon and world bosses that are camped endlessly. Let's face it, Etup had already moved on from this game as soon as he hit max level. Some of his friends didn't even bother to reach max level before they stopped playing. They aren't coming back unless IMC comes out with some new content, but God only knows when that will be, they won't even listen to the players to fix the issues everyone is complaining about.
I only wish IMC took the time to make themselves stand out from all the other F2P games out there in a positive matter, not giving themselves the negative reputation they are giving themselves now. We should have listened to the reviews on the Korean's take on KToS, about how IMC doesn't give two sh*ts about the playerbase and how they are driving their Ragnarok Online successor into the ground.
Play at your own risk of frustration and bullsh*t, but to me, it was a waste of time.

Transistor is from the creators of the Critcally Acclaimed game Bastion, Supergiant Games. Only just over an hour into the game and I have already found my GOTY. Transistor's Visuals are stunning, the hand painted look brings the characters and City to lif. The soundtrack is superb, if you've picked up the game at all you know first hand how wonderful the score is, the accompanying humming is haunting and beautiful. The combat system is innovative and fresh, it plays heavily into tactics and the game features a pleasant challenge as-is. However, like Bastion, Transistor features its own way to bring up the difficulty if you feel like shouldering more. The return of Logan "Rucks" Cunningham as your narrator adds to the dreamy atmosphere of the game. Transistor is a beautiful game, I highly recommend it to anyone who was a fan of Bastion or is looking for an action RPG with great visuals and sound, a gripping story and innovative combat.

First of all: I'm kinda a veteran in this game series and the major reason I bought this game was because of this, I was a fan of it. But after playing it a lot I simply cannot recommend it unless you get it for free, then you may kill some hours with it.
First the pluspoints: Ofc the marine battles are kinda the best advantage over the old Rome: Total War (1) and they're fun, though really messy and hardly controllable with like 40 ships (unless you pause the game). The new region boni are nice as well, the interface is good and looks nice. There might be some other good points that I forget to mention but that's jsut because the bad points outweigh everything else so hard. Let's get right into them:
First of all: The AI. Where should I start? It sucks in battle, it sucks on the campaign and sucks overall. It's diplomatic behavior is sometimes just plain stupid and senseless and it will never be able to lead a large scale war. Once you've established yourself as major power, the rest of the game is kinda grinding.
Siege battles which pose the biggest possibility for epic gameplay are - at least as defender (let's be honest: that's nicer) - just totally ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. There's still a lot of bugs in the AI's behavior with siege ladders (like not using them at all or in a really stupid way) and it's strategy; well, 9/10 games will look like this: The AI will focus all it's power on one side, even when greatly outnumbering you, you use your garrison one 2, 3 keyspots where you kill all, if any up climbing enemies and after you killed them all, the AI will rally it's cavalry for a useless, stupid attack on your gates, just to get killed by towers. I'll leave it and that, even though there's more bad about the AI.
The battles in general: Surely core of the Total War franchise, the battles still have a lot of bugs in this version (and I doubt there will be updates fixing them) which kill all the fun. One of the biggest (and probably easiest to solve) problems is the missing "Hold-Position"-button we know and love from Rome 1. This will lead to your formation breaking when you tell your units to attack and any kind of archers - let's say thay engage Legolas-style fights without his skills.
The archers... Wish that was there only problem. Not only that they always have to set themselves up facing the enemy, possibly moving into the front battle when you want them attacking flanking enemies, they also have MAJOR issues targeting enemies with any kind of obstructions (including walls, buildings, rocks etc.) nearby. "Oh, I'm so gonna lure the enemy to this cliff so my archers will send a hail of arrows down there" - nope, not happening. "I will let the enemies on my walls and then make a shooting range out of them with my archers nearby, muhaha" - ye, try it. Will work in 1 out of 5 attempts, so go ahead.
I don't know how many archer battalions (and also battles) I've lost due to unexpected, senseless behavior of these ranged units. You gotta watch them more than a pyromaniac with gas & lighter.
And now my 3 major issue: Campaign AI and diplomacy. First one advice: Like in previous TW games, allies aren't worth the trouble. Basically, they won't ever rly help you (even though there's a nice lil' "ally target" feature in diplo screen), take away cities that you desperately wanted to conquer yourself (maybe because you just lost them) and they'll only get you into wars that you do not want. You like showing mercy and building up a team of vasalls? Well, ♥♥♥♥ you. They only pretend to be your friends. I do admit that they're less backstabby than in Shogun 2, but that's probably just due to them being too stupid to succeed.
And there's the major problem with the diplomacy: Trading cities isn't possible (and there are no mods to solve it). Not only do I think it's making it less immersive, it also hinders realistic peace negotiations and worst of all, as mentioned above, allies will steal your cities, if you don't plan ahead or if you rely on their help in defense. "Oh, I just recaptured that city that surprise army conquered from you. You want it back? FU ♥♥♥♥♥, it's mine now. Just declare war on my and ruin your rep, I am after all your loyal, helping ally since ages ago."
To sum it up: Don't buy it. Don't. It's maybe fun for a really short time but if you're keen on immersion and have some standards like I do, you probably won't enjoy it for long. I can garantuee you won't fight 10 battles without some really annoying issue that destroys all immersion.

"Rome wasn't built in a day" - and apparently neither was an ethical game company. I cannot bring myself to recommend this game simply because of shrewd money-mongering and plain laziness. But let's start off with gameplay.
The combat is anything but tactical for a game that focuses so much on tactics. Depending on your unit selection, you basically have three options: a direct attack, a flank, or both. Meaning you can either send your men into the fray, watching them arduously hack away at their enemies in a jumbled, unorganized mess (unit structure and organized troop movement are what made Rome so superior!) or bait the enemy with a few unfortunate groups and flood your army around the enemy, seeing as when a unit is attacked from behind their combat effectiveness diminishes and their morale dissolves, or a mixture of both. The AI is incredibly stupid and in most cases refuses to advance on your armies even if they seem to have the upper hand.
When it comes to dimplomacy and city management, the game has become far too oversimplified especially compared to the older games. The AI is, again, incredibly stupid, and will spam you with unrealistic requests. If you are wealthy (and clearly extremely powerful) a nation with no wealth and little military power will demand money in exchange for your safety.They also won't be shy about breaking out of character: Rome's AI is extremely submissive and lets pretty much everyone around them bully them to death.
Don't even get me started on the ridiculous number of factions and overhaul it puts on the game when you change turns. It will take thirty seconds for the game to scroll through 50 different faction icons, and that's if you adjusted the settings properly. By default, you'll have to watch every single AI unit movement within your field of view, which can take up to five minutes.
And last, but certainly not least, the scamming and the penny-pinching. SEGA has done a great job at showing us just how willing they are to squeeze every single penny out of our pockets they can using any means necessary. There are over 12 DLCs (count them, 12!) most of which toss in arbitrary doodads that should've been in the game to start with (like gore... I don't want to have to pay to see a little bit of blood. Who cares about the Teen rating? Kiddies shouldn't feel sophisticated enough to play this anyway). What bothers me the most, though, are "culture" and "unit" packs. Again, little tidbits that should've been in the game ANYWAY, like being able to play as the Greeks or beings able to use war dogs like in Rome 1.
Sufficed to say they left out so much content that games before them held just so they could suck as much money out of us as they could. While I can't say I hate this game (in all honesty it's a fantastic game and I think it might be among my top five Total Wars) I simply cannot recommend it for sixty bucks. Thirty dollars? Maybe. Twenty dollars? Absolutely. An extra $86 for content that should've been included with the original $60 price tag? Hell no.

This game is fantastic! I'll start by mentioning the trite requirements to get the most out of this game:
1. Wear good, loud headphones or have loud speakers
2. Play in the dark
3. Play with as few distractions as possible
Now you're set! The story goes like this: It's the future. You're on a huge labyrinth of a ship. There may or not be a scary alien on it. Now what are you gonna do?
The game knows how to scare you the old fashioned way, but doesn't rely on it too heavily, instead creating an environment and atmosphere that allows for fantastic psychological horror. Sound is your friend in this game as well as your worst enemy. It could signal safety or certain death. Learn when to run, learn when to crouch, learn when to hide, learn when to give up. Explore the ship which has turned into an abandoned futuristic ghost-town.
The background music creates that movie-like atmosphere but personally I turned it off. Found it much more immersive, plus the music sometimes alludes to... let's say the wrong thing. It may suggest something about the game that isn't true. <-- (me trying to be vague and non-spoilery even though what i meant has nothing to do with the plot)
There are a LOT of terminals in this game, as well as QTEs and little puzzles to unlock doors and things like that. Pretty neat. Also cool weapons. You'll also find materials to craft items, but if you don't find the blueprints themselves to
the items, they might end up being useless. The nasty thing about the blueprints is that they're easy to miss and you mightn't ever find yourself
in the area they were if you ever need to make the thing. But if you don't know what you're missing then it's all good then, right? (Ignorance is bliss)

While the game nails the atmosphere of the movie, the gameplay leaves a lot to be desired. The alien does not feel like something to avoid but rather to game. There are a lot of unexplained rules that even the steam guides didn't pick up on and a lot of the time it feels like a test of patience rather than stealth. There are no given indications to how hidden you are and some of the methods to hide that you expect to work don't and the ones that shouldn't do much better. Basically, the alien is on a timer, when he's in the vents you can walk as fast as you can to an objective and when he's out you need to hide behind a box for several minutes as he never looks behind said box and leaves. Overall, the first few hours were great, but after felt like a slog fest through boring point A to point B quests to where felt safe to start "step checking" the Alien and brute forced my way through. While the first few encounters were tense, after figuring out how it moves and thinks, it gets old fast. As a fan of good stealth titles, I'm left wondering how this got a game of the year award from anyone.
Pick it up if you like the franchise, otherwise it's not a good use of time.

It was free to play, the trailer made it sound funny, so I thought I'd give it a try.
You manage a tavern, hire mercenaries and send them off to fight in a dungeon so you can get rich off them. You can largely put the mercs on auto battle and they will be fine, the A.I. is kinda dumb when it comes to offensive ability use but when it comes to healing, it's fairly sharp. It always seems to choose to heal before they are going to die and changes it's expectations based on the amount of out-going damage, healing sooner if there's higher damage and later if there's low damage going out.
This is as many other people said, an idle game. You can put the game on auto-battle and leave it 90% of the time. The only time you'd ever really need to turn off auto-battle is during a harder boss fight, right before the chest at the end of the level. The A.I. might throw the fight with a bad call, a mistake you'd know better than to make.
I clicked yes on recommend because it's free to play, it isn't a bad idea, and if you're multi-tasking and want a game to make you feel productive while you're talking to friends, reading, or doing other things online, then this might just fill that niche'.
Your main role is to make sure the characters are geared properly in the tavern before they go off on their adventure (the auto-equip does a poor job of choosing items many times, so you'll want to look over it's decisions yourself to be sure you're happy or make any changes you think need to be made). Once they are off on the adventure, as I said, your role is largely over. You can go back to talking, or whatever else you're doing online.
The music is catchy and I like listening to various levels like Fire and Ice floors so far.
I wish the setup process in the tavern was a bit more intricate and offered me more decisions to make me feel smart or creative with the gear and I think entering into the dungeon, and every time the floor-type changes (from cavern to fire, for instance), a small little "cut-scene" would have helped immeasureably. It just feels weird clicking on a dungeon and then entering into a non-stop battle gauntlet with a changing background and no sense of the characters actually "progressing through a dungeon". Seeing them go INTO the dungeon, and INTO a new door or area inbetween woulda helped alot there.
There's pay to rush in it but .. in the start, gold is too easy to get and later, you'll likely be too bored to want to invest money in the game so the pay aspect of this game is fairly self-defeating in my opinion.
It's novel and fun in the beginning but as it drags on, you'll probably get bored of it fast. But then, it's also Free to Play. So even if you only get an hour or two's amusement out of it, you still got a good deal for paying absolutely nothing.
If the developers want to try a model like this again in the future: Put a little more work into the plot, the strategy and on the presentation of the dungeon. Had they done just a bit more with every aspect of this game, this could have easily been an unexpected gem.
I think I'll find myself coming back to it whenever I can't devote my entire attention to a game but still want to mess around with something.

Great "hide'n'seek" space thriller game overall, but the gameplay itself is very linear and gets somewhat annoying and self-repetitive after a few hours (your key to survival is pretty much repeating the similar actions all the time, "hide-crawl-push the button"). Other characters / bots repeat the same phrases too often, it would be better to give them bigger dictionary. Some action parts are only cinematic, where you just watch, but can't participate (for example, an open space zip-line tour from the ship to the station).
"Alien: Isolation" game often reminded me of "Dead Space 1, 2, 3" game series, but with less action, smaller world and emphasis on constantly hiding (it's the chicken or the egg question about who should remind who, as "Dead Space" obviously took inspiration in "Alien" films, but was released before "Alien: Isolation" game).
The DLC's "Crew Expendable" and "Last Survivor" are good but short homages to the original film, where you play Sigourney Weaver's character Ellen Ripley (great to hear her real voice!), or one of the other crew members on "Nostromo". The "Survivor mode" DLC adds a few additional places to the existing maps/levels, but is very difficult to play even on "Medium" difficulty for an average gamer.
Great, but not perfect game. Overall very worth buying and playing, especially for "Alien" fans.
