Take a generic, off-the-shelf mmorpg.  Rewrite a lot of the lore. Implement some heavily unbalanced class mechanics. Employ voice actors to basically insult the player at every turn, and you have The Elder Scrolls Unlimited. For anyone not already in the know, the game is loosely broken up into two games. The aforementioned mmorpg cookie-cutter game, and the singleplayer main questline. That's right; the entire main story is not playable with friends. You cannot group for these chapters of the story. The rest of the game is really only a handful of quests repeated over and over and over again, throughout the game. The combat is fun the first few times you try it, but it's soon just another chore that takes time away from doing other things. There are four classes. Sure, you can make whatever type of character you can think of, but that character will be almost useless most of the time. You must choose and develop the character class according to very strict parameters, as laid out by Zenimax Online. I could write an essay on how this is NOT an Elder Scrolls game, but  this brief (and heavily biased) review will have to suffice. Read/watch reviews before considering this game.

If I were asked to list the most popular MOBAs that I know, the list would be as follows:
1) DOTA
2) LOL
3) Smite
I will not argue this. However, the order is also what I would consider the list from hardest to easiest. Smite is a great way to begin playing MOBAs.
Intro: Why am I somewhat qualified to say this
Well, back when Smite first went into beta, I was in middle school. I tried it out and thought it was great. I kept playing it, putting in hundreds of hours, learning every character as best I could. Almost immediately after this game came out of beta did I purchase the ultimate god pack and I haven't regret it since. So, I was one of the first players of the game, thus giving me some authority to say this
"What did you say about this being the easiest MOBA?"
I didn't necessarily say that. Recall that I put that Smite was a good MOBA if you're starting to get into MOBAs. Smite is the easiest MOBA to learn about the basics of MOBAs. Comparing the three aforementioned MOBAs, I have played all of them, least amount of time in DOTA and most amount of time in LOL. Having this play time, I can safely say that Smite has the most simple laning phase, late game, team comp, etc. If you plan on playing any of the aforementioned games, please start on Smite and work your way up, that is, playing in this order:
Smite>LOL>Dota
If you do that, and just learn over time the finer details of each game.
Overall rating: Thumbs Up

After being hugely dissapointed of the disastrous release (like so many others), this game is now a lot better with Emperor Edition. There are still some things that bugs me though, like AI intelligence being low at times and auto-resolve battles sometimes being out of touch with virtual reality. For example the enemy forces mostly want to brute force themselves  through a street filled with tightly packed phalanx units instead of assessing the situation and use other roads to enter the city. I also have had to fight unecessary many battles because auto-resolve choice results in a loss even if  I clearly have the upper hand on the battlefield.
Perhaps it was only bad play by me before, but I did not have any problems with my population rebelling because I was facilitating their cities this time. Having enough food also seemed to be easier to handle. This made the experience a lot more enjoyable. I encountered very few bugs, one of them being pretty annoying where some ranged units refused to attack enemies within range when they could fire at will.
Of the more positive things to mention is a mostly cunning enemy on the battlemap, who always tend to stay just out of reach of your troops and generally just likes to annoy you. Special abilities on the battlefield are useful, and I do not think there are too many of them. I liked the interface once I got used to it, as it for example gives you an overview over maps and situations easily. Animations on the battlefield during the clashes can be quite entertaining.
TLDR: A great game for people who are into action-strategy games, but it does not reach the very top shelf.

All the negative reviews I've read are about a few things: Not enough content, bugs, and hackers.
Tell me something, do you always purchase Alpha games and expect finished products? There is plenty of content already in the game and a lot more being designed and implemented into the game already. Obviously there are going to be bugs since we are TESTING a game in its ALPHA stage. Duh. Hackers are a problem in every Alpha game because they're in the middle of working on security and finding what works, if you have a problem with hackers call a server admin and get compensated for what was lost and get the hacker banned. Easy as that.
All in all this game is absolutely amazing and a load of fun. You build up and raid people or take the throne and when you finally get raided and lose it all you get to do it again, which is what keeps the game fun. This is obviously meant to be an open world PvP game with the ability to build amazing bases, what more could you want? I would GLADLY have paid two or three times as much money as I did and I still would have gotten my moneys worth.
Lets put it this way:
If you know what an Alpha game is and are looking for some fun, get it.
If you do not know what an Alpha game is do not purchase this game.

When I first put this game on my wishlist, I thought it would be an open-world FPS-RPG; something like GTA. I was wrong. I bought it off Steam Summer Sale 2014 and NEVER REGRETTED it. For me it was massively fun, probably because I like the Wild West theme. The game itself is FPS with a small RPG twist - the input of player levels and skill trees: with 3 different skill trees one can branch into. This sets the game apart from most general common FPS like Call of Duty, Medal of Honor etc. However, being a (somewhat) avid gamer myself, I seem to notice that most FPS these days are introducing more elements of Role-Playing; perhaps to delinearize gameplay and make things more interesting. Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is one successful title in this wave of FPS-RPG-esque genre that is hitting the gaming industry.
Aside from the usual FPS Single Player storyline, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger brings in two other game modes: Arcade and Duel; the former being a hugely popular game mode that most FPS titles in the market have in someway or another. The Arcade game mode, as an avid gamer would expect, is all about taking down enemies and scoring points in various ways such as combos, headshots, slowmo finishes etc in a single map; the usual Arcade mode stuff. The latter - Duel - is an entirely different mode which is an impressive addition, in my opinion, to the game. It has 15 different enemies/stages, all of whom are bosses from the storyline. This particular game mode is not for softcore/casual players as it requires the player to have utmost concentration, focus and peripheral vision (of the screen) - not something a casual player would want to have while playing, as it can be frustrating to new players. This game mode is NOT relaxing in any way albeit being orgas*ically satisfying everytime you clear a stage.
Duel mode, as mentioned, requires the player to concentrate on three things: the in-game character's "Focus", his "Draw Speed" and the enemy's hand. All of these are located away from each other and hence peripheral vision is required. In addition, "Focus" and "Draw" requires A LOT of skill because both elements drift randomly. "Focus" is accumulated, from 0% to 100%, by steadying a drifting reticle over the enemy onscreen. This requires the player to concentrate a lot as it requires the reticle to stay on target while accommodating for the random reticle drift. "Draw", on the other hand, is controlled by the "strafe left" and "strafe right" key or "A" and "D" on the keyboard. It has a constant rightward drift and the goal is to keep the hand above the character's holstered gun: not too much left and not too far right.
Now for the most important part: why are these two things so crucial? "Focus" affects the slowmo that occurs during the duel - meaning how long you can take to aim as well as dodging bullets; while "Draw" affects how fast the reticle changes to a crosshair - meaning how fast the you can shoot. I personally manage to achieve 100% "Draw" and 99.8% "Focus" on two separate occasions and this requires A LOT of practice. Aside from these two elements, the player also has to look at the enemy's hand to see when he is going to draw his weapon. There is a "gong" signal that will alert the player when the draw weapon window is open but the rest depends on reaction time (or memory of enemy's timings). Lastly when the Duel happens, pressing the "strafe left" or "strafe right" button allows the character to dodge - a seemingly minute but crucially important factor as it can mean a 66.67% chance to shoot a second bullet in the event the first shot misses.
In all, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a game that does not disappoint fans of the Wild West genre. Its immersion into traditional FPS gameplay can be appealing to FPS fans as well albeit lacking in the variety of weapons available. The game's singleplayer mode can be easily completed and the hard mode is not much of a challenge due to much of the in-game elements' assistance. The Arcade mode definitely promises hours of additional gameplay as one can aim to beat their previous highscore. Furthermore, the Duel mode also chips in to the additional hours of gameplay as one can be immersed in accomplishing and mastering this challenging aspect of the game. Overall, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger was a great Summer game for me.

I got this game while it was 70% off during Summer Sale 2014 after eying it for several months. After reading some reviews, watching the videos, and reading about the gameplay, I thought that it was just going to be a cool little Indie game where you work as a customs official at a newly-opened checkpoint for an imaginary Communist State.
I started the game, and becuase it was my first time playing, I was penalized for letting someone pass that I shouldn't have. It was just once, but it wasn't until the end of the day that I relized what I had done: my small error had just cost me heat for my government-issued apartment. Soon, my family was cold, and then got sick when I could not make enough to turn the heat back on, pay for food, and pay the increased rent. I kind of felt bad for them, but hey, it's just a game, right?
Wrong. It may be a game, but it embodies so much more.
For the millions of people living in the Soviet Union, poor and oppressed, situations like this one were an everyday reality. I can just imagine a poor father trying his best to make a living in a state-owned factory, his wife working another job for practically nothing, trying to support several children, and then one of them gets sick. How do you make ends meet and still keep everyone alive, healthy, and fed?
In the game, if one of my family got sick, I could pay for medicine to let them live, but what if I could only do that by not paying for heat or food? DO I let one family member stay sick so that they can all eat, or do I buy medicine to help the sick one now, and possible have the others get sick sooon from lack of food?
I am not married (therefore I have no mother-in-law) and have no children of my own yet, so I could not relate to them in the game. But when I saw my Uncle was starving, cold, and sick, I immediantly thought of my own uncle in that state, and no lie, a few tears came to my eyes. Then I thought, what if it was my brother starving? Or my mother sick? Or my father cold? What if I had to go without vital things to help my family because of an oppresive government? What if I was growing up in the Soviet Union?
I have heard about the Soviets, and the things they did, in textbooks in class, just like the Holocaust and America's wars, but this game really hit home in making me understand what living in an all-powerful state meant. It means despair. It means hopelessness. It means an everyday struggle just to survive, and a constant attack on your conscience from the choices you have to make just to get by. It means hating yourself for your actions no matter what in situations where there is no right or good option, only bad and worse.
I hate myself for turning away a man's wife in the game, desperate to immigrate and start a new life with her husband, but she didn't have the right papers, and I had to make a tough choice -- split apart a loving couple or make sure your family can eat today, and ultimately, with time running out, I had to act against my conscience to protect and support my family.
This game made me hate myself, and forced my to think about the reality faced by many of the nameless poor and numerous oppressed I constantly hear about, but can never relate to. I think I understand now a little better now. I think I understand.

So... where do I start with this game?
Reign of kings is set a medieval world, where the goal is to become king. The king can impose a tax anywhere from 0-20% on all players, on most resources. Of course, when you become king, you become a target for all players. If you ever to come to power on a fairly populated server, you will be brought down very quickly. Many kings bring several friends, and with the taxes, gear them up, and make them the king's knights. They build a huge wall to block the bridge, which is the one and only entrance to the castle. The entire server works together to bring down the tyrant king, but there is also an internal struggle, because everyone wants to be the king themselves.
There is a great building system, which unfortunately causes a lot of lag near large buildings. Players with the most fortified bases stand the best chance of keeping their gear. The normal routine for a player is to get wood armor, and build a small base. Then they move on to iron, and are alright for a while, until they realize that they need an upgrade. They fortify their base like hell in order to keep their gear safe, and they take on the arduous task of gathering and creating steel gear.
While it seems it would take an amazing warrior with the best gear to take down the king, usually the king is dethroned by one player, with little to no gear. When it comes to rising to power, it takes more cunning than brute force. I once became king with only a rope and several blocks, while there were at least 5 knights in full steel guarding the king. If you take advantage of what you have, you can easily overcome anyone.
This is the game in it's prime, but is unfortunately not always like this.
This is how your first go will probably end up: You spawn at the beach, wondering how to start, and what to do. Due to your many years of minecraft and your knowledge of games, you run up to a tree and start wacking it with a stick. After a while, you see a player, and go to ask for some help with starting out. You get beaten to death.
This repeats several times
Now, you finally have a grasp on the game, what resources you need for low-level stuff, and how to get it. You start working on your very first base. You are killed and your base and items are stolen.
This repeats several times
Now, you finally have a grasp on the combat, and how to best anyone with the same gear as you. You finally finish your first base, you set it up in a safezone, and you finally feel comfortable enough to gather higher level gear. You head out and gather all the iron you can carry, and prepare to gear yourself up. You return home only to see that someone spent 10 minutes wacking your front door, so that they could sneak in and take everything, and maybe even steal the base itself.
Back to square one.
You play extremely cautiously, knowing that people would die for the items you have on you. You think to yourself, "Yeah, I'll build in a secluded place so I'm not raided again, it will be great!"
Finally, after days of struggling, you have iron gear, a base to be proud of, and are comfortable in knowing that if you die, you can pick yourself back up again.
The game updates (as it does very frequently) and all of the servers wipe.
Now, armed with the knowledge of how to progress through the game, you ditch the official server, and join a nice, popular community server, with no KOS allowed, and other rules to help the player progress.
Throw all of those rules out the window because the admins will not do a thing, and most do not know how to access player or server logs. Rules will be broken, you will die, and you will leave.
tl;dr
Yes, this game is well made, and while it does have it's issues, it is very fun while not very forgiving. However, because of the players, whether they be bandits, admins, or whatever else, it isn't always a very pleasing experience. You will love the game to death and first, and will do anything to rise to power and get good items. But over time, the game will not treat you well, and you will leave with a bitter taste in your mouth.
However, for what the game is worth, this is a must buy. The game will last you a long time, and because of these other players, death actually has meaning. You will always feel tense and anxious playing this game, fearing that you could lose it all due to a stupid decision - but that's the best part. The players with quick thinking, good ideas, and especially with a lot of time on their hands will prosper.
10/10 would attempt (and fail) to rise to power again.

I'm a fan of Bad Metroids, but man this one is pretty bad. Its most obvious sin is that it doesn't respect your time. After finishing a boss fight, you have to slog back through the level you just took a couple of tries to get through to reach the exit without save rooms or a (good) way to regain health. But that would be fine if the game were fundamentally fun, which this is not.
I can't put it any better than describing the Eye Cube. The Eye Cube is an enemy that fires a big eye beam thing. This big eye beam cannot be dodged or avoided and takes up every available inch of the corridor. The only way to fight the Eye Cube is to stand past the extent of the beam and shoot from that point of safety, and the beam is so long that you can't actually see the Eye Cube. The Eye Cube dies after like 25 hits that you shoot blindly at an enemy off-screen. It is possibly the worst enemy I have ever seen in a video game. (For funzies, the hit box on the beam is substantially larger than the beam itself, like by the width of your character. But that is not the fundamental problem with the Eye Cube.)
There's some bullet hell going on, but movement is floaty where it should be tight. There's a "jump to the background" mechanic, but the floor of the background doesn't quite line up with the floor of the foreground, and so you need to jump before you can pop back, but the difference between the minimum jump height and the maximum jump height is so slight that you jump into ceiling enemies in a way that's more or less out of your control.
Every exploration item is misused. There's a jetpack, but you can't ever experience fun and freedom using the thing because the foreground camera is so close and there are milipedes everywhere. You get a dash mechanic, but the dash isn't long enough to avoid damage from the very irritating enemy that was introduced on the same map as the dash mechanic. There are stupid traps where you dash through a wall into a bullet from an off-screen enemy that activates only after you dash through the wall.
It's short enough that you finish before you realize how much you hate this game, and I paid a dollar for it, so I'm not *really* complaining, but it's so bad.
Oh and there's an ability you have to turn on and off several times per level. Instead of assigning a key to toggle it, you have to pause, navigate to it, turn it on, unpause, etc. Such a bad design choice.
I haven't played much of Xeodrifter. For what I have, this game is incredbile.

What you do:
Your ship is seriously damaged while you are flying through space. You are able to locate several strong energy signals which you believe will be parts to repair your ship. You start off with the choice to visit all four of these planets, but you can only progress on one of them. This game presents itself with an exploration focus of gameplay, but it turns out there is only one true path to finishing the game. Once you get a new ability, there is only one place to go to get the next ability. You find a bunch of "relics" or something and you go to this one spot where you can now go to the final boss. Not because the items do anything, but because you have the final ability which lets you enter this area. Defeating the final boss gets you a replacement warp drive so you can take your ship out of here. We aren't told who you are or why you are flying around in a spaceship in the first place. That's all there is to the story.
------------
What I Like:
+ Customizable weapon fire, progressed with found power-ups. The different options are only explained with small pictures in-game: (in order) bullet speed, bullet size, fire rate, spread pattern, wave pattern)
+ Secrets to be found in side paths, usually found with new abilities gained from the bosses. What you find will either increase your max health or upgrade your gun.
------------
What I Don't Like:
- Floaty and slippery controls, time holding the jump button to effect height has a minimal effect and jump height is too high at the lowest input level for my taste. Precision platforming is near impossible when you float off in one direction with a slight input.
- False non-linearity. The game gives you no direction, as if you are to find your own path through these environments, but actually there is only one path and you just have to run into all the dead-ends until you find it. Especially in the beginning when starting the game, going to the "wrong" planets first only to find an immediate dead end or obstacle I can't pass is annoying/frustrating. At least point me in the right direction at the start of the game.
- Only one boss type? The same boss is repeated on every planet, it is even the final boss. You destroy it each time, so it has to be different copies of the same boss.
- You can only save your game at your ship and the only checkpoints are before/after a boss. Because of this, most of my deaths were when I was backtracking the long way to my ship. And dying then makes me replay a long section until I can survive getting back to my ship before I can save my game. I think it would have been better if there were more places to save or go back to your ship.
------------
Conclusion:
I know there are a bunch of things I can point out that I don't like about this game, but I did have fun playing it. I can recommend it, but, just like Mutant Mudds, wait for it to go on sale. Keep in mind that there is a "beat the game in one hour" achievement, which is easy to get when you simply have directions, meaning this game is really short.

The game has very little to offer beyond longevity. There's no sense of community in the game. There's no zone-wide chat to cooperate with others, there's only global chat (which takes a consumable item to use) or party/guild chat.
As an MMO, it's a failure. The game doesn't rely on healers or tanks for dungeons and missions. Bosses simply get zerged while they mindlessly walk towards their aggro target and use AoE attacks. Healers sometimes can save you when potions are on cooldown, but generally they're unnecessary. Class balance is AWFUL and the AI is really bad, so if you play a pet class be ready for frustration.
Leveling goes up to 280 or so with stat points, skill points, and class progression that you cannot undo (some can be undone with microtransactions, but others cannot). Core gameplay consists of:
Questing - standard uninteresting MMO fair with minimal rewards.
Exploring - small reward for discovering 100% of a zone's map. Very difficult with the base UI, but mods make it less confusing.
Combat - hit a few cooldown with 15-60 second cooldowns. Then procede to auto attack a bunch, even if you're a mage or priest. Then use a mana and/or health potion to continue. There's no challenge to be found at all.
Dungeons/Missions - kill a bunch of trash and then fight several bosses. This gives MUCH more Exp for the time invested than anything else you can do, yet it has a daily limit of 2/3 for each. Basically this is your "daily quest."
The game is full of bots spamming their websites in town or in the global channel. Completing quests and grinding Exp can involve more waiting than killing between sitting at a bonfire for SP if you choose to and waiting for monsters to very slowly respawn. There's also the option to camp world bosses that spawn every ~4 hours, what fun!
The UI is clunky, and while there are 3 control modes (gamepad, keyboard, mouse), none works 100% correctly. The servers have awful performance despite a very small playerbase, and the game itself cannot maintain even 10fps on a GTX 970. I've routinely seen my FPS go above 120 and below 10 in a very short time period.
If you want to try the game and not pay anything, feel free I don't think that's a bad idea. Focus on doing all quests (you need to talk to NPCs, they don't have an exclamation over their head) and exploring all zones. Don't use Exp cards until you are desperate to level up.
If you wanted to spend money on this game, please don't. It's in a horrible state and probably won't improve anytime soon.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a game that was not even on my radar. I've never played the previous titles in the series, and know next to nothing about the days of the Wild West (except that I love the Leone/Eastwood trilogy.)
With that being said, this game is an absolute blast to play. The campaign is very short, but anchored by an enjoyable narrative that never takes itself too seriously while drawing from homages of the genre. Detailing fictional character Silas Greaves' efforts at revenge over the span of four decades, a quest that has him cross paths with many luminaries of the era, Gunslinger uses the drunken bar story and hazy flashback tropes to full effect, with often unexpected results.
Tonally I would compare it to something like Borderlands, with a kind of manic and subversive form of story telling that is heavy on humour and light on gravitas. There's also a good variety of settings and collectibles that provide lore for the time period (the names tended to run together for me after awhile, but again I'm a novice to the setting.)
I would say that the conclusion is a bit of a let down, because there ended up being a ton of stuff that was just blatant filler in regards to working towards the ending, but you probably aren't going to enjoy this primarily for the story.
The real standout is the combat itself. Gunslinger has a take on bullet time which really makes you feel like an invincible outlaw, and the quick time events are surprisingly unintrusive and help further the tone, calling to mind the rapid fire killings in something like the Good, the Bad, and the Ugly. There's a rudimentary skill tree (with too much focus on dynamite, which is not nearly as fun to use as you might think owing to the lack of destructible environments) and a few unlockable weapons in the three main categories: shotgun, rifle, and pistols. Pistols will be the obvious favourite, but after spending more time with the sawed off dual-wield shotguns, I grew to like them as well.
Arcade mode is a surprisingly fun take on the more memorable single player settings. You are tasked with racking up a high score by chaining combo kills across the entirety of the map. This mode requires solid tactics, reflexes, and more than a little bit of practice, but is basically just all the high-octane action from the main game without the narrative trappings.
It's worth pointing out that the duel system is somewhat awkward. It involves simultaneously hovering your cursor over an opponent to improve focus (without a focus of around 75-80% you CANNOT win most duels) while also using A-D to lower your hand to your gun, improving draw time. It's not very intuitive at first, particularly the draw speed keys which rely on you reading Greaves' movements to determine which key to push next, but it is far from luck and fairly manageable once you've had some practice. I even got all duel related achievements within about 45 minutes of practicing, and I'm far from an expert.
If you like FPS games, you will almost certainly like Gunslinger. There's no real multiplayer (arcade and duel modes come with a leaderboard and that's the extent of it,) but for a game you can currently buy at a steep discount it's definitely worth looking in to.

CoJ Gunslinger is highly underrated and one of the more enjoyable shooters I've played in recent years. There's a surprising dearth of Western shooters on the market, and Gunslinger rises above the competition.
Gunslinger's strength lies in its narrative. It centers around a retired bounty hunter telling stories of his glory days to a crowded bar. As you play through each of the levels, Greaves' voice narrates what you're doing. In this sense it's similar to Bastion, although Greaves isn't quite as talkative.
Voice acting is excellent, as is the background music.
The story touches on every Western cliche imaginable, and fans of Cint Eastwood's movies will find much of interest.
All of this would be for naught if the gameplay was poor, but fortunately, the gunplay handled well. Not the greatest or most imaginative, but good enough. The guns don't feel particularly weighty, but the concentration mechanic, which I was concerned would be gimmicky, gives a fun cinematic feel to certain fights. Doesn't make it too easy, either.
I've heard some complaints about the boss battles, which are dueling minigames. I wish there had been more instructions as to how the minigame operates, as it took me a little while to get it down, and I don't like when games bring a completely different mechanic in for boss battles. If you're looking for multiplayer, forget it. The arcade style dueling "campaign" is fun once or twice, but not too much after that.
My only other complaint is that in hardcore mode, it is almost impossible to track how much ammo you have. I appreciate the removal of HUD elements for increased realism, and the higher difficulty was enjoyable, but I was constantly concerned because there's no way of telling how many bullets you have left.
Overall it's an excellent choice, and I definitely recommend it to anyone with an appreciation for the Western genre.

Transistor, like Bastion, is all about execution - and that is what Supergiant Games does so very, very well.
The developers' strategy is to deliver amazing sound and music design on top of a polished and beautiful gameplay experience, and no one can find any fault with that. Logan Cunningham is an incredible voice actor; he's becoming something of an indie Nolan North. And Darren Korb is something of a hidden treasure when it comes to game soundtracks. These guys have a dream team and they're producing quality I'd rate at the very highest levels, even against any AAA title.
The game is well executed and allows for a good depth of strategy balanced with some twitch play. I sense that most players, like myself, will develop pet strategies as they go through the game and try to stick to those methods as much as possible. The game doesn't often do a lot to push players off-balance during the main story. Some of the challenge levels, however, do an excellent job of that.
But this game does feel like a sophomore effort in some ways. It feels like a very safe play for the team. Anyone who has played Bastion feels very comfortable within seconds of picking up Transistor, to the extent that one suspects a kind of formula or template developing behind the scenes. This doesn't subtract from the experience at all, but I would hate to see Supergiant Games go down a formulaic route and avoid taking risks. (Compare to Klei, who hasn't really repeated their game formats, save for the direct sequel of Shank 2.) And some of the environment development feels clipped or truncated, and Cloudbank doesn't seem quite as rich of a world as Caelondia, even as the former is falling apart around the player.
If you're reading this and you haven't played Bastion: go get that game immediately. Play to exhaustion, then return. Then: purchase Transistor, enjoy to exhaustion as well.

TheHunter is a very fun game but one can find many issues with it.. I appreciate that it is a free to play game and it inspired me to purchase a 3 month pass to start.
I do not like that even with a purchase, I am still limited to what I can use in the game.. I now need to purchase the guns, ammo, calls, scents, stands, and anything else I may use during my hunts.. Either allow me to pay for what I use or pay for the pass, not both.. On top of all that, a $55 pass only allows you to play the game for 1 year.. Come next year, you will have to pay again.. Even after all of this, you still dont have any extra guns or calls for your hunts.. This game really sucks your cash and I could very easily find a better use of my money..
All the cash problems aside, This game is fun.. I do wish they would put more focus into the animal AI though.. It seems as if they focus on new animals but not improving the ones already in game.. Animals do not swin, Bucks dont fight and so on.. I know plenty of hunting games that got this right 15+ years ago.. It really is a shame to see a game that is half-a$$ed and then your charged double for it..
IF, you have the pockets and the willingness to pay double for a hunting game, This could loose many hours for you.. You may even want to have a divorce lawyer ready, Because youll need one when you finally come back to reality.. Very few games cause me to get lost for hours on end and this is one of them.. Some may say that this justifies the price but I do disagree.. The Challenges are what holds you in the game.. Once you startyour first one, your hooked..
There are some great elements to this game that balance it out with some of the bad but I still cannot justify a yearly subscription that is so high, followed by guns that are roughly $5USD a piece.. Many of which are needed to play the game.. Certain animals can only be hunted with certain weapons and this forced you to open your pockets more.. I have about $50 in guns and calls and I still cannot complete half of my challenges because I dont have certain guns..
I would love to recommend this game to everyone I know because it has potential.. I wont.. I could easily see $300 not being enough to get your way through and Ive been more addicted to cheaper games to justify the transactions required.. Over all this game is a rather disappointing sequel to Dark Souls. A great example of when developers misunderstand what it was about their game that made it so popular, this game seems so focused to let you know that it is "hard" and "not for casuals" that it misses the allure of the previous souls games. First off, is that this game is rarely "hard." What you have to do is generally obvious and simple, the only difficulty comes more from the realm of cheap, than hard. Hidden enemies inside of walls that blow up with know way of you knowing they are there, rooms filled with too many enemies to realistically fight yet they are easily skippable as you merely run past them, and a whole mess of over tracked attacks. You are more rewarded for just running and skipping enemies than fighting them, as levels make such an insignificant difference to the power of your character and there are no items worth finding, that you just chain bosses from start to finish.
The bosses are all incredibly bland in design. They are, for the most part, merely tall humanoids with 3-4 hit combos which you merely circle as they do them and attack them in the back until they die. Should you actually try rolling out of danger the attacks will nine times out of ten turn into your character as you are rolling. Blocking is often not a great option as many boss attacks will pierce straight through your shield, though that was not absent from prior games either.
Just as bland, are many of the areas through which the game takes place. The ease of the fast travel system and how early, the begining of the game, you get it. Makes each zone feel seperate and completely eliminates the interconnected feeling that Dark Souls gave the player. That interconnectedness gave the feel that it was a real area, that these places were in many spots connected and interacted with each other. Dark Souls 2 instead gives a closer feeling to a Mario game of each bonfire being merely 2-4 of a completely self contained area. Thus despite Dark Souls 2 being a larger game, it's world feels much smaller.
All in all this game is not really a bad game and as a result whether or not to recommend the game is difficult to classify as a yes or no. The main issue is that it's just so wholly disappointing that it leaves one with a bad taste in their mouths. This rendered the game incompletable for myself as the whole time I just wished I could be playing Dark Souls, a game with interesting characters, a deep and well thought out plot, and an impressive world. Not a bland action role playing game where my only objective is forward and my only reason for forward is because forward.
Overall rating: 3/10

Xeodrifter decides to evoke the feel of the original NES Metroid. Anyone who knows me knows that those words aren't a compliment.
The game tells you nothing aside from telling you new ability commands. Exploration is linear but unrestrained, meaning a lot of time wandering blindly wondering where you're supposed to go. Your only save spot is on your ship, which can be a problem to get to halfway through a stage, and the only temporary checkpoints you have are immediately before and after bosses. Health refills are only right before bosses, or hidden away in alcoves like wall meat.
Oh, I'm sorry, did I say "bosses"? I meant boss. There is one singular boss that you fight in every single boss room, with increasingly more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t attacks that you have no way of properly dealing with. Mercy invincibility is almost nonexistent. Health upgrades are rare and as squirreled away as any Metroid game. Your only weapon upgrades are incremental boosts.
Maybe this game is good for you. It wasn't good for me.

The game (as far as I've gotten) is actually good. It is pretty different from Skyrim, but it makes up for it in its own ways.
+ The game is large and very cheap for the content is offers (no DLC still offers a ton of stuff to do!)
+ The community is nice, at least in my experience. I go in a cave to continue a mission and a higher leveled player jumps in and helps me, for example.
+ Contributes to the Elder Scrolls lore almost as any other Elder Scrolls game.
+ The controls are simple and the game is fun to play because of it.
+ Character creation is extremely in-depth, as always.
+ The "tutorial" is just a mission that shows you the controls while doing the mission. I like this because it didn't waste my time.
+ Makes up for the loss of weight in combat by the "stun" ability. It doesn't make up for it completely, but it certainly helps.
Many of these negatives are minor things.
- The inventory can get a bit messy, although there are tabs that put items in to categories, such as weapons, armors, potions, etc.
- As formentioned above, there is almost no weight, or "feel", to the combat, meaning when you hit an enemy they don't react like they would in any of the other recent Elder Scrolls games. They pretty much stand still.
- Quests are a tad bit "get this, get that, kill this, kill that", but it is an MMO, that should be expected.
- The in-game shop uses lots of in-game currency that is obtained by paying money from your pocket. (Almost all these items are aesthetic though, so this does have the Overwatch defense.)
- The looting system is awkward. Regular enemies have a chance of having stuff on them, and bosses (I think) have an almost 100% droprate for something. These items are usually for crafting and such, but so far I've found some good weapons and armor :).
- This is the big one. The game's difficulty can be described in one word: easy. Almost no difficulty is involved. Your health, stamina, AND magika regenerate much, much faster than other Elder Scrolls games. Not only that, but the AI can be ♥♥♥♥ing autistic. (I sat in front of a regular enemy that was my level and didn't die for 26 seconds.) That's my only real complaint.
tl:dr: The game is fun with minor errors here and there (nothing that impacts the game much), although if you're looking for a challenge, this isn't the place for you.

Transistor, like Bastion, is all about execution - and that is what Supergiant Games does so very, very well.
The developers' strategy is to deliver amazing sound and music design on top of a polished and beautiful gameplay experience, and no one can find any fault with that. Logan Cunningham is an incredible voice actor; he's becoming something of an indie Nolan North. And Darren Korb is something of a hidden treasure when it comes to game soundtracks. These guys have a dream team and they're producing quality I'd rate at the very highest levels, even against any AAA title.
The game is well executed and allows for a good depth of strategy balanced with some twitch play. I sense that most players, like myself, will develop pet strategies as they go through the game and try to stick to those methods as much as possible. The game doesn't often do a lot to push players off-balance during the main story. Some of the challenge levels, however, do an excellent job of that.
But this game does feel like a sophomore effort in some ways. It feels like a very safe play for the team. Anyone who has played Bastion feels very comfortable within seconds of picking up Transistor, to the extent that one suspects a kind of formula or template developing behind the scenes. This doesn't subtract from the experience at all, but I would hate to see Supergiant Games go down a formulaic route and avoid taking risks. (Compare to Klei, who hasn't really repeated their game formats, save for the direct sequel of Shank 2.) And some of the environment development feels clipped or truncated, and Cloudbank doesn't seem quite as rich of a world as Caelondia, even as the former is falling apart around the player.
If you're reading this and you haven't played Bastion: go get that game immediately. Play to exhaustion, then return. Then: purchase Transistor, enjoy to exhaustion as well.

Another masterfully implemented mod of the source engine, No More Room in Hell will give you a lot of fun.
The game uses a more realistical approach on the zombie survival genre while offering two game modes: survival and objective missions.
While the survival missions are quite simple, they are very enjoyable and fun, holding the zombies while you wait for extraction at wave 10.
The objective ones are more broad and offer variation within big maps, and while some are easier than others they are still a good adventure. Another fact is that such maps possess variation between rounds, so you will have another route of objectives to execute.
Most of the maps also contain secrets and special features.
You are not a superhero: you will bleed, you will be infected and you can also suicide yourself for the greater good of the group.
Overall review:
Pros:
- Free game.
- Extremely fun with friends (the more people you play, the better).
- Realistic gun mechanics and decent melee combat while keeping a good gameplay.
- Nice graphics (taking in account the fact that the game was made in 2011).
- Extremely well made animations of itens and weapons in first person.
- Very good optimization (very few bugs, and no performance issues at all).
- Good gun and attack sounds.
- Characters possess a varied soundbank of quick chat commands, giving you quick communication with your fellow survivors.
- The VOIP inside the game simulates real conversation, the far you are from another player, the lower is your voice (you can use an in game walkie talkie to communicate from afar without issues).
- Lots of maps with good level design.
- Two map types with lot of variation.
- Very good amount of guns and melee weapons (arround 20 firearms and a bow, and 20 melee weapons, there are also 3 throwable explosives).
- People still play this game to this day (so you will find people to play with you without a problem).
Cons:
- Few zombie models (you will kill the same zombies all over again).
- Some animations of ammo checking are wrong.
- Playing alone is difficult in most cases (not recommended to play alone, this is a cooperative game after all).
- Sometimes the zombie attack animation can be quite poor (depending on you position).
- The music is quite boring (my personal opinion, maybe you will like it).
While the game has minor flaws, it is a very enjoyable experience and will bring you and your friends lots of desperating moments and agony (the good kind of it).
A good adventure.

Has the same great sense of humor and looting of the first borderlands with some even more creative missions.  However, this game punishes you for not playing co-op and I do mean punishes.  Trying to play it solo is an exercise in trial and error and frustration as many enemies can basically two-shot you.  If I wanted to play Contra, I'd play Contra, but when you're trying to fight a boss that can kill you in two hits and minions are shooting at you from all sides at the same time it feels utterly unbalanced.
If I wanted a 'git gud' game I'd play the Dark Souls games.  If I wanted a shooter where stealth and being careful with my health was important I'd play Far Cry again.  This is like something that wants to be zany like Bulletstorm but brutally punishes you for ever (EVER) not using stealth and running away at all times, praying that an enemy can't sniper you with a shotgun blast while your incredibly weak shield begins to recharge.
I even played up some more advanced missions just to get the loot and my corrosive submachine gun that does more than 300 DPS and my massive shield that absorbs enemy bullets still can't even put a scratch in many bosses.
I want to keep playing, but I don't want to be forced into playing Co-op just to experience what I thought was touted as a single-player game.
Maybe I'll finish the main story, but this will be, without a doubt, my last Borderlands experience.

Borderlands 2 is one of the greatest first person shooters you will find on the market today. After 4.5 years of being released, it has been untouched by bad updates for the entire time. Not only is the game and plot amazing, but the amount of weapons and items that you will encounter are mind blowing. You will never get over this game, as the 50 hours that I have invested into this game have been over the coure of 3 days. I have been playing this game non-stop and it never gets old, especially if you're playing with friends.
My only issue is the GOTY Bundle. You don't get all of the DLC, and you're forced to spend more dollars on each Headhunter pack separately, along with all of the other DLCs that didn't come with the GOTY edition. However, you do make a profit with all of the DLCs that do come with it, so that's still a somewhat pro with it.
The story is also feels very short. Although broad and filled with fun missions and side quests to take your time with the story, if you don't do any of the side quests, the entire main story is kind of short. But, that's only if its not your first time playing it. But that's where the Expansion Packs come in. You're able to get two harder modes, True Vault Hunter Mode and then Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode. To make it even more difficult, they added 8 OP Levels, so while getting more difficult enemies and bosses to kill, you're also getting more OP loot.
The game is extremely diverse and you're also able to create as many new characters as you want, so you're able to try out every single one, and if you get GOTY, you can try the two DLC characters as well and see what you like the best. Out of all of them, I used to think Commando used to be my favorite. Now, Pyscho is my all time go-to Vault Hunter for hard situations, as his Psycho ability, after being upgraded, turns you into a Badass. Like, the skill tree clearly states you become a Super Badass Psycho, running around with a buzz axe. That's not something anyone can come up with, you have to be creative as hell to come up with something like that.
Overall, this game is freakin' amazing, and I refuse to name a better FPS then this.

The Call Of Duty series has seen better days. With releases like Ghosts, will COD die and be forgotten. Ghosts is TERRIBLE!
But this game, Modern Warfare 2, was and still is THE LAST GOOD CALL OF DUTY GAME! Every game after MW2 was not bad but not good either, except for Black Ops, maybe.
CAMPAIGN: 7,5/10
The campaign is set 5 years after the events of Modern Warfare. USA is under attack by a new terrorist, Vladmimir Makarov, and of course are YOU the only one who can save USA and the world from World War III.
You play as 4 soldiers: PFC Allen, SGT Gary "Roach" Sanderson, PVT James Ramirez and CPT John "Soap" MacTavish. "Roach" and "Soap" are from Task Force 141 and Allen and Ramirez are from the Army Rangers. The missions are different from the TF141 and Ranger missions, which isn't very surprising. The TF141 missions are more stealth missions rather then a full scale war, like the Rangers mission. If I had to choose my favorite Ranger and TF141 missions it has to be "Cliffhanger", (TF141) and "Wolverines!". (Rangers)
The story took me about 4 hours to complete on PS3, and I haven't completed it on PC. It consists of three acts, each with about 5-10 missions, in total 15-30 missions. It's a decent number of missions, but it could've been more.
The set pieces are sometimes great, sometimes not so great, but overall it's good. It's ranging from large cities to oilrigs and prisons. Overall, pretty good.
MULTIPLAYER: 9.5/10
In every COD game, is there a multiplayer feature? YES! This is definitely the best part in the entire game! With loads of unlockable perks, weapons, camos, titles and emblems, THIS IS AWESOME!

Papers, Please is a bleak game, set in the harsh world of a Soviet-esque satellite republic. You and your family suffer for your every mistake, and even your efficiency is poorly rewarded.
It's a difficult game, built on recognizing documents and analyzing them as valid, in addition to spotting discrepancies. As your money dwindles, you begin to find moral quandaries: Do you take a bribe to let someone with invalid documents inside your country, or do you keep your meager earnings and reject them? Do you help the desperate at your own peril, or do you only worry about yourself?
With each day, the demands placed on you grow, and with every person you don't process properly, you find yourself unpaid at best, and possibly penalized financially at worst. Why would you play such a game set in such an unforgiving world? Because it's brilliant. It's compelling. Every mistake you make, you KNOW it was your fault. Every unsatisfactory ending makes you want to try harder for the next time, so you can find something, ANYTHING to make this story have a happy ending, even if it seems impossible.
This game is pure brilliance, distilled into a low res form. Unless you simply must have cutting edge graphics, or can't stand a difficult game, you owe it to yourself to buy a copy.
9/10

If you like micro-managing factories, this is the game for you!
Actually, it's more like a cross between Age of Empires (minus the pseudo history) and Minecraft, with a little Starcraft thrown in for good measure.
The game is deceptively simple at first, with your factory rapidly growing to the size of a small nation within minutes. Figuring out efficient solutions to stupid problems is definitely a key part of the early stages, as you start with little more than your bare hands. Researching the tech tree becomes a fun early challenge, with automation playing a key role in making this progress at a useful pace.
By the end of my first complete playthrough I had found some wonderfully compact and efficient configurations, and was tearing through the resources like there was no tomorrow. Which there wasn't - the bugs ate me. Thankfully I saved. Lots.
The ending (yes, there's an actual ending) is a bit of a let down (statistics screen, along with "you won!" at the top), but at least there is a definite ending.

For the sake of briefness, we will mostly stick to the Grand Campaign. You got a map stretching from the Brittanic Isles and Iberia to Northern Africa and Bactria. The faction you choose will be somewhere inside this vast landscape, and your goal is to fulfill certain objectives to beat the game. The map is historically accurate, and please, show some understanding and don't complain about certain "historical cities" missing, if every aspect of history was added in this game, we would have a giant mess to deal with that would be pretty unplayable.
The gameplay is pretty complex. As your faction's leader you got access everywhere: from internal politics between parties and dynasties, to economy, to constructing new buildings, armies, navies, to recruiting agents, to foreign policies and much more. You have so much to do and so many ways to destroy or subjugate your enemies, you will never be bored. Every playthrough is unique and always something new and different happens, requiring your skills to take care of it. Diplomacy, economy, military, they all are the means to an end. Slides, grappling hooks, jump pads, teleporters, and perhaps best of all, it's community fuelled thanks to the fantastic easy-as-hell-to-use built-in map editor.
There's also no gore what so ever, it feels a lot like a sci-fi laser-tag game in that "killing" your opponent gracefully teleports them back to the finish rather than tearing them apart or dropping them to the floor. It feels very much like a sport or tournament and that's fairly refreshing to be honest!
Recommend this game to lovers of classic FPS games like Quake or Unreal Tournament, those who love to design maps and environments, or those who feel like they need something different in the FPS genre.
From the fast paced 3v3 elite mode, to the obstacle mode where u can spend hours mastering the games movement I always find myself coming back to this game.

OK, let's go through this one at a time:
Story: Cheesy, somewhat reminiscient of Rambo on steroids, but it does its job
Gameplay: I know that the game's been getting mixed reviews on this one, but here's my take: if you want a game where you can run around and blow stuff up as you please with gratifying results, this is it. The missions are pretty cool and manage not to reuse the same generic framework. Once you finish everything though (by this I mean the core game + all DLC), there really isn't much to do. Sure you could run around and try and find all the tapes / relics, but there's not much fun in this, as it feels more like running errands. If you wnated, you could just try and lure a bunch of soldiers to your position and try and make a last stand, but if you've got the time to do this, then odds are you've already got enough gear mods, DLC, and gear-modded DLC (seeking grenades, lightning guns and nigh-invincible mechs come to mind) to be an unstoppable god-avatar at this point. I'd really like it if they could add a challenge mode or something where you just have a constant 5-star heat level, but I doubt that's coming. Honestly, the best part of this game for me was about halfway through, as this was when it was enough of a challenge to be fun, but not so much that you couldn't experiment with the grapple and tether system that makes this game unique.
Side Missions: OK, why do the shrines even exist? By the time you've got the time to go after them, you've already got free fast travel to basically anywhere you want, which I find is a bit redudant. The tapes are somewhat better, allowing you to learn a bit more about the otherwise two-dimensional Big Bad of the game, and the Encounters are probably the best of all the side missions, allowing you to experiment with new and creative ways to carry out otherwise (relatively) menial tasks. My personal favourite is to bring the informant up in the cargo plane and release him once I'm high enough.
DLC: These actually add some cool new missions and gear for you to get on these, but like I said before, I'm dissappointed that it's all so OP; since if you ever attack the basic sodiers with this stuff, it'll be as one-sided as a wolf hunting legless sheep. You can't even go back to the old bases you conquered, since by then it feels like a watered-down version of the first time you conquered the base, which is another dissappointment for me.
Final Opinion: The game is pretty good, even if it leaves something to be desired with the late / post-campaign game. I'd just recommend resetting and starting over if you have the patience, but I think it might get a bit boring at that point. If you can get this game on sale like I did, then it's definitely worth it.

Disclaimer: This is my first Dark Souls game so I won't be comparing it to Demon's or the first Dark Souls.
A difficult (Japanese) Action RPG where you explore, fight and die... Lots. You fight for your humanity (literally) as you claim Souls which is used as an in-game currency (and experience for leveling up) to the world of Drangleic. You fight many monsters, often ranging in groups between 1 to 4 and will probably die in some of these encounters. When you die you drop all your Souls that you acquired and under normal circumstances have one chance to reclaim them after respawning at your last bonfire (checkpoint). If you die in that pursuit the souls are gone forever. The combat system is quite unusual by modern conventions in that it's quite slow and methodical, i.e. you really need to think as opposed to just mindlessly swinging your weapons around, a button masher; Dark Souls is definitely not. Whilst this game can be extremely frustrating, and incredibly tense thanks to how much of a risk/reward atmosphere the game creates, there's good laughs to be had; especially in the PVP section when other players invade your world to hunt you down. Also the Boss fights feel pretty iconic thanks to most modern games' desire to abolish such mechanics. Such a mechanic is truly a sight to behold as towering enemies will beat you to a bloody pulp repeatedly until you find a strategy to take them down and victory feels incredibly satisfying as a result.
Dark Souls much like life, will beat you to your knees and keep you there if you let it. But it ain't about how hard you get hit, it's about how hard you can get hit and keep moving forward. Victory truly feels like a reward in what feels like a desperate struggle to stay alive and that's why I recommend Dark Souls II.
(I reviewed this in knowing that the game is updating to be more challenging and technically a better package with all DLCs included in the Scholar of the First Sin package. However I really just wanted to review Dark Souls II to express how much I actually enjoyed Dark Souls as it is. My plan is eventually to go back and play the predecessors.)

Papers, Please is a bleak game, set in the harsh world of a Soviet-esque satellite republic. You and your family suffer for your every mistake, and even your efficiency is poorly rewarded.
It's a difficult game, built on recognizing documents and analyzing them as valid, in addition to spotting discrepancies. As your money dwindles, you begin to find moral quandaries: Do you take a bribe to let someone with invalid documents inside your country, or do you keep your meager earnings and reject them? Do you help the desperate at your own peril, or do you only worry about yourself?
With each day, the demands placed on you grow, and with every person you don't process properly, you find yourself unpaid at best, and possibly penalized financially at worst. Why would you play such a game set in such an unforgiving world? Because it's brilliant. It's compelling. Every mistake you make, you KNOW it was your fault. Every unsatisfactory ending makes you want to try harder for the next time, so you can find something, ANYTHING to make this story have a happy ending, even if it seems impossible.
This game is pure brilliance, distilled into a low res form. Unless you simply must have cutting edge graphics, or can't stand a difficult game, you owe it to yourself to buy a copy.
9/10

Well, what to say?
If youre interested in a full game experience; DO NOT BUY
If you wanna be part of the work in progress thing then you can buy it although i do not recommend it.
The island is insanely small, so youre bumping into others constantly and trying to find a quiet spot to build is not available.
The resources are extremely scarce on busy servers because they all spawn at the same exact location (in the middle), so everyone is farming there.
These things aside (which have been promised to change), i simply wonder where this game is going. There is no survival, sure you have to eat and drink but theres food and drink aplenty, so no challenge there.
Then youre left with building. It is fun, as all other similar games are. But it quickly loses any form of interest and becomes a huge, tedious grind for resources. Especially if your King sets high taxes. If you want to build a castle of more epic proportions be ready to grind an insane amount of trees and stone.
And then comes the question, to what end?  you build a castle and siege weaponry and hang some useless baubles in your newly fetched stone home.... and then go out kill your neighbour?
Im very curious what the devs are intending to accomplish with this game. As it is now, theres no point. After having built your castle, formed a guild and taken control of the island with your clan, there is nothing to do. Why would i want to log back in? I cant be arsed to build anything else (which is the main feature of the game), Being King is not really rewarding in any way (oo i got the best sword and i can get taxes).
It really is all a matter of endgame. This piece of work has none. Since there is absolutely no survival element and that building requires you to grind endless amounts of materials (unlike minecraft), you get stuck with fighting other players. And the fighting mechanics are, to say the least, not the best around.
So unless the devteam (which is credited for a similar game which has dramatic reviews for not finishing their product) comes up with something great to lead this project towards sense. I fear this one is going to get stuck in the limbo.
Im gonna put thumbs down for now, because i cant recommend buying it at this point, ill come back in 6 months to see what has happened and where this is going.

I've never been terribly interested in the Juarez franchise, but this title is just awesome. Extremely good voice acting coupled with a heavy infusion of plot and actual old west trivia in the form of collectibles made getting this a no brainer. The missions are exciting and the world is attractive to look at, although somewhat scarce of actual people. However, models for the villains look very good and the boss sequences are well done.
As a shooter, it's just okay. The guns are not as accurate as they feel they should be while villains half either impeccable aim or shoot like storm troopers. This isn't to say the challenge isn't there- just that it's uneven. Duels can be pretty tough but you're allowed to keep trying at them. I have only two real peeves. First, jumping. It's terrible. Your character has short unresponsive jumps that make getting to some areas for collectibles more difficult than it feels it should be. Second, the enemy never shuts up. I would wholeheartedly reccomend this game to anybody who's a fan of Immersive storylines, excellent sound design, and satisfying combat. All of those were big selling points for me, and in particular, the story is what drove me to push fowards. Granted, I was really invested in the characters and their story since early 2013, so I jumped on the chance to finally see what what happening. It had me guessing at each turn, leaving me wrong more often than not, and a 2nd playthrough is warranted just because of the change in perspective on the events. The only thing that I would warn anybody looking into buying this game is that, for all it's amazingly done Narrative, Transistor is not afraid to leave loose ends for you to piece together yourself. It's something that not everyone will prefer, but it certainly was to my liking.
As far as combat goes, every funciton can be used as a primary attack, an upgrade, or a passive abilty, and the game really shines in this aspect. Every time you recieve a new function, you want to experiment, and should you fail combat, the game penalizes you by temporarily cutting access to some of your currently equipped functions, which forces you to try out new combinations, which might just lead to you finding new favorites. Each new function opens up a myriad of possibilities, and you're sure to find something you love out of them all.
Last, but certainly not least, a lot of love was put into the sound design for this game, just like their work on Bastion. Obvious things aside, like the live narrative of Transistor and Ashley Barret's fantastic performances, the soundtrack itself is worth listening too, both during combat, and on it's own. Lyrics take on new meanings in playthrough 2, and the small touches, like enviornmental sounds, or Transistor commenting on new abilities, are a great polish on the already excellent sound design. One touch that I found particularly great was the option to hum. Either by holding hum, or goign into Turn() (the games plannign phase in combat), you can listen to Red hum. I'd be lying if I didn't hold Tab for at least an hour, as she sings to each song currently playing. It's bittersweet, considering the circumstances, and it's not something that Supergiant needed to do. But they did it, and I think that little touch of flair was well worth implementing.
TL:DR version, This game has sick combat, a gripping story, and I won't shut up about the OST, buy it now.

Transistor has much in common with Bastion - the game made a few years back by the same studio (Supergiant Games). But at the same time Transistor is very different and it takes all the Bastion's best feats to the whole new level.
There are two main gameplay improvements: the Turn, and the Functions.
The Turn is a kind of tactical pause during which you may plan several moves. These moves are almost instantly performed when you unpause. Then you run around and try to avoid enemy fire while the Turn cools down. So, in fact, game's mostly about tactical planning.
The Functions are a sort of replacement for weapons and skills. Every Function represents a soul of a certain VIP of the Transistor world. When you use a certain Function, you get some info about the person this Function/soul used to belong to.
It's also important that you may combine Functions. Each of them may be installed as a Passive Bonus, an Action or an Action Bonus. And each Function has different effects in all of those three possible roles.
I also was impressed how the same voice actor Logan Cunningham sounded different and new. While in Bastion he was more of a cowboy by the bonfire, in Transistor he sounds more as an old friend in a very unfriendly city.
The city itself is great and atmopsheric. It reminds me of Bioshock, Shadowrun and No One Lives Forever at the same time.

Xeodrifter is a fairly uninspired Metroid clone, without enough unique twists or personal style to really make it stand out. Still, if you're gonna rip off something, Metroid's a pretty good base to use, and the result is still somewhat amusing (if you can get it at a reduced price).
If I were to make a direct comparison to any Metroid game, Xeodrifter is probably most like Metroid Prime 3: instead of one large world consisting of tunnels and caves all networked together, the game is split up into several smaller labyrinthine worlds, and you can travel between them using your spaceship in the main hub screen. Unfortunately, unlike Prime 3, each world only has a single teleporter that will let you return to your ship, and your ship is the only place you can save your game and fully restore your health. Each world isn't overly large so you won't have to backtrack
much to return to your vessel, but it still would've been nice if there had been more docking ports unlocked as you progressed.
Gameplay is pretty standard Metroid fare too. That classic feeling of excitement, knowing that you've discovered new powers and can use them to reach places you couldn't before, never really gets old. Still, Xeodrifter does almost nothing to make it stand out from its inspiration. The only thing it does that's kind of original is its weapon upgrade system, which allows you to allot upgrade points to your firearm in one of 5 different categories: projectile speed, damage, rate of fire, spread, and wave. You can add and remove points from each category freely, and even save up to 3 presets. I enjoyed experimenting and seeing which combination worked best in various combat situations.
One combat situation that came up often was boss fights, or rather a single boss fight repeated throughout the game. Yes, there's only one boss that you fight time after time, which is something a lot of reviewers have taken issue with. It's a little odd, but I didn't really hate it, as each time the boss shows up again, it's learned a few new techniques. By the end of the game, its moveset is vast, and I enjoyed applying my accumulated knowledge of all its various tells in order to defeat it. I wouldn't have minded a few completely unique bosses, sure, but I didn't have a huge problem with the method the developers ultimately used.
Before concluding this review, and without giving too much away, I'd like to briefly mention the ending of the game. Xeodrifter is generally fairly bright and cutesy, but this is in stark contrast to an event at its climax. It presents a moment with some emotional impact on the player, but then fails to explore it, quickly sweeping the moment under the rug and returning to the game's usual happy-go-lucky ways for the credits. I'll give the developers credit for crafting a scenario that stuck in my mind, but I felt it was a mistake: adding this moment seemed unnecessary and only serves to slightly sour the overall experience.
In the end, I think Xeodrifter is
worthy of recommendation, but only on sale. The crude graphics and sound, on par with a very early Game Boy Advance game, won't impress anyone. And even if you're a slowpoke like me and take your time checking and re-checking every corner of the game world for secrets, you're probably only going to wring about 3 hours out of the experience at most, with seemingly no post-game content to keep you coming back. Still, I can't deny that I had fun playing it. It may not be that soothing ointment that cures you of your Metroid itch, but Xeodrifter will give it a brief scratch if desired.

ShootMania is Nadeo's attempt to apply the TrackMania philosophy to shooter games.  And it works... Mostly.
The gameplay is at its core pretty simple, it is your basic fps, with only zero splash rocket launchers.  The other weapons can only be used while standing on their pad.  It is an odd system, but a good one.
But ShootMania's main flaw is in its oddness.  Players often do not understand the gamemode they are playing and instead just try and kill eachother whilst ignoring objectives.  It's like playing DotA with everyone just trying for kills, and never touching lane or tower.  Each gamemode, once understood, is amazing though.  I find all of them highly entertaining, fast paced, and worth my time.
The lack of community that other reviewers mention is real, but with nadeo's recent move to a universal demo, the server numbers are increasing, and I can usually find a good game in the core game-modes.
Grab the demo for now, it is the full game you just have to put up with a one hour timer each day.  If you like it, and want to play more than an hour each day, then buy it when it goes on sale.  $20 isn't much at all, especially for what you get, and a sale price is even better.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a great, and mind you, cheap game. It's simple, but fun. If you like fast paced shooter games, you might like this game.
The story follows ex-bounty hunter Silas Greaves on his quest for revenge. It's a typical western story. As you play through the game you will hear his commentary, along with the comments of the others in which he is talking to. The game follows what he says exactly, so he might exxaggerate his story and make the game a bit more of a hassle for the player.
The game mechanics work very well. The hit boxes are perfect, which is something most moders games struggle with. The environments are beautiful, but limited for the player. There is no free roam, and the missions funnel you allong a very narrow path all throughout the game.
Killing enemies, shooting flying dynamite, and shooting chickens are just a few of the things that earn you XP while playing. There a three perk trees in the game, but XP is easy to get, and the perks are usually things like "Do 30% more damage" or "Concentration regen 50% faster".
Which brings me to the concentration mode. If you've ever played Red Dead Redemption, it's like Dead Eye. It's a slow motion bullet time which highlights your enemies in red and gives you a bit of night vision. It is regenerated through killing enemies.
Overall, the only thing this game really lacks is the "legendary freedom of choice", as Bethesda would say. What's in this game is great, but it just needs more... stuff to improve my 7/10 rating.
Extremely fun, plenty of time to be put into it if you are a completionist, but if you just want to run through once and forget about it, will only last about 5-6 hours.

MINI METROID
I got this for £0.69 in a Steam sale, and thoroughly enjoyed it.  It's a Mini version of Metroid: short, simplified, relatively easy, with miniaturised graphics.  The acid-coloured, cute look of the game was a big part of the appeal for me; judge for yourself from the screenshots.
If there was a story, I've forgotten it already - but the mission follows the Metroid template: find items that give you special powers which give you access to new parts of the map.  The weapon system is quite good: you allocate points to customise your gunfire, changing power, speed, pattern, etc.  I found that the parabola pattern was the best all-rounder.
There is the usual Metroid backtracking through parts of the map, for example when you decide you need more health or gun collectibles to defeat a boss, but I didn't find this too troublesome- the maps are quite small, and (most) of the enemies are not hard to beat once you've figured them out.
A fairly novel feature to the game is the ability to shift into the background layer at times.  This plays a part in the gameplay here and there, and it's quite an enjoyable, cool little addition.
Some reviewers have criticised the lack of save points: you have to make it back to your ship to save.  I was irritated by this at first myself, but once you know you can't just rush carelessly through a map, it adds to the challenge and tension of the game.  Can't be bad.
CONS:
Though I really liked the sound effects, I can't say the same for the music.  I've got a lot of time for chiptunes, but the music here was too basic and repetitive and became grating.
Having to go to the menu to select a different weapon seemed unnecessary.  Since the game  has Xbox controller support, why not allow weapon selection using the shoulder buttons?
COMPARISONS:
I tried Environmental Station Alpha before this, which appears to have been better-received, but I didn't like it.  The music is much better, but the graphics are too tiny and pixelated even for me, and the gameplay was less accessible.
I've also purchased Mutant Mudds off the back of this- because it has the same developer- but although it again seems to have been better-received, I'm finding it inferior so far.  Slow, a bit clunky and too simplistic.
CONCLUSION:
All in all, I'd heartily recommend this game if you're looking for a slice of retro Metroid fun.  Some reviewers here feel short-changed by the short length I think,  but at the sort of discount I got it's a no-brainer.

I am going to say this now i am a huge fan of the Alien franchise and always have been since i first saw it at the age of 6 (even if it scared me to death) but i digress i will try to remain fair in the review that follows:
This game is an honest to god glimpse into the Alien franchises universe outside of the classic vessels such as the Nostromo, this game instead takes place on board the Anesidora space station and the reason i don't say "Within" i will come to later.
You place as the daughter of the main character from the movies Ellen Ripley, this new character going by the name of Amanda Ripley is an engineer by trade and a member of Weyland Yutani corporations (you know, the bad guys), whilst on board the station you are forced into a world of danger and paranoia at every turn, people on board are acting weird and far too many of them have guns for anybody's well being, the systems on board are badly damaged and the service androids have gone haywire at the command of the space stations built in A.I.
Put all that into place and you realise what has happened, an alien has gotten on board the vessel and has slowly and methodically taken down a large amount of the crew in it's own efforts to survive, however, you are not going to become one of the many names on the deceased list, so using your skills and your natural instincts you need to avoid these threats and i mean AVOID them, at all costs.
You have little firepower, enough to take on human targets and barely able to kill those machines but the alien is far too advanced, you don't have pulse rifles like the lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ marines that you see in the movies your weapons aren't nearly powerful enough to kill this thing, simply run, hide and hold your goddamn breath and hope he doesn't spot you through that hole in the locker you're hiding inside right now... don't... move... okay he's gone; but not far.
The constant pursuit and differing environments from the dark and dreary to the flaming chaos arenas this game throws at you are a joy to behold and are beautiful to witness at times (seriously, i found myself gawking at the lights reflection on water droplets in the first 10 minutes of the game) therefore i can safely say i give this game a very high score.
I used to get mad at the game because i would die often and call these deaths out as cheap or unfair, but it was simply my lack of awareness, in this game you are prey, you must not stay still for long and you musn't walk underneath any vents... or face your doom.

Transistor is a truly different game, and that is what makes it so special. The graphical style is similar to Bastion, and the gameplay seems to be similar at first, but actually has much more strategy to it.
