At first, all you can really do is use those skills to attack the enemies in real-time, but shortly after the game begins you gain the ability known as Turn(). Turn () allows Red to slow down time and plan her attacks, which allows for very intense, strategic battles, rather than just attacking blindly. Another great aspect of Transistor is the music. I usually do not tend to care to much about a game's soundtrack, let alone end up buying it. The music is an awesome mix of jazz and techno. It is really stellar music that perfectly complements the game. Overall, Transistor is a truly unique game, the likes of which have never been seen before. If you are looking for a game with an interesting setting, amazing soundtrack, and strategic combat, then Transistor is the game for you.

Xeodrifter is a Metroid-inspired 2D-platformer originally developed for the Nintendo 3DS. I went into this game without any knowledge about it, and I was pleasantly surprised by how much fun it was.
There are plenty of neat gameplay ideas used to a great effect (which I won't spoil), but some of the late-game abilities are a bit under-utilized. However, knowing the limited size and scope of the game, it's excusable.
The level, or WORLD DESIGN I guess you should say, is pretty darn good for the most part. It uses the game's mechanics in very clear ways that rarely leave you wondering where you're supposed to go and how you're supposed to go about it. If you want to 100% this game you'll have to back-track through the same areas over and over, but unlike metroid which had big sprawling maps with tons of different paths connecting to each other, Zeodrifter is a lot more linear and limited. I got a bit tired of going down the same areas after acquiring a new ability that allowed me to reach a spot or path I wasn't able to before. I understand they wanted to extend the longevity of the game but it wasn't the most enjoyable way of going about it from a player's perspective.
Another thing the levels have are water-sections. Thankfully they're not too annoying, but they make back-tracking a chore, and I didn't enjoy them over-all.
What I do enjoy is the on-the-fly weapon upgrading system which allows the player to change their weapon's capabilities on the fly, using upgrade points you pick up from secret areas (much like Metroid). It's really quick and really intuitive, and allows you to change your weapon depending on the scenario so that you can tackle it more efficiently.
One slightly dissapointing thing is the boss-fights. Now there are multiple bosses in the game but they are all the same boss copy-pasted, palette-swapped, and with more attacks added to its move-set each time you encounter it. While the boss eventually gets pretty creative if you use the game's mechanics to your advantage, it does feel a bit cheap and underwhelming, especially since the FINAL BOSS feels no different than the ones before it.
Over-all though I think the game is great, and is totally worth the 2-3 hours of your time.
PROS:
-Vibrant and clean pixel-art visuals.
-Solid game feel.
-World-design that cleverly uses the game's mechanics.
-Challenging enemies.
-Intuitive and fun weapon-upgrade system.
-A bunch of secrets for 100 percenters.
MIDDLE-GROUND:
(most of this stuff can be excused because it is a small game made by a small studio)
-Back-tracking was a bit tedious in some parts.
-Copy-pasted bosses.
-Movement-inertia is a bit slippery.
CONS:
-Water sections are a bore.
-Ending is VERY underwhelming.
SCORE: 8/10

This could be a fun game but it feels so cheap. The only checkpoints are before bosses and these are the only points where you can replenish your health during a level. That wouldn't be so bad if the big monsters weren't placed in the most unfair ways possible.
You jump out of the water? Too bad. A big snail shoots you in the face for 2 of your 4 health points. If you die you have to play everything all over again and the levels are not fun. They are so slow, because everything hits so hard while being able to tank so many of your shots, you can't really see what's coming next and enemies will attack you from blind spots of the screen. You can't make mistakes or 8 minutes of slow grinding are for nothing. Aforementioned snail takes something like 15 hits and just shoots bullets in a straight path. The difficulty is in repetition. Jump over the bullet, shoot the snail in the face, rinse repeat 10 times and the snail is dead. If you mess up one jump, you lose half your health. This is just cheap.
Then there are the bosses. They all look the same but have some extra attacks. They can randomly heal themselves. With no counterplay on your part. Fun. Otherwise they hit like trucks and are situated in tiny rooms like old Mega Man bosses. If you managed to defeat a boss, well done. Have fun backtracking through the level while dying over and over again. You can only save at your ship. Fun.
Some could say "git gud" and maybe this game isn't for me. I usually enjoy difficult games but this one just feels like cheap difficulty to me. Take all the parts that made Mega Man or the original Metroid unfun and claim it's cool and retro. There is a reason why certain things are handled differently in modern games. All this is made more infuriating by the fixed jump height. Even in Mega Man you could vary your jumping height. It just feels like a struggle to control the character.
There is an illusion of a Metroidvania gameplay where you can choose your paths. This is however just an illusion. If you land on the wrong planet you just cannot progress by any means. You have to find out the right order in which you have to visit the planets. The path is strictly linear. If you visit the wrong one you will get stuck halfway through a level because you lack a specific power up.
So if you enjoy the old Mega Man games, especially the infuriating parts and wish to see them in cute graphics with a pseudo Metroidvania level selection, go for it. I didn't enjoy it. If you wish to play something similar but well executed, try Cave Story. That one is amazing.

When I first heard about this game late last year, I thought "how on Earth can such a game be fun?" Now that I've finally played for some hours, I have to admit my first reaction to the game idea couldn't have been much farther from the mark. The background story is quite grim, having been influenced by the not so distant history, and this brings unforeseen depth to the game. However, humor is present as well, in the myriad funny details, cultural references, and indeed, the somewhat sparse unique characters. Even the cumbersome old smuggler who kept wasting my valuable inspector-time made me smile every time he trotted in front of the desk and started rambling cheerfully. The mechanic is quite ingenious in that it forces the player to make difficult choices: for instance, is it better to buy the essential supplies that are needed for the family to survive, or upgrades to the inspector's gear that, in the long run, enable the player to gain more money with which to secure their family's well-being? Choices that at first seem good investments in the future may turn out to be little more than shortcuts to an early grave, since a certain amount of randomness in the game's events ensures that each decision the player makes is laden with uncertainty. The carefully balanced mix of random and scripted events effectively create an addictive feeling that the player's actions have real consequences for the player's character and other characters as well. Well done.

Now you too can embrace the corruption of the government. Get paid under the table for ensuring even the slightest suspicious person is hauled awaay by your loyal guards. Confiscate passports, destroy the hopes and dreams of truly desperate people. You're the gatekeeper. For the glory of Arstotzka!

What can be said about this game that hasn't been said a hundred times before. The game is a cult classic, horror driven, guns blazing, ♥♥♥♥♥ yelling, survival♥♥♥♥♥♥show filled to the brim with potential and disappointment. It's worth the experience based on the hype surrounding it alone. It has a ton of charm, atmosphere, and good intentions. That being said, this game is a case study in missed potential and for that, I need to vent.
First accuracy terrible early on. Ignore the /vg/ threads telling you to "git gud". Shift-crouched, 10 meters away, aimed at center of mass, AK-74 with regular 7.62, can kill a bandit 1/10 times. There's no gun sway, just a dice roll on how close you'll make your grouping even after the first shot. Just get a sawed off early and treat the game like FEAR until you get a reliable gun.
Next, AI ranges from fun and fair to aim bots. In close quarters, you're better off with leading sprays than you are with quick reactions. Unarmed AI like dogs or mutants are fine. Almost all of them can be herded into anomalies/traps.
The story is pretty boring as well. Truthfully, I couldn't stay invested and had to look it up. I thought I had missed something when I got to the end but, nah. There was neat build up but that was about it.
Finally, bugs. The game is sometimes unplayable or much harder than it should in vanilla. By difficult, I don't mean finding better positioning or fast reaction times. I mean quick saving every few seconds to essentially create a TAS as you manipulate AI and dodge bullets coming from AI shooting at you safely behind cover. Not to metion unwinnable quests and incredibly varied damage. If you need proof of this, get to the end of the game with a SPAZ. You'll notice after 3 or 4 firefights how unreliable a shotgun is at close range. Sometimes it's an instakill to a Military vet in an exo. Othertimes it doesn't even cause knockback to an unarmored bandit.
Buy the game. Mod it. And then tell /vg/ it's a 7/10 at best.

This was a genuinely terrifying experience. Faced with a virtually invincible enemy who persistently hunts you using heightened senses and intelligence, and who can effortlessly run you down and kill you, and who can chase you into air ducts or pull you out of hiding places, you feel as if no place is safe.
In a way that's a shame because the environments of the game are amazingly detailed, and faithful to the 80s retro-tech milieu of the original film--but you hesitate to soak in all the beauty of it because you're being actively hunted by The Perfect Organism and you have to keep moving.
The game does not hold your hand. You can only save progress at save stations, which are spread thin, and which require you to be vulnerable for a few seconds. It's likely that you'll die a lot. But it isn't unfair, and even in the most horrifying and challenging objectives there's always a way to get through. At some points you'll find yourself completely transfixed even as you sit stock still, pressing no keys, just waiting, holding your breath, and praying. The experience is not built around jumpscares (though there is one in particular which is terrifying and awesome) but rather the steady buildup of sweat-inducing, butt-clenching tension with a heavy dose of desperate peril. It's really, really well done.
I made it through in 19 hours, and enjoyed every one of them (even if they may have taken years off of my life). Buy this game!

Transistor is a truly different game, and that is what makes it so special. The graphical style is similar to Bastion, and the gameplay seems to be similar at first, but actually has much more strategy to it. As Red, weilding the Transistor, you have the ability to perform many uniqe and powerful abilities. At first, all you can really do is use those skills to attack the enemies in real-time, but shortly after the game begins you gain the ability known as Turn(). Turn () allows Red to slow down time and plan her attacks, which allows for very intense, strategic battles, rather than just attacking blindly. Another great aspect of Transistor is the music. I usually do not tend to care to much about a game's soundtrack, let alone end up buying it. The music is an awesome mix of jazz and techno. It is really stellar music that perfectly complements the game. Overall, Transistor is a truly unique game, the likes of which have never been seen before. If you are looking for a game with an interesting setting, amazing soundtrack, and strategic combat, then Transistor is the game for you.

Honestly, it's by far not the worst game or MMO in the world. It's fun in many aspects, and I wouldn't have played for hundreds of hours if it wasn't. But ultimately, the truth creeps in and you take a step back, only to see that everything you do in this game is pointless.
First is the level scaling. Basically, the difference between a level 1 player and a maxed out one is skills (which you must buy with points gained through leveling), and a few points into health, stamina or magic. At end game, you can pump some points into overall damage output/resistance and an assortment of other boosts, but at your core, everybody is the same. This makes for some very anticlimactic progression, as you never really feel weak or strong, youre always in the middle. Did I mention that as soon as you level, your equipment scales down? So all of a sudden, unless you find some updated gear, you're in fact WEAKER.
What?!
Enemies are all the same. Skeletons, bandits, thunderbugs, who cares? They are all the exact same difficulty no matter where in the world you're located or what level you are, save for a few mini bosses and ridiculous super bosses. There's no strategy to PvE mobs outside of dungeons, and no matter how interesting a questline could be, it always boils down to "Help there's "insert enemy here" attacking! Please drive them off with no difficulty whatsoever." Seriously PvE is so easy and mindless, besides the story there's no point to it.
Equipment! There's a ****ton of it. And you'll be sweapping gear out every 5 minutes. Remember in Morrowind/Oblivion/Skyrim, when you'd stumble across an AWESOME new sword that was way better than the iron garbage you had before, and then you'd never go back? Well this is not like that. Found a new weapon? Whoop-dee-doo. Add it to the stack of 30 brandless weapons and break em all up into parts. There is no thrill to finding new, better gear, as not only will it all drop into your lap eventually, but there is just so, so much of it. Your inventory will fill up so quickly with worthless stuff you'll think you were playing Diablo III.
I got this game on sale, and it was worth every penny for sure. It was fun for a while and kept me entertained. But I value a game at how it leaves me feeling after I'm finished, and although you can't really "finish" an MMO, it didn't hold my attention for long once I figured out the formula. If you're expecting an Elder Scrolls game, stay away. If you're expecting an action MMO with some cool combat mechanics but a myriad of other flaws (level scaling I'm lookin at you), then give it a go.

On this desolate frontier of gaming very, VERY few games inhabit the pioneer town of 'Decent Wild West Stuff' (A dusty and lonesome place, nice to visit but I wouldn't want to live there) Many a PC gamer has mourned the lack of Red Dead Redemption on our glorious master systems.
While Gunslinger is an entirely different beast it certainly scratches the itch of a wild west shootout. Gratutious violence, colourful characters (based on real-world figures), an amusing story and rousing score all feature to bring the game about as close to a proper silver screen Spaghetti Western as you're likely to find.
The gameplay is solid and engaging, the guns are loud and powerful and little features such as your enemies falling in slow-motion as you gun them down really add to the ambience. It features a storyline which is an enjoyable if slightly short romp through the history of the wild west told from a very original point of view and using a few narrative features which I shan't spoil but lend well to the feel of classic 'tall tales' from the old west.
In addition you can replay the story levels in arcade mode, competing against your friends for the highest score, quickest time and longest combo. Sadly it lacks any real multiplayer value other than leaderboards and a co-op would have made me happy in places I can't write about.
All in all I thoroughly recommend Gunslinger, and commend its departure from Call of Juarez's increasingly bland series.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a big improvement over the previous game in the series, The Cartel.  Gunslinger returns the franchise back to where it belongs: the American Old West. Don't let the low price tag fool you: Gunslinger packs a lot of fun into a small package.
While there are a couple of references to earlier Call of Juarez titles, Gunslinger isn't a sequel. Instead it introduces a new character, Silas Greaves, and we follow his story in flashbacks as he regales some saloon patrons about his long-ago adventures as a bounty hunter on the trail of a notorious criminal. The banter between Greaves and the hangers-on is well written and voice-acted, especially when some of the more cynical characters start questioning Greaves' story.
Why are they questioning Greaves? According to Silas, he had interactions with some of the Old West's most legendary figures, having crossed paths with the likes of Billy the Kid, Pat Garrett, John Wesley Hardin, Grey Owl, and Jesse James, amongst others. Who wouldn't question a story like that? It also doesn't help that Greaves sometimes forgets certain details or adds embellishments to his story, and when someone calls him on it he'll change the tale accordingly.  This is sometimes reflected in the level design, as the map will change slightly to reflect something Silas just remembered...or forgot to mention in the first place.
Gunslinger's story is presented well and will keep players involved, although the end plot twist is so blatantly telegraphed ahead of time they might as well have flashed "Remember this! It'll be really important later!" onscreen when it occurs. Kudos to developer Techland for making one of the saloon patrons a famous historical figure and keeping their true identity a secret right to the end, though.
As for gameplay, Gunslinger is an arcade-styled first-person shooter. The player has access to weapons like revolvers, rifles, shotguns, and dynamite, and killing enemies awards points; killing a few in a row builds a score multiplier, and the longer the mulitplier is active the more points each kill gains. Points earned can be used to unlock new skills, allowing for upgrades like faster reloads and more concentration time, ie "Bullet Time." There are a lot of skills to unlock, and it will take at least two playtrhoughs of the game to unlock all of them. Gunslinger has a New Game Plus option, which will allow players to carry over all their upgrades into a new playthrough once they've completed the game the first time. So if you want to turn Silas into the ultimate Wild West weapon, you can.
The action in Gunslinger is satisfying: the guns are enjoyable to fire (and they're loud too), and enemies die in a variety of violent ways. Enemy gunners are kind of dumb, but when there are five or six of them firing at you at the same time, you probably won't notice their lack of brainpower too much. Most levels end with a showdown of some kind, which is where the Old West legends come in. They function as Gunslinger's bosses, and can only be defeated by shooting or dynamiting them a bunch of times while running around a small arena or via an old-fashioned Wild West showdown, where the man with the fastest gun hand wins the day. The showdowns can be tense, but a bit frustrating as you try and not only build a focus meter but keep your hand close to your shootin' iron so you can quickly draw and fire when the time arrives. Expect to die several times during the duels, which were obviously meant to be done with a controller.
Gunslinger's action isn't revolutionary, but it's done well and the game is consistently entertaining. The campaign isn't long (about four or five hours from start to finish), but the wide array of upgrades, hidden collectibles, and the unlockable "True West" difficulty setting add replay value. Gunslinger also has 26 Steam achievements, and it'll take at least two playthroughs of the campaign to get the majority of them. The rest of the achievements are devoted to Gunslinger's two other modes: Arcade and Duel. Arcade is a score-attack mode where you run through short levels blasting enemies, keeping a score multiplier as high as possible while trying to earn a perfect three-star ranking and a high position on the online leaderboards. There are 10 of these maps, and fans of score-attack games will enjoy them.
Duel mode works the same as the duels from the campaign, where you take on the Old West legends one after the other in a series of showdowns.
Gunslinger doesn't have any multiplayer, but the campaign, New Game Plus, Arcade, and Duel modes offer up enough gameplay to offset that.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a pleasant surprise. Not only is it a fun budget game, but it also restores some of the luster to this mostly underrated series of games. Recommended.

I don't know what everyone is complaining about, I love Rome 1 and have played it for years but Rome 2 adds so many new features and improvements.
+New agent types and actions
+Providence system that I think adds more strategy to the campaign. It forces you to decide what resources the towns produce, where Rome 1 had cities that were money makers/fortresses/everything.
+Tech tree, simple, but there wasn't even one in Rome 1.
+Food system, need to keep it up in order to support your armies.
+Naval combat that is simple yet enjoyable.
+Land and sea battles at the same time!!!
+Leveling system for indavidual armies and generals, being able to name your armies is a plus too.
+Seige battles are so much better, so far, AI has proven to be way better than Rome 1.
+Culture mechanic, can be used as a weapon and adds more depth to city development, also gets around the terrible cultural difference that you can't get around in Rome 1.
+Touches on some inner politics, not too much but adds more immersion with the actual generals/statesmen.
+Garrison units, less micromanagement of city garrisons, more of a personal preference.
The few complaints I have:
-Rome 1 started with everyone starting with clean slates with diplomacy, had more of a sandbox feeling in how diplomatic ties developed. Rome 2 tries to force the diplomatic relations to historical accuracy.
-Instant fleets, but not that big of a deal because the ships they get are terrible. An actual navy can easily destroy them.
-From what I've seen so far, no family trees.
Overall, Rome 2 has way more features than Rome 1. I still love Rome 1 but saying that Rome 2 dumbs everything down and simplifies the game is complete ignorance. There are some things from CA that I disagree with, but as a game, Rome 2 is better.

This is essentially a standardized World of Warcraft style 'theme park' MMO with an Elder Scrolls skin.  That's worth 5 or 6 points on a 10 point scale, and if that were the end of it I'd simply refrain from reviewing this at all, because I love Skyrim, Fallout, and the rest of Bethesda's open world games, and I could chalk this up as an experience that simply isn't intended for me.
However, I've been playing MMORPGs since Everquest and never have I had such an odious experience with a customer service department.  My Steam account got linked to the wrong ESO account.  I contacted ESO customer service through their web form - there is no other way to contact them, in or out of game, no phone number, no email address, just a web form that won't get you a reply until several days later.  Long story short, after 2 months and 6 outright dismissals of my CS ticket ESO CS has still been unable to fix this issue.  They refused to so much as pretend to try until I escalated the issue repeatedly, then blew smoke up my♥♥♥♥♥for another 2 months until I gave up and quit playing their game entirely.
So that's the main issue here - in a game where you may invest months or years of your life building up a character or a guild, that complete lack of customer service is simply unacceptable.  However, that's not the only issue.
ESO lacks major convenience features that make the MMORPG genre work.  For example, despite an extensive crafting system - not a deep or nuanced crafting system, mind - the game does not have anything resembling a central marketplace.  Instead individual guilds rent out merchants, and in order to access the things those particular guilds have put up for sale you have to physically travel within the game world to speak with the merchant they've rented.  If you want to put something you've found or purchased up for sale, the game dictates that you have to seek out and pucker up to the right asses on your particular server in order to join the proper merchant guild.
This is coupled with a combat system that lacks interactivity to such a degree that the fight is either completely over in the blink of an eye or devolves into 'hold block while your allies shoot, then shoot while one of your allies blocks'.  Progression is boring because combat is boring - getting new skills does little to aleviate the repetitive nature of combat in an MMO where you only have 8 skills to use at once and most of them are limited by cooldowns or charge mechanics.
If all you have is an XBOX then perhaps ESO is the game for you.  If you're on a PC, however, there are a hundred better options - Final Fantasy XIV, Star Wars: The Old Republic, Guild Wars 2, World of Warcraft and Neverwinter are all tangibly, measurably better products than ESO.

If I had a child interested in computers like I was growing up, I would buy this game for them.
After they got hooked on it, I would explain to them that this is the best metaphor for becoming a systems engineer or a software developer that there is in game form. You start out hacking everything together manually in a very tedious manner, and every small automation early on feels like a big improvement. After you've been working there for a few years, you have your automated systems going like clockwork. Even still, you'll hem and haw over whether to automate this or that process. 'Do I use this enough to be worth it?', you'll think to yourself.  Over time, you'll learn new techniques that make your old attempts to do things look crude and sub-par. On the best days, you'll have those beautiful moments where you make a cup of tea and watch the universe unfold like it should without you lifting a finger. Then some variable changes akin to running out of ore or having giant bugs destroy your conveyor belts, and it's back to work.
If you like this game, you'll love working in tech, unless maybe you're not yet past that stage in your career when you tell people to turn their computer off and on again all day. Don't worry though, it gets better. Just keep reaching.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a big improvement over the previous game in the series, The Cartel.  Gunslinger returns the franchise back to where it belongs: the American Old West. Don't let the low price tag fool you: Gunslinger packs a lot of fun into a small package.
While there are a couple of references to earlier Call of Juarez titles, Gunslinger isn't a sequel. Instead it introduces a new character, Silas Greaves, and we follow his story in flashbacks as he regales some saloon patrons about his long-ago adventures as a bounty hunter on the trail of a notorious criminal. The banter between Greaves and the hangers-on is well written and voice-acted, especially when some of the more cynical characters start questioning Greaves' story.
Why are they questioning Greaves? According to Silas, he had interactions with some of the Old West's most legendary figures, having crossed paths with the likes of Billy the Kid, Pat Garrett, John Wesley Hardin, Grey Owl, and Jesse James, amongst others. Who wouldn't question a story like that? It also doesn't help that Greaves sometimes forgets certain details or adds embellishments to his story, and when someone calls him on it he'll change the tale accordingly.  This is sometimes reflected in the level design, as the map will change slightly to reflect something Silas just remembered...or forgot to mention in the first place.
Gunslinger's story is presented well and will keep players involved, although the end plot twist is so blatantly telegraphed ahead of time they might as well have flashed "Remember this! It'll be really important later!" onscreen when it occurs. Kudos to developer Techland for making one of the saloon patrons a famous historical figure and keeping their true identity a secret right to the end, though.
As for gameplay, Gunslinger is an arcade-styled first-person shooter. The player has access to weapons like revolvers, rifles, shotguns, and dynamite, and killing enemies awards points; killing a few in a row builds a score multiplier, and the longer the mulitplier is active the more points each kill gains. Points earned can be used to unlock new skills, allowing for upgrades like faster reloads and more concentration time, ie "Bullet Time." There are a lot of skills to unlock, and it will take at least two playtrhoughs of the game to unlock all of them. Gunslinger has a New Game Plus option, which will allow players to carry over all their upgrades into a new playthrough once they've completed the game the first time. So if you want to turn Silas into the ultimate Wild West weapon, you can.
The action in Gunslinger is satisfying: the guns are enjoyable to fire (and they're loud too), and enemies die in a variety of violent ways. Enemy gunners are kind of dumb, but when there are five or six of them firing at you at the same time, you probably won't notice their lack of brainpower too much. Most levels end with a showdown of some kind, which is where the Old West legends come in. They function as Gunslinger's bosses, and can only be defeated by shooting or dynamiting them a bunch of times while running around a small arena or via an old-fashioned Wild West showdown, where the man with the fastest gun hand wins the day. The showdowns can be tense, but a bit frustrating as you try and not only build a focus meter but keep your hand close to your shootin' iron so you can quickly draw and fire when the time arrives. Expect to die several times during the duels, which were obviously meant to be done with a controller.
Gunslinger's action isn't revolutionary, but it's done well and the game is consistently entertaining. The campaign isn't long (about four or five hours from start to finish), but the wide array of upgrades, hidden collectibles, and the unlockable "True West" difficulty setting add replay value. Gunslinger also has 26 Steam achievements, and it'll take at least two playthroughs of the campaign to get the majority of them. The rest of the achievements are devoted to Gunslinger's two other modes: Arcade and Duel. Arcade is a score-attack mode where you run through short levels blasting enemies, keeping a score multiplier as high as possible while trying to earn a perfect three-star ranking and a high position on the online leaderboards. There are 10 of these maps, and fans of score-attack games will enjoy them.
Duel mode works the same as the duels from the campaign, where you take on the Old West legends one after the other in a series of showdowns.
Gunslinger doesn't have any multiplayer, but the campaign, New Game Plus, Arcade, and Duel modes offer up enough gameplay to offset that.
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a pleasant surprise. Not only is it a fun budget game, but it also restores some of the luster to this mostly underrated series of games. Recommended.

This was a genuinely terrifying experience. Faced with a virtually invincible enemy who persistently hunts you using heightened senses and intelligence, and who can effortlessly run you down and kill you, and who can chase you into air ducts or pull you out of hiding places, you feel as if no place is safe.
In a way that's a shame because the environments of the game are amazingly detailed, and faithful to the 80s retro-tech milieu of the original film--but you hesitate to soak in all the beauty of it because you're being actively hunted by The Perfect Organism and you have to keep moving.
The game does not hold your hand. You can only save progress at save stations, which are spread thin, and which require you to be vulnerable for a few seconds. It's likely that you'll die a lot. But it isn't unfair, and even in the most horrifying and challenging objectives there's always a way to get through. At some points you'll find yourself completely transfixed even as you sit stock still, pressing no keys, just waiting, holding your breath, and praying. The experience is not built around jumpscares (though there is one in particular which is terrifying and awesome) but rather the steady buildup of sweat-inducing, butt-clenching tension with a heavy dose of desperate peril. It's really, really well done.
I made it through in 19 hours, and enjoyed every one of them (even if they may have taken years off of my life). Buy this game!

I don't know what everyone is complaining about, I love Rome 1 and have played it for years but Rome 2 adds so many new features and improvements.
+New agent types and actions
+Providence system that I think adds more strategy to the campaign. It forces you to decide what resources the towns produce, where Rome 1 had cities that were money makers/fortresses/everything.
+Tech tree, simple, but there wasn't even one in Rome 1.
+Food system, need to keep it up in order to support your armies.
+Naval combat that is simple yet enjoyable.
+Land and sea battles at the same time!!!
+Leveling system for indavidual armies and generals, being able to name your armies is a plus too.
+Seige battles are so much better, so far, AI has proven to be way better than Rome 1.
+Culture mechanic, can be used as a weapon and adds more depth to city development, also gets around the terrible cultural difference that you can't get around in Rome 1.
+Touches on some inner politics, not too much but adds more immersion with the actual generals/statesmen.
+Garrison units, less micromanagement of city garrisons, more of a personal preference.
The few complaints I have:
-Rome 1 started with everyone starting with clean slates with diplomacy, had more of a sandbox feeling in how diplomatic ties developed. Rome 2 tries to force the diplomatic relations to historical accuracy.
-Instant fleets, but not that big of a deal because the ships they get are terrible. An actual navy can easily destroy them.
-From what I've seen so far, no family trees.
Overall, Rome 2 has way more features than Rome 1. I still love Rome 1 but saying that Rome 2 dumbs everything down and simplifies the game is complete ignorance. There are some things from CA that I disagree with, but as a game, Rome 2 is better.

The story line has many branching points were you are given the choice to support the current weakened communist government or aid the well-meaning but somewhat foolish rebels, all the while deciding what to do with hordes of people seeking a better life in your “glorious” country.

This was probably one of the most "Retro" feeling games I've played in a long time. It's soundtrack reminds me a lot of Metroid and LifeForce/Gradius era games. If you were ever a fan of the NES games like those, this harkens back quite nicely.
It's difficult, yet not unforgiving. The controls are smooth, but also take some getting used to.
The short list of the good/bad:
+Great music
+Fluid controls
+Cool powerups
+Fun boss fights (but they could be better)
+Boss checkpoints
+Configurable weapon upgrade loadouts - you can choose where you put your gun points and you can rearrange them for free whenever, saved with 3 presets.
+Plane shift + run + rocket = <3
-If you die while exploring, unless you hit a checkpoint (boss chamber), you're going back. And it could mean the beginning of the map.
-All the bosses are the "same" - relatively same pattern and same form, not really a whole lot to them once you learn the patterns. fun to play them, but could be better
-health pickups are almost non-existent. You can find them from special enemies right before a boss, and hidden in walls, but there's not much else -- so don't get hit!
-it's short
It might seem like a balanced list of good and bad, but the bad are really just aspects of the game that I personally didn't care for -- those seeking a challenge will welcome it.
For the controls, the jump height is fixed -- tap or hold the button, you jump the same. It's not so much a problem, but it can be tricky to avoid certain enemies if they aren't at the apex of your jump when you need to hit them.
It feels like you're sliding on ice when you jump, but the platforming is pretty simple, so it's not a big deal. It can be meddlesome when you need to avoid enemies, but you can kill most everything.
The game is sort of linear, in that you uncover parts of the map that are accessible each time you get a power, but you have to remember all those little places you might have forgotten to check in order to come back later -- hello Metroid.
The game is rather short. I completed it in a few hours, without getting 100% of the map/items (I got all the gun powerups, missing about half the health ones).
I feel like it could be one you could replay over again to see if you can nab all the achievements or whatnot, but i thought it was extremely worth it.

So close.
Xeodrifter is ...almost there. It has all of the elements that make a Metroidish game, but lacks something in every department.
Controls: Once I mapped the directional pad to my analong stick the controls responded well. However, the lack of diagonals and the fixed jump height are kinda unforgivable in 201X and hurt playability. Almost every type of special movement being mapped to B instead of making use of the left shoulder button hurt as well.
Features: Pretty standard fare for health, 1 = 1 and all. The weapon upgrade system was neat in theory, but in actuality you're never going to allocate points to at least two of the gimmicks. The "suit" upgrades are also standard fare, which isn't bad but there was not much original about the game. Worth noting is the ability to shift from fore to background, which is probably the best executed of the upgrades.
Graphics: Neat little 8-bit style graphics, if a bit bland in spots. The ability to shift focus from foreground to background was kinda cool and done well from a graphical standpoint and deserves some praise. Some bits look like they were ripped straight from Metroid which I have mixed feelings about because hey, at least they looked good. The primary weapon could have used better looking bullets.
Sound: The music was pretty atrocious. Just a bar or two repeating for each of the zones. The SFX were also bland and repetitive to the point of annoyance. This is one area where the game could use some work by someone experienced in SFX and soundtrack. It is possible that the DLC addresses this; I can't say as I didn't spend the extra dollar.
Now... the worst bit. There are very few enemy types and only one of the standard enemies has any sort of intelligent attack pattern. The Bosses are... all the same boss but with one extra type of ability thrown into the mix and enough extra HP each time to make sure they go through the list of all of the previous attack types. This is unfortunate as unique bosses really would have helped this game feel a little dynamic.
I really want to give this game a positive review and a recommend as it is right on the verge of being a cool game. But in honesty I feel more like I wasted a few hours of my day than I do satisfied that I finished it.  For the price on sale I don't feel like I wasted money, but I wish I had those hours back.

If I had a child interested in computers like I was growing up, I would buy this game for them.
After they got hooked on it, I would explain to them that this is the best metaphor for becoming a systems engineer or a software developer that there is in game form. You start out hacking everything together manually in a very tedious manner, and every small automation early on feels like a big improvement. After you've been working there for a few years, you have your automated systems going like clockwork. Even still, you'll hem and haw over whether to automate this or that process. 'Do I use this enough to be worth it?', you'll think to yourself.  Over time, you'll learn new techniques that make your old attempts to do things look crude and sub-par. On the best days, you'll have those beautiful moments where you make a cup of tea and watch the universe unfold like it should without you lifting a finger. Then some variable changes akin to running out of ore or having giant bugs destroy your conveyor belts, and it's back to work.
If you like this game, you'll love working in tech, unless maybe you're not yet past that stage in your career when you tell people to turn their computer off and on again all day. Don't worry though, it gets better. Just keep reaching.

I was surprised how different the gameplay is from Bastion. The combat is mostly turn based and there's no environment hazards other than enemies. The system for selecting skills and upgrades is very unique and really encourages trying different combinations. I like how the complexity grows over time, but never feels overwhelming. It has the same clever system as Bastion for customizing the difficulty with debuffs for rewards.
The story is bat♥♥♥♥♥♥insane, even more so than Bastion. It turns out to be a similar sort of apocalypse, but it feels like most of the collapsing is happening offscreen. I don’t really follow how all the character including your own fits into it. At the same time this makes the world feel very massive.
I miss the destructible and animating environments of Bastion, but these are incredibly beautiful. All the character an enemy design is wonderful. The music is amazingly good, but is much harder to describe than Bastion’s mix of Indian and Western.
It’s tough to live in the shadow of Bastion. This isn’t my favorite game this year and didn’t meet my very high expectations, but I still like almost everything about it and was left wanting more. It probably the most stylish turn-based combat games I’ve ever played. It’s pretty different from almost anything else I’ve ever played including Bastion, so it’s worth experiencing for that.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger was a surprisingly fun game, all things considered. The story, while being a simple tale of revenge, did a great job of incorporating iconic figures from the American Frontier, such as Billy the Kid, Jesse James, and others. The gameplay itself is your standard FPS, with extra twists like bullet time, quicktime events to dodge bullets, and a heavy focus on the classic western duels. There is also a bit of an RPG element, where you gain experience and level up to unlock different abilities, ranging from longer bullet time to special weapons.
All in all, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is enjoyable to play, but the story is short enough that it leaves something to be desired. It does allow a harder difficult upon completion, and an arcade mode, but the replayability is very limited.
If you're a fan of FPS games, western shootouts, and reactive gunplay I'd recommend picking this up whenever it's on sale.

I was initially wary in approaching the Call of Juarez series, having only heard of its infamous "Cartel" entry. However, Gunslinger proved to be one of the sweetest, if shortest, games I've played to date. You play the life of Silas Greaves, as told by series of flashbacks, from his point of view, of course. All together a good, if short, experience.
Pros-
The narrative. Taking a page from Bastion's western-play-as-its-told narrative style, Gunslinger delivers battlefields that flow and change as the story progresses. The best way to describe it is to think of the game as a scribe, copying down every detail that comes out of Greaves' mouth, only to be set back as Greaves remebers a tiny detail or decides to mess with his audience by tossing in random facts and events. The end result is that a player actually feels like he or she is part of the story. One begins to have doubts and grows exasperated by the old man's antics, just like the folks he relays his story to.
Gameplay- Action is fast-paced and constant, with a RPG-styled level up system. Weapons are the usual Wild West revolvers and shotguns, with rifles for long range. A focus ability slows time, allowing the player to chain together ridiulous combos and reaping in points by the hundreds.
Graphics: Cell-shading completes the feeling of playing a comic book western. Very nice, prety enviroments, if a little restricted in variety. You'll be fighting through the a town, then a forest, then a desert, and back to the town more than a few times.
Cons
Length- The game, despite its pluses, only  lasts a miserly 3 hours.
Duels-The one-on-one's are generally tolerable and the ever so slight slow mo and added heartbeat add much to the intensity of a standoff. However they do crush the fast pace set up by the rest of the game. Often one goes from gunning down bandits by the dozen to standing face to face with the boss with little more than a scene transition. But that one Mexican standoff. That one standoff in that graveyard. *shudders*.
Bosses- Ranging from "easy" to "annoying", none of the bosses are fleshed out characters. In fact often it's hard to distinguish the boss characters from the mooks under their command. It's simply "there's the varmint! Git 'im!" and that's all the expostion one can expect. The only one I can remember is that one dude with the top hat and a dynamite fetish.
Conclusion: A game's not flawless, but is well worth your time. It's story is a little generic, but the way it's intertwined with the gameplay more than makes up for it. Despite a measly length and some anticlimatic bosses, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a wholehearted recommendation.

This was a genuinely terrifying experience. Faced with a virtually invincible enemy who persistently hunts you using heightened senses and intelligence, and who can effortlessly run you down and kill you, and who can chase you into air ducts or pull you out of hiding places, you feel as if no place is safe.
In a way that's a shame because the environments of the game are amazingly detailed, and faithful to the 80s retro-tech milieu of the original film--but you hesitate to soak in all the beauty of it because you're being actively hunted by The Perfect Organism and you have to keep moving.
The game does not hold your hand. You can only save progress at save stations, which are spread thin, and which require you to be vulnerable for a few seconds. It's likely that you'll die a lot. But it isn't unfair, and even in the most horrifying and challenging objectives there's always a way to get through. At some points you'll find yourself completely transfixed even as you sit stock still, pressing no keys, just waiting, holding your breath, and praying. The experience is not built around jumpscares (though there is one in particular which is terrifying and awesome) but rather the steady buildup of sweat-inducing, butt-clenching tension with a heavy dose of desperate peril. It's really, really well done.
I made it through in 19 hours, and enjoyed every one of them (even if they may have taken years off of my life). Buy this game!

This is the mmo using the name of the greatest single player series made that is standing in the way of a 6th installment to the series. Nuf said.
As far as mmo's go, it is a pretty good game. Realistically though, there is no such thing as free to play. Expect to pay to get  more than a passing glimpse at the game because of storage and a few other issues. It is an mmo so you should know ahead of time say goodbye to your spending money and most of your free time if not all to get much out of it.
One of the great points to the single player series is that you level a character based on skills you use and there are (at least before skyrim er oblivion or whatever a lot of skills.) This one has classes with a few skills. The end. It winds up being more of a gear grinder, which is ok if that is what your game is... like say... diablo. As far as character progression on it's own goes this one feels really shallow.
It has quite a bit of crafting, but see paragraph 2 about storage. My biggest peave about the crafting is alchemy just is meh. In the single player it is the go to OP skill.
If you aren't extremely active don't expect to be in a guild that gets a store bid every week so you can actually sell things and have money. In some cases you can get away with only logging in once a week for a few hours and still sell the minimum required by the guilds that successfully bid locations with stores that actually sell anything. There is no auction house so expect to spend a lot of time searching for that one piece to finish a set every few levels.
The game has its good points. The combat is pretty good and there are lots of areas to explore. Some of the boss battles are innovative and fun. They leave you feeling like you accomplished something and sometimes even drop something useful. There is a great variety of enemies. It is story and lore rich.
All in all if you know what you're getting into with an mmo it is worth it, but because of paragraph one and its many other  faults I can't give it a positive recommendation.

Many of you many be wondering how tactical can the combat be? Well, it is tactical. Most, if not all, of your combat takes place utilizing the turn() system. This system uses an "energy" bar, which once full, allows you to plan out a sequence of movements and attacks. Each movement and attack uses up a different portion of the same "energy" bar. Pros:
-Classic, Metroid-like feel. This game brought me back to my childhood, when I played Super, Fusion and Zero Mission to absolute death. The formula is so well-executed here that you could replace the main character with Samus and it would feel like something Nintendo made.
-Unique and customizable upgrade system that encourages experimentation and strategy.
-Tight, responsive controls and pixel-perfect platforming.
-Great art design that is also very much inspired by Metroid
-Brevity! It doesn't overstay its welcome.
Cons:
-...Brevity. Short games are fine, but for $10, 2-5 hours isn't a lot.
-Lack of direction at first. Instead of being set in one big world, Xeodrifter consists of four planets that may appear to be accessed in any order, but you need to play them a certain order to get the appropriate power-ups to proceed. Start with the green planet first.
-Lack of enemy and boss variety. There aren't many standard enemies, and there is only one actual boss in the game, who you fight multiple times, with a new type of attack added onto his pattern each time.
-Lack of checkpoints and save points. You can only save on your ship, and checkpoints are only granted before and after each boss fight. When you consider that most bosses take place on the other side of the map, you find yourself having to make careful mad dashes from your ship to the boss and then back, and dying can set you back a ways, especially if you're hunting for upgrades.
-High difficulty. While the game doesn't have the upside-down difficulty curve of other Metroidvania titles thanks to its health system, it's still easy to die and the game length feels padded because of that.
Overall, Xeodrifter is a fun little Metroidvania game that nails the formula to a T. Maybe not the best out there, but for what it is, it's great.

How this got a 9/10 from Destructoid, I'll never know. While this is a beautiful, beautiful game, and it has some very interesting design, the gameplay has a lot of glaring flaws. I really hope the devs actually ready these reviews and take notice, because I think that the main problems with this game happen to be a direct result of design choices, rather than simple sloppy work -- barring the bosses. I don't like fighting the same enemy over and over and over again.
Starting Xeodrifter is probably the most brutal part of the game. The starting health is absurd for someone who is just learning how the game works, and the trial-by-fire method seems to be counter-intuitive here. The fact that the developers chose to assuage the pain of this by adding in a checkpoint system instead of culling back the gauntlet, or giving the player better footing to start with is something that bothers me immensely. It says to me, "We want our game to be hard, but we don't really want to think about what that means." There are several points throughout my first hour of playing the game where exhausting enemies with the same simple pattern are simply copy and pasted. They have an absurd amount of health for what I can only glean is to test if the player can jump over the same pellet they shoot repeatedly. Now, to be fair, a few times to deal with the same attack at once is fine. Fifteen times, and you're just being mean.
I have fought five bosses, and every single one of them is the same archetype. Each of them seems to have a moveset that builds upon the last, which would be interesting if there were some other boss-type to compare them against. Since there hasn't been, I can't say that there's anything special about these additional attack patterns. What I can say, however, is that the developers seem to dislike the idea of you using phase-shifting in a fight when you're not supposed to. While there are certain moves and patterns where phase-shifting to the background is something you're clearly supposed to do, when you're not supposed to, the boss monster will go positively ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. That is to say, the game punishes you for using a tool that it has given you. That's not fun at all. It sends a clear message: There is only one way to approach this situation, and if you don't approach it that way, you are playing the game wrong. Not allowing the player to have flexibility with the tools you've given them makes using those tools boring and predictable. Bossfights are just an exasperating exercise in recognizing and repeatedly dodging patterns while shooting back with absolutely no room for personal preference or playstyle.
The weapon system would appear, at first, to be this game's saving grace. After all, you're given a measure of custimization with your guns. But from what I've tried, it largely makes no difference aside from clearing out enemies that are purposefully and awkwardly placed.
The tight mechanics might work in another setting a lot more, but I think with the way the game is set up, especially as an alien exploration metroidvania-esque game, simple and forced playstyle and plain pattern memorization just make for bland and tasteless experience. I really want to like this game more, because again, it is quite beautiful, but it's boring, meticulous, and completely unrewarding.
If you're not dissuaded by what I nitpicked at with this game, go ahead and pick it up, but for my time with this game, I couldn't and wouldn't recommend this to anyone who didn't already have their heart set on it. It's just a disappointing experience all around.

I'll start off by saying this is the first survival horror game I've beaten, I've played a few other games in the horror genre but I'm admittedly a total pansy. I picked up this game on sale and was determined to not let it gather dust in my steam library. I took another reviewer's advice and played on medium difficulty since I don't play this genre much and was anxious as all hell.
And I ♥♥♥♥ing loved the game. The atmosphere and sound design is top notch. At first I couldn't play for more than 30 minutes, but after a few encounters I loved hiding around from the alien and playing around with the gadgets. I read a lot of reviews before playing the game and I'll try to address some of the cons I noticed. The pacing kept me interested the whole game, but there's two missions in the middle of the story mode that lost my interest because you could tell you were safe to make mistakes and ♥♥♥♥ around. That's when the game felt like a 'walking simulator.' This however stopped once the tension and story picked back up, but there's definitely a lot of hiding and backtracking present in the gameplay. Really smooth, as in a buttery 45-60 fps for upwards of 16 hr sessions without any signs of studdering or crashing. Reign of Griefers and Hackers
When I first saw the trailers for this game I thought it looked amazing. An island with a throne. An objective of becoming the King. What I expected was a Game of Thrones with guilds of players working together to capture territory and to install their leader as King. Backstabbing and intrigue. And lone wolfs just trying to survive amidst it all. What I actually got was Lord of the Flies reenacted by the inmates of Aylesbury Young Offenders Institute.
I started off, found some abandoned half destroyed ruin in a forest at the edge of the island and started building it up. Repaired the walls. Built new facilities inside. Got killed finding resources but I learned from it. Built iron doors. Built a stone outer wall. Things were going great!
You use crests to mark territory, and I had a basic leather one in my base. This makes it so players cannot remove blocks from your house so if they want in they have to force entry.
I had acquired the resources for an iron one which marks a wider amount of space so I could have a big thick stone wall around my base for protection. Unfortunately you can only have 1 crest at a time even if it's in your own territory so to replace the crest I had to remove my previous one and place a new one, accepting 10 minutes of complete vulnerability until it remarked the territory.
So I remove my crest and put the new iron one down. At that moment 10 (not kidding) japanese players in iron armour came storming over, tore down my walls and took my items while I hid in my panic room. Stepping out I noticed the devestation and ina fury ran out in my steel armour with ym steel greatsword. Naturally this didn't end well for me
I was then informed that these people are hackers who ruin the game for everyone and scrolling down through the reviews I noticed that this is a common problem.
You know, up until that point I would have given this game another glowing review. But the destruction of hours and hours of my hard work have left me in an understandably bitter mood and the developers attitude towards the hacking problem doesn't help.
So 8/10 before the hack and 0/10 post-hack due to the game being unplayable. DO NOT BUY!
Edit: Against my better judgement I decided to give this game another try. Spent hours building a new base and then a new patch was released, wiping the servers and destroying my work. So I spent many more hours building another base, had to answer the phone while I was out finding resources and since your character goes to sleep in the game when you log out I logged back in to find I had been killed while I was away having a life. Got back to my base to find 2 lovely chaps had not only taken over my base but had also built a prison outside and put someone in it. Now my base was made out of wood with a top tier iron door outside. For a new player with limited access to resources (and since the stone quarry is swarming with heavily armed players looking for newbies to kill) this is basically the best I could achieve. I even put my crest inside the walls so they would have to tear them down to find it if they wanted to take over. Naturally this didn't stop these 2, whether it was hacks or high level equipment they somehow got in, found and destroyed my crest. Since the walls seemed intact they either rebuilt them exactly or they simply hacked it, most likely the latter.
Tried to force entry into my own home and they both came out. My attacks passed through them doing no damage and eventually I died. Please for the love of god DON'T GET THIS GAME!!!
Final Edit:
So after I pulled myself together I decided to give it one final try with two objectives, retake my base and be crowned as Queen!
I made a new base nearby my old one, gathered my power there then forced entry and retook it, leaving the miserable gits who took it handcuffed and sealed in a cobblestone box.
With that unpleasantness out of the way I turned my attention towards the throne at which point the server promptly shut down, one of about 2/3 of all the servers that were shut down!
So I joined another server, built a new base, then when I logged back in later all traces of my base had vanished and I was now playing as a fat bald man....
Sensing a pattern I decided not to bother building anything anymore since between server wipes, game breaking errors, servers shutting down and high level players you are lucky if anything you build lasts a few hours.
Someone had built a cobblestone wall on the bridge to the castle but I was able to get around it by building a skybridge. Passing through there I was immediately ganged up on and killed by 2 steel clad people. The only other 2 people on the server. Apparently they just wait there with the patience of the ancients for someone to log in, get through or around their stone wall, and then get killed by them both.
So I jumped servers and found a castle with a massive wall on it and a lot of player activity. I decided to get around this by gathering many cheap blocks and building a staircase behind the castle up to the top, no mean feat since the rock the castle stands on must be about 200 blocks tall! Fortunately I didn't need to waste much time on this because I ran into a bug where every approx 5 minutes my screen goes black forcing me to log out and in again, and if I was in the sea I drop to 40 fathoms below it and drown before I can get back up again
Next server had nothing on the bridge but a couple of steel clad foul mouthed kiddies. After getting massacred the first time I came up with a plan. I made a bed and ran past them, placed it down behind a rock then did an Obi Wan and lowered my club as they slaughtered me with cries of noob and nigerian.
So they ran off back to the front of the bridge to await their next victim while I respawned at the bed. I then spent 45 minutes clubbing my way through the wooden wall they had built to block entrance to the castle and seized the throne before they could get back to stop me! At that moment I felt something like overcoming an especially tough boss in Dark Souls!
I think I know now why the game ended up so far from it's vision. The game trailers give a fair amount of attention to the presences of ropes, shackles, cages and torture devices, which are clearly present for the sake of bullying and griefing. Of course these things do exist in the Medieval era and I gave it little thought. But when a bully watches that trailer they will be drawn to the game by the promise of these griefing tools.
In practice they lack the patience to craft the necessary facilities to produce these things, and simply travel in gangs attacking lone players and destroying their work with their clubs. What's more the game artwork displays caracatures of bloated troll like men acting like monkeys and the in-game character customisation option not only allows for exaggerated anatomy, but the pvp meta is of a pitch black midget with maximum size arms for the smallest target to hit with the longest reach. In the end the game advertising appeals to exactly these sorts of people who drive away everyone else and leave the community a toxic cesspool.
So I suppose in the end this game is like Dark Souls meets Lord of the Flies, except the hollows are obscenity spewing bullying ganging adolescents, and the bosses are server wipes, servers closing and game breaking bugs. That all said, I'm glad I can finally uninstall this ordeal with peace of mind that I didn't let it break me :)

This is one of those games that's hard to review with Steam's binary Recommend/Not Recommend system. Xeodrifter isn't a bad game, but it has enough little quibbles that makes it very hard to recommend unless you've dredged Steam's other Metroidvanias on offer and have ran out of Must Play ones.
First the good things: The game is fun. Even with the problems I have, I still got through its ~5 hour playtime just fine. Playing with the Steam Controller, it handled pretty well. There's a few good platforming and shooting challenges in there that don't feel too cheap. Upgrading the gun is interesting, you can level it up in several different ways, and you can un-spend the upgrade points so you can experiment to your heart's content. You can even save 3 presets, but the game doesn't really throw that many different challenges at you that you need variety. You eventually get an ability that allows you to jump between the foreground and background that feels new and interesting, but doesn't really shake up the core generic Metroidvania gameplay much.
Now the bad. Probably my biggest problem is the level design is uninspired, confusing, and tedious to navigate. The game world is stretched over 4 planets, but apart from the physical separation and change of color scheme, there's not much to differentiate them. All 4 planets have the same enemies, are mostly narrow corridors, and randomly full of water, lava, and barriers for the sole purpose to block your progress until you get a specific upgrade and necessitate backtracking. Even though you can fly to any of the 4 planets right at the start, your progress in 3 of them are blocked off until you get the right upgrade. There's only one path you can take through the game. The devs could have easily left the game as a single planet, and it wouldn't have lost anything. As it was, flying back and forth between nearly identical planets only made it harder to remember where I was and whether I found all the collectibles.
The hidden upgrades, a staple of the genre, are not rewarding to find. They are either randomly hidden behind invisible tunnels in the wall, or out in plain sight, blocked off by a lack of a specific power-up. There's no challenge or problem-solving there, you either stumble across them when you see your bullets pass through the wall, or you see them and wait until you have the right power.  Since hunting secrets is one of my favorite parts of the genre, Xeodrifter's stumbling here is pretty damning.
There's a few other quibbles I have, There's very few checkpoints and health around, which makes exploration frustrating at times. The boss is the same one over and over with little variety in between.
All in all, Xeodrifter is not terrible, but there's enough little problems that outweigh the good, and nothing in the game really stands out or makes me really excited.  There's better games out there for your money.

I'm an MMO newcomer, and I enjoy this a fair bit. It is a pretty damn good adaptation of the Elder Scrolls games into an MMO. It's VERY solo friendly, which is awesome, and some great UI mods make it immersive and exploration friendly. I use Wykkyd's Immersion and True Exploration (by Shinni) which help make it less of a follow-the-quest-arrow experience, and more like roaming through a strange, distant land. Combat is pretty fun, and rewards positioning and light tactics, way better than just managing cooldowns. Your character yells a lot in combat, making it sound like she's falling down stairs.
It's also remarkably easy to join a friendly guild, group up, and find a dungeon to run through with others. I found the level 1 dungeon I did pretty rote - the boss fight was about whittling down a health bar, and barely engaging - but the level 2 version of that dungeon, the Veteran dungeon, required close teamwork to get to the boss, and I still haven't beaten her, after perhaps 15 attempts with two different groups. That's cool, and shows the high level play can get interesting.

First and foremost, I don't know why this game has so many bad reviews, they made me wary of downloading and playing it. This game doesn't really have any major fps issues that most of the reviews drone on about.
As far as gameplay goes, the combat is mildly similar to a hack n' slash game, exploration is great - the environments are beatifully done, the art style is great (especially enjoyable for people who are fans of the old "of mana" series of games).
Quests aren't all the same like in most mmo's e.g they arent just "go here and kill this mob 10 times then come back" rinse and repeat. The boss battles, though a little on the easy side, play brilliantly.
There are some latency issues but nothing worth moaning about, as mentioned earlier, and in many overly dramatic bad reviews - there are some fps issues, but they aren't gamebreaking. Worst case scenario, once every hour or so your fps may come to a standstill for a couple of seconds.
The game is Free to Play and not Pay to Win, which is a nice change from most F2P mmo's, and although you can pay for things in game, it isn't being shoved in your face. The benefits for those who pay vs those that don't are very minor.
The game utilizes full keyboard control for playing, mouse and keyboard or a controller, which are all laid out brilliantly, so the game can be picked up and played by anyone, regardless of their preferred playstyle.
All in all this is a very promising game, and I look forward to seeing what more comes of it in the future. 8/10

Let me start off by saying that I obviously enjoy this game, with the 600 hours I've accumulated on it. It does have it's downsides compared to other games in the genre, but overall it's a good pick if you're willing to spend a little money on it or are a more casual player.
I'll start off with what I find most appealing: The amount of heroes available and the variety in them. The gods chosen from various pantheons are all quite unique and have actual history backing them, which makes it even better for people like me who find interest in mythology. Of course this is what drew me in. What kept me playing was the surprisingly unique abilities for gods. It's a lot of fun to just pick up a god you haven't played before and just mess around with their kit and come up with item builds (yeah, you do buy items  to enhance your character like in most other MOBAs) that suit it. Most gods have a couple good builds that work for them, and many are pretty flexible for different situations. The over-the-shoulder camera and controls also make it easier for newcomers to the genre to focus more on learning singular strategy and mechanics rather than the more observation-based tactics over other MOBAs. Not to say that kind of observation isn't used in Smite, it's just easier to grasp for beginners.
Now for the cons. Like every other F2P MOBA, there are a lot of heroes and a lot of cosmetics, and they're not all unocked for you at the start. While you can unlock all heroes for free and some of their cosmetic changes, there are a LOT of gods and it will take a while to grind out enough games to unlock all of them. Most of the skins have to be purchased with currency that is difficult (but not imposible) to obtain besides using actual money. There's also the whole case/loot box/chest/whatever mechanism to get some of the really good cosmetics. So, if you're really into that side of MOBAs, prepare to dig into your wallet a little bit. As for gameplay, you can't expect much hardcore high-level teamwork in most games, especially at low ranks. In my experience, people are very focused on individual skill vs. team play. While this isn't a terrible thing, it is a team game, so it comes with toxic players who blame things on others vs. themselves, even if they're not really working with the team. Balancing is rather slow sometimes, and some gods simply become overpowered with the right build, being able to tank hits, deal insane damage, and just overall mess things up. These things do get balanced eventually, but it's a bit slower than other MOBAs, in my experience.
I know this was a rather long review, and has a good bit od rambling, but I do reccomend this game for people, especially those who are new to MOBAs or even skill-based games. It's easy to learn, but hard to master.
For those who want a TL;DR : I recommend the game for it's variety of gods, items, and abilities, as well as the history and lore that's behind all the different gods. It's also very newbie friendly.

Well then, here's the short and sweet version of my Reign of King's experience, and by short and sweet I mean a sample of what myself and my guild of 15+ people (more or less, it varies due to people leaving the game because of lack in developer interest/care) had gone through during months of RoK playing.
First and foremost let me start by saying the game was a blast to play. From the beginning it was fun, simple and hacker-free with room to do whatever you want. The building was solid, becoming better as you learned which piece would fit with another to make intricate designs on castle walls, bridges, and towers. This aspect of the game was more or less 60% of your time between gathering resources and actually building it out. Combat in the beginning was lacking, and still is (but I will get to that later) and due to it being faulty, skill isn't a factor in the game and instead became all about luck. With these factors in mind, it was still playable and it kept you thoroughly entertained because these issues seemed trivial for a game in early stages. However we soon learned that mostly everything would change.
Around mid-point from where the game is now, I'd say Alpha 5 or 6, things got out of control. The combat was getting worse, hit-boxes being huge on almost every point of your characters body. This caused the poke to be an absurd way to kill someone quickly requiring no skill at all. (When I tell you the hit-box is huge, I mean imagine your head was 3 feet wide and 2 feet long.) Raiding bases was way too easy, everyone learned that trebucheting a base was as easy as getting the materials for it. You load the thing with 15 shots aim and fire, the base immediately crumbling into dust with the crest fully exposed. Now I understand completely the point of the game is to siege, kill, and build. (With added perks of being the king) However when you spent 10+ hours sometimes even DAYS building your base, just to log in one day to find it completely gone, your body dead, and your loot that took you forever to get all missing in one foul swoop, you'd immediately recognize the issue with this game. Not only was raiding easy, but during the Alpha 5-6 range, hackers became prominent in the community. Everyone and their friends had free gear, free blocks, and so many other items that the servers became laggy, and the community volatile. This was the downfall of the game, however only the beginning.
As time went by, the Developers became more and more lazy, less and less interested in what their community had to say. Alpha 7 and up became a slow trend of useless updates that did nothing to end the start of the collapse (that being the hackers) and how the game became unplayable because of ESP (player-spotting), Kill-Commanding, Player controlling hackers. The player control part was incredibly annoying, getting to a milestone of 10 hours on a server only to see a hacker turn you green, wipe your body of all it's loot, change your size, weight etc, etc. Not to mention they could also instantly teleport you into a bear pit causing immediate death, and this all was absolutely terrible. Granted, the Dev's added some new content, and eventually began working on EAC hack prevention, which let me tell you all, was a huge waste of time. EAC did nothing for the game, it lasted a total of 24 hours, a peaceful 24 hours that seemed too good to be true, and of course it was. Soon the hackers came back, only this time pretending to be a casual. As you played you would eventually come across someone who jumps you and or kills you with no questions asked, forcing a retaliation. When trying to get them back they'd turn out to be a hacker and over night would destroy your base completely with infinite trebuchet shots.
Turning away from the hacker issues there was the update on the game engine from Unity 4.5 to Unity 5, which was delayed somewhere around 2 weeks with little to no response from the Devs. The update finally came and it was lovely, the graphics updated and new items to tinker with seemed nice but ultimately was just a face-lift on what was already ruined in the first place. More bugs came from Unity 5 than its predecessor, hackers kept on hacking, and the community was scarce but toxic. Eventually they "fixed" sieging, which by that I mean they nerfed ballistas into the ground rendering them useless, and tuned Trebuchet's down to a mere 500 damage a shot, 5 shot capacity (ultimately changing nothing about sieging)
All in all, the game in it's current state is broken, battered and ruined. The community is thin and the developers seem to be off elsewhere while the whole thing crumbles. They rarely respond, their updates are useless, and if it's anything we've learned about Code}{atch is that they've sunk another game into the ground, and whether or not they acknowledge this, nobody knows. It's a shame though, because the game had great potential before all of the chaos arrived. If you ask me, I think they should sell the game to another Dev, or to the community and be done with it.
In my honest opinion, leave this game alone, and don't waste your time with it. You'll just be putting more money into the pit like the rest of us.

Controls are slippery and hard to get used to at first, but the real downfall are the bosses. Or, I should say, the boss. You fight the same boss that gains (and, as far as I've seen, also loses) some new moves over the course of the game. And it's not me trying to avoid spoilers, yes, even the final boss is that bug thing you fight in the first five minutes of the game. At times it feels more like a good flash game or a demo than a full game.
