Smite is a free to play 3rd person moba. There are plenty of reasons you should try this game, and i'm going to go over a few.
1. Smite being 3rd person really brings out a whole new feel for the game, one i've never felt before in a moba. It really feels like you have full control. I've never felt so excited hitting an ultimate that can be extremely hard to hit, or just barely making it out of danger. I really like the whole 3rd person because it adds a whole new element to the game. This is where leaps and other escapes come in, which i though was an excellent touch because it actually gives you a chance to escape if someone ganks. I can definetly say that this game has made me WAY more excited than any other moba. It just feels SO much more rewarding hitting an ultimate or getting a kill. when i played league of legends a while back, when i got a kill it never really seemed like anything special, which I think played a big part in turning me away from the game.
2. There is already a HUGE selection of gods to chose from, and more on the way. There is currently 82 gods (Soon to be 83 when Nike comes out this tuesday) and they usually release a new god every month or so. Each god has their own unique set of skills, although some gods have what can be described as a repeat (basically the same skill as another god just looks or behaves a bit differently) but ALMOST every ultimate in the game is unique.
3. One word. Roles. This is an EXTREMELY important part of the game as is you don't have a certain class or role, you can be almost certain you lost. I personally like this element because it makes you think carefully. For example, should you have your mage be for damage, or heals? Also if you don't have a tank and they do, it can be extremely frustrating as the purpose of a tank is to absorb the enemy gods abilities so that they don't hit your weaker characters, who can't take as much damage.
4. Skins. Now i know that this has nothing to do with gameplay and is completly optional since it costs real money instead of in-game currency, but i have to give them credit for the work they put into the skins. Every skin (except for recolors which i will get into in a second) looks absoloutley amazing. they each have their own theme (most of the time) and you can always tell that they put a LOT of effort into it. Now about recolors. Recolors are the skins that you can get for in-game currency (which you can get simply by playing matches) and they aren't anything special. all they are are the character's normal skin (not any extra details like things that weren't there before) just different colors. But hey, at least you can get skins for free.
5. Patch notes. Hi-Rez is extremely funny and interactive when doing patch notes. They stream them every other wednesday at 3pm est? they like making fun of each other and having fun while doing the whole thing. They also do a short Q & A at the end of every patch notes, answering helpful or just plain silly questions.
6. Events. Hi-Rez is extremely generous with their events as you can often get things like skins or icons which you would have to pay real world money for and they sometimes never have those events again so they are definetly worth it. In addition to this, they try to always have a big event going on ( which most of the time cost real world money to progress in) that you can get rewards on top of what you pay for. In addition to that addition, they pick three skins to go on sale EVERY WEEK starting from 25% off going all the way to 75% off.
All in all i could not recommend this game more. You can play it completely for free so even if you ended up not liking it it didn't cost you anything so who cares, and if you later decide to support the developers and all of the hard work and time they spend putting into this game, then why not buy a couple skins? And also before ending this review I have to say that they have by far the best deal I have ever seen to get all of the gods now and all of the ones they release in the future. You can get all the current and upcoming gods for $30 USD.

Applying the Trackmania theory of game design to FPS results in one of the more interesting arena shooters in some time. It's just as french and weird as Trackmania, and getting to see how Maniaplanet is coming together as this and Stadium release is pretty exciting.
For the uninitiated, the Mania games, when initially released, are♥♥♥♥♥♥ That's being overly harsh, but  the level that the community takes the content to is so far above anything the developers include with the games that it is ridiculous. As a result, what is currently available in Shootmania is pretty middling. You can see the groundwork and tools are there for people to make some cool stuff, but right now, everyone is still playing on the default maps and gametypes, the pro players are still talking in IRC, and the custom content creators are still figuring out what works, and what works that is also fun to play.
To give you an idea of how one gametype works, imagine a standard FFA match. In the center of the map is a big metal pole. Once someone has captured the pole, respawns are disabled for the rest of the round. Additionally, there is a bigass storm closing on the map the entire round, and touching it kills you instantly, so you have to move towards the middle of the map over time. You can get hit twice by an enemy players weapon before you are killed, as well.
OH AND THE SURFACE YOU ARE STANDING ON DICTATES YOUR CURRENT WEAPON AND WHETHER OR NOT SPACEBAR JUMPS OR SPRINTS WELCOME TO MANIAPLANET ENJOY YOUR STAY
I wouldn't start your PAID experience with the Mania games here. I do suggest you play the Open Beta by downloading the demo, however. Trackmania 2 Stadium is pretty cheap, and is heavily populated at the moment. Canyon is more expensive, and since Stadium is still a pretty recent release, it's pretty empty by comparison.
Maniaplanet is one of the most unique...things I've had the pleasure of playing, and I suggest you check it out, from one of its components or another.

This is one of the greatest survivor games I have ever played. Pay not attention to whoever is dismissing it. The game is a love letter to the original "Alien" by Ridley Scott. Unlike so many other games out there trying to emulate James Cameron's "Aliens", this game tries to capture the horror elements of the first film. It really puts you there.
The game is dripping with atmospherics, and it captures the retro-futuristic style of the late 70's with perfect grace. However, to have a better enjoyment of this game, I would recommend playing it in medium difficulty, since on hard, it's unforgivingly difficult - you'll be more time trapped in closets than R. Kelly.
The game had some similarities with "Dead Space", but to me, it felt closer to the game "Dead Space" was promoting itself to be: a survivor experience. Only that "DS" turned out to be a shooter, and "AI" is a proper horror game.

I'm a fan of the movies and really want to love this game. The foundation for something great is here but they didn't quite put it all together. Your character is also too helpless. You will die many times and never feel like you stand a chance against any of the games enemies (including fellow humans).
All that said I do keep coming back to it slowly chipping away at the campaign. The graphics engine is very well optimized and it supports cloud save so you can just quit as soon as you get frustrated and come back down the road. I actually use this game more as a tech demo than anything else because it looks great and seems to run well on all hardware. I would only recommend this to fans of the Alien universe when it is on sale.

This game is a pretty good experience. It's at the right price range and provides really high entertainment value. The story line is gripping and the action is exciting. The story really shines and it's very well written. The voice acting is very well done adding to the immersion of the character.
Visually, the game is very polished. There's no AA settings, but I'm sure that you could install SweetFX to enhance the graphics a bit more. However, no post-processing is really needed.
Two things bother me about this title - the AI is fairly predictable and the game is extremely linear. I wish the AI would attempt to flank or try something different. I think the AI is scripted to be in certain positions/locations making it fairly easy to pick them off from range.
As well, it would've been nice to have an open-level concept. However, if the level was opened, I guess the AI would have to be more complex. There is the occassional part in a level where the story adapts to the path you choose, which makes it interesting, however, it would've been more satisfying if there were more opportunities like this.
I suspect, if they make a second version of this game, they'll add in the open-world concept, smarter AI and multiplayer. Hopefully, this game was successful enough to warrant anoother "Gunslinger"
Regardless, I highly recommend this short game. It's at the right price point, so if you have a weekend free to play, this is definitely a good game to finish over a weekend.

From the makers of Bastion comes a brand new game with a brand new setting. As with Bastion, the soundtrack and art are fantastic, but now instead of a Post-Apocalyptic/Western/Fantasy setting, now it's a (post-post-?)cyberpunk-ish setting with elements of noir. The combat system moves from a typical "isometric" action-RPG to a turn-based hybrid with the "Turn" system and the new abilities (programs/characters) are incredibly versatile, giving different effects when slotted into active/passive or mutation slots, giving tactical depth and an incentive to mix up and experiment with your combat style.
The plot is something best experienced yourself, told through varied means as audiologs, "codex"-style entries (tied to varied use of the combat abilities), environment and enemy design as much as the sequence of events.
Highly recommended, even more so if you're a fan of Bastion.

I don't review many games, but Transistor, much like SuperGiant's previous title, Bastion, exceeded my expectations on all fronts.
This game is a tremendously soulful piece of work, and from the very start to the very end, is first and foremost a work of art. The music, narration, artistic style and presentation flow together in a way that I would probably say outclasses almost any other game i've played. Anyone with a quibble of curiousity and a penchant for great games, or even works of art, should immediately purchase Transistor (AND Bastion) and enjoy the ride.
To touch on the gameplay itself, the combat is inventive and blends several previously done elements (pseudo-turn based combat, action queues, tactical-execution-based combat) into a pretty seamless and enjoyable experience. It is two parts arcade, one part strategic pause-and-think game. It remains fresh and has a lot of room for player creativity due to the openly configurable nature of abilities acquired throughout the game.
What follows are some brief pros/cons:
Pros:
+Incredible Art. From music to artwork, this entire game is a masterpiece.
+Gameplay. The combat remains fresh, enjoyable, and creative all the way through.
+Difficulty.  Like bastion, difficulty is born of modifiers you can apply to enemies, which give you bonuses for being brave.
+Storyline.  Again, this is a work of art and the storyline is rich, heartfelt, and incredibly immersive.
+Soundtrack.  Incredible, as usual.
Cons:
-Length.   The game itself isn't that long, although there are excuses to re-play the game with new conditions and toy around with the combat some more.
That's really all I can see anyone really griping about with this game.
In total, I'd give Transistor a 9.5/10, as one of the most absolutely awesome pieces of work i've seen in terms of gaming. It isn't a triple-A 40 hour experience... but it's an incredibly rich, artistic romp through an engaging and incredibly envisioned city of Cloudbank.

Papers, Please is definitely an addicting game. It has 20 different endings, so there is replay value. Your first playthrough will really be entirely getting used to the system and to be as quick and efficient as possible, in order to maximize how much money you make everyday. Additionally, as a Passport Control Officer, you have to make decisions which will affect your character's, and your family's lives. Whether helping take down the government by letting terrorists through, letting people take vigiliante justice, denying people entry even though they may be executed if they return to their home country, or personally killing people to provide for your family. This is not "Passport Control Simulator." In this game, you really have to pay attention, and it is good for your brain, because you have to juggle multiple documents at the same time and remember dates and so forth off the top of your head on the fly. Not only that, it realy makes you question what you would do in these circumstances; help others at your family's expense, or only look out for yourself. Though it will get dull rather quickly, it is definitely worth the few bucks it costs.

If you ever liked Metroid games, there is a big chance you will like this game. This game incorporates nostalgic Metroid art and gameplay, where you need to backtrack to access area previously blocked due to the requirement of a certain ability, weapons upgrades, bosses, hidden items, maps, puzzles, almost everything from Metroid is there!
The game is quite short (2-4hrs), but very fun while it lasts. The major problem I initially had with this game is that there are almost no save points, the only save point is your ship, and you can visit 4 different areas from your ship. The areas themselves are quite small, so if you run recklessly you will certainly die, since the game is a bit more difficult tham Metroid, and does not provide health pickups to restore your health (except for some secret ones), unlike in most Metroid-like games where you get health back from killing creatures.
Highly recommended!

Really fun game.  It did a good job of bringing back what I love about some of my favorite NES and SNES games.
While being classified as a "Metroidvania" game, its redundant to say that it plays similar to Metroid, however there are also art and musical similarities to both Metriod and Super Metriod.
Even many of the abilities obtained are similar to Super Metriod, though don't operate the same way.
The Phase ability was really neat, it really fit the game well and it probably the best implementation of a changing active layers feature/skill/gimmick that I have seen in a game.
While similar to Metriod, I feel like there are also ties back to Blaster Master on the NES as well, starting with the main character himself and the way he moves/shoots, as well as the gun upgrades and functionality.
The game starts out pretty difficult as you have little health, and no abilities or upgrades.
You can also pick any of the 4 planets to start exploring, however you'll notice that some of those planets you will not be able to explore much until you have the right item/ability to progress, also some of the enemies on those planets are far stronger than you are at the start of the game.
This game has no hand holding at all, which is nice as I've always been the type of person who liked to explore and figure things out on my own.  The only thing that this game is is forgiving about, is giving you a check point before a boss fight, and having infinite lives.  Dying before a checkpoint however will send you back off the planet onto your ship, and you will have lost any progress you might have made.
I played just over 7 hours of this game and obtained all the upgrades, map progress and finished the game.  While the game can be completed in much less time (less than 1 hour for speed run achievement), if it is your first time playing the game, it will good for several hours at least, assuming you are working for full completion.
If I had to pick anything to complain about with this game it would be that some of the gun upgrades categories feel fairly useless.  While you can put points into different catergories which change how your gun fires, I only found 2 of them to be of any use to me.  Since you only have enough points to max out 2 of the 5 categories, the other 3 were completely ignored.  Which made having an option to save upto 3 different weapon setups to quickly swap between also a bit useless.
Aside from that the game was really a lot of fun, the engine ran silky smooth, the visuals were just how I like my pixel style games to look, the music was fantastic and there were pleanty of abilities and hidden items.
The game's video does a good job of showing you what this game is all about, so if you like the video, then you'll probably love the game.

I have went into this one with very few expectations. Not really knowing much about the game, seeing the negative reviews and seeing as the publishers completely screw the pre-order business model up, my hopes for the game were not all that high. Luckily, so far I am yet to run into a blatant intrusion into my gameplay sourced from the cash shop in the game.
[STORY]
I will be honest, while I tried following the story at the start, I rapidly ended up going back to just skipping over NPC text. As far as I can tell, the basic premise if that godesses that were once responding to the prayers of man kind went silent and distasters began to strike the world. While the premise of potentially interesting, I found that the presentation of the story wasn't the most engaging, but that could be just me.
[COMBAT]
Moving onto what is probably the most important aspect of the game, the combat is not the best. Controlls involve moving around with arrow keys/mouse/controller and using a key to do a basic attack, pressing another key to jump. Additionally, each class gets skills to use in combat that can be used from the action bar. Early on, the combat feels really repetitive and perhaps not as engaging as it should be. I can imagine that gaining more skills as you progress would probably alleviate this issue somewhat, however I am not 100% sure on how much more interesting this combat system could get.
[QUESTING]
Questing in the game so far was simple, talk to this NPC, go to this location, do this thing the NPC asked you to do. One aspect I did enjoy about questing however was the fact that most quests are hidden encouraging exploration and engaging with NPCs to find side quests.
[PROGRESSION]
This is by far my favourite bit of the game, the character progression is quite nicely done. At the start, you choose one of 4 classes, then when you are actually in the game, your progression is separated into two halves. Firstly, there is your chaarcter level which detemines your basic stats such as strenght or constitution. Then you have your Class progression which is how you advance your class and learn more skills. Every 15 class levels, you get the ability to advance your character by either developing your last chosen class, or choosing one of the two additional classes you get every 15 levels. This creates some really incredible customisation options and it's probably one of my favourite progression systems for a game of this type.
[GRAPHICS]
This is an interesting one as this game provides a very quite unique artsyle with a very charming asthetic. The game has a very old feel to it, however it looks as a fairly recent game. The stylistic choice to provide simpler animations, less complex feeling world while including a lot of detail into the design creates a very memorable feel to the game.
[AUDIO]
Similarily to the graphics, the audio used in this game is fairly unique. The tracks used for the game have a somewhat classical vibe to them, however they are much more lively, sounding like something that would play at a disco, mixed with something that would be played during an epic, fantastical adventure.
In conclussion, I think this game is definitly worth a go, in the end, its free and in many aspects, quite well done.

This game is a lot of fun, if you enjoy FPS with a Wild West twist this is for you. Just a warning, if you are looking for a complex game this is not it. This is actually a very simple FPS with only 3 types of guns and only 1 explosive. You mostly just shoot and run, just like in most FPS games. HAVING said that, this game does what it does right.
The guns feel fun to fire, the kills are satisfying, and the story is actually very interesting. The best part about it is that you play while the story is being told in front of your eyes. It is a strange concept, but it really works well in this game.
There is a sort of bullet time and doge and it really works and is a lot of fun to use. Sure, it gets repetative, but this is one of those few games where you can not get enough of it.
The duels are also very cool, hard to master. It took me a while to figure out how it works but once you do, it really is fun to play. The replay value is good, because you get a hard game mode after you beat the game and you have arcade like levels you can play over and over just having fun playing a Wild West Gun.
Even the levels are designed great, they are fun and pretty to look at. The graphics overall are quite good and the colours really make it a Wild West Feel. Though I really enjoy this game, I can not recommend buying it for full price. Right now its $15 but once it is below $10 it is really worth it.
If you can not wait, then $15 is ok too, but as it lacks MP and is very short, I really think $10 is the maximum for a game like this. Either way, it is a good addition to your Steam library

From the makers of Bastion comes a brand new game with a brand new setting. As with Bastion, the soundtrack and art are fantastic, but now instead of a Post-Apocalyptic/Western/Fantasy setting, now it's a (post-post-?)cyberpunk-ish setting with elements of noir. The combat system moves from a typical "isometric" action-RPG to a turn-based hybrid with the "Turn" system and the new abilities (programs/characters) are incredibly versatile, giving different effects when slotted into active/passive or mutation slots, giving tactical depth and an incentive to mix up and experiment with your combat style.
The plot is something best experienced yourself, told through varied means as audiologs, "codex"-style entries (tied to varied use of the combat abilities), environment and enemy design as much as the sequence of events.
Highly recommended, even more so if you're a fan of Bastion.

I don't review many games, but Transistor, much like SuperGiant's previous title, Bastion, exceeded my expectations on all fronts.
This game is a tremendously soulful piece of work, and from the very start to the very end, is first and foremost a work of art. The music, narration, artistic style and presentation flow together in a way that I would probably say outclasses almost any other game i've played. Anyone with a quibble of curiousity and a penchant for great games, or even works of art, should immediately purchase Transistor (AND Bastion) and enjoy the ride.
To touch on the gameplay itself, the combat is inventive and blends several previously done elements (pseudo-turn based combat, action queues, tactical-execution-based combat) into a pretty seamless and enjoyable experience. It is two parts arcade, one part strategic pause-and-think game. It remains fresh and has a lot of room for player creativity due to the openly configurable nature of abilities acquired throughout the game.
What follows are some brief pros/cons:
Pros:
+Incredible Art. From music to artwork, this entire game is a masterpiece.
+Gameplay. The combat remains fresh, enjoyable, and creative all the way through.
+Difficulty.  Like bastion, difficulty is born of modifiers you can apply to enemies, which give you bonuses for being brave.
+Storyline.  Again, this is a work of art and the storyline is rich, heartfelt, and incredibly immersive.
+Soundtrack.  Incredible, as usual.
Cons:
-Length.   The game itself isn't that long, although there are excuses to re-play the game with new conditions and toy around with the combat some more.
That's really all I can see anyone really griping about with this game.
In total, I'd give Transistor a 9.5/10, as one of the most absolutely awesome pieces of work i've seen in terms of gaming. It isn't a triple-A 40 hour experience... but it's an incredibly rich, artistic romp through an engaging and incredibly envisioned city of Cloudbank.

What an amazing game! Some of the best graphics and atmosphere I’ve ever seen. Its graphics still supersede most new releases which is quite an achievement for a game 2.5 years old. I’m flabbergasted why this game didn’t have better sales and more critical praise. I know that it has it’s downsides (a bit too long, probably too many Seegson simple Joes and still a few lingering bugs) but its achievements in story, sound, atmosphere, lighting, graphics, art, weapon design, AI etc. are phenomenal.
Nowadays, many single player games fail to immerse me and engage my emotions but this is the first game in a long time which has succeeded. I constantly found myself holding my breath and struggling to control my facial muscles from spasming into a grimace of fear and anguish as I tried to evade the ultra quick Alien while I literally moved at a crawl to the nearest shelter of darkness. This is largely due to the amazing sound design and graphics. Graphics don't usually influence my enjoyment of a game too much but in a game such as this where it relies heavily on its atmosphere and lighting, they really do add strongly to the immersion.
If you love survival horror, stealth and story-rich games, you'll almost certainly enjoy this experience (similar to but better than Outlast, Amnesia, Penumbra series - I've yet to play Soma). And i'm not even a big fan of the Alien movies but you don't have to be to enjoy this game - and if you are a fan of the franchise, you're in for a treat!
Lastly, to the team at Creative Assembly and everyone involved, BRAVO!

[Spoiler-Free Review]
In space, no one can hear you scream... for Metroidvania!
Xeodrifter is a bite-sized burst of platforming, exploration, and re-traversal. It took me roughly 4.5 hours from start to 100% completion, but I’d imagine the game could be completed comfortably in 2-3 if you aren’t overly concerned with finding secrets. Post-game content and replayability are basically non-existent however, so if you’re getting the game, know that there isn’t a lot to do after the end credits.
You start out on a ship surrounded by a few planets. With no clear idea of where to go, the player is left to figure things out on their own; that’s fine. The problem is, when you’re given the option to visit any planet right from the get go, you don't expect to have to bounce around between only two of them before being able to make any headway in the others. I found myself reaching an impasse on a few occasions, with no recourse but death (losing any progress/pickups collected along the way). It’s frustrating because you don't realize you aren't meant to explore certain planets until much later in the game. If a few of them were uncovered over time, this wouldn’t be such an issue.
Stages are a series of interconnected pathways and shortcuts (basically a big loop with smaller loops within it). Unfortunately, the experience of navigating through the stages is kind of cumbersome. If you revisit the boss lair after defeating it, for example, the door closes behind you and you'll have to go through a section of the map just to get back to where you started. It had me wishing for a way to cut the trip short at times. Thankfully, unlocked skills help alleviate some of the hassle of re-exploring the stages, but never enough that you feel excited to trek back down some of the longer hallways previously visited. Re-traversal with a disregard for the player's time isn’t the best design choice! An option to teleport directly to your ship would have made longer journeys a bit less grueling.
Planetary inhabitants are varied, though I think a few more types would have been welcome. Some are very clearly influenced by classic Metroid enemies, both in appearance and movement patterns. The highlight for me was the animation cycle of a snail-like creature (sometimes it’s the little things that grab your attention). Ultimately, I would have liked to see each planet house its own set of enemy occupants, rather than being reused across each stage, but in a package the size of Xeodrifter, it may be asking too much.
What’s really disappointing are the bosses, which are basically re-skins rather than completely unique in appearance and function. The design is cool, but fighting the same enemy, albeit with different special attacks and such, made for an unexciting finale to each stage. It’s one of the only things that feel cheap about the game.
The main character is very quick and has a slightly slippery feel when moving across the stage; it’s almost too fluid. Worst of all, jumping isn’t set so that short presses result in a hop, and longer presses result in higher jumps. This leads to some frustration as the character ends up feeling fatally irresponsible. Rather than a tiny hop to avoid an incoming bullet, for instance, the character jumps as high as possible (even if it means hitting another bullet at that height). It isn’t unforgivable except for the fact, certain enemy shot patterns and movements create situations where you’re going to die regardless if/how you react. Taking a hit because it’s impossible to avoid, goes against a lifetime of learned player instinct.
On the subject of player instinct, there are sections in some of the stages where you need to drop below a platform by pressing down, then jump. The game never explains how to deal with the obstacle. While experienced gamers will know this by heart, newcomers may not, so it’s disappointing to leave them without proper instructions.
Xeodrifter does a fantastic job in capturing the feeling of visiting unexplored planets, they’re strange and mysterious, with a hint of familiarity. It’s nice to see a game do mood so well. Encountering alien lifeforms and collecting artifacts and upgrades always felt exciting. The art style is incredible, and the concept, timeless.
The NES-inspired music is great! Enough so, that I remained fixated on the title screen for as long as it took to hear the entire track. Afterwards, I went straight to the options screen and credits, just to hear more.
Sound FX are suitable for the setting, save for one sound which is overused and somewhat comedic; the effect used when you destroy the enemy inhabitants. It’s rough, and is best described as the sound of a coughing dog? (or a tire braking hard while travelling at 100mph). As killing anything results in the sound, it kind of breaks some of the atmosphere, especially when eviscerating anything with a goo-like appearance (shouldn’t they emit a squishy sound?).
Xeodrifter is a competent and enjoyable take on classic Metroid gameplay. It’s somewhat short, and has its flaws, but remains an easy recommendation for players looking to scratch an exploratory itch. Get it in the hope it helps the developer create more games like this in the future.

Xeodrifter is a neat and effective little metroid-vania style exploration-based platformer. The art is very clean and the colour palette is vibrant. The game runs smoothly and doesn't waste any time holding your hand, it just lets you get on with it.

As others have mentioned, the game is quite short, I have 6.5 hours logged and have completed the game with every achievement unlocked. The first 6 hours were spent on the initial play through and locating all the unpgrades, with the rest spent on a speed run.
If you're not sure $10/£7 is good enough value for 6+ hours of gameplay then wait for a sale; the game received a 75% discount during the 2015 Steam Summer Sale, so will probably be heavily discounted in the future.

A short but sweet homage and excellent rendition of not only Metroid, but an underrated era of 2D games that existed during the tragically short GBA era of gaming history.
Precise and satisfying, the simple controls are easy to learn and satisfying to execute. Several types of enemies and varied bosses to fight, in tough but fair bouts that feel rewarding due to how excellently the physics are implemented. Controller implementation is a bit lacking.
Perfectly recreates the look and feel of the GBA era of video games. The sprite art is self limited to capture the 16 bit look, but still has a modern flair that looks beautiful. Many homages to Metroid enemies and items, faithfully recreated for nostalgic value.
The music does not capture the same effortless atmosphere and mood of the Metroid series, but is still of high quality. All sound effects have a satisfying punch to them and help to carry the experience forward.
If you ever owned a handheld Nintendo system, were ever a fan of Metroid, or indeed enjoy any short and sweet video game experience, I highly recommend this game.

Note: This review was pared down slightly due to size limitations.
Tree of Savior can best be described as a mixed bag: before you put your hand in, you better know what you’re going to get out of it. In this Free to Play MMORPG by IMC Entertainment (Granado Espada, ex Ragnarok Online developers) you start by picking one of four classes and by the end of it you’re one of eighty. Designed to be a hardcore game, Tree of Savior takes ideas from eastern and western games in its genre and blends them with varying degrees of success. Seeing all the beautiful landscapes and legends based on Lithuanian mythology might take hundreds of hours, but it feels like the game was designed so only the most dedicated players will see even half of it.
Which is a shame, because there’s no denying that Tree of Savior is a beautiful looking game. By using a mix of 2D and 3D the game treads that line between old and new and occasionally looks like a massive vanillaware game. The area design has been fairly unique from my time with it and I’ve been impressed more than a couple of times just from how it looks. Some of the monsters and items start to repeat as early as 30 levels in though which is a bit of a drag, but I figure they had to cut back a bit since there is enough content for over 200 levels of gameplay.
That’s right, 200! I don’t have a number for the amount of different maps total, but I’ve probably seen more than 40 already and I am over level 100. You do see a lot of the standard areas, like a peaceful looking field or a dungeon filled with monsters, but they change it up enough so it doesn’t get boring to look at. The max level is 280, but the quest content supposedly runs out at about 230, leaving 50 levels of straight grinding to do. That’s a tall order for anyone, let alone a regular player who just wants to unwind for a few hours during the weekend.
Regular gameplay is fairly simple - designed with a keyboard in mind (but you can use keyboard and mouse or a controller as well), all of your movements are controlled by the arrow keys and spells on the keyboard rows, but you can have more if you like. It plays like an action game where you can dodge attacks and dash and jump, just with spells instead of combos. Dodging can be kind of iffy occasionally, as hitboxes or lag make it tough to jump over ground attacks. Most classes are very skill-heavy but the given layouts are pretty comfortable. Unfortunately the only way to rebind keys right now is by editing a file, which just feels like an obvious oversight.
In fact, I’d go so far as to say that this game requires a lot of research to get the full enjoyment from it. There is no stat reset and skill resets are only purchased with real money. On top of that there are seven ranks for each class and each one has at least two different and new choices in it, so there are hundreds of build combinations per class, with no way to reset or change your mind when you’ve decided, so you better make it count. It’s very easy to make a choice you might regret later, which feels very old-school but also a little frustrating for some. I have been in dungeons where players will tell others that they should be reading this big document talking about the nuances to the combat; a lot of things just aren’t intuitive.

A lot of these minor details have been fixed by the awesome community of the game. There are addons that people have made through LUA scripting and other means that were made to patch holes currently in the game. Gibbed made an addon that shows all the sidequests that you can take, and even displays them on the map so you don’t have to talk to every single NPC or check every corner of every map for quests. Right now most of these addons are unofficial and haven’t been approved by designers, but they mentioned that addons are fine as long as they’re not exploiting the game or giving some players unfair advantages.
Up until now the messaging between players and developers has been pretty good. They listened to the community when they weren’t happy with the price of their early access server, and they are working to fix the ongoing bot problem that has already cropped up. Even though it’s a Korean developed game they are surprisingly talkative and have community representatives that are active on their forums. I think the real problem is that some of the issues the game has are going to take a lot more work to fix.
Although beautiful, Tree of Savior is a technical nightmare. I have a decent PC (GTX 760 and a 4590 intel processor) and this game runs very awkwardly, the main reason being that the game doesn’t use your graphics card at all. In an attempt to be playable on every computer imaginable, the programmers also forced the game to run only on a single core. Combined, these two choices make the game run very sluggishly and with lots of inconsistent frame drops and overall shaky performance. If there are many players nearby the game slows to a crawl. If a lot of enemies take damage at once you might see single digit frames per second. These aren’t uncommon occurrences either; even with multiple channels per area, you can usually find many crowded areas with players fighting large groups of monsters at once, which looks cool until it tanks the game’s performance like nothing I’ve ever seen. The good thing is that if you have a PC that can run the game at the bare minimum you’ll probably have the same experience as someone with a great computer, providing an even playing field for all - for better or worse.
Something about the creature AI just doesn’t feel quite right either. If I attack five monsters at once, occasionally one will just run away which is either a cute feature or an annoyance depending on how you see it. Most enemies are very slow to respond to attacks too, sometimes taking three or four seconds to react to you hitting them which feels very wrong considering how active this game otherwise feels.
Speaking of, spells in this game also feel a little inconsistent. Either a product of lag or poor netcode, spells will sometimes fail to cast even though I charged them up fully. Some spells that don’t have cast times can be interrupted mid-attack and can be put on cooldown without actually going off while others will be cast regardless, even if I get knocked down. Another annoying thing is enemies clumped together but at different heights can avoid being hurt altogether because of the way the 3D works. This is good and bad as it also allows you to avoid being hit by standing above someone, but it makes playing on hills or slopes fairly frustrating. All these are fairly common occurrences and it makes the game feel sort of incomplete on a technical level.
There’s a shocking lack of consistency in this game that really makes it feel rushed. I wish they had spent another 6 months fixing the performance and some of the other flaws I mentioned, because it appears a bit unstable. It’s a shame, because there is so much unique about it but I can’t look past the technical problems. This game feels like the result of a Korean designer’s attempt at making a game with a bit of a western feel, similar to what Dark Souls did. Between the layers of complexity and poor performance I fear it that may turn people away once they get frustrated with some of the games’ intricacies, which is a shame because it’s got a lot of cute details that make it fun and feel full of life. I would recommend trying out the game at least because it’s free, but know going into it that you’ve got a long road ahead and might have to deal with some issues along the way.

Tree of Savior is a fun game for those who enjoy the style.  The 2D sprite art is grogeous, and the isometric MMORPG game format is changed up with unique controls that favor a more action-packed experience.  Nonetheless, the controls take time to get used to.
The story is very cliche for the genre, and most people ignore it in-game, mashing through quests.  Some might find the quest system boring, while others will enjoy it over grinding.  Grinding becomes paramount after the questline closes after level 230.  More quests will be added down the line.
Build options are extensive, and the meta is somewhat variable due to the variety of skills/classes.  Still, issues exist when we review the differences between magic and physical damage mitigation.
Performance issues have plagued the game since Founder Beta, but as a game in Open Beta, it seems those issues are being fixed over time.  Also, the game initially restricted a lot of market/trade options in an effort to limit market manipulation and bot impact on the game.  It is widely accepted this didn't work.  Bots still showed up, but it seems they're being dealt with bit by bit, and no longer have a major effect on the game's economy.  Market manipulation has also been minimized.  Some restrictions have been removed, but personally I feel some restrictions are justifed to put more focus on gameplay rather than MMO economy know-how.
If you liked Ragnarok, MapleStory, Granado Espada, or any games like those, this might be the game for you.  If you are an experienced MMORPG player, this might provide a fresh experience.  If you are looking for a run-of-the-mill MMORPG, look elsewhere.

So you are thinking about buying Elder Scrolls Online? Is this your first MMO? Are you an experienced MMO player? Do you just like the Elder Scrolls series and are looking for more? Well, allow me to disappoint you.
The main storyline in many ways is interesting and a fun playthrough your first time. However, unlike many other elderscrolls, it is not something you would like to experience more than once. There are, of course, other smaller "main" storylines such as guilds, however they too lose their novelty after the first playthrough. However, there is the plus of the many PvE dungeons and trial content which allows the player to score on a leaderboard based on performance. If this is something you enjoy, you might have ONE reason to buy the game but there are other reason as to why you shouldn't buy the game, which i will discuss later on.
In terms of PvP, it is undeniable that PvP has been a mess since release. Many aspects of the PvP were flawed and its almost as if Zenimax put no thought into whether or not everything worked
. After the major glitches were fixed, it became bearable to play pvp. That is, untill the inevitable meta that we commonly see in games now adays took over and forced many to adapt or perish. What I mean is there were many builds such as Magick Nightblades who were forced to change their build, or level a new character. Not to mention the addition of Combat power (perks after initial 50 levels, meant to grant small bonuses, however the impact they have on whether you survive in PvP is large).
This next part brings the fun.
Zenimax Online Studios (ZoS for short) has absolutely no clue what they are doing with the game. They push out patches on their test server and ask for feadback from the comminity. This sounds fine, untill you realise that there are two MAJOR problems with how they do this. The first, being that they actually do not care about the opinion of the community whatsoever. The other, being that instead of small changes to something that needs nerfing or buffing, they wait 5 months at a time, and push out 50 different changes which leave us stranded to even attempt to figure out what is and isnt working.
My next HUGE beef with ZoS as a company is how they so desperately try and FORCE you buy their content. In the current patch on the test server, they completely destroyed all classes in preperation for the release of the Morrowind DLC which adds the new Warden class. This brings us back to the "adapt or perish" meta, except now it is "throw us 40 dollars or you might aswell not play our game."
To add to this, a HUGE reason as to why many of us ESO players pay for the 15$/month Subscription is the promise from ZoS that ALL downloadable content will be acessable to ESO+ members regardless of them owning the DLC. However, they've gone and played the legal game by calling morrowing an "expansion" rather than a DLC, meaning ESO+ members do not recieve access.
ESO is a good game. Some of my most favorite moments in gaming have happened whilst playing this game. However like many people in the past, I can no longer play this game due to the outrageous business practices of ZoS. To play this game would mean to support them, and I cannot agree with that

Factorio is an immersive production game with hints of city building and RTS-Battle games. The graphics are well suited to the infinite nature of the game and emulate a 16 bit style. As the game title suggests there is a substantial amount of automation and factory building to facilitate your production. The game has a very addictive nature and is incredibly difficult to organize which leads to an immense amount of time spent planning. I personally enjoy city-building games and would put them in my top three game genres. Cities:Skylines and Minecraft both come to mind when playing Factorio but it's in a league of it's own undoubtedly.
What I enjoyed:
Quick Start – I mentioned that I play many city building games which made getting started in Factorio fairly easy after a couple of well built but poorly described tutorials. When you start your first production setup you advance rapidly. As you advance you'll find that more and more components are needed for each new component and creating compound production lines becomes key. You'll find within a couple of hours you have components for research being automated into your labs while you setup new automation lines.
Logic Puzzle – The amount of logic needed for a game like this is incredible. The amount of times you'll likely restart a facility to get the perfect setup is equally incredible. I found this phenomenon to be a mixture of frustration and elation. You'll be cursing the developers each time you run hundreds of pieces of track only to find the production line isn't going to work right and you have to rebuild the whole thing. You will however sit back with a sense of amazing pride when you have 40-50  different production lines feeding into hundreds more creating vehicles and weapons by the warehouse.
Multi-Replay – There are some deep replay-ability aspects to Factorio. Players can group up and build massive complex systems together which only further increases the expansive nature of the automation. The maps are highly customize-able and mods are both encouraged as well as available in substantial numbers already. The overwhelmingly positive reviews on the Steam platform are over 8,900 at this point so it's clearly something the community is embracing.
What I disliked:
Sunken time – I've played enough games with semi-infinite to infinite formulas to recognize what is happening to me during the addictive game-play stage. I stopped myself at 30 hours of Factorio solely noticing that it could get out of hand quickly. This is not a flaw as much as a design element that has become more popular and available due to the processing power of CPU's being able to sustain "infinite" generated worlds. Minecraft is similar in that you can build infinitely and one thing I do enjoy about city building games is that once you fill the terrain you often have a feeling of completion which cannot be obtained with these infinite games.
Returning is difficult – My biggest problem with Factorio is that when you save your game after playing for hours and return to it after a few days it can be completely overwhelming. I found my first hour was often spent trying to figure out where I was in terms of the next thing to produce or the next line to connect. The seer vast nature of the game can make managing every aspect quite a task. I found that often I felt more like starting a new map than trying to figure out how the mess of wires and tracks worked from a map I played a week ago.
I found Factorio to be an incredibly deep and well designed game. The only downsides I mentioned are considered upsides by many and I can't argue that I don't see substantial upside to a game at this price point being nearly infinitely playable. There is no shortage of brain power you can spend attempting to create an efficient and massive connection of factories producing a massive variety of goods. It may be in Early Access but this game is substantially superior and more complete than many "released" titles on the platform.
Score: Buy it now

From the makers of Bastion comes a brand new game with a brand new setting. As with Bastion, the soundtrack and art are fantastic, but now instead of a Post-Apocalyptic/Western/Fantasy setting, now it's a (post-post-?)cyberpunk-ish setting with elements of noir. The combat system moves from a typical "isometric" action-RPG to a turn-based hybrid with the "Turn" system and the new abilities (programs/characters) are incredibly versatile, giving different effects when slotted into active/passive or mutation slots, giving tactical depth and an incentive to mix up and experiment with your combat style.
The plot is something best experienced yourself, told through varied means as audiologs, "codex"-style entries (tied to varied use of the combat abilities), environment and enemy design as much as the sequence of events.
Highly recommended, even more so if you're a fan of Bastion.

I don't review many games, but Transistor, much like SuperGiant's previous title, Bastion, exceeded my expectations on all fronts.
This game is a tremendously soulful piece of work, and from the very start to the very end, is first and foremost a work of art. The music, narration, artistic style and presentation flow together in a way that I would probably say outclasses almost any other game i've played. Anyone with a quibble of curiousity and a penchant for great games, or even works of art, should immediately purchase Transistor (AND Bastion) and enjoy the ride.
To touch on the gameplay itself, the combat is inventive and blends several previously done elements (pseudo-turn based combat, action queues, tactical-execution-based combat) into a pretty seamless and enjoyable experience. It is two parts arcade, one part strategic pause-and-think game. It remains fresh and has a lot of room for player creativity due to the openly configurable nature of abilities acquired throughout the game.
What follows are some brief pros/cons:
Pros:
+Incredible Art. From music to artwork, this entire game is a masterpiece.
+Gameplay. The combat remains fresh, enjoyable, and creative all the way through.
+Difficulty.  Like bastion, difficulty is born of modifiers you can apply to enemies, which give you bonuses for being brave.
+Storyline.  Again, this is a work of art and the storyline is rich, heartfelt, and incredibly immersive.
+Soundtrack.  Incredible, as usual.
Cons:
-Length.   The game itself isn't that long, although there are excuses to re-play the game with new conditions and toy around with the combat some more.
That's really all I can see anyone really griping about with this game.
In total, I'd give Transistor a 9.5/10, as one of the most absolutely awesome pieces of work i've seen in terms of gaming. It isn't a triple-A 40 hour experience... but it's an incredibly rich, artistic romp through an engaging and incredibly envisioned city of Cloudbank.

Transistor is an okay game.  The gameplay is a bit straightforward, you're simply channeled from one combat encounter to the next, with very few secret areas or opportunities for exploration.  The combat system is reasonably interesting, but nothing special.  It's also very fast-paced and sometimes hard to keep up with all the enemies on the screen.
Transistor is really only worth recommending because of its atmosphere and story.  You can tell that a lot of work and love went into the art, music, and tone of the game, because it's utterly beautiful.  The setting feels lonely and empty, but very intentionally so.  The soundtrack is amazing, and the in-game art is fantastic.

After two spectacular indie darlings, Supergiant Games seem to have found their niche- convincing worlds and characters, strategic, constantly shifting gameplay and stunning audio/visual presentation. The story is emotionally resonant, although far more obtuse than Bastion's ever was. The combat and upgrade system has impressive flexibilty and even let's you adjust "difficulty" through a risk/reward system (also much like Bastion). Aesthetically, the soundtrack will blow you away (how many games write such great, original lyrical compositions?) and you can enjoy some of the best voice acting in the industry. Created with love by a group who has swiftly become one of my favourite studios.
Taken as a whole, there is nothing out there like Transistor. BUY NOW.

Set in a fictional totalitarian country, you act as a border checkpoint guard struggling to keep your family warm, fed, and healthy.  Paid by the number of people you screen daily, you will encounter forgers, smugglers, and, even more morally challenging, people trying to visit sick relatives with improper paperwork.  Do you call to your humanity, let them through, and risk your family's welfare and imprisonment?  Or do you stamp denied on their passport to their curses and possible future retributions?

Let's talk about one of my favourite games of all time.
A game that has been out for a while, Borderlands 2 is a first person shooting game about picking one of 6 (4 in the base game and 2 dlc) vault hunters each playing significantly different from each other, collecting loot as said character and leveling up to improve your character and match your playstyle.
The game is up to 4 player coop online which is definitely the best way to play this game, although the solo experience is still really good.
In the base game alone you can play through the main game twice as a single character and max out at level 50, but if you get the ultimate vault hunter packs (which I highly reccommend) you can play the story a third time with your lvel extended to 72.
Now this is where you will notice some of the game fall apart, as some characters are going to struggle with the third playthrough while others can breeze through it. You will have to follow specific builds in order to get anywhere and farm for uniques/legendaries and go exclusively for critical locations on enemies. Thing such as some action skills and turrets become utter jokes on this difficulty because they do not scale well at all and have pitiful damage output. Some skills are honestly awful leaving not a whole lot in diversity. To top this all off not only is a bunch of the loot in this game rather bad in this difficulty but quest reward items can't properly be farmed so you will want to wait until you reach overpowered 8 level to get these but sometimes it feels like you need them to reach that anyways so you're kind of screwed either way.
If you download and run the community patch (which I highly reccommend) my above criticisms will be practically removed, bad skills either get reworked or buffed significantly and a bunch of the less effective loot becomes much better plus (while not all) a good chunk of the quest reward items are added to boss loot pools allowing you to farm them appropriately.
All in all, this game is fantastic and I love it to pieces, if my number of hours played isn't enough of an indication of the games quality. Get some friends, grab your loot, and shoot the people and creatures of pandora in the face many times.

TL;DR: Co-op Borderlands on "tough" quests is the best way to experience the game first time.
First-Person shooter that has smoothed out many issues from their first game. Textures are less muddy, hit boxes are more accurate, and the story is quite enjoyable, in contrast to the infamous lackluster final boss of Borderlands 1. The gun play is concrete with 100s of variations of weapons through the game, you'll often spend time eyeballing stats between weapons and carefully choosing which would be a more badass companion. Although, guns are really just half the gameplay, because each of the 4 classes (6 if you include the DLC) have 3 skill trees with unique playstyles for each of them (for the most part). Each class adapts to different preferences of playstyle,  if you just wanna blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and have crazy area of effect on your attacks, Berserker class would work best. If you can't aim for your life, the Anarchy class offers a skill tree where your bullets can miss and ricochet off walls, still hitting enemies. If you just want to run up and melee a badass for 250K damage, PLAY THE PSYCHO BAYBEE. Being able to cater to all play styles along with those players is a valuable design skill often missed.
Although, there are some gripes. When I did every side quest before completing main quests, I'd be over leveled for the main quest and it wouldn't be as exciting combat wise. If you are on the same level of a quest, you will steam roll through the objectives 8 times out of 10, every now and then a boss will counter your playstyle and you will actually have to try for a few minutes. BUT if you are a level or two below the quest and they label it as "tough," you will be met with a challenge that really pushes you to take advantage of all your skills, co-op synergies, weapon types, and spacing between enemies. This is where the game shines the brightest.
Co-op Borderlands on "tough" quests is the best way to experience the game first time, although it does mean that if you intended to do all the side quests for the story's sake, you'd have to miss a good portion of them during the window that they gave good xp.
Small note about the golden chest in Sanctuary. You can find Shift codes by the dozens online that will allow you to infinitely open a chest that will provide weapons with a purple rarity at minimum. While the loot is nice, finding all the good gear in a box you put in codes for really takes away the joy of finding good gear and working with it in the game. It's an entire mechanic of the game that those who use the golden chest frequently are missing out on.
Pros:
-Strong gunplay
-Unique classes and skill trees for various entertaining play styles (mostly, see neutral).
-Wonderful story and memorable characters, plenty of lore is shared through the game that you can quite literally go searching for
-Co-op even with just one other person is astounding
-Main 4 DLC are certainly worth the investment, a ton of content. Consider GOTY edition/ a bundle
-New game+ aka True Vault Hunter Mode, adds many more hours of life to the game
-The interest in playing other classes offers even more hours to the game
Cons:
-Game is too easy if you don't challenge yourself
-Netcode has a few annoying but forgivable bugs
-GOTY edition didn't provide all microtransactions, there are still some skins that weren't included. They didn't say it would be, but GOTY editions are convinent because they avoid microtransactions by bundling it all together.
Neutral:
-Axton is a class used to help break people into Borderlands from other FPS games, but in exchange they made his skill tree bland in comparison to the other Vault Hunters. Would reccomend him to a newby, but would never do a playthrough with him twice.

text:
So you are thinking about buying Elder Scrolls Online? Is this your first MMO? Are you an experienced MMO player? Do you just like the Elder Scrolls series and are looking for more? Well, allow me to disappoint you.
The main storyline in many ways is interesting and a fun playthrough your first time. However, unlike many other elderscrolls, it is not something you would like to experience more than once. There are, of course, other smaller "main" storylines such as guilds, however they too lose their novelty after the first playthrough. However, there is the plus of the many PvE dungeons and trial content which allows the player to score on a leaderboard based on performance. If this is something you enjoy, you might have ONE reason to buy the game but there are other reason as to why you shouldn't buy the game, which i will discuss later on.
In terms of PvP, it is undeniable that PvP has been a mess since release. Many aspects of the PvP were flawed and its almost as if Zenimax put no thought into whether or not everything worked
. After the major glitches were fixed, it became bearable to play pvp. That is, untill the inevitable meta that we commonly see in games now adays took over and forced many to adapt or perish. What I mean is there were many builds such as Magick Nightblades who were forced to change their build, or level a new character. Not to mention the addition of Combat power (perks after initial 50 levels, meant to grant small bonuses, however the impact they have on whether you survive in PvP is large).
This next part brings the fun.
Zenimax Online Studios (ZoS for short) has absolutely no clue what they are doing with the game. They push out patches on their test server and ask for feadback from the comminity. This sounds fine, untill you realise that there are two MAJOR problems with how they do this. The first, being that they actually do not care about the opinion of the community whatsoever. The other, being that instead of small changes to something that needs nerfing or buffing, they wait 5 months at a time, and push out 50 different changes which leave us stranded to even attempt to figure out what is and isnt working.
My next HUGE beef with ZoS as a company is how they so desperately try and FORCE you buy their content. In the current patch on the test server, they completely destroyed all classes in preperation for the release of the Morrowind DLC which adds the new Warden class. This brings us back to the "adapt or perish" meta, except now it is "throw us 40 dollars or you might aswell not play our game."
To add to this, a HUGE reason as to why many of us ESO players pay for the 15$/month Subscription is the promise from ZoS that ALL downloadable content will be acessable to ESO+ members regardless of them owning the DLC. However, they've gone and played the legal game by calling morrowing an "expansion" rather than a DLC, meaning ESO+ members do not recieve access.
ESO is a good game. Some of my most favorite moments in gaming have happened whilst playing this game. However like many people in the past, I can no longer play this game due to the outrageous business practices of ZoS. To play this game would mean to support them, and I cannot agree with that

I knew nothing about this game beforehand except that you handle paperwork, which initially threw me off, as I can imagine happened with a lot of people.
I was pleasantly surprised by this game. I read about it on a comment on Reddit talking about some of this game's immersive aspects and I had to check it out, it was on sale anyway.
I was certainly not disappointed, though not as amazing and sandbox-like as I initially imagined from what I read, it's still top notch. The whole border inspector setup is a great storytelling device. You can for example purposefully incorrectly handle an immigrant, while the game doesn't specifically ask for you to do this, and notice the effects within the story, or notice it in the next day's newspaper. It's a branching story with 20! different endings. The story has both it's funny and serious moments, and keeps it well balanced. This game has a sense of humor within a dystopian setting, which I adore. Your 'health' in this game is basically your financial situation, being able to keep up with the bills and pay for food and your family's health. If they get sick, they need medicine, which costs money. There's no arbitrary bars or meters or anything, everything is explained within the story. This is what makes it immersive to me.
The way you manage paperwork in this game is actually hilariously similar to real life. Real life shortcuts and organizational skills translate well into this game. I actually feel like being a border inspector at times, and it sounds weird to say that. XD
Stylistically, the pixel art represents the Soviet Union inspired architecture, iconography, typography, etc. really well with a fitting colorscheme.
I recommend this game to anyone who is open minded towards new experimental gameplay ideas, as this is an interesting one. It certainly holds an aspect of challenge and rewards you for actually balancing accuracy and speed. The game becomes more challenging with time and the added challenge is explained within the story.
In short: It's something different and innovating that's fun and challenging, quite immersive (if you still have your sense of imagination) and has a branching storyline that can both be funny (albeit often in a dark way) and serious at appropriate times.

What an amazing game! Some of the best graphics and atmosphere I’ve ever seen. Its graphics still supersede most new releases which is quite an achievement for a game 2.5 years old. I’m flabbergasted why this game didn’t have better sales and more critical praise. I know that it has it’s downsides (a bit too long, probably too many Seegson simple Joes and still a few lingering bugs) but its achievements in story, sound, atmosphere, lighting, graphics, art, weapon design, AI etc. are phenomenal.
Nowadays, many single player games fail to immerse me and engage my emotions but this is the first game in a long time which has succeeded. I constantly found myself holding my breath and struggling to control my facial muscles from spasming into a grimace of fear and anguish as I tried to evade the ultra quick Alien while I literally moved at a crawl to the nearest shelter of darkness. This is largely due to the amazing sound design and graphics. Graphics don't usually influence my enjoyment of a game too much but in a game such as this where it relies heavily on its atmosphere and lighting, they really do add strongly to the immersion.
If you love survival horror, stealth and story-rich games, you'll almost certainly enjoy this experience (similar to but better than Outlast, Amnesia, Penumbra series - I've yet to play Soma). And i'm not even a big fan of the Alien movies but you don't have to be to enjoy this game - and if you are a fan of the franchise, you're in for a treat!
Lastly, to the team at Creative Assembly and everyone involved, BRAVO!

Transistor is the most all-around aesthetically pleasing game I've played in some time. The visuals, sound track, and voice acting are top-notch. The story too, is very well written. This is all not to say the gameplay falls short, because it certainly does not.
The only potential problem some might have is that this game is rather short. Explanation on the "no" rating: don't buy this VERSION of the game. The developers are releasing a new one in the coming months or so, which will be more feature-complete than this. If you haven't bought one yet, get the one that's coming out soon that has all the DLC and extra features bundled in. You cannot upgrade this verison to the new one if you buy it.
That being said, DS2 is a fine game. It inevitably gets compared to Dark Souls 1, so how does it compare in my opinon? I feel that the game is, from a technical perspective, better overall. I mean as far as combat, options to PvP, and co-op with friends. It is arguably better from a graphical perspective in terms of resolution, but DS1 can be tweaked with to attain a similar result.
The drawbacks to DS2 are the level design and overall story of the game. Dark Souls games aren't big on their story to begin with, so this isn't a reason to NOT buy the game, but it definitely falls short of how the levels inter-connect with each other compared ot DS1. I would say the level design in DS2 is "easier" as far as getting from place to place, and that enemies don't respawn after you kill them a few dozen times or so.
The DLC in DS2 is fantastic and definitely worth the purchase of the full edition and not this one. I bought the season pass which included the DLC with my pre-order of DS2. The three levels add about 50% extra gameplay length-wise to the game and aren't necessary to beat to enjoy the main part. They are better designed levels, have interesting and challenging opponents and have many nooks and crannies to explore.
If DS1 didn't exist, I'd say DS2 is a perfectly good game. Just the fact that I have to caveat that makes it clear that DS1 is, I think, overall better, but narrowly. If you're looking for a game to get an idea as to what dark souls is, I'd actually recommend playing DS2 first. It doesn't share the same story as DS1, and I'd say it's easier to get into than the first. If you're up for a face-melting and laugh-in-your-face level of difficulty, then DS1 is a strong recommendation as well.
To sum up: this game is good, holds the dark souls legacy pretty well, but wait for the complete edition, since the extras are definitely worth it.

While Just Cause 2 made up for its lack of gameplay features (few weapons, lack of base variety, unpolished mechanics) with a beautiful open world, some pretty cool explosive action and great mod support, Just Cause 3 initially seemed worse to me.
Here is what I thought before getting the game for 10 bucks:
- they got rid of the roll mechanic (some of the coolest moments are with slow motion mod and dodging bullets with rolls matrix style)
- they got rid of the sprint ability (ahem... superspeed mod was badass)
- the wingsuit renders driving pointless
- other than this, the game looked just like JC2 with better graphics and bad performance
Boy, was I wrong. This game is fu(king phenomenal.
Removing the roll and sprint make complete sense to me now. Using your grapple to evade attacks is much cooler and the game overall moves faster than Just Cause 2, so there is no point for being able to supersprint.
There are performance issues, yes, but I have a modest GTX 970 and the game runs pretty solidly at almost maxed out settings, so unless you're some graphics junkie there is no reason to complain.
The star of the show, however, is the new wingsuit. Not only is it an absolute blast to fly with, but it also adds new gameplay ideas, as the parachute was never a good way to move horizontally in the last game.
There are also many cool smaller things added, such as a lot more weapons (like the Leech, fu(king amazing) and an improved rebel drop system, improved handling and vehicle models, plus retractable grapples, adding a whole new aspect to connecting things to cause mayhem. While in Just Cause 2 you could only connect things, in this one you can do this plus cause the grapple rope to tighten and crash the two objects (or people) into each other.
When the game was first released I fell in love with its soundtrack (Firestarter is so good), but the game seemed like too much of the same coupled with $hitty performance. I was wrong, and I am happy I was, because this has become one of my all time favorite games, and blows Just Cause 2 out of the water in every single way.

Alien: Isolation might be THE definitive video game in the Aliens universe (barring AvP of course). This game just OOZES atmosphere. They seem to have gotten every graphical detail right. Despite the fabulous graphics (especially lighting, fire effects, fog effects and shadows) this game looks like the movies - straight from the pre 2000 era. Humanity has conquered the stars, with lots of beeps and boops and subdued lights. Who would have imagined that in 2137 computers are older than they were when they actually made the damn movie. But that's the charm. Graphics, sounds, animations, everything fits.
Gameplay: Depending on the difficulty level you chose (from Novice to Nightmare) your experience will vary heavily. While enemies are rather tame and often don't see you even at somewhat close distance and don't react to sound that heavily, the higher difficulties (as proven in the survivor mode where you can't select any difficulty) make especially the titular enemy, the Alien, particularly deadly and irritating. Other than the ravenous Alien you will also have to compete with rampaging androids and desperate humans with guns.
The gameplay varies greatly during the 12-16 hours of game time. Sometimes it's sneaking around, hiding, crawling through vents, avoiding or fighting the various enemies, going for a space walk, trying to find your way through the station, watching your friends die...lovely. Over the course of the game Amanda gets more tools and weapons to open new paths and defend herself. Since you can often visit most areas you've already been to when you want to (instead of following the mission) you're free to explore, however, the game usually loops around anyway, so no need for that. The only things to find are some crafting items, ammo and collectibles anyway. Sooner or later you will also be able to rudimentary defend yourself with various guns. Most of those make a noise though, so killing someone usually results in the rest of the enemies (esp. the Alien) hunting you down. Combat should be a last resort, unless you're only facing androids. Once you get the flame thrower you can even scare off the big black biter.
There's also a great many things you can craft: from flares to emp and pipe bombs or noise makers, there are enough gadgets to use and gather supplies for. My biggest gripe with the item system is that weapons and items are part of the same menu and quickly switching between weapons or having an item AND a weapon equipped is not possible. This can easily spell your end, especially since you can only save at predetermined emergency stations.
The game is authentic, a lot of fun, and the difficulty can be freely modified to your personal skill level. I didn't have too much trouble playing through it apart from a few nasty situations, mostly triggered by the game. What I don't understand is why they chose to use a sort of grainy 15 FPS approach for cutscenes. The game's graphics are SO much better. Perhaps already prerendered for consoles? No idea...they take you out of the immersion completely, however.
9/10 for a genre I don't even particularly like, but this game was a blast.
As far as DLC is concerned I would stay away from those. There are two "story" DLCs. However, those are set on the Nostromo and you play Ellen Ripley or the rest of the crew in ridiculously short missions (5 euros for 15 minutes each is not worth it, if you get 15 HOURS for 50 euros with a much better narrative and missions). The other DLCs are only for the survivor mode, in which you have to - survive...and fulfill some missions. They are heavily overpriced as well imho, especially since you apparently have no map in survivor mode...

Papers, Please is one of those very pleasant, tiny surprises that comes along every now and again. And I do mean tiny: 30 megs tiny. That's four times the price of an iTunes HD episode for less than one-fifteenth the size, but believe me when I say that you'll spend more time on this game than you ever would watching any episode of any TV show.
The power of the game lies in its simple and complex art style and moral elements, respectively. Your position sees very little of any colour other than greys and blacks, probably reflecting that the morality that the game pushes you towards. Almost your money goes to rent, food and heat for your family at the end of each workday, and you get paid by how many people you process correctly. This would normally just serve to give the players incentive to pay attention and not ♥♥♥♥ up, but the game has the simple trick of any citizen just claiming what any citizen would. Maybe they want to get into the country to see their family or reunite with their significant other, and turning them away means breaking that. Of course, letting them through means you might not be able to afford heat this evening.
The game has problems, sure. If you're not the type for it, the morality system falls completely flat and you just don't care, because there's no real penalty for simply doing your job aside from citizens calling you an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in 16-bit text before disappearing forever. The booth upgrades aren't very helpful, and I can't say that this is the most thrilling game to play if you're playing on a stationary rig that can run many more exciting, if not as compelling, games. That being said, it is still surprisingly engaging for its size; I found myself able to play it (before I bought the Steam version) in class for sometimes hours at a time, just processing and processing over and over. And its size and almost non-existant graphical tax means that no matter your specs, you could run it.
In conclusion, it's more than worth recommending. The phrase "Simple, yet elegant" is thrown around a lot but it really does find a place here, amongst the endless passports and tickets that will inevitably clutter your desk. If you're the type for it, pick it up anyway, but if you're on the move a lot and switching computers, frequently finding yourself with nothing to do, I couldn't recommend Papers, Please higher. It takes some real talent to make a job that should be boring fun and captivating, and that's just what Mr. Pope has done.
Final Score: 8.5/10

I picked this up on a whim (75% off), and was pleased with it. I don't really care for elaborate reviews, so I'll keep it simple.
THE GOOD:
-The soundtrack is awesome. These feel like tunes that would've been stuck in my head from 1991.
-The weapon upgrade system is neat. It allows you to really tailor your approach.
-The gameplay. This is pretty solid Metroidvania.
-Linear difficulty curve. For an afternoon play, I got enough challenging spots without getting frustrated.
THE NOT-SO-GOOD:
-The weapon upgrade system. 3 of your 5 upgrades are worthless. Faster projectiles, maybe. But the angled shots? Why bother. Wave shot was helpful for exactly 1 enemy in the game.
-Storyline. There isn't one.
-The backtracking. Metroidvania-style games are notorious for this. However, the upgrades you get are used in every single level. So it's essentially trial-and-error to find the level that you can progress the furthest in with the set of upgrades you have.
-The same creature is used for every single boss fight. Enemies are recycled in every single level.
-The levels look different, but ultimately play out exactly the same.
-The game is very short. I registered 4.9 hours, and that's only because I spent a good chunk of that making dinner and watching TV with my girlfriend.
-A lot of wasted potential.
