You'll start off with only the ability to hire the most basic of adventurers, and as you send parties into the dungeon and defeat monsters, you'll gather loot and gold which you can spend on obtaining the ability to hire better adventurers and outfit them with better gear. This will enable you to push further into the dungeon, where you'll be able to acquire more gold and better items, allowing you to purchase the ability to hire even better adventurers and equip them with even better gear so you can push further into the dungeon, etc, etc...
Soda Dungeon is extremely repetitive, and you may end up getting bored of the combat itself. Fortunately, the game has an 'Auto-fight' feature where, once activated, the AI will take over control of all party members for you. At this point, the game could be described as a 'turn-based idle game', where you simply wait for the party to reach the limit of their endurance before collecting the loot after all party members have been defeated.
The AI doesn't do a bad job at controlling the party either; in fact, it's quite good at what it does. Although not perfect, the AI will use abilities and items in a generally intelligent and efficient manner, and for the most part, can be left to its own devices while you watch or minimise the game and do something else. After the first five or so hours of gameplay, I ended up hiring, equipping, and organising my party, sending them to the dungeon, then letting the AI take over from there. I imagine this is what you might end up doing as well, unless you really, really insist upon the idea of grinding out hundreds of levels of dungeon manually.
On another note, the aforementioned 'Auto-fight' feature can be toggled on and off at any time, so if you see a situation where human intervention is required, you can simply turn this off and control your party members for as long as you need to, then set them back to auto once you've done whatever you intended to do.
Excluding the boss floor, which occurs every 100 floors, there are 5 areas. Each of these areas lasts for 20 floors and come with their own unique backgrounds, music, and monsters. Changes in levels are announced through text, while changes in areas are announced both via text and changes in background and music.
Once the boss on the hundredth floor is defeated, the dungeon will reset and the enemies will become tougher and deal more damage.
At random points throughout the dungeon, you'll come across a 'fork in the road', giving you a choice between entering one of two doors, where one door will lead to a trap that will harm your party, and another door will lead to a room with some kind of reward or benefit. Alternatively, you can choose to ignore these doors and continue on your present path. Dungeon levels are otherwise cleared in a rather linear fashion - after clearing one floor, you'll automatically move on up to the next. This leads us to our next point. Just how far does this dungeon go? At what point do you 'finish'?
The point of the game is to fight far enough into the dungeon that you can meet and fight the boss. After the boss is defeated, you can then advance the game and proceed to the next dimension, where the next boss fight is 100 levels higher than the boss you fought in the previous dimension. Whenever you advance to a new dimension, you lose all gold and equipment in your inventory, as well as the ability to hire all the adventurers you previously unlocked. However, you'll be given two relics: one affects and benefits all party members, and the other specifically enhances one type of adventurer. These relics are permanent and continue to provide boosts to party members' statistics even if you advance to another dimension.
Some relics can only be upgraded a limited number of times, but most of them do not seem to have a limit, so it's possible to keep increasing your party members' attributes as long as you can afford it.
There are a limited number of dungeon bosses and dimensions to advance to, so you'll eventually end up in the final dimension. From here, you can simply keep on pushing higher and higher into the dungeon until you're satisfied that you no longer want to continue.
While there's a decent variety of gear to find, I feel the loot system is one of the game's weaknesses. You'll start off finding level 1 gear, and as you reach higher levels, eventually, level 2 gear will drop. An item of the next level is only marginally better than its lower-level counterpart, but requires that the player has reached much further into the dungeon in order to have a chance to drop (this is even more so the case with rare and legendary items). Additionally, some items have far worse statistics than other items that are of much lower level. A level 10 iron shield has worse statistics than a level 5 spike shield, but is far more difficult to obtain. I found the tiered weapon system uninteresting, and the power differences between weapon tiers was underwhelming.
There are also rare, legendary, and mythical items, all with their own special attributes and effects. They gave me some satisfaction in finding/farming them, and didn't render all the non-rare items completely obsolete, though I still would have preferred to see more (new) items with their own characteristics, instead of simply slightly buffed versions of the usual junk you found when you were first starting out.
There are microtransactions in this game, but they're not at all required. Soda Dungeon seems to operate on a pay-to-save-time model, where it's possible to obtain things simply by playing the game, but would take a lengthy investment of time to do so without spending any money.
Some of the things that can be unlocked/obtained through payment are:
- Special characters
- Relic upgrade levels
- Various upgrade/ability levels
+ Competent AI allows you to play the game manually or treat it as an idle game
+ Good entertainment value for the price of admission
+ The story/dialogue is mildly interesting/amusing
+ Lots of quality-of-life features (warp to specific dungeon levels already passed, automatically sell excess items, save outfits for specific classes, etc)
- Tiered loot system is uninteresting/unrewarding
- Repetitive - you'll be fighting the same monsters and visiting the same areas over and over for (mostly) the same loot, only of (slightly) higher quality/statistics
For me, the enjoyment and satisfaction in playing this game came from watching my party of adventurers grow in power, from barely being able to clear the first 50-100 floors, to eventually powering through hundreds of floors in one run. Seeing a rare or legendary item drop from a monster or chest also gave a sense of reward, as well as doing other silly things like equipping my party all with gold-boosting gear, then watching as enemies and chests burst into ridiculous fountains of gold.
I'd recommend this game to people who like hunting/farming loot and grinding dungeon levels, but not to those who are looking for deep or engaging battles. There is some variety, experimentation, and depth to be found in gear setups, party compositions, and skill use, but the fixed order in which party members have to move, as well as the lack of synergy or team abilities among the different types of adventurers means you'll probably outfit and arrange your party, pick a floor to warp them to, then leave them to fend for themselves.

Normally, I'd say, "Stop! There's a demo. Just play it." Normally, demo > review. But whether the demo fairly represents the experience of the full product is something to consider.
I hope you played the demo. I hope you experienced for yourself that this game isn't super serious realistic. The game mechanics are a bit silly with the liberties taken (e.g. automated research? You just miraculously learn something after enough resources poured into a depository?).
This game is finally on Steam. It presents itself as early access, despite being 4 years in development as I understand it. The sandbox is there. The story/campaign, imo, leaves much to be desired. If it's meant to be the slow and steady progressive tutorial, it doesn't cover all the bases. I found myself very confused as to whether steam engines were working, as the network feedback is never explained. The feedback strongly implies that electricity is only generated when something that uses electricity is connected. It constantly says the consumption = production, without clearly explaning what my max production can be, or why I'm not producing it (presumably, max production consumes more resources, and the game is just built to automatically be as efficient as possible without manual management).
If it's just meant to be a series of unique objectives that form a narrative, and provide purpose to those without sandbox self-motivation, then maybe it fairs better. I'm not ready to say, as it quickly dropped me into an objective that I had no idea how to solve ("reclaim" an empty, damaged base?  There was no enemy to take it back from, no enemy to defend against as I attempted to replace what appeared to be missing, and no indication made as to what form or function the base needed to have for it satisfy a "reclaimed" condition.)
The good news is that, from what I hear, the campaign isn't finished. It could get better at doing either of the two things a campaign should, if not both.
All that's left is to describe the challenge, which the demo doesn't adequately do. The demo tends to give you really good set-ups, but you won't get these in the full product's campaign or sandbox. The challenge is typically from resources being far apart. Ultimately, I find this game to be a logistics game. It's on you to get things where they need to be for this or that automated process to be able to happen. You won't want to try and run/walk around and do anything manually, as things will come to a halt if they depend on you for things like fuel/energy.
In sandbox, combat is optional setting, and I imagine that the enemy will hold to a pattern of generating a wave to send against you for as long as you allow the enemy generator to exist. I haven't attempted to eliminate any enemy base, though, as I'd rather just not have combat. Combat is not optional in the campaign.
For all that it isn't, for some reason this game is highly satisfying to a lot of people. There are a lot of ways to do things, inefficient as they may be. The fact that people have control over the design empowers them; it gives them ownership of the automated production that goes on without them by virtue of the fact that it wouldn't function at all without a working design.

This is a really charming game, and deffinitely worth the price. yes it's short, but it's challenging and has a couple of unique mechanics (which i won't spoil due to the length of the game)
a couple of things i really appreciate are the nature of the upgrades. you earn weapon upgrades, which serve as points for you to spend on a kind of skill tree. the devs really went out of their way to give you freedom with these skill trees:
-spending points is not permenant you can change things at a moments notice
-you have skill sets, so you can switch between two or even three play styles very easily
little touches like these make this game an A-list for me.
also, there are no checkpoints in the game, except for right before bosses, making the levels challenging, but completely cutting out the frustration should you die at the boss, since you spawn outside and can try again.
the graphics are actually really nice. at first glance they might appear to be a cheap 8-bit look to shorten dev time, but actually there's a lot of thought given to aesthetic and theme, each enviornment feels very different and vibrant.
the one nit-pick i might have is with the boss, instead of fighting several different bosses, you fight the same boss several times, but with new attack patterns. now that being said, it really works for the game and gives it a great progression in difficulty, but it still felt kind of tedious seeing the same boss over and over.

Let's talk about one of my favourite games of all time.
A game that has been out for a while, Borderlands 2 is a first person shooting game about picking one of 6 (4 in the base game and 2 dlc) vault hunters each playing significantly different from each other, collecting loot as said character and leveling up to improve your character and match your playstyle.
The game is up to 4 player coop online which is definitely the best way to play this game, although the solo experience is still really good.
In the base game alone you can play through the main game twice as a single character and max out at level 50, but if you get the ultimate vault hunter packs (which I highly reccommend) you can play the story a third time with your lvel extended to 72.
Now this is where you will notice some of the game fall apart, as some characters are going to struggle with the third playthrough while others can breeze through it. You will have to follow specific builds in order to get anywhere and farm for uniques/legendaries and go exclusively for critical locations on enemies. Thing such as some action skills and turrets become utter jokes on this difficulty because they do not scale well at all and have pitiful damage output. Some skills are honestly awful leaving not a whole lot in diversity. To top this all off not only is a bunch of the loot in this game rather bad in this difficulty but quest reward items can't properly be farmed so you will want to wait until you reach overpowered 8 level to get these but sometimes it feels like you need them to reach that anyways so you're kind of screwed either way.
If you download and run the community patch (which I highly reccommend) my above criticisms will be practically removed, bad skills either get reworked or buffed significantly and a bunch of the less effective loot becomes much better plus (while not all) a good chunk of the quest reward items are added to boss loot pools allowing you to farm them appropriately.
All in all, this game is fantastic and I love it to pieces, if my number of hours played isn't enough of an indication of the games quality. Get some friends, grab your loot, and shoot the people and creatures of pandora in the face many times.

9/10 For a specific number of reasons.
First and foremost, its combat system.
Combat is fun, fluent, and effective with /slight/ realism
I enjoy the many different types of weapons and for the
most part their stats are even.
Secondly, Building. The building system is
similar to that of games like Robocraft and
Minecraft, and is a huge part of this game.
The only complaint I have is the amount
of resources needed for some of the more
advanced items, but it still makes building a fun challenge!
Lastly, player-to-player interactions. Its hard to find
a game where other gamers aren't killing others
mercilessly for no reason. This game (With the
exception of the outliers, such as those who do
kill on sight or hack)is probably one of
the best in forcing others to work together.
Stronger guild = More land, faster resource
gathering, and so much more. I can only
imagine how insanely good some people
might become if the map were bigger with
larger player limits.
Even though the game is still in ALPHA, I
highly recommend this specifically because
the game feels complete. Unlike other
open-world games, such as DayZ, players
are easy to find, resources are in areas that
most people find easily accessible, and
the competition between others is friendly.
Last note: What other game allows you to
drag people like a ragdoll, lock them in a
cage, and force them to play a song or die?
Answer: None.

I want to start by saying that if you are a hardcore fan of Bastion (Like me), then I absolutely recommend playing Transistor. However if you have never played Bastion, or for whatever reason didn't like it, then this is NOT the game for you.
I expected a lot from this game, being from the same maker from Bastion, and for the most part I wasn't let down. The one problem with this game is the combat, which almost ruins this game entirely.
Combat is completely based on abilities you use. You gain various abilities as you progress, but there are no basic attacks. Meaning the combat revolves around these abilities or "Functions" as the game calls them. With the new combat system known as "Turn" players can stop time and maneuver the around the fight planning what moves to make. I would relate it to V.A.T.S in the Fallout games, but much more in depth. Each move comsumes a part of your "Turn bar". When the bar is empty you can no longer make a move. In theory this is a great idea for a game and I was all for it in the beginning. The problem with Turn however is that a function like this should be up to the players choice in games, but with the amount of damage enemies do and the time it takes for you to cast a single ability, it is almost impossible to finish a fight sequence without relying completely on it. Now one would think you could solve this problem by just turning down the diffuculty. Unfortunately you the difficulty is set, and cannot be changed. To make matters worse once you have used turn it goes on cooldown (based on how much of the turn bar you consumed), making all of your ability unusable until turn is usable again. There is an ability in the game that can be used during turn's cooldown, and it can be applied to other abilities as well, but once again with the long cast animations and the amount of damage enemies do, it is much wiser to simply run away and wait for Turn to come off cooldown. This makes the game have very little veriety since you have to rely completely on a single function. Turn should be giving the player a viable option to change the flow of combat and not completely dictate it.
However the ONLY problem I have with Transistor is the combat. The rest of the game is absolutely fantastic. The soundtrack is absolutely beautiful, the visuals are just stunning, the story is a little hard to follow but is interesting nonetheless, and the narration is even better than before. All of these combined are enough for me to look past the problems with the combat and continue playing.
I was expecting a game that would rival Bastion. What i got was a game that can never hope to come near Bastion's level. In the end it didnt meet expectations, but is still an acceptable game.

I know this game is a few years old, but hey
What to say about Alien Isolation.
What can I say? What words can I say that will truly give this game the justice that it deserves.
I’ll preface this review by stating that I don't normally play horror games. There is just something about the genre I find unsettling to a degree that makes me uncomfortable playing them. I’ll also state that number reviews like 9/10, 4.5 stars out of 5 and so on do not appeal to me. I think that they undervalue what a game can truly be rated at.
Now I've played a ton of video games, from Call of Duty to Battlefield, from Binding of Isaac to Unravel, and a ton of games there and in between. But none have given me the immense feeling of elation and accomplishment that Alien: Isolation has. The emotional roller coaster that this game is, it’s something that I haven’t found too often in my gaming experiences. I really got attached to a couple of the characters in the game and I genuinely felt upset when something happened to them. For me that kind of immersion is special and it is something that I hope more games can learn to adopt. Samuels is by far my favorite character.
Overall the performance of the game was superb. The game ran smoothly even during massive explosions and hectic events. The storytelling was fantastic and the way the game was written was excellent. However the game had a bit of a suspense problem and I feel it was a bit drug out in some places. There were these intense parts of suspense that had me thinking “okay that’s enough suspense I want to get back to surviving”. For instance the portions where it turned into a walking simulator to push a few buttons then slug your way back, only to find out that it was counterintuitive. By this statement you might concur that the game is really hectically slow which it is however there are reasons for the game being slow. There were just portions that were a bit over exaggerated.
Suspense aside, the game keeps its pace on survival up a majority of the time. When you aren’t dealing with the alien you have to deal with a ship, or other humans, or angry androids that remind me of an earlier model of Data from Star Trek. They were never really an issue either. More of a nuisance than anything else. You are constantly faced with problems and you have to always be on your toes for what the next problem could be. With this, I had to constantly think about what to do next, map out where to go, and how on earth I was going to get out of the pickle of a far too curious alien. More on that later.
In terms of gameplay, the way Ripley is able to interact with the environment around her is phenomenal and allows for different types of playstyles. For instance, I was having some issues with the alien being to my left in this small corridor, and their being some sort of police force below me on the stairwell. I needed to get down the stairwell to reach my objective so I simply used the alien to my advantage.  I would use the craftable items to attract the alien to the humans in my way, let it get them, then wait for it to move on. I did this quite a bit throughout my 18 hours of play.
Speaking on craftable items, the items in this game are phenomenal. They allow you different solutions to many problems and made progression a bit easier. Especially, of course, if  you are like me and throw a smoke bomb to distract the alien while I sneak past him into the server hub, or smacking a group of unsuspecting humans with a molotov. The items themselves are each unique and give the player a sense of power over the scenario they are put in. I never once felt like I had to figure out how to get around the alien since the abundance of pieces for said craftable items was a bit excessive. I can only remember one time where the alien really got me and that was because I hadn’t quite figured out the craftable items yet.
The ai for the alien was smart in the sense that if it had even the slightest inkling of where you were, it wouldn’t leave. For instance, I remember being at a point for about 20 minutes trying to decide whether or not it would be easier to just haul♥♥♥♥♥or wait for him to leave. This is that time I mentioned earlier. This happened plenty of times in my playthrough and it was such a nuisance to deal with, having to waste noisemakers just to get around the corner or waste the one smoke bomb I made the entire game. There were plenty of times throughout my playthrough in which the alien would toy with me. He would know where I was and wouldn’t move simply trying to wait me out. There were also times where the alien would, rather than go after me, allow me to bring him victims. Fortunately I allowed their deaths not to be in vain as I scurried into a nearby vent or through a door. The ai is one of the most interesting ai’s I've seen in recent years and it is certainly one that I will remember for a long while.
There are not many things to gripe on about this game. It was executed perfectly and immersed me to no end. The only issues I really had were a few crashes, map and weapon glitches that were solved by a quick restart. I would have much rather have spent the 25 or so minutes it took for all those restarts playing, but that is simply unavoidable sometimes. I found a glitch that was exceedingly annoying however, in which the flamethrower would disappear if I swapped weapons while having a weapon drawn. This caused the flame on the flamethrower to disappear as well. I found this most annoying simply because rather than using the flashlight which would have drawn enemies to me, I was using the small light the flamethrower gave off to supplement my inability to see.
Overall though the game was by far one of the best I have played in recent years and it will leave a lasting impression on me. Creative Assembly I applaud you for a job well done, and if this is the kind of quality games we can hope to receive from you, I will be looking forward to the next title you release. I hope you all have enjoyed my thoughts on Alien Isolation, have a wonderful day.

This game was always on my "2nd tier" list of games to buy.... there was always another game I wanted just a LITTLE bit more, and as a result I didn't get this game until fairly recently and then did not play it immediately.  After having finished a playthrough I can safely say that I regret not having played this game MUCH, MUCH earlier and that it is a truly unique gem of a game.  Very tense atmosphere in a way that only a first-person perspective can provide..... example- Dead Space.  Very tense game and highly freaky atmosphere.... but I just feel that if you took that same game and put it in first-person perspective that it would be much more intense and frightening.  But I digress.
They absolutely NAILED the look and feel of the locations in Alien Isolation.  Very true to my recollections of the early Alien movies... granted it's been a while since I've seen any of them.... but the environments were just PERFECT.  Dripping with details- advertisements on the walls, the different random items lying around.... if you keep an eye for detail during your playthrough (which can admittedly be hard at times when you are running/hiding for your life) you will have more than a few chuckles and you will REALLY be drawn into the environment.  I can't state enough how the devs REALLY REALLY had an attention to small details and it really makes a huge difference in terms of believability and overall atmosphere.  While much of the game takes place on a backwater space station it manages to avoid feeling like a sterile, industrial-ish, generic type location.  It feels lived in and alive, in a way that Rapture, Colombia, The Zone in Stalker... it feels like an NPC, a character as important as any major companion/character in the game.
Whereas the Dead Space games gave you a horror-filled environment and then slowly gave you a powerful-enough arsenal to start taking the fight to the bad guys, Alien Isolation DOES give you more and more tools- but fighting is less viable than running/hiding/sneaking in most circumstances.  There is no getting around the fact that you ARE the hunted, not the hunter, but as you get more and more tools at your disposal you don't necessarily feel COMPLETELY weak and powerless the entire time.... you just never get close to the Dead Space-style "Kill everything that moves Rambo-style".  There are many different people and things that you can find yourself in conflict with- don't think this is only a cat-and-mouse "Hiding from the Alien" game.  Many of your tools are better suited to being used intelligently in the right circumstances to avoid fights or trick opponents into coming into contact and fighting each other.
The game is quite long.... 30-plus hours for my first playthrough (I'm on a second one so I don't have the exact time of my first playthrough anymore).  One note about difficulty- i usually advocate playing games on Super Duper Hard.... I personally find this more immersive and fun.  This game I'd advise playing on Normal to start with..... I won't get too specific as to why because it'd be giving away something about the game- but the difficulty changes the Alien's behavior and playing Normal the first time allows you to figure out and play with your tools enough to where you can reasonably get out of most stick situations.  On Hard it changes the alien's aggression and behavior in some ways that can get a little frustrating and on Impossible the alien is even more relentless AND you find VERY few resources with which to build your tools/items with which to distract/defeat/escape your enemies.  I was hitting a wall pretty bad on Hard- switched to Normal and had a WONDERFUL experience and it was certainly still very difficult.  With what I learned I'm now doing a Hard Mode run and having decent success.... I'm just saying that THIS is one game that there is no shame in playing on an easier difficulty and I'm not the only person that thinks this if you check out the Community Hub forums.  A mod called The Unpredictable Alien Mod changes some of the aspects of the Alien's behavior... you may wish to check it out and see if it doesn't sound interesting to you.  I'm using it in my current playthrough and have enjoyed the changes.
In short- amazing game.  Very detailed, quite a long game.  Have not played the DLC yet but have heard good things about them.  Definately worth checking out but it can be a bit... tense.  It managed to keep me on edge for like 90% of the game which is pretty rare.  I'd compare the atmosphere a little bit to Dead Space.... but that's not QUITE right.... it's certainly it's own beast and if you don't mind horror-ish games I'd DEFINATELY pick it up.  One of the rare games that I think is worth the full, non-sale purchase price.

Alien: Isolation might be THE definitive video game in the Aliens universe (barring AvP of course). This game just OOZES atmosphere. They seem to have gotten every graphical detail right. Despite the fabulous graphics (especially lighting, fire effects, fog effects and shadows) this game looks like the movies - straight from the pre 2000 era. Humanity has conquered the stars, with lots of beeps and boops and subdued lights. Who would have imagined that in 2137 computers are older than they were when they actually made the damn movie. But that's the charm. Graphics, sounds, animations, everything fits.
Gameplay: Depending on the difficulty level you chose (from Novice to Nightmare) your experience will vary heavily. While enemies are rather tame and often don't see you even at somewhat close distance and don't react to sound that heavily, the higher difficulties (as proven in the survivor mode where you can't select any difficulty) make especially the titular enemy, the Alien, particularly deadly and irritating. Other than the ravenous Alien you will also have to compete with rampaging androids and desperate humans with guns.
The gameplay varies greatly during the 12-16 hours of game time. Sometimes it's sneaking around, hiding, crawling through vents, avoiding or fighting the various enemies, going for a space walk, trying to find your way through the station, watching your friends die...lovely. Over the course of the game Amanda gets more tools and weapons to open new paths and defend herself. Since you can often visit most areas you've already been to when you want to (instead of following the mission) you're free to explore, however, the game usually loops around anyway, so no need for that. The only things to find are some crafting items, ammo and collectibles anyway. Sooner or later you will also be able to rudimentary defend yourself with various guns. Most of those make a noise though, so killing someone usually results in the rest of the enemies (esp. the Alien) hunting you down. Combat should be a last resort, unless you're only facing androids. Once you get the flame thrower you can even scare off the big black biter.
There's also a great many things you can craft: from flares to emp and pipe bombs or noise makers, there are enough gadgets to use and gather supplies for. My biggest gripe with the item system is that weapons and items are part of the same menu and quickly switching between weapons or having an item AND a weapon equipped is not possible. This can easily spell your end, especially since you can only save at predetermined emergency stations.
The game is authentic, a lot of fun, and the difficulty can be freely modified to your personal skill level. I didn't have too much trouble playing through it apart from a few nasty situations, mostly triggered by the game. What I don't understand is why they chose to use a sort of grainy 15 FPS approach for cutscenes. The game's graphics are SO much better. Perhaps already prerendered for consoles? No idea...they take you out of the immersion completely, however.
9/10 for a genre I don't even particularly like, but this game was a blast.
As far as DLC is concerned I would stay away from those. There are two "story" DLCs. However, those are set on the Nostromo and you play Ellen Ripley or the rest of the crew in ridiculously short missions (5 euros for 15 minutes each is not worth it, if you get 15 HOURS for 50 euros with a much better narrative and missions). The other DLCs are only for the survivor mode, in which you have to - survive...and fulfill some missions. They are heavily overpriced as well imho, especially since you apparently have no map in survivor mode...

Getting older I don't get impressed by many games these days, but have been a gamer all my life. Factorio came out of nowhere and kicked me right in the shins, in a good way. This game will constantly challenge and reward you in so many ways you never thought possible that it's absolute brain cocaine, Will run on literally any computer in beautiful old-school 2D design, and when it comes to puzzles, strategy, research, defense, base building, production, infrastructure, etc etc etc; this game has it all. I cannot possible overstate how addictive and intelligent this game really is. Well worth the money.

Shortly after its release into early access, Factorio found itself neighbouring Stardew Valley in the Steam bestseller list. I have played both, and the contrast is worth exploring. Both are modern continuations of a classic game or genre. Both take advantage of the love of crafting, mining, building, demolishing and rebuilding again that we in the 2010s love so much. (Lord knows what our descendants will think of the generation which fantasized about throwing away all the luxuries of civilisation to dig stuff out of the ground. It's like a reverse-Billy Elliot fever dream.)
Here's the crib notes: plucked from your familiar existence and deposited squarely in the middle of 'nature', you must make a life for yourself through hard work and resourcefulness. But whereas Stardew Valley longs for the pastoral world of Thomas Hardy, Factorio prefers a gruelling 'state of nature' straight out of Thomas Hobbes. The world upon which you have crashed is wild and foreboding, and if you ever want to escape it, you'll have to exploit its resources through the kind of brutal industrialisation which has led to our real world being such a safe and well-balanced place. The native population won't take kindly to this, so you'll be encouraged to exterminate them with ever-greater firepower. Luckily for you, the barbaric hordes yield vital resources for scientific research, which can only be obtained by
. If you're getting an imperial vibe from this, you're not wrong. It would hardly be the first video game to tap into a desire for conquest and domination, though. You're no better, Minecraft: Creepers are people too.
If you want a management game which tests the reasoning and creativity of the player with ever more complex logistical challenges, you could do a lot worse than Factorio. A seemingly endless network of moving parts, conveyor belts, machines, pumps, pipes and boxes eventually reaches a point that is halfway between migraine-inducing and pure unadulterated joy. Moving up the tech tree feels compelling, and provides meaningful rewards. Resource scarcity and the constant need to find and produce new ingredients keep the player moving, exploring, and devising new ways to arrange the overlapping streams of materials. And all you fans of troubleshooting will be spoiled by an eternity of tinkering to get that perfectly optimised system working exactly the way you want.
This is a brilliantly engaging game of ingenuity, exploration, and rather dodgy colonial politics. I've already spent too much time on it, and I guarantee I'll spend much more in future. Good job.

I absolutely love this game.  If you've played a Total War game before, this is the best and you know what to expect.  While there have certainly been ups and downs in the series, TW-R2 makes up for a lot of the mistakes.  The game takes place in ancient Rome, and allows you to build an empire with a variety of different factions.  Thanks to CA paying attention to it's customers, the wait time between end of turn to the start of your turn (time where the computer factions play) has been greatly reduced.
Graphics and gameplay are quite smooth.  Gone are all of the time settlements and towns you need to manage in Empire, and instead the campaign map is organized into Provinces which makes enconmic and building management a breeze.
Multiplayer and DLC abound for this game. Some of the DLC lets you play extra factions which you can skip if you're not interested, however the Wrath of Sparta, and a few others, open up new campaigns.  I'd recommend getting the DLC on Steam sale.  *Update - Creative Assembly is releasing new DLC for this game - something unheard of - shows you the level of support this game still has! - End Update*
I always find myself coming back to this game after playing something else for a while.  I'd say that this wouldn't be a game you play constantly above all others, rather one that you play in between other blockbuster games, like a good old reliable friend.

Started out good, but then everytime I got a new upgrade to progress, I ended up going to the 3 worlds that you couldn't progress on yet, before finally getting to the world that required the upgrade. This felt completely intentional, otherwise the game would probably last less than an hour.

Xenodrifter is a 2D watered down metroid clone- you know the kind. Navigate mazes, get power-ups to access new areas, fight evil space monsters, and backtracking galore. Xenodrifter straddles the gorge with one foot on the side of neat ideas with the other firmly planted in unnecessary tedium. The major power-up and mechanical theme is lifted from an older title Renagade Kid worked on called Mutant Mudds, where the protagonist can warp from foreground to background to traverse the world. Another major feature is how you can customize the gun- the hero's main form of attack. Want the bullets to weave through the air? There's an upgrade for that. Faster Bullets? Got it. Spray and pray? Right here. You can allocate points to make your gun as “wavy” or “fast” as you like. As you progress through the game, the more of these upgrade points you find and the crazier your custom gun becomes.
However, the gameplay is fairly dull. The stages have bleak layouts with no real threats besides the odd off-screen enemy ramming you. The game just has that “autopilot” feel. Jump up ledges, stand still to shoot the bouncing baddy, move on. No real hazards, interesting enemies, or challenging puzzles. The bosses are the same creature with different colors and more attack actions. This visually makes bosses anti-climatic and their patterns obvious.  Oddly, the game feature few checkpoints- only one at the start of the stage and when you face the planet boss. This can lead to some false difficulty and more tedium as you face the same enemies, the same layout, with the same stage all over again from the beginning if you get nixed. Snore.
If you absolutely enjoy these types of 2D action-adventure games then you've played much better and far worse. Xendrifter is in the middle- it has good bullet points to pique your interest, but nothing engaging to make you stay. If your interested in playing one of these types of games, Xenodrfter is not a good first choice. A nice second just to see what an “everyday” metroid-clone feels like.
A sale, coupon, or bundle item- don't get it full price.

TL;DR: Co-op Borderlands on "tough" quests is the best way to experience the game first time.
First-Person shooter that has smoothed out many issues from their first game. Textures are less muddy, hit boxes are more accurate, and the story is quite enjoyable, in contrast to the infamous lackluster final boss of Borderlands 1. The gun play is concrete with 100s of variations of weapons through the game, you'll often spend time eyeballing stats between weapons and carefully choosing which would be a more badass companion. Although, guns are really just half the gameplay, because each of the 4 classes (6 if you include the DLC) have 3 skill trees with unique playstyles for each of them (for the most part). Each class adapts to different preferences of playstyle,  if you just wanna blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up and have crazy area of effect on your attacks, Berserker class would work best. If you can't aim for your life, the Anarchy class offers a skill tree where your bullets can miss and ricochet off walls, still hitting enemies. If you just want to run up and melee a badass for 250K damage, PLAY THE PSYCHO BAYBEE. Being able to cater to all play styles along with those players is a valuable design skill often missed.
Although, there are some gripes. When I did every side quest before completing main quests, I'd be over leveled for the main quest and it wouldn't be as exciting combat wise. If you are on the same level of a quest, you will steam roll through the objectives 8 times out of 10, every now and then a boss will counter your playstyle and you will actually have to try for a few minutes. BUT if you are a level or two below the quest and they label it as "tough," you will be met with a challenge that really pushes you to take advantage of all your skills, co-op synergies, weapon types, and spacing between enemies. This is where the game shines the brightest.
Co-op Borderlands on "tough" quests is the best way to experience the game first time, although it does mean that if you intended to do all the side quests for the story's sake, you'd have to miss a good portion of them during the window that they gave good xp.
Small note about the golden chest in Sanctuary. You can find Shift codes by the dozens online that will allow you to infinitely open a chest that will provide weapons with a purple rarity at minimum. While the loot is nice, finding all the good gear in a box you put in codes for really takes away the joy of finding good gear and working with it in the game. It's an entire mechanic of the game that those who use the golden chest frequently are missing out on.
Pros:
-Strong gunplay
-Unique classes and skill trees for various entertaining play styles (mostly, see neutral).
-Wonderful story and memorable characters, plenty of lore is shared through the game that you can quite literally go searching for
-Co-op even with just one other person is astounding
-Main 4 DLC are certainly worth the investment, a ton of content. Consider GOTY edition/ a bundle
-New game+ aka True Vault Hunter Mode, adds many more hours of life to the game
-The interest in playing other classes offers even more hours to the game
Cons:
-Game is too easy if you don't challenge yourself
-Netcode has a few annoying but forgivable bugs
-GOTY edition didn't provide all microtransactions, there are still some skins that weren't included. They didn't say it would be, but GOTY editions are convinent because they avoid microtransactions by bundling it all together.
Neutral:
-Axton is a class used to help break people into Borderlands from other FPS games, but in exchange they made his skill tree bland in comparison to the other Vault Hunters. Would reccomend him to a newby, but would never do a playthrough with him twice.

This game. Oh, this game. Look, the souls series is notorious for being the 'Incredibly, Super Hard' games, and don't get me wrong they can be really hard at most times. But in perspective I would call these games particularly "Difficult" but the learning curve of this game is -extremely- high if not the highest of any recent game. This game -will- kick you in the teeth over and over your first run through. Now, if you have an adaptive personality this game shouldn't be too difficult as, like I said, it's a huge learning curve. With all that being said, this game is INCREDIBLE...PvE wise. The Souls series is mainly a "Boss-by-Boss" type of game, meaning the main attraction to most people are the difficult boss fights. But in Dark Souls 2, the boss fights are a lot of fun, ranging from extremely challenging to♥♥♥♥♥♥easy. Normal mobs in this game are a bit different, as I will let you make up your own strategies on how to deal with them. With PvE aside, now on to PvP. My -least- favourite part of this game, and the -biggest- con in my opinion. Now...when I say Player versus Player, I mean arena-wise and I mean serious matches to either win or have fun, not "Troll-Fights" where the opponent or you is doing some gimmick to tease the other player. So let me say this: PvP is broken. Almost completely. Sure they are players who "limit" themselves, (I.E. staying at a certain Soul Level) but most people will want to keep going. Which mean that person's stats are going to be HUGE. Which goes into their DMG, and can be utterly pointless for you to even queue  for pvp. If you have high skill at this game or adept at dodging you shouldn't have too much of a problem. That being said many people don't go into the route of "making builds" rather than using a certain spam weapon. I'll let you find out and form your own -opinion- of what is or what isn't overpowered.
All that aside I UTTERLY and COMPLETELY recommend this game. 9/10! Great PvE & PvP even if PvP can be a bit frustrating sometimes.

This game is a work of art. It has been quite some time since I last played a game that was so capitivating or moving.
For what it's worth, I have never played Bastion so I won't be able to compare Transistor to it. That said, the game's aesthetics are astounding, both in terms of sights and sounds. The game's story is also very good. It essentially dumps you into the middle of events and you have to unpack it from there, tying most of it up at the end. The game's gameplay is also tied into the narrative in a nice and tight manner. The game mechanics involve using various modules that can be equipped either in active, passive, or upgraded slots. The game encourages experimentation as each module contains lore involving a particular character that can only be unlocked by using it in each of these slots. It incentivizes player experimentation in a keen way, rather than finding one tried-and-true attack. Additionally, if your health depletes in a battle it doesn't seem to outright fail you (at least as far as I've experienced). Instead, it disables one of your abilities and recharges your health. As Two Best Friends put it, it's essentially telling you that whatever you're doing currently isn't working. It's another incentive to experiment.
We're only halfway through the year, but this might honestly get my choice as the best game of 2014. I look forward to the replays ahead of me.
UPDATE 06/28
So I thought about this game some more and I want to add another reason why I like this game so much: Red seems like an actual, living person.
This is done masterfully through small things in the story. The two that stand out for me are the fact that we see her eat pizza and we see her go to use a bathroom. And I mean use *use* a bathroom, not like Silent Hill *use* a bathroom where you stick your arm down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to pull out a wallet. We see her walk into a bathroom, a fade to black with a flush, and the game returns.
This was endearing to me. Emotions and whatnot go a long way into making a fictional character appear human, but I honestly think it's the small minutiae that ultimately make fictional characters pop to life more. It's not as exciting as drama, but to me it pulses with the true blood of life: the banality of existence. I apprecaited it a lot.

Ok, so, wow...
Just finished this saga of tragedy and redemption. Just soaking in the afterglow...
It should be noted that I am a big fan of Bastion, and of narrative-driven games with saturated environments in general. So if you love such games, just buy this and drop in.
I have to admit that the first few times I picked up the controller, I didn't immediately get 'caught'; and there are reasons for that which I will explain below. The main thing is to not get discouraged if you are feeling the same way in the first 15-30 minutes.
In many ways, not getting sucked in right at the beginning is much like some of my favorite books: they take time to build. Transistor wisely knows to savor itself, not pandering to the ADD gamer just looking for the next shiney thing.
There was a critical mass moment for me, maybe 45 minutes in, where I finally got over the interface learning curve, unlocked enough powers to start to feel badass, and allowed enough of the narrative to build to really get involved in what was happening.
Look forward to this moment, because once it happens, the your gaming experience will steadily build to its poignant crescendo, leaving you both satisfied and at a loss.
Summary: the narrative is original and creative, the environments are immersive, the gameplay is unique and enjoyable, and the holistic experience is worth the price and time invested.

I want to be analed by this game.
The general jist of the game is that you crash land on an alien planet with similar recources to ours on earth. With the technology and knowledge we have, we research diffrent technologies in order to build a factory to create a ship back to our home planet.
The game is highly inspired by the technology and methods of organisation Tekkit has. (which for those who don't know, is a mod towards 'Minecraft' that add industry, additional recources) It's been around for a similar amount of time tekkit has too.
So, the styling for the game is very grimy but contrasting and bright. It's very nice to look at regardless of how simplistic it is. The way the game is able to manage a grid basis is highly effective to allow you to manage the recources you collect. It's a very simplistic layout but requires a lot of thought in order to maximise efficiency in your factory. It gives you all the tools you need to organise the factory the way you want it without anything extra to make it anymore complicated than it already needs to be to do everything you want.
The gameplay is solid. Controls are again, simplistic and let you do the job you need. I hate repeating myself, but it's hard to describe it as anything else but that because it simply is. However, getting around your factory can become annoying due to the velocity adjustment you get from conveyor belts. It's annoying, but you learn to get used to it.
The progression on the game is amazing. From the technology you learn through science labs, it's very smooth and easy to understand and build yourself up within your factories and against your enemy. Along side your own technology, the aliens on this strange planet build themselves up too accordingly to the technology you research, it makes it build up in difficulty without any sudden surge. It makes you feel like you're always progressing at a good pace.
Wanting to get everything done at all times is a disease you start to get while playing this game. There is always so much you cna do to either improve your factory or to build. I've gone a few days without eating due to how easily additicting this game is always giving you something to do.
The only current problem I find is the robots you gain access to late game. They make your factory too empty if you was to use them and make you feel like you're cheating from how easy it makes everything to make. Requesting what you want at any time without having to effectively manage what you produce.
However, my personal advice about robots is to limit what they are an allowed to do as a personal rule. It makes your factory seem like a factory, gives you a challange but allows much easier forms of automated additions towards your factory. Personally, I have fully fledged automated construction drones and only allow logistics to transport things I request on my character or to transport small amounts of ores and to transport the final products created from each section of the factory. You still have the fun of automation but keep the challange at the same time.
The only REAL problem I have with the game is the cable network system. It's overly complicated in order to complete simple functionalities and is really limited to simple mathamatic inputs created from your factory. It's a system that could use some revision to make it easier to understand with an actual tutorial to learn you how to use the system effectively.
Overall, it's a game with a lot of potential for future updates, with a very dedicated team who update the game regularly, read the fans' suggestions and bugs they're having through the forms and always look for new things they can put in the game. The game has taken ages to get where it currently is, but regardless of how undeveloped the game is, it's extremely fun.
This game is highly addictive and in general, an amazing for a game that's only in 0.12v as of it's current release. Considering that factor, I really can't wait for future updates and constantly look out for the weekly bugfixes and weekly posts on the current production status of the game.

When I saw this game appear on steam I had never heard of it. So I downloaded the demo and started playing that. 3 hours later I reached the end of the demo and was craving more.
Don't let the early access scare you off thinking the game isn't finished. It has been in development for years, and continues to get updates to this day. Even with the early access tag, it still seems like a finished product.
While this doesn't have workshop support, it does have mods and an ingame mod browser. The best thing about this is that it can automatically update all mods to updated version. Now if you are worried about a new update breaking the game because mods aren't updated yet, don't worry as the modders seem to use the beta test of new versions so when the update goes live, all your mods are already up to date.
Multiplayer. This game has it. I haven't really tried it, but a few searches online have shown people playing a game with up to 250 people at the same time.
The core of the game is all about automating anything and everything. Build a drill on an ore deposit, conveyor belt it to a place to smelt the ore, then to a machine to craft it into ammo for your gun, which gets delivered to you automatically by robots. The screenshots will look intimidating with the very large and complex factories, but they start so small and simple and grow complex over time. Then it's no longer intimidating because you grew with the factory so you just know where everything is and how it works.
This game will probably never be on sale, but it is still well worth the $20. My 446 hours spent on it say so.
Edit: Notice how I'm now over 1000 hours and most reviews have over 100? Just buy the game already.

Alien: Isolation may just be one of the nicest surprises I've ever had in all my years of gaming. It is also perhaps one of my greatest regrets that I did not play this a hell of a lot sooner.
Why you may ask? Well I'll be only too happy to tell you. So strap in folks, cause I'm gonna go a little deep on this one, I believe the title deserves it.
When it was released back in 2014 this title proved divisive, with very polarising opinions on whether it was a legitimate masterpiece, or an ambitious but heavily flawed attempt at capturing the spirit of Ridley Scott's classic 1979 motion picture; Alien.
For example, a quick look on scoring aggregate Metacritic for the PC version (the version I played) reveals this divide to a rather staggering degree.
PC Powerplay and PC Gamer awarded the title scores of 100/100 and 93/100 respectively. At the opposite end of the scale GameSpot and IGN awarded it scores of 60/100 and 59/100 respectively.
Generally speaking, it is unusual for a AAA title to have such vastly different scores, making Alien: Isolation rather unique in this regard. Thankfully, the positive reviews were far more abundant than the negative ones which brought it's aggregate score up to a very respectable 81/100 amongst the critics, with the user score average being an even healthier 84/100, with the user review count at 1600 at the time of writing this.
Regarding the user score, we can take this a step further and look to the platform you are reading this very review on. Steam user scores for this game for the last 30 days are "Very Positive" with 90% of the 412 reviews submitted in that period being a positive experience.
Further to this, the title sits on an overall score of "Very Positive", with 92% of the 16,589 reviews submitted since launch being a positive experience.
That's some pretty enviable praise from the masses to be honest. I will tell you right now, it is completely justified.
Ok, so your probably thinking "Ok, that's some interesting data but why are you sharing it with me?"
Well, I'm sharing it because it is the reason why I slept on this title for so long. Back when it launched, we really only had those critic reviews to go by if we were interested in making a day one purchase, an educated one at least. Although the title had plenty of positive ones, I will admit those damning ones by IGN and GameSpot gave me pause. I mean 5.9 and 6, that's a pretty depressing score, indicating some severe issues.
I have since then started to take scores from either of these outlets with more than a grain of salt. Although I don't think I will ever buy into the whole "Publisher X didn't pay Reviewer Y enough money to score their game well" conspiracy theory, if I were going to this would probably be the title I thought of.
So after finishing the title, I thought about the things said in both the IGN and GameSpot reviews, and the individuals it was said by, and thought about how they came to such conclusions. I attempted to at least try and be objective when analyzing the criticisms levelled at the game.
I concluded that they were more than likely working to a deadline and not in the appropriate mindset to immerse themselves into this survival horror experience. A consistent complaint between the two was that the title was overlong and too punishing. I don't believe this to be the case at all. I thought the campaign was exceptionally well paced, and the difficulty was a big part of the appeal. The fact that the Alien could be so unpredictable made it truly terrifying, and made each new save point reached a small victory.
If however, you were trying to rush through the game to get a review out I could see why you would come to loathe it. It is impossible to play this game fast, and if you try then you are just going to become frustrated. This is not a fault of the game however, but rather a fault of the player expecting the title to bend to their expectation. Just as one doesn't expect to be able to play Doom as a stealth title, one should not expect to play Alien: Isolation as a run and gun shooter.
They levelled other complaints at the game, but they are fairly meritless so I think we'll move on to my opinion of the game and conclusion. Although I'll quickly mention that GameSpot even went so far as to say it was an unattractive title, which I can assure you could not be further from the truth. I haven't played the console version/s, but on PC, this title can go up against the best of them on the graphics front.
So, my take:
This game is DREAD.
It is without doubt one of, if not THE, scariest gaming experiences I've ever had. To progress in this game was akin to crawling on my belly like a scared little rat being hunted by a predator, and I loved every second of it. The Alien is of course your main nemesis, and it does a spectacular job of scaring the ever living poop out of you when it comes calling. When it doesn't, maybe you have to contend with the Sevastopol's "Working Joe" androids instead. Let me tell you, it's not much of a trade-off. The Joe's are about as creepy as it gets, I swear sometimes these things scared me just as much as the Alien. When they stalk towards you, box you into a corner, bash your head against a wall and then start choking the life from you all whilst telling you that "You are becoming hysterical" in a dead voice you will definitely have to take a moment to mentally reset.
The save system is excellent, the inability to save when and where you want raises the stakes considerably, and makes the encounters with the Alien and Joe's even more fraught with peril as you try not to lose your progress as well as your life. Even the way it takes 3 seconds to complete the save, whilst perhaps telling you that the Alien is nearby, is pure genius, and made those three seconds the longest ever.
Graphics; Amazing. I'm a spoilt gamer, I have a great PC and I've got pretty much all the latest and greatest games. So please trust me when I say that I have a lot of titles to draw from when making mental comparisons. This title from 2014 still has drop dead gorgeous looks. The Sevastopol is incredibly realised here, with painstaking attention to detail and a true sense of authenticity. The textures and lighting are top notch. The Alien is perfect, it looks all kinds of menacing, but graceful as well, with some absolutely first class animation.
Sound: Incredible. Voices range from being decent to excellent, but the sound effects and the way they are integrated into the game with regards to the Alien itself is masterful. The station's creaks and groans can keep you on edge, but the sounds of the creature in the walls or above you or its carapace shuddering as it searches for you as you cower under a desk are just super unnerving. The music is perfect as well, completely upholding the franchises excellent pedigree and being applied sparingly but at the right times.
Gameplay: This is survival horror, and it is survival horror done right. You are in a constant state of distress, you are hunted, you are weak, and you are scared. Mechanically speaking it is very well done, no complaints at all.
Performance: Sublime. Truly, the fact that a game can look this good and run this well is quite honestly kind of staggering in this day and age. I had it maxed out, 1440p, never dropped from 144fps, which is what it was capped at to match my monitors refresh rate. I have no idea how much higher it could go, but I'd wager a lot given its ridiculous stability at 144Hz. Super well optimized game here folks.
So, that's it, if your still here thanks for taking the time to read my review. If I've helped sway you towards purchasing this title then that is fantastic, it's an experience you won't regret.

Alien: Isolation teaches us that you can't trust the majority's opinion. This game has been praised to high hell, but I found it severely disappointing. I thought I was buying a game about  Aliens, but what I got was a half-baked stealth/walking simulator. After just two hours, I couldn't take it anymore. It made me want to scream at the sheer amount of mediocrity assaulting my eyeballs. Don't buy it!
★STORY★
It's like they spent an afternoon developing the story for this game at a pizza hut. You're playing Ripley's estranged daughter. Your motivation is the promise of finding your mother that's been missing for years. That's about it. Yep. That's your motivation for risking your life on a broken♥♥♥♥♥space station with a psychotic monster on-board. Everyone is dead or dying or killing each other. Does this make you want to stop, turn around, and get the hell out of there? Nooope.
★GAMEPLAY★
Omg the gameplay is just the worst. Most of my time was spent wandering empty halls wonder where the ♥♥♥♥ I was supposed to go, because the waypoint system is complete garbage. Most of the time, I was given an objective with no clue where to go or how to achieve it. I've never had to resort to Youtube guides within the first hour of a game before. Everything is so ♥♥♥♥ing dark that you can't see anything, even with the gamma turned up to max.
You can't jump and are often blocked by TINY BOXES, fallen pipes, or sealed doors that serve as a barrier to keep you from exploring too far, so there's literally NO exploration to this game. In one instance, instead of hopping over a knee-high barrier, you're forced to climb through a fallen vent that has collapsed onto said barrier to get past it. I mean, come on. That's just awful.
Once you pull out your flare, there's no way to put it back. If you accidently push the X button, oops! There goes your last flare. Too bad, so sad. Guess you'll have to use your flashlight that gobbles up batteries so fast it only lasts a few minutes.
★SOUND & MUSIC★
The production value of the music and sound effects are truly the only saving grace of this game. It's really top notch. But unfortunately, it's not enough to save the game.
★BUGS & BOTHERS★
It really bothers me that this game is being sold as a cutting-edge graphics engine that will knock your socks off. Well, that's a lie. The use of lens flare and really, really, REALLY dark gamma correction is used to cover up the flaws like a makeup on a cheap hooker. Once the cutscenes (of which are too frequent for my tastes) take over the screen, you get a good look at how bad the graphics really are.

Not worth full price. I'd also stay away from DLC. It doesn't expand the universe or story. They're just timed challenges which is lame as hell. All in all, the story is just oozing with info that if you're an Alien fan, this is ideal. I'd give this game 8/10.

Take a Metroid game, spread it across four different planets, and make it bite-sized, and you have Xeodrifter by Renegade Kid.
What makes Xeodrifter cool and separates it from other Metroidvanias is its abilities, one of which borrows from their back catalog. There's no other Metroid-like game where your character can turn into a submarine, or can switch between foreground and background layers. The plane shifting allows for great map design that often sneaks secrets right past you in plain sight. Just pay attention you goof!
The weapons system allows you to spend (and respec) points on different attributes, from rate of fire to power to... inaccuracy? That one's a little weird. You also get to store three different presets to suit whatever playstyle you feel like. Plus you get a charge shot, Mega Man X-style, which can help take out some of the tankier enemies (like that BAT. THAT STUPID BAT, WHY. GO TO HELL, BAT).
It looks good, the music is great, it's compact and doesn't overstay its welcome, the only downside is that the boss is recycled over and over (but it does gain new attack patterns each time). Good game to buy in a sale, a fun little title.

Eeehh... this is definitely one for the "meh" pile, and what pushes it into negative review territory especially is the short length and the fact that you can do so much better for the money.
The first problem I noticed almost immediately. Fixed jump height. No. Stop. Wrong. There's no reason to make jump height fixed, especially in a game where you have to aim while jumping. Way too often I was jumping higher than I wanted to be and hitting my intended target was more trouble that it was worth.
The second is that the game is very linear. You can explore around a bit, but there's always only one specific spot of the game you can go to, regardless of the fact that it starts off with four planets to visit. It gives the illusion of freedom without offering you the slightest bit.
The third is the boss design. For the one boss. That you fight seven times. Sure, he gets new attacks. That suck. Aww yeah, shield attack that makes him invincible and takes 30ish seconds each time it occurs, great. Oh man, slamming attack that is hard to figure out how to dodge and can take an eternity as well (though he's at least not invincible). Oh good, spawning more enemies that fire 2-damage bullets.
The fourth is the artificial difficulty. There is exactly one save spot in the game; on your ship. The only other checkpoints are entering/exiting boss rooms. On all but the first planet, there's quite a distance between your ship and any given boss room. And there's very little in the way of healing; there are hidden full heals sparsely scattered around the planets, and enemies that drop health spawn right before the boss room. What this means is that you have to go a fair distance without getting hit more than a few times.
And despite that, the game's still easy as heck. I cleared it in a few hours and 100%'ed it only a little while later. Hell, I didn't even go past 5 HP until right before the final boss and didn't really struggle much for it. The "secrets" of the game are all hidden passageways that give no real indication that they exist, and aren't even worth hunting down unless you're going for 100% completion. I couldn't be bothered to prod around the (not even that large) game map to find them all, because what's the point? They're no fun to find, there's no sense of discovery, you just have to poke at everything until you find what you're looking for. I got bored and just looked them up after a while.
I don't think this game is awful, though. It's far better than Mutant Mudds. It's decently enjoyable. But it's nothing special; the only slightly original mechanic is the multiple layers one from Mutant Mudds, and while it's done better here than there it's not that special of a mechanic; swapping between two layers has been done before in many other games, it's just visually displayed as separate layers here. Other than that you have pretty stock powerups; submarine for water travel, dashing and rocket jump, a charge shot, and a short dash that lets you phase through walls, that you only need to use about 5-6 times anyways.
I wasn't impressed. I don't hate this game but I'd say pass unless you're desperate for more vaguely-metroidvania-ish gaming, For an equal or lower pricetag you can get Environmental Station Alpha, Outland, Knytt Underground, and quite a few other better metroidvania-type games.

A short and well crafted Metroid-like game. Xeodrifter is basically a mini-metroid game meaning it heavily focuses on exploration and backtracking to find hidden goodies. I really enjoyed the well crafted levels as they helped create a feeling of organic exploration throughout the game. I also found the equipment system (or however you'd like to address it) very interesting and appreciated that I was able to customize certain aspects of how my character shot bullets at enemies.
As a warning, Xeodrifter only takes 2-3 hours to complete, so if you will feel shafted buying it for 10$ (or your regional equivalent) I would recommend getting it on sale. Otherwise, if you tend to enjoy metroid-like or metroid-vania games this may be a game that you'd enjoy.

Gamefeel is pretty nice, but there's no variable jump height and you can't move while aiming up, which are both annoying.  Difficulty felt just right to me.  Like Super Metroid, exploration is generally fairly easy, with moderate difficulty bumps for boss fights.
Weapon customization feels kinda pointless to me.  Using anything other than the two DPS stats just seems like a waste.  You also have to enter the menu to toggle your super blasty gun, and to swap gun stat presets.  Why not use LB and back/select for these?
Exploration is pretty simplistic.  Four small, fairly straightforward planets that you move between via a glorified level select screen.  Keeps up the pace, but really limits the trailblazer feel that makes Metroid so satisfying.
Overall it's fun and well put together, but honestly kinda forgettable.  Grab it on sale and play through it in an afternoon if you're into Metroid.

Dark Souls II is a great game, no matter what anyone will say. It is -not- the same as the first Dark Souls though. Level design is linear, a lot of mobs and bosses are poorly designed and forgettable (though there are a few hidden gems). On the other hand, the PvP is infinitely better than the previous title; fastrolling Havelmonsters are still a thing, but lagstabs are... Slightly less of an issue, and even though From has been a bit heavy-handed when managing their balance tweaking, nerfing some things so hard as to make them unusable and buffing others to the degree of nonsense (Looking at you, here, Red Iron Winblade), it remains a wonderful game.
If you enjoyed Demon's or Dark Souls, you will enjoy this. But you might not enjoy it as much if you are one who likes to focus solely on PvE. Though you might want to wait with buying it if you haven't already, and instead wait 'til April for Scholar of the First Sin edition.
TL;DR: Great game, albeit with worse PvE than previous titles. On the plus side, improved PvP.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

A beautiful game, and a worthy successor of Bastion. Gorgeous soundtrack that only Darren Korb could provide, intruiging characters that don't shove themselves down your throat and allow you to learn about them on your own time, and a combat system you can customize with more variety than you would expect from such a short game. I beat it the first time in maybe 4 hours or so, but eagerly started it over again to explore more deeply and experience the game again. And, of course, as expected from the creators a Bastion, a story that buries you in emotion.
For a short game that will break your heart and a combat system more flexible than a member of Cirque De Soleil, play Transistor.

If you liked Bastion, you'll like this game. All the elements that made Bastion so beautiful are alive and well in Transistor. Beautiful hand drawn graphics, a great soundtrack, and exquisite narration are all well done. SuperGiant manages to keep Transistor fun in it's own way by keeping the gameplay original. The Turn() mechancics give the game an interesting edge and make you feel like a badass as you unleash a series of moves in a split second before enemies can react.
Definitely recommend this game.

Transistor is one of those beautiful surprises that you find over there from time to time... It is a game packed with action, but, in fact, is a game to behold, to enjoy its amazing soundtrack and its superb art. You are taken through the history and discovers the plot as you go through it, just like a good movie, a good book. There comes a time when it is impossible not to want to know how it will end, resulting in an unbelievable ending. For those who love a good story, good music and a fantastic art, you have to play this one.
