Alien: Isolation may just be one of the nicest surprises I've ever had in all my years of gaming. It is also perhaps one of my greatest regrets that I did not play this a hell of a lot sooner.
Why you may ask? Well I'll be only too happy to tell you. So strap in folks, cause I'm gonna go a little deep on this one, I believe the title deserves it.
When it was released back in 2014 this title proved divisive, with very polarising opinions on whether it was a legitimate masterpiece, or an ambitious but heavily flawed attempt at capturing the spirit of Ridley Scott's classic 1979 motion picture; Alien.
For example, a quick look on scoring aggregate Metacritic for the PC version (the version I played) reveals this divide to a rather staggering degree.
PC Powerplay and PC Gamer awarded the title scores of 100/100 and 93/100 respectively. At the opposite end of the scale GameSpot and IGN awarded it scores of 60/100 and 59/100 respectively.
Generally speaking, it is unusual for a AAA title to have such vastly different scores, making Alien: Isolation rather unique in this regard. Thankfully, the positive reviews were far more abundant than the negative ones which brought it's aggregate score up to a very respectable 81/100 amongst the critics, with the user score average being an even healthier 84/100, with the user review count at 1600 at the time of writing this.
Regarding the user score, we can take this a step further and look to the platform you are reading this very review on. Steam user scores for this game for the last 30 days are "Very Positive" with 90% of the 412 reviews submitted in that period being a positive experience.
Further to this, the title sits on an overall score of "Very Positive", with 92% of the 16,589 reviews submitted since launch being a positive experience.
That's some pretty enviable praise from the masses to be honest. I will tell you right now, it is completely justified.
Ok, so your probably thinking "Ok, that's some interesting data but why are you sharing it with me?"
Well, I'm sharing it because it is the reason why I slept on this title for so long. Back when it launched, we really only had those critic reviews to go by if we were interested in making a day one purchase, an educated one at least. Although the title had plenty of positive ones, I will admit those damning ones by IGN and GameSpot gave me pause. I mean 5.9 and 6, that's a pretty depressing score, indicating some severe issues.
I have since then started to take scores from either of these outlets with more than a grain of salt. Although I don't think I will ever buy into the whole "Publisher X didn't pay Reviewer Y enough money to score their game well" conspiracy theory, if I were going to this would probably be the title I thought of.
So after finishing the title, I thought about the things said in both the IGN and GameSpot reviews, and the individuals it was said by, and thought about how they came to such conclusions. I attempted to at least try and be objective when analyzing the criticisms levelled at the game.
I concluded that they were more than likely working to a deadline and not in the appropriate mindset to immerse themselves into this survival horror experience. A consistent complaint between the two was that the title was overlong and too punishing. I don't believe this to be the case at all. I thought the campaign was exceptionally well paced, and the difficulty was a big part of the appeal. The fact that the Alien could be so unpredictable made it truly terrifying, and made each new save point reached a small victory.
If however, you were trying to rush through the game to get a review out I could see why you would come to loathe it. It is impossible to play this game fast, and if you try then you are just going to become frustrated. This is not a fault of the game however, but rather a fault of the player expecting the title to bend to their expectation. Just as one doesn't expect to be able to play Doom as a stealth title, one should not expect to play Alien: Isolation as a run and gun shooter.
They levelled other complaints at the game, but they are fairly meritless so I think we'll move on to my opinion of the game and conclusion. Although I'll quickly mention that GameSpot even went so far as to say it was an unattractive title, which I can assure you could not be further from the truth. I haven't played the console version/s, but on PC, this title can go up against the best of them on the graphics front.
So, my take:
This game is DREAD.
It is without doubt one of, if not THE, scariest gaming experiences I've ever had. To progress in this game was akin to crawling on my belly like a scared little rat being hunted by a predator, and I loved every second of it. The Alien is of course your main nemesis, and it does a spectacular job of scaring the ever living poop out of you when it comes calling. When it doesn't, maybe you have to contend with the Sevastopol's "Working Joe" androids instead. Let me tell you, it's not much of a trade-off. The Joe's are about as creepy as it gets, I swear sometimes these things scared me just as much as the Alien. When they stalk towards you, box you into a corner, bash your head against a wall and then start choking the life from you all whilst telling you that "You are becoming hysterical" in a dead voice you will definitely have to take a moment to mentally reset.
The save system is excellent, the inability to save when and where you want raises the stakes considerably, and makes the encounters with the Alien and Joe's even more fraught with peril as you try not to lose your progress as well as your life. Even the way it takes 3 seconds to complete the save, whilst perhaps telling you that the Alien is nearby, is pure genius, and made those three seconds the longest ever.
Graphics; Amazing. I'm a spoilt gamer, I have a great PC and I've got pretty much all the latest and greatest games. So please trust me when I say that I have a lot of titles to draw from when making mental comparisons. This title from 2014 still has drop dead gorgeous looks. The Sevastopol is incredibly realised here, with painstaking attention to detail and a true sense of authenticity. The textures and lighting are top notch. The Alien is perfect, it looks all kinds of menacing, but graceful as well, with some absolutely first class animation.
Sound: Incredible. Voices range from being decent to excellent, but the sound effects and the way they are integrated into the game with regards to the Alien itself is masterful. The station's creaks and groans can keep you on edge, but the sounds of the creature in the walls or above you or its carapace shuddering as it searches for you as you cower under a desk are just super unnerving. The music is perfect as well, completely upholding the franchises excellent pedigree and being applied sparingly but at the right times.
Gameplay: This is survival horror, and it is survival horror done right. You are in a constant state of distress, you are hunted, you are weak, and you are scared. Mechanically speaking it is very well done, no complaints at all.
Performance: Sublime. Truly, the fact that a game can look this good and run this well is quite honestly kind of staggering in this day and age. I had it maxed out, 1440p, never dropped from 144fps, which is what it was capped at to match my monitors refresh rate. I have no idea how much higher it could go, but I'd wager a lot given its ridiculous stability at 144Hz. Super well optimized game here folks.
So, that's it, if your still here thanks for taking the time to read my review. If I've helped sway you towards purchasing this title then that is fantastic, it's an experience you won't regret.

★OVERALL★
Alien: Isolation teaches us that you can't trust the majority's opinion. This game has been praised to high hell, but I found it severely disappointing. I thought I was buying a game about  Aliens, but what I got was a half-baked stealth/walking simulator. After just two hours, I couldn't take it anymore. It made me want to scream at the sheer amount of mediocrity assaulting my eyeballs. Don't buy it!
★STORY★
It's like they spent an afternoon developing the story for this game at a pizza hut. You're playing Ripley's estranged daughter. Your motivation is the promise of finding your mother that's been missing for years. That's about it. Yep. That's your motivation for risking your life on a broken♥♥♥♥♥space station with a psychotic monster on-board. Everyone is dead or dying or killing each other. Does this make you want to stop, turn around, and get the hell out of there? Nooope.
★GAMEPLAY★
Omg the gameplay is just the worst. Most of my time was spent wandering empty halls wonder where the ♥♥♥♥ I was supposed to go, because the waypoint system is complete garbage. Most of the time, I was given an objective with no clue where to go or how to achieve it. I've never had to resort to Youtube guides within the first hour of a game before. Everything is so ♥♥♥♥ing dark that you can't see anything, even with the gamma turned up to max.
You can't jump and are often blocked by TINY BOXES, fallen pipes, or sealed doors that serve as a barrier to keep you from exploring too far, so there's literally NO exploration to this game. In one instance, instead of hopping over a knee-high barrier, you're forced to climb through a fallen vent that has collapsed onto said barrier to get past it. I mean, come on. That's just awful.
Once you pull out your flare, there's no way to put it back. If you accidently push the X button, oops! There goes your last flare. Too bad, so sad. Guess you'll have to use your flashlight that gobbles up batteries so fast it only lasts a few minutes.
★SOUND & MUSIC★
The production value of the music and sound effects are truly the only saving grace of this game. It's really top notch. But unfortunately, it's not enough to save the game.
★BUGS & BOTHERS★
It really bothers me that this game is being sold as a cutting-edge graphics engine that will knock your socks off. Well, that's a lie. The use of lens flare and really, really, REALLY dark gamma correction is used to cover up the flaws like a makeup on a cheap hooker. Once the cutscenes (of which are too frequent for my tastes) take over the screen, you get a good look at how bad the graphics really are.

- Short version:  you grind in the dungeon to make money that you use to buy upgrades to help you grind better.
The game is a free download.  There are no advertisements.  All upgrades can be obtained in-game without spending real money - or - upgrades can be purchased in-game with real money through steam for a few dollars per upgrade.

I decided the game was worth at least $5, so I chose wich upgrades I wanted to purchase for that amount and bought them to send some money to the game's creators - just my choice as I could have easily spent some time and gotten the upgrades in-game without spending real money.

CONS:

I have played this game for a about 2 years now (almost exclusively outside steam). I have made good friends within the community and enjoyed thousands of hours in this game.
General characteristics of the game:
The Hunter is a game trying to find a balance between a realistic simulator and a fun game. It is not fast paced and it might take some time before you understand the mechanics of the game. You can play in any way you want; some people focus on winning competitions or getting on the general leaderboards, others enjoy luring in birds or just walking around in a reserve, tracking and calling for the animals they love to hunt.
Downloading this game for free will give you very limited options, you will recieve a weapon that only allows you to hunt 1 species. However, if you are willing to pay for some licenses and gear, you can hunt all of the species you like and use the weapons you are fond of. The achievement system depends on the animals you shoot, and the weapons you use. Killing animals and using different weapons gives you HunterScore, which is the basis for your position on the leaderboards.
If you wish to have all the weapons, it will cost you a lot of money. However there are some great bundles that give you good weapons and permission to hunt all species in the game. Buying licenses for specific species is something I would advise against. If you buy membership packs, you get permission to shoot all species for a certain time + some nice weapons and gear. Furthermore, this game has two types of current EM$ and GM$; the EM$ can only be bought with real money and allows you to buy everything in the store, the GM$ is earned by doing missions and special events, and can be used buy consumables that improve your game or a special shotgun.
If you are thinking about buying things from the ingame store, don't hesitate to message me on steam, I can give you some advice on what to buy.
Pros:
- There are many different species (A-typical and rare colored animals can be found [albino, melanistic etc.] )
- There are many different weapons (incl. rifles, handguns, bows. Modern and old)
- Very nice reserves
- Good graphics
- Many competitions in which you can compete with fellow hunters
- It's challenging
- It will keep you off the streets for years if you enjoy it
- Frequent updates
- Many special events (Holidays with special competitions and store discounts!)
- Many great people in the community
- A very active forum, where all your questions can be answered
Cons:
- It has bugs, it often takes a long time before they are fixed (Some of these have been around for a long time)
- Server is down a few times every month for a few minutes to a few hours
- It's expensive if you want to have a lot of gear
- Very limited options for character customisation
Cheers, Gierenhart (Grafzerk in theHunter)

Okay, well firstly I should probably mention that I'm not a big fan of MMO's in general.  I'm more of a Single player fan or playing with a small group of friends on a self hosted game, privately.  My past experiences with MMO's or similar are games like WoW, GW and Neverwinter Nights; persistent world servers.  Like I say these really are not my cup of tea except for Neverwinter Nights being played with decent modules privately, either by myself or with friends.
As for the Elder Scrolls games, I am a massive fan of Oblivion and Skyrim.  I love playing these, however I do not love playing Elder Scrolls Online and I shall explain why.
I'm sure that I was not the only one who had high expectations of Elder Scrolls online when it was first announced and expected it to be an Online Skyrim of sorts.  Both Skyrim and Especially Oblivion were fantastic games.  Not just because of the Fantasy World for which they were based, but mainly for the Game Play.  They have a great formula of Game play mechanics that made them fun, immersive and addictive.   This is where TES online falls short.  It's not the same game at all. It's an Elder Scrolls Game on the outside, but on the inside it's something completely different.  The only thing that makes TES online a TES game is the Fantasy setting and lore it borrows from the previous TES games.  Apart from that the entire game play, mechanics, combat, User Interface, character design/levelling... EVERYTHING is a completely different game and in my opinion does not feel fun.
Here I shall have just a short rant about the gaming industry these days: I don't know what it is these days that makes the AAA game developers of today make such a mess of things.  Are they trying too hard to innovate that they simply forget to check if what they are making is actually fun?  It's like they are rolling a dice and guessing what people will like instead of actually maintaining what works and building on it.  What happened to the good old days, back in the 90's and 00's?  Every sequel to a game was an improved version of the previous game.  They would pay attention and learn what made that game great and then they would keep those awesome features and simply improve on them or add to them.  What happened to that?   These days it seems they throw away good solid game play mechanics and replace them with new ones that suck.
I feel that TES Online is yet another product of this kind of random development mentality.  Skyrim and especially Oblivion were great games with awesome successful game play mechanics(Although they did nerf out some good mechanics a little with Skyrim making Oblivion still that little bit better).  Already good solid fun game play mechanics there.  Why ignore this fact?  Why not re-use and create a version of those mechanics that work in favour of Multiplayer?  Why create something completely different that old TES fans will not feel comfortable with?  Was TES Online aimed at a different audience?   Did Bethesda nefariously do this to get regular MMO players of other games onboard and expect that old TES fans would still pay for this simply because it's called "The Elder Scrolls"?
So now I'll elaborate on the game play mechanics I wasn't pleased with. The character stats and levelling is pretty poor and uninteresting IMO. When you level up you get one point to place in either Magicka, Health or Stamina and a few points to place into skills.  From what I can remember the skills are simply special moves.  I'm not very entertained by this.  I prefer being able to put points into Attributes that give an overall improvement to various things that your character can already do, like in Oblivion.  And I miss the variety of the Feats you can choose in Skyrim.  It seems to be completely different system and to me very basic, bland and uninteresting as I have found in other MMO's.  Again I'm not a fan of MMO's, so bare that in mind when reading this review.  I'm sure many other experienced lovers of MMORPG's will also love this game for its features.
Quickslots are for the Skills/Special moves.  But wait where are the quickslots for weapons and potions?  Oh that's right, there aren't any!  And you are not allowed to switch weapons during combat!!!   WHAAAAAT???  This is a horrible mechanic and eliminates any chance of strategic combat.  The weapon you have been fighting with is the weapon you finish fighting with.  No choice in the matter!  So if you find yourself in a scrap with a fireball casting mage or an archer and you are holding a sword, don't expect to engage in a ranged fight by switching to a Bow or Magic Staff!   Mind you the ranged AI Mages like to stupidly teleport straight in front of you, so you can smash them to death easily.  What?  Yes really!
My other gripe is with the rapid firing pistol bow.  Yes the Bow fires like a Pistol!  No need to press and hold to pull back the string to enhance range and there is no arrow dip.  Just keep smashing the mouse button like as fast as you like and your character will shoot that thing like an automatic weapon!  And there is no need to get arrows!  It fires them infinitely out of thin air!   It's like a fricken hack!  Pathetic!  No skill required.   The magic staves are no better.  They run on infinite charge and can also be fired like a rapid fire laser gun.  They are like Unreal Tournament Weapons!
After starting the game it seems to take a very long time to acquire any armour.  I was running around in rags for hours before I finally scraped enough loot together to sell it for a bit of armour from a large town I found.  And it seems like every time I bought a piece of Armour I would soon after get rewarded with that same type of armour after completing a quest!  e.g. just bought a cuirass and then I get rewarded with a cuirass... Just an unfortunate coincidence, I am sure.
The other thing I found or didn't find were recipes for food.  They seemed to be extremely rare early in the game.  Such a simple form of crafting, you'd think cooking would be something your character could start jumping into straight away.
On a plus I do have to say that this was still a lot more interesting and fun to me than playing WoW and GW.  The quests were not as lame as those games and I definitely appreciated them more.  I was soloing them too, which is great, but it did feel odd seeing other players that I wasn't teamed up with running around doing the same quests at the same time as me.  It didn't really make much sense and kind of broke the immersion for me, but I guess I am more of a Single player fan and feel that Oblivion and Skyrim work better for me.
Now just a quick Rant about the hype of MMO's: Just my opinion, but when people say they get immersed in these MMO's, I don't believe them.  I think they are getting Immersion confused with Social Interaction.  These big online games just feel like big public virtual playgrounds where people can meet and socialise and partake in mediocre game play on the side.  Which is fine, but it's not my cup of tea.  Social interaction to me involves other preferences and Video Game play is separate.  But I do enjoy a good social a face to face board game occasionally.
The other big plus with TES Online is the first person perspective view that is classic to the other TES games.  This is something that is sorely missing from other MMO's or just not done right.
There may be a lot more I could talk about on this Game, but I think I've covered all that I need to.  I'm really glad and thankful that Bethesda give me a chance to try TES Online out for free, so that I can make an informed decision about whether or not to buy it.  I had seen reviews and had heard it wasn't that great, although I do prefer to form my own opinion and now I have it.  My conclusion is that just because you may love Oblivion or Skyrim, does not mean you will like this game.  TES Online is not for me.

I'll admit I hadn't expected this game to pull itself out of the dumpster fire it threw itself into upon release in 2014. It has come a long way since then. I find myself walking through the world excited to see the markers for new quests because they are so much fun. The voice acting for each and every character is pure joy upon the ears. It isn't your typical MMO, while there are skills to be used, the skill tree is definitely nothing in comparison to something like WoW. It's an inviting first time MMO, not too complicated and with simple controls and mechanics. I think at this point it has finally delivered on its initial promise of being Skyrim, but with friends. I actually think that some elements are better than Skyrim and I hope that they will be incorperated into the next Elder Scrolls game, whenever it is released.

This is a decent little Metroidvania.
Pros: It's got some interesting new mechanics, which the videos on the store here show off nicely.  It's well-polished and easy to get into, with solid platforming controls and pretty smooth presentation for a pixel-art game.
Cons: The game's biggest flaw is that it's ultimately fairly shallow.  I finished the whole thing, including finding nearly all of the optional power-ups, in under 4 hours.  There aren't that many enemy types, and you'll see the same basic behaviors over and over as you traverse the game world.  Worst of all, the boss fights are incredibly repetetive; every new boss is a palette-swapped minor enhancement on the last, right up through the end of the game.
Overall, this game provides a decent if repetetive few hours' of amusement.  Probably worth the $10 asking price if you have the cash lying around, but only barely.  Grab on sale if you can.

If you can stomach the super irritating false sense of freedom that snares a labyrinth around just a few planets, Xeodrifter is an action-adventure akin to Metroid like few others, where unlocking new capabilities opens new paths. Bright and clean pixel art along with a rhythmical soundtrack help a great deal as well:

Neat gun upgrade system
Short length (~3 hours)
Only 1 boss that you fight 7 flavors of that gains new more frustrating/boring moves. Special mention goes to the blue shield that renders them invincible for 30 seconds that they can use several times per fight. There is an upgrade than can break it, however.
5/10 get it on sale or in a bundle and have no expectations.

Xeodrifter is a lot of fun, but is a little short. Let's make a quick list for you.
Good:
- Gun upgrades - They are kind of ambiguous, but it actually forces you to try out the different combos of how you can create your gun and allows you to choose really different build paths. Pretty cool feature!
- Fun skills - You pick up skills as you progress through the game that not only help you through levels, but help you do them quicker and more efficiently. You can also manipulate them creatively to take on bosses!
- Secret rooms - If you're anything like me, you'll love finding the secret rooms in here. The first secret room I stumbled upon was completely by accident
. See what you can find!
- Level builds (also see "not so good") - The level builds are creative and once you start earning your upgrades, you're going to really appreciate the way they are constructed. There aren't many levels, but you'll be able to revisit them with your upgrades to explore even more!
- Achievements - GET THEM!
Not So Good:
- Short game - I don't have much time down on this game and once it was done, I found myself hoping there was more, like maybe some extra content once it's beaten.
- Level builds - Some of the levels builds are pretty in-depth, which is pretty awesome while you're exploring, but when going back to look for secret rooms or upgrades, some of the levels can be really long and it takes a long time to get back to the spot where you would find the secret/upgrade. I found myself sort of annoyed that I had to go through that level and run all the way back just for 1 item. Having said that, it's not a terrible feature, just "not so good."
- Boss algorithms don't change much - [Minor Spoiler]
Though I wouldn't say that it necessarily takes away from the boss fights being fun.
Overall, 8/10. Wish there was more, but I was engaged and excited every time I was playing this game. The devs definitely get props for this one. They made this game so refreshing and fun.

If you loved Metroid, you'll love Xeodrifter as well. It's got the same exploration-rewarding run-and-gun gameplay, the same feeling of isolation on a distant world, and it brings a few nifty new mechanics to the mix, like the "plane shift" ability which lets you move between the foreground and the background, and the customizable weapon loadouts. Well, I suppose Super Metroid let you customize your weapons, but not to the degree that this game does! Just two downsides - the maps are a bit small, and teleporters (from which you can access your ship to save) are few and far between.

Liked the game, has an old school metroid vibe to it, but it suffers two flaws in my opinion:
It's too short and the bosses are all the same with incremental patterns (i.e. the second boss has all the patterns of the first plus some new ones, the third boss has all of the patterns from before and his own, etc...)
The modular weapon upgrades that one can change at wish is great, but there is never enough game to allow for multiple combinations try outs. It just comes down to maximizing damage and then fire rate to increase DPS.
What sentiment do I retain from playing this? Slight disappointment, as it is too good a game to be this short.
If the difficulty would have been extreme then I would understood. Kinda like VVVVVVVV being short and it not bothering me as much. But the game is fairly easy and straight forward. There's no back tracking unless you want to catch some extras and even that is not something that is going to make me go back.
For less than two euros I guess I could recommend it, but paying more and becoming disappointed of not having enough is just not worth it. As someone else already pointed out in a review. As soon as one is having fun, the game just ends. There is no time nor new environments in which to test the new found abilities for a satisfactory time.
Sum up:
+Graphics: nice and neat old retro pixel art (loved it)
+Gameplay: Nervous, adaptive, not frustrating, if it's game over there is only oneself to blame, abilities are well thought and fun to use, modular upgrades mechanic is a nice idea
+Sound effects: great chip tune shooting and enemy sounds
+/-Music: Good chip tune but not enough variety
+/-Environments: Some are better than others, too linear though with 4 planets having one or two ability focused design. Maybe one big environment would have made for more backtracking and the metroidvaniaesque feel
-Enemies: too little different enemies overall, varied ones could have required different upgrade builds, bosses are a joke of code copy pasting and color changing, could have used more creativity
--Lifetime: too short for a good game, makes us want more

Ok, so, wow...

It should be noted that I am a big fan of Bastion, and of narrative-driven games with saturated environments in general. So if you love such games, just buy this and drop in.
I have to admit that the first few times I picked up the controller, I didn't immediately get 'caught'; and there are reasons for that which I will explain below. The main thing is to not get discouraged if you are feeling the same way in the first 15-30 minutes.
In many ways, not getting sucked in right at the beginning is much like some of my favorite books: they take time to build. Transistor wisely knows to savor itself, not pandering to the ADD gamer just looking for the next shiney thing.
There was a critical mass moment for me, maybe 45 minutes in, where I finally got over the interface learning curve, unlocked enough powers to start to feel badass, and allowed enough of the narrative to build to really get involved in what was happening.
Look forward to this moment, because once it happens, the your gaming experience will steadily build to its poignant crescendo, leaving you both satisfied and at a loss.
Summary: the narrative is original and creative, the environments are immersive, the gameplay is unique and enjoyable, and the holistic experience is worth the price and time invested.

And, of course, as expected from the creators a Bastion, a story that buries you in emotion.
For a short game that will break your heart and a combat system more flexible than a member of Cirque De Soleil, play Transistor.

If you liked Bastion, you'll like this game. All the elements that made Bastion so beautiful are alive and well in Transistor. The Turn() mechancics give the game an interesting edge and make you feel like a badass as you unleash a series of moves in a split second before enemies can react.
Definitely recommend this game.

Transistor is one of those beautiful surprises that you find over there from time to time... It is a game packed with action, but, in fact, is a game to behold, to enjoy its amazing soundtrack and its superb art. The plot is also full of surprises: is not a game that teaches you the mission objectives at the beginning, as in a conventional game. You are taken through the history and discovers the plot as you go through it, just like a good movie, a good book. There comes a time when it is impossible not to want to know how it will end, resulting in an unbelievable ending. For those who love a good story, good music and a fantastic art, you have to play this one.

When I saw this game appear on steam I had never heard of it. So I downloaded the demo and started playing that. 3 hours later I reached the end of the demo and was craving more.
Don't let the early access scare you off thinking the game isn't finished. It has been in development for years, and continues to get updates to this day. Even with the early access tag, it still seems like a finished product.
While this doesn't have workshop support, it does have mods and an ingame mod browser. The best thing about this is that it can automatically update all mods to updated version. Now if you are worried about a new update breaking the game because mods aren't updated yet, don't worry as the modders seem to use the beta test of new versions so when the update goes live, all your mods are already up to date.
Multiplayer. This game has it. I haven't really tried it, but a few searches online have shown people playing a game with up to 250 people at the same time.
The core of the game is all about automating anything and everything. Build a drill on an ore deposit, conveyor belt it to a place to smelt the ore, then to a machine to craft it into ammo for your gun, which gets delivered to you automatically by robots. The screenshots will look intimidating with the very large and complex factories, but they start so small and simple and grow complex over time. Then it's no longer intimidating because you grew with the factory so you just know where everything is and how it works.
This game will probably never be on sale, but it is still well worth the $20. My 446 hours spent on it say so.
Edit: Notice how I'm now over 1000 hours and most reviews have over 100? Just buy the game already.

Xeodrifter is a short but sweet Metroid-like game where the player must explore 4 unique planets to find new abilities and a number of power-ups in order to find their way home. Taking a page out of Metroid Fusion the map is separated into 4 different sections with a hub (the players ship) rather than the Super Metroid approach of a single interconnected world. Each of these levels has a number of routes which can be opened with new abilities and contain power-ups to give the player an easier time.
Xeodrifter controls rather well but does suffer from a slightly floaty feel in regards to the movement. Having only used an Xbox controller I found it intuitive but would probably advise against using a keyboard.
One of the power-ups the player can find is a Gun Mod. Each of these is a single point which can be used to customize the way your weapon functions. By mixing and matching these point (which can be refunded and re-added at any point) you will be able to increase the damage, firing rate and spread or even make the bullets fire in a sine wave. You can also save 3 varieties of firing modes for quick use in the future.
The planets are filled with a wide array of beasts which will try and impede your progress, many of which have attack patterns players which have experienced a Metroid game will recognize. All of them have different ways of hindering the player and there was rarely a time I found myself annoyed at their placement in the world.
The downside to this game is of course its length, you can probably beat this game in well under 3 hours. There is also only a single boss to battle. However each time you fight it there is a new move or 2 added to its library, making it slightly more difficult. Another variety of boss or two would have helped keep it fresh though.
A final complaint is the construction of the fourth world. While all of the others have a few branching or looping paths this one is almost entirely linear. This planet just doesn't seem to have had the same attention put into its creation which is a bit of a shame.
Overall anyone who is a fan of Metroid-like platform games should definitely check this one out and not be put off by the short playtime provided. Xeodrifter, while short, does not overstay its welcome and the abilities you collect from the bosses make revisiting old locations for new gear a joy.

Good: Great "metroidish" game, but with a new twist. Espescially the feature to switch between foreground and background is awesome. Great level design. Great pixel art. Cool music. Very fun and rewarding.
Not so good: Fullscreen mode does not work when having high DPI mode enabled in Windows. You only see the upper left part of the actual game. There is only one boss enemy that you have to beat 7 times. It does have some new tricks every time, but it is still the same sprite every time, just a different color. A little more variety would have been nice. Some overpowered enemies (the pink fly).
Bad: No save points, only check points before and after each boss fight. Because of that, you will have to repeat some sections very often because you cannot save and the enemies do not drop any health pickups. There are some hidden health stashes, but those a pretty rare and most of the time not in the place where you would need them. This is what bothered me most. I don't like repetitions, even if it was state of the art back in the 8-Bit days. This is one thing I do not miss from those times. ;-)
Conclusion: Looking forward to a sequel!

I love the visuals. I loved the feeling of being a badass gunslinger, dishing out hot lead left and right to any who stood in my way. Silas does change as a main character, and it is interesting how that pans out at the end, with a final battle followed by 2 endings. I also liked how the ending I picked felt final to me. There were no plot holes, and at least for me, it seemed like a happy ending, which made it more likeable for me. I'm also a little proud to say that I figured out the ending a couple hours in and saw it coming, which made me anticipate it even more. I finished the story in almost 5 hours I think, so it is a short game, but I think it was a good investment. The AI are predictable, running into cover then popping out to shoot, and sometimes you'll encounter shotgunners and occaisonally a stick of dynamite will be thrown your way. I'm a lazy gamer, I'll admit it, and I like being an unstoppable juggernaut that blows through my foes, so the stupid AI was fun for me ( ._.). I'd rate Call of Juarez Gunslinger a 10/10, because it had beautiful visuals, an interesting (at least to me) storyline, and I got to shoot the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of hundreds of guys. ♥♥♥♥ yeah.

TL;DR: Great concept.  Bad follow through (so far.)  Wait for release + 3 weeks.
Hacks are everywhere. Development is slow and working off a history of abandonment.  New game additions are focusing on fluff and not optimization and key issues.  Overall combat is poor and has very little depth.  During a raid you will mostly be fighting vs naked fresh respawns that will zerg you and spam mouse click for an easy win.
Sadly, base design and security eat into artistic design freedom.  Due to a lack of good physics, you'll see mostly squared flat buildings or floating islands for bases.
Game optimization is very poor. While servers do support 30+ people, there are often disconnects when people group up which results in your character sleeping in the open with a high likely hood of being killed for all your items.  Many people have also run into terrible FPS as people start to gather over groups of 8-10.  I personally do not see this till 15~ people come in so your millage may vary.
However, if you want a medieval Minecraft built on Unity 5, this isn't a bad pick.  You need to go into the game and be accepting that you are likely to lose many hours of your time investment through hacks, getting stuck, and bugs.  This game is also coming from a publisher with a history of abandonment.  For that reason I wouldn't recommend this to anyone until at least a few weeks into release.

I'm not sure why anyone would want to play a hidden object game without a goofy, awkward, nonsensical story to it, but those people can rejoice for they have Millionaire Manor. Freed from the oppressive shackles of plot and narrative, players can click through the many game modes offered in rapid succession. If you need a quick item-hunting fix it'll get the job done but honestly just scrounging items is not what I'm here for. Consider this a pretty tepid recommendation based solely on the strengths of the game modes and the impressive scenery-chewing of one major character.
I was being a little facetious, there IS a plot, it's just arranged so that all it does is bookend bouts of object hunting. The verbose title, Millionaire Manor: The Hidden Object Game, refers to an old game show that your character's grandfather used to enjoy. It's off the air, but you get a call from him saying he's going to be on it. Rather than calling the nursing home you chase him down and discover that he and a handful of other people have been captured by some jerkoff in a top hat who's doing his best Andrew-Divoff-in-Wishmaster impression. Seriously, this guy is great and a big highlight of an otherwise bone-dry game.
If you want to free these wayward souls, you'll have to play top-hat's games and I don't need to tell you they involve a lot of obfuscated items. The appeal of Millionaire Manor lies in its many game modes. You must complete 6 games to release each of the 5 prisoners, and for each game you spin a wheel of the 10 different modes available. There's the standard hidden object search with a list to complete, but you'll also encounter riffs like hunting silhouettes or sets of three, combining items to make new ones, finding letters or solving riddles to learn what objects you need, or even spot the difference rounds. You'll frequently have to do double rounds to score a victory, and occasionally triple rounds, but each of these is guaranteed to be a different mode.
During each round you can also trigger bonus scenes by clicking glowing text that appears. In these you have all of 12 seconds to find pieces of chips that earn you more hints, tokens to skip specific modes, and unlock new modes. These searches can be pretty tricky due to how well the chips blend in, and honestly the base game isn't much easier. Millionaire Manor is a little dated in looks, with lower-res, washed-out graphics that hide more than a few pixellated objects in the backgrounds. While I wouldn't call it hard by any stretch, you might have a tough time getting through it without burning hints.
You might also have a tough time chugging along to the end, even if you're digging the different game modes. Lacking any kind of exploration or adventure elements, Millionaire Manor feels much more hollow and disconnected than most games in the genre. There's no big conclusion at the end, just a victory screen. You do unlock the ability to play any of the modes on any scene once you win, and it does bother to track which ones you've beaten for the rare completionist that wants to 100% their hidden object game. Honestly between this and the different modes to try, I'd say this one is still worth a look. It's not the sharpest or prettiest HOG out there, but the variety of modes helps to make up for its other shortcomings.

All in all I like this title.  It is based on a concept that you are playing a gameshow and trying to rescue previous contestants that lost but it isn't a strong story line that keep pulling me back into the game.
What does keep pulling me back into it are the new ideas Gogii added to the Hidden Object game genre.  Like I said this isn't a strong story driven game much like Artifex Mundi games BUT it does add many new concepts when looking at the same scene; match 3 (adds an extra 2 items somewhere), find 10 like items (adds another 9 items to the scene); Find Alphabet Letters to spell words of objects you must find; Riddle (you need to decipher a sentence to know what to search for), Puzzle (yes puzzle pieces that make up the scene), Combine (kind of deciper an easy meaning that translates to 2 items in the scene), List & Sillouette to name most of them but not all of the modes.  There are 12 modes.  Also as you play, you get a chance to play 15 second bonus games that let you earn hints, unlocks (to unlock a new mode) & skips (if you didn't like a particular mode).  Going back to comparing Artifex Mundi, there isn't any map to this game.  It is mainly a game show theme much like 'Discovery! Seek and Find' where the scenes change and not your position on a map.  (Thus you don't need to remember where to use an object because you don't pick up any objects to carry around.)
The scenes keep changing rapidly so you don't feel any staleness in looking at scenes or for objects.  I also find this game moderately hard to find objects and I've needed to use hints.
If you like HO games and you want to try something different in the HO genre, I'd suggest trying this game out.

If you like hidden-object puzzles, it's a pretty good pick up!

Game at it's current state is barely playable.
- there are game-breaking bugs present at every turn
- server latency is worse than you'd expect from an indie game running out of somebody's garage
- at least half the content is either disabled or unplayable
- there is literally no balance in either PvE or PvP (with the latter being non-existant except for guild wars)
- several game mechanics introduced mke the experience even more unpleasant then it needs to be
- there is literally no endgame to speak of
If you are looking for a game that will allow you to create a character and solo through 280 levels of killing monsters and occasionally clicking on an NPC to pick up a quest then this is the game for you.
If you are expecting social interactions, a free market, balanced content, finished content, WORKING content or even PLAYABLE content - this is not the game for you.
I'm not saying you can't get several hundred hours worth of playtime out of this - you can - I am a good example of that.
However you will find that it amounts to nothing in the end. The more you progress the more you notice that the game makes no effort to keep you playing, but rather just teases you to start and then says "oh well, you got me, I got nothing".
Not to be called out on empty words let me give you JUST A FEW examples of what you might expect later on:
- for those familiar with RO (Ragnarok Online, which this game tries to be but fails on all accounts by the way) you will remember that gear was enhanced with cards to add interesting ways of grinding monsters or make fun builds. In this game the concept is copied using "monster gems" that add 1 skillpoint to a skill. That's it, there no variety or special effects to that. Most importantly those gems cannot be traded and as such you are forced to look for a 0.01% drop for yourself each time you need one. And yes they do drop off monsters that are as rare as a decent MMO.
- If you played any MMO you will be familiar with the concept of an Auction House / Market that allows you to sell items to other players. In this game however the developers decided they know better than you , and as such you are not allowed to set a price above or below what their algorithm picks up from the game. As such, given the fact of bots, RMTs and simply people not knowing the worth of items in the beginning you are now unable to sell most items simply because nobody will pay the set price and you are not allowed to sell for less.
- Recently the game has been moved from the Eastern US to several servers across the world. I can only speak for the server I play(ed) on, which is the EU one (located in Germany), but the latency varies between 20 and 800ms. (yes 800!). This issue is omnipresent and does not in any way limit itself to people with poor internet connections or located in specific places. It is also not at all dependant on the server's current capacity, since you will get a ping of 20 at midday and a ping of 600 at 3am seemingly at random. Latency changes (spikes/drops) can cover a variance of +-300 over a span of 20 seconds. It's a true rollercoaster ride of lag.
- Game mechanics itself is beyond unfinished. With several ways to control your character (mouse, keyboard, mouse + keyboard, pad) depending on the class you choose to play you will end up with a multitude of issues. Skills will not register, skills will lock your character in place, switching weapon will lock up the game for several seconds, latency changes will make you rubberjump all over the place. Most keys on the keyboard can be used to bind skills, but only a handful will work properly. Attempting to bind most skills to keys on the right side of the keyboard will render them unusable or make them trigger once/10tries if used in combination with the movement arrows (does not depend on your keyboard, just on the way the game handles I/O requests).
- Optimization and stable FPS are things that will not be found here, even by the likes of Sherlock Holmes. Simply turning on the map can drop your FPS to 5 for several seconds. Turning on the map AND trying to run or attack will plummet the FPS to a grinding halt almost always. At this moment over 90% of the players are using the lowest available settings and the developers have since added several options to disable most of the graphics "fanfare" you might have seen in the videos - it did not help a lot. The game still uses a single core regardless of the CPU you might have and will (while still laughing at me with 30fps) force my Intel i5 to encounter temperatures that it has never experienced before. After several hours in the game (even if only at the login screen) your PC will be ready to serve as an oven/hearth for all your culinary desires.
I could go on, but honestly, try it out for free and leave as soon as you can. Do not spend money on this heap of camel dung. Don't get swayed by the first 100 levels that look and feel almost fun - check all the issues I've described above , and if they all pan out just know they are only about 5% of it.
1/10 would not get scammed into founding again.

TL;DR It's a very long story, but this company doesn't care about its players at all.
The long story:
I purchased a founder's pack to Tree of Savior and was there the moment the doors opened (after having stayed up all night to secure a desired team name due to them not being prepared to launch their game on time). While more games are managing to launch without any issues, it is still relatively expected that there will be some kinds of hiccups at launch (although I expected this to be less likely since they've already launched the title in South Korea).
Due to even more issues at the moment of launch, I could not log in to the server my friends wanted to be on (Klaipeda). However, I could log in to a server called Orsha. At the time, the FAQ on their main site mentioned that team names would be unique to each server. I figured I could go ahead and grab my desired team name on Orsha since Klaipeda didn't seem to be online at the moment. I grabbed my desired team name on Orsha and soon found out that their FAQ was not accurate; They had changed team names to be unique to each region. They also changed the official FAQ a week later (after the early access launch) to reflect their new changes.
I have sent in six tickets asking what can be done to get my team name from Orsha to Klaipeda. The first ticket was automatically closed without a response. The second ticket was given an autoresponse that did not at all answer my question. With the third ticket I was a bit rough with the customer support and basically said "You are wasting both my time and your time by giving an unrelated response rather than trying to work through the issue". I then asked if it was possible to do a server transfer for the team since they had said they would allow a one time free server transfer for all founder accounts. The customer support answered and said it was not possible at this time to do server transfers. I waited a long time to file a fourth ticket; The ticket was filed when the EU servers opened up and they were allowing transfers from Klaipeda and Orsha to the new EU servers (but were not allowing Klaipeda to transfer to Orsha or vice versa). I did not receive a human response to this ticket; however, I was given an auto-response saying:
"Q. Why is my ticket still "Unanswered"?
A. The transfer tickets will be answered after the transfer process is complete."
I received this response on the night before the server transfers happened. I had filed the ticket on 4/15/2016 and the auto-response was given on 4/25/2016. I was excited that it appeared that they had manually transferred my team during the maintenance, but upon attempting to log in I found that my team was still on Orsha. So this is when I sent in the fifth ticket.
I asked, once again, if I could please transfer to a different server. They replied:
"We understand that you want to transfer to a different server. Unfortunately, we regret to inform you that all request for server transfer has ended. We are no longer accepting request for Server Transfer. For future news and announcements regarding server transfer, kindly visit our official website"
For my sixth "ticket", I sent a private message to a CM politely asking what my options are (even if that option is to hang tight for another ___amount of time___). I expressed that I simply desired to join my friends on Klaipeda with my Orsha team name. (I have not made a character and I have not redeemed any of the founder's pack items). I sent this private message on April 27th, and the CM did not bother responding to the message. The "free server transfer" that was advertised with any founders pack has been amended to apply only to server transfers IMC wants to do. Originally, there seemingly weren't any constraints on which server they would allow the free transfer to apply to. Now, it seems they will only allow you to go from Orsha or Klaipeda to the EU servers, or the SA server.
I'm not necessarily upset about their lack of ability to do something that at the moment they just can't do. I'm upset about how they've been flaking me off for well over a month without giving me any answers as to what can or can't be done. In my ticket responses they've made me feel like I'm the one entirely responsible for my predicament when they're the ones that had an incorrect FAQ entry on something as important as team names at the moment of launch. If anything, it is a shared blame, but they have done NOTHING in an attempt to cooperate with me and fix the situation.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

There is love in this game. Love in the design, the story, the music. The essence of what was great in Bastion has been refurbished to fit the environment of Transistor. They are noticeably similar, but all-together different. Bastion is more of a hack and slash, while Transistor relies on tactics and positioning to make combat the most effective. A familiar aspect, Logan Cunningham, the narrator of Bastion has returned to voice the narrator of Transistor. While the voice is the same, the tone and style of it is noticeably different. "Rucks" of Bastion speaks like a storyteller, full of authoritative power and wisdom. In Transistor, the narrator is a large sword that holds great technological power. This narrator speaks in the constant present, holding conversations, granting advice, but there is a totally different feel to it as it seems like the narrator is more of a changing character than Rucks was. The point that I am attempting to make is that this is not Bastion 2, but still very similar to an experience that was obviously Bastion-esque. It is slower going at the beginning in my opinion than Bastion was, learning the new combat and leveling mechanics, but it is certainly worth the initial learning process.
Supergiant Games has made two of the most wonderfully designed games with Transistor and Bastion. It will be worth following their future developments, as they have made unique experiences that are worth supporting.
Also, press Tab when you're in the game. It's just that little extra aspect that makes me love this game.

Absolutely superb game. From the off it pulls you into it's world with a crisp, warm palette, some in medias res storytelling as well as a mesmerising soundtrack and a mute protagonist with a talking sword to boot. It can be a little difficult early on to work out what works best with your functions (abilities you use in the game's combat system) but incredibly satisfying once you master the "turn" or real time based gameplay. Again this is totally up to the player, and most people will find either one style or a mix which suits them best. I loved the little nuances and pieces of story hidden in the game via the ovc terminals, or the more blatant observation areas which just develop the background a little more and add some depth to the games world. The storyline is interesting if confusing in parts though the finer details of the plot are there to be found if you look hard enough. VA's are top notch, the humming is a wonderful little addition (oh, there's a hum button, did I not mention that?) and the option of a new game plus will stretch out the games lifespan somewhat. I clocked in around 6 hours on first playthrough and apparently this is about average. Like Bastion, the games spirutual predecessor, there are challenges and ways of altering the games difficulty, but these are optional and add a little more to the game for the masochists of you out there. My only great criticism is that I wish it were longer, though the new game plus adds an extra dimension through tougher enemies and more options for combat, it would have been good to see more of the world and I would have gladly payed extra to do so. Can't recommend the game enough, so don't let me hold you back any longer and go and experience cloudbank yourself.

Right, here's how it goes. This game is a STEAL for £15 and here is why;
You start up the game, you find the tutorial levels in campaign mode and you think along the lines of "Ah cool, so it's a complex minecraft? Gotcha."
Nope. You see, Minecraft at least gives you the honour of making all your stuff with nothing but your own bare hands. The objective in Factorio on the other hand is to make a complicated and efficient layout of conveyor belts, furnaces, mining drills, steam engines, boilers, oil refineries, component factories and many, many, MANY more things that makes all your stuff FOR you.
You try to make this highly efficient and economic factory floor and instead, all you've managed to do is make what looks like a scrambled ball of yarn AND the back of your cranium explode due to severe confusion. And yet, what you have made is enough - what you have created will suffice.
THAT'S what makes Factorio special. You don't need an engineering degree to play and eventually finish this beast of a game and yet, when you do beat the game with a layout that mostly resembles a lump of spaghetti and you push aside the mountains of coal that have built up around you, the game seems to challenge you to do it better.
You exit the current game, you press New Game and you rise to that challenge... only to realise that it is now 3:30am and you have in fact managed to transform what felt like a cople of hours into what is in fact a day.
This does not stop you.
10/10

If you're looking for a Skyrim with buddies type of game then you're going to have to wait for a long time. If you're looking for Skyrim in a bigger world, Skyrim with more dungeons, Skyrim in any way, shape, or form really, then you're going to have to wait. This game is not Skyrim. It's not Oblivion. It's definitely not Morrowind.
The Elder Scrolls Online is fun in its own ways, but like many of the games that have come out in the last four years it is really only fun when you've got some friends with you.
QUESTING
The quests are not very well designed, they are all relatively "fetch quest" formatted, and feel too simple. Every quest in the game feels kind of hacked apart and put together again to make a "new" quest, when really all that separates them is the dialogue given to you by the npc's. I believe this occurs because there simply aren't enough little interactions in the game. You simply hit the action button and a simple recylced animation plays which in turn completes the objective. Quests with puzzles are simple. Quests that ask you to search for something are spoiled by the large floating waypoints and the "hints" in your quest journal which tell you exactly where to go. Ultimately, the quests in this game feel very unsatisfying.
EXPLORING
If you want to walk around and enjoy some pretty scenery then this game is right for you. You want to explore a large environment filled with monsters at every turn (literally every turn, it's a little annoying) then play this. The environments are all very well put together. They are designed well and the assets are used efficiently. Textures are good and model detail is good, especially when you consider that this is an MMO. Combine that with some great lighting, the water reflectivity, foilage, and (given your rig can take it) the massive draw distance then you're looking at a very pretty game.
COMBAT
Combat is very repetitive and grindy. You essentially can attack and block just like you do in Skyrim, but now you have up to five different skills you can use that consume either stamina or magicka. Combat in first person perspective is down right difficult simply because most of, if not all of, the enemies you fight have one variety or more of an AOE (Area of Effect) attack. These attacks are marked with a red circle that are difficult to see in first person perspective. Combat in third person is where the game shines. It's fun, easy to get into, and you can see where enemies are attacking and respond accordingly, which, for a sword and shield guy like me that is important.
VOICE ACTING
This game has some of the worst voice acting I've ever heard. It's brutal. It makes my ears bleed. I have such a hard time stomaching the voice acting that it nearly does me in, I just can't take it. I play under the Ebonheart Pact, and therefore don't interact with some races very often, but I've plenty of experience talking with Nords, Dunmer, Argonions, and Khajiit. Nords sound either like your cliche viking which is super irritating to have to sit through. Dunmer sound pretentious up the♥♥♥♥♥♥and it's also irritating. Then you have the Argonions and the Khajiit, and they just sound painful. I feel like the voice actors had to really force every line out, like their voices aren't able to make those accents with ease. I don't know who did the dialogue for those races in the single player Elder Scrolls installations, but those folks should have been brought on board, cause the guys Zenimax used in ESO are just not the right pick.
OVERVIEW
The game has pitfalls, I've listen them above. But among those, and countering them very effectively, are numerous enjoyable things boasted throughout. Rich lore is one of them, and that for me can take a game miles. I love the lore of the Elder Scrolls universe and so to be able to dive back into it makes me very happy. That, along side with the beautiful environments, solid musical score, and just TONS of content make this game one to keep. The game initially was very grindy in a lot of ways, and I hear horror stories from my friends who've been playing since launch at how bad it was. Zenimax has since made changes that have greatly helped the game and gotten rid of the grindy nature of it all, which is a huge win for me. Accessability on the MMO front is a good thing, it makes it more approachable, which is vital when you're competing against giants like World of Warcraft.
So, yes, this game is worth owning. For fan of the Elder Scrolls series you won't be short of things to enjoy, not by any means. For newbies to the series you are looking at a solid entry to get your foot in the door, especially since cronologically ESO takes place before many of the other Elder Scrolls games.

This game is one of the few Metriodvania's I've seen or played that gets as close to original NES Metriod as humanly possible. The graphical style and music are 100% retro, so much so that this game could have honestly come out on the NES with little issue. That's not a knock on it all, in fact it's kind of refreshing since a lot of "retro" games are simply newer games mechanic and gameplay-wise with that pixelated outer coating masking the fact it's just another modern indie title.
It isn't anything too difficult, but you'll have to work a little bit if you die a lot because there are very few checkpoints within the worlds themselves, only back on your ship when you leave the planet or before boss fights. It's a decent enough throwback to the more difficult era of NES gaming all considered though.
The game itself *is* short, but again that's kind of dictated by how many times you die and need to replay portions of a world and how fast you game in general. I've played almost three hours so far and I'm not halfway done because I take my time. In all honesty though, this game would wear thin after the 10 hour mark, as most Metriodvania's usually do, so it's a logical choice to make it shorter. Having purchased this game for a discount on Humble Bundle, I feel it's well worth the price of admission, definitely one of the better and more fun games of this type currently on Steam.

After playing this game alot, i have decided to make a true review of this game. At the time of writing this, i have played a total of 489 hours (this game wasnt always on steam, so i have played it before it were), so my word can be trusted.
To start things off, this game, theHunter, is aimed to be a hunting simulator. Although there are a few arcade-like functions, this game is mostly what it aims to be. Some people call this a "Pay-to-Win" game, but i will tell why it is not in a few seconds (or minutes, depending on your reading speed). This game offers alot of variety to paid users. If you buy, lets say, the Trailrunner membership (often best for thoose who are new and needs a great start), contains alot of usefull items. It gives you a few very usefull weapons, one camo set wich is very good against deer, license to hunt all species (there are many) for a year, diverce items and equipment. The weapons you recieve is mostly made up of: .300 Bolt Action rifle, .270 Bolt Action rifle, Compound Bow "Snakebite" (most powerfull compound bow, although not most powerfull bow after all) and the .30-06 Lever Action rifle. Theese are not all weapons, but they allow you to hunt almost all species in all the reserves. This game offers alot of different ways to track, spot, stalk and kill prey. You can use lures to attract most species to get them closer to you so you can kill them with a bow, a shotgun, a pistol, or you can use the .300 with a 3-9x scope to pick them off at range. A wide variety of weapons are available to be purchased ranging from a .22LR air rifle to take down small bird and rabbits, to the 9.3x62mm Anschütz rifle and shotguns using slug ammunition to take down the biggest of bear and moose. To buy theese weapons, you need an in-game currency called em$. This currency can be gained in a number of ways: Purchasing it for real money and earning it from competitions and certain offers. The easiest way is to purchase. You can also purchase tents to spawn in, treestands/blinds/tripods to sit in to take down prey without it noticing you, and other different tools that may aid you during hunts. Free users only start with the .243 Bolt Action rifle. A weak weapon, but still capable of taking down the most basic free-to-play animal: the Mule Deer. Although Mule Deer is not the only free-to-play animal, it is the only one you may take down using the .243 rifle. There are a huge number off different species, all with their own unique behaviour and pelt characteristics. This game cannot be a "Pay-to-Win" game, as there is no real true goal. Its like a open world sandbox, although with the characteristics of hunting. This game can never be completed fully, wich is why you can never win. I will not keep writing this huge text so much more, as this would take alot of time.
Pros:
-Fun and interesting gameplay.
-Get to have a slight feel to hunt animals.
-Feeling the adrenaline rush when you spot that Roe Buck with thoose huge antlers.
-Many different gameplay mechanics to track, spot, stalk and kill your prey.
-Fairly realistic.
-Free to play.
Cons:
-Fairly expensive if you want to get the most out of the game, although not as expensive as titles like World of Warcraft.
-Still a few interesting (although harmless) bugs and glitches.
-Animal behaviour could be better.
-Ballistics could be better.
-Weapon mechanics could be better.
-In-game skills is very, VERY, time consuming to level up.
Conclusion: A great game that i would recomment people to try out. Start as a free-to-play, and if you feel this game is for you, get a membership. Get serious in playing. This game is not for everyone, so i cannot promise any user to be satisfied. I am personally in love with this game, and have inspired me to enter high school with a education line in "Hunting & Wildlife Preservation". Devs are also happy to assist on their social networks. I cannot be more happy with this product, and i hope you will find this review of use. Also i cannot thank the devs behind this game enough, it has given me litteratly days of fun in total. Give the game a try, atleast it begins as free-to-play. Thanks to GunninGamerz for letting me post his beginner tutorial, you can watch it

I usually pride myself on being quite tolerant when it comes to games. That is to say, I enjoy a wide variety of them and rarely have trouble finding something to like even in a game that doesn't appeal to me. Yet, this game is, quite simply, so boring that it nearly put me to sleep almost as soon as I started playing. Unfortunately, the situation didn't improve any as I tried to keep playing on. Finally, after a short time that felt like far longer, I did ultimately give up and quit. If I had actually bought it rather than getting it in a bundle, I'd be kicking myself right now. But, I understand that my opinion alone isn't all that helpful. So, some info on the game:
The gameplay - This game is incredibly simple to play, but that is a big part of what makes it almost unbearable for me to play. The description makes it sound as though your actions and directions, as the player, ultimately create and shape the story. This is true, but in the weakest way possible. Basically, it goes like this: the characters on the screen have speech bubbles pop up for you to read and/or click through, and after several of these, one or more "cues" (little labelled pictures) will show up at the top of the screen for you to select one of in order to cue the next action, usually with little to no indication of the relevance or role of most of them, after which you get another series of speech bubbles followed by another set of cues. Rinse and repeat, and that's about it. To make it worse, many of them are in a loop of sorts, so you basically get routed back to the same choices until you make the "right" one to continue the story, after reading more speech bubbles each time, of course. Also, if you make a true "wrong" choice and hit an "ending," you just un-cue your choice and choose something else. It quickly becomes tedious, and it doesn't take long to just stop caring.
The story - As it says in the description, you're a witch that opens a yarn store. Beyond that, the characters and storyline are mostly quite shallow and unengaging. I didn't care about any of them, beyond wanting to take tape and seal their mouths shut, as they talk way too much. I did come to a couple early "endings" that apparently happen if you choose the "wrong" cues, but they didn't really make a whole lot of sense in terms of the sequence of events, so while I cannot comment on the longer storyline that (hopefully) is to be found if you stick with it and choose the right options, I don't hold out much hope for it. In any case, my lack of playing time means I can't comment on the story much.
The really sad thing is, I truly did want to like this, as it sounded interesting and unique. I don't even mind "reading" games if the story and gameplay elements are interesting and fun. But, this was a disappontment on every count. If you really want to play it, I highly recommend watching for a bundle, or at least a really good sale. That way, at least the loss is minimal.

As someone who has enjoyed Supergiant's previous work, Bastion, I'm impressed by everything Transistor has to offer to its players. My only gripe with the game is its battle system which I did find a little lacking, as the player isn't able to do pretty much anything after executing a Turn()* besides moving away from surrounding enemies while waiting for the Turn() meter to recover.
What amazed me, on the other hand, was the deep, well-planned power-ups, also known as Functions in-game, that allows the player to mix-and-match them to his/her liking. Say, your character has a weapon-based attack which stuns surrounding enemies and a skill which allows your character to teleport short distances. In Transistor, you can combine these two, and get a skill which teleports your character AND stuns surrounding enemies upon reaching its destination. It's that awesome.
In overall, it's a great game well-deserving its place as the successor to Bastion, and there's no doubt that Supergiant has once again raised the bar for the action RPG genre just like they did three years ago.
*In Transistor, enemy battles are real-time but the player has the ability to "freeze" time and plan a limited number of movements and attacks. Once the input is given, the battle system would execute each move in real-time but the ability to do so would be put into a recovery period before it can be used again. In addition, all offensive skills (bar one, through the use of a power-up) are disabled during the recovery period.

Transistor is an amazingly crafted action-RPG combining hack&slash with tactical combat. It shares the same genre as Supergiant's previous game, again with memorable characters, well written story, and great soundtrack that enhances the experience. Like in Dark Souls, Transistor's plot is vague on purpose, leaving a lot of room to interpretation and speculation. I especially loved the impressively complex combat system of this game. With 16 Functions (skills) that can be used in a variety of ways, you have multitude of options to dominate the battlefield. Transistor is one of the best games I've played this year, fully reccomend it.
