MW2 contains nothing new. Very similar multiplayer to CoD4 (same formula) and very similar single player to CoD1 (exact same formula). Infinity Ward has proven once again that it has no idea how to innovate. Of course, why should they, with one of the best selling franchises of all time. And if these were all of my concerns, this would still be a pretty damn good game. However they only scratch the surface.
Graphics/Audio/Presentation- The graphics engine for the series has not visibly changed in nature since call of duty 2. Despite what infinity ward says, I have seen no visible innovation or improvement in the engine, with the exception of new skins or slightly higher resolution models. This is because of the limiting hardware of current consoles. The game consequentially looks mediocre at best and is not well optimized on the PC. It runs rather poorly. The cinematic effects of course are rather good, with blood splattering your screen when you are hit and good usage of the first person perspective in cutscenes. The audio is for the most part good, with voice acting being quite good, but the gun sounds are rather tinny and canned. They don't really sound like real guns if you've ever fired one before.
Story- The story is complete trash. Straight up. CoD 4 had a ridiculous premise, but at least it was somewhat coherent and it made some sense. Mw2 is even more over the top and makes NO SENSE AT ALL. no exaggeration, the plot seems to have been written by someone with a penchant for cinematic effects and a complete lack of storytelling ability. I wasn't even sure who I was (or why it mattered) more than half the time. I had to look up several articles online to even get a sense of what the plot was about, but it still doesn't make any sense at all.
Single- The single player gameplay itself is very linear, and really hasn't changed since CoD1. Regenerative health is maybe the only exception. ridiculous amounts of enemies shooting at you, and only you, ineffective allies, chase scenes etc. nothing new here. Exciting, but old and incredibly unrealistic
Multi- The multiplayer is clearly the game's greatest strength. They have taken their addictive FPS/RPG multiplayer leveling system from CoD4 and refined it, and for the most part, it works very well. Unfortunately. The PC version of the multi is incredibly deficient. No dedicated servers, no mod support, no server browser. No choice of which map to play, or any choice. You are matched using P2P technology with other players on a random map in the gamemode of your choosing (what a luxury) and are forced to deal with whoever is selected by the system is host. It is an insult to PC gamers everywhere. In addition, the game costs 60 dollars, and the map packs are 15 bucks each for 4-5 maps, which any decent company would include for free in content updates. Multi is also completely infested with hackers, and VAC is unlikely to do anything about it.
Coop- spec ops is a nice addition for playing with a buddy and can actually be quite challenging at times.
Overall, the game is CoD, through and through, and if you don't mind the thought of the unchanged gameplay, the price tag, the lack of servers, the hackers, and the overpriced map packs, you will have a good time, and get many hours of fun out of this game.

In the short time I have spent playing this, I can already tell this is an amazing game.
Pros:
+ Fantastic post-apocolyptic enviroment. It consistently feels like nowhere is safe.
+ Huge variety of enemies. Mutated animals galore and distorted humanoids. Militaristic bandits and factions run different areas and all provide a different challenge.
+ MASSIVE map with tons to explore. Every location has something of interest so it is worth exploring everything possible.
+ Plenty of weapons, armor, ammunition types, and consumables.
+ In-depth inventory managment. You can only carry so much weight before your movement speed slows. Take time to determine which medical items are the most important and which weapons are vital to where you are heading. You need everything but don't get the privilage to bring everything.
+ Still looks decent for being over a decade old.
+ Weapon damage is done differently in this game. The harder the difficulty, the more damage bullets do to both you AND the enemy. Easier levels are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥because you need more ammunition which takes up inventory space and fills up your weight limit. If you want a legitimate S.T.A.L.K.E.R. experience, play on the harder levels.
Cons:

Everybody knows by now that the atmosphere in this game is amazing, because it is. Everything works, yet looks unique giving each area a certain character. Gameplay wise, the game takes a while to gain moment and complexity, but once it reaches that point the possibilities for completing a mission are endless. This is thanks to the crafting system and the excellent "peep" mechanics. The enemies are challenging, and each in their own ways. I found myself being relieved at each interval when I would switch from Joe's to the Xeno or even humans. It keeps it fresh. What holds it back is the glitches that are a little to frequent to ignore. The only horror game I keep getting back to.
This game does so many things right. The atmosphere is absolutely captivating. The sound design in combination with the 70's Sci-Fi aesthetics make it so haunting and fascinating, you'd wish a spaceship like this would exist. Creative Assembly perfectly recreated (and expanded) the looks of the Alien movies. The art team did a fantastic job. I found myself many times just looking at the rooms and details that they have filled it with.
But where the game really shines is when the Alien is around. Everything gets taken up to eleven in terms of feel and atmosphere. And there's also pressure. Lots of pressure. While some websites talked about the game being worse when the Alien was around, due to its unpredictable behaviour and immortality, I couldn't disagree more. The goosepumps you get while trying to hack a door, while not knowing if the Alien is around is great. It's the positive kind of pressure. Barely being able to do something for the most time is one of the big pluses of this game. It's not like you are completely defenseless though. You can use Molotovs to scare it away or throw flares to distract it. But not more. It can't be killed, which is why the fear of it feels real and is apparent throughout the entire game. The items you can use have variety but all have the same effect in the end. Like I wrote earlier, the sound design is absolutely stellar. This applies to the Alien as well. The crawling vent sounds or the muffled sounds of the steps the Alien takes while you are hiding under a desk or in a locker, while getting louder with each step is a haunting experience.
The AI of the Alien is also really, really good. It's unpredictable at times but also fair for the biggest part. You should invest some time since hiding takes up a good chunk of gameplay. Not having any quick save possibilities also add to the gameplay since you really want to survive just to get to the next save point. A bit frustrating at times but you'll forgive the game since it's so good.
However, there are some downsides to this game. They are mostly minor though.
I'm not exactly a fan of Amanda's voice actress. I think she's trying but I found her voice to not be a perfect choice. She's just fine. It could have been better.
The gameplay with the androids is not really fun. Partially because they are not great to fight against/deal with. Most of the time you are running from them (like the Alien) but I simply found the levels with androids to be less fun to play, since there are mostly many of them in a single level. And maybe because seeing them smiling while they choke you to death is rather infuriating.
The campaign feels artificially extended. You could just feel that the story was written for a 8-10 hours experience, the game however went into the 12-14 hours route. You could see this as a negative (or positive), I enjoyed playing it for a longer period despite realizing that it could have been shorter and thus more focused. The story is also not that great. A company in the background wants the Alien and manipulated the androids to turn against the people. Not many huge surprises during the game. Standard Alien stuff.
Other things that could have been improved: Hacking, it's okay but gets tiring after while because of the missing variety. The facehuggers are trial-and-error sometimes, since they pop up out of nowhere at parts and you have to be very quick or it's suddenly game over. Characters are mostly  pale, but you do end up liking some such as Ricardo and Samuels but overall they are rather weak. Gameplay and atmosphere dominate while story and characters are more in the background.
Overall: Highly recommended, especially for horror fans. Buy it and we might see an Alien Isolation 2 even if the chances are really low, according to Sega.

TLDR: This game is good. Buy it.
If you are at all in to game critique and understanding games as an art you've probably heard of a term Ludo Narrative Dissonance. To explain it simply, it's when the gameplay and the narrative of a game are at odds with each other. Like in Bioshock (1) the narrative says you are stronger if you kill the Little Sisters, but in reality if you leave the Little Sisters alive you actually end up getting a lot more atom over the course of the game and end up WAY stronger.
So lets talk about the exact opposite of that. Ludo Narrative Resonance. When the gameplay and narrative work together.
This game is basically the personification of Ludo Narrative Resonance. In the Aliens universe, Xenomorphs (aka the aliens) are terrifying killing machines! In this game, yes...they are in fact terrifying and unstoppable killing machines.
So, what makes this game great?
1. You are not a soldier.
You are not a killer...(though you probably will kill a lot of things during this game) You are Amanda Ripley. An engineer.
You know one of the funny things about role playing shooters, like Fallout 3. There is no reason to holster your gun. Like realistically, it's actually pretty tiring to keep your gun out and ready all the time. This game did a brilliant decision to represent that in gameplay. You have to hold a button to keep your gun out.
In fact, that's one of the beautiful things about this game. The controls are complex. Not terribly complicated, but complex enough to make a tense situation with a Xenomorph more intense. You'll have to hold a button down to pull out your motion detecter. You'll need to press another button to make the background in focus, so you can see just what that blip on the radar actually is. Oh no! But what's this! The blip on the scanner is actually something hostile, you need to stop pressing that button so you can pull out your gun! Oh no, it's the crappy♥♥♥♥♥revolver and you didn't reload it! Hold down a button to open your inventory! Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ no time for that, you got to hide! Just so you have enough time to find the flamethrower. God this game's controls are stressful. And its all the better for it.
2. The Xenomorph are immortal.
It's very fitting for the Xenomorph to be immortal. After all, it was effectively unkillable in the first Alien movie too. But makes it work in a game context is that it's now no longer about defeating it, it's about managing resources to get around it.
Ever play Resident Evil 3? In that game there is an immortal monster that chases you around Raccoon City. Its an amazing game, but Alien: Isolation here takes it to a more logical extreme. So Nemesis (RE3 monster) can appear at any time in the game and will follow you from room to room. However, in this game, running is a terrible idea, because the Xenomorph is faster then you. Also, do to the limitations of the Playstation 1, you couldn't really hide from Nemesis. In Alien: Isolation, you have to hide. But don't be stupid about it.
When I first encountered the Xenomorph in a non-scripted way, I ran straight to a locker to hide from it. The alien clearly saw me, and promptly murdered me. So you have to break line of sight, and sometimes just go for the quickest hiding place, like behind a box and then just pray the Xenomorph doesn't find you.
It does get a bit annoying as sometimes the Xenomorph is relentless, and you just have to wait. Or sometimes you have another enemy in the area, then you get placed in to an impossible situation. And at that point, you need to use your resources to distract your enemies, so you can GTFO.
3. Just when you think you've won, you're dead wrong.
There are so many false signs that you're almost done with this game. But then it keeps going. Not only does it keep going, but it keeps getting worse. Every time.
Some people don't like that about this game. But screw them. Because it captures the feeling of the movie to the nth degree. Its insane how close you get to victory only for it to be snatched away from you. It makes sense, and it fills you full of dread. It's wonderful.
All in all, the game took me about 22 hours to beat. And I definitely missed a lot, and only beat it on normal. Honestly, I had so much fun, I think I might come back to this game on the hardest difficulty and see if I can't take on the challenge of beating the game with a more aggressive Xenomorph, and it should force me to use my resources smarter. The game was really fun despite how stressful and frightening the game is.
It's all of these things that come together to make the game absolutely amazing. Whether it's feeling like you just outsmarted an android trying to kill you, or maybe the shock and horror of dying because you didn't take the time to look around. It really does feel like you're in an Alien movie and you need to survive.
Just buy this game, so Sega can make us a sequel.

I have played factorio for 67 hours at the time of writing this review and i have been really enjoying this game. I will be writing this review based off of my own playthrough where i managed to launch 2 rockets with sattelites into space. I also devided production of resources into diffrent outposts to maximize the use of trains.
When you first start off in factorio you need to mine some coal, iron, copper and stone
. This process of getting resources yourself is slow and painfull it makes you want to automate the mining and smelting of resources. Once you built your first mining operation and smeling setup that converts ore into plates all by itself you can start to research things.
Research in Factorio is done by making
. You put these into a lab and it researches what you selected to research. Its a good way for this game to make sure you keep using your resources because that is what factorio is all about getting resources to build rockets and launch them into space.
You will be running into problems where the ore patches on the ground are totally used up. At this point in the game you will start using trains. Trains can be hard to understand and setup at first but once you get the hang of it you will see all the things you can do with trains. If you have played OpenTTD you will know exactly how to use the trains in factorio, they work almost identically.
At that point in the game the aliens will start comming for you because you have been making far too much pollution and the aliens have had enough. They will start attacking in waves of biters and spitters. Their name suggest what they do, the biters bite you, the spritters spit at you. you wont be able to hold the aliens off yourself and so you will need to build turrets and walls to shoot them down when they come for you. Ofcourse the turrets need ammo, for ammunition you need iron and if the biters take down your mining operation, well, good luck.
These aliens can be set to peacefull, they will only attack you if you attack them. But its more fun with the aliens. The aliens also bring a constant fear and a constant production need of ammunition and power. If one thing in the chain gets broken, the whole machine breaks and falls undel the alien regime.
The goal in the game is to launch a rocket into space with a sattelite attached. You do this by having the
craft a rocket for you. You will need alot of resources, ALOT of resources. And this is good, because again factorio is about building massive factories that make enough resources to constantly build rockets. And after you have built and launched your first rocket, the new goal is to launch as many rockets as possible.
The graphics in factorio really make you want to exploit the natural resources and make you want to leave the planet. The environment is very ugly, infact Sips from the yogscast called the planet &quot♥♥♥♥♥♥stained", that should say it all. The tree's on the planet aren't particularly beautifull either. they dont have a nice vibrant green colour but a kind of faded dark green colour which makes it look ugly.
The aliens look great, for the style. They are worm like creatures that will attack your pollution making machines. The aliens have diffrent tiers or evolution levels. They get bigger and have more badass colours starting with the default brown, going to a red like colour to blue to purple (I think purple is the colour of the new tier).
This does
mean that the game is ugly, its quite pretty in its own way. It has developped an art style and stuck to it. The planet itself looks ♥♥♥♥♥♥, the way it should be, it makes you want to kill the aliens and makes you want to leave the planet, which is the goal of the game. I would say they did a really good job of the graphics.
Factorio uses 2d sprites, which is why there can be such complex machines without impacting framerate. The sprites itself, from what i could tell are 3d models all rendered from the same perspective. This mean it looks like the objects are 3d with high quality lighting when in reality they are 2d sprites.
The sound in factorio is great, it can be a little loud at times but i mean, you would be deaf in real life if you stand next to a launching rocket. and the music also gives you this feeling that you want to leave the planet. overall great sound and music.
Factorio is absolutly great, if you like sandbox puzzle games. It really comes down to that, because you will be building factories to automate things and then troubleshooting those factories because either something has gone complely wrong or the balancing of resource productiond and consumption is off. The graphics are reallt nice (if you dont zoom in too far). The graphics, sound and music really make you want to leave the planet and exploit it to its maximum capacity while you are there.
All things considered i give it a solid
because the art is on point, sound and music is great, and the Gameplay is solid and pretty balances already. The game is in early access which in this case means tha game is still being worked on and regular updates are released to only make it better and add more cool stuff to the game.
Great game, much graphics, wow sound and music, so 9/10.

The short description of this game could be "Teen Ages of the 2000s simulator". On the long run it could be described as a nostalgic trek through the relationship developments via instant messaging, specifically because it gets you tiping on AIM while using a 8-bit version of Windows XP, complete with all the sound effects we've come to love over the years. Gameplay has you chatting with a high school friend named Emily, in an experience that has sufficient depth to make you feel like you're really the one talking to your long-time friend. The game spans several years of the character's online - and real - relationship with Em, which makes it feel like you're reliving the contact with that one long forgotten friend/crush.
When I began to write this review I really felt like giving this game a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ grade and a gigantic steam thumbs down. Finishing it for the first time and going through it again revealed that the dynamic of choice is nowhere near as influential as one would make it out to be.
But then I stopped to realize that, sometimes, people inevitably grow apart, regardless of what you do. Along with that epiphany, came the harsh and cruel truth: it wasn't merely a sad ending to my character, it represented the drifting away of
I had forgotten as life went by. By getting quashed by that brutal truth was that I could really understand the true beauty of this game.
So although I feel like cursing at the game and at its developer for not making it have a happy ending, I'd be also cursing at my younger self for not taking the time to enjoy those times with people I've left behind.

An amazing single-player first person western shooter. I've had more fun with this game in the first 3 levels than I ever have with most games.
The gunplay is solid, allowing you to go long ranged with rifles and accurate shots, rush in berserker style with shotguns or go full rambo raining bullets onto the enemy as a dual-wielding desperado. The tech tree is divided into these three categories, each with their strengths and weaknesses. The guns sound solid, look solid and, while not being realistic, give a definite feel of playing through a western movie.
A definite positive is also the game's aesthetic. The cartoon stlye intro is nice and over the top and in general the game provides some nicely detailed locales with middling textures but a beautiful variety of colours. The lovely style with the fairly mid-range textures and details does mean it stays at a solid 60 fps on high at 1080p on a pretty mid-range card (r9 270).
The secrets are well hidden and encourage exploration of the nicely varied maps, the narration is well done and lends endearing character to the protagonist you're playing and I like the overall story-time style of the game, which will have you playing a segment for a good 10 minutes just to tell you "nope, that didn't happen".
That would be my major point of criticism for the game too. I really feel that the game too often takes away control from you to tell the story, often throwing you into QTE-ladden cutscenes. I understand this is part of the style but sometimes breaks the flow too much for me. Thankfully, these sections never last more than 10-20 seconds, allowing me to get back to headshotting countless bandits or running in and splitting them in half with th deputy sheriff's "mean♥♥♥♥♥shotgun".
TL;DR: Highly recommended, great style, great gameplay, runs well, looks good, railroads a bit. Stupid fun and worth your money.

Game is pretty much unplayable at this point. Most servers ( cannot speak for all) are extremely unstable. SEA Server is basically a hit or miss thing. Ping spikes, DCs, crashes, you name it. The game is basically an early alpha product. Its extremely unpolished and rushed to make quick buck. It IS playable and you can like it for what it is, but if you have any standarts you will quickly notice the flaws and its gonna put you off. theres currently more cons than pros if you compare to any other "Free" mmo out there.
The support is generally bad. Ive asked a lot of questions and reported a lot of bugs that affected my character in various ways (mostly negative). The community is sadly not one of the best out there. Just go through the official forum and see for yourself.
The game design gets basically "worse" the higher you get in levels. Quests become more and more annoying, and the pace slows down. Lacking endgame content, or actual high level content, forces players to grind out their remaining levels. Theres no real PVP in the game (no rewards whatsoever). Guilds currently also no real value aside from being a community and having access to some minor things that no one makes use of.
ITOS (steam) also currently does not get ANY balance patches that kTOS gets, so the games balance is currently very well thrown off and you are better off not playing melee characters, unless its for tanking. Theres also no ETA when those balance patches will come.

Though a much shorter game than Bastion, as I managed to get through this in a mere six hours; transistor offers some of 2014's best indie gameplay. The story is compelling from beginning to end, with mystery intertwined throughout. The combat mechanics are outstanding, but very fiddly; a lack of control can be the difference between death and living to see another Turn(). The landscaping is beautiful, as expected from Supergiant, and will always take your breath away; when you have one after all the combat.
The narration, voiced by the same guy that did Bastion's narration, is still some of the best. Those that have played Bastion may find it offputting though, as the same voice in two different contexts always will be. The soundtrack is where the game shines, as 23 different tracks blend together to place you into Cloudbank, and truly understand the desperation that the city faces. The vocals, all by Ashley Barrett are amazing and definately coveny emotion throughout. My personal favourite, In Circles, will continually make you come back for more.
If you're really stuggling to pay £21 for both the game and the soundtrack, it might be best ot buy them seperately. the game is available from Supergiant Games' website for around £10, and the soundtrack is available from their Bandcamp page, for around £6. Overall, a good game with a lot of replayability, worth the time spent. 8.5/10

TLDR: This game is good. Buy it.
If you are at all in to game critique and understanding games as an art you've probably heard of a term Ludo Narrative Dissonance. To explain it simply, it's when the gameplay and the narrative of a game are at odds with each other. Like in Bioshock (1) the narrative says you are stronger if you kill the Little Sisters, but in reality if you leave the Little Sisters alive you actually end up getting a lot more atom over the course of the game and end up WAY stronger.
So lets talk about the exact opposite of that. Ludo Narrative Resonance. When the gameplay and narrative work together.
This game is basically the personification of Ludo Narrative Resonance. In the Aliens universe, Xenomorphs (aka the aliens) are terrifying killing machines! In this game, yes...they are in fact terrifying and unstoppable killing machines.
So, what makes this game great?
1. You are not a soldier.
You are not a killer...(though you probably will kill a lot of things during this game) You are Amanda Ripley. An engineer.
You know one of the funny things about role playing shooters, like Fallout 3. There is no reason to holster your gun. Like realistically, it's actually pretty tiring to keep your gun out and ready all the time. This game did a brilliant decision to represent that in gameplay. You have to hold a button to keep your gun out.
In fact, that's one of the beautiful things about this game. The controls are complex. Not terribly complicated, but complex enough to make a tense situation with a Xenomorph more intense. You'll have to hold a button down to pull out your motion detecter. You'll need to press another button to make the background in focus, so you can see just what that blip on the radar actually is. Oh no! But what's this! The blip on the scanner is actually something hostile, you need to stop pressing that button so you can pull out your gun! Oh no, it's the crappy♥♥♥♥♥revolver and you didn't reload it! Hold down a button to open your inventory! Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ no time for that, you got to hide! Just so you have enough time to find the flamethrower. God this game's controls are stressful. And its all the better for it.
2. The Xenomorph are immortal.
It's very fitting for the Xenomorph to be immortal. After all, it was effectively unkillable in the first Alien movie too. But makes it work in a game context is that it's now no longer about defeating it, it's about managing resources to get around it.
Ever play Resident Evil 3? In that game there is an immortal monster that chases you around Raccoon City. Its an amazing game, but Alien: Isolation here takes it to a more logical extreme. So Nemesis (RE3 monster) can appear at any time in the game and will follow you from room to room. However, in this game, running is a terrible idea, because the Xenomorph is faster then you. Also, do to the limitations of the Playstation 1, you couldn't really hide from Nemesis. In Alien: Isolation, you have to hide. But don't be stupid about it.
When I first encountered the Xenomorph in a non-scripted way, I ran straight to a locker to hide from it. The alien clearly saw me, and promptly murdered me. So you have to break line of sight, and sometimes just go for the quickest hiding place, like behind a box and then just pray the Xenomorph doesn't find you.
It does get a bit annoying as sometimes the Xenomorph is relentless, and you just have to wait. Or sometimes you have another enemy in the area, then you get placed in to an impossible situation. And at that point, you need to use your resources to distract your enemies, so you can GTFO.
3. Just when you think you've won, you're dead wrong.
There are so many false signs that you're almost done with this game. But then it keeps going. Not only does it keep going, but it keeps getting worse. Every time.
Some people don't like that about this game. But screw them. Because it captures the feeling of the movie to the nth degree. Its insane how close you get to victory only for it to be snatched away from you. It makes sense, and it fills you full of dread. It's wonderful.
All in all, the game took me about 22 hours to beat. And I definitely missed a lot, and only beat it on normal. Honestly, I had so much fun, I think I might come back to this game on the hardest difficulty and see if I can't take on the challenge of beating the game with a more aggressive Xenomorph, and it should force me to use my resources smarter. The game was really fun despite how stressful and frightening the game is.
It's all of these things that come together to make the game absolutely amazing. Whether it's feeling like you just outsmarted an android trying to kill you, or maybe the shock and horror of dying because you didn't take the time to look around. It really does feel like you're in an Alien movie and you need to survive.
Just buy this game, so Sega can make us a sequel.

So this game is easily a contender for best game in the Alien franchise but I had some real issues playing through the game that kept it from being the best without a doubt.
First off, the game is beautiful. They did a really solid job doing the retro rectreation of the original movie. I felt like I was watching a movie at some points but this is because there is no HUD on nightmare mode. Which brings me to my second point, I played through my first time on Nightmare.
I really enjoyed no HUD, no autosaves, and VERY little supplies. However, no map made this game really frustrating on some parts. Most of the time there are actually signs posted above the area you need to go but sometimes there is nothing at all so its really confusing where you are suppose to go and it doesn't help that all of the scenery looks the exact same and cannot be told apart from one another. This does add to the tension but sometimes it just became frustration and I would of appreciated if they would of left the map in but disable the markers.
That aside, the one thing I did NOT understand is why they do not display your health in any way. There is no way to tell if you get hurt because she doesnt make noise and theres no strawberry jam on the screen. I wish they would of just added the health bar when you pull up your item and crafting selection. There was a point that I kept dying over and over to fire that was on the frame of a door in the security office and had NO idea what I was doing wrong. I figured that since everything was an instant kill that health was disabled but no, they just don't show you. I didn't mind not finding supplies all the time as it made finding the supplies you did need feel like christmas and each present is a bullet. On the other hand, I thought it was kind of goofy to not give you any supplies in some of the locked supply caches that you find the codes for via terminal log files.
The Alien A.I. is a joke. There were times that literally i was against a wall in the open and just pressed the lean key and it didnt see me standing right next to me. I was more scared of the humans and androids than the alien itself to be completely honest. The humans would see you and shoot you on site, and the androids were slow but ridiculously tough so they could be outran but in numbers were rough. The alien was a total joke though, I wasn't scared of it just annoyed by it. This really ruins the atmosphere of the game, and made it feel mediocre.
The third and final point will contain spoilers, the story. The game offers what I am assuming is an alternate time line where the message at the end of Alien is actually much longer and is directed towards her daughter. That part I don't mind, but the end of the game is just terrible. Amanda Ripley doesn't die, but I doubt she lives. In the movie Aliens, she apparently dies from old age in a scene that was cut from the theatrical release but in the gamee they leave it ambiguous. Thats fine, the reason why I think the end is terrible is because the game just drags on and on after you reach the hive. I literally thought the game was going to be over 4 different times and eventually just quit caring and had to finish this game in segments. I completely lost interest because each time the game should of ended but didn't was more stupid than the next. It was like they were just desperate for ideas but they should of just ended it after you leave the hive. That part was terrifying and you can't top that so why are you dragging it on for several hours doing the same stuff you have been doing the entire game.
Over all, I would recommend this game to hardcore Alien fans for sure, however I'm not too sure the casual gamer would really give a♥♥♥♥♥♥after a certain point because the game just gets boring as ♥♥♥♥. There are some really great things about this game and some really mediocre things, but over all I would say give it a play through when its on sale.

Let's start with the great. From the moment this starts, you're back in Alien again. Not the sequel (unpopular opinion, but Aliens was far inferior to Alien), not the third one (seriously, shovels to drive the Xenomorphs back?), not the rest of them I try to forget. The original. The low-fi, giant CRT monitors, everything digital done in green and black, phones you need change for that have a receiver, everything. It's like stepping on the set and being able to wander in that universe. This is one of the most beautiful, well designed games I've ever played. Everything looks and feels like a movie straight out of the late 70s. (Bonus: they got the original voice actors from the original Alien to do very brief cameos.) But there's a large problem.
And it's the ♥♥♥♥ing Alien.
This one takes a moment to unpack because the original premise was that they wanted to go back to the original movie: that feeling of constant fear, constantly being hunted. But in the original movie, the Alien was always a looming threat. It was there, picking people off, but it wasn't on screen constantly. In this game, the Alien is CONSTANTLY on screen. And it isn't scary, it's just ♥♥♥♥ing annoying. The game specifically limits you in how you can fight it, so most of the early game is spent huddled under tables or in closets, waiting until it goes back in the vents. Then you walk on through. As a result, VERY short levels are artificially lengthened by hiding under a table for 5-10 minute stretches. Later, when you get a flame thrower, it comes down from the vents, you torch it, it scurries back in the vents, and you walk on through. This game wanted you to be afraid, but the Alien (of all things) is what prevented you from ever getting to that emotional state. Which is ♥♥♥♥ing sad, because the parts of the game where the Alien IS looming but you're having to deal with a space station falling to pieces is where the game shines. In fact, the last two to three missions (where the Alien is scripted more heavily and not left to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI) are REALLY good. But even that gets spoiled by ham handed lipservice to the original Alien and then one of the most egregious non-endings I've ever seen in any medium.
The problem with it comes down to this: in a movie, despite having a general idea of how it'll turn out because of certain constraints of the medium (ie, the Alien can't kill everyone in ten minutes or this movie will be boring♥♥♥♥♥♥, you can place your characters in situations which threaten them and make the audience sit on the edge of their seat. You can lean on the fear and the looming terror of the characters as the audience gets attached and then has those characters ripped away. That doesn't work NEARLY as well in a game where you're overexposing the villain and where any sort of death is undoable - you reload from your last save, now you know what to avoid, ♥♥♥♥ this♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm out, yeah?
So how do I feel about it? Eh. If you love the original Alien (♥♥♥♥ the sequels), there is enough nostalgia combined with incredible design to see this as kind of a "true sequel" and make it worth the purchase (on sale, for 10-12 dollars, don't pay more). But if you're looking for either a more palpable terror experience or simply an awesome game, there are way too many things that prevent this from being an unconditional recommendation. YMMV with this one.

Installed the game and loved many elements of it until I met the alien, after I encountered the alien I had great difficulty accepting the behavior of the dynamic AI into what I had come to expect as a well constructed continuation of the ideas in the original film (alien), in large part this review is based with inclusion of the mod "Unpredictable Alien AI mod"...
Liked:
Voice acting was believable
Graphics are to a high quality on max settings.
Graphical theme and atmosphere follow the original film
Suspense and evasion (modded!) match the original film ideas very well
Lack of emphasis on using weapons to fight, a great game of stealth.
An interesting station design with enough elements to construct a great virtual world
Revisiting areas of the station throughout the game adds to the permanence of the station as a real world.
Great range of gadgets that enhance gameplay
Incorporation of gameplay elements like new weapons and blueprints through the game that add depth to the game
Fantastic level design for evading the Alien with plenty of lockers and desks and obstacles to hide from it
Fantastic incorporation of noise making elements to attract the alien through negligent movement
Requires a slight element of thought to play the game, much better than other games.
Lighting and shading is fantastic
Some great jump scares and a great game to play at night.
Overall a brilliant experience.
Disliked:
I played through the entire game with a mod that changes the aliens behaviour, this mod unleashes the alien from being attached to the players vicinity and allows it to roam around each level in a manner that I found more consistent with the behaviour of the alien in the original film and more realistic in that it didn't seem to cheat.
I found the original behaviour of the alien very game like, it would often not deviate very much from me hiding in a locker despite waiting 5 or more real life minutes, it would move away from me then erratically return running to where I was on multiple occasions producing a frustrating experience. The alien behaved as if it knew my location at all times despite not making any noise, as if it was leashed to my position and not sources of interest / noise.
I found the behaviour changed an experience that immersively followed the intent of the original film into "just" a computer game. Without the mod I wouldn't of bothered with playing the "game" much at all.
Installing the mod made everything work, though I couldn't make much noise for risk of attracting the alien, so long as I played thoughtfully I could play smoothly through the level, only being hunted when I drew the aliens attention to my area, but with sufficient time of evasion the alien would return to the vents and another part of the level, freeing me to play on.

The combat in this game feels very solid. Everything from the range of weapons to sound design ensure that every bullet you fire feels different and has an impact on the enemies.
Furthermore, the aesthetic fits the game well. It's stylized look douses everything in bright colors, and everything seems to pop out a little more because of it.
The story is surprsingly intresting, and is told as a sequence of memories. This means that during the middle of a gunfight the narrator may remember something new, drastically changing the playing field.
Considering that this is a very cheap game for what it is, I'd give this game a look if you were intrested in a good old fashioned shoot em up.

While the sampling size of Western themed FPS games is pretty much nil and as a person who has played the first two Call of Juarez games, I think it goes without saying that Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is the best Western themed FPS I've ever played. You play an old bounty hunter telling his tales of his past the western frontier to the patrons in a saloon and I won't go any further as the game is filled with many twists, turns and surprises throughout. The good is that the story is very good with excellent voice acting, nice gunplay and beautiful cel shaded graphics. While some of the environments do repeat themselves  (mostly due to how the narrator is telling the story) you'll still do battle in valleys, forests, gold mines, swamps and of course a train. One of the unique points of this game is the duelling and it definitely takes some practice but you'll get better as you go which adds satisfaction to when you win. It took me about eight hours to compete but I was scouring the levels for the unlockables, which give you some real life history of some of the characters you come across. If you enjoy the old west, this is definitely the game for you. The MSRP is $14.99 which is quite fair but if you can get it for 66%-75% off well that's just a (train) robbery. 9/10 from me.

Sadly there's likely to be frustration over the weapon balance, since a significant amount of people exploit what the game offers, and create
combinations. Be aware also that there are no dedicated servers, only matchmaking. This piece is not without flaws, but it is still a joy to play. Nice job Infinity Ward.

I enjoyed many things about this game, but the game has a long way to go to be worth playing as a long term MMO. You might enjoy playing this game for the first 160 levels if you do some homework and pick a cookie cutter build. You might even enjoy the game for a very long time if you have friends to share the experience with. At best I can recommend trying the game for 50 hours. Eventually the problems will add up and you'll ask yourself if you want to spend hundreds of hours to this game.
Everybody has their own reasons for quitting a game. I personally quit because of the class balance, lack of respecs, and lack of endgame content. I have devoted hundreds of hours of my time to maxing out multiple characters on other MMOs but I couldn't see myself doing that in this half finished game. It's bad enough that you can't fix small mistakes with your build. You can't share your items between characters and rerolling means throwing away all of your work. Planning your character means nothing when you can't account for future patches or nerfs. None of the classes are balanced in a sane way, either. Wizard is especially intollerable to level up. Why play an MMO where rerolling is forced and takes hundreds of hours to level up and you can't transfer gear between alts? I see this game eventually being dominated by botters and a toxic community that hates casuals due to the class imbalance.

First off, this is not Dark Souls 1.  It was made by a different team, and should in no way be considered a sequel.  The name in and of itself is a lie, and leads to false expectations.  However, it is named as a sequel, so comparisons to Dark Souls 1 must be expected and accepted.  Moving on.
The game is a good game, that can't be denied.  I wish steam gave the option to call it a "neutral" opinion, because that most reflects what mine is.  As it is, I'll be posting it as a negative review.  Let me just lay out my thoughts on the game.
Pros (not many):
-Jump button can be bound to left thumbstick.  Thank god.
-Left handed weapons are actually useable.
-Larger variety in armor.
-Connecting is fast and simple.
Cons(a lot):
-Movement on controllers at least feels very 8-directional.  Unlike DS1, where it had a very 360 degrees feel to it.
-Rolling is now a stat.  Rolling.  A stat.  Now you have to buy your i-frames?  I don't have much issue with it because I just kill dragonrider first and get 20 adp, but still it feels like a completely unnecessary addition to the mix.
-There are far too many stats.  It feels like they wanted to make it different than the other games in the souls "series" and they succeeded at that.  However, for that difference we are stuck with a confusing mess of numbers and modifiers.
-There is no poise system.  To be fair, poise shouldn't have been implemented in ds1, but they tried to keep some movesets and that led to some stunlocking that just feels frustrating and loose.
-Endurance is almost nonexistent.  In DS1 and Demon's, endurance feels like it's actually realistic.  In this game, it just feels like my guy can't run more than 15 feet without needing a break.
-Enemies feel like they've just been dumped into random places.   In Dark and Demon's, enemy placement was strategic.  The games were difficult not because a lot of enemies, but because the enemies were well-placed.  This game just puts piles of them against you as if it were trying to be God of War.
-Pvp latancy is absurd.  I have a good connection, roughly 20 ping.  However, I consistently get hit from 5-10 feet away.  Hit registration needs to be fixed.
-The art style feels like a huge downgrade from Dark Souls 1.  Sure, the game runs great on my laptop.  But I'd rather run steady 30fps instead of 45 and actually have more detail in the game.
-Boss AI is awful.  You expect an upgrade from game to game, but the ai seems the same as DS1.  No improvements made, limited set of actions, very predictable.
-A lot of recycled content.  To be fair, Dark Souls 1 had the same issue with many of the bosses being the same as Demon's (Asylum Demon and Bed of Chaos I'm looking at you).  Dark Souls 2 is no different, taking bosses from Dark Souls 1 (Sif 2.0) and Demon's Souls (Dragons, everyone?)
-Soul Memory.  God, Soul Memory.  I understand why it was implemented, to stop twinking, but at least take it out in NG+ so I don't have to fight max levels all the time?
All in all, DS2 was a dissappointment.  I don't regret paying full price to get it on release, but it could have been so much better.

Short version: If you like Bastion, you'll like Transistor... because you've already played it.
Long version: Transistor is like a high-tech, watered-down version of Bastion, with Art Deco in place of mysterious rising bits of landscape. There's visually a lot more going on in Transistor, if the frame rate on my computer is any indication [chugging somewhat at the lowest resolution], but the game is completely linear, where Bastion allows a choice of what land to visit next. To make up for it, the Transistor is capable of equipping and "upgrading" four different attacks ("Functions"), which double as life extensions (lose too much life, and a Function overloads--Red dies if all Functions overload). The Idols in Bastion reappear in Transistor as Limiters, providing additional experience at the expense of added difficulties.
What sets Transistor apart from Bastion the most is the Turn() action, which is by default automatically activated at low health, though it can also be activated at will. Turn() is a Frozen Synapse-style "freeze frame" where Red can plan out a set number of attacks at leisure before enacting them, at the penalty of leaving herself unable to attack until her Turn() meter resets. Mastering Turn() can mean the difference between winning and losing, especially in the Sandbox tests. The most fun is experimenting with stacking Functions for effectiveness in battle, and finding all the cute flavour text hidden throughout the stages.
Once again, if you like Bastion, you'll like Transistor... because you've already played it.

A player is gifted with a set of tools and a sandbox to play in, and told to destroy everything in sight. It's Just Cause - the anti-Minecraft. It’s not cerebral, it’s the GTA-clone stripped down to its core elements – get rid of the story, get rid of the characters, get rid of the nuance and go blow things up, please. It’s one of the most sandbox-y of all the GTA-type sandbox game series’ out there, and this factor is responsible for all that is good and almost all that is bad about the game.
Firstly:
Is JC3 better than JC2?
- Yes.
Are you just buying the same game?
- On the surface the formula is quite similar, but the product is not the same.
Is it as buggy/janky as everyone says?
- I suppose this depends on your particular experience, but yes and no. My playthrough was very functional, although I did experience one or two game-breaking bugs in 35 hours, and a few non-critical but noticeable bugs throughout. In other words, I found there to be some visible, but not ruinous, issues.
There have been a number of key improvements in JC3 that make the game worth recommending over and above JC2. The best part about this game is that you don’t need to have played the others, so if you’re new to the series, I’d seriously recommend just starting here. Apart from the protagonist there is only one returning character, otherwise there is almost no connection to any of the other games. On top of that, JC3, more than any other entry in the series, makes an effort to delve into Rico’s back-story, which brings me to my first point:
The characters are better…which is a breath of fresh air given that anything and everything story-related in JC2 was not just a waste of time, but often actively irritating. The plot was so thin I often had little idea of what I was doing and why, and the characters were so poorly developed and executed that when I did, I didn’t care. At least in JC3, Avalanche have put some effort into developing the relationships between the enjoyably quirky characters, as well as between the characters and the setting in which you are playing, grounding the 30-odd hours you’ll pump into a playthrough in a way that feels like they’ve *tried* to motivate the action. The downside is that the cutscenes generally come in two flavours: too short (amounting to literally a handful of lines before throwing you into a mission), or pointless (either stripping you of control for no reason, or breaking to give you control for a moment of time, only to take it from you again seconds later). And while this may delight those who are here for the ‘boom-boom’, they often felt rushed to me, and poorly considered.
But you’re not playing a Just Cause game for the plot, are you? No, you came here to blow a lot of things up, which is just as well, because the game is really, REALLY good at letting you do that. The graphics are, for the most part, wonderful, and I had quite a few ‘wow’ moments in my time. The game is quite taxing/poorly optimised depending on who you talk to, and getting a smooth 60fps might be a struggle, but there really is nothing like seeing a mushroom cloud light up the night sky as it stretches hundreds of feet into the air before you. It’s mesmerising. The arsenal of weapons is extensive, although you’ll likely only stick to a few, and the line-up of destructive vehicles is varied, and each have their own little balancing trade-offs. While the action itself is repetitive, I never felt like I was hurrying to finish. I enjoyed myself far more than in JC2. It’s kind of zen, in a way, in that you can switch your mind off and slowly and methodically clear out the islands one-by-one. And there is plenty of island to clear - travelling from one end of the map to the other ought to take a good 10-15 minutes in the fastest vehicle. For at least half of my play-time it felt like there was less scenic variation than in JC2, as most of the lower half of the map is all Mediterranean countryside. But once you reach the top end, you’ll find enormous snowy mountain peaks, strip mines and smouldering volcanic craters. It makes a bit more sense than letting the snowline rest a calm 2 minute drive from the nearest tropical beach, although if you’re like me and enjoy avoiding fast travel, flying or driving can feel like a slog at times.
The downsides to the game are similar to those of the previous. The driving in JC3 is some of the worst I’ve ever experienced, and you NEED to master the touchy drifting mechanic to corner properly. It’s not a pleasant experience at all, and you will likely stick to the air most of the time. There are also some elements that shriek ‘rushed development!’ as well – little bugs like lights remaining mid-air after you destroy an antenna, or cars bouncing into the air after an impact. The island as a whole feels quite empty apart from the designated destructible areas, and there are few surprises to be found exploring. Also, like JC2, JC3 has a whole bunch of busywork by way of collectables and activities, although the potentially mind-numbing nature of these is mitigated by some progressively unlocking in-game rewards for completing them - most importantly, completing activities unlocks enhancements for your weapons and skills. These increase the fun-factor ten-fold, and are a good motivation for completing those activities that aren’t as enjoyable as others.
Finally, a nice surprise is that, whilst the ending is decidedly abrupt and lacking in gravity, the end-game allows you to ‘re-oppress’ any settlement, and destroy it all over again with your new arsenal of end-game weapons. The nuke-launcher and the gold-plated chopper are hilarious fun, and single-handedly kept this game on my hard drive after I finished the story.
TL;DR – JC3 is JC2 but better. I can definitely recommend buying it, especially if it’s on sale, and if you haven’t played any before – start here. I did experience some bugs, and the frame rate can be hard to lock down on high settings, but with a bit of tweaking I had a very stable, functional time, and lovely-looking time. It's repetitive, but there's enough fun and spectacle that I rarely got tired of the action, and I was never playing just to get it over with. To be honest, I’m a little bummed that I’m done with it, and if there were a new game + I’d probably start again tomorrow.

Read alot of reviews, both negative and positive, about the game and decided to confirm / debunk some points made by others.
Walking simulator? No, it's alot more than that.
Buggy? The game is 99.99% bug free. I only encountered one camera angle issue which was resolved easily.
Extremely scary horror game? There are scarier games, that's true. Still, there are some exceptionally scary moments in this game (both scripted and non-scripted). It takes a while for the Alien to make its appearance (as to be expected, so this is no spoiler really), some people find the game before that happens boring, but this period simply sets up the atmosphere and the story.
About halfway throughout the game you find a means to at least combat the Alien a bit better (not kill it, not fight it, just... have it take a chill pill) and it is this moment where the game changes from a hide/seek game to a being chased / hunted (some people use the word 'annoyed', which I can understand) game, where you can easily see the gameplay and level design are built around the fact you no longer have to hide constantly from the Alien (though it's still highly recommended).
Another complaint I read alot about this game is the length and the way it's made to be a long game. Single player adventure is about 20-25 hours first playthrough (assuming it is blind, and you take your time to investigate every cabinet and computer, get a good grip on the story, backstory, etc.) on Normal/Hard difficulty. Recommended first playthrough is on Normal, after that Hard is a worth a try. Differences are most about the occurrence of Alien leaving the vents to try a more 'hands-on' approach to find you. On Easy he hardly makes an appearance (which in a way makes the game more scary I guess), on Hard he will be constantly in your face, obstructing your route to the next waypoint (which will end up to annoy you more than scare you, especially after halfway throughout the game when you found a way to deal with the Alien  more directly. You will be saying 'Get the hell outta my way, you idiot' more often than 'omg, the horror!')
Anyway, about the length: it's true that right towards the end the game exhausts you a bit with the Alien pop-ups, but still, the story is interesting to keep you going to the end. Also, the story fools you quite a few times thinking it's the end, but no... more stuff to explore and do before you are safe. Again, this was a complaint by some people, I can understand it, even though I didn't experience it that badly.
Graphics and audio are excellent, not just from a technical view but also from a scenic view. The game is a TRUE homage to the first Alien movie, and also gets some inspiration from the second movie (both story and location wise, sort to speak). Smoke from vents, creepy shadows from lights, beeps from computers, it all fits together.
If you loved the Alien movies (especially the first and second) this game is a must have. If you loved other horror games, you will like this as well.

VERDICT: Frustrating at times, but ultimately a rewarding, tense and visceral experience. Recommended purchase given it's regularly on sale, but expect to test your patience.
TYPE OF GAME: Linear stealth game with emphasis on atmosphere. Played with keyboard and mouse.
PROS:
* Runs well on modest PCs with high frame rates. Graphics are nothing special but certainly work well in the game. Staring out the window at the gas giant the Sevastapol is orbiting is a brief moment of pleasure in an otherwise tense game.
* Fantasic sound effects, The creaking, groaning sounds of the disintegrating Sevastapol station are great, along with the hair raising sounds of the Alien itself. Limited music in game, with some tense music that, although certainly works well, is a little overpowering at times when you need to concentrate on more subtle sounds the most. The androids are particularly creepy.
* The jump scares are not excessive or pointless and really work well where used.
* Genuinely difficult game, especially when difficulty is ramped up.
* Some flexibility as to how you approach roadblocks, be it humans, the Alien or androids. For example, a loud noise triggered near some adverse characters would allow for the Alien to clear the room for you.
* Great effort has been made to have the game integrate well with, and be faithful to, the original Alien movie (well worth going back and watching the movie after playing it). It almost feels like canon for the Alien franchise.
CONS:
* Sometimes I found it difficult to understand what was required next. Although that may be a positive/challenge for some, it is applied inconsistently throughout the game, meaning I would often wander around for a long time backtracking to see if I had missed anything at certain times in the game. This resulted in a little too much reliance on walkthoughs for me (but, hey, that's probably my fault for lack of observational skills).
* The interface at times resulted in me pressing the wrong button (i.e. craft item instead of use item at the worst possible time).
* Limited save points, spaced inconsistently. Hell, even reaching a save point and saving with an Alien close by gave your nerves a run.
* Speaking of Alien, its omnipresence made it difficult to read the stories on terminals, etc. So getting an in depth experience with the game isn't easy to achieve and you skim read to not be ambushed by an android or alient (yep, they can attack you even when you are logged into a terminal).
* A little long for me. I find the sweet spot for most linear games around 15 hours, but up to 25 hours if it is an engaging story. I completed this in 27 hours, but often got lost or missed objectives, resulting in some unnecessary backtracking (on top of the mandatory backtracking that seems to endlessly happen throughout the story).

Striking a balance between overwhelmingly flawed and vastly improved in comparison to the first Dark Souls game, Dark Souls II rides on the coattails of the Souls franchise to still end up a pretty great game overall. Despite being what I consider to be a fairly mediocre Souls game, it’s still a fantastic game to be experienced. Greater overall game performance, notable gameplay tweaks, and a series of exceptional downloadable content chapters added post-release raise Dark Souls II to greater heights. The combat is still tight, exploration is still satisfying, and death is still just right around the bend.
Dark Souls II is likely the weakest of the Souls series so far, with a story that feels flat and empty, as well as environments that make little to no sense. You ride an elevator up from a windmill perched atop a poison-filled swamp, and emerge to… a castle immersed in lava? Uninspired boss battles, mostly consisting of giant dudes in armor, round the game out to be pretty disappointing… and yet I still recommend it. Why? Because it’s still immensely fun. The strengths overwhelm the weaknesses, and Dark Souls II still comes out on top.

As I write this review, I hear the constant generic pixelated RPG sound effects going off as this game literally plays itself in the background. I downloaded this game in the morning to find something new and exciting, and at first, I thought I had found it. It is now late evening, and I see through this game's clever facade. It's just another one of those clicker games, like Cookie Clicker or Adventure Capitalist, the ones that are♥♥♥♥♥♥easy to program and require either an arbitrary amount of time or a few micropayments in order to get anything cool. You may think that it is a fun Final Fantasy Style RPG game with cool characters and fun gameplay. Soon enough, however, you'll realize the "Auto Play" function at the bottom of the screen, and watch in utter shock as the game starts playing itself for you, and reasonably much better than a new player could. I'll admit, beating my way through dungeons and getting better gear does have its appeal at first. But as you eventually revert to Auto Play to get through dungeons and such faster, you'll see the monatany of it all. Once you get past the first dungeon, nothing changes. No innovations, no interesting mechanics, no new ways to play, nothing. I suppose that since it is free, and it isn't a scenario in which you have to use micro transactions to do anything of significance, then it gets my recommendation, because the feeling of progression at the beginning feels good, the idea is pretty neat, albeit not ground-breaking, and the art style is visually appealing and clearly had a lot of effort put into it. But if you try to argue that this game is in any way game-changing or monumental, I think you haven't spent enough time in the Steam Free Games list, you creaton.

Set in the wild west, with an art direction that can only be described as eye candy, Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a point-racking arcade shooter with a lot to offer.
The choices the player can make that makes their game feel free and character unique are, in fact, slim to none. However, you will be able to pick perks that supplement your favored playstyle, and many of the perks synergize with other equipment choices. Any complaints of linearity aside, what makes Gunslinger shine is very much the narrative story line and spectacular visuals, combined with the rich and detailed history in the form of 'hidden nuggets of truth' placed throughout the stages.
As a general suggestion; if you're looking for a complete wild west experience, Gunslinger is probably not the best place to look. However, it doesn't take away from the merits, being that Gunslinger is a lovingly crafted homage to the tall tales birthed from American history.
Also, as a final thought, I read a lot of reviews before making my purchase and found that a common complaint was with the dueling mechanics and with the lack of horse riding. I have to say, that none of the settings really called for horseback riding. The scenes are short and you often find climbing up structures, or entering buildings. All of the travelling (which would very much interrupt the episodic stories) is done offscreen.
The duels were cinematic and intense, and added to the overall excitement and pacing. "Your mileage may vary" as is often said.
Edit: After completing the game, I realized two things.
1. The soundtrack is awesome.
2. This game is awesome.
I was only slightly disappointed that NG+ promised hints about the story. While the promise was delivered, these additions were only additional loading screen tidbits.
If you know what you're buying, and considering the easiness - I honestly think Call of Juarez: Gunslinger is a 9.6/10. Great game.

Okay I will admit that this game didnt have the most successful launch but it sure did a good job of getting back up ( In my opinion ). This game has so much to offer, plus the mod support alone makes it a worthy product to be bought. Graphics Improvement, New Political System etc are a few examples of the new features in this TW game! Overall the DLCs are pretty fine as well, especially the Caesar in Gaul DLC. What I dont like is (this is just a teeny tiny prob) is the fact that agents can very much bring your armies to a halt. I've had 10 armies completely stopped from marching because of agents. Well until I found a "No Agents Mod" of course.  Everything is eye-candy and the battle mechanics have been improved compared to older patches of the game. AI can bring you down to your knees, attacking you with 5 full stacks and actually flanking you with heavier infantry and veteran cavalry units. Its quite good really. The factions are diverse giving players the opportunity to create an empire in any region of the world depending on the culture they choose (Latin, Greek, Celtic etc). Also the game provides a considerable and essential amount of tooltips everywhere giving you various info of whats gonna happen if you click this or doing that. Siege battles are okay but wall battles are like complete slugfests so battering rams are always a must if you dont want to send wave after wave of poor tier 2 infantry up against a tier 2 spear unit defending. I know there are some people that say the new TW games are definitely not what TW was known for but I for one still find it enjoying and interesting enough for me to play hundreds of hours on them. I hope the upcoming TW Titles will bring the "small bits" of past TW Titles like, Medieval 2's Assassination scenes, or the Closeup Pre-Battle Speeches or even the Diplomatic Option to give regions :D
Overall Rating: 8/10 - A great addition to the franchise!

Transistor does exactly what you'd expect from Supergiant Games after their first big hit "Bastion": A action-RPG-style game with an interesting story, beautiful art and wonderful music.
The game revisits many elements from Bastion (varied attacks, modifiers for your attacks, difficulty increases for challenge and more XP), but improves upon all of them. The story is more interwoven with the mechanics than the last time (and you get rewarded for experimenting with the mechanics with story snippets) and art and music are more refined than the last time.
And, much like with the last game, by the time you're getting to the ending, you feel the climax coming on, you feel the emotional resonance, it's a good pay-off, it feels like you earned the ending.
One big change is: the game is a good bit shorter than Bastion, though better. It's not lacking in content, it's short in the same way a short story is short. I like that, but if you're looking for something that fills dozen of hours of play, this is not it and it doesn't try to be.

Let me start off by stating that I play my FPS games on the console. I just love the layout of the controller as opposed to the keyboard/mouse combo. That said I won't play this game online because I'm well aware of the disadvantage us controller wielding players have so this is a review for the spec ops and single player portions of the game.
The biggest gripe I have, and actually the only one is that there is no native support for the controller so you have to either use the keyboard and mouse or download other drivers and they have a tendency to jump around at times when you try to use the controller. If you're a FPS console guy like me just don't go online with it and you'll be fine and if you're a PC FPS gamer then you're golden.
The campaign for MW2 is hands down the best in the series. Pretty decent length, they do a very good job of getting you to feel attached to the characters so when something happens to one of them you're feeling the loss of a buddy out there not just some random NPC. The story is deep, the music is excellent and the gameplay is very well done. I'd recommend the game for the campaign alone.
Spec Ops mode adds a lot of time and replayability to the game. There are 23 missions spread across 5 categories with each mission having a completion grade of 1-3 stars. The more stars you get the better you did and the more difficult missions you can unlock. The missions are based mostly around events that happen in the campaign but there are a few (including my favorite,
) that are from COD 4. 21 of the 23 missions are single player and 2 of them are co-op.
All in all a great game even without touching multiplayer and still has great replayability. Even after you get all 69 stars in spec ops mode a lot of those missions are still fun to go through. Modern Warfare 2 is a classic and a worthy member of the Call of Duty franchise.

A player is gifted with a set of tools and a sandbox to play in, and told to destroy everything in sight. It's Just Cause - the anti-Minecraft. It’s not cerebral, it’s the GTA-clone stripped down to its core elements – get rid of the story, get rid of the characters, get rid of the nuance and go blow things up, please. It’s one of the most sandbox-y of all the GTA-type sandbox game series’ out there, and this factor is responsible for all that is good and almost all that is bad about the game.
Firstly:
Is JC3 better than JC2?
- Yes.
Are you just buying the same game?
- On the surface the formula is quite similar, but the product is not the same.
Is it as buggy/janky as everyone says?
- I suppose this depends on your particular experience, but yes and no. My playthrough was very functional, although I did experience one or two game-breaking bugs in 35 hours, and a few non-critical but noticeable bugs throughout. In other words, I found there to be some visible, but not ruinous, issues.
There have been a number of key improvements in JC3 that make the game worth recommending over and above JC2. The best part about this game is that you don’t need to have played the others, so if you’re new to the series, I’d seriously recommend just starting here. Apart from the protagonist there is only one returning character, otherwise there is almost no connection to any of the other games. On top of that, JC3, more than any other entry in the series, makes an effort to delve into Rico’s back-story, which brings me to my first point:
The characters are better…which is a breath of fresh air given that anything and everything story-related in JC2 was not just a waste of time, but often actively irritating. The plot was so thin I often had little idea of what I was doing and why, and the characters were so poorly developed and executed that when I did, I didn’t care. At least in JC3, Avalanche have put some effort into developing the relationships between the enjoyably quirky characters, as well as between the characters and the setting in which you are playing, grounding the 30-odd hours you’ll pump into a playthrough in a way that feels like they’ve *tried* to motivate the action. The downside is that the cutscenes generally come in two flavours: too short (amounting to literally a handful of lines before throwing you into a mission), or pointless (either stripping you of control for no reason, or breaking to give you control for a moment of time, only to take it from you again seconds later). And while this may delight those who are here for the ‘boom-boom’, they often felt rushed to me, and poorly considered.
But you’re not playing a Just Cause game for the plot, are you? No, you came here to blow a lot of things up, which is just as well, because the game is really, REALLY good at letting you do that. The graphics are, for the most part, wonderful, and I had quite a few ‘wow’ moments in my time. The game is quite taxing/poorly optimised depending on who you talk to, and getting a smooth 60fps might be a struggle, but there really is nothing like seeing a mushroom cloud light up the night sky as it stretches hundreds of feet into the air before you. It’s mesmerising. The arsenal of weapons is extensive, although you’ll likely only stick to a few, and the line-up of destructive vehicles is varied, and each have their own little balancing trade-offs. While the action itself is repetitive, I never felt like I was hurrying to finish. I enjoyed myself far more than in JC2. It’s kind of zen, in a way, in that you can switch your mind off and slowly and methodically clear out the islands one-by-one. And there is plenty of island to clear - travelling from one end of the map to the other ought to take a good 10-15 minutes in the fastest vehicle. For at least half of my play-time it felt like there was less scenic variation than in JC2, as most of the lower half of the map is all Mediterranean countryside. But once you reach the top end, you’ll find enormous snowy mountain peaks, strip mines and smouldering volcanic craters. It makes a bit more sense than letting the snowline rest a calm 2 minute drive from the nearest tropical beach, although if you’re like me and enjoy avoiding fast travel, flying or driving can feel like a slog at times.
The downsides to the game are similar to those of the previous. The driving in JC3 is some of the worst I’ve ever experienced, and you NEED to master the touchy drifting mechanic to corner properly. It’s not a pleasant experience at all, and you will likely stick to the air most of the time. There are also some elements that shriek ‘rushed development!’ as well – little bugs like lights remaining mid-air after you destroy an antenna, or cars bouncing into the air after an impact. The island as a whole feels quite empty apart from the designated destructible areas, and there are few surprises to be found exploring. Also, like JC2, JC3 has a whole bunch of busywork by way of collectables and activities, although the potentially mind-numbing nature of these is mitigated by some progressively unlocking in-game rewards for completing them - most importantly, completing activities unlocks enhancements for your weapons and skills. These increase the fun-factor ten-fold, and are a good motivation for completing those activities that aren’t as enjoyable as others.
Finally, a nice surprise is that, whilst the ending is decidedly abrupt and lacking in gravity, the end-game allows you to ‘re-oppress’ any settlement, and destroy it all over again with your new arsenal of end-game weapons. The nuke-launcher and the gold-plated chopper are hilarious fun, and single-handedly kept this game on my hard drive after I finished the story.
TL;DR – JC3 is JC2 but better. I can definitely recommend buying it, especially if it’s on sale, and if you haven’t played any before – start here. I did experience some bugs, and the frame rate can be hard to lock down on high settings, but with a bit of tweaking I had a very stable, functional time, and lovely-looking time. It's repetitive, but there's enough fun and spectacle that I rarely got tired of the action, and I was never playing just to get it over with. To be honest, I’m a little bummed that I’m done with it, and if there were a new game + I’d probably start again tomorrow.

As my 2 hours hold strong in Reign of Kings as of 5/13/2015, I have experienced..... interesting things at that.
++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
Starting off in the game really isn't so difficult, sure there might be that one annoying guy that charges you with javelins or slightly better items than you and angers you due to you just earning a full set of armor after spending an hour gathering resources. Yet the real point is the game allows you to have fun, yes I had been mad when I runt charged me with javelins but the real fun had been exploring and using your resources at hand intensifying the game play making not only yourself more interested yet bringing excitement and achievement to the table. Imagine having a full scale war, now imagine having a full scale war with no items. In my opinion having no items wouldn't be smart yet in Reign of Kings that is exactly what you are doing, you are starting some kind of revolution whether it be creating a civilization etc. Another negative I have seen may not occur on most servers yet the two I have explored had an overuse of blocks either floating or broken into due to them being raided (they had been set up in bad positions so honestly I cannot complain against the attacker). Back to the experience of the game, most games I have interacted with give you pointers or leave you stranded and from having some bit of time in DayZ I knew survival would be something to riot about. Yet in Reign of Kings there is a vast amount of ways to stay alive, through berries through water, through killing a bunny stuck in a corner scratching oneself until little Ulti finds the poor thing and stabs it to death splattering blood throughout the small stronghold I discovered I mean... never mind that the game puts you in a barbaric situations unlike most games brought to the table and I have to admire the beautiful scenery plus extreme combat systems. Despite the feud of CodeHatch creating Starforge I feel this game in itself is already a new height in the gaming business and with a bit of support maybe we will see updates and recover from the repetitive hopes of other games (wink wink) Don't even get me started on how joyful I will be once I get a few friends to join me in Reign of Kings, through making strongholds and mobbing people will just intensify the day at hand, yet that is for another post.
