One of the best games i've ever played.
It's a short game, you can complete in about 5/6 hours, where you fight sets of enemies (called "Process") as you progress through the story.
You fight the enemies with your abilities, that the game calls Functions. The interesting thing about it is that even though you have a set of abilities, the same ability can be used in different ways: as an active ability, as an upgrade to another ability or as a passive ability. The game tells you what each ability do in each of those 3 roles. This leads to an endless number of possible ways you can combine your abilities. Not only that but it does it in a very good way, since there's not exactly an obvious choice of "loadout" and multiple alternatives are viable and effective to fight against the enemies. It really leaves space for you to use the abilities the way you fell more comfortable with. In the beginning it might be hard to figure out which abilities to use and how you will use them, the amount of choices you have is a little bit overwhelming, but as you play you will learn the weaknesses and strengths of each one until it's really no longer a problem. The game helps you with that, you are given only a few abilities to use at the start and you unlock new ones little by little.
The combat itself is very innovative. You can use your abilities just pressing its button, just like in an mmo or Diablo. But more often than not, you will be using the Turn() mode. In this mode the game is paused and you can plan your movements and the attacks you will do, then execute the plan. The game has no difficulty selection, but you can customize how hard the game can be by using the Limiters, some of them buff your enemies while others nerf the player in general. By choosing Limiters, the combat will be harder but you will receive more experience and level up faster as a result.
This makes up the core mechanics of the game, which i greatly enjoyed.
But an excellent mechanic is not only what this game has to offer.
The visuals and the art style is incredible, i would dare to say it is the most beautiful isometric game i've ever saw. Really really good. The soundtrack is also very good, not only it is good on a musical standpoint as it also fits the game perfectly and contributes greatly for a better immersion.
I would highly recommend this game to anyone, if you are still not sure, wait for a sale, otherwise buy it full price. And you may also want to grab the soundtrack. You will want it after playing the game.

actual game itself -- a very good pc port, surprisingly, aside from the mouse controls (easily corrected by autohotkey, in my case), runs at medium graphical settings (which looks better than consoles lel) on my not so great computer at a surprisingly stable, silky smooth 40-60 fps. seriously, it so nice to see that after how horribly ds1 was optimized, oh my god.

Indeed, the game (which is, in my opinion, a spiritual successor to Ragnarok Online) has an interesting, if somewhat simple, fairy-tale-like story and similarly beautiful art direction, injected with an energising, yet somehow appropriate soundtrack. Sadly, those are just about the game's only good aspects.
gameplay restrictions, regular FPS and server-side lag issues, a growing Bot and Gold Selling problem - these are only some of the negative points in an otherwise
Korean grindfesty MMORPG.
From a development standpoint, gameplay is solid but superficial and sometimes repetitive. There are more than enough classes (and customization thereof) to play around with, but generally they all fill a similar trinity-like role, with the exception of some world-mechanic requirements (Templar for guild creation, Pardoner for purchasable buffs, that sort of thing). The large variation of skills are bright and colourful, but they scale rather poorly into the later stages of this release of the game.
From a publisher's point of view (oh boy), IMC leaves much to be desired. Firstly, some of their restrictions plainly don't make sense. I feel like a lot of them are methods or workarounds to handle the already large amounts of Bots and/or Gold Sellers found on servers. This defeats the purpose, though - you are removing the aforementioned in order to improve player experience, by limiting player experience? Restricted dungeon runs, minimum/maximum market sale values, timed withdrawals on your items, severely hampered alternate character slots and storage systems...
As an example, without the game's "Freemium" 30 day installment, you are limited to 2 (
) dungeon runs per day. In total. Not per dungeon, no - in total! That's ridiculous. Paying what seems to be around $20 for the Token (which can also be purchased with the in-game currency of silver) let's you run that dungeon once more per day. What's worse is that the drop rates of useful items are so very slim, much more so than any other MMORPG I've played before.
Leveling has been painless thus far (I currently have two level 100+ characters) and therefor I am thankful, because the grind is real, ladies and gentlemen. I just haven't hit that part of the game yet, but if the leveling guides/Reddit is to be believed, I better strap myself in for what I can only describe as a boring rotation of skills for hours on end...
The Reddit community is decent, the in-game community is non-existent. With a very small cap on maximum guild members (25-35), getting into one isn't the easiest of tasks - creation of guilds harder still.
I recommend trying this gorgeous game when it goes Free-to-Play, without spending a cent of your valuable money until you hit at least level 115. Not a moment before should you give IMC a dollar's worth of time - not until they start listening to the community - who have already made more than a few viable suggestions, which, while they may not cure the botting problem, will certainly curb the influx to an extent where the game can be considered playable.
RATED SCORE: [ 5/10 ]
Once I have a few dozen hours' worth of end-game content, I will re-evaluate my current position. The ball is in IMC's court, after all...

Early Access games can be hit or miss sometimes, and this one is definitely a hit.
tl;dr Absolutely the best $20 I have spent on an Early Access game. The devs update regularly and are very transparent about the behind-the-scenes stuff, and I am very excited to see where it goes from here.
This game is all about logistics and automation; getting resources from place to place, and feeding them into machines to build large quantities of stuff, and even research cool new technologies.
While there is a very rudimentary story (crash landed on a planet, have to build and launch a rocket with a satellite to call for help), the game is very much a sandbox game with a win condition, which I love. The one problem I run into with sandbox games is once I get to all of the high-tier stuff, I'm left asking "...Now what?" But Factorio provides a fun, but very challenging, way to end it.
You can also mess around with the generation settings via a GUI that is super easy to figure out. Want hostile alien nests to spawn everywhere at ridiculously high rates? Want large patches of resources so you can build a ton? Just mess around with the drop-down boxes a bit, and voila! A game customized however you want it.
The tutorials are fun and teach you the basics; the controls take a little getting used to (or at least, it took me a bit to get used to them), but it isn't hard to get the hang of how the game works.
I've found that multiplayer lags a little bit, which makes it hard to drive cars or tanks, but it's entirely possible that that has more to do with the network I'm using than the game itself.
I haven't even messed around in the map editor, but the idea of setting up a challenging (or otherwise entertaining) scenario is always cool.

I haven't yet spent too long in this game, but I know for certain I will spend much more time here. The game's tiered crafting system is very reminicent of Chris Sawyer's Locomotion, a long time personal favorite, while also feeling very unique and fresh as a concept. Wonderfully frustrating and challenging when you are trying to fit as much as you can into a small space, this is a great mental workout that seems to beg for even more time spent with it.

I really enjoyed Call of Juarez: Gunslinger.  The voice acting is great and the shooting mechanics are spot on.  It's incredibly satisfying to get a string of headshots with the revolver.  There is a skill system progression that lets you increase the amount of time you can focus for headshots, lets you dual wield revolvers, and unlock special versions of each gun.  The music is great and nails the old-west setting.  The story is pretty simple, but well told in flashbacks.  You can also find "secrets" in each level that tell the real historical story of each character you meet in the game, so it's pretty cool to learn a little bit about the old-west history as you play.  The graphics are reminiscient of Borderlands 2 in that they are cel-shaded; I thought the graphics were really pretty and the lighting was impressive.
I completed the game in about 7 hours.  By the end the shooting was a little repetitive, but I definitely felt motivated to finish the game and see the story's conclusion.  Definitely recommended for the price!

This is definitely one for those who like atmopsheric games.
Pros:
-The game creates a believable atmosphere on an old, partly decomissioned, deep space station. The retro 70s sci-fi theme of the original film is captured extremely well in game; clunky noises and animations play as Ripley interacts with the old monochrome green-screened gadgets that litter the station.
-The game's sound design is phenomenal and you can hear the alien as it loudly thuds around the station and crawls though the vents above you.
-There are often a few different ways to sneak past the alien and other hazards, such as making use of crafted gadgets like smoke and EMP bombs, as well power boxes which allow you to reroute power from less important systems in order to cause distractions or open doors. Frightened and confused human NPCs, many of which are hostile, can be used as unfortunate bait for the alien if you create noise in their direction to attract it.
-The game's story is relatively simple, yet engaging. Discoving old tape recordings and abandoned computer terminals will allow you to piece together the station's background and its decent into chaos with the arrival of the creature.
-Manual save stations are the only way to save. I have seen some people complain about this and it can sometimes be a little frustrating, but in my opinion it helps create more tension, as dying actually has a consequence.
-The game is pretty terrifying at first particularly for the alien's first couple of entrances, although as the game goes on and you become more familiar with the alien, it becomes less scary.
-I actually found Ripley's character to be quite refreshing in comparison to many other video game protagonists. She is determined but also obviously very scared and makes her character more relatable.
Cons:
-There were a couple of times where I was incredibly well hidden and the alien still killed me, which is annoying since it is a one hit kill. It can occasionally feel like there is a little bit of luck involved.
-The game probably lasts about a couple of hours too long. The game reaches what seems to be a pretty natural climax, but then just keeps on going. This is not necessarily a problem, but the pacing here just felt a little off.
I overall really loved this game. The game was able to create a very immersive atmosphere that should be very enjoyable to those who like sci-fi and in particular the first Alien film, which Alien: Isolation is very faithful to.

[No Spoilers] Papers, Please is a pretty cool game, but it's too simple for the price tag. I would only recommend you get this on sale. There is a lot of replay value in the game, as there are 20 endings and a bit of random generation throughout, but there is no achievement for unlocking all 20 endings or a log to keep track of it if you are a perfectionist like I am.
The overall gameplay would be completely different for every person however. Every mistake or choice can lead to a different outcome and experience for each player. That's why I like this game, and although the mechanics are simple, it's still very fun. But I just feel that there could have been much more impactful elements added into the game. There were a lot of opportunities to add immersion to the character in the game, like giving more detailed backstory on the government, making the daily events directly affect you and your family (not just your work), and actually having a benefit to moving to higher class apartments, etc.. I know this game was like a runner up for Game of the Year with Gone, Home, which I have heard has little mechanics and just story, so I was a bit dissapointed that this game wasn't overwhelming me with story elements along with it's gameplay.
You WILL have fun playing this game, I still do recommend it. I will definitely purchase the sequel if it's released. But comparing this to a game like Binding of Isaac, which is $5, this game is not worth the $10 price tag at all. The fact that Gone Home was $20 and these two games were mentioned a lot together makes me suspicious as hell. Not sure why they are so overpriced.
TL;DR STILL A GOOD GAME. Just wait for a sale.

Arthouse games get a bad rep, not because they try to make videogames into a serious form of art, but because most of them are pretentious as ♥♥♥♥. Because of this, there are only two games other than this one that I consider "art", Shadow of the Colossus and Limbo. But SotC and Limbo both have similar atmospheres and worlds, something that Papers Please doesn't bother trying to set up to the same extent.
Papers Please works instead as the videogame equivalent to Albert Camus's "The Stranger", in that you have to choose what is morally right and logically right. There's no real answer to any of the major border holdups you encounter throughout the game. By supporting a totalitarian regime you help secure your family's safety, but at the price of the immigrants and revolutionaries crossing the border. By helping the underground resistance movements, you put yourself and your entire family at risk, without the closure of knowing you became a martyr for a bigger cause.
So there's the holdup. Do you go with what is ethically right, appealing to your emotions to do what's best in the grand scheme of things? Or do what is logically right, sacrificing your own humanity for protection and security?
Game's pretty fun too.
SImple, no frills... low-fi, deadpan... and yet oddly addicting.

What can be said about this game? I bought it when it was on sale purely on the recommendation of yahtzee, who does zero punctuation. "Paper, Please" is an interesting concept, and it's done fairly well. Everything that needs to work does, and it's kept at whatever pace you set. This is not a game to blaze through, you should go into it expecting a lot of reading, and a lot of failure.
If you hae patience, and want to try something pretty refreshing, I recommend it. If you want a fast paced mindless game this is not for you. Like I said before you need to be very aware and cautious, because there isn't much room for error. If you are not dilligent than small mistakes can cost you, which can mean your family dying. There are several decissions to be made based on your morals in game, and risk vs. reward played a big role in my playthrough, With all that in mind, if none of that scares you, check this game out, It's made by one guy, support indie developers.

So, the most asked question first - Is this Bastion 2? Absolutely not!
Transistor has a few things in common with Bastion - Great voiceover, compelling world and story that reveals itself through the narrative, the solitude of the main character, interesting art style and unique enemies and the combat is similar (yet at the same time completely different).
Transistor is beautiful (if you like this animation style), the music of the game is simply fantastic and the story flows well towards the inevitable conclution. The fighting is innovative and clever and makes you want to try out all the combinations.
The game is not without flaws though - it is highly linear and constantly pushes you through the quite short story arc. Exploration is not really present so if you want to rush through the game you can do so quite fast.
Is the game worth buying? Yes! Especially for the price point of this game I highly recommend it!

Unfortunately, the game is so focused that you're not offered the opportunity to really explore or experience this world. I can't help but feel Cloudbank has more mysteries to experience and villains to combat, and that Transistor was only the beginning of something larger than this single game. Read full review here
You liked Bastion? You will love Transistor. Graphism, OST, gameplay, everything is just perfect.

Do you want to play a game with very interesting combat mechanics and a huge amount of customization options? Never fight battles with the same skills and passive combos twice!
Do you like your games to be intelligently written with an intriguing plot and accompanied by a wonderful soundtrack? Do you want an organic way of learning about the setting and the plot without massive plot info dumps?
Do you want to play a game with a beautiful and bold visual design?
If so, Transistor is the game for you. Grab it during a Steam Sales if you have not done so already!

Demon's Souls is the fifth installment of the Armored Core series that is made by From, probably the BEST WRPG creator's out there. In Demon's Souls, there is plenty of PvP action, however, they have sadly broken some of the weapons and items going for a PvE style even though the game is purely for multiplayer. My review of Steam Reviews is zero stars, it didn't let me write as much as I wanted so here is the dummies version.
My review of Tree of Savior is that it is absolutely worth trying.
The art and world style are very nice but would be offputting to anyone who cannot handle more whimsicle and ridiculous world and enemy designs.
Class designs are very reserved in comparison and Tree of Savior mostly lacks the mile high shoulderpads and chainmail bikinis of other MMO universes.
I would be lying if I said there were no Pay to Win aspects
Tokens are essentially a one month premium membership with numerous powerful benefits that can be traded once.
If prices were made to match the Korean version of the game, they may cost the equivelant of $17.
There are also much cheaper Enchant Scrolls that add random stats to cosmetic headgear.
The issue is that the potential to get a good result is all up to chance, and the chances aren't good.
Now I must be blunt, he game runs terribly.
The visual effects in Tree of Savior should be able to run on a phone but will put a modern four core processor with a mid level dedicated graphics card in a bad place.
Getting sixty frames per second in a party is a feat worthy of applause.
Control methods are varied and mostly but not quite equal.
Keyboard and Gamepad controls are essentially on a level playing field but Mouse controls are blatantly better for archers and arguably better for all other classes.
Mouse controls are however incredibly glitchy when attempting to interact with objects in the world, most instances of these glitches have not been fixed since the Alpha tests.
Gameplay involves fetch quests and grinding.
You will do a lot of fetch quests and grinding.
However, some of us are OK with that so we played.
Classes feel varied and interesting
Combat is action based and movement is paramount however basic grinding activities don't offer much challenge.
Class and Build diversity is effectively enormous, but builds deemed practical or valuable in serious situations may yet prove to be very limited. The MMO community is notorious for promoting cookie cutter solutions after all.
Developer to Player interaction is interesting.
It seems obvious to me that IMC are fumbling in the dark with every decision they make regarding the international version but I believe the absolutely want the best for the game.
In this past month they have established a Southeastern Asia, South American, and European server according to demand.
Before that they held a poll to decide exactly what it would cost and how long the Founders program would run.
I worry that they listen too intentively to the vocal minority and make changes too quickly, but they are making those changes for the community making them.
I would certainly recommend installing and trying Tree of Savior for a few days on the 10th of May when it becomes free to everyone.

NMRIH is a game that can sometimes fall victim to the general grouping of 'another zombie game'. This is a game where you group up and survive either waves of zombies or complete an objective, but there is a part of this game that brings it out of the 'L4D clone', which is the real threat of losing any amount of HP. A singlen scratch can cause you to become infected, which can cause you to either search for pills, have the party kill you, or surprise the squad when you turn (which is ill advised). NMRIH has made a name for itself, and with a second game on the way, this comunity of modders and players will only continue to grow. I would say that this is a must play for any group of friends, and I would recomend anyone to pick it up (for free) and give it a chance. I give NMRIH a 9/10 for being a generally innovative game and creating many fun filled hours.

This game has the potential to be very entertaining and as the anti-hacking tools got installed I hoped the real game would begin to shine but instead I found the game became stagnated. You will invest a huge amount of time in building a small base whilst trying to avoid being killed by other players, along with trying to make alliances to get more people on your team and the ever present thirst and hunger battles. Almost invevitably, as soon as you have any kind of half completed base you will become a target for ganking. I made several attempts on official and community servers to get to a point where I had a base to hide in and build up my armory, each time this process was stalled (usually 5-6 hours of pretty dull resource gathering gameplay later) you barely had the front door on when fully armored broadsword wielding players in groups of 3-5 would come and kill my team of 2-3, destroy our crest and then take all our resources. If you have several friends who are willing to sink several hours of gameplay into repetative resource gathering to begin building a base then you might be  able to enjoy this game (no guarantee), if not you will spend much of your time respawning and mourning your lost resources. Now that I've beaten Alien: Isolation, I can finally talk about it. Basically, I can understand why PC Gamer gave it such a great review, because this game is what every fan of the franchise wanted. It carries so much of the same exact atmosphere and raw intensity from the first film that completely taken aback. I haven't played a game this good based on a film or film franchise since GoldenEye. And the fact that this was developed by Creative Assembly, best known for the Total War games, just makes it that more surprising at how good it was. I don't think they've ever developed a first person game.
About the game itself, you play as Amanda Ripley as she is abourd the Torrens, a private courier ship hired by Weyland-Yutani to pick up the recently found Nostromo flight recorder from the ship Sevastapool. When you wake up, you meet your crew, Samuels the android, Taylor the legal person, Connor the communications officer, and Verlaine, the captain and owner of the Torrens. After attempting to make contact with Sevastapool, you get a static response and decide to try and board anyway. Samuels, Taylor, and yourself put on EVA suits and use a line to cross from the Torrens to Sevastapool. This is where things start to go awry and you start to realize that Sevastapool is having serious issues. The line is cut, you're seperated and the real gameplay starts here, once you're aboard Sevastapool.
Similar to BioShock, you can learn about the history of the ship and the inner workings of it by listening to audio messages left on computers and tapes. As you make your way through the ship before finding your first friendly, you find out that the ship has recently been decommissioned and sold and people started looting and rioting after an accident. Without getting too much into the plot, you eventually learn that the accident was the alien, a xenomorph got on board and started causing havoc, creating an every man for himself situation. You get your first real taste of the alien after some gruesome cut scenes and this is where the stealth mechanics of the game kick into high gear.
The stealth mechanics in this game are great in that you'll really want to hide. Because the xenomorph is terrifying. Just absolutely terrifying. I was scared. I mean genuinely scared. The xenomorph is such a forbidding enemy and the way it creeps around as it searches for you whenever you make the slightest noise had me on edge so many times. There are other enemies in the game as well, specifically humans that don't like strangers, and faulty androids.
As the game progresses, you learn more about the problems and end up doing this and that (it's a lot of plot, this game is really story heavy).
I really loved this game. The atmosphere was intense, the music was great, the sound design was unreal, the animation was pretty good (I thought some of the walking animation for the xenomorphs was kind of clunky), and the level designs were fantastic to the point that some were eerily made to look like tech from the first film. Just fantastic work put into this game.

I really enjoy this game overall, and would recommend it to anyone.

So the problems I have with this game are the same I have with most of the genre. And to illustrate and best explain it, let me tell you about my first day.
I spent all day gathering wood and building my house and trying to get moderately situated for a peaceful existance in some woods away from all the fighting. An hour in, I'm killed in all my nakedness by a dude in full iron and a big steel axe. Why? I didn't hear him say hello. Did I have any chance to not die? Not really. One hit killed me with his axe. So I recover, play for a few more hours, and then with my house all secure with a door and everything, log off. About 13 hours later, after a little sleep and some work, I log back in. My door was busted down, I was killed in my sleep, and all my stuff was stolen. Could this have been prevented? Not really. Unless I wanted to play for another 10 hours last night to get stone walls all around my house and a metal door, and even then it's only a matter of time for people to break it down.
My problem is, being new is a huge disadvantage, and there's no sort of protection. If you're new, you're fodder unless you can play long enough or make enough friends that you're safe. It's not challenging in a fun, fair way, it's punishing in an unavoidable, painful way. It's crushing when all that time you spent playing is just ripped away because screw you for starting to play the game. If you're looking for a game where you can, and have to, join a large group to survive, great, this game might be your thing. If you're looking for a game where you can play on your own to some degree, this really won't suit you well.

Now that I've beaten Alien: Isolation, I can finally talk about it. Basically, I can understand why PC Gamer gave it such a great review, because this game is what every fan of the franchise wanted. It carries so much of the same exact atmosphere and raw intensity from the first film that completely taken aback. I haven't played a game this good based on a film or film franchise since GoldenEye. And the fact that this was developed by Creative Assembly, best known for the Total War games, just makes it that more surprising at how good it was. I don't think they've ever developed a first person game.
About the game itself, you play as Amanda Ripley as she is abourd the Torrens, a private courier ship hired by Weyland-Yutani to pick up the recently found Nostromo flight recorder from the ship Sevastapool. When you wake up, you meet your crew, Samuels the android, Taylor the legal person, Connor the communications officer, and Verlaine, the captain and owner of the Torrens. After attempting to make contact with Sevastapool, you get a static response and decide to try and board anyway. Samuels, Taylor, and yourself put on EVA suits and use a line to cross from the Torrens to Sevastapool. This is where things start to go awry and you start to realize that Sevastapool is having serious issues. The line is cut, you're seperated and the real gameplay starts here, once you're aboard Sevastapool.
Similar to BioShock, you can learn about the history of the ship and the inner workings of it by listening to audio messages left on computers and tapes. As you make your way through the ship before finding your first friendly, you find out that the ship has recently been decommissioned and sold and people started looting and rioting after an accident. Without getting too much into the plot, you eventually learn that the accident was the alien, a xenomorph got on board and started causing havoc, creating an every man for himself situation. You get your first real taste of the alien after some gruesome cut scenes and this is where the stealth mechanics of the game kick into high gear.
The stealth mechanics in this game are great in that you'll really want to hide. Because the xenomorph is terrifying. Just absolutely terrifying. I was scared. I mean genuinely scared. The xenomorph is such a forbidding enemy and the way it creeps around as it searches for you whenever you make the slightest noise had me on edge so many times. There are other enemies in the game as well, specifically humans that don't like strangers, and faulty androids.
As the game progresses, you learn more about the problems and end up doing this and that (it's a lot of plot, this game is really story heavy).
I really loved this game. The atmosphere was intense, the music was great, the sound design was unreal, the animation was pretty good (I thought some of the walking animation for the xenomorphs was kind of clunky), and the level designs were fantastic to the point that some were eerily made to look like tech from the first film. Just fantastic work put into this game.
9.7/10

Nutshell: 8/10 - If you have a computer capable of running this game, it's an awesome game and honestly a better screwing-around game than GTA 5 even.
Pros:
- One of the largest open worlds in a game - Seriously, this map is around 400 square miles in size, that's absolutely massive, guaranteed it will take you forever to explore the entirety of the map.
- Beautiful graphics - It isn't Battlefield 1 graphics, but it's enough to be a beautiful sight and really is a nice touch, it's definitely a good game for looking around
- Lots of stuff to do - Once you finish the story, you got plenty of fun ways to goof off in this game, be it attaching rockets to the butt of a cow, or using your grapple hook to glue bad guys together, or maybe try and ride a car off a plane and land it (resulting in a 2.4km long jump)
- Partially-destructible environments - Some stuff (not all, but quite a few structures) are destructible, meaning it gives you some rewarding explosions that are always unique.
- Loads of vehicles and aircraft to try piloting/driving - It's lots of fun trying and experimenting which vehicles are good getaway vehicles in this game.
Cons:
- A little glitchy/some bugs - The bug in particular I wish to mention as it's possible to fix, is that this game vsyncs at 30fps, so even if you got an awesome computer (like me), when vsync is enabled you'll never get more than 30fps. The simple fix to this bug is to disable vsync in the video settings and never touch the vsync button again. Other noticeable bugs (that I can't fix) I ran into were road textures not loading when I drive in an F1 car for too long at 200+kph (or other fast vehicles in the game, they loaded again when I slowed down). Another big issue was large chunks of the map not loading when I sail over to other islands, forcing me to restart the game before going between islands. Every other glitch I ran into is negligible.
- Won't run on all computers - This game requires a beefy computer, my computer scored only 40fps on medium settings, by the way my computer can run Battlefield 1 on max settings in 4K resolution at a steady 60fps so... Yeah, talk about a demanding game, if you use a laptop or low-end computer, forget it.
- No first person - More an opinion on something they should add when they get these bugs fixed than a con, but seriously, if they added first-person this would be one killer game.

While many enjoy the Total War games because of their unique blend of real-time strategy combat and standard-setting visuals or their incredibly high production values, what makes them truly fantastic is that one can easily invest hundreds of hours into just one entry of the series and likely never grow tired of its addicting mix of fighting and management. I have spend many hours on Rome II and yet I still keep coming back for more. Whether it be to try a new faction, a different early game strategy, change up my research priorities, focus more on naval prowess rather than raw manpower, empower trade over combat as a continent-spanning empire or mix up my tactics in the battles themselves.
The Total War games are packed with content, like the unique scenario battles that represent a key conflict in history, narrative campaigns and tutorial campaigns that each require a few hours or more of your time at the very least while presenting a mostly distinct experience, many entirely separate factions each with their own various traits at both a regional and cultural level, and the grand campaigns.
Each of these is a massive undertaking and has almost endless permutations for the path to total victory, dependent on any number of the factors mentioned above. You can even use the skirmish battle system to try out all different tactics and unit combinations from any of the numerous factions present in the game against a battle AI that you can freely adapt to your tastes in terms of difficulty. Lastly, Rome II offers an expansive suite of multiplayer options to back up its gargantuan single-player offerings, allowing you to play challenging battles against your friends or compete for global domination through the usual turn-based campaign system, even if the multiplayer isn't as functional as I would like! I have put many hours in every single Total War game and each new entry is both fresh enough and packed with quality to easily justify that kind of investment time and again - truly, this is a franchise that knows how to eat up the small hours of the day. If ever you needed a game to kill time in while trying out multiple different approaches to victory, allowing you to succeed either through making friends or destroying enemies in equal measure, then Rome II has been tailor made to match your desires.

Soda Dungeon is a hero management / idle game with a lot of strategic options and, thankfully, a minimum amount of clicking required to proceed.
Your job is to hire adventurers to fight their way through the dungeon for you. You do this by upgrading your tavern, purchasing new sodas, and paying heroes to fight for you. You control which hero classes to hire, what equipment to use, and how you distribute points amongst your relics. You're given fairly fine control over how to set up your party, and then you let them loose in the dungeon and see how far they go.
Graphics are in a low-res style and are fairly decent - at least they don't use the same sprite pack that every person and their grandma use in their 8-bit games these days. The music is good as well, but perhaps a bit repetitive, not that this can really be avoided when you need to power power through 4000+ levels like my party does. Gameplay is intuitive and you're given very clear tutorials on how everything works, but you're also given a lot of freedom to outfit your party and recruit your heroes to meet a specific strategy. Amount of content is good, there are five zones spread across one hundred levels which continuously repeat. There are a fair amount of different enemy types and bosses which have different movesets to keep you on your toes. There are also 10 bosses which appear every time you enter a new dimension (ascend).
Overall, Soda Dungeon is great for those who like the idle game genre. Unlike other idle games, however, the achievements in Soda Dungeon are actually designed to be achievable without sinking several thousand hours of real playtime. For that reason, Soda Dungeon is much more accessible than games like Clicker Heroes which require constant ascensions just to progress.
Note: This game does contain microtransactions to unlock content early, but it should be noted that you absolutely don't have to make any purchases to finish the game. Everything is unlockable at some point, and by the time you reach the end-game, you certainly won't need to spend any money to get the last few unlocks.

Gunslinger is arcade-style FPS shooter set in the wild west. There are no fancy cutscenes (they are mostly just drawings) but there is still a quite large story. There is a lot of dialog and voice acting is well done.
The game kinda borrows features from other games, and I'm not saying this negativily because it still works. From Bulletstorm we got the "skill shot" system. Making skillful shots and defeating many enemies quickly gives you combo and that translates into more exp (or points in arcade mode). You use the exp for three different skill trees, and that is quite a lot like Borderlands. The game's art style is a little similar to Borderlands, with those dark outlines giving it slightly "drawn" look and it looks quite nice actually!
The action is fun and that is pretty much all that matters, because there is not much else to see here. You sometimes get to play the dueling mini game several times during the story, but that is kinda most boring part of the game. There is also an arcade mode what might still keep you playing after clearing the story, and I'm very glad this mode was added! I'm a big fan of game modes like The Mercenaries from Resident Evil, so this offers you similar high score hunting as it did.
Negatives include small amount of weapons. Three revolvers, two shotguns and two rifle variants (that are almost the same, just normal and sawn off version). I would have liked a little more variety in this part, after all the game is all almost nothing else than shooting action with those same weapons.
The game was made as a budget release from the beginning, it was about 15 dollars during the release date and you should be able to get it a lot cheaper during steam sales. If you want some arcadey shooting and like the wild west atmosphere, this is a good purchase!

Nutshell: 8/10 - If you have a computer capable of running this game, it's an awesome game and honestly a better screwing-around game than GTA 5 even.
Pros:
- One of the largest open worlds in a game - Seriously, this map is around 400 square miles in size, that's absolutely massive, guaranteed it will take you forever to explore the entirety of the map.
- Beautiful graphics - It isn't Battlefield 1 graphics, but it's enough to be a beautiful sight and really is a nice touch, it's definitely a good game for looking around
- Lots of stuff to do - Once you finish the story, you got plenty of fun ways to goof off in this game, be it attaching rockets to the butt of a cow, or using your grapple hook to glue bad guys together, or maybe try and ride a car off a plane and land it (resulting in a 2.4km long jump)
- Partially-destructible environments - Some stuff (not all, but quite a few structures) are destructible, meaning it gives you some rewarding explosions that are always unique.
- Loads of vehicles and aircraft to try piloting/driving - It's lots of fun trying and experimenting which vehicles are good getaway vehicles in this game.
Cons:
- A little glitchy/some bugs - The bug in particular I wish to mention as it's possible to fix, is that this game vsyncs at 30fps, so even if you got an awesome computer (like me), when vsync is enabled you'll never get more than 30fps. The simple fix to this bug is to disable vsync in the video settings and never touch the vsync button again. Other noticeable bugs (that I can't fix) I ran into were road textures not loading when I drive in an F1 car for too long at 200+kph (or other fast vehicles in the game, they loaded again when I slowed down). Another big issue was large chunks of the map not loading when I sail over to other islands, forcing me to restart the game before going between islands. Every other glitch I ran into is negligible.
- Won't run on all computers - This game requires a beefy computer, my computer scored only 40fps on medium settings, by the way my computer can run Battlefield 1 on max settings in 4K resolution at a steady 60fps so... Yeah, talk about a demanding game, if you use a laptop or low-end computer, forget it.
- No first person - More an opinion on something they should add when they get these bugs fixed than a con, but seriously, if they added first-person this would be one killer game.

I absolutely loved playing this game.  The game is perhaps not as good as Just Cause 2, but free roaming the island and destroying everything you find is a ton of fun.  Unfortunately, Square Enix chose to take the low road and released this so-called AAA game in an unplayable condition.  Players are reporting varying amounts of success getting the game running, but one thing is certain: the game will crash on you eventually, and when that starts, you're very unlikely to be able to continue.  My game survived a glorious 12 hours of chaos and destruction.  Now it crashes within 10 minutes of startup.  That's not enough time to finish a mission, so I am completely unable to progress the game.
The game has several game-crashing bugs that make the game unplayable. Most notably is memory leakage that causes the game to slowly fill up all your available RAM before it crashes your entire computer. There are several other issues that cause framerate stuttering, flickering graphics, and save file corruption. Square Enix is aware of these issues, and has been for a long time, but is doing nothing to fix them. In fact, the most recent patch they released actually caused more issues.  I submitted a support ticket and all they did was accuse my system of being at fault.  My system is way above the minimum specs for this game, so I know it is not my hardware.  (That, and the fact that thousands of other players are reporting the same problem should be a clear giveaway that it isn't a hardware issue!)

This game deserves a decent review, rather than complaints about the"free to play" terminology.
First, the "free to play" terminology.  Yes, you can download it and hunt one type of deer.  If you see other animals, no; you won't be able to kill them.  Ignore them for now.  Track and hunt the deer to see if you will like the game.
If you *REALLY* want to enjoy the game and think you would like a hunting simulator, spend a few bucks on it.  Get one of the memberships for a few months, which gets you all the weapons you need to start enjoying the game.  Like most free to play games, there are other items for you to buy; guns, cosmetic gear, etc.  but none of that is really needed.
The graphics and environment are amazing.  You track animals by their sounds, their droppings, and (of course) their tracks.  As you get close, you crouch down; move slowly; and scope in on the target.  Its pretty wild to watch the animals move around; often in groups.  When you fire, the game has a pretty realistic wound simulator.  If you hit them in the head, they drop immediately.  Heart or lungs?  They take a few steps and drop.  Graze them?  They run away leaving a trail of blood behind them (the tracking continues).
Speaking of the wound simulator, my last went like this:  I scoped an elk in the distance; took aim, and fired.  I went up to take a trophy photo of my kill, only to see she wasn't dead.  She was very much alive, just wounded.  I had to finish her off (head shot), and then I got credit for the kill.  Then the stats screen showed me where I hit her: first, the spine, which is why she couldn't run away.  Then, of course, the brain.
So that's the game.   Pretty hardcore.  It isn't for everyone, but I've had a blast with it.
Good luck.

This is not a good game. This is not even a good
of a game. Someone thought that because both clicker games and JRPGs have a lot of grinding, they would be good together, but they didn't put in the effort of both so we end up with a pixelated mess that isn't good at either.
You build a team of adventurers, equip them with items, and go into a dungeon, wailing on enemies until your party dies. Then you repeat the process. You manually build your team and equip them with items every single time (there's an auto-equip option but it prioritizes level over quality of equipment). There's an auto-battle option, but the AI is shoddy, having dark mages use melee attacks and clerics refusing to heal status effects, and it will never use the third and fourth abilities of a character (which include group healing).
There's no real offline progression (there's a way to earn gold, but it works inconsistantly and doesn't actually help in any way). There's too much grind and repitition to keep your attention, but if you look away there's missable dialogue and plot, gimmick bosses which the AI can't work around, and if you go AFK you'll have no idea what killed you or how to prevent it from happening on your next run.
There aren't any hotkeys. Leveling up relics and such is done manually. There are stats, but you can only see some of them: HP, MP, Attack, your gold, your Essence. You have to dig around to find your Caps (premium currency). Other stats are hinted at with modifiers, but you can't see the numbers themselves. The game has trouble displaying numbers in the five digits, anyway.
Stay away. It isn't worth the effort.

I reccomend this game only if you were a fan of the original Rome: Total War and would like to play a more graphically-improved sequel. However, be warned that the base game is bland for the most part. I would highly reccomend using mods, because you will find that this game has a few missing features from its predecessor, Rome I.
Also, before you buy, you might want to consider a few problems on this game:
1) Compared to Rome I, Rome II's campaign is watered down and has some of the dumbest ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you could ever imagine. Remember when I said the game feels bland without mods? Here's why:
-There is a limit to how many armies a faction can have on this game. If you want to increase that limit, you have to conquer a specific number of regions. This really is the dumbest BS you can add to a game like this. The devs lack brain cells and fail to realise that this limit they added is useless and just makes the game dumbed down. You should be able to build as many armies as you want in regards to the state of your economy, just like the older titles. Adding an army limit to all the factions on this game means that you might be fighting less battles than you did in Rome I. The developers were too stupid to realize that if we wanted to fight less battles, we could have just used the auto resolve button just like the previous titles. There's no strategy involved with a limit like this...
-On the campaign map, you can't split armies into smaller groups like you could in the previous titles. This is another incredibly stupid feature that makes the campaign overly simplified. For example, let's say an enemy army containing only 3 units shows up in your territory, and the nearest army you have to counter them contains 20 units. Since this army is so puny and would be destroyed in no time with, say, three of your higher quality units, you'd think it would make more sense to just send in 3 units to counter that army. Well, in this game, you can't do that anymore. You have to move your ENTIRE ARMY if you want to get rid of them, which is a complete waste of time because you could be using the rest of your units for more useful purposes. You simply can't split armies to cover more territory, scout unknown parts of the campaign map, or provide support to another army. You're just commanding completely immobile armies that have had their strategic potential neutered by this ♥♥♥♥ing stupid mechanic.
-Just like armies on the campaign are unable to split up, they are also unable to merge with other armies. This means that if an enemy army containing 20 units, for example, is in your territory, and you have 2 armies that each contain 10 units, you can't merge them into one strong army of 20 units to take on the enemy army. Instead, you'll have to go through the BS of having your two separate armies stuck on two different sections of the battle map, wasting precious time trying to get them where you need them. Once again, the strategic value of this game has been further watered down...
-It is mandatory for every single army to have a general. Now, I don't mind having generals in all of my armies, but it'd be nice if you could have some of them under the command of captains and turn them into generals after a few battles like in Rome I and Medieval II.
-You no longer have the choice to build walls in your settlements. Only a certain number of cities will have walls by default. Once again, the strategic value of this game has been watered down a by the diminished brain cells of the developers.
2) The soundtrack of the base game is your bland, run of the mill dramatic tryhard collection of the works of a composer desperately trying to become the new John Williams. The developers should have kept the composer from Rome I. Thankfully, there is a mod for this game that allows you to use the soundtrack from Rome I itself.
3) Voice acting on this game is♥♥♥♥♥♥ In Rome I, different factions from different parts of the campaign map actually had their own accents, giving them a unique identity. Instead, there are only two accents on this game. Basically, 'civilized' factions like the Romans and Athenians have the same old, plain and boring British accent. 'Barbarian' factions like the Britons and Suebi just sound like a bunch idiots.
4) The Greek City States are a mandatory DLC, so you can forget playing as Sparta or Athens without paying extra money. CA, like your average AAA developer these days, just loves to manipulate its fanbase by locking content on a game and calling it "extra" content.
5) In battles, projectiles fired from archers and slingers don't look deadly and fast at all. The devs came up with the stupid idea of putting tracers on every single projectile thrown. None of them look dangerous at all, and when you zoom in on the unit of soldiers being attacked by arrows or rocks, the sound effects don't sound like any of these projectiles were able to hit anything with a great amount of force.
The only good things about this game are this:
1) Better graphics.
2) There are mods.
Use as many mods as you can if you're still reading this review.

It requires teamwork of a group of survivors, from 2 to 8 to work together and cooperate.
Your objective is survival and escape. Pretty simple, except it's not always so...
Surviving in this is never easy, and that's what makes it fun.
It poses a challenge, and sometimes can be the cause of random roleplay moments which I have encountered, although not very often, seen as it has randomly generating objectives, to "answering the phone" to "Go through the graveyard" and so on, throwing runners and children zombies your way.
Survivors are forced to work together at times, which makes teamwork the most valuable. Teamwork among new players is what makes them survive longer than experienced players rushing ahead, thinking they know what they're up against.
The game servers you can join have gamemodes of their own aswell, such as Dodgeball. You kill zombies to throw them back to the other side, and it just pings back and forth. More and more zombies are added in, and there will be a point either one of the two teams gets overwhelmed and die, or just die depending what the enemy team does.
The game also has a multi-cutural community. Lots of people from Russia, Australia, the UK, USA, Mexico, Poland, everywhere you can think of, has a lot of players of different types, and can be interesting to meet (Yeah, seems something obvious to point out, but it's always nice to see this sort of stuff, doesn't it? It shows a great side of that community, that it isn't just one side. That it has multiple angles you can look from.)
You can also select your own survivor that suits you best, and there's various characters (mostly male characters) with different voices you can add to them to suit your character that best fits you. I swear one of them is voices by Harry Callahagn...
It's also a great first person shooter in general. Nothing more satisfying than causing a zombie's head to split into two.

I've been gaming since the mid-80s and longing for something as brilliantly executed as the Half-Life series or System Shock 2. This is it. I'm a huge fan of the original movie, and have played most of the game adaptations. With the exception of a little-known ZX Spectrum game 'Alien' from the early 80s (which was suprisingly successful at producing the heart-in-your throat tension of the original movie) every game has been a disappointingly formulaic multiple monster-shooter. This could not be further away from being a shooter if it involved nothing more than inserting daisies into the gun barrels of a row of soldiers at an anti-war protest.
Not only is this not a shooter, it is effectively an anti-shooter. Your weapons are so ineffective against anything other than a human that you will actively avoid using them because the noise will soon attract the arch acid-slobberer himself. This is an out and out stealth game - a 'hider' not a 'shooter' - but the ever present threat of immediate and fatal violence is all the more oppressive because of it. In this way, the gameplay, although apparently derivate of stealth games feels original and utterly compelling. It is no exaggeration to say that the main reason I put this game down to write this review was to gain some relief from the persistent state of anxiety I experience while playing it.
Visually it is beautifully realised and entirely faithful to the original movie. Aurally, it is every bit as impressive, not least because after a few hours of play you will be relying on your ears as much as the motion sensor to figure out where the alien is and whether you are in immediate danger. That too is remarkable. Many games have tried, most have ultimately failed.
The scripted story mode is unusually long (I'm half-way at 14 hours played on 'Hard') and the DLC, although expensive at full price, adds enough interest to keep you coming back for more. The only thing lacking is some kind of multiplayer/co-op mode, but really this is all about sitting alone in the dark and knowing that no one is going to come to your rescue.
Finally, I must take my hat off to whoever designed the graphics engine. My laptop, which just fails to meet the minimum recommended spec, runs this smoothly with all the effects set to 'ultra' at 1366x resoluton.
Take care: In space, no one can hear you scream...
...On Earth you will wake everyone in the house.

Convinced a friend to buy JC3 recently due to it being on sale and saw that the reviews on this game were mixed and decided a proper positive review was needed. Cons First.
This is an open world game which means, yes, there will be some bugs from time to time when making a particular movement as you're reacting with a particular piece of the environment. And no, this game should not be purchased if you're strictly looking to play the multiplayer mod. When an open world game has little outposts, and takes little time to beat, it is criticized. When the game has many outposts over a large map it is also criticized as being repetitive. So, take that as you will. Story line isn't crazy juicy.
Now let’s get to the good stuff. The main objective of this game is f*ck $h*t up. I can remember a time in every single video game I've ever played were I wish I could have blown something up to the next level or do something more epic than the game allowed. JC3 is a platform for this to happen, it's actually a platform that was made for this to happen. Like most open world games, a leader has taken control of the land presented in the map and the people within it. This place happens to be the main characters, Rico Rodriguez's, home. The campaign missions don't have a 10/10 story line but the missions themselves put you in some awesome situations where you can do some pretty badass stuff. Regarding the map, all outposts must be taken by force as a one-man army destroying everything in your path. You will find a fair number of outposts to liberate across this HUGE map. Seriously this map is massive on a land, sea and sky level, larger than even the newer Wildlands map. You have access to numerous weapons including a wide variety of guns, a never ending retractable grappling hook, a never-ending parachute, a sick wing suit, C4 packs, tanks, helicopters, and planes that can be used as assets in your♥♥♥♥♥kicking and liberating. When an outpost has been liberated, side missions in that area then become available to you. In my opinion, side missions are the down fall of most open world video games. JC3 provides you with great side missions including; wing suit courses, land races, sea races, air races, aim courses, destroy everything in sight ASAP missions, drive explosive cars into objects and bail right before hand missions. Each side mission attempted is rated on a scale of 0 to 5 Gears depending on your success rate. Each type of side missions allows you to upgrade a particular skill as you earn gears in those missions over time. Some learnable skills include; easier and fun wing suit movements, turbo charged vehicles, jumping ability is boats and cars, etc. I found myself wanting to complete more and more and take advantage of everything the game threw at me. I also enjoyed messing around on the map and blowing things up for no reason or using your grappling hook to make some dude drag from a car or something silly. DLC on this game was AWESOME as well, so definitely recommend the XL version. The DLC expands the same great map by adding one new island, a sky fortress (Think SHIELD in the Avenger’s movies), and a washed-up sea bound operation. While also introducing some great new vehicles and weapons.
Overall this game is just a blast, 100% recommended. Praying JC4 rumors.

Summary: This is a tough one.  In the end there's enough Alien film in Alien: Isolation that I give it "thumbs up".  But, warning!  This is a tedious game of door-gating and errand-running.
===========
Things Alien: Isolation does well.
-Sounds and music.  Great atmosphere.  This game builds suspense nicely.
-Beautiful visuals and art.  Humans, synthetics, the alien, technology, and space visuals provide an almost immersible Alien experience.
-Clever hacking minigame mechanics that can add to suspense.
-Carrying out building and tool operation in real time adds another nice layer of suspense.
-Stealth mechanics.  It's not Metal Gear level, but not bad.
-Story.
-There were times where my heart was pounding.
===========
Things Alien: Isolation does poorly.
-Logic.  Sadly, this game follows the tropes of other suspense games.  Flashlights will die from battery use in minutes, if that.  Manual saving is done via phone stations, adding a layer of cheesy gameness.  Most items are static immovables with occasional useless bump-only clutter, making the environment feel superficial.  Want to move that object that's on wheels?  Nope.  Expect NPCs to drop pocket lint, even if they literally have useful equipment or guns.  Androids malfunction in the films, but in Isolation no amount of damage (even headshots) will cause that.
-AI is painfully simplistic.  NPCs seem to be limited to the following:  Bad standing idle.  Random/scripted patrol.  Hunt player while X condition.
-Few choices.  Obviously, this is the opposite of an open world game.  It's as railroad as they come.
-Saves.  Why didn't they just roll with being able to have multiple saves while saving anywhere?  If they wanted to add another suspense layer, add another suspense layer.  If they wanted to make death more tragic, find a different way to make death more tragic.  We don't need classic horror game homages.  Most of the time, they just don't make sense.
-Traversing the environment.  Controls are average, at best.  There's no jumping and limited climbing.

Alien: Isolation is a very pleasant return to the atmosphere of the original Alien film before the horror got sucked out of it. instead of appealing to other aesthetics it remains true to the retro sci fi visuals and audio of the film. but perhaps more than that it provides game play that is actually survival horror that is very reminiscent of frictional's SOMA and the original Resident Evil games.

OK then.. Alien Isolation is a nasty and brilliantly horrific game! Especially if you know the franchise, the history and the universe.
So first of all I would recommend you watched the films because that way you can appreciate the small details and hints like the audio side of the game which is sooo good.. If you don’t know the story, Alien is just like any other monster horror game, but if you’ve seen the films you know why it’s so scary to encounter this nightmarish creature.
Yes, the first couple of hours it is abit slow, but that is what Alien is about. Building up tension and building up a story and person gallery which is really well copied from the iconic first film from 1979. It is not about spray and pray and a bug hunt like so many other games.. it is about being and feeling isolated against a ruthless and intelligent enemy with no ways to run on a claustrophobic space station that ebbs of chaos, panic and fear. You are no soldier.. you have no weapons that can defeat this creature. Your only hope is your ability to outsmart the hunter before it oursmarts
.
The second thing I would recommend: Play it on nightmare or at least one of the two hardest difficulties and get that actual “Alien feeling”. The Alien AI changes when you change the difficulty – it becomes more intelligent in everything from search patterns to analyzing the ways you’re countering it. On medium and easy it is hardly ever around (from what I’ve read in reviews and seen on Youtube) , but on the harder difficulties it is always around somewhere.. lurking in vents, dark corner, making noises etc. On medium you can walk and sprint without the Alien reacting but on the two hardest settings it will react to any sounds like shots/breathing/sprinting and normal walking.
If you are an Alien fan this is a must buy, must play and must "scream your lungs out" game..
9.5/10 from a Alien fanatic that is normally hard to satisfy.

Alien isolation is a survival/action/horror game in which you craft instruments and gadgets while sneaking around enemy threats with a constant, overpowered, looming sense of dread from a xenomorph threat. The game revolves around your ability to tackle every situation differently, as you have many settings and problems to adapt to. I have never felt a bigger sense of tension in any other horror game than this.
Not to mention this is one of the best optimized/looking titles on the market right now. CA has captured Ridley Scotts original terrifying retro-futurism low fidelity science fiction aesthetic with perfect execution, and rightfully so. The audio is not something to be taken for granted either as i would reccomend wearing a headset at all times to capture the atmosphere that the devs have worked so hard to portray.
The storyline on the otherhand kind of gets wonky after about mission 10, when the game starts faking you out with (what you think to be) perfect endings to this fiasco aboard Sevastopol Station. I feel like the last 8 missions could have been great side content, or pushed back before mission 10 with M10 being the ending. None the less, it still is a phenominal title and deserves to be played by any aliens fan, or survival/action/horror game fans.
It feels like Creative Assembly singlehandedly ressurected the Alien games with this survival horror title, and to that i say thank you :)

Before you take my play time into account, just know that I have thousands of hours played on console. I just recently got a PC and plan on playing it all over again, even though it means restarting. That should show how much I do appreciate this game, and enjoy playing it.
Anyways, I just wanted to point a few things out to the people who are hesitant on purchasing this game, at the moment.
- The questing in this game is fantastic. They keep you entertained, especially if you enjoy the story that they have to offer you with each quest. Not to mention the beautifully done voice-acting that accompanies it.
- There is a plethora of possible gear combinations, making your character feel that much more unique. Especially with the gear you can obtain through the Undaunted chests and Veteran dungeons. The gear looks fantastic, as well.
- The crafting is important, so if this is something you enjoy in these types of games, you are in luck. You can make some of the best gear sets in the game through blacksmithing, woodworking, and clothing. Also, it can make you a lot of money in the long run. It is worth the time and effort.
-  The dungeons are fun. They provide you with a challenge, as well as a great story to follow along with for each and every one. Truly great content to be played.
- The PVP is massive and very entertaining. Hundreds of people in a large scale battle, with the three different factions, where you breach castles and defend yours. You can also duel people at any point in the game, in a 1v1 brawl. (Should also note that Battlegrounds PVP is coming very soon)
- The combat system is enjoyable. Not the best that I have played with, but it is not Tab-Targeting, so it's actually fun.
- The fashion items in the game are fantastic. If you are one for Roleplaying, then you will be happy with ESO, as there are a lot of cosmetics that are very good looking.
- You won't have to worry about getting "ahead" of friend in this game, as the level scaling is amazing. You can be Champion level 400 and play with a level 30 friend. Quests, dungeons, you name it. Your levels won't seperate you, or stop you from having fun.
- You'll never feel obligated to buy Crowns (The paid currency in this game), as it has little affect on your in-game character. Aside from the beautiful mounts, pets, and outfits, of course. So, no worries about a "pay-to-win" situation.
Even though I talk up this game quite a bit, there is negative side, as well.
- As of now, there are only 4 classes to choose from. Which is a downgrade, compared to a lot of other MMO's out there. (5th coming soon)
- The skills are lacking. There aren't many things to choose from. It gives the illusion of choice, but a lot of the skills are just straight up bad to use. Meaning, your character and someone else's character are not going to be too different, aside from the outfits.
Overall, I give this game an 8/10. I love it, but it does need a little more variety. It is getting better and better, as time passes.
Also, if you do play the game and enjoy it, without a doubt, get ESO Plus. It is well worth the fee. The craft-bag changes the game entirely.

I absolutely love this game!!
But I am getting ahead of myself. First of all: I did not play the first two games in the Just Cause series, so I can't compare this one to them (so I wont).
But what I can say is this:
Just Cause is a game to have fun with. The entire game is designed to be as ridiculous, funny and explosive as possible.
The Wingsuit is the best, most awesome way in a videogame to traverse (okay, second. right behind the Arkham series) and though a little rough to steer at the start, you get used to it really fast and from that point on, it is pure fun. "But Cap, flying in videogames often gets pretty boring pretty soon".
Well, due to the fact that you have to constantely grapple to the ground with your grappling hook, we will come back to that later, to maintain speed, you are always in danger of hitting the floor with Ricos beautiful face; Or as Nerdcubed put it: "They made geting around the place amazing."
The parachute, for me, is more like a link between wingsuiting and walking, you will now what I mean when you play the game, but it can also be a way to unload your bullets on the enemy without them being able to do anything against it. Well, unless they have a ac♥♥♥♥ (anti-aircraft-gun), that is... or a sniper... or a chopper with missiles..... or a tank... thinking about it, maybe you should not do this in a big base (of which there are many in Just Cause 3).
But the grappling hook is the mechanic that makes Just Cause 3 to a Just Cause game. You can use the device in several ways: you can use it as a way to move around the place, which you will do quite often, since Rico can not sprint; you can use it to get enough speed to use your wingsuit or parachute; you can use it to maintain speed during parachuting/wingsuiting, you can use it to latch on to enemies (or friends ;D ) and kick them Batman-style; you can connect to objects and pull them together; you can tear down Watchtowers or pull Containers onto soldiers...the possibilities are nearly endless.
Of course, you dont have to be creative while killing. You can also use the "normal" ingame-weapons. There are many types of weapons. From small semi-automated pistols over to grenade launchers with 5 grenades to literally a nuke-missile. And if you like DLC there is also a laser-guided missile-launcher and a few more toys.
Speaking of DLC: I bought the day-1-edition, so many of the additional contents i have were cheaper or free for me,so I will now try to review them while having the money in mind.
There are 3 big DLCs and a few small ones. the latter contain said missile-launcher, a semi-automated assault-rifle with explosive ammo, a buggy and boat with miniguns, a sportscar with missiles and a few other things.
The 3 bigger DLCs are the Skyfortress DLC, the Land Mech Assault DLC and the Bavarium Sea Heist DLC.
The first one adds a Helicarrier, a drone that rico can use, a new machine gun and a Jetpack for the Wingsuit which basically turns Rico into Iron Man (including missiles and guns).
The second one gives you a new set of Islands in the North-west of the map and 3 Mechs (one of them is controlled remotely) with Force-powers (yes, the Jedi-sort of Force).
The last one adds a Seabase and a rocketboat with 10 heatseaking missiles.
I will say that I think the first one is a must have, although it sometimes is nice to disable the Jetpack and go back to the roots of wingsuiting, the second also is very cool and the third one is...meh...not worth the money, altough still really fun, since it adds the ability to boost with the wingsuit underwater.
Another important aspect: the Story. Sadly, the story of the game is nothing special and very short, and the missions are pretty repetitive. But I almost think thats on purpose. Avalanche did not focus on the story, because the game itself is more than enough fun. But if you are a story-guy, or gal, maybe you should reconsider your choice, or just lower your expectations for this one.
To come to a conclusion; Just Cause 3 is an awesome, fun game with severyl unique and exiting features and mechanics. It is a game that does not just give you the fun you want (except for when a NPCs car crashes into the oncoming traffic next to a petrol station and...well, just find out for yourself), you have to get the fun you want, meaning YOU have to do funny stuff and explore/experiment, but if you do that...boy, are you in for a treat. Though the story isn't nearly the selling point, the sandboy aspect, which is quadrupled after completing the story, more than makes up for that.
So, if you like explosions, chaos, fun, exploration, eastereggs, more explosions, carnage, more eastereggs, action, even more explosions, Michael Bay, gigantic Maps (I honestly believe it is the biggest Map of a videogame, yes bigger than Witcher 3 or Skyrim) and firepower, this most definetly is not a game for you, but THE game for you.

Summary: This is a tough one.  In the end there's enough Alien film in Alien: Isolation that I give it "thumbs up".  But, warning!  This is a tedious game of door-gating and errand-running.
===========
Things Alien: Isolation does well.
-Sounds and music.  Great atmosphere.  This game builds suspense nicely.
-Beautiful visuals and art.  Humans, synthetics, the alien, technology, and space visuals provide an almost immersible Alien experience.
-Clever hacking minigame mechanics that can add to suspense.
-Carrying out building and tool operation in real time adds another nice layer of suspense.
-Stealth mechanics.  It's not Metal Gear level, but not bad.
-Story.
-There were times where my heart was pounding.
===========
Things Alien: Isolation does poorly.
-Logic.  Sadly, this game follows the tropes of other suspense games.  Flashlights will die from battery use in minutes, if that.  Manual saving is done via phone stations, adding a layer of cheesy gameness.  Most items are static immovables with occasional useless bump-only clutter, making the environment feel superficial.  Want to move that object that's on wheels?  Nope.  Expect NPCs to drop pocket lint, even if they literally have useful equipment or guns.  Androids malfunction in the films, but in Isolation no amount of damage (even headshots) will cause that.
-AI is painfully simplistic.  NPCs seem to be limited to the following:  Bad standing idle.  Random/scripted patrol.  Hunt player while X condition.
-Few choices.  Obviously, this is the opposite of an open world game.  It's as railroad as they come.
-Saves.  Why didn't they just roll with being able to have multiple saves while saving anywhere?  If they wanted to add another suspense layer, add another suspense layer.  If they wanted to make death more tragic, find a different way to make death more tragic.  We don't need classic horror game homages.  Most of the time, they just don't make sense.
-Traversing the environment.  Controls are average, at best.  There's no jumping and limited climbing.
-Errands and door-gating.  This feature is BY FAR, the WORST part of this game.  You will be doing these the entire playthrough.  It feels like they got worse as the game went on.  Thanks to Alien: Isolation, I hate generators and using keycards.
===========
In the end: 7/10, if that.  The tedious nature of this game really takes away from how great it could have been.

Alien: Isolation is a very pleasant return to the atmosphere of the original Alien film before the horror got sucked out of it. instead of appealing to other aesthetics it remains true to the retro sci fi visuals and audio of the film. but perhaps more than that it provides game play that is actually survival horror that is very reminiscent of frictional's SOMA and the original Resident Evil games.
Together these things create an experience as classic as the original Alien movie complete with the masterpiece by H.R. Geiger.
It is terrifying, tense, and it makes you think and requires you to be bold in parts. this improves upon the simple mechanics of Frictional's horror survival where you are required to cower until you learn the mechanics of the monster. it also provides more complex gameplay than the original resident evil games. it has a mechanic where you build various objects that distract or damage certain enemies from materials in order to avoid them and stay alive. you will have to do more than any other survival horror game in a beautiful game. not to mention it has a story driven feel that keeps you going that narates events that mirror the movie.
with many references to the movie and following the events of the movie and all of the masterfully done parts of the game i cannot simply not reccomend it.
however i reccomend you see the original movie first.

OK then.. Alien Isolation is a nasty and brilliantly horrific game! Especially if you know the franchise, the history and the universe.
So first of all I would recommend you watched the films because that way you can appreciate the small details and hints like the audio side of the game which is sooo good.. If you don’t know the story, Alien is just like any other monster horror game, but if you’ve seen the films you know why it’s so scary to encounter this nightmarish creature.
Yes, the first couple of hours it is abit slow, but that is what Alien is about. Building up tension and building up a story and person gallery which is really well copied from the iconic first film from 1979. It is not about spray and pray and a bug hunt like so many other games.. it is about being and feeling isolated against a ruthless and intelligent enemy with no ways to run on a claustrophobic space station that ebbs of chaos, panic and fear. You are no soldier.. you have no weapons that can defeat this creature. Your only hope is your ability to outsmart the hunter before it oursmarts
.
The second thing I would recommend: Play it on nightmare or at least one of the two hardest difficulties and get that actual “Alien feeling”. The Alien AI changes when you change the difficulty – it becomes more intelligent in everything from search patterns to analyzing the ways you’re countering it. On medium and easy it is hardly ever around (from what I’ve read in reviews and seen on Youtube) , but on the harder difficulties it is always around somewhere.. lurking in vents, dark corner, making noises etc. On medium you can walk and sprint without the Alien reacting but on the two hardest settings it will react to any sounds like shots/breathing/sprinting and normal walking.
If you are an Alien fan this is a must buy, must play and must "scream your lungs out" game..
9.5/10 from a Alien fanatic that is normally hard to satisfy.
