ESO is a game I wasn't touching for a long time because I'm more into casual gameplay and peaceful features like housing, decoration and things that need some actual skill without being stressful or grindy. And I dislike very much if I'm led around by the nose because I've outleveled an area I like. I prefer the settle in a MMO, not run on rails ...
When ESO introduced One Tamriel, were content was changed to level-scale, and announced the housing system I had gotten really tired of the sexist armor in BDO and jumped in. That was almost 5 month ago now. I still enjoy ESO a lot, especially the thieving is something I do excessively. Usually I am very poor in MMO's and level only slowly, and despite sometimes being years in one (looking at you EQ2) I have never ever reached level cap. Not even remotely. In ESO I just spend my time doing whatever I like doing and spending time in my favorite areas stealing everything not nailed down - and leveling just happens on the side. I'm currently Level 50 Templer with Champion level 30, another novum for me as I usually really dislike melee. But somehow this Templer with all its ability-customizations really works for me. And I am a valuable addition even if I come late to a world boss fight a 300-champion already started and we are alone and not grouped. That makes it very smooth and enjoyable.
Plus the option to be in five guilds at once, while it seemed strange at first turns out to be great to not be stuck in a guild whose membership might be waning. People move between guilds more easily and you have a much higher likelihood to meet likeminded people even if you prefer small guilds. I'm very impressed by the large number of RP guilds and RP events as well, I've happened to stumble upon quite a few people doing (safe for work style) RP in the world.
The quest writing is in my opinion some of the most eloquent, rich and high quality in any (!) game I have played. And yeah, I'm doing this since a few decades now... The vocabulary and lore is so amazing, that I'm learning even new words that are not commonly part of conversation or news or such. And yes, I skip over quest text in many games because it is so cheap and redundant. But in ESO I go for even the additional voluntary dialogue parts, because the lore makes sense, is deep and very well written.
So if you are like me and like to take your game time as time off from the real world without pressure, raid group training needs or mandatory online time, wide array of gameplay options and a very beautiful world that has hidden things to discover in pretty much every corner (treasure chests! thieve troves! quests! lore books! trader!) - go for it!
There are a few things that I think the tutorial is severely lacking in explaining though so let me state a few things I feel are important for enjoying ESO:
Motifs are for equipment and very commonly available for little money at guild traders. Equipment (except jewelery) can be crafted at workbenches and you can add special traits to it. But traits need to be researched first at the respective workbench - which needs an equipment piece with it that is lost in the process. Researching takes time (counted as real world time).
Recipes you only need for cooking. Those you can buy for 10-30 gold at guild traders everywhere or get them from daily provisioner task rewards. Or if you have the thieves DLC you can steal them quite frequently from containers as they are common. And the basic ones for provision quests are sold at NPC (cook and brewer).
For furniture/decoration you need designs/blueprint, those are indeed not so common and still quite valuable.
Inventory: if you want to craft, then really get the subscription, because it gets you an unlimited bag for crafting ingredients. Looting does not really provide anything crafting-related ... You get crafting ingredients pretty much exclusively from crates, barrels and in the world from logs and such. Looting mobs yields (except hides and some alchemy items) almost exclusively equipment/money/consumables. But you can research equipment for learning the traits and you can break equipment down for resources (both at the work benches). Or you steal equipment from shops and break it down or use it.
You can buy backpack upgrades for ingame money at pack merchants and bank upgrades at banks, quite cheap initially. And stable masters allow you to increase your inventory every 24 hours real world time for 250 gold as well. I've 200 slot inventory by now, 100 or so bank and the crafting bag from the subscription - it is a complex game. With that inventory size even extensive thieving sprees are nice now. :D

Skill/Leveling System: 6/10 - The skill system is as varied as the class system but I feel like it doesn't offer as much customization as I'd like it to be. The scaling is aweful. The Leveling is fresh as it depends on the skills in your skill slots. Grinding is aweful.
Class System: 10/10 - So many Races with their own perks and abilities combined with Item dependent skills make it very enjoyable.
Quest System: 4/10 - Quests scatter and unorganized.
Optimization/Performance/Graphics: 8/10 - Surpirsed at how well it is performing considering the degree of details the game graphics has to offer.
Lore: 10/10 - Elder scrolls have one of the best lores in the market.
Battle/PVP system: 6/10 - It's not a true hack and slash. Once you are identified as a target by mobs especially ranged ones, you can only dodge certain kinds of attacks ( or it's just me, since I'm playing under 400ping all the time)
Crafting: 10/10 - simple yet very very very immersive.
All in all, the game is slow at the begining, but once you get a knack of things, you'll get drawn in easily.

TheHunter. Best hunting game available as far i know. And everyone complaining about the buying thing, it's kinda true, but look at the game, are you expecting this to be 100% free? Developing this game is not easy or free. Sure they would have 100% free game if they only could, but they can't. So to the review now.
Free To Play Hunting Experience
In TheHunter, when you get into your first game, you will have .243 rifle and a navigator called Huntermate at your disposal. With huntermate, you can track every animal in the game (Some of them are in different reserves), and you can only hunt one animal as a free to play, mule deer.
The mule deer is located at Logger's point Hunting Reserve. You can shoot rabbits (Both european and cottontail ones) as a f2p, but you are not allowed to shoot those with your .243. Other animals you don't have license to. You can buy licenses with ingame currency called gm$, but i more likely recommend buying wayfarer bundle or 3kk membership. Why? You may ask. I will get to that next.
Member Hunting Experience
As a member, you can hunt every single animal in every reserve. Of course you need a right gun for right animals. My personal recommendation for a weapon is 8x57 Ansutch rifle. You can shoot everything from a deer to a bear with it.
Bundles, oh bundles what is so different with them? In bundles, you get some extra stuff with your membership! You only should buy one bundle, (I recommend pathfinder) becouse after that you don't get any extra with your bundle.
The Money Thing That Everyone is Crying About
With ingame currency called em$, you can buy anything between bear bait and clothing. Basically every item in the game is purchaseable with em$. Most of the items in the game can only be bought with em$. Few animals require you to buy things with em$. You can't hunt mallard without buying the callers and decoys.
Results: 9/10, super good game if you have a lot of spare time and money. Remember what i said earlier, devs need money. Don't let the mostly negative disturb you. Have fun!

Denuvo DRM ruins the experience. There is essentially no TRUE offline mode in any game that utilizes Denuvo DRM due to the fact that if you either change hardware, update Steam, or update Windows you are forced to go online and re-authenticate the game's license through Denuvo's servers. The authentication ticket could also simply expire without any updates made to hardware and/or software as well, so either way, you're screwed if you're not connected to the internet about 99% of the time.

Forget DOOM and forget FALLOUT 3, 4, NEW VEGAS...
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL is the best first person shooter AND the best post-apocalyptic game. WAIT, WHAT?
Yes, you heard right.
Firstly, SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL is the most atmospheric game I've playerd since the original SYSTEM SHOCK. It features a real post-apocalyptic world that is the most immersive I've ever seen, unlike Bethesda's FALLOUT series it takes itself fairly serious which works to its benefit. While the Bethesda games are quite good in there own way, they are nowhere near as captivating. Their over-the-top humor feels completely out of place, here it is not present.
The enemies are tough, and unlike DOOM or other fps you are not a bullet sponge. Most enemies can one or two shot you. A simple bandit with a sawed-off shotgun blasting you from close distance will kill you with one shot even with a full health bar.
I felt reminded of the good old days when I was a teen crawling through space station Citadel, carefully peeking around the corner in fear of bumping into a very powerful enemy. Unseen dangers, be it invisible mutants or traps (anormalies) also await the careless stalkers.
There is an interesting backstory and lore to satisfy RPG/adventure fans as well. Tons of loot. You need to eat/sleep/rest. There is no fast travel here, it's an open world to explore on foot and you WALK - no poppin' up the map and "teleport" to section A.
Creatures have a decent AI and behave realatively natural. Some mutants are extremly creepy and powerful, requiring a bit of tactics to take out, goin' Rambo on most foes is simply not an option here. Several factions can be joined, and this requires some planning as well, unlike FALLOUT you cannot be everybody's darling.
NOTE: SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL has its flaws. In its vanilla state it is an unpolished gem. I STRONGLY RECOMMEND one of two mods (from
: either Autumn Aurora (2.x) or Complete (2009), which eliminate several flaws and bugs of the game and upgrade the graphics.
Secondly this game is quite difficult and I recommend playing this on one of the more difficult settings for the full effect of adrenaline and fear.
SHADOW OF CHERNOBYL also spawned two inferior sequels, CLEAR SKIES (avoid) and CALL OF PRIPYAT (good, not great, but only with mods).
I am very hard to satisfy when it comes to games, so far this is only the 3rd game that has been able to draw me in for several hours and keep me interested, the other two being SYSTEM SHOCK 1 and DARKEST DUNGEON.

I love this game. The visuals are gorgeous - every frame would make a great wallpaper. The music is hypnotic - the soundtrack will probably be the best this year. And the combat is a great mix of strategy and customization, with plenty of variety in how you equip the different abilities. It may only be about 5 hours for a single play through, but it was well worth it the cost.

Simply put, Transistor is beautiful. The soundtrack composed by Darren Korb buzzes with electric, jazzy energy. The painted artstyle, courtesy of Jen Zee, drenches protagonist Red's world of Cloudbank in a gorgeous Art Nouveau - meets - cyberpunk atmosphere. If you played Supergiant Games's spiritual predecessor Bastion, you'll recognize Rucks's silky-smooth narration as the voice within Red's attendant sword, the titular Transistor. If nothing else, the game has an irreversible sense of style - from the way the Transistor, the titular weapon, trails along the ground, to the novel option to hum in time with the background music. Mute though she may be, Red - and the player - leave their voices imprinted upon the Processed world.
Gameplay is innovative, and expands upon the isometric action style that Bastion perfected. The core of Transistor's mechanics are various Functions that represent an in-game concept - breaching, crashing, even calling for help. These translate into active abilities - a damaging linear attack, a single-target disable, and the ability to summon a robotic helper, respectively - as well as traits used to modify functions- the ability to extend range of functions, addition of a disable utility to functions, and modifying the trait to spawn weak allies when an enemy is killed - and passive abilities that can be used to modify yourself, which, for the sake of length, will not be mentioned. Combat is also made more strategic by the Turn() ability, which, when activated, allows the player to go into a pseudo-"planning mode," halting battle and allowing the player to input a certain number of Functions and movements. Upon deactivation of the Turn(), Red activates all of the moves near-instantaneously, but is vulnerable and has most Functions disabled until the Turn() meter passively regenerates. Players can choose to either maximize their Turn() potential, packing their moveset with tons of burst and evasion Functions, choose to play it real-time using sustain and distraction Functions, or a mixture of the two.
Story is intimately tied to gameplay, as leveling up, using Functions, and empowering the enemy Process with certain upgrades allow for greater fleshing out of the world - a storytelling device that encourages the player to experiment with different approaches to the game. It does, however, mean that the story suffers somewhat in terms of actual content - a speedrunning player will find the plot threads to be confusing and sparse. Once one unravels all the various story threads though, , a greater plot does begin to emerge from the tangled network of Cloudbank's world.

If any real criticism can exist for Transistor, it may be that it does not quite live up to Bastion, in terms of sheer narrative clarity. The characters, perhaps, never feel as fully realized as the Kid, Zia, or Zulf (though perhaps the incredible ending sequence will object.) But Transistor is its own subroutine, and to contradict a certain quote, when nothing changes, well - nothing changes.

If there is in the world the game, that obliged by its name to inspire holy shock, the "Dark Souls II" surely is it. In general, I'm not fan of hardcore games. Quotha!

As before, it is the best to play "Dark Souls II" with sword and shield(I think so) - the only way the game throws a real challenge to your reflexes. The combat system hasn't changed: weak punch, strong attack with a shield, roll and "first aid kit to eat." All. No complicated combo, no racks like in "Assassin's Creed" - you use only shield, sword, and, OF COURSE, your head.
The only thing, that annoys me personally in this game, - the interaction with other players. It is interesting idea with the invasion of red phantoms in your world, but, GUYS, SERIOUSLY, I don't like to be summoned to my friend's world. I get used just to connect to my friend and that's all. But only in "Dark Souls" I need to get some stuff, check my soul memory and after that my friend and I can be connected to each other. I cannot stand it.
Now let's think about why we love such games, which make us die about a hundred and fifty times at the same place? And the answer to this question is freaking simple. This game is the only one.
"From Software" proves, that the gameplay is the most important thing in game. And I fully agree with that opinion.

Broforce is a hysterical and fun pixel based shoot 'em up sidescroller. I have to emphasize just how funny this game is, it doesn't take itself seriously at all and it's one of the funniest games I've played in a long time, there's plenty of laugh out loud moments. Besides consisting of well-done sophomoric humor/parodies, there are also instances of satire found within the game. One example would be how your commander says "the people from this country, look, speak, and act differently to us. Let's move fast, bros!". I'm sure most of you have encountered similar or possibly the same exact saying elsewhere, but it fits perfectly well in this game.
In Broforce you frenetically wreak fierce havoc upon terrorists and two enemies that come out of left field much later in the game. This frantic gameplay style mixed with destructible environments leads to very exciting moments. Not only is the gameplay exciting due to the mayhem that you can possibly create, it could also be used as a viable strategy to get through tough situations.
Speaking of tough situations, there are plenty of moments that will test your skills. Many people dislike tough video games for many reasons, but Broforce offers tough but fair gameplay. Despite being fair, there are many levels in which you will have to trial and error your way through it, you will die a lot. The deaths aren't really a problem as long as you have more lives. After you die you'll essentially respawn as a different character in the exact spot where you died, which is especially helpful during boss fights.
The boss fights in Broforce are interesting not only because of the variety of bosses that are encountered, but also because they all vary in difficulty. Some are quite easy to get through and some are frustratingly hard, it all depends on your playstyle and which character you feel best fits the situation.
You mainly play as a multitude of characters that are throwback references to popular 80s/90s action movie stars with the occasional 2000s hero thrown in. I honestly don't know how many characters there are, but it's interesting just how many playstyles are offered. Some of these characters consist of Rambo, The Terminator, Dirty Harry, Neo/Mr. Anderson and Indiana Jones. The funny gimmick in regards to the names of these characters is that their names are altered to fit "bro". For example, Rambo is Rambro and Leon the professional is simply "The Brofessional".
Though many may view this game as infantile, playing through this game will show you just how well thought out it truly was, based on the overall gameplay. I've played through other games that include popular characters from movies/cartoons, but it's obvious that much thought didn't go into truly depicting how the character is in their source material. The characters in Broforce all have three attacks, a main attack, a special attack, and a melee attack. As previously stated, all of the attacks fit well with the character that's being used. For example, Dirty Harry uses a powerful revolver like he does in the movies, the terminator uses a large/recoil heavy minigun, and Indiana Jones uses a whip along with a piercing revolver.
Despite having a multitude of characters in this game, they're essentially chosen at random, it's a bit of a double-edged sword. At the start of the levels you don't know who you'll play as and as you save imprisoned "bros", the equivalent of getting an extra life, your character is switched and you begin to play as another. There are pros and cons when it comes to this, do you ignore the necessary extra life, or do you stick to the character that you're currently playing as because you favor their playstyle? That is one question you'll most likely ask yourself while playing through this game.
Overall, I greatly enjoyed Broforce due to its highly entertaining gameplay and humorous story. I give it a 4.5/5 and I recommend it if you're a fan of pixel based side-scrolling shoot 'em ups.

This is the most fun I've had with a game in a long while.  I generally stay away from third-person shooters, and somehow I missed that this was a third-person game when I bought it.  But after giving it a chance, I can see why the game was made this way -- it really does make for a better experience, and it works well the way it was constructed.
I have a pretty new machine, and I am not experiencing any problems playing the game as others have said, except for one thing: my keyboard mapping periodically gets over-written.  (You can solve this by just copying your keyboard map file, so it isn't a huge issue, but I digress.)
One very surprising thing about this game for me was how well almost everything in the world blows up.  The physics on destroying things and soldiers really is fun and allows you to use your imagination in your destruction.  At first I didn't like how some things give infinite missiles and bombs, but I think it turns out more fun this way.  I really like that you aren't penalized for destroying civilians, and in some cases it's hilarious ("Rico! You could have just asked for my car!")
Once you figure out how to use your cables for destruction and moving around... well, for me there was no turning back!  I'm now in the middle of my second go-around with this game, and still having loads of fun with it.
I definitely recommend: Get this game.

Call of Juarez Gunslinger is great, albeit short, FPS narrating the story of Silas Greaves, a cowboy bounty hunter seeking revenge after his brothers were murdered. The game takes place in Western-times and it is basically a shoot-them-all type of FPS, and even though I hate these kind of FPS, there's something about this one that I loved. Perhaps it is the fact that Silas narrates the story as you play and it is so well written it encourages you to play to find out more. I love how he changes parts of the story and you have to play them again from another perspective. There's also something in his character making him very lovable.
You don't get a lot of different guns, but they are more than enough to go thru the story. I particularly loved the rifle and the quickshooter pistol. There's also a sawed-off shotgun, a shotgun, and some other pistols. You can upgrade the guns and your reflexes/combos by gaining EXP, which adds some twist to the shooting portion of the game. You also get dynamite, making it lots of fun to blow bad fellas up. Even though the firing is quite good, there's something about the game that bothers me. It seems that you gotta get the scope spot on or you will miss the shot... if you miss the aim by 1 mm, it'll be a loss, even with the shotgun, which doesn't make sense. There's also something weird about the ironsight in which you have to aim lower than the sight to get headshots. Anyway, you get used to that quickly.
The only thing I really hated about the game is the duels. They are based on crippling the player by making your aim move randomly and you just have to click when the other one pulls out his gun, then aim and shoot, which is really weird and most of the times it seems based on luck rather than skill. This really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off. I hope the find another way to do this in the next game.
Another downside is that the game is really short. I passed it in 8 hours and I didn't rush it at all (I tried to get all nudges of truth in every chapter). Being used to 15+ hour-games, this one felt really, really short, but damn, did I get a good time playing it.
I hardly ever replay games unless something new to the story is brought in, but I am now replaying it in the western (I think) difficulty mode, which removes the hud and crosshair. There's also an arcade mode and a duel mode I haven't tried yet, but the first one looks fun (I think it's based on combos and scores).
I highly recommend this game to anyone that likes FPS with a good story and encouraging characters. You'll definitely have a good time.

Where do I begin with this game? After sinking over 800 hours into it, there is a lot I could say, but I will try to keep it short. Overall, the game is great, and there are many improvements from the original Rome Total War. Being able to have large 40 unit armies during the period of Ancient Rome is somwthing I have enjoyed for many many hours. The campaign map's size alone is also very impressive. However, some things bother me about this game. While there are bugs, just like every game, there are things that they left out/got rid of from other Total War games that were great features. 1. The ability to customize your army/general, like in Shogun 2. This feature was one of my favorites from the Total War series, as it made me feel like i was really in control of my army. 2. I can never understand the online multiplayer in Total War games. It should be possible to play campaigns online with way more than two people. Especially considering the size of the campaign map in Rome 2, there should be a possibilty of at least up to 8 player games. 3. PAYING FOR BETTER BLOOD AND GORE. I mean really? You have to charge for that? I paid for it, but it definitely should have been an update not paid DLC.
So, i would recommend this game, but only to those who enjoy Total War games. If you are looking for a good RTS game, you may want to look elsewhere, only because the mechanics of this game are not the greatest I've seen. If you are looking for a good Total War game to start with, I would suggest Medieval 2, or Shogun 2. This game is still too pricey for someone looking for a good game.

First off: About this version of Dark Souls II
There's going to be a Re-Worked version of this game being released on April as of this review.
The name of it shall be " Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin " and it will be a re-worked version of this game.
Before I get into details on that let's talk a bit about this version.
Was it as good as it was advertised to be?
No... The Graphics, the Matchmaking, and even the way the map was said to be actually worked to take away a lot from the game and made it feel very limiting, with-in your first day of playin (If you've played the first.) you can already feel like you were playing within a Park instead of the Branching Open World that it was said to be and especially the vast open world the previous tittle was.
Did it have the mechanics it said it would have?
Yes... (Albeit sometime it was wonky at best.)
The window for the dodging mechanic did feel a lot smaller, that being a good thing for me compaired to the first game.
Meaning you had to be smarter when were to dodge in this game, but of coarse that came with having to memorise when abilities and weapons actually deal their damage.
... and there in lies the problem...
For the most part I've found that there's more then a few weapons that have a delay to when the damage is applied compaired to the actual animation.
Then on the other hand there's more then a few that deal their damage before the animation even implise it.
Now I would of said this was a matchmaking connection problem but why would it always be on those certain weapons?
Now yes admittingly I didn't play much of this game... Even with Pre-Ordering it...
It just didn't feel worth it, it felt empty and devoid of the Dark Souls charm from before.
It mimiced it, yes, but it didn't get it down packed.
There was something about it that was not as fun as when I played the first one that had me coming back to it for so long.
I don't know about other players but to me something felt missing from what made this game really feel like Dark Souls.
Could have just been myself needing to adjust to the new looks of things...
... and speaking of the looks...
Did it look good on max settings?
Absolutly not, I think there was an article that I ended up reading that showed technics from the year 2000 that showed games actually looked better on those then they did on here.
But I'm not going to open that can of worms, to me the graphics where horrible and murky, no not murky as in a griddy look I mean murky as in the textures were not applied correctly and as well as the fact that they used a lot of low resolution textures in the game...
I have a NVIDIA GeForce GTX 660 Ti with an Intel Dual Core Proccessor... To me... That says that this game is not that demanding on resourses if my computer can keep up with the settings.
Yes I would studder at times here and there, but that was like what? Every twenty minutes at most.
So again while good for me that I could run it all at max, it just shows that the graphics in this game are not that high at all to begin with.
To be honest, to me... It felt like Dark Souls looked much better then Dark Souls II on almost all acounts aside from the character models (Though the textures of the models weren't that good.) and the background designs.
Now I did look up to see if it was just me, that if it was just that with my Rig there were settings that were locked away behind a script or something around the lines.
But from what I've looked up everyone's games looked the same as mine, even with some using the Titan Series Graphics cards.
The game still looked horrible and just a murky mess of stretched graphics.
Now this is all I have to say about this version, these were my problems I had, the way the story was told is still Dark Souls-esk where you need to be the one reading and looking for all the clues as to what happened with in the area.
Reading the descriptions and everything that was before you in an attempt to piece together the much larger picture of what happened.
Second off: About Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin ( Dark Souls II 2.0 )
Half a year after the release of Dark Souls II the Devs anounced that they're re-working on their release Dark Souls II.
That they were unhappy with what was done with it, how things were handled with by their publisher and of how DLC was being treated.
They admitted that all three DLCs that are currently out were supposed to release straight out the gate with the game, and yet their publisher said no and to cut it up into DLC to sell seperatly...
Now with the money that's left from Dark Souls II sales they're re-working and trying to undo the changes that their publishers forced them to make.
From improving the graphics back to what was planned originally to improving the mechanics of the game to be more responsive.
Even the maps, models, weapons, and NPCs will be re-worked from the ground up.
The Devs are promising an entirely new game to don the Dark Souls II name, something that they themselves are proud of.
Now I saw this happen before with EA's Dead Space series, where by the Third title the Devs had 0 control over the cretion of the game and we all know how that turned out...
So I'm glad to see the devs take up arms and try to undo the damage that their publishers caused them.
( Yes, publishers have more influence over a game's creation then most people may think... )
So what's being promised?
Improved Mechanics
Improved Textures
Improved Modeling
Added Content that was originally Cut completly from the first version.
Include the three DLCs into the game right on release.
Add a lot more weapons
Add alot more armors
More NPCs
Improved AI
Added More Creatures that were not given a chance to develop
As well as ontop of all this they promise to add an Expansion's worth of original new content.
So will this next version be worth the money?
I think that hands down it will definetly be worth the money.
Just wished we didn't have to pay 60 - 120 dollars to Beta test it before its release. :/

First things first, I have over 800 hours total on this game at time of writing with over 700 hours coming from outside of steam.
The negative review is going to be for a few reasons, despite loving this game and spending a lot of money on it over the past year and a half.
My biggest gripe is the view distance and the devs insistence that nothing can (will) be done about it, despite it being something that many many players are calling for and leaving the game upon realising it won't be improved.
This claims to be the most realistic hunting game and, while that may be true, it's only because there is no competition from other hunting games to take the crown.
The view distance for animals in the game is 220 meters, which means that they abruptly disappear when they walk or run past that limit. It's quite laughable when zooming in on a bear you've just shot, only to see him completely disappear on you.
The worse part of it though, you can be looking across a field that is maybe 300 meters across or a lot more, thinking that there's no animals there, yet there could be a whole herd of Elk standing there, just past that 220 meter borderline and you'll never know unless walking towards them when they will suddenly appear in front of you. The likely outcome of this is a spooked herd when you too suddenly appear to them.
Hunkered down in the bushes, looking across a field, knowing that everything past that 220m line is pointless to even look at, totally ruins the experience and realism of the game/simulation. Hunting in real life you would scan everything in the vicinity and most of the time plan your approach to animals from a long distance away, so forget about that. Using a high powered rifle from inside this 220m range is no fun, there's not going to be any significant bullet drop so there's little challenge in the shot placement, a massively missed opportunity. The air rifle and bows do however give you that back, with bullet drop and wind both being a challenging and welcome aspect of the game play due to the weapons lower range.
There are many hunting towers placed around the reserves but again the 220 limit makes this laughable with many towers looking out onto open fields stretching way beyond that limit. Just knowing this, is a game ruining experience, and the cause of me asking myself "why am I playing this crap?"
Yet I still play it because the core experience is so good. The devs say that extending that 220 meter range would have a massive impact on performance but this day and age I cannot see that being a concern for many of the games players. I run the game at maximum settings in 4k and only one of my three 290x being used and I still get a solid 60fps with v-sync on. All of my AMD control panel options have been maxed too, to try to push the most out of this game and there's never a single dip in fps. This game could easily be pushed up to at least 320m ranges which would make it acceptable and more realistic. I doubt anyone would want to take a shot at an animal past that range anyway.
Another thing players have been asking for is an updated engine. Whilst the scenery looks lovely it is lacking in depth on certain objects like the trees, and there are many trees in this game. A game based on DX11 would solve this issue and give us the fur on the animals which would bring the game up to modern standards. A lot of the game does look amazing though, sometimes you'll lose yourself in the scale of the forests and the swaying grass and trees are majestic and unequaled.  Yet again though it is let down by stupid stuff like floating rocks which brings you straight back down to reality again.
I spent countless hours getting screenshots of these rocks and taking the time to get them uploaded along with the gps coordinates and posting them on the bug reporting forum, only to keep experiencing the very same bugs after a year as the devs have not done anything about them. There's no profit in spending hours on bugs is there but to me that would be a priority, quality over quantity every time to keep your current customers happy.
The rest of it though is all good, there's little wrong with the game and if you like hunting you should give this a shot as the free to play aspect will at least give you the chance to see if you like the game. Be aware of these issues mentioned though and you can make a choice as to whether or not they are issues that would ruin your experience, before spending hundreds of pounds on the game.

Truth is, when it comes to FPS, I tend to be of the fussy end. I have a lot of experience on many different ones but Call of Juarez Gunslinger tops them all off by far. It does not reinvent the wheel, no, more like makes it even rounder than what it was. The mechanics in this game are simple and the shoting is as smooth as it can get.
There's a little RPG depth as well thanks to the leveling system and even though it is a modern shooter, with regenerating health and all that jazz, it's far from being a boring one with an ultra-serious tone and everything. The leveling gives you a chance to use your skill points on new skills that better your damage or enchanse your concentration meter - a tool to be used to recreate the speed and accuracy of a gunslinger. There's also the 'sense of death' ability, which lets you dodge an otherwise lethal bullet once the meter's full. Truth is, after more than five playthroughs, I still think it's awesome as hell! Also, as I have played Call of Juarez Bound in Blood, I can seriously say that the people at Techland have really thought about the duel system. While in Bound in Blood it was quite easy on the computer, Gunslinger throws a lot more challenge at you as you have to use your mouse to hold the aim, and A and D keys to move your hand. Also, you can pull before your opponent does, but seriously, that's just cheap, and does not guarantee your victory. Not only that but you can, given you have the chance and willing (and balls), shoot a bird before your opponent, or let him fire first and attempt to freaking EVADE the bullet. Now if that's not cool, I don't know what is. Also, I think you should know that you even get to try your luck and skill at a Mexican standoff.
The storytelling might take a little to get used to but Techland has taken everything out of the first person narration; you are walking towards a mountain and "I found an entrance to their hideout" after which the entire mountain moves away. Sometimes the story backs up a bit as Silas has trouble remembering exactly what happened, or somebody else wants to add their take to the story.
The wild west athmosphere is brought well into this game: each weapon, even if there are not many different types, fires off with a satisfying explosion. No BB-guns up in this b*tch! Each have varying statistics and each are useful in their on way, depending on your play-style and also the environment. All in all the sound design is great; some of the soundtracks are from the previous CoJs and some are original to Gunslinger, there are eagles, chickes, cows and whatevere the hell you can find in the wild west. Bullets make those Hollywood style effects when they hit near you or fly past. The graphics are bright and colourful, a little like Borderlands as many others have written as well.
Now, I have listed good things about this game. The bad things? Well, I can't find any. Gunslinger is by far the shortest Call of Juarez but then again, it costs only 30 bucks. And trust me, that money is well spent as you get to enjoy an FPS so fresh, so smooth and so goddarn brilliant it will leave you buying a horse and riding into the sunset. I'm just sayin'!

Factorio is simply amazing, and it is only getting better. Just look at the amount of time played by some of the reviewers, or of friends on your friend list who own it. In terms of value - I could only dream of living in a world where developers put this amount of time, effort, community collaboration, and content into their work. In this day and age where quality early access games are few and far between, and microtransactions filled free to play games domintate the market in terms of sheer numbers, drowing out smaller and newer developers, it is such an amazing refreshing feeling to see a game like Factorio.
Factorio is a sandbox openworld building game where your goal is to automate everything. It shares a similar concept with many games, in such that each resource requires a combination of resources that come before it to create. You start small, but believe you me, you get big! Towards the end of the tech trees when your factory gets really big, it is truly astounding that it actually functions and that YOU actually made it! It reminds me a lot of lego's in a sense, and also the human body, in that each little part does its function and as a whole they create this amazingly complex machine. You actually learn a lot while playing it too, in an engineer'ish type way. Sometimes changing just one thing creates this huge butterfly effect, and rather than reverting it back, figuring out why and making it work is so much more fun. With multiplayer (which I will talk about a little more down below) you can see in real time how people look at the same problem and solve it in different ways, which I find fascinating.
There are a million ways to play this game, but personally I (and I know so many others do too, as this is one of the core concepts that draws people like us to this genre) love figuring out how to make each little contraption work as efficiently as possible. I also loved making my first factory as symmetrical as I could, just because it looked so cool. Copper on the left, iron on the right in the exact pattern. Oil up the middle with some green chips on each side just because it looked cool!
If you have even the slightest bit of OCD this game will turn it on overdrive, but in a bizzarly fun way...I can't really explain it, just trust me xD
The developer is constantly adding to the game, and listens to the community feedback, which is in my opinion neccesary in 2016. There is so much more I could say about this game, but I will just add this one final and AWESOME end note....It already has *PERFECTLY* working multiplayer, which makes it just THAT much better. These are my absolute favorite types of games, and I have always wanted a good open sandbox game to play with my friend(s), and now I have one.
If you are even considering buying this game for whatever reason, do yourself a favor buy it. These are exactly the types of dev's we need in the gaming world today, our support means everything!
*An easier way to use muliplayer is being added in one of the next updates, but as of now just use the program "evolve" which allows your to share an IP address with whoever you party with, and just join a party with whoever you want to play with.

Supergiant games has struck lighting again with their latest entry in to the action Rpg genre, Transistor.
The makers of Bastion brings you to the cyberpunk city of Cloudbank, a city despite its color and flare, has a few things going on. The main character, and the character you control throughout your adventure, Red, is a songstress that has a bit of a rough night, from dealing with an assassination attempt on her life, to losing her voice, and is now in possession of a weapon which now contains the data of the person who helped her narrowly escape. Both of you wade through the city, fighting a group of mechanical creatures called the process, who has taken over the city in the meantime. It all adds up to an action filled journey as you try to seek retribution for the attempt on Reds life, and the connection between the process and the transistor.
The story also isn't told in a conventional sense, as from the very start of the game you are thrown into the middle of a situation and left to figure things out on your own. You could probably complete the game a couple of times and still not understand everything around you. The only narration is through the sword itself, which is voiced by Logan Cunningham, the narrator of Bastion. The narration though isn't really narration as this time he is accompanying you on your adventure instead of talking about things in a past tense as it was with Bastion.
The game doesn't fail to please the eye with its distinct art style, which fits the tone of the story that show great resemblance to Blade Runner, with a touch a Tron, you will traverse through the roof tops, and city streets, and even the inside of a beast. Each location has some sort of hidden secret or a puzzle for you to solve in order to get through to the next area, they are pretty simple though, so don't expect anything too tough on the brain. There is a sanctuary of sorts that you discover that has training rooms for you to get better at the speed, planning, and learning how to survive more efficiently.
Which brings us to the true meat and potatoes of the game, is its combat system which mixes both real time combat, and turn based combat, with the latter being the most efficient way to get things done. Even some of the story is connected to the combat as you collect abilities, called functions, as each function has a character bio of a previous owner of the transistor or just noteworthy citizens of Cloudbank. You can unlock more of that character's background by equipping a function into an active slot , abilities that can be used in battle, upgrade slot, or a passive slot which encourages a lot of experimentation with abilities. It takes a little bit to get adjusted to, and while learning its not hard to win fights, its hard to win them with style. But once you get the hang of things you can always get the biggest bang for your buck. The combat system encourages experimentation, as when you lose all your health during a fight, you dont exactly die, but instead you lose a function and it gets taken out of your rotation for a while, while this may seem like a debilitating feature, this keeps players from the dull nature that min maxing brings and puts them right back into experimenting with other abilities.
While you can use abilities outside of the planning phase, the fact of the matter is that in most cases there are usually more mobs than you can handle, which in turn makes plan mode the only choice in dealing with most fights. Great for those who like to be strategic in their battles, not so great for those that just want to run in there and hack and slash. The game does have a new game plus feature for those that want to continue to go for achievements, and maybe to take a hidden path or two that you may have missed your first time around. There is no difficulty setting, although the higher level you go more mobs are thrown your way with upgraded abilities. To give your self more of a challenge, you have the option to apply limiters to your self, which is essentially a handicap feature. You can make the Process do more damage, make more spawn in a fight, or you can limit the amount of abilities that you have access to, to do get the results you want. It can get pretty rough, with quite a few limiters on, but each limiter adds a percentage bonus to experience that you get...and give you bit of bragging rights.
The story also isn't told in a conventional sense, as from the very start of the game you are thrown into the middle of a situation and left to figure things out on your own. You could probably complete the game a couple of times and still not understand everything around you. The only narration is through the sword itself, which is voiced by Logan Cunningham, the narrator of Bastion. The narration though isn't really narration as this time he is accompanying you on your adventure instead of talking about things in a past tense as it was with Bastion.
Supergiant games could have rested on the laurels of their success with Bastion, but decided to take a good risk and mix up the formula a bit with Transistor, which works good in some areas, and fall short in other. But all in all its a well made game with a bit of re-playability. I give Transistor a 4/5.

(For people who just want a quick summary, pros and cons are listed below. )
Do you love the original Ragnarok Online? Was Ragnarok 2 a bitter dissapointment? If yes....you can download this in a hardbeat because this is pretty much it's spiritual successor. This game was conceived by Ragnarok's original project lead  Kim Hakkyu who founded IMC Games when he left Gravity game studios. This game just has the original Ragnarok vibe all over.
If no this game is still pretty compelling. You see I love MMO's but I'm not that fond of endgame. What makes this game pretty unique is it's class system. You start with one of the four base classes Archer, Cleric, Swordsman or Wizzard. Your max class level is 15 and every time you hit this you can either take a second or third rank in your current class or you can take a different class. New classes get added each time you hit class level 15. This makes your character very custimizable to your own taste. Currently there are 7 total class rank (including your base class) but more will be added in the future.
Tho not all class combinations are optimal all of them are pretty much viable. I personally think the class system adds a lot of fun to the game.
Honestly I did expect a lot of grinding from a Korean MMO but it does not become grindy until level 130-140 ish. Up until then there is a lot of content to go through. There is a sort of subscription you can either buy with real money or either with ingame currency which gives extra benefits. But nothing game breaking, of the group of friends the person with the highest level was the one that did not have premium even tho premium gets you +30% mob experience.
Yes going full free to play has it's limitations but nothing mayor....some of the limitations are imposed to make the job of Gold Sellers more difficult. Tho I think it's a nice try it does not currenly have the desired effect.
All in all I can give this game a recommendation, especially when the games free to play launces. I will list some of the pro's and cons below. Just give it a go once the free to play launches because well...it's free. This will definitely be one of the better free to play MMO's. It has been able to keep my attention more then any other MMO is recent years and I've tried many.

First off: About this version of Dark Souls II
There's going to be a Re-Worked version of this game being released on April as of this review.
The name of it shall be " Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin " and it will be a re-worked version of this game.
Before I get into details on that let's talk a bit about this version.
Was it as good as it was advertised to be?
No... The Graphics, the Matchmaking, and even the way the map was said to be actually worked to take away a lot from the game and made it feel very limiting, with-in your first day of playin (If you've played the first.) you can already feel like you were playing within a Park instead of the Branching Open World that it was said to be and especially the vast open world the previous tittle was.
Did it have the mechanics it said it would have?
Yes... (Albeit sometime it was wonky at best.)
The window for the dodging mechanic did feel a lot smaller, that being a good thing for me compaired to the first game.
Meaning you had to be smarter when were to dodge in this game, but of coarse that came with having to memorise when abilities and weapons actually deal their damage.
... and there in lies the problem...
For the most part I've found that there's more then a few weapons that have a delay to when the damage is applied compaired to the actual animation.
Then on the other hand there's more then a few that deal their damage before the animation even implise it.
Now I would of said this was a matchmaking connection problem but why would it always be on those certain weapons?
Now yes admittingly I didn't play much of this game... Even with Pre-Ordering it...
It just didn't feel worth it, it felt empty and devoid of the Dark Souls charm from before.
It mimiced it, yes, but it didn't get it down packed.
There was something about it that was not as fun as when I played the first one that had me coming back to it for so long.
I don't know about other players but to me something felt missing from what made this game really feel like Dark Souls.
Could have just been myself needing to adjust to the new looks of things...
... and speaking of the looks...
Did it look good on max settings?
Absolutly not, I think there was an article that I ended up reading that showed technics from the year 2000 that showed games actually looked better on those then they did on here.
But I'm not going to open that can of worms, to me the graphics where horrible and murky, no not murky as in a griddy look I mean murky as in the textures were not applied correctly and as well as the fact that they used a lot of low resolution textures in the game...
I have a NVIDIA GeForce GTX 660 Ti with an Intel Dual Core Proccessor... To me... That says that this game is not that demanding on resourses if my computer can keep up with the settings.
Yes I would studder at times here and there, but that was like what? Every twenty minutes at most.
So again while good for me that I could run it all at max, it just shows that the graphics in this game are not that high at all to begin with.
To be honest, to me... It felt like Dark Souls looked much better then Dark Souls II on almost all acounts aside from the character models (Though the textures of the models weren't that good.) and the background designs.
Now I did look up to see if it was just me, that if it was just that with my Rig there were settings that were locked away behind a script or something around the lines.
But from what I've looked up everyone's games looked the same as mine, even with some using the Titan Series Graphics cards.
The game still looked horrible and just a murky mess of stretched graphics.
Now this is all I have to say about this version, these were my problems I had, the way the story was told is still Dark Souls-esk where you need to be the one reading and looking for all the clues as to what happened with in the area.
Reading the descriptions and everything that was before you in an attempt to piece together the much larger picture of what happened.
Second off: About Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin ( Dark Souls II 2.0 )
Half a year after the release of Dark Souls II the Devs anounced that they're re-working on their release Dark Souls II.
That they were unhappy with what was done with it, how things were handled with by their publisher and of how DLC was being treated.
They admitted that all three DLCs that are currently out were supposed to release straight out the gate with the game, and yet their publisher said no and to cut it up into DLC to sell seperatly...
Now with the money that's left from Dark Souls II sales they're re-working and trying to undo the changes that their publishers forced them to make.
From improving the graphics back to what was planned originally to improving the mechanics of the game to be more responsive.
Even the maps, models, weapons, and NPCs will be re-worked from the ground up.
The Devs are promising an entirely new game to don the Dark Souls II name, something that they themselves are proud of.
Now I saw this happen before with EA's Dead Space series, where by the Third title the Devs had 0 control over the cretion of the game and we all know how that turned out...
So I'm glad to see the devs take up arms and try to undo the damage that their publishers caused them.
( Yes, publishers have more influence over a game's creation then most people may think... )
So what's being promised?
Improved Mechanics
Improved Textures
Improved Modeling
Added Content that was originally Cut completly from the first version.
Include the three DLCs into the game right on release.
Add a lot more weapons
Add alot more armors
More NPCs
Improved AI
Added More Creatures that were not given a chance to develop
As well as ontop of all this they promise to add an Expansion's worth of original new content.
So will this next version be worth the money?
I think that hands down it will definetly be worth the money.
Just wished we didn't have to pay 60 - 120 dollars to Beta test it before its release. :/

Before purchasing the game there are some things a new player should know.
Bag space is very limited unless you also purchase the Plus Subscription. Whilst playable it makes crafting difficult as there are many crafting materials. The subscription costs $24 (NZD) a month.
Some quest lines I.E. Dark Brotherhood, Thieves Guild are DLC and have to purchased with crowns ranging $20-40 each. Or you can buy the Gold version of the game for a cheaper deal. More ways to suck money out of an unsuspecting new player who chose the cheaper option to begin with.
There a lot of basic features missing from the game that require third-party addons to remedy. I.E. a minimap.
There are some game store items to make life a lot easier (portable banker or merchant) but also are not cheap ~$40 each.
Last but not least: refunding is almost impossible. Launching the game brings up the game's launcher which proceeds to download ~40GB of patches. If you've got a slow connection your 2 hour refund window is gone before you can even play. That doesn't include the hour you could spend creating a character or the hour spent in the tutorial area.
Please do yourselves a favour and read the other negative reviews for the real story before purchasing.

"This game ain't got no depth" Bob "Killjoy" Flannhegan spat out.
I wasn't gonna take this slander lyin' down. My hand hovered near my sixshooter. Every nerve in my body was taut with rage as I considered every potential response to such slanderous accusations as he was levelin'.
"There ain't no character depth" he continued, disregardin' the look on my face. It was a look that woulda told every right thinkin' man and woman that they was enterin' a disagreement the likes of which they was woefully underprepared for. I marshalled my words carefully as I sipped my whisky with the hand the wasn't preparin' to put a bullet in this fool's face. A misplaced word would spell the end of me, and the end of the journey I had undertaken so long ago.
"Now, seems to me, that's just your opinion, fellah" I answered in most level tone I could muster. It took all my willpower not to draw right there and then.
"The plot sure got me involved." I said with a wry smile. "As did the gameplay." I continued.
"Ohhh, the gameplay, is it then?" Killjoy replied with a face that made me wanna empty all my bullets into it there and then. "The gameplay ain't nothin a first person shooter hasn't done a million times before."
The smug smile lingered on that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Bob's face, lookin' like an armadillo that had just won a Nobel prize in the field of oustandin' twattery.
"It's a goddamn entertainin' game and you knows it!" I pressed on, ignorin' the objections of all the folks who don't like me writin' in phonetics.
Right then, in one fluid motion, ol' Killjoydrew upturned the table and fired first.
"Too linear!" whizzed past my head as I ducked behind the overturned table. I dodged just in time by statin' that the game itself was entertainin' enough to sustain interest beyond a single playthrough.
"No character development!" hit my impromtu table fortress, sendin' splinters flying into the air.
Half shutting my eyes against the wooden sharpnel I carefully took aim.
"The skill levellin' system is fun." I plainly stated, lookin' right in his eyes. I saw in them the look of a man who knew his argument was doomed. It was the look of a man that was too far in and quietly prayin' that God would forgive his trespasses... because he knew I wouldn't.
"And there are enough twists on the ol' first person shooter dynamics to keep it interestin'" I stated almost apologetically.
But it was too late for apologies. My argument caught him squarely in the forehead, burrowing into his brain like a hot mole into butter. I'll never forget the look on Bob "Killjoy" Flannhegan's face. It was a look of defeat. A look of betrayal. But there was no going back now; in entering the argument I had committed myself to this path.
"Lord forgive me" I murmered, "But I think this game is worth a replay."

Denuvo DRM ruins the experience. There is essentially no TRUE offline mode in any game that utilizes Denuvo DRM due to the fact that if you either change hardware, update Steam, or update Windows you are forced to go online and re-authenticate the game's license through Denuvo's servers. The authentication ticket could also simply expire without any updates made to hardware and/or software as well, so either way, you're screwed if you're not connected to the internet about 99% of the time.

Note: I have about 300 more hours in this before it came to Steam.
I really, really like this game. It is not perfectly balanced (what game is) and it has some toxic people in the player base (what MOBA doesn't). However, it is still incredibly fun. You might think, "It's just another MOBA with a different control set", and yes, it is. But shifting the camera to third person actually makes a huge difference with positioning and vision. Also, ALMOST everything is a skill shot (including basic attacks and excluding Nu Wa's entire kit) which, to me at least, makes it much more fun than a traditional MOBA. There are also a bunch of different game modes.
Conquest is your standard 3-lane MOBA map.
Arena is a bit like deathmatch. Still has minions, but mostly just 5v5 fighting in a circle arena.
Assault is ARAM.
Clash is a little weird, but also kinda cool. Ends up being a mix of arena and conquest.
Joust is 3v3 on a smaller, conquest-like map.
Seige is 4v4 on a special 2-lane map, with seige minions that add some excitment.
...and...drumroll...
MOTD (Mode of the Day) is sometimes weird, sometimes boring, sometimes great, but always INTERESTING. It rotates to different things, with the more popular modes returning fairly often. Common variants are different numbers of teamates, super low cooldowns, infinite mane, draft and bans in modes that don't usually have it, everyone plays the same god, or whatever (April fool's day is EPIC). Helps keep the game interesting for those days that you are bored of conquest.

*** Review as of May 3, 2016 ***
The game is absolutely gorgeous. Many different monsters and a coherent backstory, with more endgame content coming. Most maps have 3-7 NPCs with quests you can do (for best EXP, be within +/- 5 levels of the map's level.) This makes questing and the story a bit linear, but personally I was still immersed in the world because of the art and overarching storyline.
MAKE SURE you read online and do some research for a class path you'd like, since there are 80 to choose from! Be VERY careful when choosing classes and abilities. (Main online resources include the subreddit r/treeofsavior, the fan site
, and the TOS official site news and forums. These are invaluable for getting the most out of the game.) Choosing an optimal build can make the grindy leveling easier. But all the grinding and the careful class and abilities selection can make your character really feel like your own, and form the core draw of the game for many players. Both DPS and healers are wanted in parties. If you're a healer, joining a party to level up together can make leveling easier. The classes aren't 100% balanced at the time of writing, but future updates may change that.
There are other ways to reduce the grind and repetition - for example, when you start out in either Klaipeda or Orsha towns, you can buy a Klaipeda or Orsha scroll to warp to the other respective town, and then warp back and forth between the regions near those towns as you progress to higher-level maps. This means you may not need much grinding before level 100, since quests give so much EXP. The key system is flexible and the defaults are nice, such as 'M' for the map you're currently on (showing objectives) and 'N' for the world map. You also get EXP rewards if you explore a map 100%, and since there are hundreds of maps already, exploration makes the game feel more open-world. (Just be sure to run by all the edges and corners while exploring, to ensure 100%.)
To be social, you can join a party, especially a dungeon party, or a guild. You can engage in PvP content when your guild goes to war with another guild. And your guild has a special guild house to socialize in! More chat features are needed, like per-map chat, but all the basics are covered, like all chat, whispering, and megaphones. The emotes are good (helped by the polished avatars) and you can have custom phrases per emotes (10 quick-access emote slots). You can also like other people. And you can rotate while sitting.
IMC has shown they can listen to community feedback, so recent updates have lowered bot numbers, server lag, and monster respawn time. Hundreds of bots are banned every day, and new regional servers like in Southeast Asia and Brazil have reduced average server lag time. Now, some of the other negative reviews have brought up some bugs and legitimate game components that still need polishing. And at the time of F2P launch, there's no telling how the servers will react to all the new players. For me, a drawback was having to switch channels occasionally on crowded maps to hunt all the monsters I need. IMC still needs to increase the spawn rate for some maps. But from the perspective of the next few years, and the MMO genre, Tree of Savior is an exciting release and I hope it lasts for 20 years at least!

Other reviews have covered the great parts of Transistor, and I agree that is a beautiful game with an immersive story and great gameplay, etc. I do want to give a bit of a warning, though:
The story can be overly subtle, especially if it's not fully explored. I enjoyed unlocking snippets of character backstory and interacting with out-of-the-way terminals and scenery, but anyone who doesn't do so is going to miss out on a lot of the story. Even those who read and interact with everything are going to find themselves with questions. The story is too important to the gameplay to be ignored, so if you buy Transistor give it your full attention and you'll be rewarded.
It is a short game and replay value is fairly low. Already on the second playthrough (even with Limiters and New Game+ spicing up my possibilities) I felt less "magic" than the first time--I already knew what was going to happen, after all, and so much of the excellence of the first playthrough was in the plot. Casual players ought to expect six to eight hours of gameplay in a single playthrough, only the most dedicated are likely to get more than 12 or 16. I think that for most people Transitor will be enjoyed once or twice and then set aside.
The mechanics, like the story, are immersive and require dedication. It is tempting to find a single combination and use it through the whole game in the same way, adding on a single new power or slightly altering your layout with each level increase. There's a reason, though, that you're prompted to change your skillset every time you reach a checkpoint. The upgrade and passive ability system offers so much customization that by the end of the game I was finding testing new strategies and messing around in the skill menu at least as much fun as pulling off a well-executed combo (which, though awesome and enjoyable, did get a bit repetitive after ten hours).
If you're not put off, though, please do buy Transistor with all haste. It is magnificent, artistic, mechanically brilliant, and intensely enjoyable.

Joust is 3v3 on a smaller, conquest-like map.
Seige is 4v4 on a special 2-lane map, with seige minions that add some excitment.

You won't find a better single player Call of Duty game around, except maybe Black Ops 2.
Should you buy this? Maybe. See the section on the Multiplayer for the big warning about this game.
This is a great single player game, because it's such a well-rounded experience in general. The gameplay feels sharp and responsive, and incorporates and improves on Call of Duty 4's mechanics. The levels in the story, and the spec-ops bonus missions, are well planned, well-designed, and varied, taking the player all over the globe from South America to the White House, all over Russia and to the Middle East. The plot is far beyond what you would expect from a mil-shooter today, willing to subvert the jingoistic American Police State that these games often build up. It's not Shakespeare, and at times falls to pleasent stupidity, but again, it generally rises above the rest.
The multiplayer.
If you want to buy this game for the multiplayer, DO NOT. This game is quite old now, and several new generations of COD have come and gone. The game also features console-style P2P gaming, so the lack of players has hit the possible pings hard. Half the game modes will be empty, and the other half will be playing against people across the globe. There are mods out there to reinvigorate the multiplayer with servers instead of P2P (rightfully so, as it is insanely adictive otherwise). Look into these options before you buy this game, because to get anything out of MP, you'll need to download one of them.

As for the gameplay, they did a fantastic job of letting you absolutely tear through people as a reward for accuracy without ever letting you get lazy. Every enemy is a threat and they WILL kill you if you aren't fast enough (I do recommend playing on Hard though. I didn't touch normal.). My only complaint is the duel mechanic that quickly grows to be tiresome though you only have to do it at the end of levels. The campaign should keep you busy for 4-5 hours by which time you will unlock a New Game+ mode that lets you keep leveling up and play on the "True West" difficulty. If that's not enough, there's the relentlessly fun arcade mode that is essentially a score attack mode where accuracy, speed, and combos are key.
9/10 - a surprisingly complete package for $15 or less.

Grading this game is very hard. It is really difficult for a person to speak objectively of what is perhaps their favourite game ever. Age has been kind to Shadow of Chernobyl for sure, as no other game (bar its sequels and mods) has ever managed to quite match it.
It is a flawed gem of a game. Released buggy, unstable, now fixed (due to its community's love) but still unpolished and not without questionable design choices. With that being said, when it works, it is simply peerless, without an equal even 10 years later. Very few games can elicit such strong emotional reactions on almost all levels of game design as S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl.
Graphical Fidelity and Audio: Back when it came out in 2007, it was a very good looking game. The advanced weather and dynamic lighting were second to none and the sheer size of the world, combined with its AI and physics was impressive. One also has to applaud that the game had good scalability and even terrible computers could at least play it (even on potato graphics). It was very demanding and unoptimized though if one wanted to utilize higher settings. Furthermore, the game's dated animations were a bit of an issue. Outstanding 3D sound processing and the best choice of API gives it a massive edge over most games. On a somewhat unfortunate note for SoC, 2007 saw the release of Crysis, which at the time featured by far the best visual quality in almost every single aspect, as well as BioShock and Penumbra: Overture which to this day have the best sound quality of all time. Despite all that, SoC was still noteworthy, but could never claim the crown. 18/20
Presentation: Some of the best art style and ambient sound design in gaming. Fast and efficient UI design, reasonable amounts of options customization. Built like a PC game. It could have used even more guitar tracks and used more of its OST songs, but the quality here is immense. An FOV slider is missing, even if the default FOV strikes a good balance for any gamer. I want to make it clear that this score is given for the fully patched game with the Zone Reclamation Project bug fix mod. At release, SoC would have done far worse in this category, but these days it makes little sense for a first time playthrough to not use ZPR. 18/20
Storytelling: I am very mixed on what to give the game here. On the one hand it dabbles in complex, advanced themes and uses a lot of its environmental design and gameplay to accentuate them. This means it is really using gaming's potential as an art form fully and some of the mechanics of its storytelling are almost peerless within the industry. But the problem is that for all of its possible depth, for all the lore, the advanced concepts and themes, it is not efficient in telling its own main plot. Open world games have an issue with this in general, but Shadow of Chernobyl's smart secondary writing and excellent world design can not fully compensate for the rushed and unpolished main storyline. 17/20
Gameplay: One of a kind, but not without its shortcomings. Stealth is often buggy and some mechanics perhaps needed to be rethought, the "weapon ladder" used is a bit counter-intuitive to its universe. It could do with more weapon variety, as machine guns are missing entirely and so are important types of rifles and more. On the other hand, the A-Life system, the structure of its world, the game is bigger than the sum of its parts. 17/20
Lasting Appeal: Obviously Shadow of Chernobyl will score top marks here. The world is so dynamic, always changing due to the A-Life system. It is not only a long game, but offers grade A replay value. Add to said replayability the incredible, top tier modding community and you get what is for all things considered an absurd amount of content and longevity. A decent (though now abandoned) multiplayer mode is appreciated but most of its players are on the other games of the series now. 20/20
Overall: 90/100 - One of Gaming's brightest shining flawed gems!

Textbook example of an uncut diamond. Simply an amazing game.
Story & Atmosphere:
STALKER games are known for being very atmospheric shooters, and quite tough ones too. But they are also pretty unstable. The first game, Shadow of Chernobyl (SoC), kicks off the series with your character "Marked One" waking up from a roadcrash. He was found at the crashsite of a so called "deathtruck". A fellow stalker (a scavenger) was surprised to find Marked One alive among the dead bodies that are usually in those trucks. Marked One has amnesia, but apart from being alive among the dead ones at the truck, he also has a very curious PDA on him. A PDA with a single task description: Kill Strelok. With the "mutual" help of the local trader Sidorovich, Marked One starts his journey to find out about himself and the many mysteries within The Zone. But the real showstealer here is The Zone itself, consisting of the ghastly exclusion zone around the Chernobyl NPP, dripping with an amazing atmoshpere. The sounds and the music, the creatures roaming the area, its all real good. Stalkers gathered up around a campfire, playing their guitars and telling jokes in russian, the group of howling dogs in the distance that are munching away on their recently caught prey... Everybody does their own thing, their AI is impressive at times, and it feels pretty alive to me. The grim look of the terrain, the spooky underground sections... the unique atmosphere is simply amazing and very few games do this as well as Stalker does.
Gameplay:
The game itself plays as a semi-open-world FPS shooter with RPG elements. The shooting is challenging and quite satisfying. The starting weapons like the makarov pistol can be really bad, but i think that it adds to the survival aspect of the game. However, later weapons are more accurate and deadly. The bulletarcs actually drop abit over distance, making longer ranged weapons like the Vintorez difficult but fun to use. The game can be pretty punishing, with deadly creatures (humans and mutants alike) and many dangerous areas. Like the radiation pockets for example: Radiation can slowly build up when you stroll through it and it can kill you later if you dont deal with it. Your gear keeps deteriorating depending on use, so make sure to check and loot enemies, check stashes and search the area whenever you get the chance. Not everyone is your enemy though, so theres no need to go guns blazing at every moment. There are neutral stalkers and different factions with their own standing towards you. If you scratch one of them off, you count on the others to act agressive to you aswell. But being nice to other stalkers might even give you discounts when you trade items with them. The game has several fairly large areas with loadingzones to connect them with, and the mission sequence is fairly lineair. But you're free to travel between practically every area, though some areas require some sort of progress to access. This could be a specific mission item, or simply better gear to survive.
RPG?:
The further you go up north, the more dangerous the Zone becomes. This shows the RPGesque parts of the game. Marked One doesnt level up or gain exp, but gathers up better gear little by little. STALKER has alot of items too. Not just different guns, but suits, ammotypes, medkits, vodka etc etc. Some items are better geared for some situations then others. Hazmat suits for example provide better protection against radiation and extreme heat while Spetznaz suits mostly offer better bullet and explosive protection and even the lower tiered bandit suits can be useful for being very cheap etc etc... Marked One can also make use of the valuable "Artifacts": these are strange items found in the Zone, attracting the flock of stalkers for the value these items have in the outside world. Artifacts can offer the user various status effects, but their effects are balanced out by side-effects. For example, there is an artifact that regenerates health easier, but causes the user to be weaker against certain other kinds of damage. Or an artifact that boosts endurance but decreases electric protection, or radiation reduction vs weaker to bleeding etc etc. So the benefits of these artifacts depend on how well you manage them.
Buggy & mods:
I think the worst part of this game is how unstable it can be, with all sorts of crashes and glitches. Alot bugs are patched by now, and the community does a good job of fixing alot too with mods, but some are still there and can still be frustrating (and even amusing) at times. The community brings me to another point, and that is the ridiculously huge amount of content it creates. Some files are easy to edit, (you can make some easy tweaks yourself in no time) so this leads to lots of content and a large games series with a near infinite amount of modcontent out there. AMK adds more to the vanilla SoC experience, ZRP focuses on bugfixes, and thats just for SoC alone. Lost Alpha is a (very buggy but very interesting) reimaging of how SoC should have been, and Call of Chernobyl adds all the areas from the 3 games combined into 1 massive modular sandbox.
Theres so much to say about this game, but heres the gist of it:
Pro's:
+ Truly amazing atmosphere
+ Freedom to wander in the Zone
+ Challenging
+ Item managing
+ Lot's of different mechanics
+ Impressive AI
+ Near infinite amount of content by community
Cons:
- Notoriously unstable
- some mechanics unrefined/tough to get into
If you're not afraid to get your hands dirty on it's learning curve, ageing graphics and some of it's trouble shooting, then you should definitely try this gem and the rest of the series... Even if they can feel uncut at times.
