You played Bastion. You loved it and can't wait to play Transistor, but hold on. This game is not what you expect it to be. That doesn't mean its a bad game by any means, but this is a completely different experience from what you are expecting. Combat is mostly turn based and the game runs on rails for the most part. The game is also not fully fleshed out. Its obvious they ran out of ideas, time or money because the game doesn't quite set up the story as well as their previous one. You get character biographies from using skills but there is nothing more. The moments you do encounter other characters are brief and you will never get the answers you want about the setting. Where does this take place? What is the process? What were the Camerata's goals? The game teases at an explanation but stops short of actually filling in the blanks. Buy this game on sale and enjoy it for the brief distraction that it is. You will probably enjoy it.

TL;DR: Transistor is good, you should pick it up if you liked Bastion or, in other words, if you like challenging combat and interesting storyline.
That being said, what is transistor? It's an action-rpg game, where you have only one weapon, but it is very flexible and customizable. Leveling also affects weapon, there is no "character skills" whatsoever. The mechanics is unusual, it's a mix of time based and real time combat. At first I was sceptical about this, thinking that one of the modes will be way better, but that's not the case. Both modes are good, you can use one, other, or mix or them depending on your playstyle.
The "default" combat is not very hard, as it was obviously designed for those who want to just see the story. But we are speaking of SGG, so they added a mechanics very similar to Bastion's Idols - Limiters, which can be activated/deactiated at any time, and will affect the strength, numbers and AI of enemies.
The story is good, there is not much to say about it, the only downside being its length. This is arguably a downside, however, because the game doesn't feel too boring, and overextended.
Also, the famous narrator is here, so this is definitely a big yay, imo.

Just Cause 3 is an open-world, destruction, fun simulator. You can literally do whatever you want in this game. It has so many possibilities that you never get bored of it! I have played it a few hours and still don't have explored all. A lot of people say it's a Michael Bay Simulator... Indeed, it is! The giant explosions; sometimes "Just Caused" by a simple flick, will let you AGAPE! You can choose to follow the story of the campaign, which I think is really cool and entertaining, or you can choose to spend your time exploring the majestic, giant and beautiful world.
The graphics? They are just amazing. I have rarely seen graphics that nice in other games... (I've made so many screenshots in the game to remember all the delicious places I've met...) You also have a menu to spawn weapons and vehicles where you want on the map. The tall choice of this menu is very pleasant. From the bike to the giant army plane, going through the assault tank! Also, the wingsuit and the grapple system is something you can only find in Just Cause... It's one of the most important gadget in the game, allowing you to go everywhere on the map with much fun!
The only thing that is missing yet, is a multiplayer mode. Sharing with your friends your crazy experimentations and funny nonsenses is something very pleasant. Just Cause 2 multiplayer mode was much fun... Bring it back, developers!
By the way, you will have to play it with a good computer, otherwise the graphics will not be as beautiful as I said, and it will crash many times if you get too crazy with your experimentations!
Finally, if you want a game that never bores you and where you can have much fun, playing an entire day, stop looking for it. This game is Just Cause 3.

This game is a stunning work of art that while different from Bastion in most aspects does create a narrative experience of equal caliber. It is not as accessible as Bastion because the narrator is now more of a present character instead of the omnipresent Rucks, leaving it up to the player to explore. This does not detract from the base story of the protagonist revenge tale as that is very easy to follow, but gives the player the option to how immersed into the world that he/she that adding more depth. The gameplay is incredibly innovative being a combination of RTS and Action-RPG, allowing one to combine attacks to create different movesets. When attacks are used in different ways the player gets lore, so by playing with one of the game's core mechanics you are adding an optional narrative layer to your game. In conclusion, Transistor is a beautiful game that has remarkble gameplay as well as story. And if you are not gonna buy this game, please buy the soundtrack because Darren Korb is an absolute genius. The soundtrack really gives the world atmosphere bordering on near impressionism and is absolutely beautiful. Everything in that soundtrack is fantastically done from the production work to the vocal talents of Ashley Barret who gives the voice of Red. It is a masterpiece.

SMITE is a really great game:
It's not perfect but not everyone will be out for your blood as soon as you make a mistake and after trying LoL and Dota it's nice to see someone actually helping and giving tips to new people instead of raging because they lost the game by half a inch.

Each one is different and you can find what you really enjoy.
Smite doesn't really have its own lore, because it takes everything from existing religions, myths and legends, which is really cool and can get pretty interesting (like, who knew the chinese had that many gods?)

Well, I hope you will buy this game, or at least go watch it on youtube! Despite the bads things, its still a must have in your survival game collection.

Overall, it's a game where, if you want to kill some time and keep it in the background checking it occasionally i'd reccomend it, I'f there were still visible goals for end game i'd say it would be fantastic idle game, but it's an idle game, it's entertaining for a few weeks, and then you move on. Being a fan of neither Elder Scrolls nor MMOs, there's not much here to change my mind about either.
Disclaimer: I played with a couple of friends. Review spoiler warning: The game is probably even less fun if you go in alone.
Just like many (all?) of its kind, you run around working on chores that for some reason NPCs feel very compelled to trust a complete stranger. You spend a huge amount of time running around at a pace that has no place in a map this big, occassionally fighting shallow battles that don't feel different from each other. I can't speak for the whole map since you can clearly see I didn't play for long, but what was there in the noob training grounds looked fairly generic. Pretty graphics, though. Thoroughly boring art, but nice graphics.
The combat, again at least in the beginning, is not unlike a p**** comparison contest: If your measurements are greater than your opponents', you win. You don't have to do much. And because it's difficult to find stuff that has your exact d*** size, everything is either served in a silver platter or splatters your vital organs all over the place. Mostly the former, since of course they want to get you invested in the early game. Later on I suppose there's value in combining your member and your mates' members together to form an even bigger, gayer wood, but that's not to say it's not boring. A game whose main gameplay is watching numbers grow is not unlike watching the grass grow.
I saw a lot of people in town riding horses, and eager to solve the pacing issue, I tried googling how to get one. I found an article stating these very exact words:
It's like, are you serious? Is this not a joke? I find it very adorable that people refer to core gameplay as a "ton of pain and suffering". Also, if you're the patient type, you will realize that $20 is more than what you have to pay for THREE FULL games, even AAA ones, on Steam. Also, the horse starts at a measly 15% speed increase and needs to be leveled up. Enjoy your inane busywork, I suppose?
This might sound baffling to you MMO players, but did you know that there are actually fun games out there? Games that you play because they are designed to be fun, not designed to be addictive. You guys really should learn the difference between the two. One is good for you, and the other one is not. I am no one to dictate how you should be spending your lives, but if you've already decided to waste it on videogames, then I feel like you should probably try to make it fun ones.
That's for how the game stands as a general videogame. As far as MMOs go, it's alright, I guess. Rather unoriginal, but what's there, it's well implemented I suppose.
Fun and time consuming game, There are plenty of bugs that should be fixed by the Devs like some launcher issues or the in-game glitches and bugs. But Ignoring the issues I'd rate it a solid 8/10.

Well, my review is mainly for beginners who have just started this game or willing to buy it. This is also for them who had stopped playing it after some trivial hours of trying.
A great game but yet I think the enjoyment will depend on how you are playing it! All that I mean, if you want to get the fullest essence of this game then play with suitable co-op partner(s). Some who enjoys solo, they may say different but as I played solo because I had none to play with, so I felt even boring in some point and so also I felt how much the experience would be better with suitable co-op partner(s).
This is a hard-core game for hard-core gamers. Death and incapability may happen every now and then… but again the number may be reduced dramatically if you have your co-op partner(s). There are some other advantages too to play co-op (such as, better loot, or think that while you are reloading your gun, your co op partner still firing and thus you will be less hurt by enemies) and the game itself prompts for co-op although everything can be done in solo except few achievements.
This is a long game, including DLCs and need patience to finish them all. However, as I said before, this is a hard core game with almost a lot enemy everywhere, so, at some point you can feel frustrated if you don’t have proper levelled equipment and so you should farm for right things enough. Here again comes the advantage of co-op; such as you 4 people if farm for 4 weapons and then you can make duplicate of those [though it is a glitch] and you 4 can be well equipped… which chance does not exist in solo and so can be a lot time consuming and monotonous to be advanced.
For new players, as I was when I started this game… may be a problem to understand the architecture of the game. At the very beginning the game starts in NORMAL mode. Once you will finish the main game… then TVHM [True Vault Hunter Mode] will be unlocked which you can take as medium difficulty. Re-playing the game in TVHM mode from the beginning once you reach at level 50 and then so also if you have finished the last mission of main story, then UVHM [Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode] will be unlocked for you. So take this as hard mode. There are over power [OP (1 to 8)] mode also where you can think it as very hard difficulty mode where enemy is up of your level. but that can be unlocked once you reach the ultimate level of the game, i.e. level 72. So, the main game will take you upto the level 50; The UVH pack 1 will take you upto 61 and UVH pack 2 will take you to level 72.
Addition as on 30th June: Since I have just finished the main mission of main game in UVHM mode so I shall suggest you if you are playing UVHM then you must carry 2 blue pistols: Potent Rubi and Potent Gorg Nozzle and always keep one of these at your one slot. Whenever you are low in health start shooting using it.
This is the review basing on my present experience of nearly 400 hours; I can update this review in the future as I shall get new experience.

Supergiant came out of nowhere with Bastion, and it was amazing.  Would they be able to recapture the magic with their sophomore release?  In short:  mostly.
What made Bastion memorable to me was the music and atmosphere.  Mechanically solid, but aurally and visually delightful.  With Transistor they flip this a bit.  The real hook, the most fully formed part of the game, is the combat mechanics.
Make no mistake, the audio is still miles ahead of most competitors.  Darren Korb does superb work with the music, though admittedly my tastes favor the folk blues of Bastion to the synth jazz of Transistor.  Logan Cunningham once again able to run laps around most voice acting in games.  Overall the entire atmosphere and audio portions of the game fall secondary to Bastion, but there is no shame in taking second to a game as strong as that.
The mechanics are the area where it stands on it's own.  They use a unique system of abilities, with each function able to take either the form of an ability, modifier for another ability, or passive support role.  The myriad ways these interact can lead to many tactical situation.  The game also strongly encourages mixing and experimentation, as the narrative is largely unlocked by using an ability in each of the 3 roles.  There doesn't seem to be any overpowering combo, though each can feel that way when used correctly.  Many games feature a wide array of abilities you can equip, but few do as good of a job encouraging you to experiment and resist using the same strategy throughout.
Overall, a hearty recommendation.  While I rate it slightly lower than Bastion, their idea of a sophomore slump is still to embarrass the competition in writing and audio.

I finished the game, so here i go.
Let me just say upfront, it's an interesting game, with beautiful atmosphere, a convincing word and matching characters.
That said, this title is very inconsistant and suffers from some annoying game (breaking) mechanics and bugs.
Even though it did have potential, it's not worth it. Here's why:
- The "maps" (not open-world) are interesting at times, but traversing trough it can often times feel like a unnecasery chore. Quick travel would have helpt alot.
- Characters will yell the same sentence over and over and over and over and over again, untill you go mad. ( "Get out of here Stalker!" ) It's funny at first, but after a while... not so much.
- The A.I. will be a perfect shot one time, then another time will shoot in a completely different direction from yours.
- Quick saving is handy, but can bite you in the♥♥♥♥♥due to the enemies suddenly spawning behind you if you reload after death. Wich can cause an infinite loop of you dying over and over..
- The Main story is short and flawed, nothing particularly interesting going on.
- Dont bother with the side-missions. They are a waste of time, and will probably only draw out the experience more that you'd care for. They have no (good) story, and are just for cash grinding.
- Mutants that roam some areas where a nice break from the generic soldiers over-and-over. But those encounters where far en few in between.
- environmental hazards (anomalies) are just there to prevent you from progressing to fast, and can insta-kill you. the tornado ones are the worst, and just lead to pointless deaths.
- The inventory system is a nightmare. You're over burdened way to quickly, wich shortens your stamina bar alot.
You will always need the stamina for running, since there is no quick travel and there is ALOT of boring walking from A to B. Its a constant trade-off between loot, and stamina.
- Sometimes missions cant be completed because the A.I. where your supposed to turn it in can die during that mission. The mission will stay there in your mission panel, and will promt you to turn it in all the time even though you cant.
You'll forget about it and traverse the enitre map just to find out it's still bugged and wasted your time going there.
- Gunplay is decent but the accuracy on the weapons is terrible. You'll shoot an entire magazine at one enemy just to score a headshot. The A.I on the other hand will have no trouble landing one, even though their gun has a worse accuracy stat.
Even though i experienced all these problems with the game, i did finish it.
In the end it left me pretty unsatisfied and i wont be revisiting the game for a second playtrough.
Once finished, it has no real re-play value.
Its a shame really, because this game had alot of potential but got spoiled by the above mentioned problems.
If this didnt convince you and do decide to buy this game, buy it on sale and, QUICK SAVE... ALOT.
At current price, it's not worth it.

Right, allow me to review based on every seperate emotion I felt while playing.
'Wow.'
This game looks, sounds and feels incredible. The level of detail is out of this world, from the odd, atmospheric tunes to the facial expressions of characters, to the Sevastopol station and the surrounding space... it is all just one great decision after another. The motion tracker, that serves as your main tool of survival throughout the game, can be focused on with your point of view just like I am focusing on my computer screen to write this, so the background is vague, right? This is the first game I have seen where it is possible to focus your gaze on something behind the object, which gives it a very realistic and extremely eery feel to it.
'Oh, just like...'
This game is a hommage to the first Alien movie from 1979. I watched it after playing for a couple of hours and I recommend to watch it beforehand, although most of the core elements are embedded in this game anyway, but it's always nice to catch some little jokes now and then.
Butt-clenching fear
Make no mistake, this is the scariest game I have ever played. Remember the motion tracker example I gave above? Imagine trying to track the Xenomorph with that, watching the green blop go around the area, than seeing something vague in the unfocused distance behind glass. You focus your gaze on the background instead of watching the tracker and you see the ♥♥♥♥er walking towards you. Instinctively, you turn around and run for the nearest hideout like a retard, which exposes you and turns you into minced meat. That was my first death and I was too terrified to load my save.
In fact, after five to six hours of progress  I was about to play another session and I realized that my brain was like "Are you sure? This♥♥♥♥♥♥is really stressful. Why not watch a comedy instead?". Never had that before either.
Comedy
It is incredibly satisfying when some dumb musclehead survivor shoots you on sight without asking so much of a question and he and his buddies get jumped by the Alien who went after the sound. While they are being torn apart on the other side of the room, you thank them for the distraction and walk along your path like nothing happened.
Also, why does the Alien kill everyone if he doesn't eat them? (I may have studied him)
'Am I there yet?'
The game is a tad overly long, just like this review. I would have skipped at least one sequence. It also turns kind of in a ridiculuous action movie at the end, but I guess that is fair if you want your audience to experience a buildup throughout the entire game instead of being disappointed that the scariest part was in the middle.
I admire how the devs tried to keep the game interesting by having some variety in there as well - that is incredibly difficult to do for a game that, let's face it, mainly revolves around avoiding an Alien. Building suspense is difficult enough as it is, but keeping it for 18 hours...
♥♥♥♥ this Alien / poor Amanda
I don't usually care for protaganists or antagonists. Amanda is kind of boring and gets walked over by people, but by God I was still with her along the way. I never wanted any virtual enemy destroyed so badly!
9/10

So... Call of Juarez, Gunslinger.
Straight up arcady western shooter with a lot of aim and reflex based cowboy gunslinger shootouts, mixed with a shallow character advancement and a minimal upgrade system.
The graphic is solid for modern standards and the cell shading (aka, 'comic') graphic style really worked well with the game.
It's strong points are, no doubt, the actual gunplay, which is fast and furious and VERY rewarding as you gun down dozen after dozen of bandits, throwing dynamte in between and shooting it mid-air for a devasting airburst combo... and the story.
Well yeah, you wouldn'T expect it from an ARCADE SHOOTER, but CoJ:Gunslinger has a quite decent storyline... and the best storytelling I've yet seen. And unique at that.
You don't just get multiple-choice dialogs or cutscenes. You get narrated 'comics' and, more importantly, have the entire gameplay narrated. Additionally, you often encounter spots in the game where the narration 'jumps' as your 'listeners' (bar patrons) ask 'But how did X happen?' and suddenly the entire level changes to accomodate to the new focus of the protagonists storytelling.
Of course, the game doesn't come without weaknesses: First of all, the gameplay is a bit repetitive. It's all about shooting stuff, with minor variations. There's no stealth like in the first CoJ, nor does leveling the 3 offered path's change much. You get the occasionall turret / dodge+nade / bossfight, but that's it.
Another downside could be called the lack of multiplayer. The game merely offers you a 'time attack' mode which has online highscore tables. Lack of a multiplayer is not necessaryly a killerpoint for a good singleplayer game...
But the biggest issue is CoJ's content: About 4-8 hours for the campaign, depending on how good and fast you play it. Of course you can now replay the campaing on a higher difficulty (and with the + option which keeps your unlocked skills), but for a linear-story based game, that's not all that great.
As result, I would say CoJ:Gunslinger is a nice wild west arcade shooter with an unique style of storytelling that really is worth giving it a try. It won't last you throught a week, but if you can grab it for cheap (in my case I paid 5€, which may even be too much), I can recommend it.
Rating 7/10 (mainly because of it's subpar price-playtime ratio)
PS: I see Steam labels it with 3h on my account, but I can't but feel that is wrong, I played 2 evenings of 2-3 hours each...

There’s four big things to do in this game: story mode, liberation, collectables, and challenges.
The story mode really isn’t much, even compared to Just Cause 2.  Most of the characters aren’t very interesting and the missions really aren’t that novel but they do provide a break from the other parts of the game.
The liberation is the big thing Just Cause has done for so long.  Basically, go in and blow up all the stuff with red paint on it.  But it ISN’T basic at all!  JC3 provides loads of ways to get that done from simply shooting at them to rocket launchers to tanks.  When you blow up all the red stuff in a base, your fellow rebels instantly swoop in at take over.  Liberating towns is a bit more complicated but only a bit more.  Every time you liberate a town or base, some challenges open up.
There are several kinds of challenges from car/plane/boat races to handing you infinite ammo and seeing how much you can destroy in 2 minutes.  Depending on how well you do, you earn 0 to 5 stars (gears – whatever).  These are totaled up over different challenges to earn upgrades to your equipment like being able to hold more grenades or adding a nitro boost to vehicles you request.
There are also many ad-hoc challenges that you can earn anytime just by playing the game.  These are things like number of kills without reloading, car jump distance, and distance travelled in a soap box car.  They will pop up in the upper right when one of them is getting near or above your personal best.
It isn’t just your own score up there, though, and it isn’t every person that ever played the game including dozens of cheaters.  It’s your friends that have played the game plus a few random people (which will be replaced by more friends if they start playing the game).  I’ve enjoyed that quite a bit – it hit just the right mix of challenge and attainability for me.
The collectables are mostly pretty blah.  I did enjoy collecting vehicles simply because some of them are a real challenge to get to the chop shops but the rewards for finding all the tapes/vintage parts/shrines didn’t seem to come anywhere near justifying the work you have to do to get them and there's not much fun in homing in on them or flying to a ? mark on the map.
The game's grapple hook is hugely fun!  This is where your own creativity really gets a workout.  With the grapple you can pull yourself quickly forward, latch on to a car and pull yourself on top of it, latch yourself to a ledge and pull yourself up, and lots more.  You can also hold down the button after attaching and attach the other side of the grapple to something else, tethering them together.  Holding down shift then pulls those two things together.  It’s amazing what you can do with this simple mechanic!
A word on the controls, which have been getting a pretty bad wrap.  The controls for the wing suit, grapple, and airplanes seem pretty bad at first.  The grapple just has a lot of functionality, though, and the wingsuit/airplanes are simply supposed to be hard to control.  You’ll get used to the grapple pretty quickly and some practice will get you flying well enough in the wingsuit and airplanes.
There’s definitely some not-so-good stuff.
First the specs.  A lot of folks with minimum specs are getting really poor performance.  If you’re anywhere near the lower bounds, keep your finger on the Refund button.  If you’re having performance issues you can try a few tweaks but don’t go over that 2 hour limit!
For whatever reason the game makes you sit there for several seconds before it finally decides to get on with loading the game.  It’s nice in that you don’t have to interact at all to get into the game but why does it make you sit and watch Rico on the beach for so long!?  At least you've got time to go make a drink while the game loads up.
There’s also just one and only one save.  If your save gets corrupted or you aren’t thinking and start a new game up… oops.  Be sure to go into the Documents\Square Enix\Just Cause 3\ folder and back up your save folder every now and again, just in case.
There are some other nagging bugs but nothing too terrible.
At full price the DLC might be a bit expensive for what you get but they are pretty fun and well worth it if you find them on sale.  (The XL version of the game includes all three.)  You’ll have access to them about a quarter of the way through the game and they’ll be a pretty good challenge at that point.  You might want to lay off some of the weapons you get, though, because they are devastating.  (Though it’s nice to be devastating from time to time.  ;)

This review will cover the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series including: S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Clear Sky and S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat as I don't intend to spoil the story and there is no need to review the same game concept three times.
The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is the ultimate way to release your inner slav!
Some have referred to this series as the Russian version of Fallout however, unlike Fallout, the game is based in and around a real event i.e. the Chernobyl disaster zone in modern-day Ukraine, formerly the Soviet Union. The series as a whole is an intense, atmospheric, story-driven FPS set in real, open world environments that you could visit today... given a proper tour guide and a rad suit. In addition to the immersive experience the games are undoubtedly going to glitch and contain graphics that look like they came straight out of the Soviet Union but just like taking a swig of fine vodka; it burns on the way down but leaves you feeling great in the end. One can expect to sink about 20-30 hours a game on vanilla, considering you don't speed run it, and can potentially sink many more in if you experiment with the vast modding community that does everything from fixing graphics/errors to completely overhauling the game into a 100-hour epic (Pripyat-Misery mod). With the reasonable sale price of $20.00 USD (or less) for the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. bundle, you will undoubtedly get your monies worth.
A recommendation if you like slavs, vodka, immersive story-driven FPSs and having a good time.

"Control" is the name of the game this time around. Proper use of the Turn() system allows you to master the flow of every battle, and can result in some amazing combos. You also have complete control over all of your abilities; since each ability has an active, passive, and upgrade version, there's hundreds of different ways to play the game, and you're incouraged to mix and match all of your abilities. You even have control over the enemies; removing "limiters" from the Process in order to increase both the risk and reward.
The story starts out in media res, which can lead to some confusion, but if you're paying attention (and with Logan Cunningham  providing narration again, why wouldn't you be?), the plot fits nicely together by the end.
The one real problem I had with Transistor was how shot it was; you can clear it in about six hours. But with New Game, optional challenges, and a boatload of skill combinations you probably didn't get around to using the first time, there's plenty of game to enjoy.

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 is the main game we point the finger at when we look at the negative aspects of Call of Duty, and rightfully so. Before I delve deeper, I would like to start out by addressing the controversy between Call of Duty and Battlefield. While I do prefer Battlefield, I do NOT despise the COD franchise. I had moderate enjoyment with Call of Duty 4, and a blast with Black Ops 2. However, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 is easily my least favorite in the franchise. Without further ado, lets dive in.
What does Modern Warfare 2 do wrong? The first place is the campaign. While the story was decent in the game, it was a big disapointment. To no suprise, it is a linear corridoor shooter, as you mow up enemies and stop evil Russian men. Nothing new here, and there is no motivation to play the campaign. The only REAL motive I can think of is if you took alot of enjoyment in COD 4 campaign, and want to see what happens to your favorite characters in the franchise.
Next we have Spec Ops, which is a spectacular addition to the game. The minigames are superb in this game with great level design, and is a blast with friends. I took alot of enjoyment holding off enemies, mostly due to the replayabilty and freedom of this gamemode, in contrast to the Campaign, which forces you to put rockets on certain targets.
Finally we have the multiplayer, the heart and soul of the game. And let me tell you, is it horrid. This is not because the game is not "realistic" enough - come on, we are in an arcade shooter. It is because mechanics are bad. Yes, they gel well, and the game doesn't feel clunky, but they are just flat out bad design choices. The first issue is create-a-class, which looks very dynamic at first, but essentially boils down to a handful of gun and attachment combos that are overpowered. This makes gunplay boil down not to skill, reaction time, or map knowledge - but who has the best overpowered gun. Same goes for perks and deathstreaks. I would have much more enjoyment in making a class, and finding a setup that suits my playstyle, in contrast to this game.The game also has no emphasis on teamwork, mostly due in part to killstreaks that cater completely towards racking up more kills. Not to mention, hacking in this game is horrid - but that is a whole 'nother story within itself.

To conclude, Spec Ops is not worth purchasing this game. While it is fun while it lasts, you will be forced into multiplayer, which is terrible. The games' mechanics only allow a handful of good classes, and that is the only way to do well in the game.  Combined with a lack of emphasis on teamwork, the game becomes a muddled mess more than a competitive arcade shooter. If you want the best experience possible, I would highly reccomend picking up Black Ops 2, which fixes many of the problems addressed above.

--Why I'm a not reccomend--
I really want to reccomend the game but for it's biggest glaring flaw.
The constant cycle of loss.
Like Rust, the game is currently too hostile to anyone who doesn't have all the time in the world and the inclination to spend it in the game, who has a big group of friends who are likewise in the same boat, and thus can overcome the current flaws in the game and prosper.
You start the game off naked and with basically nothing on a beach, and I guess the goal if there is one is to gather resources, craft and build your way up to a bigger and better base, with bigger and better equipment and maybe even take the throne and become king.
It's nice to have a sort of ultimate goal, but as you know only one can be king, and because of the amount of time and effort required to build up, most of you will never see that crown on your head. Most of you will never see the top teir building blocks and equipment either.
You'll spend your evenings when you play building up, only to log out that night and leave your character "sleeping" in the game world.
Come the next time you log in I can basically guarantee you will have lost everything.
Your base will be gutted if not in ruins, all your gear stolen, your character killed and even your bed (spawn point) and crest (lbasically a land deed) destroyed.
You will log on in the same position you did when you started the game. Naked and on a beach with sweet F-all to your name.
This is pretty much the deal-breaker, since the game is effectively about building up, but inevitably you are always shot right back down to to the bottom. Your time is thus in all meaningful ways, wasted.
It's true that joining guilds helps, but on most servers the established guilds aren't recruiting, and they dominate all the other guilds/individuals in a textbook pyramid of haves and have nots. It would make Rust blush.
Even then, being in a guild is no garuntee. Sure you may have friends to play with (which make any poor game better anyway), but if the guild isn't big and powerful enough, it's too easy ultimately for another guild to break in and ruin it for your group instead of just yourself. The only upside is you'll have people to share your greif and sense of loss with.
The more peaceful servers are roleplay servers and thus PvP is heavily restricted. This may not be entirely a bad thing as long as they have active admins and events and stuff, but most of these are going whitelist which means you cannot just join up when you have free time and feel like playing, because whitelisted servers require applications.
Any public RP server may be a more pleasant environment but due to their public nature still suffer from raiders wrecking/taking your stuff when you're logged off.
Basically (and I don't mean to be rude to those who do have the time) if you have a life and find the efforts of hours of gameplay undone every time you log off, this game isn't worth the purchase.

However, the gameplay is solid, as are the mechanics. It really does feel like a true extension of the Souls series. There are a few issues though. The hit detection can be slippery at times. I'm not saying this because I'm not good at the new dodging mechanics, I'm saying this as a veteren and (what I would consider) a fairly decent player on this game. Some attacks, when dodged properly, just don't feel like you are really going to hit the IFs, and sometimes you don't. The Smelter Demon is a prime example of this. Other little things also bring this game down as well, things that can be nit-picked abd scrutinized. Forest of Fallen Giants spearmen, nuff said. For immersive RPG fans, this game also suffers from a lack of not feeling connected or in-tune with your character, which is a huge bummer for gamers like myself.
Now some of the good things. Weapon and armor variety is solid. You can honestly take almost any gear to endgame. The game isn't nearly as exploitable as Dark Souls. There's a bit more of an actual soft-class feel to the building system, which I personally like. It can be a really fun experience, especially when doing bro-op playthroughs with friends. There's a substantial amount of replay value as well. granted, it isn't as much as other games I've played in the past like Dead Space 2 and other such nonsense, but nonetheless, still a good deal of it. There's always time to try new builds and collect new gear. Some crucial game mechanics have stayed in this installment, such as stun-locking, counters, IF dodging (though slippery at times), and others have been tweaked to provide an overall more challenging gameplay experience.
When all is said and done I give this game an 8/10. It didn't quite live up to what it could have been, and missed the mark in a lot of places, and in some, even feels rushed. It can never compare to the magic we all experienced while playing Dark Souls for the very first time, as much as a PTSD simulator as it was. We should take this game for what it is. Though it falls short, it picks its self back and and gets right back into the fight. Just as you will, over, and over again. It is still, first and foremost, a Souls game,

There’s four big things to do in this game: story mode, liberation, collectables, and challenges.
The story mode really isn’t much, even compared to Just Cause 2.  Most of the characters aren’t very interesting and the missions really aren’t that novel but they do provide a break from the other parts of the game.
The liberation is the big thing Just Cause has done for so long.  Basically, go in and blow up all the stuff with red paint on it.  But it ISN’T basic at all!  JC3 provides loads of ways to get that done from simply shooting at them to rocket launchers to tanks.  When you blow up all the red stuff in a base, your fellow rebels instantly swoop in at take over.  Liberating towns is a bit more complicated but only a bit more.  Every time you liberate a town or base, some challenges open up.
There are several kinds of challenges from car/plane/boat races to handing you infinite ammo and seeing how much you can destroy in 2 minutes.  Depending on how well you do, you earn 0 to 5 stars (gears – whatever).  These are totaled up over different challenges to earn upgrades to your equipment like being able to hold more grenades or adding a nitro boost to vehicles you request.
There are also many ad-hoc challenges that you can earn anytime just by playing the game.  These are things like number of kills without reloading, car jump distance, and distance travelled in a soap box car.  They will pop up in the upper right when one of them is getting near or above your personal best.
It isn’t just your own score up there, though, and it isn’t every person that ever played the game including dozens of cheaters.  It’s your friends that have played the game plus a few random people (which will be replaced by more friends if they start playing the game).  I’ve enjoyed that quite a bit – it hit just the right mix of challenge and attainability for me.
The collectables are mostly pretty blah.  I did enjoy collecting vehicles simply because some of them are a real challenge to get to the chop shops but the rewards for finding all the tapes/vintage parts/shrines didn’t seem to come anywhere near justifying the work you have to do to get them and there's not much fun in homing in on them or flying to a ? mark on the map.
The game's grapple hook is hugely fun!  This is where your own creativity really gets a workout.  With the grapple you can pull yourself quickly forward, latch on to a car and pull yourself on top of it, latch yourself to a ledge and pull yourself up, and lots more.  You can also hold down the button after attaching and attach the other side of the grapple to something else, tethering them together.  Holding down shift then pulls those two things together.  It’s amazing what you can do with this simple mechanic!
A word on the controls, which have been getting a pretty bad wrap.  The controls for the wing suit, grapple, and airplanes seem pretty bad at first.  The grapple just has a lot of functionality, though, and the wingsuit/airplanes are simply supposed to be hard to control.  You’ll get used to the grapple pretty quickly and some practice will get you flying well enough in the wingsuit and airplanes.
There’s definitely some not-so-good stuff.
First the specs.  A lot of folks with minimum specs are getting really poor performance.  If you’re anywhere near the lower bounds, keep your finger on the Refund button.  If you’re having performance issues you can try a few tweaks but don’t go over that 2 hour limit!
For whatever reason the game makes you sit there for several seconds before it finally decides to get on with loading the game.  It’s nice in that you don’t have to interact at all to get into the game but why does it make you sit and watch Rico on the beach for so long!?  At least you've got time to go make a drink while the game loads up.
There’s also just one and only one save.  If your save gets corrupted or you aren’t thinking and start a new game up… oops.  Be sure to go into the Documents\Square Enix\Just Cause 3\ folder and back up your save folder every now and again, just in case.
There are some other nagging bugs but nothing too terrible.
At full price the DLC might be a bit expensive for what you get but they are pretty fun and well worth it if you find them on sale.  (The XL version of the game includes all three.)  You’ll have access to them about a quarter of the way through the game and they’ll be a pretty good challenge at that point.  You might want to lay off some of the weapons you get, though, because they are devastating.  (Though it’s nice to be devastating from time to time.  ;)

There are few bugs here and there (mostly concerning sidequests), and you must learn to play the game without tutorial, so apart from knowing different weapons, what ammunition they have and how to manage your inventory, so you can run when needed and most of all, do not take all loot you find, only the best, throw away old weapons because if you will follow main quest you will find better, and armour too.
The thing about this game is, there is radiation all around world and closer you get to your final mission, more protection you need to effectively survive and apart from that, protection fighting enemies is also essential if not loads of medications for different injuries, and also food to recover health and stop hunger.
While you can play this unlimited time because enemies respawn when you travel there and back through locations, sometimes you will meet stronger enemies in your beginner area and always be careful not to step into anomaly or trap, because it is pretty deadly even if you wear strong armour.
Bigger armour you wear more capacity you get for inventory while you will lose ability to run and it is not really capacity efficient when armour weighs 1 fourth of your inventory.
I like this game very much while it aches me when I struggled in the beginning and did not know how to proceed to main mission and such.
So little tip for you, press P, press double on your mission to track it, find or buy some anti-radiation, sell and save on every opportunity because most NPCs have limited money and do not buy weapons and ammunition from you.
Do not shoot your allies. I accidently sniped down ally so all his allies turned to enemies and now everytime I go to prievously friendly areas where were merchants I find them guarding.
And it is also more rewarding when you use your knife on enemies, you will not make mistake using it on ally. Though, most of enemies will be aware of you because they will have allies near.
Important note is you make noise all the time. All you hear as audio is noise you make that enemies hear, if you want to surprise them, watch the indicator down left. Beeping means there is anomaly nearby.
Be aware, time passes quite slow and you do not want to appear in the middle of nowhere in dark with no directions and ammunition. Plan your route and spend all your money because you will stack a lot of them early on, though you will be able to buy some super expensive armour, you will soon find it somewhere lying hidden, though those treasures are very few. There are also few weapons you will not be able to buy but find instead.
Have fun.

Hello everybody, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for Light Apprentice by Amazu Media.
Light Apprentice is a game that mixes multiple genres together. Most notably are RPG’s, Adventure Games and Visual Novels. The game’s story plays out like a comic book with various panels showing various scenes. Battles also take place within the boxes of the comic book, as does the exploration phase.
The story follows a young man from the past named Nate and a blueling called Tlob as they journey across a barren wasteland of a planet to save the environment and the people that live there. The story is very environmentalist friendly and it talks about various issues that impact our own planet today. It also covers themes like slavery, greed and imperialism.
Even though the story covers these rather serious topics, it does so in a way that makes it enjoyable yet poignant. It doesn’t feel forced and the characters are great as well. The story in this volume is 4 chapters long and I imagine that there will be much more story to this game in the future.
The gameplay portion of the game is split into two different areas. The first area focuses on exploration and plays like a point and click adventure game. In this mode you can interact with the world, activate switches, open doors and chests, and attack enemies.
The second portion of the game is combat. Combat in Light Apprentice plays somewhat like Costume Quest mixed with some Final Fantasy (Classic FF). You have the option to attack, defend, use items or use skills. Skills are unlocked whenever you need to make an important choice in the story and each requires a specific amount of spirit to use. Spirit is obtained when you hit an enemy or when an enemy hits you. The max spirit you can have at any time is 10. The stronger the skill, the more spirit you’ll need to use it. You’re also limited to 3 potions during a battle and they don’t replenish automatically so if you use one you’ll need to manually add a new one.
If you happen to die in battle the game gives you the option to replay the battle until you defeat it.
I’ll also mention that the game can be pretty buggy at times. Most notably in the first and fourth chapter. There are random slowdowns in both which affects playability.
Overall, Light Apprentice has been an enjoyable adventure. Like a few other games that I’ve reviewed, the game touches upon real world issues. It’s done really well and in a pretty lighthearted way. The story is entertaining but poignant and I felt it was done really well. The slowdowns that I encountered were a bit of a pain (Especially in chapter 4) but most of the game played well for me. I definitely recommend the game but it might be wise to wait for a couple patches to fix these issues first.

First Impressions / Gameplay

I would definitely recommend this game, however, this is also available for free on Android and iOS. It's so unique that anyone who enjoys a good story and RPG should check it out. This is an Early Access Report, meaning that it will be revised after the game leaves Early Access.
Even the 3D world is connected by boxes, much like a comic strip. When you’re exploring, the camera slides between panels the way one’s eye would when reading. So cool.
It’s your typical save the world situation, but the story is well written nonetheless. The presentation style really helps in delivering the significance of the events that occur. Combat scenes, reflections of the past, and  exchanges between characters are all presented in still images over which the text appears and then the next panel is presented when you click.
A party of young adventurer who you’ll grow fond of over the course of their journey.
There are mini games associated with every skill and spell and a timing ring when you attack or defend. This makes it so that
You can kill every monster in sight or you can stun them and make a run for it, leaving them unscathed. You could even do a combination of the two—the decision is yours.
Your character levels up and gains stats. You have no control over distribution, unfortunately. You also find equipment in chests, which can be equipped to your characters. Only the weapons are character-specific.
These come up in the normal course of play and range from finding items from a list to circumventing obstacles in order to progress. Much of the time, the answer to these puzzles can be found by exploring the surrounding area.
It's seriously catchy and oftentimes I'll recognize the base tune even though it's been sped up, slowed down, or changed in pitch to suit the scene it accompanies. I really, really like it.

How can a game about a border control booth be interesting? It's the characters involved. The premise is simple enough, point and click your way through documents making sure people have all the correct papers required to enter your glorious nation. Earn enough money to feed your family and keep them safe, and everything else is just secondary... or at least that's what you think.
As you play through this game familiar faces are formed, characters and their stories start to become apparent and a small morality check starts to creep across your thoughts - do I keep my family safe or do I help this stranger out?
This game might not be for all, as it's simple graphics and audio might put some people off, and it's not the most 'exciting' of games, however if you don't require constant action and zany cutscenes than you might find something different in Papers, Please.

Factorio is simply amazing, and it is only getting better. Just look at the amount of time played by some of the reviewers, or of friends on your friend list who own it. In terms of value - I could only dream of living in a world where developers put this amount of time, effort, community collaboration, and content into their work. In this day and age where quality early access games are few and far between, and microtransactions filled free to play games domintate the market in terms of sheer numbers, drowing out smaller and newer developers, it is such an amazing refreshing feeling to see a game like Factorio.
Factorio is a sandbox openworld building game where your goal is to automate everything. It shares a similar concept with many games, in such that each resource requires a combination of resources that come before it to create. You start small, but believe you me, you get big! Towards the end of the tech trees when your factory gets really big, it is truly astounding that it actually functions and that YOU actually made it! It reminds me a lot of lego's in a sense, and also the human body, in that each little part does its function and as a whole they create this amazingly complex machine. You actually learn a lot while playing it too, in an engineer'ish type way. Sometimes changing just one thing creates this huge butterfly effect, and rather than reverting it back, figuring out why and making it work is so much more fun. With multiplayer (which I will talk about a little more down below) you can see in real time how people look at the same problem and solve it in different ways, which I find fascinating.
There are a million ways to play this game, but personally I (and I know so many others do too, as this is one of the core concepts that draws people like us to this genre) love figuring out how to make each little contraption work as efficiently as possible. I also loved making my first factory as symmetrical as I could, just because it looked so cool. Copper on the left, iron on the right in the exact pattern. Oil up the middle with some green chips on each side just because it looked cool!
If you have even the slightest bit of OCD this game will turn it on overdrive, but in a bizzarly fun way...I can't really explain it, just trust me xD
The developer is constantly adding to the game, and listens to the community feedback, which is in my opinion neccesary in 2016. There is so much more I could say about this game, but I will just add this one final and AWESOME end note....It already has *PERFECTLY* working multiplayer, which makes it just THAT much better. These are my absolute favorite types of games, and I have always wanted a good open sandbox game to play with my friend(s), and now I have one.
If you are even considering buying this game for whatever reason, do yourself a favor buy it. These are exactly the types of dev's we need in the gaming world today, our support means everything!
*An easier way to use muliplayer is being added in one of the next updates, but as of now just use the program "evolve" which allows your to share an IP address with whoever you party with, and just join a party with whoever you want to play with.

More of the Just Cause magic, without quite the same...magic.
I like to play this as a madness simulator, not a combat playground. A big part of the fun for me is watching everything go sideways. I'm pretty god damn good at this, and things still regularly go haywire for me. I suggest just embracing all of the chaos and seeing it as a generative madness simulator.
And the only time I find the game to get repetitive is when I get focused on achievement and box ticking. When I'm just zooming around and doing what I feel like, everything is great. (I recommend turning off the HUD except for reticles. This removes the annoying "CHAOS" popup every time you destroy something, and lets you see just how damn gorgeous this game is.)
I've been taking out oil platforms and really enjoying the frantic scramble through them. They're like big insane puzzles with bullets flying everywhere.
I'm a little let down by the lack of visual variety and the lack of density on the main island. I think the smaller archipelagoes are incredible in both senses - the second island, to the west, is particularly impressive, with all those amazing caves and cliffs. But the big island is just...empty. It's weird to have so much room to...not do anything in. Just Cause 2 ended up being almost too MUCH, but this is weirdly desolate in the north.
Finally, there's also something missing in this game, that last 5% of magic that JC2 had (though maybe it's just that JC2 was my First Time, and is therefore beautiful and special. Yep, 70+ hours worth of beautiful). I think it has something to do with the town/installation takeover mechanic. It encourages me to identify the big high value targets in the area, go eff them up, and go to the next one, where JC2's more diffuse '100% everything you come across' meant I didn't see things as pieces of larger regions, but strings of experiences. It meant I went from one thing to the next organically. Here in JC3 I see the ruined towns and have a moment of 'huh, sad' for what they represent - crushed rebel bases, razed towns - but because they're not targets, they mean nothing. They're backdrop. I move along and head toward the towns and bases filled with red explodey objects. Whereas in JC2 everything was a target. Everything. There were too many, perhaps, but there was no reason not to have gameplay everywhere.
It's a luxury problem, for sure - this game is incredible - but I miss that sense of everything being full of promise and play.

I pre-ordered the game, I followed all the videos and promotional content they released before launch. I didn't complain about the pre-order DLC. From Rome 1 and Medieval 2 I had a very positive experience with CA and so I let the whole thing slide and show faith.
How do I feel now? I feel like my girlfriend I was with for five years tells me the night I propose to her, that she is running off to marry my best friend whom she was dating for 2 years behind my back. I feel THAT cheated.
Why?
Promotionally CA did its best to lure us to buy a game with high expectations: "40% higher budget", "it will look much better at launch, this is pre-alpha footage", "our goal is to make Rome 2 the best Total War game yet"
We trusted them and gave them money for a product we have not seen.
What did we get?
I'll state my positives so to be fair:
- Cinematic camera
- Addition of naval warfare (it is unplayable but is the best in the series :P)
- Depth and number of factions
To the important stuff:
Battles:
- Super awkward formations and unit movement
- No realistic collision between clashing units. Ironically Rome 1 had more realism than its successor
- Animation seems idiotic and fake
- Individual persons interact only 1v1, so if even if they are outnumbered one unit can survive waves after waves of enemies
- When charging, units awkwardly stop and lose momentum instantly (and this applies to the entire unit)
- Music is unspirational and does not change with battle conditions
- Control areas in open fields (whaaat??). Instead of playing the enemy and thinking strategically, you run to a controll area, stay for a little time and you win the battle
- Battles are super short
- AI is stupid beyond imagination
- Buggy and laggy as hell
- Naval battles are even more broken and buggy
- UI makes no sense, all units look exactly the same
- One spot for unit condition, so you lose precious time to understand all the status ailments of a unit e.g. fighiting, taking fire, firing etc.
- and much more
Campaign:
- AI is even more stupid than that in battles
- Diplomacy is broken with out any explanation of what led to an ally's/enemy's particular decision. AI decisions are spontaneous
- Very easy even in high difficulty level
- Building system makes no sense
- Loooooong wait turns
- and much more
Overall, Rome 2 is a beta game. It is blunt, boring and uninspirational
I attribute the fiasco to awful project management, but I can only speculate
I understand CA tried to mend it with continious patching, but a game so flawed in its core is unfixable no matter how you try to improve specific features. Also, when you talk about patching at launch, means you should not have launched in the first place.

Turn-based RPG Adventure
Medium-Hard
7/10
The main game consists of two modes, adventure mode and battle mode.
Adventure mode is a point-and-click mode, where you move around interacting with different objects and characters.
Battle Mode is a turn-based combat mode, where the player will select which potion, spell, ability or attack to use on the enemy.
The battles in Battle Mode can be won in two different ways.
The pacifist way, where you will drain their stamina and thereby stunning them. Once all enemies are stunned at the same time the battle can be won peacefully.
The aggressive way, where you will drain their health and thereby killing them. Once all enemies are killed the battle is won.
Each attack, spell and ability has it own unique mini-game and success in the mini-game determines the degree of success (or failure) the attack, spell or ability has. This is where the games origins can be seen the most, as this game was ported from mobile to PC and the mini-games shows this. This is not a mad thing, the game has full mouse integration and the only issue you may encounter is timing and precision.
The few puzzles there is in Adventure Mode is fairly straight forward.
8/10
The Narrative is presented in cut-scenes in the form of animated comic book pages.
The player is presented with multiple choices along their journey which influences how the story turns up in the story and which abilities different characters learns.
The story is brilliantly written. it will make you laugh and cry and everything in between.
8/10
As previously mentioned cut-scenes are shown in the form of animated comic book pages. The adventure mode and combat mode is pre-rendered 2.5D with bright colors in a cartoon style.
7/10
The music is most fitting for the game. The music in cut-scenes drives the emotion and the music in combat mode has your adrenaline pumping. The sound effects are top quality and very fitting for the game.
7.5/10
If you are looking a great take on classic RPG adventure games with an amazing story, adorable graphics, relatable characters and lovely music, this is the game for you.

is a roleplaying game with a story told in a comic book style. It’s a fun game with likeable characters fighting to try and save the world. An important feature is that of choices as what you do during the game affects your play style and story. I enjoy games where “choices matter” and in this RPG they can literally affect which skills you can and cannot use in battle which helps shape your characters and gameplay styles. While the game premiered on mobile devices, I played the Steam release on my computer. My review is based on the Early Access build, and -at the time of publication- only volume one is available to play. I’ll update this when the game changes.
The story starts of with a young girl named Tlob, who is a mage and healer, looking for the Light Apprentice who happens to be our main character Nate. Nate has been in suspended animation for three hundred years and the world he awakens to is not what he remembers. War and pollution have ruined the once beautiful planet and Nate vows to set things right with Tlob’s help, doing so means finding the other Apprentices. The story is a bit heavy handed with its environmental message and the moral system of “choices matter” pressures the player to not be a jerk.
As of this moment, there is only one volume of the story available to play, the game promises three in total. This first story arc mainly serves to introduce us to the characters and the world around them. Besides Nate and Tlob there is also Mya, the Fire Apprentice, and K-Ken who half human and half monster. While we get some flashbacks for Nate, this volume doesn’t have much in the way of character development aside from showing us their basic personalities. For me, the story started off slow but built up as things progressed leaving me wanting more.
The first thing players will notice about this game is there are two modes. The story mode which feels like a comic book, and the adventure mode where you wander around and fight bad guys. On the computer, I played with my mouse since I didn’t feel the need to use a controller, but it’s an option, and a nice option to have. Battles are turn-based, however, and to perform attacks or skills or even defend you have to pay attention to the screen because of quick time mini games. You’ll either love them or hate them, I was personally alright with them but they became tedious. It seemed very gimmicky and tacked on; it probably made more sense on mobile.
As mentioned before it takes a “choices matter” approach. During the story mode this can be choosing to take a certain side in a conflict to figuring out what is the best way for Mya to make money in town. It isn’t always expressed which chose is the best or even what might happen. Taking the side of a corrupt politician or a race of creatures who have been slaves sounds easy, figuring out if Nate or Tlob should talk to frog people not so much. Your choices affect how the story flows and also certain ones unlock certain skills. Choices also matter in battle, you can fight aggressively or passively which means defending and then “forgiving” the enemy. This was my biggest issue. I found the battles to often be unbalanced to the point where I had no choice but to defend just to survive. There are no random encounters so grinding isn’t easy and your stats are directly affected by the gear your character wears which you can’t purchase, only find. By the end of the first volume I had a very unbalanced team and couldn’t even bother to use skills often because I needed the energy for healing just to keep people alive.
The story itself is mainly told through a comic book presentation with panels and dialogue. The artwork is colorful and inviting, perfect for gamers of all ages. The adventure mode and battles have a more 3D feel to them and all of the animation in the game is pretty smooth. Monster design is a bit repetitive but this isn’t a huge issue at all. The game has no voice acting in it but does have a wonderful soundtrack that fits the aesthetics very well. I honestly have nothing negative to say at all in terms of graphics and audio, for a game originally on mobile devices it ports beautifully to the PC.
+ Lovely graphics and music.
+ Comic book-style storytelling method really works well.
+ Choices truly matter and help shape the game you play.
+ Story is well written and a tale of caution and hope.
+ Characters are enjoyable to follow on their adventure.
- I found the battles to be frustrating and sometimes limiting in how I could play.
- No Steam trading cards or achievements at the moment.
- Currently the price does not match the amount of content the game offers.
shows a lot of promise. It has what all good RPGs need, a solid story with interesting characters. Whatever issues I have with the gameplay weren’t enough to stop me from completing volume one because I wanted to see where the story went. It’s a fresh take on the role playing game, giving players more control over how their experience plays out. As it’s still Early Access there may be some glitches, but I didn’t find any game-breaking ones. While I do feel the price is a bit steep for the game in its current state, I feel the completed version will be worth it in the end.
7/10

After playing through and beating the original Dark Souls last spring with a friend, I was extremely excited to start playing Dark Souls II when it was released last year. School ended up getting in the way, and so I never really had a chance to play it until last December.
Wow. What a game. I enjoyed it as much, if not more, as the original Dark Souls. The mechanics were improved upon from the first game, and the graphics were significantly better. While there was no Blighttown like there was in the first game, there were some incredibly frustrating areas to navigate, such as the areas before the Executioner's Chariot, mostly due to poison.
Like the first game, I had a couple of choices to go to do my quest, and I opted to complete all three DLC areas after collecting the four primal souls. I enjoyed the areas opened. In my opinion, the boss at the end of one of the DLCs (I can't remember which) was the toughest boss in the game. It was the dragon that breathed toxin, took significantly reduced damage, and caused your weapons to wear down faster. That fight was the one I was most frustrated over, and was the most rewarding one to finish.
I did have a few complaints with the game, however. I felt a lot of the bosses were too easy when summoning in other players or NPCs. I understand that having more players makes a fight easier by default, but I felt that, compared to the first game, allied help made the bosses too much easier. I also did not like being invaded while a hollow, because I do not enjoy PvP in the Dark Souls games, and in the first I had the option of avoiding that if I chose to not be human. I chose to do a Strength build in this game, after doing a Dexterity/Pyromancy build in Dark Souls I, and I found that I used the Homonculous Mace (came as a preorder bonus) for pretty much the entirety of the game. Perhaps it was my play style, but I could not find any better weapons to use for my shield/one weapon build.
The graphics were nice. They weren't fantastic, but they could have been better. In some unreachable areas, it was very obvious the same texture was repeated frequently in plains and rocks. Graphics do not generally make or break a game for me, and the textures had a small fuzziness to them, but overall, I found the game quite beautiful.
I found this game a lot of fun. It took me 63 hours to beat it, and I did not partake in any soul farming like I did in the previous game. In fact, I often found I had sufficient souls to do what I needed to. I loved the mechanics and gameplay, and I would play this game again.

I got this game two days ago at the writing of this review, after seeing Markiplier play it on Youtube. It looked fun, so i got it. I rate if games were worth buying by the price/hours played. When i have got less than one pound per hour, i consider that game to have been worth it. The only game i reached that point faster in than this was Fallout 4, and thats only because i had more free time.
While it might be a bit overwhelming, looking at the ad for it and thinking "how will i ever manage all that?", you start small and grow with your factory, constantly learning new things. You will get frustated at times, but always due to a problem thats easily fixed. One exception to this is if its a problem in your circuits and conveyers, but that means its your fault, not the games.
The aliens come suddenly at a certain research level, so make sure to build defences ASAP to avoid getting caught off guard. Alien swarm sizes grow with your tech, so be sure to keep building.
The car takes a bit of getting used to, but is VERY useful.
Perhaps make oil a little more common? I have literal mountains of iron and copper, but am having to push far into enemy territory to try and make an outpost for oil. Maybe just bad luck.
Very fun game, if you play with a friend prepare to check the wiki on how to connect, i found reddit useful for that, and prepare to be annoyed when they break your circuit or ruin your plan.
I give it 9/10. I expect to pour hundreds of hours into this, alone and with friends. Great game, great progression, great gameplay, great fun.

From the creators of Bastion comes their next game, Transistor, which is not directly related to its predessor except for its artwork, some of the voice work, and the amazing soundtracks which both games provide.  Like Bastion, Transistor has a unique combat system all its own, a hybrid strategy/real-time combat where you can customize your build almost all the time, and can choose to use "Turn()", a way to pause time and plan out attacks while your enemies are in slo-mo, or go at it like an action game and take things as they come.  The storyline keeps you moving, and encourages diversity of the combat to fully unlock the lore of the world, integrating gameplay with story in a unique and satisfying manner.  While not necessarily quite on par with Bastion, it is still a truly amazing game that you will want to hear the music of long after you've set it aside.

I would recommend this game simply on its approach to storytelling.
As an FPS, it's ok. It doesn't do anything revolutionary, has the "Red Dead" style focus system & a few duels thrown in for good measure, which works well with the setting.
The story is set up in a manner where main character is infamous, and is retelling his story to a group of locals in a saloon. He sometimes has to fill them in on how certain events played out, as the game plays cleverly with the idea of the legend Vs the reality.
I also love the 'nuggets of truth', which are a set of collectables with (I assume) real facts and stories about the people & life in the old west.
Thusfar in, i'd hardly call the story itself award winning, but the method in which its told means I cant wait for my next venture in the old west.

A "sequel" I think, but more of a "big fish" side story (like "big fish" the movie). It's narrated by the older brother (whatever his name is I can't remember) and is told in a manor that obviously favors... well himself. In his story he's a legendary gunslinger that you get to play and in which you have to hold true to his "big fish" version, which is no harder than the Call of Juarez game and has similar 12 o'clock noon shooting standoffs... mechanics slightly tweaked.
All that aside, it feels pretty good playing a badass even if it might be a lie, and there's an impossibly predictable twist (in my opinion) that proves that some of it might have actually been part way true. Regardless, it's a fun shooter and the story is fun, so fiction or fact really makes little difference (hell all games are fiction anyway, but its odd how when a game lets you know that it changes things somewhat). In additon, it throws some notes in history that are interesting, which are not necessarily fact, but make you wonder the credibility of "history" regarding the "facts," which are not facts to begin with... they're only "his story" right...?

First impressions:
I love, loved the comic-stylings of this game so I *had* to give a shot and I wasn't disappointed! I thoroughly enjoyed every moment of my short (so far) playthrough of this game. I intend to do more episodes and get through to Chapter 2!
But seriously, if you like comic books and games, give Light Apprentice a go! It's seemingly taken the best aspects from other games (at least I thought so) and employed them very well indeed!

I've written a review for Light Apprentice here -
But, I will also say that if you like Visual Novels, or Turn-Based RPG's then Light Apprentice is probably for you :) I also greatly applaud the Dev's use of a morality system like in Undertale, as it is an option that is heavily underrated.

So, after having the developer respond to my earlier review I feel like I can now recommend this game whole heartedly.
My previous complaints were that the way the inventory system works can potentially leave you in a spot that makes it impossible to progress.  In short, whenever you use an item in your inventory that item is gone forever, even if you exit the game and reload.  As it turns out, there is a way to acquire more healing potions and other items necessary to progress, though the way you do so, while allows you to avoid getting stuck forever, brings with it a whole host of lesser problems.  Basically, there's a "Quest Mode" in the main menu, which you can hop on over to at any time and fight a series of enemies which allows you to grind for XP and healing items.  The obvious problem with this is that it basically forces the player to exit the main game and grind the items necessary to continue.  And while I have nothing against grind, so long as it's optional and the player is allowed to do it at their own volition, it is never a good idea to force the player into doing it.  Because while there are people out there who find the exercise fun (I being among them) there's a whole host of others who will find it very tedious and very tiring very fast.  To a lesser annoyance, this mechanic also forces you to exit the main game mode and play what basically amounts to a side activity before you can continue, which breaks the flow of the game somewhat.  The annoyance is lessened in this instance since the loading screen are few and brief, and you'll be back in the main meat of the game relatively quick, but it's still there, and I still can't help but feel this whole problem could be avoided simply by allowing items to respawn after you die in combat, or reload your game.
Now this has been a lot of negativity so far, but I put it up front because these were serious problems which prevented me from enjoying the game as fully as I'd like to, and the last thing I want to do is give the impression that this game is not worth your time, because it absolutely is.
The combat mechanics are very well executed, similar to other turn-based games such as Final Fantasy, Dragon Quest, and Stick of Truth.  And like all good turn based RPG's you'll start off being able to get through by bashing your way through brute force, but sooner or later you will have to adopt a strategy to go along with muscle, and you'll need to think through each of your actions in order to succeed.  It starts off simple enough but quickly becomes more complex and difficult as more characters are introduced and new combat mechanics are thrown in.  Turn based strategy nerds will find themselves right at home here, and there's also a nice learning curb for newcomers as well.
What sets this game apart from its contemporaries, however, is the unique art style and overall aesthetic of game and story.  It literally feels like you're playing a comic book, which may sound like a concept which has been done before, but not like this.  Infamous was done in a comic book style, but it didn't feel like you were playing a comic book.  TellTale games are done in comic book styles, but they don't feel like you're playing a comic book.  This, from beginning to end, feels like you're literally playing a comic book.  From the cartoony art style of the characters to the how the whole story is told using speech bubbles and pop-up text, to how every cutscene and even gameplay sections are transitioned using comic book panels, every detail has been fine tuned to give off this vibe colorful comic book goodness.  The developer really should be applauded for how much thought went into every detail to make the game feel this way.
Story wise, Light Apprentice is your basic fantasy affair, though with some slight alterations to make things a little more interesting.  You play as Nate, a boy who's been trapped in time for a few hundred years, and is suddenly awakened in order to save the world with his mystical power granted to him by the earth.  Yes, I'd be lying if I said I didn't see the avatar similarities as well.  But where avatar was sort of Disneyfied in its storytelling Light Apprentice is a little darker, allowing you to choose whether to kill or spare your opponents and even decide on some other moral choices throughout the plot.  These moral choices spice up the story, though they're not really as complex as we've seen in other games like The Walking Dead, nor are they played around with like they were in Undertale.  It's a good addition to the game, but not as well implemented as it could be.
Overall, I would absolutely recommend this game, especially if you're one for a good story and unique style this is a definite buy for you, and I look forward to what the developer has in store for this game as well as their future endeavors.
