Whew where do I begin... To start off I had played Ragnarok Online for a couple of years an had plaed other MMOs as well. So let's start off with the Pros:
1. Good Graphics - artistic and unique
2. Satisfying gameplay - gameplay is really satisfying since most skills will often have a substantial effect on opponents and allies. There are still some skills that need tweaking and bug fixing; however, I woudl say that the game's gameplay is still really solid.
Cons:
1. Grind- I have reached level 190. I can tell you that I have reached several grind walls already but the grind in this game is absurd. What happens if you're 10 levels above or below a monster? 10 levels above a monster = less exp (starting from being 5 levels below or above a monster); however,  being 10 levels below will make the monsters hit you harder in addition to having much less exp gain. It's gotten to the point that you really have to read on guides on how to use the exp cards efficiently due to the nature of the grind of this game and how unforgiving it is in terms of gaining experience due to leveling restrictions.
To top it all off, skill resets are only allowed through the use of premium currency, which is extreemely poor taste due to how much grind is involved and how the skill descriptions are really poor.
2. Trade restrictions - My god... I have never seen a game so heavily restrict on it's trading before. You can list only 1 item on the market (non premium user) and you can only trade with other players without the use of the in game currency, which prompts you to barter. Access to the market is only in towns as well. This makes market use cumbersome and often not worth using for the most part, at least from my experience.
3. Pay to win- sever items from the cash shop give combat advantages. Token = movespeed. Enchant scroll = provides you headgear with stat increases. Mind you that these increases are quite substantial, regardless of what people tell you otherwise.
4. Techinical issues- bots, server instabilities, etc. Can be fixed
5. Class Balance and equipment balance - can still be fixed; however, I really will say that the items and class balance are really out of whack right now. As an example for equipment, I am loaded with recipes but I have no materials to craft them even though I keep killing monsters, which often have spawn rates or mob densities that want us wanting more in normal maps. Not that the materials have any value on the market anyway nor can I actually sell them anyway due tot he trade restrictions hahaha.....
Overall, the game is still really rough around the edges and has still to go through a lot to improve. Currently, seeing how this is going to lift it's limited access soon to F2P players, I want to warn prospective players that this is brings in a lot of the archaic and not so good aspect of past MMOs and fails to bring the sandbox feeling of RO in the game with all the restrictions involved.
TL;DR - remove restrictions, improve archaic and obsolete MMO design (e.g. old world boss design, market access, bad spawn rates, etc.), make the grind more bearable, and balance issues in terms of skills and equipment aquisition.

I've played this for a good portion of the past two days, so here's my review so far
It's your typical MMO, it has problems with "bots"... Although, at the moment, I'm pretty sure it's just some dude at an internet cafe, in the Phillipines copy-pasting links to sites to try and scam people. I haven't seen any bot-like behaviour from "players" while outside of towns though, but KS'ing is a problem on the higher population servers/channels.
Anyways...
Unlike your typical MMO class based system, ToS uses 4 classes, but each class has numerous ranks for you to chose from and, you can switch between these ranks to gain specific skills. This allows for numerous unique builds that will either succeed or fail depending on the way you play.
Your first character will likely be a throw-away, to get you learning the game, unless you do a ton of research or follow a build guide. So far during my experience(lvl 25), ranged characters are OP in terms of PVE, as long as you are mobile(this is where the controller comes in handy), mobs can't get close enough to hurt you. I find myself going after mobs that are anywhere between 5-10 levels higher than me and aside from the higher HP, I don't struggle to kill them.
I would recommend this game to people who enjoy MMO's, that either want something a little more involved, or something with controller support.
PROS:
-Well done controller support.
-Graphics are simple, but well made.
-Combat is fun and involved.
CONS:
-No visible EXP bars. (This is a pain in the butt because of the next con)
-Leveling up pushes/damages mobs around you, so it's easy to aggro mobs on accident.
-GUI can't be customized/moved around.
-Camera position/zoom/field of view is very limited.
-Chat has very limited options/you cannot right click a name to "mute" a player.
-Players can stack on warp points, making it difficult to mute and/or report players that are spamming.

After playing through and beating the original Dark Souls last spring with a friend, I was extremely excited to start playing Dark Souls II when it was released last year. School ended up getting in the way, and so I never really had a chance to play it until last December.
Wow. What a game. I enjoyed it as much, if not more, as the original Dark Souls. The mechanics were improved upon from the first game, and the graphics were significantly better. While there was no Blighttown like there was in the first game, there were some incredibly frustrating areas to navigate, such as the areas before the Executioner's Chariot, mostly due to poison.
Like the first game, I had a couple of choices to go to do my quest, and I opted to complete all three DLC areas after collecting the four primal souls. I enjoyed the areas opened. In my opinion, the boss at the end of one of the DLCs (I can't remember which) was the toughest boss in the game. It was the dragon that breathed toxin, took significantly reduced damage, and caused your weapons to wear down faster. That fight was the one I was most frustrated over, and was the most rewarding one to finish.
I did have a few complaints with the game, however. I felt a lot of the bosses were too easy when summoning in other players or NPCs. I understand that having more players makes a fight easier by default, but I felt that, compared to the first game, allied help made the bosses too much easier. I also did not like being invaded while a hollow, because I do not enjoy PvP in the Dark Souls games, and in the first I had the option of avoiding that if I chose to not be human. I chose to do a Strength build in this game, after doing a Dexterity/Pyromancy build in Dark Souls I, and I found that I used the Homonculous Mace (came as a preorder bonus) for pretty much the entirety of the game. Perhaps it was my play style, but I could not find any better weapons to use for my shield/one weapon build.
The graphics were nice. They weren't fantastic, but they could have been better. In some unreachable areas, it was very obvious the same texture was repeated frequently in plains and rocks. Graphics do not generally make or break a game for me, and the textures had a small fuzziness to them, but overall, I found the game quite beautiful.
I found this game a lot of fun. It took me 63 hours to beat it, and I did not partake in any soul farming like I did in the previous game. In fact, I often found I had sufficient souls to do what I needed to. I loved the mechanics and gameplay, and I would play this game again.

After 375+ hours of gameplay i though it was time to make a review of this game, probably my favourite one of all time. Let's start:
First of all i'm going to talk about the gameplay:
-Good port to PC, i don't use a ps3/xbox controller, i use the keyboard and mouse and you can play perfectly with that (not like DS1 where it was unplayable).

-Despite the downgrade of the graphics from the demo of dark souls to the final game, they are pretty good and really enjoyable

-Brilliant masterpiece, shown in item descriptions and short talks to npc's, maybe its not too deep as it was in DS1 but if you enjoy this kind of story and the "soul series" it's still a masterpiece

I started playing DSII right after beating DS. I didn’t go far as I decided replaying DS would be more rewarding, so what I’m sharing here are my initial impressions after playing the game for a couple of hours only. If I play further and change my mind, I will write a new review.
Right from the start I noticed some strong emphasis on elements from the first game that were praised by the community. Unfortunately it didn’t work out in DSII's favor. For instance, the npcs eventually bursting into laughter during the dialogues was a great touch to DS, it added an extra layer to the haunting atmosphere of the game; on DSII every npc laughs after every line spoken, and it comes across as forced and artificial, by the time you have talked to a couple of npcs in Majula it’s just annoying. DS was praised for its difficulty and it’s well known that dying is part of the game’s mechanic (in case you didn’t know they released an edition called “prepare to die” to make sure you are warned). On DSII they go as far as bragging about it in-game: the old woman in the opening scene tells you that you will die a lot and laughs about it. That’s quite silly and unnecessary if you ask me, it communicates on a very unsophisticated level that takes away from the atmosphere and lore of the game, it states the obvious to please the stupid.
The intros for both games show a difference in tone. The DS intro is a masterpiece, I watched it several times while playing and each time I learned more, it made more sense. The intro for DSII, with the old women laughing and being complacent towards the player, was probably meant to be haunting and scary, but for me it was just silly and anti-climactic. For someone who had just faced Nito, Gwyn, Manus, Seath, all those mythological forces that seemed far beyond the grasp of a simple undead human, the old women from the DSII’s intro surely didn’t make an impact.
Back to the difficulty issue, yeah, the first game was often challenging, but in DSII they just tried too hard. One of the first challenges the player will face leaving Majula is 3 hollowed soldiers plus a sniper, attacking all at once at the top of a ladder in the FotFG. The player will get killed the first couple of times and each time the difficulty increases because his meager hp will be further reduced. Challenge is good, but this is frustrating. I understand it’s a statement, I just think it’s a silly one.
The combat on DS was one of the strengths of the game. The camera would eventually add some extra-difficulty, which always felt unfair, but overall it didn’t provide a lot of fodder for frustration. The lock-on solution for battles could be a pain sometimes, but it worked ok and made it possible for the camera not to be locked on the character’s back, in a way that the astonishing landscapes of Lordran could be better enjoyed. The way the lock-on feature was implemented on DSII is different though: the camera won’t quickly move so you face the locked target, instead it will move very slowly. This is very annoying when you’re surrounded by a group of enemies, the time it takes for the camera to move so you can identify which target is locked is too long. In a very annoying part I was jumping down to a lower platform, and it is not possible to turn while falling, the direction you’re facing the moment you jump is the direction you’ll be facing when you arrive at the lower platform, so I always had my back to an enemy that I knew would backstab me. This means I had to turn quickly to face him, but when I tried to lock on him it would lock on a third enemy on a level below instead, one who wasn’t even part of the fight, and the camera slowly moved towards him. With this mess I would get hit and killed, and it’s extremely annoying when the enemy poses no threat, but you keep struggling with badly implemented mechanics such as camera view and lock-on feature. The combat on DSII also feels kind of like “on rails” compared to DS, in part because strikes come in “combos” now, as in freakin’ Street Fighter. I don’t know how poise affects this, but if one strike catches you with your guard down, you can expect to be trapped defenseless and take a couple more hits. Your attacks seem to follow the same “combo” logic, even backstabbing has become a combo-like succession of hits.
But all the changes to the combat mechanics, as annoying as they are, wouldn’t be a problem if other aspects weren’t also nerfed. Having just arrived in Lordran on DS I knew instantly I’ve met some memorable npcs. The meeting with the knight of Astoras, however brief, made an impact. Snuggly takes you away from the Asylum, and after a couple more travels there and back again, a bond between man and bird is created. And good ol’ Crestfallen, it is through his rather disinterested and mocking attitude that the player is introduced to the world of Lordran, a perfect introduction to such a somber, forlorn and hopeless world, certainly leaves a mark on it... What do we have in DSII instead? An annoying woman whose dramatic tone and clichéd dialogue are quite boring and who will lecture you on some nonsense EVERYTIME you just want to quickly level up and get lost. A blacksmith who will send you in an errand-boy quest for a key (perhaps the most boring, pointless and obvious quest EVER?), and who later keeps his arms in a weird position while talking to you. A cat obsessed with your scent. The covenant guy by the sea, perhaps the less uninteresting npc in Majula, but by the time I got to him I was already bored to death by the other npcs. And of course the old women before Majula, who makes up for the silliest start ever. I wish I could have created my char without that puerile, pointless prologue…
Moving on to the FotFG, the area is a conceptual mess. Every ten steps you get a completely different landscape, it goes from cave to dungeon to river to fortress to something else in a matter of seconds. It made me miss Undead Burg. Again, the developers seem to be trying too hard. It’s not impressive at all, it’s messy and unpleasant.
The abandonment of the lore from DS is also dispiriting. If they wanted to make something different, something more akin to Demon’s Souls, why not call it Cursed Souls or something? I was excited for more DS lore, but nothing matches, the premise is a different one altogether. To begin with, there’s no humanity in this game. Weren’t the Dark Souls that gave the name to the game *SPOILER ALERT* fragments of the dark soul found by the furtive pygmy? What means that the Dark Souls were, in fact, humanities? How can they make a Dark Souls game without freakin’ dark souls? (I might be talking nonsense here, I know nothing about the DSII lore).
Another bad move was the world structure. While on DS you experience this interconnected world with all areas linked to each other (with the same giant hollow tree appearing on many of them), and you have to make long journeys to go from one area to another before acquiring the Lordvessel, on DSII you can just teleport between bonfires from the beginning. This causes the size of the world not to be experienced, you wouldn’t notice the space around you as much if you could just teleport everywhere, and that’s what happens in DSII.
I guess that sums up my first impressions of the game. Unfortunately, this is not a game I’m jumping in and playing the crap out of until it’s finished and beaten like DS. I’m not saying it’s not a good game, I haven’t played enough to judge it fairly. All I’m saying is that it failed to capture my imagination like its predecessor, and I was willing to like this game, I wanted the journey to go on. Maybe it catches up later, but I can’t say anything positive about it. As a sequel to DS it stands as a huge disappointment atm.

It starts as a linear "stamping simulator" but, actually the game diversifies a lot from that starting point. You can simply play the game mechanically, doing your job, or you can try to approach it from other angles. I mean, the core mechanics it´s always the demanding  validation of documents with different rules being thrown at you. But at certain point the money you do is not enough to support your family. Your son will get sick, your wife cold and you have to decide how you're going to manage your money and most importantly, you will be tempted to get corrupted.

And it´s in that point that the game gets more interesting. It´s impossible not to get corrupted, but how will you manage your corruption? Will you be content with the petty government corruption? Will you go for high level corruption earning more money but risking more? Will you get involved with drugs?
And there´s also the more "emotional" side. Will you risk a share of your salary by wrongly stopping someone from entering the country because you know he is a human slaver? Will you allow the illegal wife of a legal immigrant to enter the country knowing that your denial will sentence her to death? Will you get involved in a conspiracy to overthrown your oppressive government, and if so, how much will you get involved? Will you kill for it? What comes firts, liberty or family?
All this, and not knowing the ramifications of your actions, because sometimes an innocent thing can end up being not so harmless, gives this game a depth like very few games I´ve played.  It´s not a "boring job simulator", but it does a superb job of putting you on the skin of someone with a boring job and showing that what defines one person is much more than the most immediate layer of his existence. But above all, it an amazing sociological tool to understand how easy it is for a system to get systemically corrupted, and most importantly, why this happens.

CONS :
- Most of the weapons have unrealistic damage and deal a low amount of damage to the enemies
- Money are very difficult to earn without cheating because the artifacts,weapons and any other items can be sold for ridiculously low sums
- Top-notch gear like weapons and armor are extremely expensive and are nearly impossible to buy without using money cheats
- The graphics of the outer zones of the map are very bad
- Repetitive NPCs dialogs and quotes
- Some bugs and glitches that can't be fixed without using mods (even the latest patch doesn't deal with everything)
- Inconsistent AI
- The ammo for top-notch weapons like RPG7 AND G36 is very scarce,not to mention the rarity of some useful items like scientifical medkit
- Lack of an autosave feature
So despite all those flaws I strongly advise you to buy this game and enjoy it.

Stalker SoC is definitely a fun game made with good intentions, but holy ♥♥♥♥ is it broken and outdated. First off, love the world of Stalker; very semi-apocalyptic and Russian, full of nasty, well-made mutants and bandit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. The story was better than I expected it to be also, especially the true good ending (although going through the level that leads to the ending was a major pain in the♥♥♥♥♥.
And then there's the rest of the game. There's a really annoying view-bobbing when walking, and the map is pretty ♥♥♥♥ing big so you'll be walking a LOT, and you can't turn it off. There are only THREE actual merchants in the game (guys who actually buy your loot) and they're extremely spread apart between the huge map (except for 2 of them). For some reason guns and armor have durability yet there is no repair system at all so you'll have to constantly keep switching gear or use some "trick" to repair stuff. You can't toggle the lean buttons so they're basically useless. In the main menu the framerate goes to the thousands for some reason which causes coil-whine in my GPU (really annoying). The inventory weight is extremely anti-fun compared to something like Fallout and you can only equip two weapons at a time (one of them being a pistol and all of them are useless). Stealth is almost completely broken which makes no sense when there are two different crouches. All enemies, even bandits, have insane accuracy even when using pistols or shotguns from far away and are bullet sponges making most fights really drawn-out peek-a-boo contests. You also definitely need a scoped weapon most of the time if you ever want to hit anything that isn't a fat, blob mutant.
Despite all that, and maybe a few more complaints and bugs, SoC is still pretty fun and "interesting" to play through at least once (for under $10). Maybe I'll even replay it completely modded someday.

A lot of people will say bad things about this game. Maybe not on the reviews, but the "true Dark Souls" fans. They'll say this game isn't hardcore enough, that it's lore can't even hold a candle in the direction of the original Dark Souls, and that generally the game is worse than it's predessesor.
I disagree to a point, to a certain point, I can see where the original fans are coming from.
When looked at on it's own, when not being compared to Dark Souls, Dark Souls 2 is a fantastic game that you can truly immerse yourself in just by sheer amount of time playing it. I find myself trying to think about how I want to plan out future builds for PvP or PvE or Co-op, whatever. I digress, the game itself has a very, very refined combat system, easily the best I've ever utilized in a game. Every realistic melee weapon you could want is probably in this game in some shape or another. Magic is interesting and varied and there's multiple ways to approach each given encounter with enemies. Through this game, you will experience frustration and anger, but when you finally achieve victory, it really gives off a feeling of true satisfaction. You beat that boss that was kicking the crap out of you before and now he lies dead on the floor, it's a good feeling to get from a video game and it's difficult to describe in words. This game's movement system, combat system, it's different bosses, are all top level awesome.
Anyways; Pros and Cons
PROS:
-Fantastic PvP system, easy to get into a game, easy to leave games, etc.
-Loads of initial choice, what path do you want to go to reach your inevitable destination?
-Movement system is extremely refined and feels very fluid
-As does the combat, still extremely refined
-Extremely interesting lore if you decide to take the time out to read various item descriptions
-Extremely engaging and time consuming, the mentality of "just one more match" or "just one more boss" is really addicting
CONS:
-Soul memory system isn't great, although with a more recent update it's been fixed
-Extremely foggy pathing at times. There's a few headscratching moments where you sit there thinking to yourself "huh, what do I do now?" and the game barely hints at it
-Some extremely broken (in terms of PvP) weapons that, when used can almost assure victory for it's wielder
-Apparently this game takes a dump on Dark Souls lore, which I don't know much about, but we're looking at it as a standalone game
Overall 9/10. It's my most played game on Steam and I personally love every second of it. I recommend it to anyone who likes RPGs and has been feeling the need for more challenge or more "UMPH" to their RPG experience.

It starts as a linear "stamping simulator" but, actually the game diversifies a lot from that starting point. You can simply play the game mechanically, doing your job, or you can try to approach it from other angles. I mean, the core mechanics it´s always the demanding  validation of documents with different rules being thrown at you. But at certain point the money you do is not enough to support your family. Your son will get sick, your wife cold and you have to decide how you're going to manage your money and most importantly, you will be tempted to get corrupted.

And it´s in that point that the game gets more interesting. It´s impossible not to get corrupted, but how will you manage your corruption? Will you be content with the petty government corruption? Will you go for high level corruption earning more money but risking more? Will you get involved with drugs?
And there´s also the more "emotional" side. Will you risk a share of your salary by wrongly stopping someone from entering the country because you know he is a human slaver? Will you allow the illegal wife of a legal immigrant to enter the country knowing that your denial will sentence her to death? Will you get involved in a conspiracy to overthrown your oppressive government, and if so, how much will you get involved? Will you kill for it? What comes firts, liberty or family?
All this, and not knowing the ramifications of your actions, because sometimes an innocent thing can end up being not so harmless, gives this game a depth like very few games I´ve played.  It´s not a "boring job simulator", but it does a superb job of putting you on the skin of someone with a boring job and showing that what defines one person is much more than the most immediate layer of his existence. But above all, it an amazing sociological tool to understand how easy it is for a system to get systemically corrupted, and most importantly, why this happens.

If you hate this game, then you also hate America. Your job in this game, is to decide who is allowed to move freely in your country. Half the fun of this game is that you get the privilege of being a cold callous bureaucrat, a corrupt official with his finger in every illicit pie. For a change, you get to be the one giving everyone the business and not the one looking down the business end of such and such thing!
You can also be kind and benevolent and let every person through who has a sob story. Just know, that no matter how you choose to play this game, you (your character, not 'you' yourself) are the most miserable scum of the earth and you're damn lucky to have a job!

Trixxter Reviews:
From the developers behind the highly artistic and well-written game "Bastion", Supergiant Games have returned once more to bring another magical peice of art in the form of "Transistor".
You play as the main character "Red", a famous singer who has had her voice stolen by the syndicate known as "The Camerata" as you wield the weapon "Transistor", a weapon with a sentient soul trapped inside of it in a world that is slowly crumbling to "The Process". Along the way you encounter key characters the unveil the storyline behind Red's missing voice, why the city of CloudBank is succumbing to The Process, and the true purpose and identity of the Transistor.
Supergiant Games have made a combat system with ease of access and a very easy-flow of combat. Visually the game is amazing with equally stunning music composed by Bastion and Supergiant Games' Darren Korb. Naturally with all games there comes some form of downfall.
Pros:
•Amazing visual and musical artwork.
•Fluid free-form combat with ease of use
•Emotionally deep storyline
Cons:
•The combat system isn't very well introducted during the game's "Tutorial" and takes some time to get used to using the combat mechinism as well as the Turn() function.
•Although the storyline was vivid, there was many points through-out the game that could have been explained better, such as the Transistor's introduction, the background behind The Process and the Camerata's motives and background.
All-In-All, This game is still worth the affordable price, as well as the Soundtrack DLC Avaliable from both Steam and Supergiant Games' website.
I personally give it 8.5/10 Circuits, and encourage people to see the masterworks of this art.

Followed the prints until they went into a huge cluster of wolf prints again, Thought to myself, maybe there is a water source nearby and this is a high traffic area. Have played this in the free week and I am a bit confused about the amount of bad reviews that this game is getting.
Yes, it is a HUGE download; I left it overnight to fully dowload and then the last few files that install during the launcher took less than an hour. Not too much of an issue for a one time task. Some people have had issues with the launcher not installing properly and getting caught in loops, but I cannot speak to this as mine went smoothly.
As for the game itself, I am only a few hours in but I think it is great! As someone who hadn't played an Elder Scrolls game for years prior to this, it felt at once familiar and fresh. The quests are very interesting and long enough not to feel like a 'Go get/kill this, come back, have loot' and I can see a deeper story emerging that I can't wait to find out more about.
Microtransactions are a thing (I'm sure you could probably buy horse armour somewhere) but given the low sale prices at the moment, I wouldn't necessarily begrudge spending a bit on crows to get a few extra items. Plus there is no monthly subscription so if you need to justify it to yourself, set aside £9 a month and tell yourself it's Warcraft (is Warcraft £9?).
Really recommend it, even if you haven't had chance to try it in the free week. I've spent a lot more money on a lot worse games and have no regrets in buying this game.

The graphics and music are, of course, a tad crappy. But that's the point! The game is set in an alternate version of the 1980s, so I presume it's been designed to emulate the feel of games in those days. Furthermore, it provides real evidence towards the fact that a game doesn't need to look all spangly to be captivating. In fact, I genuinely believe the game benefits from the simplicity of its style.
The game isn't overly hard, and probably could be made more testing in later levels without destroying the fun, so a possible update from the developers in that way would be a lovely thing. But even if they never do, I will cherish my time at my checkpoint in Arstotzka. Yes I will.

This is the ultimate mining / supply chain / production / logistics / tower defense game.  Gameplay is complete and extremely well-balanced.  All aspects of the game (mining, production, logistics, and alien attacks) ramp up simultaneously and at an even pace that you largely control.  It's very satisfying to go from mining individual units of ore with a pickaxe at the beginning of the game, to having hordes of flying robots on your character that carry out your construction projects for you instantaneously after 40 hours of gameplay.
The single win condition requires having a fairly sophisticated supply chain and robust mining and transport facilities (i.e. a rail network) to produce thousands of high-level items.  Or you can join multiplayer servers and build super-factories, as seen in the screenshots -- though I haven't tried.
Replayability is very high.  By the time I finished one game, I'd have new ideas for how to organize everything better, so I'd be excited to build a new factory from scratch.  Plus there's extensive modding support.
The game's optimization and moderate resource usage is impressive.  My huge factories run with no problem on my 3-year-old Macbook Pro laptop.  (By the way, I've spent hours playing with a trackpad -- of course, if you have a huge monitor and a real mouse, that's nicer.)  The visuals are nice and the animations are smooth, but of course I didn't expect it to be graphically demanding; what impresses me is that it can simulate a huge factory without making the cooling fans on my laptop run like a jet engine.
The one downside is the lack of documentation.  There are some nice tutorial scenarios, and there's a wiki, but for details on the mechanics (or even the purpose) of some of the advanced game objects, you'll have to comb through the forums, or just experiment.  That said, I wouldn't characterize the learning curve as particularly steep, since you can safely ignore the more complicated mechanics on a first play-through, and you largely control the pace of the game anyway.
It's hard to see how anyone could make a better game in this genre.  Paying $20 for (at least) dozens of hours of enjoyable gameplay is a no-brainer.

Clannad is a fantastic visual novel with a case of poor pacing for a lot of the routes (which to get the true ending you need to do every single one).  The game focuses on life and romantic relationships with 0 erotic content.   It is an "All ages" visual novel which is perfectly fine by me.
The game follows a day format which works fine for the primary story but for some of the branches you can tell that they did their best to fill in the days where not much happened.  For me, this turned into a feeling of disinterest where I needed to put the game down for a bit and come back to get reinvested.
Don't misunderstand,  I love the game and recommend it to anyone who takes visual novels or reading seriously. However, it is a long game.   I believe the game is reported to have over 1.3 million English words in the script.  Which put it at 30% more than the 7 Harry Potter books combined and more than the Bible.
What I am getting at is that it isn't 2 hours pick up and put down thing.  If you buy it you're getting your monies worth for sure but if you hate reading or are expecting any sort of erotic material you will be much sad.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Personally,  while this is a high tier visual novel to me.  It doesn't feel top tier and although I played through this prior to the anime with no information going in... Unlike games such as Fate, I felt that the extras from the visual novel didn't expand on the story as much as it  could have.   The anime brings a lot of life and expression to a very solid story in a much more digestible format. Since the story focuses primarily on the people and not on some larger over-arching plot... expression and personality are so very important.
This is coming from a person that almost always believes in source material over adaption because most of the time something is lost in the middle. As well as someone who has enjoyed visual novels for many years when even completely clean VNs were seen as smutty due to some of the related material in the genre.
Something else worth talking about is the art style is not for everyone.  This is a visual novel from early 2004 and it looks like it was made in the late 90s.  Characters tend to look a bit off and while not an issue for me as suspending disbelief is a part of any partaking in fiction.  I have had many people comment to me asking about "What is up with the art".
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
There is also a dark undertone to a lot of the story in the visual novel specifically with the protagonist that maybe requires some knowledge in psychology to really feel out but... without spoiling anything I just don't feel like the visual novel version of the protag is a good person really and on deeper reflection many of the plot points that are billed to you as positive have some very uncomfortable undertones when looked at closely.  Not that there is anything wrong with creating a character that is complex but it sort of betrays the narrative a lot of times in the context of the plot itself.  However, that is a nitpick about a character and not to be confused with the quality of the product.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Overall this is a very solid although, sometimes slow visual novel.
Plan to read this over a longer period of time as it averages out to around 80 hours or more depending on reading speed to get everything out of it.
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Make up your own mind.

As you watch the show or play the visual novel, you’ll get attached to the characters due to the amazing character development. These are characters dealing with real issues, and you’ll be able to relate to them. They run into hilarious scenes with well written comedy, so you are kept entertained. They are characters with interesting interactions with others, and with interesting personalities. Clannad builds them up so well..... then throws a curve-ball to the situation to create drama and tension, which is done equally as well. These scenarios are well written with great pacing, interesting back-stories and moving themes; no matter how many times they pull off the formula in the show, the impact doesn’t really lessen. The reactions, personal monologues, and dilemmas of the characters show development. This development is something that I really appreciate, and it makes Clannad stand out. The pacing is fantastic, enough for each character without feeling dragged out or rushed. Even though it may be slower paced than what some people want, it’s an enjoyable ride. The themes of family, bonds, friendships, relationships, etc. have a lot of impact, and they just make this show something special, something that is memorable, something that is amazing. They all add up to a very moving and excellent package that you will enjoy, and if you are like most people, you will cry. You will feel ALL THE FEELS!... unless your heart is made out of stone.

Trixxter Reviews:
From the developers behind the highly artistic and well-written game "Bastion", Supergiant Games have returned once more to bring another magical peice of art in the form of "Transistor".
You play as the main character "Red", a famous singer who has had her voice stolen by the syndicate known as "The Camerata" as you wield the weapon "Transistor", a weapon with a sentient soul trapped inside of it in a world that is slowly crumbling to "The Process". Along the way you encounter key characters the unveil the storyline behind Red's missing voice, why the city of CloudBank is succumbing to The Process, and the true purpose and identity of the Transistor.
Supergiant Games have made a combat system with ease of access and a very easy-flow of combat. Visually the game is amazing with equally stunning music composed by Bastion and Supergiant Games' Darren Korb. Naturally with all games there comes some form of downfall.
Pros:
•Amazing visual and musical artwork.
•Fluid free-form combat with ease of use
•Emotionally deep storyline
Cons:
•The combat system isn't very well introducted during the game's "Tutorial" and takes some time to get used to using the combat mechinism as well as the Turn() function.
•Although the storyline was vivid, there was many points through-out the game that could have been explained better, such as the Transistor's introduction, the background behind The Process and the Camerata's motives and background.
All-In-All, This game is still worth the affordable price, as well as the Soundtrack DLC Avaliable from both Steam and Supergiant Games' website.
I personally give it 8.5/10 Circuits, and encourage people to see the masterworks of this art.

Much bolder artistically and taking a lot more risks than Bastion, I admire pretty much every decision they made with this game. This feels like the most modern JRPG i've ever played, like it came from an alternate universe where Squaresoft instead merged with some western devs that grew up loving Diablo.
The mechanics (and atmosphere) can be quite a lot to take in, but this is a game meant to be played multiple times.  Some parts of the game are more vague and potentially confusing than others, but this was completely intentional.  This is a game that treats you as a capable thinker and has enough respect to let you figure out (and most importantly, IMAGINE) things for yourself.  This game is right up there with Silent Hill 2 for game narrative done correctly, it keeps a strong narrative focus, but also embraces the fact that your imagination will always be better at filling in the fine details.
Sound, visuals, music, voices, etc... are firing on all cylinders, but it can be hard to remember that at times since there is just so much in this game begging for your attention.  It may even be too dense and atmospheric for some players, which is a criticism(?) I'm delighted to get the chance to give.
And please immediately replay this game after finishing, the second playthru is significantly more sad than the first, even though it's exactly the same game.  It's so cool how they managed that, I love this game.

It took me an hour to tear myself away from my computer to take a break from Soda Dungeon. The game has unique mechanics that make it feel fresh and independent, like it didn't take anything from other games. The pixel graphics affirm that this game can stick in your mind for quite a while. The gameplay is addictive, making you want to get right back to dungeon crawling. The goals you set for yourself are just as satisfying to complete than the goals the game sets for you. Its hard to stop playing once you've started, making it one of those games I like purely because its so addictive. Its charming, fun, and really good, and I believe it could be a budget title, maybe around $4.99, but the game is free, making it easy to access and just start playing.
Overall, the game is entertaining but, is kind of forgettable. The story is virtually non-existent, and the game doesn't throw many new combat options, making it a total button masher. Plus, Steam has a large library of much more popular games that easily overshadows Soda Dungeon. You could argue that that goes for a lot of other free games in the Steam Store, but Soda Dungeon makes it easier, being a turn-based RPG style pixel graphic game, making it seem extremely underwhelming at first sight. Have I mentioned the story? I never felt like I was fighting for anything, just hiring convientely placed mercanaries to go into a dungeon to fight to give ME money. Wait a minute, this is kind of reminding me of something. OH YEAH. This game is extremely overshadowed by a similar game that requires money, Darkest Dungeon. And I'd rather purchase a much better reviewed and recommended game rather than download a free game I'm just gonna delete after a few hours, or just let it sit in your Steam library. Soda Dungeon's whole mechanic is like Darkest Dungeon, making it feel ripped from the game.
6/10-Okay
:)  Addictive                             :(  Lack of Story
:)  Charming                             :(  Gets Old Fast
:)  Interesting Mechanics         :(  Easily Overshadowed By Other Great Free Games
:)  Fair Difficulty                        :(  To similar to a much better game
:)  Potential to Age Well
Soda Dungeon is a good title to kill a few hours with, say on a plane ride or a lazy Sunday, but is not recommended for the kind of gamer who wants hours of gameplay. Trust me, just go BUY a different game like Darkest Dungeon. Ultimately Soda Dungeon is an entertaining but forgettable and kind of underwhelming experience that lasts a few hours, then is forgotten, and thrown into the back of the closet of everyone's library. I do recommend it, however, because it offers some interesting and addictive gameplay.

Broforce is a lot more indepth than its machismo parody might lead you to believe. Each character has unique abilities that drastically change how you approach obstacles, the stages are designed so that you can literally carve your own paths through them, the asthetic is  retro but crisp, and the references and over the top dialogue are clever while still being overt. The entire game is an homage to the cheesy and glorious action movies of the 80's, and I adore that.
That being said, the sheer chaos of explosions and attacks can easily obscure your view, making it easy to get hit by stray projectiles, and the balance of the different characters varies wildly which, when combined with the random nature of which characters you have access to at a given time, can greatly affect the level difficulty. For some this is a positive, but for me it meant some runs were better off not finishing because the roster of characters I had acquired for that level was not up to the task.
God speed broforce... gods speed!

I've been burned way too many times with Early Access that I rarely if ever purchase EAs any more. This game was an exception I'm glad I made.
It's part factory efficiency/planning simulator with laying out production chains and part RTS with defending yourself against the wildlife. You can tell a decent amount of thought has gone into all aspects of design which really makes for an enjoyable experience.
Pros:
- Very nice "ant hill" effect. Lots of bits and pieces moving around your production chains that it's a pleasure to watch and can suck you in if you're not careful.
- The wildlife attacks keep you on your toes (unless you play in peaceful mode which is also a nice touch) and ramp up in difficulty so you can't plop down some defenses and forget about them.
- All items have a use, even the basic ones that can be upgraded. The basic versions use fuel (usually coal or wood) while advanced versions use electricity. Pros and cons to both approaches.
- Lots of helpful technology. Conveyor belts are fine, but trains are much better across large distances. Drones that do your bidding. Logic systems to sort and filter items. Capacitors to store excess energy. Just to name a few.
- Very complex and deep research tree. I've barely scratched the surface and I'm excited to see more.
- The UI is very helpful. Everything is either WASD, uses keys near WASD, or uses the mouse. Very intuitive and didn't take long to figure out. Also each item tells you exactly what it needs, how long it takes to make, where it is made, and even what base materials are required if refinement is needed.
- While most items are made in assemblers, you can make a lot of things "in your pocket." This really helps to fill in gaps or unplug blockages in your production chain.
- If you need materials from your production chain, you can just run around and "vacuum up" the items you want.
- Lots of customization if you want to do freeplay. You can set things up just how you like.
- The price is $20.00, not $19.99. A small thing, but appreciated nonetheless. No mind games or trickery.
- Special shout-out for the trailer. Shows actual game footage that conveys the game very nicely in a short amount of time. I sure hope other game makers take note.
Cons:
- The tutorials need some love. The first tutorial is very good in that it holds your hand and tells you exactly what to do and how to do it. The next campaign feels like a more in-depth tutorial that slowly reveals more of the tech tree, but they include extraneous techs in the tree. It's hard to know what I should do next. There isn't enough hand-holding and explanation for a new player like me. I had to go view some YouTube videos to figure things out like trains and oil production. IMO, that should be done in-game by a good tutorial, not out-sourced to fans. Also they need someone who speaks English to go over their text. Some grating grammatical issues that make it hard to read at times.
- There is currently not a whole lot of scripted content (campaigns). The initial campaign is nice (minus the issues mentioned above) but left me wanting a whole lot more. There is player content, but again that seems like a lazy cop-out. Also, this is EA, so perhaps there's more coming?
So as you can see, a lot more pros than cons in my mind. A very polished game for EA. Definitely worth jumping the gun.

Call of Juarez has at best been a series of middling highs until CoJ Gunslinger, a game that smartly works within the confines of a budget shooter's scale with sharp storytelling and a slick sense of style. I've never been a fan of Wild West games bar Red Dead Redemption because the majority of them have been shooters set in a time where guns weren't exactly designed for the kind of shooter gameplay I gravitate towards.
Gunslinger however feels fantastic as you sling its small variety of firearms. Everything in Gunslinger feels polished, slick and well-executed. The narration takes cues from games like Bastion and subtely plays with your expectations about where the game is going. It kept me involved in the story long after the simplistic shooting wore out its welcome. CoJ Gunslinger may take the shooting gallery concept to its logical extreme, but that doesn't stop it from getting repetitive by the end of its 3 hour campaign. Though it has an score-attack mode for you to amuse yourself with, the gameplay is lacking the depth to provide any long-term value.
You come for the story, which is strange to say in the context of a Call of Juarez game. It tells a relatively simple tale superbly and for a shooter, let alone a downloadable FPS, to pull that off with gusto is pretty admirable.

Trixxter Reviews:
From the developers behind the highly artistic and well-written game "Bastion", Supergiant Games have returned once more to bring another magical peice of art in the form of "Transistor".
You play as the main character "Red", a famous singer who has had her voice stolen by the syndicate known as "The Camerata" as you wield the weapon "Transistor", a weapon with a sentient soul trapped inside of it in a world that is slowly crumbling to "The Process". Along the way you encounter key characters the unveil the storyline behind Red's missing voice, why the city of CloudBank is succumbing to The Process, and the true purpose and identity of the Transistor.
Supergiant Games have made a combat system with ease of access and a very easy-flow of combat. Visually the game is amazing with equally stunning music composed by Bastion and Supergiant Games' Darren Korb. Naturally with all games there comes some form of downfall.
Pros:
•Amazing visual and musical artwork.
•Fluid free-form combat with ease of use
•Emotionally deep storyline
Cons:
•The combat system isn't very well introducted during the game's "Tutorial" and takes some time to get used to using the combat mechinism as well as the Turn() function.
•Although the storyline was vivid, there was many points through-out the game that could have been explained better, such as the Transistor's introduction, the background behind The Process and the Camerata's motives and background.
All-In-All, This game is still worth the affordable price, as well as the Soundtrack DLC Avaliable from both Steam and Supergiant Games' website.
I personally give it 8.5/10 Circuits, and encourage people to see the masterworks of this art.

Much bolder artistically and taking a lot more risks than Bastion, I admire pretty much every decision they made with this game. This feels like the most modern JRPG i've ever played, like it came from an alternate universe where Squaresoft instead merged with some western devs that grew up loving Diablo.
The mechanics (and atmosphere) can be quite a lot to take in, but this is a game meant to be played multiple times.  Some parts of the game are more vague and potentially confusing than others, but this was completely intentional.  This is a game that treats you as a capable thinker and has enough respect to let you figure out (and most importantly, IMAGINE) things for yourself.  This game is right up there with Silent Hill 2 for game narrative done correctly, it keeps a strong narrative focus, but also embraces the fact that your imagination will always be better at filling in the fine details.
Sound, visuals, music, voices, etc... are firing on all cylinders, but it can be hard to remember that at times since there is just so much in this game begging for your attention.  It may even be too dense and atmospheric for some players, which is a criticism(?) I'm delighted to get the chance to give.
And please immediately replay this game after finishing, the second playthru is significantly more sad than the first, even though it's exactly the same game.  It's so cool how they managed that, I love this game.

Later on I came back into that area and saw the guns floating in mid-air. THE GAME SAID NO LOOKING.

It's 15 years after the first Alien film and Ripley's daughter, Amanda, is travelling to deep space to investigate her mother's disappearance.
Cue some of the best Alien environment/ graphics/ sound I have ever seen. They hit the mark. It's all replicated with love. The reproduction of what we thought future technology would look like back in the 1970s is just perfect. The strange beep (alien) sounds is almost breath taking. The motion tracker can be used with abandon. The flamethrower makes an appearance.
The large almost orchestrated sound that initiates any time the Alien appears is designed to give you a heart flutter. Make sure you check your blood pressure before playing this game.
As a fan of the films, I LOVED IT.
Despite all this, almost straight away you will realize it is all a facade. Smoke and mirrors. 95% of the environment cannot be interacted with. 100% of the locations are used again and again.
Thus begins a battle within yourself to pretend you are in one of the films rather than in a very cleverly disguised rat in a maze following a single path. The only path.
They have included a crafting mini-game where you can collect all sort of junk to create bombs and healing kits. You can go around collecting IDs of the crew. Possibly the worst type of collection game in existence. There is no explanation or information about who these people were. Just names. Pathetic!
The space station where most of the game is based really does feel huge. There are lifts to other levels and it even hosts a train station type location where you can catch a ride along to the furthest edges in quick time. The station also houses the different type of zoning areas one would expect such as medical, engineering and residential. It is well done.
As I progressed through the game more and more weapons and items were made available to me. Some locations that I could not access before could later be entered once I had, for example, access to a welding torch or electronic hacking devices.
The Alien was pretty amazing. Hiding under tables was amazing. Adjusting the environmental controls to reduce the light or air filtering was amazing.
Playing a game where I was hiding in a locker and trying to look through its cracks was pretty amazing.
Trying to hold my breath in game and simultaneously in real life was pretty AMAZING.
Despite the developers trying to randomize it's behavior as much as possible, somewhere along though you will sense the Alien's patterns. At one point I was running through every new location to see if it was safe to do so.
The game carefully treads the tightrope between shooter and stealth very well. It reminds me a bit of Deadspace and System Shock 2. More stealth than anything else because for a long, long time you cannot survive any confrontation with the Alien.
It's all good until you slowly realize that you are stuck in a maze following the only path set up by the gaming gods.
27 hours in I would like to continue the game and complete the story. But I can guess what will happen. And I am no rat.
Recommend to purchase on sale for the experience only.

This is utterly terrifying.  I first played the game in 2014 when it first came out which then only had Easy, Normal, and Hard difficulties available.  While I played it on normal it was still very tough to get through.  The AI for the Alien truly makes it an enemy like no other.  You'd think you'd be tailing it as it walks down a corridor until suddenly, and without warning, it'll turn it's head in your direction then you're Alien chow.  Or you'd walk along another section and hear the Alien thumping around in the vent, to all of a sudden drop down right in front of you.
When this game first came out I thoroughly enjoyed it as it really sells that retro-future ascetic used in Ridley Scott's first film Alien.  A lot of people I've seen play this call the first Alien film a 1980's film.  It's not.  Production started in 1977 and was released in 1979.  The decor and architecture of browns and greys was "the thing" back in the day.  That makes the film a 1970's film, not the physadelic colors of the 80's.  Yet another look this game nails.  Wondering around the Torrens and Sevastopol station you'll see many reminders of where this game gets its backbone from.  The seats and walls are emblazoned with the drab 2-tone covers, the monochromatic monitors displaying text and basic graphics common in 1960's and 1970's computers.
And then, and THEN the music starts playing.  The music is adaptive to your situation.  In an area devoid of enemies you'll usually hear a calming melody which sets the mood that, yes, while you are in a dangerous environment you're not alone and not in immediate danger.  But then the alien gets near, you hide, the alien gets nearer still, then the music changes.  The trombones and horns start singing as you hind in that locker or under a table, you can't move and only hope the alien will move on.  And in a couple of sections of the game you'll even hear little ditties that came straight from the original firm to further emphasise you're in space and deep in the Xeno-verse.
The vanilla game is truly epic with some only a couple of scripted scenes with the alien, the alien is pure unfettered AI looking, sniffing for you.  A really tough challenge is to play the game on Nightmare difficulty, however as I write this review, I've started playing the game yet again this time with the Unpredictable Alien and No Motion Tracker mods.  It's bad enough the alien is "somewhere", and the motion tracker can only approximate it's position especially in maps with multiple levels to it, but try playing this game with only audio clues to try and keep tabs on the alien as it scuttles each level you're on.
The game isn't without faults though.  Bipedal NPCs seem "stiff" while walking.  No so great when seeing humans walk like that but is a great effect on the Working Joes.  Talking of which, the game is called Alien: Isolation, not Attack of the Working Joes.  There's far too many in game, though like in Deus Ex are best left alone as they can be really tough to take down without the right tools, and neigh on impossible if they don't like you while the Alien is nearby.
Voice acting is film quality but while in-game (not when a cut scene is being played out) lip-syncing is a hit-and-miss.  Though that's not a problem on the 'Joes as they have no lips to sync.  There are also a few missions where you have to traverse the same map 2 or 3 times, I'm not talking about maps you play early in game you have to play later on in the story with different enemies oh no.  I'm talking about you enter a level, you get set a waypoint on the map (not available in Nightmare difficulty) for the exit, you get there but the exit is locked.  So you have to go to another point on that same map, do something and return to that exit.  I understand Creative Assembly are trying to keep the tension up by prolonging it for as long as possible but it can get very tedious for speed runners.
I love the Aliens franchise and this is THE DEFINITIVE Alien game for any one who loves the lore like I do.  A masterpiece on it's own, but with the few mods that are available, you can make it so much more terrifying like never before.

What can I say that hasn't been said already? Alien: Isolation is a love letter to fans of the original 1979 film that started it all. The alien is a hulking, unbeatable beast and no doubt the protagonist of the game, but if you look past the fabulously accurate recreation of the film's aesthetic, you have a fantastic cat-and-mouse stealth game that had me terrified throughout almost the entirety of the experience. The game is clearly too long, and while it has many tricks up its sleeve, it has such a huge amount of time to spread them out in that the campaign does eventually become somewhat stale in the final third or so. It's still a wonderful game - just an excessively long one, at around 25-30 hours if you're doing a completionist playthrough when it really ought to be in the late teens.
Either way, this title kickstarted the comeback of AAA horror. It's the first good game the Alien franchise has had in years and by far the best one; it excels as a horror game; it excels as a stealth game; it excels as a film series-to-videogame adaptation. This isn't a review as much as me just gushing over one of my favourite games, but the "Overwhelmingly positive" consensus that Alien: Isolation has (at the time of writing this) is pretty much what my opinion aligns with. If you enjoy horror, stealth, the Alien series or just good looking games, I absolutely recommend this.

Your first impression of the game will be monotonous and fastidious but very soon you will develop a rhythm of being a proficient immigration inspector.
This game requires your undivided attention and quick reflexes; you will have to take notice small details. When you play this game, you are going to enter a mesmerising state of mind and the music is very appeasing; you won't notice how much time has passed.
This game is not just about being a immigration inspector, its about the struggle of making moral choices. Would you condemn this lady to die, with expired passport, by refusing her entry or deprive your sick son of medicine by losing your paycheque? Would you let a wanted murderer pass because revenge driven father wants to kill him or would you get him arrested, where he might not be sentenced justly for his crimes? Would you help the terrorist organisation EZIC over-throw the corrupt government or  stay loyal to the dystopian Arstotzka? These are but a few of the question you have to ask yourself. The story is not that long but the best part is that you can start a semi-new game from any day and make different choices. Clannad is an awesome visual novel. Set aside at least 50 hours and get ready to cry.
The story is excellent. There are quite a few routes, and all of them are required to be completed in order to unlock the (long) epilogue chapter. Most are fantastic, and a couple are mediocre. I wouldn’t recommend playing the game if you aren’t going to see it through to completion.
The writing is quite sharp, and the translation is great. I lost track of how many time I laughed out loud after twenty-something. I rarely find writing that is this funny, so it was a real treat.
The characters are quite enjoyable for the most part. None of them fall too deeply into stereotypes or tropes, and the routes are long enough to tell interesting stories with the characters. The characters’ visual designs are also pretty good.
Lackluster art is probably the biggest weakness the game has. The characters are well designed, but the art that you see in-game for them is not very good looking, which is a shame since you’ll be looking at them for 50+ hours. The CGs look fine though.
The music and voice acting are top notch. The score does a really good job setting the mood appropriately. It’s the type of soundtrack I want to download and listen to afterwards. The voice actors are a huge reason why the game is so funny and emotional. No complaints whatsoever in this department. All characters besides the protagonist are fully voiced.
Some of the routes (especially some of the more joke endings) have somewhat arbitrary choices required to enter them. There are some order-specific dependencies (some routes can’t
be fully completed unless other routes are done first). This is kind of annoying and might lead to have to replay some routes if you don’t consult a walkthrough.
This game is super sad. Pretty much every route has some serious tragedy or heartbreak involved. For the most part they have happy endings, but be warned that you will cry like a baby many times unless you have a heart of stone.
Overall, I highly recommend it if you have the patience and desire for 50+ hours of reading.

I would only recommend this game if you really know what you're getting yourself into. I marked "Yes" because It was a fun game to play and I'm familiar with the series. While the game had its fair share of problems, if you're a fan of the series you'll enjoy yourself. Unfortunately, in my opinion, it is a downgrade from the sequel. If there was a "mixed" option, I would probably choose that instead. I purchased this game while it was 75% off, and I highly recommend that you do the same if you really want it.
If you have a high end system, don't worry about the people complaining about memory leaks.
I have 16GB RAM, GTX 1070, and Intel 6700k and experienced no real issues regarding memory leaks.
However, that does not change the fact that the game was very glitchy. Enemies spawn in right before your eyes at times, physics glitches are not uncommon, and the game is generally unstable (in the lovable Just Cause sort of way). I will still able to maintain a consistently high frame rate despite this. I have crashed to desktop 1 time, and had to force close the game due to it locking up 2 times in my 24 hours of playing it, so it's really not all that bad.
They somehow managed to make the driving even worse than how it was in Just Cause 2. Once you get used to it, it's not so bad. Motorcycles are especially horrible to drive, you will never get used to them. The vehicles have a really strange momentum/weight to them, and it's very difficult to drive with a keyboard and mouse unlike in games like Grand Theft Auto 5 or Saint's Row. The driving mechanics also depend way too much on using your hand brake, and of course that is a pain since the controls are frustrating. Be prepared to not use your space bar for hand brakes. They also got rid of the Stunt Jump mechanic from Just Cause 2, which is a major disappointment. It's a lot harder to hijack cars and vehicles, and it's very frustrating trying to enter cars via grappling hook alone. Rico also has a very cool habit of only walking while on boats and planes. Since there is no more Stunt Jumping, this makes it very tedious and frustrating to actually enter the cockpit of boats and planes. In Just Cause 2, you could just press the Stunt Jump button to have Rico quickly and automatically grapple his way into position to enter a vehicle and drive it, but in 3 you have to actually walk over to the cockpit or car door for some reason.
This game was clearly not optimized for PC. The game will never let you know about keybind conflicts, and with so many different keys and functions, things get very difficult to manage. I actually ended up binding "contract tether" to one of the rudder controls for air vehicles by accident and realized this halfway through the game. The game will also not let you know if chaning one bind for one control will change another. For example, if you want to change your parachute button while on foot to something else, this will in turn change your parachute and bail buttons for driving as well, and the game will not notify you of this. Also, there are many binds that are linked, such as jumping onto the roof of a car and bailing by parachute. The game will list these as separate binds although they will always be bound to the same button no matter what. This was one of the biggest annoyances of this game. The keybinding in Just Cause 2 was leagues better than this.
It's repetitive, but such is the nature of Just Cause. However, since the story is lackluster, none of it really feels like it's worth it. Sure, it's fun to destroy bases and liberate towns at first, but then you start to realize the copy/paste nature of many areas in the game world, and the game starts turning into a chore. There are also many annoying parts of combat. Enemies with shotguns can temporarily stun Rico from quite long ranges for some reason. Also, hitting the ground while using a wingsuit is very annoying. No matter how fast you go, Rico will get stunned, unless you unlock the ability to retract your wingsuit when going slowly near the ground, which should have been a feature by default. Be sure not to get stunned while on a mountain or something, or else Rico will go into an uncontrollable tumble for an annoyingly long amount of time. The stun mechanics in the game are horrible and annoying. You will find yourself getting frustrated every time Rico falls over.
There are also many challenges that you must do to upgrade tools and equipment, which also (surprise!) gets annoying quite quickly. By doing challenges, you earn "gears" which act as currency towards upgrades of different kinds. If you do a racing challenge you unlock gears for cars, gun challenges unlock gears for guns, and so forth. You actually have to unlock things like precision aiming, which should have been available from the beginning by default, and things like increased tethers, which should have been unlocked as the story progressed. A lot of the unlocks are also very underwhelming and were clearly meant to be filler/padding for the more interesting and useful upgrades. Oh, I unlocked the ability to get a supply drop faster? Wow, because they were
to begin with.
The story was pretty nice, but the ending felt incredibly rushed. Things will be developing at a certain pace and then it will ramp up out of nowhere and end unexpectedly. The ending is unbelievably underwhelming compared to the ending of Just Cause 2. Spoilers:
The game also lacks the charm of Just Cause 2. Just Cause 2 felt like a campy B-movie, and Rico felt like the stereotypical lead to that kind of movie, his voice actor fit the role perfectly. You could practically see him doing the sign of the cross after taking out baddies. Now, Rico is this rugged manly man with a new voice actor whom I'm not entirely fond of. Rico is still Rico, though. He's still out fighting for the greater good and trying to end corruption, taking the obvious moral high ground as always, and I love him for it. Just Cause 3 story-wise is basically Just Cause 2, but with less of the B-movie charm. It is nice to finally get some answers regarding Rico's past, as well as somewhat of a conclusion to it. I really enjoyed the setting and premise of the story, but felt that it was lacking in a few areas.
If you want to just kill time with a game revolving around mindless action and chaos, and dont mind the occasional glitch and can stand mediocre controls, then go for it. It was fun to play but it could have been a lot better. If you haven't played Just Cause 2, I would HIGHLY recommend that you do before playing 3, it'll make you appreciate 3 a lot more.

Set in the old west the story follows the life of a bounty hunter named Silas Greaves. The main storyline of the game is narrated by Silas as an old man in a run down salon. As an interesting mechanic the game can change based on the narration, some of these changes are amusing. Often you will play a mission as one of your audience explains the well known story only to then have to replay the same mission as Greaves say "Well that's an interesting story but what happened was....."
Gameplay wise it is a very linear game and is a sequence of shooting galleries. Reach an area and a number of enemies will spawn and rush you. You have 3 main weapons and upgrade trees, pistols (inc dual wielding), rifle and shotgun. Kills also earn concentration which can initiate a 'bullet time' slowdown allowing you to target and fire at multiple enemies. The boss fights are a mix between bulletsponges and duels, The duels are by far the best of these. I find the difficulty of the duels to be just right, often I would require a couple of attempts to complete but sometimes succeeded in the first attempt.
Outside of the storyline there is also a couple of leaderboard style game modes. Arcade which is a level you need to clear with the highest score possible. Score is a combination of points for chaining kills and things like headshots and time to complete. There is also a pure dual mode where you need to complete 15 duels with 5 lives. The main game is still the main draw card but they additional modes are fun.

To tell you the truth I never thought this would be my favourite Call of Juarez game of all the 4 titles available. Well, if you look at the western-themed games there are just 3 out there - we can disregard The Cartel which is set in modern day Los Angeles for the sake of this review.
What I like about the game is that it does not take itself seriously. Silas, our protagonist, goes to a saloon and starts the telling of many tales with the involvement of all the legendary Wild West outlaws. Silas either killed, wounded these people or just rode alongside them. Every level is a different tale with a different setting and outlaw.
Now, about the gameplay: slow-mo is more frequent than in previous games and duelling is easier and more exciting. You have more collectibles hidden throughout each level and these so-called "nuggets" fill the in-game database with a lot of information on the era: everything you wanted to know about every outlaw, the steamship, the gatling gun, etc.
Killing people with precision and speed allows you to obtain more experience points - levelling up lets you pick a skill / upgrade which aims to take you to the land of specialisation. You'll be an expert of weapon handling so you are free to pick which weapon will be the most suitable for you. With the shotgun you can be the master of close-quarter combat, with the rifle you can further enhance your precision aiming and become the ultimate sharpshooter and with the dual-wielding of pistols you can really become a true cowboy.
Levels can be played separately, after finishing the story just for the sake of obtaining more scores to compete with your friends on leaderboards. The same goes for duels - one duel after another during which you have a limited number of lives: Do you have what it takes to win all of them without reloading?
Techland's Chrome Engine offers us more colourful visuals than ever. The game has vivid colours and overall you can see more attention was put into detail than in any previous CoJ game. Not only does it look good but it runs at a smooth 60 FPS.
This has been the best CoJ game to date. The story is forgettable but let's be honest we only play a western-themed game for its shootouts and Gunslinger has just claimed the throne.

WARNING: SLIGHT SPOILERS, SO IF YOU HAVE WEAK METABOLISMS, READ THE LAST PARAGRAPH!!!
Supergiant Games have done it again. Transistor is a beautiful game that blends both gameplay and story so fluently that I forget that I am playing a game at times. The story begins with a mute singer who has just experienced her attempted murder, only to be saved by a bystander. The savior's voice and soul are transferred to the sword, which she carries around to find out what is happening to her city, and off you go.
One thing that stood out to me was the narrator's voice this time around makes more sense to actually hear, instead of Bastion's narrator, who you just sort of, could hear all the time for no real explanation. I know this really wasn't much of an issue in Bastion, but I like to see how the writers have grown up even more than Bastion's amazing story, which leads to another improvement: terminals. We've all been there trying to collect audio logs, but this time around, it's a bit different. Since Red has no voice, these terminals provide ways to communicate with the Transistor, which gives the player more motivation to go after them, rather than just skim over the story. Personally, I think this is a genius way to integrate both the present and the past stories of the game into one.
With such a great story, there has to be some glitches involved. My main problem is after the ending. And don't get me wrong, I LOVED the ending. I never thought how that would be the end, and it was a good conclusion to the arcing story between Red and her sword. But the problem is afterwards, the Recursion. In Bastion, there was a reason to play it over, as there were references to how you ended the game before, and as such have a different experience as before. But now, the game was ended with only one choice, so there really was no point to replay it, except for gameplay value. I guess the developers were going for a more linear story, which is perfectly fine, but I just expected a similar weave to the story as Bastion.
Now, I mentioned gameplay before, and it is good. Not amazing, but good. It takes Bastion's hack-and-slash type and mixes a bit of turnbased action. When a Turn is activated, one can move freely across the field setting up attacks, using up your meter above to do so. Once you are done, you then watch your actions and hopefully dominate the field. The catch with using this system is that you must wait for the meter to fill up again before you may attack again, in Turn or out of. I find that is a good balance, but if you aren't able to dominate a powerful enemy in your Turn, then you are pretty much screwed. Luckily for me, I actually liked the Turn system, but if you don't, you may not have fun with the game, especially towards the end with Man enemies, and the final boss. Which brings up what happens when you die. When Red is defeated in a battle (hence the Turn meter is down and you lose all health), she loses a function that you have under the abilities bar, and you can't get it back until you reach two different function stations. This is an interesting aspect, but it can be quite annoying, as it is often random on what you lose. For example, I once lost my main attack function, and was left with my dodge and my load functions, which do nothing in battle without a good attack. I guess this is the point as it punishes you for losing rather than just spawning you to the last checkpoint, but in my eyes, it is ultimately just wasting my time as it adds not much towards my experience except annoyance.
Another issue is the extensive upgrade system. There were many combinations that one could make with their functions, but the problem was the GUI. You had to go through each function one at a time to see what upgrade you could add to a function. This could've been simply fixed by the ability to compare the upgrades with each function, rather than the other lengthy way. Not much of an issue, but it can be hectic near the ending when you have ten functions you have to go through at a time.
Lastly, the art style. Remember Bastion's art style? How alive the world felt? Well, magnify that by 10, and add some city elements towards the environment, and you got Transistor. The colors vibrate off the screen, and you wish that the city, maybe even the enemies, were existent. Really, there isn't much to say, but to just look at. I once just stopped playing and watched the background for a good minute. The artists know to not mess with a good formula, and luckily they didn't.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NO MORE SPOILERS AFTER, LAST PARAGRAPH/VERDICT
Transistor truly adds more to the Bastion formula, but it still latches a bit too closely towards Bastion. However, this isn't a bad thing, as Supergiant Games are playing it safe and not making a completely different game, which is what we want. We want the same feel of atmosphere from Bastion, which we got with more interactions but less replayability. We want the same gameplay feel, which we got with more options but less hack-and-slash. And we want the same story and experience, which we got with more passion but less nonlinearity. So, do I recommend Transistor? If you liked Bastion and like a bit of change, you'll love this new addition. I sure did.
