Supergiant's new game Transistor is perhaps the best singleplayer RPG game I've played in the past few years. This game has it all - Outstanding story, amazing music, breathtaking artwork, and great gameplay to go along with it. In particular the fact that you could control the difficulty as the game went on with limiters made the game insanely fun, and the story that you could really only fully understand by taking your time to read the OVC terminals and function archives made it that much more interesting. I would recommend this game in an instant to anyone who was looking for nice, laid back singleplayer adventure. 10/10, 4 stars, 2 thumbs up. It's an amazing game.

I liked the gameplay. It has good voice acting, good story, beautiful artwork, and entertaining puzzle violence. The music is fantastic, and the context of the music-- the voice of our otherwise voiceless Red -- is haunting when first presented.
I was so disappointed by the ending that I waffled on whether or not to recommend the game. I will attempt to explain my criticism without serious spoilers.
Red never quite got to be the story protagonist she first seemed to be. I felt like they were on the verge of presenting an awesome girl action character, but ultimately her character's only consistent context is her relationship; even her voicelessness, (which you'd think was a pretty huge deal for a singer), is not explored or explained; could they not think of dialogue for her? Why take her voice away and make her a singer if that's not going to even be discussed in the story-- to give her a tragic past? She doesn't save herself, or anyone, or accomplish anything she set out to do, or react to the things she wasn't able to do, god damn it.  She doesn't complete a hero's journey, even though she fights the whole way through a fighting game-- the Red we have at the end of the game is doing different things, but without context it can't be said that she DEVELOPS, more like she reacts until she's tired. She sets out to do something, then finds she can't do it, so she moves on without comment. That's fine, but a hero it does not make. SuperGiant could have done so much more with this character, and I feel like they must've along the way and then left it on the editing room floor.
If you identified with the sword's story you probably wouldn't notice everything that was wrong with Red. And that would be fine; Logan Cunningham is a great voice actor and his Transistor is a good character. But I wanted a female protagonist and I thought SuoperGiant had delivered. They did not.

It's 15 years after the first Alien film and Ripley's daughter, Amanda, is travelling to deep space to investigate her mother's disappearance.
Cue some of the best Alien environment/ graphics/ sound I have ever seen. They hit the mark. It's all replicated with love. The reproduction of what we thought future technology would look like back in the 1970s is just perfect. The strange beep (alien) sounds is almost breath taking. The motion tracker can be used with abandon. The flamethrower makes an appearance.
The large almost orchestrated sound that initiates any time the Alien appears is designed to give you a heart flutter. Make sure you check your blood pressure before playing this game.
As a fan of the films, I LOVED IT.
Despite all this, almost straight away you will realize it is all a facade. Smoke and mirrors. 95% of the environment cannot be interacted with. 100% of the locations are used again and again.
Thus begins a battle within yourself to pretend you are in one of the films rather than in a very cleverly disguised rat in a maze following a single path. The only path.
They have included a crafting mini-game where you can collect all sort of junk to create bombs and healing kits. You can go around collecting IDs of the crew. Possibly the worst type of collection game in existence. There is no explanation or information about who these people were. Just names. Pathetic!
The space station where most of the game is based really does feel huge. There are lifts to other levels and it even hosts a train station type location where you can catch a ride along to the furthest edges in quick time. The station also houses the different type of zoning areas one would expect such as medical, engineering and residential. It is well done.
As I progressed through the game more and more weapons and items were made available to me. Some locations that I could not access before could later be entered once I had, for example, access to a welding torch or electronic hacking devices.
The Alien was pretty amazing. Hiding under tables was amazing. Adjusting the environmental controls to reduce the light or air filtering was amazing.
Playing a game where I was hiding in a locker and trying to look through its cracks was pretty amazing.
Trying to hold my breath in game and simultaneously in real life was pretty AMAZING.
Despite the developers trying to randomize it's behavior as much as possible, somewhere along though you will sense the Alien's patterns. At one point I was running through every new location to see if it was safe to do so.
The game carefully treads the tightrope between shooter and stealth very well. It reminds me a bit of Deadspace and System Shock 2. More stealth than anything else because for a long, long time you cannot survive any confrontation with the Alien.
It's all good until you slowly realize that you are stuck in a maze following the only path set up by the gaming gods.
27 hours in I would like to continue the game and complete the story. But I can guess what will happen. And I am no rat.
Recommend to purchase on sale for the experience only.

This is utterly terrifying.  I first played the game in 2014 when it first came out which then only had Easy, Normal, and Hard difficulties available.  While I played it on normal it was still very tough to get through.  The AI for the Alien truly makes it an enemy like no other.  You'd think you'd be tailing it as it walks down a corridor until suddenly, and without warning, it'll turn it's head in your direction then you're Alien chow.  Or you'd walk along another section and hear the Alien thumping around in the vent, to all of a sudden drop down right in front of you.
When this game first came out I thoroughly enjoyed it as it really sells that retro-future ascetic used in Ridley Scott's first film Alien.  A lot of people I've seen play this call the first Alien film a 1980's film.  It's not.  Production started in 1977 and was released in 1979.  The decor and architecture of browns and greys was "the thing" back in the day.  That makes the film a 1970's film, not the physadelic colors of the 80's.  Yet another look this game nails.  Wondering around the Torrens and Sevastopol station you'll see many reminders of where this game gets its backbone from.  The seats and walls are emblazoned with the drab 2-tone covers, the monochromatic monitors displaying text and basic graphics common in 1960's and 1970's computers.
And then, and THEN the music starts playing.  The music is adaptive to your situation.  In an area devoid of enemies you'll usually hear a calming melody which sets the mood that, yes, while you are in a dangerous environment you're not alone and not in immediate danger.  But then the alien gets near, you hide, the alien gets nearer still, then the music changes.  The trombones and horns start singing as you hind in that locker or under a table, you can't move and only hope the alien will move on.  And in a couple of sections of the game you'll even hear little ditties that came straight from the original firm to further emphasise you're in space and deep in the Xeno-verse.
The vanilla game is truly epic with some only a couple of scripted scenes with the alien, the alien is pure unfettered AI looking, sniffing for you.  A really tough challenge is to play the game on Nightmare difficulty, however as I write this review, I've started playing the game yet again this time with the Unpredictable Alien and No Motion Tracker mods.  It's bad enough the alien is "somewhere", and the motion tracker can only approximate it's position especially in maps with multiple levels to it, but try playing this game with only audio clues to try and keep tabs on the alien as it scuttles each level you're on.
The game isn't without faults though.  Bipedal NPCs seem "stiff" while walking.  No so great when seeing humans walk like that but is a great effect on the Working Joes.  Talking of which, the game is called Alien: Isolation, not Attack of the Working Joes.  There's far too many in game, though like in Deus Ex are best left alone as they can be really tough to take down without the right tools, and neigh on impossible if they don't like you while the Alien is nearby.
Voice acting is film quality but while in-game (not when a cut scene is being played out) lip-syncing is a hit-and-miss.  Though that's not a problem on the 'Joes as they have no lips to sync.  There are also a few missions where you have to traverse the same map 2 or 3 times, I'm not talking about maps you play early in game you have to play later on in the story with different enemies oh no.  I'm talking about you enter a level, you get set a waypoint on the map (not available in Nightmare difficulty) for the exit, you get there but the exit is locked.  So you have to go to another point on that same map, do something and return to that exit.  I understand Creative Assembly are trying to keep the tension up by prolonging it for as long as possible but it can get very tedious for speed runners.
I love the Aliens franchise and this is THE DEFINITIVE Alien game for any one who loves the lore like I do.  A masterpiece on it's own, but with the few mods that are available, you can make it so much more terrifying like never before.

Bought this after playing a pirated copy about 4 times, so my total playtime is really around 80-100 hours.
What can I say that hasn't been said already? Alien: Isolation is a love letter to fans of the original 1979 film that started it all. The alien is a hulking, unbeatable beast and no doubt the protagonist of the game, but if you look past the fabulously accurate recreation of the film's aesthetic, you have a fantastic cat-and-mouse stealth game that had me terrified throughout almost the entirety of the experience. The game is clearly too long, and while it has many tricks up its sleeve, it has such a huge amount of time to spread them out in that the campaign does eventually become somewhat stale in the final third or so. It's still a wonderful game - just an excessively long one, at around 25-30 hours if you're doing a completionist playthrough when it really ought to be in the late teens.
Either way, this title kickstarted the comeback of AAA horror. It's the first good game the Alien franchise has had in years and by far the best one; it excels as a horror game; it excels as a stealth game; it excels as a film series-to-videogame adaptation. This isn't a review as much as me just gushing over one of my favourite games, but the "Overwhelmingly positive" consensus that Alien: Isolation has (at the time of writing this) is pretty much what my opinion aligns with. If you enjoy horror, stealth, the Alien series or just good looking games, I absolutely recommend this.

Papers, Please is a hard sell, after all the sentence "Eastern Bloc immigration official simulator" sounds anything but fun, let alone something that will maintain interest.  Yet despite this apparent handicap, the game is totally engrossing, as you decide who can enter Arstotzka - and it really is a matter of life or death in some cases - and it poses so many questions about the gamers' ethics and morals.
Even though it seems to be a drudgery sim, with you doing little more than stamping passports for the duration, there's several storylines that run through the game and a sly streak of humour amidst the oppression and the dystopian greyness that stops the game feeling grim.
It may not be for everyone, as the game requires you to concentrate on the papers in front of you as well as keep a good memory of the nations and cities around you, but this gives Papers, Please an old school charm from the era where taking notes would get you through a game successfully, so if this is up your proverbial street this is a game for you.  Be warned, though: you will be humming the theme tune for days.

I would only recommend this game if you really know what you're getting yourself into. I marked "Yes" because It was a fun game to play and I'm familiar with the series. While the game had its fair share of problems, if you're a fan of the series you'll enjoy yourself. Unfortunately, in my opinion, it is a downgrade from the sequel. If there was a "mixed" option, I would probably choose that instead. I purchased this game while it was 75% off, and I highly recommend that you do the same if you really want it.
If you have a high end system, don't worry about the people complaining about memory leaks.
I have 16GB RAM, GTX 1070, and Intel 6700k and experienced no real issues regarding memory leaks.
However, that does not change the fact that the game was very glitchy. Enemies spawn in right before your eyes at times, physics glitches are not uncommon, and the game is generally unstable (in the lovable Just Cause sort of way). I will still able to maintain a consistently high frame rate despite this. I have crashed to desktop 1 time, and had to force close the game due to it locking up 2 times in my 24 hours of playing it, so it's really not all that bad.
They somehow managed to make the driving even worse than how it was in Just Cause 2. Once you get used to it, it's not so bad. Motorcycles are especially horrible to drive, you will never get used to them. The vehicles have a really strange momentum/weight to them, and it's very difficult to drive with a keyboard and mouse unlike in games like Grand Theft Auto 5 or Saint's Row. The driving mechanics also depend way too much on using your hand brake, and of course that is a pain since the controls are frustrating. Be prepared to not use your space bar for hand brakes. They also got rid of the Stunt Jump mechanic from Just Cause 2, which is a major disappointment. It's a lot harder to hijack cars and vehicles, and it's very frustrating trying to enter cars via grappling hook alone. Rico also has a very cool habit of only walking while on boats and planes. Since there is no more Stunt Jumping, this makes it very tedious and frustrating to actually enter the cockpit of boats and planes. In Just Cause 2, you could just press the Stunt Jump button to have Rico quickly and automatically grapple his way into position to enter a vehicle and drive it, but in 3 you have to actually walk over to the cockpit or car door for some reason.
This game was clearly not optimized for PC. The game will never let you know about keybind conflicts, and with so many different keys and functions, things get very difficult to manage. I actually ended up binding "contract tether" to one of the rudder controls for air vehicles by accident and realized this halfway through the game. The game will also not let you know if chaning one bind for one control will change another. For example, if you want to change your parachute button while on foot to something else, this will in turn change your parachute and bail buttons for driving as well, and the game will not notify you of this. Also, there are many binds that are linked, such as jumping onto the roof of a car and bailing by parachute. The game will list these as separate binds although they will always be bound to the same button no matter what. This was one of the biggest annoyances of this game. The keybinding in Just Cause 2 was leagues better than this.
It's repetitive, but such is the nature of Just Cause. However, since the story is lackluster, none of it really feels like it's worth it. Sure, it's fun to destroy bases and liberate towns at first, but then you start to realize the copy/paste nature of many areas in the game world, and the game starts turning into a chore. There are also many annoying parts of combat. Enemies with shotguns can temporarily stun Rico from quite long ranges for some reason. Also, hitting the ground while using a wingsuit is very annoying. No matter how fast you go, Rico will get stunned, unless you unlock the ability to retract your wingsuit when going slowly near the ground, which should have been a feature by default. Be sure not to get stunned while on a mountain or something, or else Rico will go into an uncontrollable tumble for an annoyingly long amount of time. The stun mechanics in the game are horrible and annoying. You will find yourself getting frustrated every time Rico falls over.
There are also many challenges that you must do to upgrade tools and equipment, which also (surprise!) gets annoying quite quickly. By doing challenges, you earn "gears" which act as currency towards upgrades of different kinds. If you do a racing challenge you unlock gears for cars, gun challenges unlock gears for guns, and so forth. You actually have to unlock things like precision aiming, which should have been available from the beginning by default, and things like increased tethers, which should have been unlocked as the story progressed. A lot of the unlocks are also very underwhelming and were clearly meant to be filler/padding for the more interesting and useful upgrades. Oh, I unlocked the ability to get a supply drop faster? Wow, because they were
to begin with.
The story was pretty nice, but the ending felt incredibly rushed. Things will be developing at a certain pace and then it will ramp up out of nowhere and end unexpectedly. The ending is unbelievably underwhelming compared to the ending of Just Cause 2. Spoilers:
The game also lacks the charm of Just Cause 2. Just Cause 2 felt like a campy B-movie, and Rico felt like the stereotypical lead to that kind of movie, his voice actor fit the role perfectly. You could practically see him doing the sign of the cross after taking out baddies. Now, Rico is this rugged manly man with a new voice actor whom I'm not entirely fond of. Rico is still Rico, though. He's still out fighting for the greater good and trying to end corruption, taking the obvious moral high ground as always, and I love him for it. Just Cause 3 story-wise is basically Just Cause 2, but with less of the B-movie charm. It is nice to finally get some answers regarding Rico's past, as well as somewhat of a conclusion to it. I really enjoyed the setting and premise of the story, but felt that it was lacking in a few areas.
If you want to just kill time with a game revolving around mindless action and chaos, and dont mind the occasional glitch and can stand mediocre controls, then go for it. It was fun to play but it could have been a lot better. If you haven't played Just Cause 2, I would HIGHLY recommend that you do before playing 3, it'll make you appreciate 3 a lot more.

Dark Souls II isn't a bad game, but it is definitely an incomplete release.  With the release of the Scholar of the First Sin update, soon to be followed by a version with improved graphics and re-imagined enemy placement, it's dreadfully apparent that this is not a complete version of the game.
That this game was released at a AAA new release price point, yet required additional item descriptions and an entirely new character to complete the lore, implicitly admits the story to this game was not completely fleshed out. That the graphics had to be improved (when, at the very least, PC players could handle DX11 graphics at launch) and the level design had to be revised to move and add to enemies implicitly admits the game design was incomplete.
If this game were released in it's initial state as an early access title, or at a lower price point, I would be less irritated. If many of the changes were offered as an update, rather than a full blown re-release, I would also be less irritated.  As it stands, Miyazoe (and by extension From Software) misled fans in these statements:
Source:
It remains apparent that those who bought the game on day one did not receive a full experience, and won't unless they buy the Scholar of the First Sin edition.
If you don't own it yet, I don't recommend this title at all.  I recommend that you wait for the complete version of the game, and not waste your money buying twice.

Darn good fun whether you play the Story, Arcade or Duels you'll find something to enjoy. The main Story is short, around 6 hours gameplay, although the price of the game refects this. Graphics are good and stylised a little. I've played the Hard and True West difficulty, completed the Duels and love running the Arcade gauntlets. The AI isn't that much harder to beat at the "maximum" level, it can be pretty predictable, but the real fun of this game is in the plot devices used to tell a yarn about some famous Wild West gunslingers, outlaws and even a few Injuns – the voice acting is great, witty and represents some classic Western humour. The "rewind and replay" events which occur a few times when the story is told from different angles is really amusing. Nice to see a short game with a few Achievemets thrown in, for those who like bagging them.
I would love to see a sequel in the same style, or even a DLC, in order to have a fresh campaign to play through, with some new guns and skill. Some horseback or stagecoach riding would be nice, or even a new game with a similar design but set in a non-linear open world, in the style of "Gun" would be interesting – a "gun for hire" format Western FPS instead of the usual WW2 or zombie shoot 'em ups would make a nice change.

Broforce is a lot more indepth than its machismo parody might lead you to believe. Each character has unique abilities that drastically change how you approach obstacles, the stages are designed so that you can literally carve your own paths through them, the asthetic is  retro but crisp, and the references and over the top dialogue are clever while still being overt. The entire game is an homage to the cheesy and glorious action movies of the 80's, and I adore that.
That being said, the sheer chaos of explosions and attacks can easily obscure your view, making it easy to get hit by stray projectiles, and the balance of the different characters varies wildly which, when combined with the random nature of which characters you have access to at a given time, can greatly affect the level difficulty. For some this is a positive, but for me it meant some runs were better off not finishing because the roster of characters I had acquired for that level was not up to the task.
God speed broforce... gods speed!

The Elder Scrolls Online: Tamriel Unlimited is probably the mmo with the most interesting singelplayer content and quest (as far as I no, all voiced) out there rigth now. I'm not going to talk about graphics here, it's COD, it was fairly shiny at release but nothing special, framerate locked to ~90 + standard player.cfg file (use it to modify those ping bars - useful for identifying ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hosts).
Single player is fairly engaging when played for the first time, although once you play through it for nth time and get all of the intelligence pieces, you can finish the campaign on veteran in roughly 4 hours :)
Coop system is OK, parts of the campaign cut out and given some extra context, interesting implementation of stuff like sentry guns and predator missiles here and there.
Multiplayer which I spent over 700 hours on (lol) is a strong average (lol2), no dedicated servers mean host-based matches with average pings in the 100-150 range that sometimes give you the 'realistic' bullet travel effect, you do get used to it after a week or 2. Prestige system was hacked immediately, if you have a friend with some hacks, just ask him to host a server and get prestige 10 to unlock all weapon slots (only benefit of prestiging, IMO). The incredible amount of lag and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ lobby management at release made my parents question the existance of god. It has been fixed after time though.

Atmospheric
I have quite an extensive selection of categories in my steam library, and one of them is 'Atmospheric'. After completing Alien Isolation, it made me think about all the games in the category and compare them to this. Do they have the right to be in this category. This is such a solid product, but I cannot recommend it to everyone. Before playing watching the first Alien movie is a must. Watching all the other Alien movies is unimportant, as this game mostly uses the world and the xenomorph from the first movie.
First of all. The game has five different difficulty levels, novice, easy, medium, hard(recommended by developers) and nightmare. Novice and Nightmare were published later in a patch if I understood correctly. I first played with Hard to mission 5, then medium to mission 5 and then completed it with Easy. The reason I am mentioning this is the fact that the game is a totally different experience if played on different difficulties. With harder difficulties, the Alien is an all-present terror, that you need to trick and bypass almost constantly. In easier difficulties the Alien is more of an unseen terror that pops out every now and then, especially when someone has to do something noisy or important. Added to the Easy difficulty, I also was doing achievement that required no humans killed by me, that meant also no stunning. So these two heavily effected my experience of the game and therefore my review. Some of the things mentioned above are only valid if played with the same difficulty.
Basically the game is first person stealth-game with survival being the aim of the game. Your aim is to survive in a hostile space-station filled with scared people, immortal xenomorph and androids with anger management issue. The game consists mostly avoiding enemies, by hiding in certain objects or behind cover. To accomplish your goals, you can use some items or weapons. Most of the game consist of crouching behind objects or walking from hiding place to hiding place since the main antagonist, the omnipresent xenomorph, is immortal, cannot be killed or harmed. It is afraid of fire though so after receiving flamethrower and molotovs, one has some chances to repel it for few seconds, enough to escape and hide.
The environment of the game is brilliantly done. The station is claustrophobic, horrible and beautiful all at the same time. The graphics are still looking good, level design is great and the sound effects build constant terror while the music is great homage to the first movie. Almost from the start I got shivers because the music brought the first movie into my mind. Occasionally the music can be a bit of pain in the♥♥♥♥♥by playing too loud while one tries to hear the xeno's movement. Although the game is mostly quite linear, one can backtrack quite a lot if they want, although there isn't much to gain from it. Also the game cleverly builds the maps so, that after visiting a new place you almost always end up in a previously visited place from a new direction. It kind of reminded me of Dark Souls but in a more claustrophobic way. So eventually you will visit some places many times, but almost never it feels like a chore. During the last missions I hated the station, not because it was boring but because it was so terrifying. I honestly could relate to the character. I didn't want to go on to another deadly place because I was alive in this current one. Yet I had to go on to actually get out of the station and complete the game.
The main gripes this game has received is it's antagonist, the xenomorph. Unlike most survival horror games, the developers took a different approach. Instead of totally scripted moments, the alien is almost always there. If you make too much sound, it will jump down from the vents and start looking for you. While you can hide, it is said that the alien in the game can learn from your manouvers and essentially the more you succeed avoiding it, the less likely you will succeed in later game. This was something that was mostly missing from Easy difficulty. Although I could kind of prove it by luring the alien many times a row and repel it with flame thrower. Each time I had to use more of the precious fuel to repel it and eventually it killed me just by ramming me. Although it's not explained how the alien knows to start looking from closets if it never found you there, it gives the game a constant tension. Instead of learning all the tricks he can do, he learns all the tricks I can do and the game keeps staying intensive, although I'm given new ways to deal with it. The more time you spend going about, repelling and luring it, the more harder the end game becomes.
But the gripe isn't about the learning, it's about the prevalence of his appearance. On harder difficulties the alien roams the hallways and rarely goes to the vents. On easy he stays more in the vents and roams less. That means, the harder the difficulty, the more the player has to play aggressive to avoid it and yet progress in the story. The problem is the game is quite unforgiving, some save stations are far and between and there are only few ways to avoid the xeno in the first few missions. So the game isn't easy and it punishes the player for any mistakes. **  So if you have found this game too irritating or hard, I suggest trying the lower difficulties that change the game quite a lot. It's not about damage and amount of items, but the whole game mechanic that comes different.
There are some flaws that I can point out. The biggest of all, the xenomorph is a bit blind. This isn't obviously clear from the start, but it can mostly see only infront of it. This means that one can almost sneak right next to it without it seeing you. Also it cannot see the player if she's behind a small object or a table. At some points, where the alien is scripted to linger in the area(in easier difficulties too), the common tactic is to find a box or a small table and just go around it while the alien walks the other side. The blindness of the xeno is sometimes almost baffling, he can walk just right by you and then the next minute he finds you from the vents or from a closet. So the core mechanic of the game encourages to do gamey things. It's less intelligent to hide in a perfectly dark closet instead of hiding under a small table or behind a small chair. In my opinion this kind of breaks the immersion instead of creating it, although the music seems to love me being so close to the alien on the open.
The minigames are a bit of a chore as they are mostly only related to going through door or opening some computer or hatch. There's rarely any rush and they are quite easy. The power junction mechanic seems a bit underused and underpowered to justify it's presence in the game. I encountered a couple glitches that gave some comical relief but mostly the game was rock solid with no major bugs or problems.
So for me this was one of the best games I played this year. It was the most atmospheric game propably of all time. I'm terrified enough not to play it again anytime soon and have to recommend it to anyone with a love for Alien, survival horror as a genre and computer games in general. Although if you hate any of the three mentioned above and have little patience to somewhat challenging game mechanic, you propably will have a better life with out experiencing this one.

I absolutely could not recommend this game more. To me,
is one of the best games of 2013, and one of the most unique games I've had the pleasure of playing. At it's face it seems like one of the most boring concepts imaginable for a video game--you play as a lottery-chosen man serving as a checkpoint official for a communist country, and to most people a game emulating government work wouldn't really seem like a blast.
Right from the first few in-game days, though, it provides an interesting challenge that slowly meshes with a branching storyline that depends on how you choose to play the game. Will you play as a patriot, proudly serving your country and preventing dangerous individuals from crossing your iron border, or will you sneakily aid a government-proclaimed "terrorist" organisation in fighting against your country's tyrannical political system. How you perceive the situation will depend on you, as all in all it's a setting clouded by grey much more than black and white. There is incentive and reason behind running the checkpoint well, too, as you must manage entry properly to earn your salary, which is necessary to keep your family healthy and safe throughout the story.
In conclusion, this game was absolutely worth the ten-dollar price tag, and more, really, and has a reasonably amount of replayability to it because of the numerous endings. You'll probably manage to come across several in your first playthrough, because the way the save system works allows you to continue from the beginning of any day you've progressed to. I would guess that the average player who enjoys this game and plays it two or three times will probably get a reasonably eight to ten hours of gameplay out of it--the average full run for me seems to be about four hours, and I've so far gotten about 16 hours of enjoyed time out of it. I can't promise you'll enjoy
, but I'd be willing to bet you would.

While many enjoy the Total War games because of their unique blend of real-time strategy combat and standard-setting visuals or their incredibly high production values, what makes them truly fantastic is that one can easily invest hundreds of hours into just one entry of the series and likely never grow tired of its addicting mix of fighting and management. I have spend many hours on Rome II and yet I still keep coming back for more. Whether it be to try a new faction, a different early game strategy, change up my research priorities, focus more on naval prowess rather than raw manpower, empower trade over combat as a continent-spanning empire or mix up my tactics in the battles themselves.
The Total War games are packed with content, like the unique scenario battles that represent a key conflict in history, narrative campaigns and tutorial campaigns that each require a few hours or more of your time at the very least while presenting a mostly distinct experience, many entirely separate factions each with their own various traits at both a regional and cultural level, and the grand campaigns.
Each of these is a massive undertaking and has almost endless permutations for the path to total victory, dependent on any number of the factors mentioned above. You can even use the skirmish battle system to try out all different tactics and unit combinations from any of the numerous factions present in the game against a battle AI that you can freely adapt to your tastes in terms of difficulty. Lastly, Rome II offers an expansive suite of multiplayer options to back up its gargantuan single-player offerings, allowing you to play challenging battles against your friends or compete for global domination through the usual turn-based campaign system, even if the multiplayer isn't as functional as I would like! I have put many hours in every single Total War game and each new entry is both fresh enough and packed with quality to easily justify that kind of investment time and again - truly, this is a franchise that knows how to eat up the small hours of the day. If ever you needed a game to kill time in while trying out multiple different approaches to victory, allowing you to succeed either through making friends or destroying enemies in equal measure, then Rome II has been tailor made to match your desires.

Just Cause 3
A game filled with some of the best highs and most disastrous lows of any recent game i have played.
Upon getting this game on release day i was hyped. Loved just cause 2 with at least 3 playthroughs completed on ps3. Arrived at a new triple A title only to find no SLI support... okay. This meant i was using a 680 instead of a 690. On release day this game was nothing short of unplayable. I just love 30fps medium settings at 1080p,, trully glorious. After waiting for some drivers and a couple of patches I got stuck in, and was having great fun. Stuttering on a 4790k aside, i was having fun.
So lets talk gameplay.
- The wingsuit, was a very logical and good edition to Just Cause, it aloud for mobility (without vehicles) to be increased         massively, although difficult at first, a lot of fun once mastered.
- Vehicles feel a lot better than in just cause 2 mostly down to the work of Criterion Games who did a fantastic job, except motorbikes, they are horrendous and easily one of the worst things to drive in any game. Lots of vehicle choice with plenty of detail.
- Challenge scores and Feats that once set your friends can try and beat, a lot of fun to be had. However many of the challenges are incredibly buggy (especially bomb blasts) this 9 times of 10 stop them from being fun and make them more of a chore and an absolute nuisance.
- Upgrades, not much needs to be said, they are great edition and really help with a sense of progretion throughout the game, good job.
- Graphics, oh my. Run in 4k on a Titan X Pascal, its nothing short of stunning. Render distances could be improved but apart from that a true feast for the eyes.
- Story, no spoilers, is a lot of fun but has dodgy characters and terrible pacing with live rendered cutscenes that most of the time go wrong in some way.
Now, comes for the real problems. Im currently running a 5960x at 3.3ghz and the game doesnt stutter at all even in massive moments of destruction. However it should not be necessary to owen a £1000 cpu just to get the game to be smooth. The developers need to get there act together. My game would crash after about 4 hours of play without fault, there are still VRAM leak bugs that havnt been bothered to be fixed. And although I would say compared to most people my game ran well I know a friend with a 6700k and GTX 1080 and the game would flat out refuse to run in full screen without crashing.
However many hours of enjoyment I have had out of this title I cannot overlook the fact that the Devs released a broken game and have refused to fix it.
Overall I would give this game a 5/10
p.s. Dont get me started on the DLCs what a cash grabbing joke, 60% of the time they are absolutly horrendous and the rest of the time they are crashing. They break all of the balance in the game and unless you can get them all for under £5 i wouldnt go anywhere near them.

As much as I want to, I cannot recommend this game. I've played through Just Cause 2 mulitple times and enjoyed each moment of it, but this? This has been a horrendous mess. Before I go on, I should point out that i'm using an i7-6700k, 16GB of RAM, and a GTX 1080, displaying onto a 1080p screen (I really should go to 4k). Not even this could handle the s***storm that is Just Cause 3.
I hadn't even started playing the game when I encountered my first problem. The game would crash on boot in fullscreen mode. A little bit of tweaking meant I could boot it in borderless windowed mode. After getting to the main screen I set everything at ultra and selected play, to which I was instantly greeted with 25 FPS constantly. I rebooted the game multiple times, turned down all of the settings, made sure I was on the latest video drivers, and even rebooted the system, yet nothing worked. A fresh install did nothing and i decided to call it a night.
12 or so hours later, I decided to try again. Oddly enough, it decided to run at 60fps with everything on ultra. Happy with the outcome, I went through the intro again and began playing. 1 mission in and the game was already experiencing bugs. After the helicopter that was supposed to pick me up didn't arrive (which I actually found rather funny), the game decided to crash. I brushed this off and tried again, yet it crashed after an hour or so of gameplay. I gave up.
Later that day, determined to play a game that looked so beautiful and so much fun, I tried once again to keep the game running. I opened all of my monitoring software up to make sure I wasn't running out of resources and began playing. Of course, it didn't crash for about 5 hours. When it did, none of the software was showing any problems with the computer, so it must've been the game.
I continued to play for a few days or so, and each time it would crash after 4-5 hours of gameplay, which while it is annoying if you spend long periods of time gaming like me, wasn't as bad as the game running at 25 FPS. Several of the challenges I attempted within the game had a couple of bugs here and there, which was a pain to get around, especially within the crash bomb challenges as the bomb explosion is tiny and does very little damage for an explosion so big. It was only after the game crashed in the middle of a mission for the third time that i decided it was time to write this review.
I will admit, there are some parts of the game I did enjoy. The wingsuit mechanic is very well done and while difficult at first, once mastered, does become a very useful tool for getting around the place. The upgrade system works well and the leaderboards feature is a great way of competing with friends and adds an extra challenge to the game to complete in your free time if you wish. The vehicle models and mechanics (well, maybe apart from the bike mechanics) were very well done and made me want to actually drive around instead of wingsuiting everywhere. Additionally, the character models and the scenery in general is beautifully done and really captured the mediterranean atmosphere.
If you can look past the problems with the game and really enjoyed the previous one, pick it up, although wait for it to be on sale just in case you do have problems with it, as spending £10 on a broken game is better than spending £40 on a broken game. The problems I had will not be there for everyone and if you do pick this up, you may have no problems with it at all, but due to my experience with it, I cannot recommend purchasing this game.
I will eventually complete this game and attempt to 100% it, but for now, I think I'm going to give it a break.

Here's a smal disclaimer before reading my review. If Dark Souls Prepare to Die Edition was never made, and this was the first "Dark Souls" game, I would have thought this is the best game ever.
Dark Souls II was a long anticipated release for me. I was aboard the hype train the second it was announced. However when I played it I was immediatley greeted with disappointment. The level designs didn't flow or connect well at all. The bosses weren't actually hard, and the ones that were hard were either a damage sponge, or fromsoft just decided to put more enemies there, instead of making it challenging. These aren't even the worst offenders. What really offends is the story. In Dark Souls 1 we had an enviornment very literally DRIPPING with atmosphere that told a story of its own, just as we explored the bowels of its cruel world. And some of that is true for Dark Souls II, but the bits of story it actually gives you seems to make little sense, and has no real meaning. Perhaps that's what they were going for? I'm truly still unsure close to a year later. But this wasn't how Demon Souls or Dark Souls was made. The Covenants were nice if they ever worked, not to mention the whole lack of penalty for leaving a covenant. The new Parrying system was absolutely pointless, they had it right in the first game, and this one just seems to want to break up the action. I liked the idea of degenerating health upon death, however there were simply too many ways to avoid it. Combat seemed fine enough and that is a core mechanic of the game, but I fail to see any saving grace for it, when the developers "balanced" the combat.  The game isn't a PVP experience first, it's a PVE first, and you don't need to mess with that. I suppose the best parts about this game for me were actually the Expansion Packs. The Areas flowed well and kept my attention, but this was after the fact and it felt like a new team worked on them. At the end of the day, Dark Souls II was a good game if you didn't play Dark Souls or Demons Souls. But for those of us returning to the series, we have nothing to find but disappointment and hand holding.
10/10 Game of the Year

Not tl;dr
Now since that is out of the way, Transistor is an action rpg in an asemetric perpective that follows the story of Red in the city of Cloudbank. This game has an extroadinary soundtrack composed by the one and only Daren Korb and has a very interesting take on its gameplay. There are two ways to aproach combat, one way is to approach enemies in real time, and the other is during the "turn" mode. In this turn mode it freezes time and you can strategically move and perform attacks which will each diminish a portion of your energy bar. Many times i would find myself just waiting for my "turn" to recharge and then atack but others may prefer the real time combat opposed to the "turn" combat.
Next, the astetic of the game is beutiful. With most of the assets hand drawn it brings to light a unique world with tons of character that definitaly stands apart from other games. Also, the characters are very interesting and the plot does not seem cookie cutter or monotinous.
However the game does still have some problems. For example, some attacks do feel very overpowered and some players may find themselfs only using a specific itemset and not exploring other oppurtunities.
In the end, the conjunction of the different ways and lore you recieve from abilities, visually appealing world, and fun combat i reccomend you give this game a try.

I'm not going to talk about graphics here, it's COD, it was fairly shiny at release but nothing special, framerate locked to ~90 + standard player.cfg file (use it to modify those ping bars - useful for identifying ♥♥♥♥♥♥ hosts).
Single player is fairly engaging when played for the first time, although once you play through it for nth time and get all of the intelligence pieces, you can finish the campaign on veteran in roughly 4 hours :)
Coop system is OK, parts of the campaign cut out and given some extra context, interesting implementation of stuff like sentry guns and predator missiles here and there.
Multiplayer which I spent over 700 hours on (lol) is a strong average (lol2), no dedicated servers mean host-based matches with average pings in the 100-150 range that sometimes give you the 'realistic' bullet travel effect, you do get used to it after a week or 2. Prestige system was hacked immediately, if you have a friend with some hacks, just ask him to host a server and get prestige 10 to unlock all weapon slots (only benefit of prestiging, IMO). The incredible amount of lag and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ lobby management at release made my parents question the existance of god. It has been fixed after time though.
On a positive note, there are new guns, with much higher level of customizability, but the idea of a shotgun being secodary weapon vs e.g. a pistol gave me mixed feelings (not that I wasn't using one). Perk system has both improvements and flaws, with marathon/lightweight/commando combination being the worst, where enemies on small maps simply run around knifing you from time to time, same goes for One Man Army with GL, tactical insertion and good camping spot -  it's just as annoying.
New killstreaks including the infamous nuke which pretty much makes you a cheater and make everyone leave the lobby is easy to earn with any 'static' (sniping is not camping!, just because you can quick scope, doesn't mean you should) class and a Harrier/Chopper or AC130/Nuke combo.
I was banned for unknown time period (for"cheating" - using AK-47 with FMJ on campers) back in 2010, but after installing the game recently I found that I can play again, although the playerbase has dropped significantly since then.
Lastly, I could recommend this game for anyone who is flexible enough to get over all multiplayer flaws and master all maps to easily own enemies, or wants a few days with a nicely executed campaign and co-op mode.
P.S This was the last COD I have bought, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥has clearly shown us why (both projects have been closed due to "copyright infringement" ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t).

It took me a while to get into this game. I found it a bit repetitive and quickly resorted to a guide to avoid having to constantly replay between save stations and for fear of missing critical objects or triggers.
But once the alien turns up those frustrations come about and become acceptable for the most part.
And dare i say i did really start to enjoy it. Being part of the alien universe while being hunted by one of the most fearsome monsters ever dreamt up is fun indeed. And it is without doubt the best game of this franchise yet.
But It appears what this game does well is simply owed to Scott and Camerons  genius. Most of what makes AI good are the elements dragged out of those first 2 films. Infact at times its more complete repeats of scenes from the first film!
The game itself doesnt really bring anything new that will have you thinking it could actually add to the universe. (thats a bit unfair as some of the enviroment is new and quite good at times)
As for the game itself one of its greatest strenghts is what it doesnt do....
That is doom 3 style 'its dark so a monster is going to jump out... o look a monster from the dark.. again'
and the usual horror game trick of making you utterly useless and defencless. In this game Ripply is quite happy to take hard approach if pushed, just like her mother.
By not falling into those 2 traps means this game roles along in an enjoyable and almost beleivable fashion.
Although the Alien not being killable is probably a bit silly overall. 2 pipe bombs, a molotov and 4 shotgun rounds at point blank range and it just drops a spoonful of blood and runs off for a few seconds.
What really wins it for this game as far as recomendations go however is it brings a good Alien enviroment to our PC's. For you youngsters, go watch the first 2 films. Youll be blown away. Then enjoy the game.

The narrarators are very good in their delivery, and the conflicting views of the narrarators (which is a group of men at a bar) on top of the main character being vague and sometimes almost senile leads to some fun, humorous, and misleading moments. It is a relatively short game, but it was massive replay value with New Game + allowing you to keep your skills gained, give you another chance to collect the hidden items that give exposition and history tid-bits (if that's you're thing), and also giving information about the game's story, making things clear if you couldn't piece them together on your first playthrough.

-The best part of the game is the fact the developers are making every attempt to release a solid title. They fix what's broken in a realistic time. No, they don't shut the game down everytime something goes wrong with a mechanic. That's unrealistic and would frustrate everyone off who isn't having problems with that area of the game. They do address most problems on a weekly basis. Whether it's botters, real world item traders, or a messed up dungeon queue, it has been delt with, maybe not completely irradicated, but delt with. Show me an MMO that doesn't have similar problems and I'll show you a liar.
-The game play isn't trying to reinvent the wheel, but it isn't a WoW clone by any means. The leveling system is different, but effective. The class system keeps you interested in leveling. The grind is real in the game, but they take the grind and make it fun. You level up with quests, dungeons, and eventually PvP. There are so many different combinations of character builds with 4 core character classes. There is something for every type of mmorpg gamer.
-The game so far doesn't feel like it's pay2win, but that may be just because the currency for the in game cash shop hasn't been released yet. A pay2win title is typically only a problem for people who don't have a job or don't feel like spending money on entertainment is worth their investment (these people live boring lives or are amazing at entertaining themselves).
-There are things in the game that are still being worked on. I believe the adjustments to the games graphics will be overhauled and the friend list/buddy list reworked. The developers, IMC, are more worried about releasing a solid game, versus complete at this time, because so many people were demanding for the release. All in all, the game should be recommended to anyone that enjoys Fantasy MMOs. The developers care, the game play isn't unfamiliar, but is unique enough, and what's broke will be fixed.

I expect this review will be a little controversial, and I'll probably get lots of thumbs down, but in my opinion Transistor is kind of average. Not terrible, but not deserving of all the hype.
The combat is fun. Plenty of freedom and variety. Along the way you unlock lots of different powers, each one has three different uses - either as a primary attack, a buff for a different primary attack, or a passive buff for your character. You can choose to combine these powers in whatever way suits your playing style and can adjust the combinations at checkpoints.
In the later stages of the game I had a long range attack with a damage buff that also charmed the target to fight for me for a few seconds (allowing me some breathing space while the other enemies attacked the charmed one). I also had a cloak that would hide me from enemies, which also triggered an explosion in a radius around me, and then gave my next attack after de-cloak a further damage bonus. Meanwhile I was passively regenerating health, although I wasn't getting hit much anyway thanks to those other 2 combinations.
There is some nice enemy variety as well, some are able to heal or shield others, cloak themselves, abilities that influence your own tactics in terms of which enemy to target first. The difficulty is also flexible because of the "limiters" system. These are unlocked through level up and either make enemies stronger or yourself weaker when equipped, and then grant bonus XP.
But the story really dragged the game down for me. I have to admit, I don't really understand much of what happened. It throws you straight into the action without any setup and most dialogue feels like people talking in riddles. Lots of words without actually explaining anything. I guess there's a sword that can absorb dead people's souls (how? no idea) and some bad guys that are erasing the world (how? why? no clue). I kinda lost interest after a while. As much as I enjoy killing things, my favourite games are those that give context to my actions, give me a reason to care about why those things need killing, or why the world needs saving. Transistor completely failed in this respect. (Although, its indie, so I guess I'm just not intelligent enough to understand the deeper meaning or whatever).
Overall ... well, everybody else in the gaming industry seems to think the game is super amazing, so I guess my recommendation wouldn't be worth much. I regret buying it for full price, but I would say pick it up on a 50% off sale if you like tactical combat.

A terrific story, a moving conclusion, and an environment that draws you in and wraps you up in a fantastic and colorful world slowly being white washed. It's hard not to love this game and all its little moments, from the way the music matches a gorgeous environment that wraps you up, to the little bites of this world that help make it seem more than a game board that you slide your character across.
The combat system is quite charming; with a system built in that helps regulate difficulty as well as a time freezing trick that you can toggle when needed. The result is something that can delight everyone from the twitch player looking for the adrenaline pump of rapid tactical choices, to the labored perfectionist who tries to build just the right combination of steps to create the final satisfying conclusion. Both styles are rewarded well through Transistor's clever mechanics which was a delight to see and play with.
The story did seem a little odd at first, as you start in media res a tense escape against unknown assailants in a world unfamiliar to you; but everything comes together quickly and it's not long till the pieces start fitting together. The characters are a wonderful match; Red as the ever capable fighter whose voiceless dialogue told a wonderful story of the sort of person she was, and the Transistor itself voiced by the ever amazing Logan Cunningham who plays the perfect counterpart of being both helpless and ever hopeful lover who is really just forced to watch from the sidelines as the world unfolds around him.
I'll confess choking up when Red delivers her choice at the end of the game, and I found myself both understanding, dreading, and cheering it. Something which one doesn't always find when they embark on any narrative.
In short; I loved Transistor. It may not be for everyone, but it's a fantastic experience with a colorful narrative and characters that you'll fall in love with.

Before this the only Total War I had real experience with was Medieval 2, and I've gotta say, I'm glad I picked this up. Thank you, franchise sale, because Rome 2 is my favorite strategy game experience ever.  The world map management feels like a combination of Sid Meier's Civ V and Total War, and the research tree is a cool addition to the building. My only complaint about the world map is that it does feel a little oversimplified; definitely do your campaigns above "normal" difficulty if you want a real challenge.
Diplomacy is easier to do than ever before and it actually makes sense; your standing with a particular faction and its allies will actually affect what kind of treaties they'll enact with you, if any at all, and you're less likely to encounter random backstabbing. (Although why my client states maintain military alliances with countries I'm at war with I'll never know)
The actual battles are the same as before, with a pretty UI that tells you all you need to know and the addition of abilities - not just the formations, phalanxes, fire arrows, and stakes that we had before - but things like war cries to rally your own troops and intimidate the enemy all makes battles feel better and grittier.  All the different types of battles are great too, and it's awesome having an online battle work out when you're the reinforcing navy coming rescue your teammates :P
All in all, would totally recommend this game, especially as a good starting point into the Total War franchise if you want something that's actually historical and cool

Silas Greaves is probably full of♥♥♥♥♥♥ but that’s OK. He’s a bounty hunter with a million stories to tell, and happy to share them for a whisky or five. Like the times he rode with Billy the Kid, or when he won the praise of Injun magic men, or that shootout he had with Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (simultaneously). In short, tales of hanging out with just about every celebrity in the Wild West... and convenient excuses for why nobody can quite remember seeing him there.
This isn’t just a framing device for Gunslinger’s nine missions, but a big part of what helps this downloadable budget title wash away the foul taste of Call of Juarez: The Cartel. As expected, it’s a linear shooter set in a romanticised version of the Wild West (which the game itself at one point admits is complete balls). It’s also a shooter Greaves and his audience comment on throughout, the narration routinely changing the world to fit the story on the fly. At one point, for instance, you fight through a mine full of dynamite that only an idiot would go into with guns blazing. “That’s why I didn’t,” rasps Greaves, rewinding the story to tell it ‘properly’.
This doesn’t disguise the linearity, but it does make the straight path much more interesting. My only big complaint about the execution – aside from the fact that the dialogue was recorded as individual lines, and so usually fails to mesh into a smooth narrative – is that Techland didn’t use this gimmick on a full-budget game with scope for even bigger, more varied setpieces.
Restricting Juarez to raw gunplay certainly doesn’t hurt it, because the shooting is excellent. While not rewriting the rules of FPS, there’s a real weight to the weapons, while the action is a mix of regular shootouts and switching to a special slow-mo Concentration mode to take out whole groups in the blink of an eye. This ability regenerates quickly, providing an interesting power balance where you can’t take much damage, but regularly get to go full ‘Angel of Death’ on whole crowds. There’s also a very clever system where, with enough charge, you get a 50/50 chance of dodging a slowed-down incoming bullet that would normally be lethal. Get it right and you stay in the fight.
Combined, the two parts work beautifully. The story keeps things slightly off-balance and constantly throws up interesting moments, while the minute-by-minute gunplay makes murdering your way through that story intensely satisfying.
Yes, the graphics – and the cutscenes illustrated with static, hand-drawn images – are constant reminders that this is a budget game. Far from being diminished by that, however, Gunslinger impresses with just how well it spent its pennies. And, more impressively still, it makes the idea of another Call of Juarez game at some time in the future surprisingly appealing.

Free week review (just under 30 hours in - level 15)
First off it seems like a bunch of you need to take a class on time management, I started the download while I was at work for the day and when I got back, it took maybe 20 more minutes to get it installed and patched, I have an SSD and a 25mb internet speed connection, nothing crazy but seriously I don't understand all the complaints people are having with download/install time.
I have a GTX 970 and decent enough hardware to run everything at max and get a steady 100 fps in the world and about 40fps when in town, even when it drops to 25 during big battles I don't really notice any frame skipping, it's actually pretty impressive whatever they're doing on the server load here. I've never experienced any lag or rubberbanding (I've also not partictipated in any of the big alliance wars though yet) The most people I've seen on screen probably 20-30? during a portal fight.
Gameplay - It's still taking some getting used to, but I'm having a lot of fun with it. It feels a lot like any other elder scrolls game and again, I don't understand all the hate here, it's not going to be the same "quality" when you're talking about a MMO compared to the single player games, so stop comparing them. But honestly I have no qualms, it's scratching the itch I've had after beating Skryim awhile back and I couldn't be happier. It feels really easy right now still, but I've died a couple of times when 3-4 mobs start attacking me or I try to take on "Group" bosses. Which I later figured out that is what they're called, who have their own place on the map that are just chillen waiten for people to kill. The game does allow you to play alone or with friends, I've tried to play with 3-4 of my friends together but they all play at different speeds, I have one that has to search every freakin crate and barrel and steal everything, while I have a friend who races through the dialog and wants to get to the next area ASAP, and another friend who has to spend 10 minutes wondering if he should change his skill set because he just got a new weapon that does +1 more damage... But when we do get on together we can move through areas much more quickly, plus even if you are alone, most of the time (though this may be rare because of the resurgence of the free week) there are a some people around you doing the same quest so you're inadvertently helping eachother out because most of the quests aren't really "instanced"
World - My first character is a wood elf, who is apart of the Aldmeri Dominion Faction. I've been through the first little island (which can take 2-10 hours) to clear depending on how immersed you want to get. I've been having fun on the 2nd area exploring and picking up all the side quests. The environment might not be as Dark or enriched as the single player games, BUT AGAIN, we're talking about a freaking MMO, you have to understand that there is going to be some trade off of quality here for stability, but even with that said, I'm still really impressed with towns and the world that they've put together, the voice acting is top notch and even NPC's that have one lines are all voiced. I don't even have a mount and I'm don't mind running around the vast area because everything looks great.
Story - Not Great, but also not horrible. The side quests are ok as well, nothing like (go here and kill 10 of this), more like Go here and talk to this person, and go to that cave and kill something. But again everything has a little backstory and you get to decide who lives or dies most of the time.
Bag inventory/Crafting supplies - Inventory management is frustrating but I also don't expect to have the ability to pick up and hold onto everything. This game encourages ALTS when I was reading up on Champion Levels. I really don't expect one of my characters to have MATS for every profession, maybe 2 or 3? I'm doing all professions right now (but havent invested any skills points yet other than woodworking) and I have had no trouble completing all of the daily profession quests (6 of them) so far. (My bank is constantly full haha)
Honestly though I don't understand all of the hate this game is getting, maybe it's people who got burned when it first came out or before it became subscription-less. IDK - all I have to say is stop letting some of these people sway your opinion.
I will definately be picking up the GOLD edition for 30$, hell even if I never play it again I've already gotten my monies worth.
But really, what do I know?

I love Tamriel. I spent hundreds of hours in both Morrowind and Skyrim. I just started another playthrough in Morrowind, and I still love it, it feels immersive, interesting, thrilling, fascinating, soothing, deep, aesthetically pleasing (especially with the fantastic overhaul some dedicated fans provide).
Memorize these adjectives. Pretty much sums up what ESO is fundamentally lacking.
Not only in comparison to ElderScroll games, but even to contemporary games in general. Including the shoddy low- budget end of the market.
I consider it quite a feat to achieve this, given the vast story background of the Tamriel Saga, and the fact that ESO is set in an age not featured yet, but where decisive  events for the history of Tamriel take place. To take part in them was a main reason why I let myself be persuaded to purchase ESO. Ok, it´s an MMO, and I am more the SP-type, but could be interesting, just ignore that the maps will be flooded by tourists.
I never thought i could be disappointed by Tamriel to that extent that I am now.
I installed the launcher. It then told me that I am to download and install the actual game. Which is a whooping 60GB (!) download. With installation time to match. Installation broke. I validated the game files...and DID IT ALL AGAIN!
Ok. Next weekend. Now we are ready.
Character customization: really great, stunning graphics. Big anticipation. I spent the better part of 2h building an Argonian that looked exactly like I envisioned, and fit his fictious vita: a grizzled, aged veteran, witch some scars and a serious paunch he collected over the years.
--SPOILER: Now I spend my time mostly under my first self-assembled helmet, that does not fit the character model at all, is way too big to be of any practical use, covers most of the areas I spent time on designing, and, frankly, looks like a boiled-leather pisspot that I, I realized, won´t get rid off any time soon.
I searched the forums for a way to supress the model (possible in many games), and I found serious discussions by "veteran" players against the opinions of newcomers like me, arguing that such a feature would be "unrealistic". In a fantasy game soaked with magic. ROFL! guys.....come ON!
Ok, so now here my proud, stout Argonian battle veteran roams Tamriel: Two pathetically blinking lizard eyes under the shadow of a boiled leather thundermug. Looking like he was very recently bullied HARD in the schoolyard, or is a very enduring elder sibling. But anyway...oh well, what the hell, MMORPG, I was prepared to put up with stuff like this.--
I started the game.
I was spawned into some kind of hellish dungeon, and, without explanation, singled out and picked up by a strange, rather good-looking (considered the location, and the fact that we are dead), if somewhat grimy, Nord woman to embark on an enigmatic, mostly unexplained tutorial mission that turned out to be absolutely nonsensical to the point of hilarity, and became crowded with utterly clueless folks till the end.
Ok, hey, tutorial mission.
We all gotta start somewhere, and it IS hard to make a tutorial mission somewhat immersive and non-generic...well...first fail here.
Ok, we get spawned into the REAL Tamriel...and nothing changes...the game stays the same...generic, nonsensical, devoid of any motivation to start climbing the near-inexistent learning curve.
Where ElderScroll-Games had an intricate system of object properties to explore, experience to gather, character skills to develop, that really changed how the game felt and how you would behave in-game, ESO is watered down to a point where the RPG in MMORPG isn´t even fun any more: Whereas in other games, you need a specific set of materials, to built a piece of equipment with somewhat unique properties, in ESO, any object from a class requires the exact same materials, and styles are merely distinguished by a special ingredient you have to buy or loot...but then again, styles don´t make sense anyway, as the objects have comparable properties across the styles, and you can wear what you like (or loot).
You learn by buying or reading books. Point. Ya, right... not much incentive to actually play the game, is there?
Battle experience is used to unlock some nifty moves. Not like, getting more efficient with certain weapon types. Noooo, nonono. Nifty moves for your quick-draw.
Quests and missions: OMG. This is it, I think. That broke me. I can´t play longer than 2h, or else my brains start seeping out from my ears and nostrils.
Some start nice, like a wife being distraught over her husbands disappearance. Then you follow the family dog (nice move, but, like, couldn´t she have done that herself?), around the corner of the barn, and there is someone severly injured lying on the beach a few yards away. It turns out to be her husband, who tells you a horrifying story about how he almost died several times in the last few hours, and on your question how you might offer help, answers" Thanks for talking to me", jumps to his feet and RUNS HOME, to a wife who doesn´t notice...
Most are the generic usual: Get quest, rush there, encounter hordes of low-level, unmotivated  enemies nobody warned you off, rip, snarl, tear, pounce pounce pounce, loot, bloody loot, there is the marker, stand in line for your objective to respawn, press "E", done, off to the next.....what was it, we actually did there? errhh..no idea, doesn´t matter.
No, it really does not matter, because the assignments I so far encountered where invariably so generic, nonsensical, uninspired, daft and shallow, I quickly stopped reading and listening, because it HURT, even more so as I was in actual bloody TAMRIEL, the continent and history of my dreams! At times even preferable to my everyday life. Down to history, politics and religion.
Ah, politics, yeah. There was said to be some grim civil war between three (nice move to avoid the black-and -white scheme, btw. If it only worked...) factions unfolding. Well there are some sinister figures lurking around, with clearly evil  intent, that we must protect our citizens from, and occasionally slaughter for the greater good (ours).
Thats it. We: good guys. Empathic, caring, in danger of loosing home and loved ones. They: Evil, greedy, sinister, brutal. To be killed on sight.
What a bummer, compared to Skyrim or Morrowind, games that regularly made you second-guess your loyalties and morals...
There was said to be some consequence to your choice of loyalty, but that apparently vanished. Most guild memberships appear to be restricted. Ok. Guilds that merely exist to trade collectibles, or stand around and chat. Ok, here my being an SP-type shows: I can´t seem to get the hang of MMO-guilds. Never did. I am interested in the games. And in people sharing interests with me. 2Mio folks on the server is just an anonymous mass I can´t connect to, not even in the confinements of a 3k-ppl-guild of folks i don´t know, and probably never will meet, and of which ~98% are way too far up in the game for me to actually play WITH them. As in, "together".
And I really enjoy figuring games out by myself, and not being told at every step what the most efficient (stats-wise or creds-wise) next move is. That apparently makes me antisocial in extant MMOs. Fair enough.
It feels like a rather nice texture mod applied to the popular first part of an MMORPG by NCSoft. Except that there the missions worked, and the story line, albeit shallow, made sense somehow.
If you play MMO as a chatroom with facultative farming if nobody talks to you: give it a try.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl is a game that was released in March of 2007, over ten years ago, by the company GSC Game World. The game is set in "The Zone", the areas around Chernobyl after a second accident in 2006.
The world is very atmospheric and realistic and can even be terrifying at times when exploring the labs around Chernobyl. The game features extremely difficult and realistic gunplay where one shot to the head will kill anyone but it will do the same for you. The game is completely open world, you can go almost anywhere from the very beginning of the game and do almost anything. A lot of the gunfights and NPCs you will encounter on your journey through the zone will be completely unscripted leading to massive amounts of fun and replayability. It is at times buggy, but this can be fixed through a number of unofficial patches. This game also features a massive mod community and has tons of mods to enhance your experience and add thousands of hours of gameplay to this already huge game.
This was truly an amazing game, I just beat it for the first time at 12 hours, but i completely rushed through the game doing only the main story, i missed a lot of stuff I should have done and I am for sure going to replay this, because it has so much replayability. If you are a fan of open world, survival horror, or just FPSs in general, then buy this game.
