My early impressions of this great game:
This title is more polished and flat out fun to play than most supposed "A list" games costing upwards of 40 to 60 bux. The battle and stealth mechanics make for a unique playing style that I thoroughly enjoy. This isn't a typical button masher, to say the least. The story line is solid and keeps you hungering to progress to learn more and the artistic graphics are beyond good. They're top knotch and fit the tone of the game like no other style ever would. All of this and I've barely cracked the surface of what Transistor has to offer. Intrigued? Yep, so was I. Buy it and have fun!

If anyone played this in the first few days, the bugs (stuttering, save game issues) have been completely fixed. They are kind of metaphorical though -- Transistor is, in more ways than one, not as polished as Bastion. The story never completely takes off, and if you are unwilling to put in the work to uncover information in-game then you may be completely confused. Still, it's hard to do anything but laud SuperGiant's ambition. This is a beautiful game, with amazing music to boot. Also, it's honestly fun to play, with a pseudo-strategy bent and a focus on mixing-and-matching abilities creatively. Sometimes I just turn it on and play around in test rooms, which is really an achievement for such a story-oriented game. So, it's definitely worth playing, though not quite the tour de force that Bastion was.
This game is just as good as Bastion!

Have you played Bastion? No? Then go play Bastion. Then get Transistor. If you enjoyed Bastion (which you should), you'll love Transistor.
The game play is phenomenal. The hybrid turn-based combat is super fun, and makes for a perfect balance of challenge and fun. The powers system is also really well done, and actively encourages you to experiment. Whether it's to find out more information about the characters in the game, or because you're forced to after "dying", you will want to try out every combination you can with all the abilities you get.
And the music... oh man that music. Darren Korb returns from Bastion, and knocks it out of the park again with Transistor.
tl;dr: It's an excellent game, just try it. It looks amazing, it sounds amazing, and it plays amazing. And it's only $20! Although trust me, you'll want to spend the extra $10 for the soundtrack.

Thrown into a beautiful world that you know nothing about and the first thing you see is a "dead" man with a swordlike weapon, which seems to know you, stuck on his chest.
Once again you have million questions and on your way to find answers to them you are confronted by countless waves of "Process".
The main protagonist "Red" has lost her voice and Logan Cunnigham narrates the game as her swordlike weapon "Transistor".
Story is mostly told by the "Transistor" and the antagonists but you will get more info about the city through OVC Terminals and it's citizens by inspecting Functions.
Game is a Sci-fi Action-RPG in which you battle the enemies either in or outside Turn(). It also has a leveling system which lets you choose from different Functions, Limiters and Passive slots or MEM to use Functions, each time you level up.
Turn() is a system that will freeze all the enemies and gives you a chance to plan out your next couple moves. Each function (which skills are called) will use a certain amount of Turnpoints (amount will change with some Function combinations and you may extend the overall amount by placing a Function as passive) and after all of them are spent you may activate your Turn() and watch as you rip your enemies apart with different combinations of Functions. When Turn() is on cooldown you may only use Jaunt() or Functions that are upgraded with Jaunt() and because of this and the difficulty of the enemies, fighting outside Turn() is hard and risky and I recommend you to just evade with Jaunt() untill Turn() is usable again. There are also enemies that will stop you from using Turn() which will become lethal especially on your second playthrough.
Functions act a vital part in this game since you cannot attack without them and when your health reaches 0 one of your active Functions will overload and save your life. Overloaded functions can be recovered by accessing new Access Points(save points). Losing all your active Funtions will lead to a game over. There are 16 different Functions in total and each of them are "voices" of the former citizens of Cloudbank. Each Function may play its role in Active, Upgrade or Passive slots with varying effects. By combining Functions you can create 3360 (or 3840 on your second playthrough) different active Functions. The amount of different skillsets with 4 Active slots, which have 2 Upgrade slots each, and 4 Passive slots is just insane. So you will find yourself changing your skillset after each encounter and experimenting for the combination that suits your playstyle the most. Game also encourages you to try out different combinations by giving you info about the citizens when you have played through an encounter with the Function in a different slot. And to get all the achievements you must play with every Function and try out their Active, Upgrade and Passive effects.
There are Limiters which give you different handicaps and award you in EXP if you survive the encounter with Process. It has a system similiar to that of the Function that gives you info about the varying types of Process. There's also an achievement if you survive 5 encounters with all the Limiters on which makes each battle a struggle for life. Be prepared to lose atleast one active per encounter when you're trying to get this achievement. There are also 4 levels of each Process type and when you play the game for a second time the enemies levels won't reset and you will encounter even the endgame Process from the very start.
There's also a secret room that you may access from different locations throughout the game after the first boss battle. It has multiple doors with different challenges varying from speedbattles to fighting a copy of yourself with all your Functions. For each victory you are awarded with a piece of the games soundtrack that you may play at the central hub of the secret room.
After 13.7 hours of gameplay and starting my 3rd playthrough I have still not found the final version of the Process which should be Level 4 and I'm missing few duplicate Functions even though I'm level 28. So yeah.. There's still stuff to do.
I though that the game would get boring in the second playthrough since normally it would mean that you get to fight the normal starting enemies with overpovered skills but was happily suprised since the game was still getting harder even though I had full MEM and slots.
Turn() system is unique and amazing since I have always loved the combination of action and strategy.
Artwork is similiar to their earlier work, Bastion, but this time in sci-fi setting and the music is amazing and fits the theme very well.
I'll also applaud Supergiant Games since they were able to make the final boss (both battle and the character) very interesting and after the varying types of Process (even boss versions) the final boss will be something totally different.
Conclusion:
Is playing through a linear game with beautiful graphics and awesome music while slashing through endless waves of Process and fighting epic boss battles worth 19€?

The game is not going to be for everyone, no doubt about it. All i can say is please try it yourself if you are in doubt, you might just love it. I dont feel that the "10 hours played" reviews could possibly have enough insight as to what is good or bad with the game. I would suggest you read the ones with at least 100+ hours invested.
Pros
+ Graphics, i just like this oldschool style. Very cute.
+ Soundtracks are awesome, especially in some places !
+ Combat is fun, and different.
+ Community, ive only met nice people this far, seriously.
+ Alot of different paths you can build your character, tho some are "cookie cutter" (but thats always the case)
+ Huge world map with many different layouts.
+ Tons of Boss battles.
+ You can be a tank, healer, buff supporter, caster, ranger, "totem" user, Melee. Just about anything you can think of.
+ Skins of customes for different classes look really cool, some more then others ofc :)
+ IMC. Yes they are truly listening to the community, they have improved the game massively already in many
differents areas. Mobs respawn rate, Trading for none token users, compensation for unexpected maint, to name a few.
Cons
- The main thing is just opimization. The game has FPS issues for some reason. Its weird, annoying and its bad.
- Bots. I havent noticed it alot out in the world fighting monsters. In towns and in all chat its constant spam tho.
- Game freezes for a short duration sometimes, for example when opening the world map.
- The chat itself is pretty buggy sometimes.
- Huge buffs and nerfs back and forth, making and breaking builds.
- Trade restrictions
- AH
- Class advancement, if you chose wrong, there is no going back.
- Targeting can be a bit annoying (using mouse and keyboard) Even certain quest items are unclickable in mouse mode.
- Class balance. Everyone has something that make them special and good for grouping, however some supports simply cannot solo level at a certain point. DPS classes can kill a quest boss in seconds, for me as a support wizard some of them took up to 20min, and there were quests or bosses i simply could not do.
All said, its really fun, and even tho there still are issues, the game is only getting better each patch.

Call of duty: Modern Warfare 2 (CoD MW2) is the game that ruined Call of Duty Franchise.
Let's start with singleplayer. Singleplayer and escpecially Co-op missions were still somewhat ok, but singleplayer also had many things that I didn't like. First of all the singleplayer was filled with too many cutscenes. At least I play games to play them and not to watch movies. Of course the plot is important, but too much of cutscenes is just too much.
Another problem was that the plot was just too ridiculous. This is connected in many ways with with the third problem. The thing that I really liked in previous Call of Duty games and especially in the first Call of Duty game was the feeling of fighting with other soldiers (unlike in most early FPS games, in which you are a lone wolf) or how it was said in the cover of the manual of the very first Call of Duty game: "No one fights alone". This no longer applies in CoD MW 2 and the games following it. In CoD MW 2 you no longer fight with large group of fellow soldiers. Instead you fight alone or with only a couple of guys at most.
Now to multiplayer, which was the real disappointment. In the first Call of Duty game the maps were larger and more open but for some ridiculous reason the maps kept getting smaller and had more and more bottle necks as the series progressed. I could somehow cope with that until this game and i might have coped with it still if it had been the only problem, but it wasn't. The main problem that I have with this game are its ridiculous killstreak rewards and killstreak requirements. In CoD 4 the killstreaks were still somewhat acceptable, but CoD MW2 is no longer an FPS game. It is a game of killstreaks rewards. That is just not fun. The CoD games after this one have continued the usage of ridiculous killstreak rewards and because of this I will probably never again buy Call of Duty games. (To be honest, I predicted that this game was going to be horrible, and as a result I didn't buy this game, but instead got it as a gift.) Multiplayer part of MW 2 also suffers from decision to not to have dedicated servers.
Grade for Singleplayer: 6/10
Grade for Multiplayer: 2/10

Before this the only Total War I had real experience with was Medieval 2, and I've gotta say, I'm glad I picked this up. Thank you, franchise sale, because Rome 2 is my favorite strategy game experience ever.  The world map management feels like a combination of Sid Meier's Civ V and Total War, and the research tree is a cool addition to the building. My only complaint about the world map is that it does feel a little oversimplified; definitely do your campaigns above "normal" difficulty if you want a real challenge.
Diplomacy is easier to do than ever before and it actually makes sense; your standing with a particular faction and its allies will actually affect what kind of treaties they'll enact with you, if any at all, and you're less likely to encounter random backstabbing. (Although why my client states maintain military alliances with countries I'm at war with I'll never know)
The actual battles are the same as before, with a pretty UI that tells you all you need to know and the addition of abilities - not just the formations, phalanxes, fire arrows, and stakes that we had before - but things like war cries to rally your own troops and intimidate the enemy all makes battles feel better and grittier.  All the different types of battles are great too, and it's awesome having an online battle work out when you're the reinforcing navy coming rescue your teammates :P
All in all, would totally recommend this game, especially as a good starting point into the Total War franchise if you want something that's actually historical and cool

I find this game is quite a bit better then it's reputation or Steam review score would suggest. I had first tried to play it on OS X and it was a total laggard which caused me to put it down, but switching over to Windows I'm getting excellent performance and it's a whole 'nother experience.
Maybe some things were streamlined, but there's tons of depth here as well and I have to say I feel it's a bit more complicated to open up and get my bearings in compared with Shogun 2 - and that's a good thing. There were lot's of bold design decisions that were probably met with resistance more for being new than for being poorly conceived or executed. Pre-Steam, I have loads of hours on Medieval 2 and Rome 1 within the more traditional TW structure, but I have to say I really like a lot of these new design decisions. Maybe some are a bit limiting, but I believe they balanced accessibility, world building and strategic decisions nicely.
And don't think that they just dumbed things down and made them easier across the board as some elements - like Public Order - actually make things quite a bit more difficult (and atmospheric for that matter). It's also worth noting that the median playtime for TW: Rome II is almost 43 hours (per Steam Spy), which is tremendous and suggests quite a bit of both value and depth.
Only thing is, don't get it and try and play on a Mac without Bootcamp no matter what your hardware is. I have a top-spec late 2015 iMac and it was absolutely awful on OS X. However, moving over to Bootcamp, I went up to Ultra settings from High settings, turned on AA and still more or less doubled my FPS (20-30 up to 45-60; I'm sure I could get a constant 60 if I cared and wanted to diddle with the settings, but it looks great and feels fluid to me).
Pity that I've only started to play a few weeks before Total War: Warhammer is coming out as it strikes me as being worth a couple hundred hours of gameplay. Ah well, I think I'll be coming back to this after that.

It took me multiple attempts just to set the graphics properly without it either reverting into windowed mode (or just out right refusing to enter fullscreen) and then zooming in the window to the point where only the top left hand quarter of the window was viewable.  Finally after getting it set properly, the game bugged on the third leg of the very first quest and would not let me advance any farther, so I reset from the previous checkpoint and redid that section, and finally when it did let me progress, the game crashed altogether, and my graphics driver along with it.  Too buggy, and just flat out unplayable.

There were a lot of fun-sounding ideas here, like the wingsuit, ridiculously melodramatic action, a GTA-style ride-any-vehicle mechanic, plus the huge open world. However, the poor execution of all of the above absolutely ruins this game. If the devs had been given a much larger timeframe or a much smaller world to work with, I think this would be a much more complete and enjoyable game. As it is, it was obviously pushed out too early for what they were trying to do with it.
While my PC can run it perfectly fine, I still experienced tons of bugs where vehicles wouldn't respond to controls, the wingsuit wouldn't deploy when I pressed the button (which led to some admittedly hilarious faceplants), and other weird control glitches.
On top of all that, the combat simply wasn't fun. There was absolutely no challenge to it at all--I could be running in the open and soaking up bullets like a sponge. One time I was right next to an enemy, and didn't do anything  to him at all and he still couldn't kill me after several shots.
I didn't get very far into the game before getting bored, so I can't speak much for the story, but there wasn't anything there to keep me interested, at least at the start.
The graphics are nice, but that just adds to the feeling of lost potential on this game.
In summary, Just Cause 3 had a huge budget and poor direction. Play Tomb Raider instead.

best MMO ever made. It even beats Funcoms The Secret World which was, until recent company decisions, my all time favourite game ever.

There is no "best" armour or "best" style of play. You can play how you like and still do amazingly well, although there are well optimized builds out there to minmax your gameplay.

Dark Souls 2 is amazing. Amazing enough that I had the patience to actually get every achievement in the game. I've played through multiple times, and the 252 hours I've put in on Steam doesn't include the few times I beat it on the PS3 first.
First, this is a lot different than Demons Souls and Dark Souls. In general, it is NOT as hard, but it is just as much fun. There are some things in the other games that I think were better, but at the same time DS2 has improved ona  number of things as well. As a whole, this game is great and I can't recommend it enough, especially if you are looking for a challenging game. Not hard enough? Join the covenant of Champions or place restrictions on yourself, like a level cap or using only specific weapon types to fit a character concept.
As for the recent negative reviews, I haven't found anything to confirm these. There will be a seperate dx11 release but I havent seen anything that says that dx9 users wont be able to play with them. Also, almost all the features of the new content (Scholar of the first sin) are available as a free update. Only some of the features are not available for those running older versions. This could be a big issue, but only time will tell.

Highly recommended, however, I'd suggest waiting for the new version coming this April.
The game is a shinning example of what gaming should be: Hard, but fair and consistant. If you die, it's your fault. Do better next time. The game demands you take an active role in playing while a lot of games today feel like, "push X to win."
And while I suppose I can see why people are mad about the re-release being a sepperate game from this version (saves do not carry over and you can't play online with people with a different version) but for me, I don't mind it. No, it's not like I have cash to spare (quite the opposite really) but I will throw money at quality games. I bought this game for PS3, then when I moved to PC gaming, I bought this version, and when the re-release comes, I'll be buying that. Why? Because to me it's worth it. Maybe not to others, but that's them. If you can find this version on sale, buy it to see if you like it, and if you do, buy the next version this April.

Transistor is another exceptional title from Supergiant games, taking all the elements that made Bastion successful and molding them into another game that stands on its own. The combat is engaging, deep and fluid, encouraging the player to experiment with all sorts of wild combinations that only get more complex as the game progresses. Level progression is smooth, providing a challenge at all stages of the game, even when you think you’ve unlocked the broken combo. Transistor’s story, along with it’s brilliant voice acting and gorgeous presentation, Truly Supergiant games are going from strength to strength with their releases and I simply can not wait to see what they produce next.
Read my full review here:

I played this game start to finish in about 4.5 hours, and when I say start to finish, I mean I literally did not get out of my chair. So that tells you two things: this is a short game, but it's also a very good one.
The story is... not sparse, but there's a lot of background detail left for you to fill in, kind of like Dark Souls. Bastion was the same way, but this is even more so.
The combat is enjoyable; you can go real-time, use the Turn() system to plan out all your attacks (but then be mostly unable to attack while Turn() recharges), or some mixture of both.
The music is aces and I highly recommend buying the soundtrack.
Overall, if you've played Bastion, this is more of the same, but that's not a bad thing at all.
If you are not playing Transistor, you are not living well.

For those wanting a dynamic take on RPG-styled combat, in a sci-fi universe where nothing is quite as it originally seems, Transistor is a great game to buy. With an average time of 6-8 hours for a first playthrough depending on how much you elect to explore and read to digest extra information on the story, the game doesn't ask a great deal of commitment while still providing an excellent and engaging story to follow. Transistor also boasts a combat system that is easy to approach but complex to truly master, and offers more hardcore gamers a difficulty setting in terms of "Limiters" that can do anything from change how AI will behave and spawn to change how the game punishes you for losing fights. And, on a final but brief note, I'll always recommend a game that manages to make a simple-on-the-surface but intricate-in-the-nitty-gritty combat system without dragging players through a marsh of ridiculous tutorials for you to learn how it works.
Transistor drops you in the game and promptly leaves you to explore in your own time, and with a beautiful soundtrack, fantastic art direction, good voice acting and a fluid combat system, it's a considerable steal at the price it's being sold for. Pick it up!

One of my favorite strategy, RPG titles ever. I have never experienced a game that manages to pull RPG action and a moving story so well. The vibrant aesthetics, epic soundtrack, and unusual power combinations, polishes this game up to its very finest. Words just don't do the justice; you have to experience the journey yourself! This is one indie game you don't want to miss out!

Fantastic story, visuals, and interesting and new combat system. I'd definitely recommend this to anyone who enjoys indie games. Just to emphasize, the artwork in this game is brilliant and captivating throughout the game, from the cutscenes to normal gameplay. It will keep you interested.

Honestly, I want to like this game. It has a lot of excellent features to it after all, it's just the the cons far, far outweigh the pros at this point.
Example - if you happen to roll a swordsman, you better have some skills in tanking (see, Peltasta class), otherwise you dont get into any teams late-game. Also, you might want to forget about DPS, even the most DPS heavy swordsman is going to lose to archers, mages - and even some cleric builds.
The economy is also terrible. Thanks to a minority of people controlling entire aspects of the market that are needed late-game (and unless you're a high level w/ near end-game gear and a party of the same you can't compete), bots having driven up the prices on items to crazy levels and exceedingly low/grindy drop rates (some items are literally 1:18000 and untradable).
Then there's the bots. For every bot that's banned three more spring up in their place. They're like hydras that IMC seems to take a very passive stance on. Sure, they have an algorithm that bans bots sometimes. But seems to always miss the same bots that plague some areas for days/weeks at a time.
Class balance - No. There's really not any.
Customer support - In this game it's terrible, at best. Aside from more or less ignoring support tickets, they don't exactly let players know when/what is happening with regards to major issues. There is next to no GM/Staff on the forums, or facebook, or anywhere else that can be considered 'reasonable' to contact/get input from/to.
Player community - Run while you can. You're not going to find a community more toxic/racist outside of low-end FPS games.
RNG - Do you like running dungeons for no reward? You should, because 95% of the time, that's literally what you get. That other 5%? Better hope RNG is on your side, since you randomly get between 12-20 items, and if it's not for your class - too bad! Late game you can't even trade/sell the recipes. Wouldn't be quite so bad if they didn't have an absurdly low global dungeon cap (3) you could run per day.
Stability - Expect to crash. Often. More often when trying to do missions/dungeons. CommanderLoadFail is real, and he hates players.
All this and more, which really is a shame. The game feels very much like a new Ragnarok Online. The artwork is excellent, some zones are absolutely stunning and the music is fantastic. The idea behind so many classes is amazing, and from the outside it looks like an excellent game. Right now though, I'd suggest steering clear until they fix up some of the glaring issues and get some more stabioity patches in.

I have been playing this game for around six years now, before it was released on steam. I played it for free for a long time with the only huntable animal being mule deer on whiteheart island. This game has come a long way since then. It is truly a great hunting game!
Here is a list of pro's and con's for anyone  interested in checking this game out.
Pro's:
-Even though many reveiwers complain that its not free to play, they are false. As a guest you start with a 12 gauge shotgun, and .243 rifle with scope. The 12 gauge can use birdshot, buckshot, and slugs, which makes it possible to shoot nearly every animal in game. You start off with unlimited license for whitetail deer, pheasant, and european rabbit. And every week there is a rotation of two different species to hunt, so you get to hunt 5 species for free! You can earn GM$ by completing missions which make it possible for you to buy other licenses so you can hunt even more animals for free. Just exploring the amazing scenery is enough to play for free in my opinion!
-The game has massive maps to explore such as arctic alaska, australia desert, deep forest in washington state, lousiana bayou, alpine mountains in europe, etc.
-There are many unique species you don't see huntable in other games and many species have unique challenging hunting methods. Species so far that are included are Arctic Fox, Red Fox, Snowshoe Hare, European Rabbits, Cottontail Rabbit, Coyote, Polar Bear, Brown Bear, Black Bear, Fwral Hog, Wild Boar, Ibex Sheep, Pheasant, Rock Ptarmigan, Willow Ptarmigan, Mallard Duck, Pintail Duck, Gadwall Duck, Black Duck, Canada Geese, Whitetail Deer, Blacktail Deer, Sitka Deer, Mule Deer, Elk, Red Deer, Moose, Roe Deer, Red Kangaroo, Turkey, Bison,Reindeer, did I miss any?
-The devs are updating nearly every single week. And each year they are adding many species, features, equipment, and a new map. Every time you decide to upgrade a membership its like you are buying a new game!
-The game runs great! I rarely experience major glitches or low frames, and I am pushing my computer on higher graphics. My computer runs crappy on other high end games, but great on thehunter.
-You can hunt alone in single player or online with up to 8 players!
-You can purchase hunting dogs to aid in retrieving of small game +birds and blood tracking of a wounded animal.(more to come in the future). They are just great as hunting companions, and function great!
-The memberships are cheap. Three month membership with unlimited ammo and all licenses to hunt is only $10. If you buy bundles you get lots of gear that you keep forever with your membership.
-The community is great with active devs who listen to peoples suggestions. You can join the forums from thehunter website to suggest ideas and get to know community members better.
-There are tons of statistics, achievments, gallery of trophy shots, daily tournaments for EM$ and player created tournaments(on forum), leaderboards, missions for GM$, which just make the game that much more enjoyable!
-Tons of great equipment for purchase and sales are available often. Sometimes they do give out a free peice of equipment so I suggest you keep up with the news updates each week.
-There are rare type of fur, feather, and non typical antler variations for each animal  that give you an excited feeling of hope, each hunt to find something rare .
-You can stumble on collectables for fun such as mushrooms, ancient coins, etc
-Every year during holidays there are events with missions and fun easter eggs to find in the game.
-My favorite thing about this game is how it is not all arcadish like other hunting games. Animals get spooked easily, and can smell or see you from a distance if you are not cautious.  But once you get good and learn the animals, it can become easy to hunt many of them. But the great part is that there are always those rare monster trophy size animals that seem to have super senses and make the hunt even more challenging.
Cons:
-Equipment can be expensive if you don't want to wait for it to be on sale.  I suggest you don't get oeverwhelmed feeling like you need to buy everything,. Just buy the basics to hunt the animal you are after or for your style of hunting. You do not need to pay to win, I have won competitions with very basic stuff.
-Some things can be a little confusing for new members, so I wish they would make better tutorials and such.
People want the developers to make this game a one time fee, but I am so thankful they have not. If they did it would turn out like all the other crappy hunting games I have played. Rather it is great because they have money to pay their bills, pay staff, and make a career out of what they are doing. They are happy to make this game great and keep it updated because they are making money.
In conclusion I recommend anyone who has been looking for a realistic beautiful hunting game to give this a go and to not miss out on this gem!

Alien: Isolation is one of the most intense and terrifying games I have ever played. Ever since Amnesia: The Dark Descent the first person horror genre has become quite big with many titles such as Outlast following it up. Alien: Isolation manages to make itself feel distinct and unique among all of them. The environments look incredible and feel right out of Ridley Scott's 1979 film and make you feel like you are in the film. Yes all the retro futuristic things are still here such as the old style computers. Ever since Aliens the franchise itself has been on a rocky slope of quality but this is hands down the best the franchise has been since Aliens. The Xenomorph is absolutely terrifying and had my heart racing anytime it was near. The best thing the game does to differentiate itself is have very unpredictable AI. While the humans and androids may patrol set areas the Xenomorph has no limits and can show up or be anywhere at any time. For example, if some humans start shooting at you, you better hide because the Xenomorph is going to show up at the location of the sounds any second. The working joe androids are also incredibly unnerving and very difficult to take down. On the more technical side of things the game ran flawlessly at max settings and I never had a problem. The game is visually stunning and one of the best looking games I have played. The sound design is also quite phenomenal as you can hear the Xenomorph moving around in the vents above you and other small things that really make it top notch. One common criticism of the game is its length and I certainly agree with that. Sometimes the game has you do various tasks and it seems like it just gets to be too much at times. However I would certainly take too long over too short and the game took me a whopping 18.5 hours to complete which is far more than most horror games. If you are a fan of the Alien franchise or just want a terrifying horror experience then look no further than this. 9.5/10

First things first, this game has an awesome amount of potential. However, the way the devs are handling the hacker and exploiter issues could very well kill it long before alpha is finished. EVERY public server you join will have the telltale signs of hackers; stone fireplaces and trebuchets littering the main fields. They can build up an impenetrable base in a couple hours, seige every other castle on the server and then take the throne for themselves.
All that aside, the game can be fun. Building huge bases, raiding others. Claiming the crown for yourself and raising taxes to ludicrus amounts is all in good fun. I played this game start to finish in about 4.5 hours, and when I say start to finish, I mean I literally did not get out of my chair. So that tells you two things: this is a short game, but it's also a very good one.
The story is... not sparse, but there's a lot of background detail left for you to fill in, kind of like Dark Souls. Bastion was the same way, but this is even more so.
The combat is enjoyable; you can go real-time, use the Turn() system to plan out all your attacks (but then be mostly unable to attack while Turn() recharges), or some mixture of both.
The music is aces and I highly recommend buying the soundtrack.
Overall, if you've played Bastion, this is more of the same, but that's not a bad thing at all.
If you are not playing Transistor, you are not living well.

For those wanting a dynamic take on RPG-styled combat, in a sci-fi universe where nothing is quite as it originally seems, Transistor is a great game to buy. With an average time of 6-8 hours for a first playthrough depending on how much you elect to explore and read to digest extra information on the story, the game doesn't ask a great deal of commitment while still providing an excellent and engaging story to follow. Transistor also boasts a combat system that is easy to approach but complex to truly master, and offers more hardcore gamers a difficulty setting in terms of "Limiters" that can do anything from change how AI will behave and spawn to change how the game punishes you for losing fights. And, on a final but brief note, I'll always recommend a game that manages to make a simple-on-the-surface but intricate-in-the-nitty-gritty combat system without dragging players through a marsh of ridiculous tutorials for you to learn how it works.
Transistor drops you in the game and promptly leaves you to explore in your own time, and with a beautiful soundtrack, fantastic art direction, good voice acting and a fluid combat system, it's a considerable steal at the price it's being sold for. Pick it up!

Such a well-made game. It's charming, pretty, and surprisingly fun to play for a single player FPS. The duelling mechanic makes something incredibly simple as staring at someone and shooting at them after a few seconds incredibly complex and challenging, but not so complicated that it stops being fun. It's a very intense moment and it's very entertaining in that regard.
The skill system leaves something to be desired as the perks are pretty easy to choose (there's one that lets you get free headshots after like 5-10 kills, come on), but considering the length of the game I wasn't expecting much form it anyway. It does it's job.
The little things like the narration changing the scenery and the gameplay as it happens is a very nice touch, it makes the game feel very unique and immersing. I've never been a big fan of old Western stories but I found myself caring a lot about Greaves' story.
As for weapons, you don't get a lot to choose from, but that's okay. They all handle very nicely and fill the niches they are made for very well. They even let you got akimbo-revolvers. You can't go wrong with that.
A very big YES to this game. More, please.

Papers, Please is possibly the most fun you can have in the most mundane setting.
It's 1982, and after the six-year war between Arstotzka and Kolechia comes to an end, the Grestin border checkpoint opens, reuniting families and allowing the safe passage of all sorts of characters. As the checkpoint inspector, it is your duty to approve or deny people based on the documents they have and the details therein.
Not only does Papers, Please immerse you in the fascinating world of excessive bureaucracy, but it forces you to make moral choices throughout, determining the fate of travellers and immigrants, aiding or hindering subversive elements, all while ensuring the survival of you and your family.
Such is life in
finally a game that helped me see differences in text

This game. Is so good. A true one-man tour-de-force. And how ironic that it simulates one of the most boring, frustrating, and time-consuming jobs on the planet, and revels in the fact that many of us come home from one of these jobs and play Papers Please for fun. How post-modern. How Orwellian.
First of all, this game has an overall meaningful story and meaningful choices to be made through all of the paper grind. This is what really drives the game and makes it a game. Holding out (and looking for) the decisions that will change your future and your family's future is strangely compelling. The game engages very well with Dystopian ideals.
Finding discrepancies and doing a good job is rewarding in its own right, however. There is something about a job well-done after all. Developing a 'system' of dealing with the papers that works for you has quite a learning curb. The gameplay itself has a good difficulty curb, but is so terrible at the start as you learn the names of the countries, the issuing cities, the passport layouts.
Visuals are wonderful! I can't express how-- iconic-- the people are in this game. Though it's a bit frustrating when you let someone through with a fake ID because it's a bit difficult to tell a male from a female (unless you take a clotheless picture, lol).
Sound is also stylized and well thoughtout.
Pretty much EVERY decision the creator made in this game gave it a dark, bitter flavour like a fine coffee.
10/10. I'm so happy that games like this are still developed and that there is still room for one person with an idea to take that idea and make it into such a meaningful game.
Very recommend to play,  story is great, dialogues are great. A heart touching visual novel of all time.

Medici. An idyllic backtrop as your sandbox to the adventure, Just Cause 3 asks you to blow everything up. Everything that is marked in red, that is. Yes, when you see red, you blow it up... over and over again.
The game is amazingly large, beautiful and modestly detailed. The sunsets, vistas, and landscapes can be quite striking when careening over the side of a mountain in your furious fire fights. While pretty visuals aside, it's the explosions that take center stage. And through its 30-ish hour campaign, remarkably, blowing stuff up doesn't get old, even when considering you spend about 90 percent of your time blowing stuff up. It's the combination of fun weapons and extremely fluid movement options (planes, grappling hooks, parachutes, helicoptors, etc), coupled with such awesome explosions that are the meat of this game. What story there is, and it's as ridiculous as its gameplay, is only there to give you reason to island trot to blow more stuff up.
If you're into blowing stuff up, the island of Medici is ready to be freed (which means blowing it up).

Call of Duty MW2 was undoubtly the top of the series - or at least in my honest opinion. The sequel to the award winning MW had to deliver something special. It did. With a great single player (considered it's a FPS, then I'd like to call it great) continuing the events from MW1. Not that I'll spoil these events since it's your task to discover.
Furthermore MW2 has a "new" (at the time it was released it was new) coop. Treyard had their zombies in WAW, so Infinity Ward had to make their own coop, what they made was the so called "Spec Ops". It's missions where you have a special objective to do. Either get from A to B fastest, kill all enemies etc etc. It's very fun when you're playing with a friend!
The multiplayer in MW2 was the best COD MP in the series. Adding some "Kill streaks" to the game, made it various, and it wasn't only "shoot'n run". Now you could call in a "Predator Missile", "Helicopter" or even a "Nuke". The weapons felt balanced, and they had different kinds of maps.
Sadly the servers are almost empty, and you'll have to wait for eternities for joining one. But when you do, you'll probably think it's quite fun.

Its probably not a free to play in the true sense. Your experience as a Guest Member will be quite limited, as it only allows you to hunt 2 species of animal.. Mule Deer, and Cottontail Rabbits except you cant kill Rabbits with the default gun you are given, which means either spend money or just hunt Mule Deer.
Not everything is buyable with gm$ (the earnable in game currency) so you are going to have to get your credit card out to buy em$ (real money currency) ...
Want to hunt something other than Mule Deer / Rabbits .. then you need a licence and the appropriate gun / bow. Buying a license is very expensive, so its better to become a member which allows you to hunt everything in the game, as long as you have the weapon to kill it.
Lets be honest .. the business model of this game is awful (no one month subs, equipment is very expensive to buy, etc)
The gameplay however is great, tracking and killing an animal is hugely rewarding, but sometimes frustrating. The environment is beautiful and atmostpheric, the way animals roam as herds, sniff the air to detect you, bolt once they have spotted ... you gives you the impression a lot of effort was put into the gameplay and artwork.
So in summary .. its a great game, held back only by its terrible nickel and dime business model.

Oh holy ham sandwiches, this game is absurd. First of all, the art style is simply amazing. I mean did ya look at it? It's fabulous. Secondly, the soundtrack is WHOASH. You might end up not enjoying the game but still love it because of how good the music is. It's off the chain man.
The gameplay. Let's just say that it's a real sauce ball platter when it comes to this aspect. Transistor uses a battle system that is both unique and delicious to the stomach. It allows you to attack enemies in real time or using the neato "Turn" ability to plan out your attacks. Both options are viable and they are both quite satisfying.
Transistor is not without it's flaws however. The game is pretty short only taking me around 7 hours to beat. The game is also extremely linear offering no sense of exploration. The game will keep you going on the path of destruction without much say. HOWEVER, transistor's replay value is boosted thanks to it's wide selection of weapons which allows you to experiment and find tons of different strategies and slam dunk homeruns to use throughout the game. So you don't get to explore the world much but you do get to explore your vast arsenal of abilities. Making different loadouts was pretty fun, and that's where a lot of the replay value was found for me.
For those of you who played Supergiant's last game Bastion, you should be right at home with the new role that voice actor Logan Cunningham plays in this game as the voice inside the transistor.  Similar to Bastion, the main character is silent and the voice in the transistor will speak for her as she journeys through the city of Cloudbank. It is a slightly different role compared to the role of the narrator from Bastion, but it is executed very well and at the end of the day I was just as impressed.
The story is also one of the biggest dunks this game has to offer. I found it very interesting and engaging, however once the game had ended, I was left with many unanswered questions that were never resolved.  This may annoy some players, but I actually found it refreshing that the game challenges you to think about these questions and come up with interpretations for yourself.
At the end of the day, this game is GODLIKE.  For those of you who are looking for a large amount of content in this game, the 20$ price tag may be too steep. And that is okay, but I believe that this game is such an awesome experience that the price tag is justified even if it doesn't last you as long as most games.
So yeah, Transistor gets a rating of "11/10 reverse gorilla dunk". Thank you for your time.

TRANSISTOR is really cool. It follows in the footsteps of Supergiant's previous game, Bastion, yet doesn't feel derivative. It has some of the best ARPG combat I've ever seen, masterfully blending real-time and turn-based combat, the first game I've ever seen succeed in doing so. It's very well paced, never forcing you into story or combat segments for too long. It manages to sidestep many of Bastion's pitfall, including art that feels much less repetitive, and more meaningful choices in combat loadout, as well as maintaining an excellent story without acting pretentious or shoving it in your face with overly long, motionless cutscenes. Overall, I'd give it a 94/100, the only con about it being some minor issues with balance in regard to attack combos.

This game just oozes character and atmosphere. It's a fairly straightforward cover based shooter, but with a wild west setting, using real outlaws as the enemies, which is really interesting if you're in to wild west culture. The graphics are beautiful and stylized, and it's optimized to run well. When you're not running through a mountain pass or desert trail, gunnin' folks down, you are in a duel, to see if you're a quicker draw than your enemy, which were REAL people I might add. It's nothing spectacular, but for the $15 this game asks, it more than makes up for it with it's great game feel, interesting narrative, and funny humor. A few deaths seem cheap or just stupid, but there are checkpoints strewn about often. If you really want a challenge, put it into True West difficulty, which removes most of your HUD and makes the game a ton harder. With a bonus arcade mode, and duel mode, this game has a decent amount to offer for $15. So it earns an 8/10

Not as good as Dark Souls or Demon's Souls, but still a good game.
Compared to Dark Souls:
-Worse combat. There's some neat aspects, like being able to move-and-shoot with bows, dual wielding, double-bladed swords, etc. But overall it's just not as clean and nuanced as the previous games.
-Worse map design. No more clever loopbacks and tight interconnected regions, just a big haphazard sprawling map with bonfires scattered throughout which you can freely warp between right off the bat.
-Worse boss design. Mostly just different kinds of humanoid monster things, or things we've already seen. Nowhere near the imagination and creativity of the previous games' bosses. And the bosses you fight aren't very well embedded into the story/setting either. Sometimes you fight things...just because.
-Worse multiplayer. Pretty disappointing.
-Worse story. There's some good aspects to it, but it's done a bit ham-handedly.
-Worse mood/feel/emotional reaction. It's pretty flat.
But it's still a good game? Yup. Demons Souls and Dark Souls 1 just set the bar high. Out of context, just playing this by itself, I'd give it a straight B+. It's super good. But most of what makes it good is just what's been carried over from the previous games.
Rating: C+ (I'd much rather just play through Demons Souls/Dark Souls 1 again for the billionth time than play through this a second time, but if you're craving more Dark Souls, it can sort of scratch that itch).

After nearly 400 hours of playing Borderlands 2, I can say that while there are some really terrible voice acting moments, such as during the mob waves of Where Angels Fear to Tread, this is quite possibly the most fun game I have played in the past six months. I picked it up after hearing about the Community Patch, and it has only improved on the game in the best ways possible. Borderlands 2 is a game that gets better as you get deeper into it. You can't enjoy the normal playthrough nearly as much as the UVHM playthrough. The more perks you have access to, the more varied your gameplay can get.
The art style of BL2 keeps it from looking dated as the years pile on. The graphics of the game don't look too different even from the BL3 demo we were given some time back, with the exception of lighting.
The story of the game gets a little grating after about 200 hours, but the endgame of Borderlands 2 is quite possibly the best experience of my gaming career.
I highly recommend looking into the community patch, loading up the randomizer mod, and charging through a few playthroughs. It would be both frustrating and fun in the best way a video game can offer.
All in all, the game's ok. 5/7.

Michael Benjamin Bay (born February 17, 1965)[1] is an American filmmaker known for directing and producing big-budget action films characterized by fast cutting, stylistic visuals and extensive use of special effects, including frequent depictions of explosions.[2][3] His films, which include Armageddon (1998), Pearl Harbor (2001) and the Transformers film series (2007–present), have grossed over US$5 billion worldwide.[4] He is co-founder of commercial production house The Institute, a.k.a. The Institute for the Development of Enhanced Perceptual Awareness.[5] He is co-chair and part-owner of the digital effects house Digital Domain.[6] He co-owns Platinum Dunes, a production house which has remade horror movies including The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003), The Amityville Horror (2005), The Hitcher (2007), Friday the 13th (2009) and A Nightmare on Elm Street (2010).[7]
Despite his considerable success at the international box office, Bay's work is generally held in low esteem by film critics. While The Rock (1996) and Transformers (2007) received moderately positive reviews, his other films, including the three Transformers sequels, have been received negatively by critics.

Early life
Michael Bay was born in Los Angeles. He was raised by his adoptive parents Harriet, a bookstore owner/child psychiatrist, and Jim, a Certified Public Accountant (CPA).[8] Bay was raised Jewish.[9] His grandfather was from Russia.[10] His cousin, Susan Bay, is the widow of the late Star Trek actor Leonard Nimoy (whom he eventually cast as the voice actor for Sentinel Prime in Transformers: Dark of the Moon).[11] He attended the exclusive Crossroads School, in Santa Monica, California.[12] Bay often traces his interest in action films back to an incident during his childhood. As a boy, he attached some firecrackers to a toy train and filmed the ensuing fiery disaster with his mother's 8 millimeter camera. The fire department was called and he was grounded.[13]
Career
Bay got his start in the film industry interning with George Lucas when he was fifteen, filing the storyboards for Raiders of the Lost Ark, which he thought was going to be terrible. His opinion changed after seeing it in the theater and he was so impressed by the experience that he decided to become a film director.[14] He graduated from Wesleyan University in 1986, majoring in both English and Film.[15][16] He was a member of the Psi Upsilon fraternity and a favorite student of film historian Jeanine Basinger.[17] For his graduate work, he attended Art Center College of Design in Pasadena where he also studied film.[18]
Michael Bay began working at Propaganda Films, directing commercials and music videos, two weeks after finishing his post-graduate degree.[18] His 90-second World War II-inspired Coca-Cola advertisement was picked up by Capitol Records. His first national commercial for the Red Cross, which won a Clio Award in 1992.[19][20] He directed Goodby, Silverstein & Partners "Got Milk?" advertisement campaign for the California Milk Processors Board in 1993.[21]
Bay's success in music videos gained the attention of producers Jerry Bruckheimer and Don Simpson, who selected him to direct his first feature-length film, Bad Boys. The film was shot in Miami in 1994 and starred Will Smith and Martin Lawrence. The action film proved to be a break-out role for Smith, who was segueing from television to films at that time. Shooting in Miami was a good experience for Bay who would later own a home in the city and spend a great deal of time there.[22] The film was completed for $19 million and grossed a remarkable $141 million at the box office in the summer of 1995.[23] Bay's success led to a strong partnership and friendship with Jerry Bruckheimer.[24]
His follow-up film, The Rock (1996), was an action movie set on Alcatraz Island, and in the San Francisco Bay area. It starred Sean Connery, Nicolas Cage and Ed Harris. It was also produced by Jerry Bruckheimer and Don Simpson, the latter of whom died five months before the film's release. The film is dedicated to him.[25] Connery and Cage won 'Best On-Screen Duo' at the MTV Movie Awards in 1997 and the film was nominated for an Academy Award in the Best Achievement in Sound category for the work of Greg P. Russell, Kevin O'Connell, and Keith A. Wester.[26][27]
Michael Bay on the set of Transformers
In 1998, Bay collaborated with Jerry Bruckheimer again, this time as a co-producer, as well as directing the action-adventure film Armageddon.[28][29] The film, about a group of tough oil drillers who are sent by NASA to deflect an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth, starred Bruce Willis, Billy Bob Thornton, Ben Affleck and Liv Tyler. It was nominated for 4 Oscars at the 71st Academy Awards including Best Sound, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound Editing, and Best Original Song.[30] The film earned 9.6 million dollars on its opening day and a total of 36.5 million through the first weekend.[31] The production budget, $140 million, was one of the highest of the summer of 1998. Armageddon went on to gross over $553 million worldwide, becoming the highest-grossing film of that year.[32]
In 2001, Bay directed Pearl Harbor. It starred Ben Affleck, Josh Hartnett, Kate Beckinsale and Cuba Gooding, Jr. The film was released on Memorial Day weekend in 2001. Again, Bay produced the film with Jerry Bruckheimer. The film received four Academy Award nominations, including Best Sound, Best Visual Effects, Best Sound Editing and Best Song. Again, Kevin O'Connell received another nomination for Best Sound, but he did not win. Pearl Harbor won in the category for Sound Editing, making it Bay's first (and, to date, only) film to win an Oscar.[33] Michael Bay also directed the music video for nominated track "There You'll Be" by vocal artist Faith Hill.[18]
Bay reteamed with Will Smith and Martin Lawrence for Bad Boys II, a sequel which also marked Bay's fifth collaboration with Jerry Bruckheimer. The film grossed $138 million domestically, enough to cover the production budget, and $273 million worldwide, almost twice as much as the first movie. In 2005, Bay directed The Island, a science fiction film starring Ewan McGregor and Scarlett Johansson. It was the first film Bay made without Jerry Bruckheimer as a producer. The Island cost $126 million to produce and earned $35 million domestically and $172 million worldwide. Bay stated that he was not comfortable with the domestic marketing campaign, as it confused the audience to the true subject of the film.[34]
Bay filming Transformers: Age of Extinction; actresses Abigail Klein, Melanie Specht and Victoria Summer are walking in a corridor.
In 2007, he directed and teamed up with Steven Spielberg to produce Transformers, a live action film based on the Transformers franchise. The film was released in the U.S. and Canada on July 3, 2007, with 8 p.m. preview screenings on July 2. The previews earned $8.8 million, and in its first day of general release it grossed $27.8 million, a record for Tuesday box office attendance.[citation needed] It broke the record held by Spider-Man 2 for the biggest July 4 gross, making $29 million. On its opening weekend, Transformers grossed $70.5 million, amounting to a $155.4 million opening week, giving it the record for the biggest opening week for a non-sequel.[citation needed] As of November 2007, the film has made over $319 million domestically and over $708 million worldwide. Bay returned as director and executive producer for Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen, which was released on June 24, 2009 and went on to gross over $832 million worldwide.

One of the best visual novels I've read. Well written, with a good mix of humor and pathos. It follows the trials of a high school boy in his final year, who has no long term goals and spends more of his time skipping classes and annoying his teachers than attending to his studies. It's quickly made apparent that his home life is a sad affair, with a mother who died in his infancy, and a distant, slovenly drunkard of a father who makes genuine but ineffective attempts to repair the seemingly long broken relationship with his son. A chance encounter with a girl on the way to school sets the game's events into motion.
This is equal parts a coming of age story for the protagonist, a story of reconcilation, and a story about taking responsibility and learning the meaning of family. It's very much in the romance and slice of life genre, with a lot of detail given to mundane, yet character building moments.
The game is split into two distinct parts, the first of which follows his life through that final year of school. Though still good, this part is the weaker of the two and firmly adheres a little too rigidly to the standard conventions of visual novels. In this part you will make choices which affect the ending, which for the most part are distinct in that each one will end you up in a relationship of some description with one of the female cast.
The problem with this part is that not all of the arcs are as interesting as the others, with some characters being a little too one dimensional. The other problem is that for the most part, particular choices arbitrarily lead you to specific endings and you will need to do a lot of trial and error, save scumming, or consulting online guides to help you reach them. Lastly, the other issue with this part is that there are a lot of shared events between the different arcs, and you will be skipping a lot of text on subsequent playthroughs. There is no feature to skip already viewed events quickly other than a 'fast' text option, which for a game as text heavy as this is not fast enough.
The second part is where the game really shines. It follows the time after the protagonist leaves school and begins adult life. It is much more focused than the first part, with more developed characterisation and a better structure overall, with a much tighter, cohesive narrative arc. Partly this I think is owing to how it treats one of the possible routes in the first part as canon, so it doesn't have to spread itself so thin and concern itself with tying together various plot threads. Choices, though still infrequent are much more clear in their consequence down the line.
The ending of this visual novel is excellent and will stick with you. My only issue with the ending is that some parts of the major plot development as it's written are underdeveloped. For me this slightly blunted the impact of aspects of the ending overall.
This is a very long visual novel and it took me about 120 hours to complete it, with the multiple routes of the first part taking me about 90 hours to complete and the second about 30 hours thereafter. It has good production, with the entirety of all dialogue other than the protagonist being voiced, with attractive art - though I know some people are turned off by the some of the character designs, I personally liked them. If i had any problem with their designs it would be that a lot of characters look a bit too young, especially in the second part when the characters are getting into their twenties but some still appear to be children (Fuko stands out especially). This is not something that I typically play, as mostly I have played VNs with more focus on action or intrigue such as Steins;Gate or Type Moon games, but as someone less familiar with this genre I thought this was excellent.

Whether you prefer Single Player, CO-OP or Multiplayer, this game has all three of them. I have reviewed all three parts of the game if you are considering buying this.
CAMPAIGN REVIEW (Single Player):
The campaign is about 6 hours long roughly. It can be shorter or longer depending on your selected difficulty. The story itself is very good and is set 5 years on from Call of Duty 4: Modern Warfare. It is not a Hollywood Blockbuster but at the same time it is not some random quickly written story that was put together in a few hours. Every mission has different objectives and you can feel the climax building up to the finale of the game. Every level is action filled and there is never a dull moment in the campaign. As you progress you will play in different locations in the world such as: Afghanistan, Brazil, Russia, the Atlantic Ocean and the United States. Even after completing the story there are Intel collectables to find and of course Steam achievements. There are also quite a few Easter Eggs in the campaign levels. The story for this then continues on into Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 3
SPEC OPS REVIEW (Single Player / CO-OP):
The Special Op missions are mostly the campaign levels but switched the other way round and with different objectives in the level. There are a total of 23 spec ops missions in MW2. 21/23 of these can be done on your own or with a friend. There are 2 Spec Ops missions that can only be done with a 2nd player. The missions get harder and harder as they go on. Some of the levels in this have been re-used from COD4. There is no matchmaking for the Spec Ops so the only way to find another player is to invite / join a friend and begin playing. There are also quite a few Steam achivements for this like with the Campaign.
MULTIPLAYER REVIEW (Multiplayer):
The Multiplayer is what is considered the strongest part of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. Unlike COD4 this time the game uses Steam Cloud, so your rank will all be stored online and will sync every time you close MW2. The highest level you can reach is level 70 with the addition of 10 prestige levels. When you reach Rank 4 you will have the ability to create your own classes where you can choose your main weapon, secondary weapon, perks and equipment. You can also stick attachments to pretty much all of your weapons on here. You can also unlock weapon camos for your main firearms, which some look very cool when placed on. You have the ability to join friends in a session and vice versa (provided there is space) and host your own private matches for this.
Conclusion: I highly recommend buying this game if you are reading this out of personal interest or if the game has gone up for sale. I recommend playing the Campaign before going to Multiplayer to get a feel of the game, but it is of course entirely your decision.
Things to be aware of -
There is no direct controller support for this game.
If you are considering the DLCs, it should be noted that there are less players than that of 2009 - 2010, so the only two main playlists are the base game and those who own both of the DLCs. If you only buy 1 DLC, you will find literally 0 games on there.
MW2 Multiplayer has no dedicated servers. It uses a matchmaking system that will pair you up with other players in the same playlist and game mode as you.
This game uses VAC. So if you are banned for cheating / modding the game, your ban will be permanent. There is no way to lift a ban. You have been warned.
At the time of posting the Multiplayer peak for this is around 10,000 players which is more than enough to find a game and play. Campaign / Spec Ops population doesn't go above 5,000.
If you have any questions or concerns with the game feel free to leave a comment.

Multiplayer Hub -
Thank you for reading and enjoy the game if you decide to purchase!

I bought this on release but got to a certain point and never went back - something else must have taken my interest around then. I also found the game unbearably tense once the Alien starts hunting you and decided I just wasn't enjoying it, especially with a new baby in my life back then.
Having completed Dishonored 2 I was reading a post where someone mentioned this game as a classic stealth game, and I decided to come back and finish it, which ultimately meant playing another 20hours or so from that point. My enthusiasm was also improved by using a mod to fix the horrible antialiasing, and it looks stunning in 21:9. Just keep the film grain up to help make the scenes look more realistic and less like 3D modelling. For the final third I switched to a 3D monitor using nVidia 3DVision and the awesome fix at helixmod.blogspot.co.uk. Once you go to 3D there's no looking back.
The reviews had stated that the game felt over-long and that is true. You could criticise the pacing, but maybe the devs just wanted to give the story its due, and also the buyer value for money - and that shouldn't be argued against. I think however that it is perhaps feels too long for a game where you are terrified almost all the time. There are sections where the pressure feels eased off just a bit, but it is rare that you ever think that you are safe to explore and read the logs in peace. Talking of exploring, the ship is all connected and there is a little bit of MetroidVania you can do, but there's little incentive beyond achievements for log-finding plus some equipment upgrade recipies you can manage without, and I never really got a sense of how the ship linked together in my head. That's likely quite realistic given how sprawling the Sevastopol Station is. There's a map on the wall in some places I screenshotted that gives a basic linking between the zones, but unless you've noted a door you can't open you're unlikely to ever find it again as when you're backtracking you might not realise it is an area you've already been to given that things look fundamentally similar.
Technically the game is very well made, and the art is perfect. It is hard to imagine a more fitting tribute to the Alien franchise, though judging by the
ending maybe they hoped they'd get a sequel and a chance to bring in the
. One of my favourite things about the game is the feel of the character's movement. I played with the gamepad and at times the keyboard, and the main character always moved in a very satisfying and weighty manner. When she starts to run something about the momentum and the way the view leans slightly feels just right.
If you enjoyed S.O.M.A. but just wished the game had been twice as long with a less cerebral plot this is a no brainer purchase. If you like the first Alien film and want to know what it is like to crouch terrified in a locker listening to lots of banging desperately trying to work out if the coast is clear, this is a no brainer purchase. If you have a weak heart stay well away. It's not that there are cheap jump scares, but the extremely tense atmosphere will not help.

It’s Borderlands 2, like do you really need to read a review to know if you want to buy this game?

You do? Okay … where to start, Borderlands 2 capitalize on what was good in Borderlands 1 and greatly expands upon the core premise and the co-op fun. If you like playing games co-op with friends then you definitely need Borderlands 2, skip Borderlands 1 as it may put you off from the series but definitely play Borderland 2.

The game has a very diverse skill tree system to make your character a bit more unique and along with it the way you play.

Oh and the Badass system is really Badass, it's essentially a profile based leveling system where your player profile has its own level apart from your character, so when you play with a different character (as long as you use your profile) it will carry over the benefits you have in your badass rank, really makes you want to play again and again as you are getting stronger every time you play the game.

Hmmm, what more to say … It has amazing DLCs (Tiny Tina Assault being the most out there and wackiest and most fun of the bunch) and they should all also be checked out, as they carry along the comedy and story of the game (to some extent).

Oh, I forgot single player, I played through the whole game (and DLCs) solo first and I would highly recommend others to do so as well, the game has a really good story and some of the best in-game comedy I have experienced. And when playing co-op you miss out on the comedy and plot of the game because you're focusing on playing with your friend and skipping the quest info and dialogue in the game.

So yeah, 5/5 from me, excellent game, one of the most fun games out there especially with friends :).

I was introduced to Total War only last year, and since then I have played Medievil 2, Shogun 2, Attila, and Rome 2.  Of those, I have to say Rome 2 is by far the worst.  While it can still be fun, the game is just a sloppy mess that tries it's best to suck the enjoyment out of itself.
We'll start with the good things.  The time period is fantastic.  This is Rome during the height of their power, not the shadow of glory that is present in Attila.  You can re-enact the war against Carthage, you can play as the ancient Greeks or Egpyt if you like, or even try to reclaim Alexander the Great's empire as one of the successor kingdoms.  As I said, the time period is great and the map size is awesome.  I love how at the beginning of the campaign there are dozens of different factions trying to fight for control of the ancient world.  And the game is still a Total War game, with all of the positive things that that entails.
Now onto the negative.  The game is a broken, complicated mess.  Mechanics don't work as they should.  Fortify stance giving you +50% reinforcement range?  No, it doesn't.  Units tend to blob up despite the use of a "formation attack" toggle.  Morale mechanics are broken, I've had units at over 50% break and route even though they were "winning decisively."  Your general is useless, he will always be one of the first troops to fall if his unit is attacked no matter what angle it's from.  Sometimes units won't even follow orders.  I had a unit of Roman Cavalry that I was telling to attack a unit of enemy slingers.  Despite the fact that they registered the order, they stopped thirty feet from the slingers and stood there.  No matter how many times I told them to attack they just sat there until they finally routed from losses garnered by standing in the line of fire for ten minutes.
Other battlefield mechanics make no sense.  How are slingers dropping my Super Heavy Spear Infantry locked in a shield wall from the front?  Then there is the truly broken:  Pikes.  You know your game has severe balance issues when multiplayer rooms are usually tagged with "no pikes allowed" because Pikeman > EVERYTHING.  Without a doubt.  I once had a unit of heavy swordsmen in a shield wall acting as an anvil for a unit of light pikemen.  I then hit those pikes from behind with a unit of heavy melee cavalry.  Both of my units routed without the pikemen taking any significant losses.
The campaign map isn't much better.  Buildings are overly complicated with their bonuses and negatives, turning empire-building into a game of hardcore addition and subtraction.  Capturing territories is extremely slow because the public order system is designed to bog you down.  Generals will pick up negative traits for idling in cities after only one turn.  The "political intrigue" system is boring, time consuming, and doesn't really have any effect on the rest of the campaign.  The entire game just feels...Broken.  This isn't even mentioning that half of the playable factions are locked behind a paywall.  So you charge me $50 for a broken game that isn't even close to the whole package, then charge me an additional $35 to unlock the rest?  What a joke.
What makes this worse is shortly after I played this I bought Attila.  Attila is everything that Rome 2 should have been, which is even more upsetting because rather than fix the broken piece of junk they charged everyone good money for, they went ahead and just made another game that actually worked and said, "Sorry guys if you bought the crap that was Rome 2,  go ahead and buy Attila instead!  It works!"  Don't get me wrong, I'm not hating on CA, I understand that♥♥♥♥♥♥happens sometimes..And since Rome 2 they've really stepped up their game.  Look at how TW: Warhammer is shaping up!  Not to mention that they're walking everyone through that development every step of the way!  I am, however, hating on everything that happened to make Rome 2 the piece of♥♥♥♥♥♥that it is today.  This is the black stain on your record, CA, and you owe everyone by making sure that this fiasco never happens again.
In short, don't play this♥♥♥♥♥♥  Either get Attila or Warhammer instead, or go with one of their older titles.  Those actually work.
OVERALL:  4/10

As someone who pre-ordered, originally, I could not have recommended the game, as I essentially paid for a Beta in terms of bugs and polish. This still galls to this day and I would not pre-order a Total War game again.
After many patches and post-polishing, I can cautiously recommend this as a decent addition to the Total War franchise. Its overall mechanics aren't super, such as the nerf to culture change, where you now have default culture that cannot be converted, leaving permanent unhappiness in conquered territories of a foreign culture.
The battle mechanics are solid, although there are some clear carry-overs from Shogun 2. They never did families or the in-depth politics as promised. Despite that, the game is still fun, although it can get a bit stale when you get to a big empire stage against other similarly big empires. The AI does not always function as intended still, although the related game-breaking bugs have at least been eliminated.

Michael Benjamin Bay (born February 17, 1965)[1] is an American filmmaker known for directing and producing big-budget action films characterized by fast cutting, stylistic visuals and extensive use of special effects, including frequent depictions of explosions.[2][3] His films, which include Armageddon (1998), Pearl Harbor (2001) and the Transformers film series (2007–present), have grossed over US$5 billion worldwide.[4] He is co-founder of commercial production house The Institute, a.k.a. The Institute for the Development of Enhanced Perceptual Awareness.[5] He is co-chair and part-owner of the digital effects house Digital Domain.[6] He co-owns Platinum Dunes, a production house which has remade horror movies including The Texas Chainsaw Massacre (2003), The Amityville Horror (2005), The Hitcher (2007), Friday the 13th (2009) and A Nightmare on Elm Street (2010).[7]
Despite his considerable success at the international box office, Bay's work is generally held in low esteem by film critics. While The Rock (1996) and Transformers (2007) received moderately positive reviews, his other films, including the three Transformers sequels, have been received negatively by critics.
